articles.title: Traumatized teens sue school, cops after Doritos bag triggers AI gun alert
articles.text:
In October 2025, four Black high school students were sharing Cool Ranch Doritos after football practice, winding down and waiting for their rides home. It was then, in the lull of a moment any teen with after-school activities knows well, that the school’s AI gun detection system suddenly flagged one teen holding a bag of chips as a potential gunman.
Within two minutes, Baltimore County Public Schools officials who reviewed security camera footage linked to the alert determined there was no actual threat. They recognized the Doritos bag and canceled the alert, which notified not only other school officials but also the Baltimore County Police Department that no response was needed.
The false alert could have ended there—before a traumatizing campus clash with police—but it didn’t.
According to a lawsuit filed by the current and former students, Taki Allen, Yui-Osa Ogbeide, Devon Thompson Jr., and Keith Winfield III, due to “both technological and human errors,” school officials called police to the scene anyway, and the cops responded with force.
At least six patrol cars arrived with lights flashing, and some cops emerged with guns drawn. The teens froze and cooperated, confused and scared for their lives, their lawsuit said.
“No one told the students what they were suspected of,” the lawsuit said. “Officers separated the students, ordered them to their knees on the concrete, handcuffed them, and searched their persons and property.”
Only after the cops failed to find a gun did students learn that it was the school’s AI gun detection system, Omnilert, that triggered the police response. Allegedly, one of the responding officers muttered, “stupid AI cameras” and “fucking Omnilerts,” while another told the students that “AI is not the best.” Finally releasing the students, one officer seemed to acknowledge that they had put the teens in danger.
“Hey, thanks for not running away, that would have been a real problem,” the officer allegedly said. Walking away, another joked that the boys should remember to “be careful with your chip bags.”
Teens traumatized
The cops did not just target the suspected gunman but apparently told the other teens that they were guilty “by association” when they asked why they were searched.
Suing to stop any other teens from facing allegedly life-or-death situations due to officials’ blind trust of AI, the teens have asked for an injunction barring BCPS from using Omnilert until they can effectively establish protocols to prevent police responses to false alerts.
The lawsuit alleged that students’ constitutional rights were violated, as students were unlawfully searched and detained.
Damon Hewitt, president and executive director of the Lawyers’ Committee for Civil Rights Under Law—a nonpartisan nonprofit that’s representing the teens in the suit—said that “overreliance on artificial intelligence technology mixed with inept communication and coordination among key officials is a toxic mix.”
The complaint noted that BCPS was among the earliest adopters of Omnilert, and officials have touted it as “the largest deployment of AI visual gun detection” as a means to supposedly protect students. Instead, they alleged that Omnilert is marketing a defective product as triggering “near-zero false positives” without effectively requiring the adequate human review that claim depends on.
“We need a reckoning on how AI is being used, especially concerning public safety and kids,” Hewitt said. “We are fighting to deliver justice in this case, but it also holds lessons for educators and police officials across the country who should think twice before putting our children’s fate in the hands of AI.”
All the teens feel less safe on campus and less trusting of police following the incident. They also suffered from physical pain—including ”deep red marks” on their wrists from handcuffs—as well as “acute and lasting emotional distress, fear, anxiety,” and “humiliation.” Further, the teens report that rumors follow them around, falsely claiming that there was a gun and damaging their reputations.
Car pick-up will never be the same. The student falsely flagged as the gunman, Taki Allen, “no longer feels safe waiting for rides or spending time outside the school after hours” and “frequently pays for rides home from private car services to avoid waiting for rides from friends or family.” Keith Winfield’s house was very close to the school, but his mother, Frieda Winfield, said his anxiety was so bad that he would call her “multiple times after football practice ended to confirm that she was on her way to pick him up.”
Frieda Winfield called for change following her son Keith’s chilling interaction.
“The police told my son this could have been a real problem,” Frieda Winfield said. “No child in Baltimore County should face this kind of danger while waiting outside his own school for a ride home from his mother.”
What went wrong?
The teens’ lawsuit targets Omnilert and responding Baltimore County Police Department officers. It also challenges Baltimore County Public Schools and individual school officials who allegedly failed to establish proper protocols to prevent a police response to a canceled alert.
In a later investigation, the Office of the Inspector General (OIG) for Education concluded that Omnilert’s system had no “bias.” But OIG acknowledged that the “delegation of authority” process that Kenwood High School set up didn’t stop its principal, Kate Smith, from noticing the alert, failing to see it was canceled, and texting a school resource officer to deploy police 15 minutes later—all while acknowledging in that text that the object in the alert was “maybe not” a gun. Smith apparently was never trained on the Omnilert system, OIG’s report indicated.
The OIG agreed with teens that things should change. Immediately after the incident, an internal Omnilert training link was shared with BCPS staff, and OIG recommended that schools conduct biannual trainings moving forward.
They also recommended that the BCPS Department of School Safety “review its protocol” and reduce the number of individuals who receive campus gun alerts. That could help ensure “internal notification controls are followed” and police “are fully informed of a verified threat,” the OIG said.
Without changes, the OIG acknowledged that “the loss of alert notification controls could place not only BCPS staff and students at risk but could also place responding law enforcement in a potentially tragic situation.”
Another change offered a technical solution that may have prevented the tragic event. The OIG recommended that school officials switch to using the Omnilert app. Since Smith opened the alert in a text message window on her phone, they suggested that she could easily have overlooked the cancellation text message if her first instinct were to enlarge the image or review the camera footage.
These recommendations aren’t enough for current and former students suing, one of whom remains an active student who claims the principal never apologized and instead made light of the incidents using cry-laughing emojis in texts with other school officials. Teens alleged that Smith should have known that more than “99 percent of OGD Alerts in Baltimore County Public Schools were false positives that required no police response,” as the OIG’s report said, and she should have prioritized students’ safety and verified the threat before calling in police.
“BCPS’s failures amounted to deliberate indifference to the constitutional rights of its students,” their lawsuit alleged.
The teens asked a court for an injunction barring the use of Omnilert until BCPS staff and police are adequately trained. In their complaint, they alleged that none of the officers on the scene had reviewed the camera footage before responding, and none of the officers informed of the alert cancellation intervened.
BCPS silent; Omnilert defends tech
BCPS declined to comment on the lawsuit, pointing Ars to a statement issued to parents following the incident. That statement did not directly apologize to students but did say the school would provide “ongoing counseling and emotional support” to them while promising to take steps to prevent future incidents.
Blake Mitchell, Omnilert’s vice president of marketing, told Ars that Omnilert is reviewing the complaint.
“What these four students went through on October 20, 2025 should not have happened, and we are truly sorry for the fear they and their families experienced,” Mitchell said. “We understand why they want answers.”
Mitchell said that Omnilert is “built to send anything that could be a firearm to trained people for review, because missing a real gun is the worst possible outcome.” He also reiterated that the OIG investigation found no bias in Omnilert’s system and seemed to agree that it was the school’s authority delegation that failed the students, not necessarily the technology.
“In this case, the school’s designated safety staff reviewed the alert and canceled it within about two minutes, and everyone who received it was notified,” Mitchell said. “That is exactly why human review matters, and why a canceled alert must stay canceled.”
Len Kamdang of the Lawyers’ Committee representing the teens told The New York Times that teens want BCPS and Omnilert to acknowledge that “what happened to them was unacceptable.”
“This case is ultimately about how human beings allowed AI to substitute for their judgment,” Kamdang said.
As a mother, Frieda Winfield told a local news outlet that she was shocked by the incident, despite deliberately teaching her son to be cautious around police. The boys’ caution “saved their lives in my opinion,” she said.
“I was angry. I was fearful,” Frieda Winfield said. “The biggest part was fear, because they’re young men. Young Black men, and they were at school, and they didn’t understand why what was happening, happened to them.”
Kamdang told NYT that “for anyone with children, that is a scary, scary situation. For a Black student, especially a young Black man in America, that is a life-or-death situation.”
As AI tools are increasingly positioned as public safety solutions, the Lawyers Committee is pushing for police reform when cops or officials appear to be blindly trusting AI, their press release said. They noted that “this injustice also raises a broader concern regarding the use and reliability of AI-powered technology in public safety where accuracy is essential in life-and-death situations.”
Ashley is a senior policy reporter for Ars Technica, dedicated to tracking social impacts of emerging policies and new technologies. She is a Chicago-based journalist with 20 years of experience.

articles.title: I've found the 35 best Black Friday deals at Amazon UK — Switch 2, Kindles, Lego, Sony, Philips, Ninja, and more
articles.text:
Live
All the best Black Friday deals at Amazon UK — 35 top offers on Switch 2, Kindles, Lego, Sony, Philips, Ninja, and more
All the best deals from the retailer's massive sale
The Amazon Black Friday sale is here. After several days of build-up, the retailer's full end-of-year deals event is officially underway — and I've got all of the best deals right here for you. There are some huge discounts up for grabs on smart home tech, TVs, Kindles, appliances, headphones, toys, essentials, and so much more.
As you would expect, the event is heavy on Amazon devices, with some of the largest price cuts available on Ring doorbells, Blink cameras, and even a record-low on the brand-new Kindle.
Other highlights include big savings on a Nintendo Switch 2 bundle, best-ever prices on top-rated headphones from Sony and Shokz, and cheap appliances from brands including Shark, Dyson, Ninja, and De'Longhi.
Now that the full sale has started, it might take me some time to dig through it all to uncover all of the best deals, but that's what I'll be doing right here, with live updates over the next couple of weeks from myself and the TechRadar team.
Amazon Black Friday sale — quick links
- Amazon Prime: get a 30-day free trial
- Amazon Devices: up to 67% off Ring & Blink
- Amazon Haul: 30% off
- Appliances: up to 40% off Ninja & De'Longhi
- Beauty: up to 70% off Philips & Oral-B
- Computing: up to 35% off RAM & CPUs
- Essentials: up to 50% off cleaning & groceries
- Fashion: up to 50% off
- Gaming: up to 33% off PS5 & Switch 2
- Headphones: up to 50% off Shokz & Sony
- Kindle: up to 40% off
- Laptops: from £159.99
- Tablets: up to 50% off Alexa tablets
- TVs: from £109
- Vacuums: up to 50% off Shark & Dyson
- Wearables: Fitbit & Oura from £58.99
As TechRadar's senior deals editor, I've covered major sales events such as Black Friday and Amazon Prime Day for almost a decade so I've learnt what to expect and how to make the most of each one. I'm here to help you save money, bring you the best products for the lowest prices that we've tested and love here at TechRadar, and uncover those hidden bargains you don't want to miss.
My top 35 Black Friday deals at Amazon UK
I've seen a lot of people talk about and use Loop earplugs lately so if you want to see what the fuss is all about then this entry-level pair is down to a record-low price. Use them to block out noise on a commute, help you focus in the office, protect your ears from loud music at bars or concerts, or help you create a better environment for sleep. They're reusable and can last for up to five years so a good investment if you'll be a regular user.
Read moreRead less▼
One of the cheapest Switch 2 bundles available in the Black Friday sales is this Nintendo Switch Sports Resort version. It simply includes a Switch 2 console and a copy of the latest sports compilation, featuring games such as tennis, volleyball, golf, bowling, archery, and more.
Read moreRead less▼
This excellent value bundle includes the latest version of the Ring Video Doorbell and a Ring Indoor Camera for a cheap and easy way to get started with home security. We've tested these and have been impressed with the video quality, high zoom, and night vision colour, but it's a shame that some of this device's value is only usable with a Ring Protect subscription. However, if you're fine with paying for a subscription or already using a Ring-based home security system, it's worth the cost.
Read moreRead less▼
Treat yourself to one of the best pairs of bone conduction headphones at their lowest-ever price. Not only do the Shokz OpenRun Pro 2 deliver outstanding sound, but they're also incredibly comfortable. They're highly recommended by our Fitness & Wearables Editor, Matt Evans, and are now more affordable, making them a great buy for runners and gym-goers.
Read moreRead less▼
As a way to get started, this box of 790 Lego pieces is a great beginner kit. With a variety of brick types and extras, you can start building whatever you please. You also get a very handy brick-shaped box to store everything in once playtime is over, all for under £30.
Read moreRead less▼
The Suri Pro Sonic Electric Toothbrush is 20% off at Amazon for Black Friday. This is a strong offer for the fantastic, eco-friendly alternative to other electric toothbrushes. In fact, we scored it four-and-a-half out of five in our Suri 2.0 Sonic Toothbrush review. As I've found with the original 1.0 version, it performs and cleans well, offers an impressive 40-day battery life, fast wireless charging over USB-C, a useful pressure sensor, and comes with handy extras like a magnetic wall mount and UV cleaning travel case.
Read moreRead less▼
This entry-level electric toothbrush is a solid pickup while it's less than half price in Amazon's latest sale. It doesn't boast many impressive high-end features but it has the basic ones you really need to brush your teeth effectively and efficiently, including a two-minute timer and a visible pressure sensor. Plus, you get a handy carry case and a spare brush head included for free.
Read moreRead less▼
Amazon's brand-new Kindle has only been available for a few weeks, but it's already discounted to a record-low price for Black Friday. This "thinner, lighter, and faster" Kindle scored four stars in our review, making it a solid choice for most readers — even if older models might offer better value, upgrading to the slightly more expensive Paperwhite could be worth it for the extra features.
Read moreRead less▼
The Ninja AF300UK remains an extremely popular and number one best-selling air fryer all these years after its release — and it's now back to the lowest price we've seen all year at Amazon. It's an excellent offer for a large dual-basket air fryer that can prepare multiple foods at once, while being faster and arguably healthier than other conventional cooking methods.
Read moreRead less▼
Amazon's newest 4K streaming stick is already down to its lowest-ever price — less than two months after launch. Considering it's only slightly more expensive than the basic HD version, you might as well pay for the upgrade to get a fancy new remote and access to higher-resolution streaming — as long as you have a 4K TV. It lacks a few premium features found in the more expensive Plus and Max models, such as improved Wi-Fi and Dolby Atmos, but this is more than enough to cover general everyday use.
Read moreRead less▼
The original Sony WH-1000XM4 were our pick for the best over-ear headphones ever for a long time. This refreshed model of the classics offers top-notch audio, excellent comfort, and effective noise cancellation all at a reasonable price point that's over £100 cheaper than the newer Sony XM6. We still rate these as the best headphones for most people, exactly because you can find them at a price like this when they are on sale.
Read moreRead less▼
LG reclaimed the top spot on our best TV guide with the C6, as it boasts fantastic overall picture quality and excellent all-around performance, making it the number one pick for most people's needs. Contrast is top-tier, with vivid colors and rich blacks, while motion is handled expertly. No matter if you're watching films, streaming TV shows, playing games, or watching sports, it's up to the job.
Read moreRead less▼
It's always handy to have a portable charger to take with you when you're on the go, and this 10000mAh one from popular brand Inui is a smart buy in my eyes. For starters, it's small and super-slim, making it easy to carry around in a pocket or slip into your bag, while still offering enough juice to charge some of the latest phones and tablets to above 50%. It has two USB-C ports and one USB-A, meaning you can charge multiple devices at once. There's even a handy detachable USB-C cable included for free.
Read moreRead less▼
With a new model on the way, the last-generation Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition falls to a record-low price on Amazon. Upgrades in the 2026 version are fairly minimal, mostly improving the design and offering a replaceable battery, so I'd be tempted to go for the older version while it's at a great budget price. You still get a bright and easy-to-read seven-inch glare-free display, an auto-adjusting front light, space for thousands of books, handy wireless charging support, and a thin, waterproof design. And it's all for around £100 less than the new model.
Read moreRead less▼
Ideal for younger gamers, the Nex Playground comes with games ready to play out of the box, such as Fruit Ninja, Whac-a-Mole, and more. It's now down to a record-low price at Amazon. This neat little console relies on intuitive motion controls and is a locked-down system designed specifically with young children in mind.
Read moreRead less▼
The Philips OneBlade 360 is a quick, simple and affordable electric razor that's suitable for a wide variety of face and body grooming needs. This jam-packed bundle was a little cheaper over Prime Day, but today's offer is still a solid one. This bundle includes the handle, as well as a spare blade, a five-in-one comb, a body kit, and a USB-A charging cable.
Read moreRead less▼
If you want to give your home heating a boost, then I can recommend this Dreo Electric Heater, which is down to around £40. We haven't tried this model in particular, but Dreo is one of the top brands for fan and air quality products – and this seems no different, judging by the thousands of positive reviews on Amazon for its compact size and efficient heating.
Read moreRead less▼
Here's a great discount on Ninja's newest and most portable air fryer. This bundle includes the PowerPod lid, plus a resealable glass container to carry your dishes until you're ready to cook. According to our testing, it cooks exceptionally quickly, is easy to use and a breeze to clean, making this one of the best air fryer deals I've seen this year.
Read moreRead less▼
The 50-inch Amazon Ember TV is the mid-sized version of the budget-friendly 4-Series range and it's now down to its lowest-ever price. It's a nice buy if you're on a budget, as the premium 4K resolution delivers excellent clarity and picture quality for TV shows, movies, sports and general viewing. All major streaming apps are ready to go, too, plus there's voice control support through Alexa. It's an all-around solid TV for the price that I'd buy if I needed an affordable and capable display.
Read moreRead less▼
A fantastic low price for a pair of smart plugs that offer a suite of features to control your devices and monitor your energy use. You can use them with any existing socket and connect an assortment of devices such as chargers, lights, small appliances and more. Remote control, voice control, schedules and more are all handled in the free smartphone app. Today's offer is just £1 away from the recent record low.
Read moreRead less▼
I actually bought a Levoit Core Mini for myself when moving into a new house that hadn't been lived in for a while to get rid of the dust and debris, and I also think it works as a great option for any allergy problems. What I like most is that it's small and quiet, so it is perfect for all sorts of spaces, such as the living room and bedroom. It's now also very affordable at 25% off.
Read moreRead less▼
The standard PS5 DualSense Controller has a strong discount right now on Amazon. Other colours are available for slightly more, but if you just want the classic design for a great price, you can't go wrong with this Black Friday deal.
Read moreRead less▼
I'm a little tempted by the £20 price reduction on this well-scoring blender. While it can't chop ice, it creates velvety smoothies out of fresh and frozen fruits hassle-free. On top of this, the build quality and performance impressed us, and the fact that it's only a few quid more than it was last Black Friday makes this an even sweeter deal.
Read moreRead less▼
I've got one of those AnySharp knife sharpeners to keep my kitchen knives up to scratch, but if you want to go all the way with a convenient knife block with a built-in sharpener, then this is a great price for a premium set from Ninja. You'll never suffer from dull knives again with this extremely handy kitchen gadget, with its six-piece set of stainless steel knives and included paring scissors.
Read moreRead less▼
Yes, there's apparently a "deal" on this high-end set of Crucial RAM, but when you look back and see that similar sets were under £200 in late 2025, it feels terrible to even consider buying at these prices. Still, if you're in desperate need of some quality RAM, it likely won't get any better than this for a while.
Read moreRead less▼
Always a hot item during holiday sales events, Amazon has the best-selling Revlon One-Step hair dryer on sale for a record-low price of £25. Thanks to the unique oval brush design, the hairdryer delivers a salon-like blowout with brilliant shine and extra volume.
Read moreRead less▼
Display: 13.8 inches
Processor: Snapdragon X2 Plus
RAM: 16GB
Storage: 512GB
Microsoft knocked it out of the park with its latest range of Surface Laptops — and now you can pick one up for a fantastic price at Amazon following this £550 saving. It's a powerful mid-range version of the device, too, with the super-efficient Snapdragon X2 Plus processor and 16GB of RAM ensuring speedy performance and lengthy all-day battery life. Storage is reasonable at 512GB, too, which is more than enough for essential files and applications, especially if you rely on a lot of web services such as Google Docs.
Read moreRead less▼
Amazon has taken the biggest step up in terms of quality with its latest Omni Mini-LED Series Fire TVs. That's clear in the price, which puts these very close to top-end OLED displays from the likes of Sony, Samsung and LG. However, you still get a lot for your money with this Amazon option, including a large 55-inch Mini-LED panel that boasts fantastic contrast, colors and image sharpness, a 144Hz game mode for a fast and responsive experience on consoles, and smart features.
Read moreRead less▼
As big fans of the previous Nothing Ear (a), we were excited to see what was in store with this latest model. And yes, they offer the same excellent audio quality and impressive ANC for the price, making them an even more tempting buy following this £40 discount. It's just a shame the privacy concerns with the Audio Snapshot and Call Recording features tarnish what should be a pair of easy-to-recommend budget earbuds.
Read moreRead less▼
This excellent value bundle includes a Blink Outdoor 4 security camera and a Blink Video Doorbell at an incredibly low price. It's one of my top picks if you want to dabble with some cheap smart home tech. The 4th-generation outdoor security camera features two-way audio, a two-year battery life, and works with Amazon Alexa for hands-free control and interconnectivity with other smart devices. Meanwhile, the Blink Video Doorbell is a cheap and easy way to get alerts on your phone when motion is detected or when guests are at your door.
Read moreRead less▼
Promising simplicity of use, the De'Longhi Magnifica Evo has a straightforward touch control panel that allows you to brew your favourite cup of coffee with the minimum amount of effort. It also has a silent integrated grinder with 13 settings, plus a handy milk frother, so it’s a good all-in-one solution for those who love a cup of joe but want to skip all the faff of making the drink. We liked it enough in our De'Longhi Magnifica Evo Next review, in which we awarded it four stars out of five.
Read moreRead less▼
Amazon's Echo Spot smart clock is down to within £10 of its record-low price for Black Friday. As well as a time display and wake-up alerts, this compact bit of kit can play music, check the weather and control other smart devices throughout your home.
Read moreRead less▼
Here's the first-ever discount on the latest Samsung Galaxy Watch 9 for Black Friday. The new wearable boasts improved vitals and health tracking, including sleep apnea and blood pressure monitoring, smart AI assistance, a comfortable fit, and a lengthy 40-hour battery life.
Read moreRead less▼
I did a lot of research before picking up this pressure washer for myself a couple of years ago and it's been an excellent buy for simple cleaning tasks around the home, such as patios, decking, walls and cars. While we haven't tested this model at TechRadar, it's been praised elsewhere for its solid build quality, strong water pressure and portability. You also get a good selection of attachments in this bundle, including a patio cleaner, wash brush and detergent nozzle.
Read moreRead less▼
Get the highly rated Renpho smart scale on sale for under £20 for Black Friday. The smart scale has over 300,000 reviews on Amazon and holds a solid 4.5-star rating. You can use this smart device to measure your body fat ratio, BMI, and weight via the Renpho app.
Read moreRead less▼
LIVE: Latest Updates
The best soundbar under £300
The Sony HT-2000 is the best budget soundbar in our view, if we view budget and meaning under £300 with this discount. (The Sonos Beam 2 is also excellent, but is slightly over this crucial price barrier.)
It's impactful, delivers clear dialogue, and immersive 3D elements to movie soundtracks — all from a compact body.
Sony HT-S2000 soundbar: was £399 now £269 at Amazon
The best kitchen purchase I ever made
I think somebody already posted about this Ninja air fryer below, but I'm going to share it again anyway — because it's awesome.
I'm talking about the five-star-rated Ninja AF300UK, which is a dual-basket air fryer, meaning you can cook two things at once. Chips in one and (veggie) sausages in the other? Yes please! It's revolutionised my cooking (on the days when I don't do actual cooking) and right now it's at a super-low £119.
Ninja AF300UK Air Fryer: was £199.99 now £119 at Amazon
Apple's mini marvel is on sale
I bought a Mac mini M4 a couple of years ago and it's one of the best tech purchases I've made — so dinky, so stylish and well crafted, but packing tons of power inside and available for a bargain price. That bargain price is unfortunately not a thing any longer — the RAM crisis has put paid to that — but it remains a great choice of desktop computer.
Amazon currently has it on sale for £804 in its 256GB guise, which is a mere £5 above the lowest price we've seen for it so far and a handy saving of £95.
Apple Mac mini M6, 256GB: was £899 now £804 at Amazon
An oldie but goldie espresso machine
I don't have a great record of buying my partner gifts, but she has described her Sage Bambino Plus as the best thing I ever bought her, and if pushed I think she would now choose it over me. I don't drink coffee, but she assures me that it makes a fantastic espresso, and to coffee lovers that's an important thing, I gather.
This is far from the lowest price we've ever seen for it — it was £224 soon after its launch in 2018 — but it hasn't been lower for a couple of years, and £40 is still £40.
Sage The Bambino Plus: was £399 now £359 at Amazon
That's no moon. It's a Lego Star Wars Death Star
This is simultaneously the best and worst deal I've ever written about.
Best because if my parents had bought me one of these as a kid then I would have known happiness beyond that which any human has ever experienced. Come on, look at it! It has 9023 bricks! It comes with 38 Minifigures! It enables you to recreate iconic scenes such as the trash compactor and hangar bay!
Worst because it's £808 and really, can anyone justify that? Still, it is currently £91 off at Amazon for Black Friday, so that's something.
Lego Star Wars Death Star: was £899 now £808 at Amazon
A child-friendly tablet for less
One thing I quickly discovered when my kids were young was that a good tablet can be a lifesaver. Don't worry, I wasn't one of those parents who used an iPad as a babysitter — screen time was controlled, as was the content they consumed. And I did that with the help of Amazon's excellent Fire Kids tablets.
Fire Tablets are no more, replaced by the Amazon Kids Tablet 8 and Tablet 11, and these devices offer several upgrades including — finally! — the fact that they run on full Android rather than Amazon's Fire OS. That means access to the riches of the Google Play Store, but you still get all of the parental controls you need, plus the much-needed colourful bumper case and a 1-year subscription to the Amazon Kids+ service. Oh, and both models are on sale for Black Friday — so what are you waiting for?
Amazon Kids Tablet 8: was £199 now £149 at Amazon
Amazon Kids Tablet 11: was £289 now £199 at Amazon
Start your stargazing journey here
One of my hobbies is taking photos of space, a pursuit I've enjoyed far more since the arrival of smart telescopes a few years ago. I've used and written about two of the best at the more affordable end of the spectrum — the Seestar S30 Plus and S30 Pro — and both are now available for less at Amazon. Either would make a great Christmas gift for a budding astronomer!
Seestar S30 Plus smart telescope: was £449 now £426 at Amazon
Seestar S30 Pro smart telescope: was £649 now £616.55 at Amazon
The Fire TV Stick deals have begun, and they're big
Good evening, Marc here to take on live blogging duties for a few hours.
Amazon's usual Fire TV Stick discounts have arrived, and I expect that this is the lowest price we'll see for these models — I don't expect a second drop on Black Friday itself. But when you look at the size of the discounts, that seems fair enough! 
Amazon Amazon Fire TV Stick 4K Select: was £64.99 now £21.99 at Amazon
Amazon Amazon Fire TV Stick 4K Plus: was £79.99 now £34.99 at Amazon
Amazon Amazon Fire TV Stick 4K Max (newest Gen): was £99.99 now £46.99 at Amazon
The eco-friendly plaque-buster
See that picture? That's a look inside the box of the Suri Pro Sonic Toothbrush 2.0, the top model with a sustainable angle. Suri brush-heads — made of plant-based materials — can be sent back to the company to be recycled via freepost.
The brush itself has a magnetic mount, four-week battery life, a powerful motor behind a simple sonic movement, and a case packing a UV cleaning light. We gave it 4.5 stars in our review, and right now, you can save 22% on its sticker price.
Suri Pro Sonic Toothbrush 2.0: was £89 now £68.98 at Amazon
Save £50 on the Ninja Crispi 3.8L 4-in-1 Glass Air Fryer
As well as the Ninja Foodi Dual Zone, there's another stellar discount from Ninja — this time on the Ninja Crispi. This 4-in-1 air fryer clips onto the top of its glass case, which is dishwasher safe for easy cleaning.
Described as a 'portable cooking system', the Crispi allows you to simply click a lid on the glass container after frying for easy storage and transport. And it's glass, so you can see it cooking without stopping the process!
Ninja Crispi 3.8L 4-in-1 Glass Air Fryer: was £149 now £99 at Amazon
The best Black Friday Garmin deal you're likely to find this year
Sticking with smartwatches for a moment, it's going to be hard to beat this deal if you're after a Garmin watch. The Garmin Fenix 8, although now a couple of years old, is an incredible high-performance smartwatch. I wore it for months as my daily driver, and gave it five stars in my Garmin Fenix 8 review.
Considering the watch used to start at £949 before being lowered to £699.99, the fact you can now find it for under £500 means it's an absolute steal. It's labelled as one of Amazon's Black Friday Big Deals, and you can find all the details below.
Save £200 on the Garmin Fenix 8 in its 43mm size and Whitestone colorway, bringing it under £500 for the first time. At this price, it's a must-buy for any amateur athlete or hobbyist adventurer looking for their next watch. The 43mm is wearable for smaller wrists, and is less obtrusive even for larger wrists if the wearer's looking for something for everyday use too.

Garmin Fenix 8 (51mm) Black: was £779.99 now £549 at Amazon

Watching the deals

Apple Watch Series 11 (46mm) GPS-only: was £349 now £299 at Amazon
Foodi for thought
Air fryers are always popular choices on Black Friday, and this particular deal is a doozy: right now, you can save 40% on the Ninja Foodi 6-in-1 Dual Zone Air Fryer, down from £199.99 to just £119.99. That's an £80 saving.
In our Ninja Foodi Dual Zone review, our reviewer Emily Peck rated it a massive five stars thanks to its ability to cook two different foods, at different temperatures, and have them ready at the same time. Now you can get a five-star air fryer for almost half price. Black Friday may be over a week away, but we believe it's highly unlikely to drop further in price, so would recommend you snatch it up and make your holiday dinners a doddle.
Ninja Foodi 6-in-1 Dual Zone: was £199.99 now £119.99 at Amazon
Floored by the ring deals
The undisputed champ of our best sleep tracker guide, the Oura Ring 5 offers unparalleled insight into your sleep habits. Not only does it track 50 health and wellness metrics to help you understand your ZZZs but its app makes discovering key insights super intuitive. On top of that, it's also a total stunner, easily passing for a standard piece of jewelry in everyday wear. And currently comes with a massive £100 off in every style, with the cheaper finishes reduced to £299 and more premium ones priced at £399.
- Oura Ring 5: was £399 now £299 at Amazon
Another sweet-sounding deal on earbuds
As big fans of the previous Nothing Ear (a), we were excited to see what was in store with this latest model. And yes, they offer the same excellent audio quality and impressive ANC for the price, making them an even more tempting buy following this £40 discount. It's just a shame the privacy concerns with the Audio Snapshot and Call Recording features tarnish what should be a pair of easy-to-recommend budget earbuds.

There's a reason the LG C6 sits at the top of our guide to the best TVs. It offers cracking picture quality — not only can it produce beautifully contrasty images with inky blacks and vibrant color, but it's a dab-hand when it comes to motion as well. articles.title: Uber tests rides for kids as young as 10, with extra pay for drivers | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Uber has opened its ride-hailing service to children as young as 10 in three U.S. cities as the company tests whether there’s a market for shuttling tweens without an adult by their side. The program, called Uber Kids, launched quietly over the past few weeks in Austin, Texas, Nashville, Tennessee, and Madison, Wisconsin.
The program, which builds on Uber’s existing teen ride-hailing service for passengers ages 13 to 17, is the latest bid by Uber to expand its customer base. Uber is describing this as a limited pilot program, which means it may never expand beyond these cities or even exist by next year. But if successful, it could open up a potentially lucrative market for Uber: busy families with active kids.
The Uber Kids program is stacked with mandatory requirements for parents and drivers. Parents or guardians are the only ones who can order a ride for their child, which they can do by adding the child to their family profile and completing a mandatory onboarding that explains the built-in safety features. A parent or guardian must be present at the pickup locations for the trip to begin and also have to include a note to the driver that explains the drop off.
Meanwhile, only highly rated drivers who have been invited are allowed to participate. Those drivers are required to complete an education module that includes step-by-step instructions and must be opted into live video streaming so parents can watch the trip in real time, according to Uber.
Uber said it also requires PIN verification for every Uber Kids trip, and says all recordings will be encrypted and not available to the driver, and will use sensors and GPS data to detect if the ride goes off course, stops unexpectedly, or ends early.
Drivers who are willing to adhere to those rules to shuttle kids will get a pay bump for the effort, according to Uber. Eligible drivers will earn $7 more on every Uber Kids trip compared to a standard one, the company says on the dedicated Uber Kids webpage. Drivers will receive an extra $20 for the first Uber Kids ride they complete.
The extra compensation underscores a key challenge Uber faces as it expands into this younger age group — how to convince drivers to take on that added responsibility. If the program does expand it could eventually compete with existing transportation services such as HopSkipDrive and Zum.
Uber first opened its ride-hailing service to minors in 2023 when it launched Uber for Teens, although the company had conducted early pilots several years prior. As the program expanded nationwide, Uber introduced a live video streaming feature.

articles.title: Amazon SageMaker AI now detects latency drift, idle GPUs, and missed optimizations on your inference endpoints | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Amazon SageMaker AI now detects latency drift, idle GPUs, and missed optimizations on your inference endpoints
Every inference endpoint is well tuned the day it goes into production. Teams choose an instance type, serving configuration, and scaling settings that suit the model and its traffic at launch. With the endpoint serving smoothly, they understandably move on to the next priority. The workload, however, rarely stays still. Traffic patterns evolve, prompts grow longer, serving engines such as vLLM ship new releases, SageMaker inference develops new optimization techniques, and new fine-tuned checkpoints change the resources your model needs. Over time, a well-tuned endpoint quietly drifts. Latency and time to first token edge upward. A configuration that was never quite ideal keeps missing available performance gains. A GPU provisioned for demand that never materialized sits idle week after week. Because nothing has failed, no alarm sounds, and the drift goes unnoticed until users feel it or the bill reflects it.
Amazon SageMaker AI now monitors your generative AI inference endpoints and tells you when a change could improve performance or lower cost by using Generative AI optimized inference recommendations feature with Agentic experience in Amazon SageMaker Studio. Monitoring is on by default for SageMaker AI inference endpoints using vLLM serving containers and GPU instances, with no setup required, and you can opt out of endpoints. SageMaker AI looks only at operational signals: latency, GPU utilization, and the endpoint’s serving configuration. It does not read your requests or responses. From those signals, it surfaces three kinds of findings:
- Latency drift: A week-over-week rise in median (p50) end-to-end latency or time to first token.
- Unused capacity: GPUs you pay for that sit mostly idle.
- Configuration gaps: A serving container that’s missing newer performance improvements or security patches, or an optimization such as speculative decoding or GPU kernel tuning that your model supports but the endpoint doesn’t use.
SageMaker AI sends a finding through AWS Health, with one notification per endpoint that covers that endpoint’s findings. When a notification arrives, you can act on it in one place. It opens the SageMaker AI agentic experience in Amazon SageMaker Studio with the endpoint, and its recent traffic already filled in. From there, you run inference recommendations to benchmark your current configuration against alternatives and compare them side by side on response time, throughput, and cost per million tokens. That turns a judgment call into a decision backed by data. Benchmarks run on separate compute, and nothing changes on your endpoint until you choose to apply a result.
In this post, we show how SageMaker AI monitors your endpoints and how to read the notifications it sends through AWS Health. We then show how to go from a notification to a benchmarked decision in SageMaker Studio. We walk through three example scenarios, show how to apply or dismiss a recommendation safely, and explain how to opt an endpoint out of monitoring.
Solution overview
SageMaker AI inference recommendations follow a four-step loop: observe, notify, recommend, and decide. Each step is designed so that you stay in control, and your production endpoint isn’t changed without your explicit action.
- Observe – Monitoring of latency and capacity usage is on by default for eligible endpoints. It doesn’t read your requests or responses, and it carries no additional GPU cost.
- Notify – When there is something worth acting on, you receive a plain language notification in AWS Health, plus email, explaining what was observed, why it matters, and a recommended next step.
- Recommend (opt in) – One selection opens the SageMaker AI agentic experience in SageMaker Studio, prefilled with the endpoint and its observed traffic, so you can benchmark alternatives on separate compute.
- Decide – Compare response time, throughput, and cost side by side. Production is not changed until you apply a result.
The feature produces a few types of findings. The following table summarizes what triggers each one and what gets tested when you choose to benchmark.
| Finding | What triggers it | What a benchmark tests | 
| Latency drift | Response time moves relative to the endpoint’s week-over-week trends | Tensor parallelism settings and alternate instance types or sizes | 
| Underutilized GPUs | GPU utilization stays well below capacity over the window | Cheaper instance types and smaller sizes at observed peak traffic | 
| Speculative decoding not enabled | Model and container support it, but it is off (configuration based) | Current configuration compared to speculative decoding enabled | 
| Serving container | The endpoint’s serving container has a newer version with a performance improvement and security patches for critical and high finding Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs). | Current compared to updated container | 
| Untuned GPU kernels | Kernel configuration is not tuned for the model and hardware | Default compared to tuned kernels | 
Prerequisites
Monitoring itself needs no setup, it is on by default. The following prerequisites apply when you choose to act on a finding by running a benchmark and, optionally, applying a change:
- Access to AWS Health and the AWS User Notifications console.
- A SageMaker Studio domain and AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions to run inference recommendation jobs and update endpoints.
- Sufficient service quota for the benchmark instances you want to test.
Cost note: Monitoring has no GPU cost. Benchmarks use standard SageMaker AI charges, or your machine learning (ML) reservation if you have one.
Understand a finding notification
You receive notifications in AWS Health on the console and by email and each one follows the same structure, so it’s quick to scan:
- Endpoint: Which endpoint the finding applies to.
- What we noticed: The observation, stated plainly, with estimates clearly labeled as estimates.
- Why it matters: The impact on latency, capacity, or cost.
- Recommended action: A single selection into the agentic experience in SageMaker Studio to investigate.
Notifications report observations and label estimates. No benchmark has run at this point. A representative notification reads as follows:
| Subject: [Action may be required] SageMaker AI inference improvements for your endpoint SageMaker AI tracks the latency and capacity usage of your inference endpoints by default, and found improvements for one of them. It does not read your requests or responses. What we noticed: Over the past week, time to first token on this endpoint increased compared with the week before. Recommended action: Open SageMaker Studio to benchmark alternatives on separate compute. Your production endpoint is not changed. | 
Cadence: Each endpoint gets one notification that covers the applicable findings. You get at most one notification per endpoint at a time, covering all its findings, and SageMaker AI limits how many an account receives at once. Notifications are AWS Region specific, so you see an endpoint’s findings when you’re signed in to that endpoint’s Region.
Walkthrough: From notification to decision
In this section, we review a few scenarios of endpoint optimizations that will trigger findings to be reported.
Scenario 1: Catch week-over-week latency regression
A team runs a chat assistant on a single SageMaker AI endpoint. They add retrieval to improve answer quality, so every request now carries pages of retrieved context and prompts get much longer. Nothing breaks, and no alarm they set trips, but responses start more slowly.
SageMaker AI compares the endpoint’s median (p50) time to first token and median end-to-end latency with the previous week. When either one rises enough over the week, it flags the change. Because the comparison is against the endpoint’s own history, the team doesn’t need to set a threshold in advance.
- Notification: AWS Health reports that time to first token increased relative to the prior week.
- Studio session: One selection opens the agentic experience, prefilled with the endpoint and its observed traffic.
- Benchmark: The session tests tensor parallelism settings and other instance types or sizes on separate compute.
- Decision: The team compares latency, throughput, and cost, then applies the winning configuration to one variant.
The following screenshot shows an AWS Health event for a latency drift finding. The message reports that median time to first token rose about 200 ms week over week, and the Recommended actions pane links to SageMaker AI to run inference recommendations.
Scenario 2: Turn on an optimization your traffic can benefit from
A platform team hosts an internal code-completion model on a SageMaker AI endpoint. They deployed it with default serving settings and never revisited them. The model and serving container support speculative decoding, a technique for faster responses, but it isn’t enabled. SageMaker AI flags this as an opportunity. Whether it helps depends on the endpoint’s traffic, such as how many requests run concurrently and how long prompts and responses are. The notification recommends running inference recommendations, which benchmarks speculative decoding against the endpoint’s recent traffic and shows whether it’s worth turning on.
- Notification: AWS Health reports that a technique designed to make responses faster is supported but not enabled.
- Studio session: The agentic experience opens with the endpoint configuration loaded.
- Benchmark: The session compares the current configuration with speculative decoding enabled. Results may differ at peak compared to off-peak traffic.
- Decision: If the gain holds at the traffic that matters, the team applies it. Otherwise, they keep the current configuration.
The following screenshot shows an AWS Health event for a speculative decoding finding. The message reports that the model and serving container support speculative decoding, but the endpoint doesn’t use it. The Recommended actions pane links to SageMaker AI to run inference recommendations.
The notification explains that speculative decoding can make responses faster, and that the benchmark compares response time with and without it on the endpoint’s recent traffic.
Scenario 3: Right-size underutilized GPUs
A summarization endpoint was sized for a launch that drew a fraction of the planned audience, so its GPUs sit mostly idle for a week. This scenario also shows a case where the right decision may be to make no change at all.
- Notification: AWS Health reports that the endpoint paid for GPU capacity that largely went unused.
- Studio session: The agentic experience opens with the endpoint and its observed peak traffic.
- Benchmark: The session tests cheaper instance types and smaller sizes at observed peak traffic.
- Decision: The team weighs the monthly savings against the headroom they want for planned growth and may decide to keep the current size.
The following screenshot shows an AWS Health event for an unused capacity finding. The message reports that for most of the week, even the endpoint’s busiest GPU used 12 percent or less of its capacity. The Recommended actions pane links to SageMaker AI to run inference recommendations.
You can choose Open in SageMaker AI from the recommended actions as shown in the screenshot above to apply or dismiss a recommendation. Lets walk through this in next section.
Apply or dismiss a recommendation
You stay in control throughout, and nothing deploys automatically. When you choose Open in SageMaker AI from a notification’s recommended actions, Amazon SageMaker Studio opens a JupyterLab space and shows the prompt that will run in the agentic chat. The following screenshot shows the prompt for a latency drift finding on an endpoint that also runs an older vLLM serving container:
When you choose Run, the agentic experience opens in a chat panel in JupyterLab space in SageMaker Studio. It summarizes the finding in plain language, restates what you asked it to do, and checks with you before it takes any action. The following screenshot shows the agent summarizing the findings and asking to continue:
After you confirm, the agent generates a notebook that creates an inference recommendation job for the endpoint. The notebook uses the SageMaker Python SDK, takes the model from the endpoint and the traffic profile from its metrics, and tags the job with the AWS Health event so you can trace the results back to the finding. Each step is a separate notebook cell, so you can review or edit it before you run it.
The following screenshot shows the notebook cells that record the job details and start a recommendation job across three candidate instance types.
When the job completes, you can compare your current configuration with the alternatives on response time, throughput, and cost. When you are ready to act on a benchmarked result, we recommend a safe rollout pattern:
- Review the proposed change before applying it, including the configuration difference and the benchmarked latency, throughput, and cost.
- Apply to one production variant first and keep the current configuration available for rollback.
- Holding or dismissing a finding is a normal outcome. The notification stays in your AWS Health event history.
Manage monitoring and notifications
You can manage monitoring and how you are notified:
- Manage how you receive notifications in the AWS User Notifications console.
- Optionally, schedule recurring recommendations, for example monthly.
What is and is not collected: Monitoring reads aggregated latency and capacity telemetry at the endpoint level. It doesn’t read your request or response content, and it carries no GPU cost.
Opting out of monitoring: If you don’t want SageMaker AI to monitor an endpoint, set the OPT_OUT_TRACKING environment variable, with a value of your choice, on the model’s container. You set it in the Environment map when you call CreateModel, either on PrimaryContainer or on another container in the model.
If a container on the endpoint carries this variable, SageMaker AI collects no monitoring telemetry for that endpoint, including engine metrics, GPU metrics, and startup configuration details. As a result, it sends no notifications for that endpoint.
Clean up
To avoid ongoing charges, clean up the resources you created while following this post:
- Delete any test endpoints or resources you created for the walkthrough.
- Remove benchmark artifacts in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), if applicable.
- Revert any test configuration changes you applied.
Conclusion
With SageMaker AI inference recommendations now monitoring your endpoints automatically, optimization moves from a point-in-time snapshot to an ongoing signal.
Your endpoints keep telling you when they have drifted, when they are missing an improvement, or when they are paying for idle capacity. A single selection takes you to a benchmarked, side-by-side decision that you control.
For more information on how to get started, visit Amazon SageMaker AI and see the Amazon SageMaker AI documentation.

articles.title: How Dhruv Sayani built Ccigmaa Lifestyles into a five-brand personal care business
articles.text:
How Dhruv Sayani built Ccigmaa Lifestyles into a five-brand personal care business
Starting with Rs 30 lakh and a salon-focused haircare brand in 2018, Mumbai-based Ccigmaa Lifestyles has expanded into men’s grooming, children’s personal care and skincare, with a network of over 27,000 salons across 86 cities.
Hair and water composition can change significantly every 100 kilometres across India, affecting how haircare products perform. It was this observation, made while researching premature greying in his 20s, that led Dhruv Sayani to build Ccigmaa Lifestyles, a Mumbai-based personal care company.
Sayani found that keratin, the protein that makes up most of human hair, responds differently to these regional variations, something he believed conventional haircare formulations did not adequately address.
In 2018, he launched KT Professional, a salon-focused haircare brand developed specifically for stylists. Since then, Ccigmaa Lifestyles has expanded its portfolio with three more brands, KT Men, KT Kids and KT Derma, each focused on specific personal care needs.
The company, founded in 2018, aims to inspire “millions of minds” through Indian-made personal care products, according to Sayani.
Build credibility before distribution
Proving the regional-formulation premise required evidence a lab alone could not generate.
Rather than build retail distribution first and let salons discover the brand afterward, Ccigmaa Lifestyles went the other way around, giving hairstylists across Indian cities access to formulations, and letting their feedback, not a marketing brief, decide what shipped outside the production.
KT Professional was launched with Rs 30 lakh of the founder’s personal savings in 2018, exactly that route. Nearly a decade later, the company works with more than 27,000 salons across 86 cities, a distribution footprint built one stylist and salon relationship at a time rather than through a single national launch mode.
Turn specialization into a growth engine
Once KT Professional’s salon-first model was validated, the more conventional path was to push that single brand harder, deeper into more cities, more product lines, more advertising.
Sayani chose a different growth mechanism instead: apply the same underlying logic, that a mass-market, one-size-fits-all product underserves a large share of its actual buyers, to categories beyond haircare.
That decision produced KT Men and KT Kids as standalone brands rather than product extensions, a materially harder path since each requires its own credibility, its own distribution relationships, and its own reason to exist, rather than borrowing KT Professional's. It is also, by most available market evidence, the better-timed one.
Redseer projects India’s beauty and personal care market reaching $40 billion by 2030, positioning India as the fourth largest such market globally, with Gen Z and Alpha consumers becoming the largest beauty-spending cohort in that growth. A market moving toward younger, more specific buyers rewards brands built around a defined need far more than it rewards a single brand trying to serve everyone.
Position KT Men around performance, not vanity
Sayani says most Indian grooming brands have built their positioning around attraction or plain cosmetic vanity rather than performance, a framing he believed increasingly out of step with younger, fitness-oriented male consumers.
KT Men was built to compete on the second premise instead of the first, launching at an accessible Rs 399 entry point before extending into a higher Rs 699 to Rs 999 band through its G.O.A.T Edition range, a licensing partnership with the Argentina Football Association built around Lionel Messi, Julian Alvarez and Enzo Fernandez.
The brand has since disclosed a Rs 36 Crore marketing investment behind that range, against a Rs 200 crore revenue target over 18 to 24 months, sitting on top of KT Men’s original Rs 100 crore first-year ambition. Whether that specific target lands on schedule matters less to the decision itself than the positioning bet underneath it, that performance, not image, was the underused argument in Indian men's grooming.
Design for two customers at once
Children’s personal care carries a structural complication most categories do not: the person buying the product and the person using it are rarely evaluating it the same way.
A parent checks an ingredient list and asks whether a formulation is genuinely mild enough for a child's skin. A child has no interest in either question and decides on nothing more sophisticated than whether the experience of using it was enjoyable.
Rather than let KT Professional’s existing haircare range absorb a children's line as a smaller variant, Ccigmaa built KT Kids as its own brand, formulated specifically for children rather than adapted from adult products, and has run two entertainment-licensing partnerships in 15 months, first with SpongeBob SquarePants, then with Peppa Pig, timed separately rather than bundled, each aimed at a distinct age band.
The decision to treat that dual-audience problem as its own category, rather than a footnote inside an existing one, is the same underlying instinct that produced KT Men, applied to a harder version of the same question.
The company created five brands with one method to connect them: identify a specific need a generalist product is failing to serve, validate the idea against real, direct feedback before scaling it, and build a dedicated brand around it rather than stretch an existing one to cover it.
Ccigmaa's next test is whether that method holds as a repeatable business engine rather than a run of good individual calls, since a Rs 40 billion market moving toward specificity will reward the companies that can keep making this decision correctly, not just the ones that made it once.

articles.title: De Vice City a los pantanos: qué lugares podrás recorrer en el mundo abierto de GTA 6
articles.text:
GTA 6 llevará a los jugadores por Vice City, cayos tropicales, pantanos, zonas industriales, pueblos en decadencia y parques naturales dentro de Leonida, el estado ficticio inspirado en Florida que Rockstar Games creó para la nueva entrega. El mapa de Grand Theft Auto VI irá más allá de una gran ciudad y reunirá entornos con actividades, personajes y riesgos propios.
La amplitud de Leonida importa porque cada región tendrá una identidad distinta y condiciones climáticas que pueden alterar la conducción, la navegación y la exploración. Desde los neones de Vice City hasta las aguas turbias de Grassrivers, GTA 6 propone un recorrido que combina zonas urbanas, carreteras secundarias, áreas costeras y espacios naturales.
Leonida será la versión de Florida dentro de GTA 6
La relación entre Leonida y Florida sigue el modelo de otros escenarios de la franquicia. San Andreas tomó elementos de California, mientras Liberty City se inspiró en Nueva York. En esta ocasión, Rockstar plantea una reinterpretación satírica del estado estadounidense.
El mapa incluirá playas, manglares, cayos, fauna tropical, urbanizaciones de lujo, carreteras extensas y comunidades apartadas. También recogerá parte del imaginario asociado a Florida, un territorio conocido por sus contrastes entre turismo, vida nocturna, zonas rurales y sucesos extravagantes.
Grand Theft Auto VI no se limitará a recorrer calles urbanas. El jugador podrá pasar de áreas con edificios residenciales y puertos a pantanos, zonas agrícolas y bosques del norte del estado.
El sistema meteorológico reforzará esas diferencias. Las tormentas tropicales, la lluvia y la niebla afectarán cada área de manera localizada. Un trayecto por carretera, una salida en barco o una incursión en los pantanos no tendrán las mismas condiciones según la región.
Vice City recupera playas, neones y una vida nocturna actualizada
Vice City será el principal centro urbano de GTA 6. La ciudad retoma elementos asociados a la versión anterior, como palmeras, playas, luces de neón y arquitectura art déco, aunque ahora se inspira en una Miami contemporánea.
Rockstar confirmó lugares como Ocean Beach, una referencia a Miami Beach y Ocean Drive. También aparecerán Little Cuba, vinculada a la presencia cubana en la ciudad, el mercado de Tisha-Wocka y VC Port, una zona conectada con la industria de cruceros.
La ciudad reunirá edificios residenciales, clubes, puertos y calles con actividad nocturna. Será uno de los espacios donde el jugador encontrará una mayor concentración de tráfico, peatones, negocios y actividades vinculadas con la historia de Jason y Lucia.
La niebla marina podrá alterar la vista al océano en South Ocean Beach. La iluminación global y los reflejos sobre el asfalto mojado cambiarán la apariencia de las calles cuando haya lluvia o tormentas.
Los Leonida Keys conectarán islas y rutas sobre el mar
Al sur de Leonida estarán los Leonida Keys, una versión de los Florida Keys. La zona estará compuesta por pequeñas islas unidas mediante puentes y carreteras que atraviesan el océano.
El entorno incluirá embarcaciones, pesca, bares y una apariencia de vida relajada. Sin embargo, también tendrá una vertiente criminal. Jason mantiene vínculos con esta región y trabaja para Brian Heder, un contrabandista que utiliza su astillero para mover mercancía.
Las condiciones meteorológicas influirán en el desplazamiento por los cayos. Las lluvias intensas pueden reducir la visibilidad en carretera, mientras las tormentas tropicales generarán oleaje en las zonas cercanas al Rusty Anchor y dificultarán la navegación.
Los pantanos de Grassrivers esconderán caimanes y aguas turbias
Grassrivers representa los Everglades dentro de Leonida. Allí desaparecen los edificios y las avenidas para dar paso a extensiones de agua, manglares, viviendas aisladas y embarcaciones impulsadas por grandes hélices.
Los caimanes serán parte del paisaje, aunque Rockstar advierte que no siempre serán el principal peligro. Las tormentas pueden enturbiar todavía más el agua de Pelican Valley, lo que hará más difícil detectar animales y otros riesgos en el entorno.
La región muestra cómo el mundo abierto buscará ofrecer algo más que una ciudad rodeada de espacios secundarios. La navegación, la fauna y la baja visibilidad cambiarán la forma de recorrer los pantanos.
Port Gellhorn y Ambrosia mostrarán otra cara de Leonida
Port Gellhorn retrata una zona vacacional venida a menos. Hoteles baratos, atracciones cerradas y centros comerciales deteriorados forman parte de un paisaje que recuerda a una época turística anterior.
Ahora, la región vive de negocios de menor escala, con gasolineras, alcohol barato, medicamentos y actividades criminales. Es un escenario de carreteras secundarias y lugares alejados de la imagen lujosa de Vice City.
En el centro del estado estará Ambrosia, una región industrial y agrícola dominada por la refinería de azúcar Allied Crystal. La empresa concentra buena parte del empleo local, mientras una banda de moteros controla actividades ilegales.
Mount Kalaga National Park ampliará la exploración al norte
Mount Kalaga National Park será la zona más alejada de los ambientes urbanos. El parque reunirá bosques, ríos y espacios para la pesca, la caza y la conducción todoterreno.
También albergará comunidades rurales y personajes que prefieren mantenerse lejos de las ciudades, entre ellos grupos paranoicos y hostiles hacia el Gobierno. Con estas regiones, GTA 6 convertirá Leonida en un mapa de contrastes, donde Vice City será solo una parte de un territorio más amplio.

articles.text:

articles.title: Auf der Sonnenblume gelandet: Dieser Flugroboter wiegt weniger als eine große Büroklammer
articles.text:
Leichter als eine große Büroklammer: Dieser Flugroboter landet auf einer Sonnenblume
Forscher:innen des Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in Cambridge im US-Bundesstaat Massachusetts und der Cornell University in Ithaca im US-Bundesstaat New York haben nun einen vierflügeligen Mikroroboter mit eigener Sensorik und Rechentechnik gebaut. Wie in einer im Wissenschaftsmagazin Science Robotics veröffentlichten Studie zu lesen ist, hat das Gerät etwa das Format einer kleinen Diktierkassette und wiegt samt Elektronik 1,29 Gramm. Das ist weniger als eine große Büroklammer.
Bisherige Roboter dieser Gewichtsklasse mit schlagenden Flügeln konnten sich nur in engen Laborbereichen bewegen, weil Kameras im Raum ihre Position von außen verfolgen und externe Computer jede Flugkorrektur berechnen mussten. Das bis dahin leichteste Fluggerät mit eigener Orientierung und Steuerung an Bord war eine 18 Gramm schwere Minidrohne mit Propellern und damit mehr als zehnmal so schwer.
Künstliche Muskeln verschaffen dem MIT-Mikroroboter mehr Auftrieb
Damit der 1,05 Gramm leichte Grundkörper das 244 Milligramm schwere Elektronikpaket tragen kann, überarbeitete das Team um den MIT-Elektrotechnikprofessor Kevin Chen die künstlichen Muskeln der vier Flügel. Als Antriebselemente, in der Fachsprache dielektrische Elastomer-Aktuatoren genannt, dienen weiche Kunststoffröhrchen, die sich unter elektrischer Spannung verformen und die Flügel 330-mal pro Sekunde schlagen lassen.
„Es ist sehr schwierig, die Aktuatoren zu vergrößern, ohne dass die Ausgangsleistung des Systems sinkt und sich die Auftriebskräfte verringern“, erklärt Chen in einer Mitteilung der Hochschule. Indem die Entwickler:innen Länge und Radius der künstlichen Muskeln um 50 Prozent vergrößerten, wuchs die nutzbare Hubkraft um 46 Prozent. Die Flügel erzeugen nun das 1,9-Fache dessen an Auftrieb, was der fertige Roboter wiegt.
Andere Insektenroboter nutzen oft starre Antriebe aus sogenannter Piezokeramik, die beim Vergrößern gemessen an ihrer Kraft überproportional schwer und sperrig werden. Die weichen Kunststoffmuskeln behalten ihr Kraft-Gewichts-Verhältnis dagegen auch in größerem Maßstab bei und überstehen leichte Zusammenstöße mit Blättern oder Zweigen ohne direkten Schaden.
Drei Sensoren und ein Sieben-Milligramm-Chip ersetzen Laborkameras
Im Zentrum des Rumpfes sitzen drei biegsame Leiterplatten mit den Messgeräten für die Orientierung. Oben erfasst ein knapp 14 Milligramm schwerer Lagesensor, ähnlich wie in einem Smartphone, 480-mal pro Sekunde jede Drehung und Neigung des Körpers. An der Unterseite misst ein Lichtsensor über die Laufzeit kurzer Lichtsignale den Abstand zum Boden, während ein optischer Bewegungssensor wie bei einer Computermaus den Untergrund abtastet und daraus das seitliche Tempo ableitet.
Eine 0,4 Millimeter dünne Platte aus Glasfaser dämpft das Rütteln des Flügelschlags, damit sich keine Messfehler aufschaukeln. Auf der mittleren Platine wertet ein sieben Milligramm schwerer Steuerchip mit zwei Rechenkernen die Daten über stark vereinfachte Formeln aus, denn viele schnelle Korrekturen pro Sekunde halten den Flieger stabiler als langsame Detailrechnungen.
Mit aktivem Bordchip absolvierte der Roboter zehnsekündige Schwebeflüge sowie kurze Pendelflüge und wich dabei im Schnitt gut zwei Zentimeter von der vorgegebenen Route ab. Die Elektronik nutzte weniger als 25 Prozent eines einzigen Rechenkerns und verbrauchte mit 120 Milliwatt lediglich sechs Prozent des gesamten Strombedarfs von gut zwei Watt. Der Rest floss in die Flügelantriebe.
Landung auf der Sonnenblume gelingt nur mit Joystick und Stromkabel
Für mögliche Einsätze wie die künstliche Bestäubung steuerte das Team den Roboter außerhalb des Labor-Kamerasystems um Pflanzen herum und setzte ihn nach 30 Sekunden auf einer Sonnenblume ab. Allein flog das Gerät dabei allerdings nicht. Die Bordsensoren hielten zwar das Gleichgewicht und regelten die Höhe über Hindernissen, doch den Kurs zur Blüte gab ein Mensch per Joystick über einen externen Computer vor.
Eine Kamera zur selbstständigen Erkennung von Blüten fehlt dem Prototyp ebenso, und in einem vom MIT veröffentlichten Laborvideo erleichtert eine schwarz-weiß gemusterte Unterlage dem optischen Bodensensor die Orientierung. Vor allem bleibt der Flieger an dünne Stromdrähte gebunden, da seine künstlichen Muskeln Spannungen von bis zu 1.900 Volt benötigen.
Für eigene Batterien samt Elektronik, die schwachen Batteriestrom auf diese Hochspannung hochregelt, veranschlagen die Wissenschaftler:innen 1 bis 1,5 Gramm Zusatzgewicht. Der Roboter müsste dafür künftig um 15 bis 35 Prozent wachsen. Finanziert wurde die Entwicklung neben der US-amerikanischen Wissenschaftsstiftung National Science Foundation auch von den Forschungsämtern der US-Marine und der US-Luftwaffe, was nahelegt, dass solche Kleinstflieger ebenso für militärische Aufklärung in engen Räumen interessant sind.

articles.title: Age verification laws might have resurrected adult DVD sales
articles.text:
Ripple effect: Since age verification systems became mandatory in many territories, users have found various ways to circumvent them and continue accessing social media, adult websites, and other content deemed harmful to children. While most resort to VPNs or seek help from adults, recent sales data suggest that others are turning back to physical media.
A major adult film producer and a retailer recently told Mashable that adult DVD sales have surged in regions where governments have passed laws requiring online services to implement age-verification systems. The news adds to growing evidence that these measures have had limited effectiveness.
David Eliason, who owns three adult video stores in South Dakota, reported a 20% to 22% increase in sales over the past year. South Dakota passed its age-verification law last June.
Eliason confirmed that other stores had stopped selling DVDs due to the widespread availability of online adult content, but age-verification laws could slow that trend. Lewis Adams, director of adult video distributor Pulse Distribution, also confirmed an increase in sales in states with age-verification laws, including Texas, Florida, and Tennessee.
Age-verification laws in Australia, the United Kingdom, and numerous US states require websites hosting adult content to verify visitors' ages using methods such as facial scans and ID checks. Many adult users are reluctant to share personal information with these services, some of which have suffered security breaches, and have quickly found ways to bypass the requirements.
VPN use has skyrocketed in these regions, and Utah has even attempted to restrict VPN access in response. Some users reportedly resort to mannequins or 3D models to fool facial scanners, while others switch to non-compliant websites or pirate adult videos through torrents and Discord. Some privacy advocates argue that device-level age verification is the least intrusive approach.
In a recent Youth Endowment Fund study, roughly one-third of teenage respondents reported having bypassed age checks. Of those, one-quarter admitted to accessing adult content. While requiring an ID at an adult video store is technically another form of age verification, at least DVD players don't track their users online.
In related news, Best Buy recently begun testing a return to the market. So far, only The Odyssey is available in stores, but other titles including Project Hail Mary, Interstellar, It's a Wonderful Life, Top Gun, and Obsession are available as Blu-rays and 4K Blu-rays through the retailer's website.

articles.title: Nintendo Switch 2 com EA FC 27 entra em promoção de Black Friday na Amazon • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Nintendo Switch 2 com EA FC 27 entra em promoção de Black Friday na Amazon
Switch 2 tem proposta multiuso e vem com o game EA Esports FC 27 nesta oferta da Black November 2026; console da Nintendo recebe desconto de 19% no Pix
O Nintendo Switch 2 está saindo por apenas R$ 3.779 no Pix na Amazon. O novo console da marca, que oferece experiência de uso de várias formas e inclui no bundle o game EA Sports FC 27, recebe um raro desconto de 19% sobre o preço original de R$ 4.669 durante a Black November 2026.
O Switch 2 é um console que destaca a experiência de uso versátil: ele pode ser usado conectado à TV por meio da dock, como portátil com os Joy-Cons afixados, ou como semiportátil apoiado sobre uma mesa.
Sua tela LCD de 7,9″ possui resolução Full HD e taxa de 120 fps. Ligado à dock, a plataforma reproduz games em até 4K a 60 fps, ou 1080p/2K a 120 fps, com HDR10 em TVs compatíveis.
O hardware inclui um chip Nvidia T239 customizado, 12 GB de RAM e 256 GB de armazenamento expansível com cartões microSD especiais. Os Joy-Cons podem ser usados como um mouse quando apoiados em uma superfície, e a porta Ethernet nativa da dock suporta conexões de rede mais estáveis.
O Switch 2 traz um código para download do game EA Sports FC 27, a nova edição da série de futebol que é uma das mais populares de todos os tempos. O título traz seleções e clubes atualizados de todas as partes do mundo, torneios oficiais e cinco ligas de futebol feminino.
Sua bateria de 5.200 mAh resiste a até 6 horas de uso, segundo a fabricante. A dock é capaz de carregar o sistema quando usado como console de mesa, sem interromper a jogatina.
O Nintendo Switch 2 (apenas R$ 3.779 no Pix) tem acesso ao Nintendo Switch Online, serviço que oferece jogos em rede e benefícios exclusivos para assinantes, e suporta uma vasta biblioteca de games exclusivos da companhia japonesa.
A edição 2026 da Black Friday chega dia 27 de novembro, mas lojas como a Amazon oferecem cupons de ofertas em eletrônicos com condições especiais durante todo o mês, como parte da campanha da Black November.
