articles.title: From learning to leaderboard: How Cisco upskilled 1,200 engineers in agentic AI with AWS AI League | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
From learning to leaderboard: How Cisco upskilled 1,200 engineers in agentic AI with AWS AI League
Cisco, like many large engineering organizations, is adopting generative and agentic AI to change how its engineers build software. The hard part is no longer access to the technology. It’s helping thousands of engineers move from watching a demo to confidently building with it. Recorded sessions and slide decks rarely close that gap. Engineers learn fastest when they build something real, see it fail, fix it, and try again.
AWS designed AWS AI League for exactly that. It turns hands-on AI learning into a gamified competition, where participants customize models and build agents on AWS, get instant feedback on a live leaderboard, and compete in a game-show-style finale.
Cisco is one of the clearest examples of what this looks like at scale. In 2025, Hemanth V, a Cisco software engineer, went from an internal Cisco event to being crowned the first AWS AI League Champion at AWS re:Invent 2025. In 2026, 1,200 Cisco engineers competed in an AWS AI League tournament at Cisco Transformation Fest 4.0. The winner, Nishanth Aluhonnu, earned a full event pass to AWS re:Invent 2026 in Las Vegas.
In this post, we share how Cisco and AWS used Cisco Transformation Fest and AWS AI League to build a lasting culture of learning by doing. We previously covered this program in From theory to delivery: How Atos upskilled 400 engineers in agentic AI, and here we look at Cisco’s experience. We walk through Cisco’s journey, share technical lessons from the 2026 winning agent, and explain how your organization can host its own AWS AI League.
What is AWS AI League?
AWS AI League helps organizations build advanced AI skills through competition. Each league follows three steps:
- Learn – A hands-on, 2-hour workshop led by AWS experts introduces the tools and the challenge.
- Build – Participants experiment at their own pace and submit to a live leaderboard, with an automated evaluator giving real-time feedback after each submission.
- Compete – Top finalists take the stage in a live, game-show-style grand finale.
Although AWS AI League offers multiple use cases, at Cisco it offered the following two challenges:
- Agentic AI challenge – Participants build agents with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale with any framework or model. The agents move through a maze-like grid, solving challenges on the way to a treasure chest. The challenges map to real-world tasks such as handling inappropriate content, running code, retrieving information from the web, and extracting structured data. Builders can choose models for supervisor and sub-agents and add tools such as AgentCore memory, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and AWS Lambda Event Functions. Builders use Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to apply safety controls to their agents.
- Model customization challenge – Participants fine-tune models in Amazon SageMaker Studio using the latest training recipes. The challenge awards points when an automated evaluator rates a participant’s customized model as more accurate and comprehensive than a reference model on the specific tasks in the competition.
Finalists are scored on time efficiency, accuracy, agent planning, and token consumption efficiency.
The Cisco and AWS partnership
The AWS AI League story at Cisco grows out of a deep engineering partnership. Cisco and AWS bring together networking, cloud, security, and observability for shared customers including:
- Cisco SD-WAN, whose controller architecture runs on AWS and serves customers globally as a software as a service (SaaS) application.
- Cisco Meraki, Cisco Spaces, and Cisco’s IoT and smart buildings group.
- Cisco Cloud Control, a cloud-native, AI-powered application integrated with AWS services that brings together security, networking, observability, and collaboration.
- Cisco AI Defense, where Cisco’s security team uses Amazon Bedrock and Amazon SageMaker AI to embed AI governance and guardrails across the Cisco portfolio.
The two companies have also published joint deployment guides and Cisco Validated Designs across networking and AWS. A recent example of co-innovation is SD-WAN fabric on demand across the AWS backbone, built to deliver the resilience and uptime customers expect.
        “When you see that many business units independently choosing to build their next-generation platforms natively on AWS, that’s not a vendor relationship anymore. It’s a true engineering partnership.”
— Kumaril Kapoor, VP of Engineering, Cisco
Cisco’s VP of Engineering Kumaril Kapoor and AWS Industries India leader Chandra Balani sit down to discuss the AWS and Cisco partnership story, from co-innovation across networking, cloud, and AI to enabling thousands of engineers through the annual Cisco AWS Transformation Fest.
Cisco Transformation Fest: Enablement at scale
As the partnership grew, it extended beyond technology to people. Working closely with Cisco teams in India, AWS saw a strong appetite for learning and experimenting among Cisco engineers across many business units. The question was how to scale that impact beyond the day-to-day touchpoints of the partnership.
The answer was Cisco Transformation Fest, first held in 2022. The program is built on five tenets the team summarized as SCALE:
| Tenet | What it means for Cisco engineers | 
| Share | Share what you know with peers across teams. | 
| Connect | Connect with engineers across business units. | 
| Adopt | Adopt new skills and AWS services. | 
| Learn | Learn by building, not by watching. | 
| Experiment / Engage | Experiment hands-on and stay engaged with the technology and each other. | 
Transformation Fest brings together several formats: AWS GameDays, AWS AI League, sessions where Cisco leaders share best practices and success stories with peers, and sessions on Amazon and AWS culture. What began as a single event is now an annual, three-day program that has completed its fourth edition and reached around 2,000 engineers. AWS continues to engage Cisco teams with hands-on workshops and experience-based accelerations.
        “It has been genuinely valuable for us, and it’s really a journey, but I appreciate most is the intent behind it. It’s built around our people. It gives our engineers the time, the space, and the hands-on support to grow real skills on AWS. For us, it has turned into a lasting culture of learning by doing. It’s not a one-off event.”
— Kumaril Kapoor, VP of Engineering, Cisco
Where enablement becomes execution: AWS AI League at Cisco
Of all the Transformation Fest formats, AWS AI League has had the most visible impact. Its gamified, hands-on structure puts engineers to work with Amazon SageMaker on fine-tuning, model customization and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore for agent building, against a clock and in front of their peers. Participants leave with practical experience and genuine confidence in their AI skills.
        “This is where enablement actually turns into real execution.”
— Kumaril Kapoor, VP of Engineering, Cisco
2025: From the Cisco campus to global champion
Hemanth V, a software engineer in Cisco’s switching core platform team, had an inspiring journey that set the benchmark for Cisco.
His journey had two stages:
- AWS AI League at Cisco AWS Transformation Fest 3.0. He competed against more than 600 participants from Cisco in a model customization challenge, fine-tuning a small model in Amazon SageMaker, and won the title.
- Global grand finale at AWS re:Invent 2025. In Las Vegas he faced a completely different challenge: the agentic AI track, where he built an agent to navigate a dynamic, game-style maze. He took first place and was recognized during the re:Invent keynote.
Hemanth finished ahead of Ross Williams from Aqfer (second place) and Deepesh Khanna from Capital One (third place).
        “You don’t need to know everything beforehand. You will learn a lot of things on the way. The only thing that matters is your curiosity and willingness to learn.”
— Hemanth V, Software Engineer, Cisco, and 2025 AWS AI League Champion
2026: 1,200 engineers, one champion
In 2026, Cisco Transformation Fest 4.0 hosted a full AWS AI League agentic AI tournament. The AWS account team ran pre-event training so that engineers with no prior agentic AI experience could compete from day one. The format was designed to narrow a large field down to a single winner:
| Stage | Format | Winning result | 
| Qualifier | 1,200 participants across four cohorts. Top 5 per cohort advance to semifinal | 1st in cohort 3 with 15,906 points (98 submissions) | 
| Semifinal | 20 participants compete for 3 finalist spots | 1st with 16,321 points | 
| Finale | 3 live rounds on stage in front of Cisco and AWS leadership | 1st with 27,008 cumulative points | 
Nishanth Aluhonnu, a software engineer at Cisco, finished first at every stage and earned a full conference pass to AWS re:Invent 2026.
The finale itself showed why the format works. Participants could not change code, tools, or prompts during the finale, only a short steering instruction before each round. Success depended on how well each agent made decisions on maps it had never seen before. Nishanth lost the first round, then won the second by a wide margin by ignoring a board full of low-value coins in favor of a single high-value challenge.
Examining what it takes to win an agentic AI challenge
The 2026 winning agent offers lessons that go well beyond the game. Each design choice maps to a decision teams face when they run agents in production.
Output tokens are the real cost
The agentic AI challenge scores agents on challenge points, a treasure bonus, remaining lives, and a token bonus, computed as tokenBonus = 1000 - (totalOutputTokens / challengesVisited).
In the qualifier, the top four agents all solved the map. The first-place agent emitted 1,220 output tokens and the second-place agent emitted 1,430, and the final margin was only 16 points out of nearly 16,000. After every agent can solve the problem, efficiency decides the winner.
To understand which tokens mattered, Nishanth built nine variants of the same agent, changing one thing at a time. The result was clear: tool results and the system prompt didn’t count against the score, but everything the agent wrote, including tool call arguments, did. Each tool call carried roughly 52 tokens of fixed overhead on top of its arguments.
This mirrors real-world cost. Generating output is sequential and is typically priced several times higher than input, and in an agent loop that cost compounds across every step. A long, well-structured system prompt (which you can also cache) is cheap. A chatty agent isn’t.
One agent, not five
A common architecture for this challenge is a supervisor agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that delegates to specialist sub-agents for navigation, computation, and web retrieval. It’s a sound pattern for many production systems. The winning design used a single agent with no sub-agents. Instead, the prompt began with a short dispatch table that matched each challenge type to the right approach in a single turn.
The reasoning was simple: every handoff between agents is a message the model has to write, and in this challenge every written token is scored. The lesson isn’t that sub-agents are bad. It’s to choose your architecture based on what coordination costs you. When coordination is expensive, a flatter design can win.
The following diagram shows the AWS reference architecture for the agentic AI challenge: a supervisor agent with specialist sub-agents. The winning design deliberately didn’t use this multi-agent pattern.
In this reference architecture, a supervisor agent runs in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and coordinates three sub-agents, with Amazon Bedrock Guardrails and AgentCore memory connected to the runtime. The supervisor and sub-agents route through the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, to four tools: a navigation tool, browser tool, code execution tool, and custom tools using AWS Lambda functions.
Put deterministic logic in tools
Route planning was not left to the model. It ran in an AWS Lambda function that treated the board as an optimization problem. Each tile carried an expected value: the points it paid, minus the lives it could cost, minus the tokens the agent would spend to solve it. The planner respected constraints, such as collecting a key before its door, and refined the route within a time budget.
This is a useful pattern for most agents: let the model handle language and judgment, and move search, math, and rules into tools where they are faster, cheaper, and repeatable.
Make decisions on value, not habit
The second finale round was designed as a trap. A seven-by-seven board was almost entirely covered in coins worth 25 points each, while a single scheduling challenge tile was worth 1,500 points. Habit said to collect the coins. The planner’s value table said the coins were noise. The agent went for the high-value challenge and scored 7,537 points in that round, compared with 5,953 for the next finalist. That round built the lead that carried the agent to the overall win.
Impact for Cisco
Across two years of AWS AI League at Cisco, the impact shows up in skills, culture, and recognition:
- Hands-on AI skills at scale. 1,200 engineers took part in the 2026 tournament, building agents on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, many of them with no prior agentic AI experience.
- Connections across business units. Engineers who would otherwise never have met competed in the same tournament, shared approaches, and learned from each other.
- A lasting culture of learning. Now in its fourth year, Transformation Fest has become an annual commitment rather than a one-off hackathon.
- Recognition, two years in a row. A Cisco engineer won the 2025 AWS AI League global title, and the 2026 Cisco champion will attend AWS re:Invent 2026.
- Leadership visibility. The 2026 finale took place in front of Cisco and AWS senior leadership, giving engineers a real stage for their work.
For Hemanth, the biggest takeaway was confidence. You do not need to master everything before you start. You learn by getting hands-on.
        “Technology alone isn’t enough. You need people who are empowered to experiment with it. Transformation Fest created that enablement environment, and AWS AI League created the opportunity for execution.”
— Kumaril Kapoor, VP of Engineering, Cisco
Conclusion
In this post, we showed how Cisco and AWS turned enablement into execution. Cisco Transformation Fest created a space for engineers to learn by doing, and AWS AI League gave them a real challenge, a scoreboard, and a stage. The result is a culture of hands-on AI building that reaches thousands of engineers.
To get started:
- Learn how to host a tournament in your organization on the AWS AI League page.
- Build your agentic AI and model customization skills with the AWS AI training catalog on AWS Skill Builder.
- Follow the AWS AI League 2026 global finale at AWS re:Invent 2026 in Las Vegas.
We look forward to seeing what your teams build.

articles.title: Desativou o histórico do Gemini? O Google salva mesmo assim • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Desativou o histórico do Gemini? O Google salva mesmo assim
Empresa atualizou tempo que suas conversas na IA ficam registradas de três dias para dois meses, independente da configuração de histórico.
O Gemini agora “lembra” seus últimos dois meses de consultas na plataforma, mesmo que você tenha desativado completamente seu histórico. O Google atualizou suas políticas de privacidade para a inteligência artificial na terça-feira (17/11) e aumentou o tempo que suas interações ficam salvas: de 72 horas para dois meses.
Você ainda pode ajustar por quanto tempo deseja reter as trocas. A configuração dá a opção padrão de 18 meses, além de opções de três ou 36 meses, além de deixar esse limite indefinido ou totalmente zerado (mas nem tanto). Independente da sua escolha, a nova política garante pelo menos dois meses de mensagens salvas.
Segundo o Google, a mudança tem como objetivo usar as interações para “proteger o Google, seus usuários e o público”. Ao avisar sobre a novidade, a empresa fala ainda em “ajuda de revisores humanos”, dando a entender que pessoas reais teriam acesso ao que você pergunta ao Gemini.
O acesso às informações trocadas com a IA não é uma novidade. Uma recomendação comumente dada por especialistas na área, inclusive, é não fornecer dados sensíveis nessas consultas à IA, como números de cartão de crédito, documentos, entre outros exemplos.
A revisão dessas mensagens por humanos também é algo padrão das IAs, e está previsto na política de privacidade do Google. Empresas como a Anthropic publicam relatórios frequentes trazendo exemplos de mau uso a partir de revisões do tipo. O próprio Gemini assume que algumas interações são checadas por pessoas reais, mas sem identificação dos usuários.
A retenção de mensagens também é algo comum no mercado. Segundo o Gizmodo, Anthropic e OpenAI falam em 30 dias, por exemplo, mas afirmam que podem manter as interações salvas por mais tempo se necessário. O Google cita motivos de segurança para manter esses logs, mas não explica como isso pode significar uma proteção maior ao usuário.
Mesmo com a retenção obrigatória pelo Google, você pode eliminar seu histórico e desativar o salvamento automático. Apesar de ficar disponível internamente para fins de “segurança” e funcionamento da IA, não será possível acessar as conversas anteriores na sua conta. Para apagar e interromper o salvamento desses chats, siga o passo a passo:
Você também pode configurar a exclusão automática de mensagens de até 3 anos atrás. A opção fica disponível em “Excluir atividades com mais de…”, logo abaixo da configuração de desativar o salvamento. Basta selecionar o período desejado e confirmar a ação para finalizar.

articles.title: Meta’s AI agent Muse is mixing up conversations and could be exposing private data, report says | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Meta employees have raised concerns that the company’s AI agent Muse has been mixing up conversations across different accounts and exposing private user data, according to a new Reuters report that looked at internal company posts.
In some of these instances, employees said Muse surfaced messages about childcare requests they never made, career advice they never asked for, product orders they never placed, and bank account balances that didn’t belong to them.
One employee told colleagues that Muse had randomly sent an extra message in a chat about weather and tide information, saying: “BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5899.57.”
In another example, an employee using the AI agent on her personal phone received a reminder from Muse to respond to a message from her sister on Signal, the popular end-to-end encrypted messaging app.
“This seems like an extreme privacy violation. I definitely did not grant it access to other apps, or recall being asked about this,” the employee said in her post, according to the report.
“Employee testing is core to the product development process and the entire point is to get feedback, so we can implement safety and privacy protections and improve products,” a Meta spokesperson said in an email to TechCrunch. “Importantly, employees have access to different versions of Muse than the public, so they’re often reviewing features, functionality, and behavior not available elsewhere.”
Launched in September, Muse is one of the fastest-growing apps on record, with more than 10 million downloads.
Update 11/19/2026 12:05 PM PT: The article was updated to include Meta’s comment.

articles.title: Keep inference running through regional capacity shortfalls with cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Keep inference running through regional capacity shortfalls with cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI
Serving a model from more than one AWS Region is a well-established pattern for highly available inference: when one Region runs short of GPU capacity, requests move to another. The pattern is simple to describe and hard to operate. Until now, if you served models on Amazon SageMaker AI managed endpoints, cross-Region routing was a piece you still had to build yourself.
Today, we’re introducing cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI. It uses a new resource, the inference router, that gives your application one invocation path across the endpoints and inference components you already run, in one or more AWS Regions and AWS accounts. You register the destinations that serve a model, and your application invokes the router instead of a specific endpoint. The router keeps requests in its own Region while the local destination is healthy, shifts new requests to another registered destination when it isn’t, and returns traffic gradually after recovery.
In this post, we explain how cross-Region inference routing decides where each request runs, walk through an example with one model in two Regions, and cover monitoring, limits, and what you pay. For a cross-account deployment that serves several models, see How Salesforce is advancing global-scale model serving with cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI.
When one Region runs short of capacity
A SageMaker AI endpoint runs in one AWS Region and one account. When autoscaling can’t add instances of the type your endpoint needs, requests throttle and time out, even when the same model has spare capacity in another Region. To use that capacity, your application must detect a struggling endpoint and switch Regions, decide which errors are safe to retry without running the model twice, move traffic back after recovery without flapping, and manage access to endpoints in other accounts. That code sits on the critical path of every request, and every team serving models across Regions maintains its own version of it.
How cross-Region inference routing works
Cross-Region inference routing is based on a few core ideas:
- You decide where your model might run – For each model, you choose which endpoints and inference components the router might use.
- SageMaker AI decides which destination serves each request – The router prefers its own Region and shifts new requests to another destination only when the local one can’t serve reliably.
- Your endpoints stay the same – You deploy endpoints as you do today, with the same models, configurations, instance pools, and autoscaling. Direct InvokeEndpoint calls keep working, and the router passes InferenceId and CustomAttributes through, as InvokeEndpoint does.
- You can see every decision – Each real-time response tells you which destination served the request and why.
A few terms describe the pieces:
- Inference router – A Regional SageMaker AI resource in your account that your application invokes.
- Routing target – A name for one logical model on a router, such as fraud-model. A router can hold many routing targets, and each fails over independently of the others.
- Destination – A real-time endpoint, inference component, or asynchronous endpoint registered under a routing target, identified by its full Amazon Resource Name (ARN), which tells the router its Region and account. A routing target holds either real-time destinations, which can mix endpoints and inference components across Regions and accounts, or asynchronous endpoints only.
- Local destination – A destination in the router’s Region, preferred while it’s healthy.
- Routing reason – A value returned with each real-time response that explains where the request went and why.
The Region you create the router in is its local Region. To prefer a different Region, create a router there. The router doesn’t create capacity, scale your endpoints, deploy models, or copy model artifacts and container images. Each destination must already be running in its Region.
How routing decisions are made
The router considers only destinations that are registered on the routing target and that it’s authorized to invoke. Among those, it prefers destinations in its own Region, and when more than one local destination is healthy, it spreads requests across them evenly. Requests leave the Region only when local destinations can’t serve reliably. To detect that, SageMaker AI calculates a health score for each destination from its recent requests, measured in the destination’s own Region. Server errors (5xx), throttles, and timeouts lower the score. Errors from the SageMaker AI platform (for example, failed health check) lower it the most. Errors caused by the request itself, such as invalid input, don’t lower it, because the same request would fail in any Region. Model latency isn’t an input, so an endpoint that keeps returning successful responses keeps its traffic. Signals such as failed instance launches or an endpoint running fewer instances than its autoscaling target make the router react faster, but only after the destination starts failing requests.
The router evaluates each destination’s health and publishes it to Amazon CloudWatch as one of three states. A healthy destination serves normally. An overloaded destination still serves, and the router moves part of its traffic away. A degraded destination is failing or can’t serve, so the router moves most of its traffic away and keeps a small share to detect recovery.
SageMaker AI manages failover thresholds and timing, so you don’t need to tune any thresholds. If health information for remote destinations goes stale, the router keeps traffic in its own Region, so a gap in monitoring never moves traffic on its own.
When traffic moves, and when it comes back
The more requests fail, the more traffic moves, so a destination need not fail outright first. Traffic starts to move within about a minute of sustained errors, or longer for a destination with little traffic. Traffic that leaves the local Region is spread across the healthy remote destinations in proportion to their health. You can’t set weights or a fallback order. After recovery, traffic returns over several minutes, more slowly than it left. Requests in progress aren’t interrupted.
When a destination fails a real-time request without running the model, the router retries that request once on a different destination. This covers, for example, a throttle, a 503 error, a model that isn’t ready, a rejection by a cross-Region traffic cap, or access denied by the destination. The router never retries timeouts, 500 errors, or model errors.
For asynchronous requests, the router tries each eligible destination once, local destinations first, until one accepts the request.
Figure 4 shows where requests were served in one of our tests with a test model.
What you can route
The following use cases show common ways to use cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI.
- Keep serving when one Region runs short of GPU capacity. When your G-series instance type runs short in US East (Ohio) during peak traffic and requests start to throttle, the router shifts new requests to the same model in US West (Oregon), where autoscaling absorbs the overflow, and moves traffic back gradually after US East (Ohio) recovers.
- Route across endpoints owned by separate AWS accounts. When a central platform account owns the router and other accounts own the endpoints, each endpoint owner grants access to one named router, and requests reach those endpoints only through that router. We cover the setup after this list.
- Serve many models from one router. Create one router with one routing target per model, each listing that model’s destinations, and pass the routing target name on each request. Each model fails over independently.
- Put the router behind your own gateway. If you operate an API or model gateway, you can point its SageMaker AI integration at the router, so SageMaker AI handles Region selection for SageMaker-hosted models while your gateway decides when to use a different provider. For example, see the Salesforce post.
- Route asynchronous requests. Asynchronous endpoints, in the router’s account or in other accounts, can be destinations. Your application calls InvokeInferenceRouterAsync with the routing target name and the Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) input location, and gets back an InferenceId and the output and failure locations, as with InvokeEndpointAsync.
- Protect a receiving endpoint from other Regions’ overflow. On a real-time endpoint, you can set an optional cross-Region traffic cap so that requests from other Regions can use only part of its capacity. Your endpoint’s local callers keep the rest. We cover the details later in this section.
When a destination belongs to a different account than the router, both accounts must allow each request. On the endpoint side, the owner attaches a resource-based policy that allows the router account to invoke the endpoint, and the sagemaker:SourceInferenceRouterArn condition key limits that access to one named router. The following policy allows only my-router in account 444455556666 to invoke the endpoint. Its second statement has no router condition and lets the router account read the endpoint’s status. Without that statement, the destination shows its status as unknown.
In the router account, callers need sagemaker:InvokeInferenceRouter (or sagemaker:InvokeInferenceRouterAsync) on the router and sagemaker:InvokeEndpoint (or sagemaker:InvokeEndpointAsync) on every destination, because the router invokes each destination on the caller’s behalf. A router never gives a caller access to an endpoint they couldn’t call directly. For DescribeInferenceRouter to report each destination’s status, callers also need sagemaker:DescribeEndpoint on endpoints and sagemaker:DescribeInferenceComponent on inference components. Applications in other accounts call the router by assuming a role in the router account. For a walkthrough, see How Salesforce is advancing global-scale model serving with cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI and User Guide on cross-account destinations.
Protect a receiving endpoint with a cross-Region traffic cap
When the router moves requests away from a Region that’s short on capacity, those requests land on endpoints that already serve their own Region’s callers. By default, a receiving endpoint accepts any amount of cross-Region traffic, so a surge of overflow can push it into throttling. With a cross-Region traffic cap, the endpoint owner decides how much of the endpoint’s capacity other Regions might use.
You set the cap in CreateEndpointConfig with CrossRegionTrafficConfig, which takes two required values. MaxInvocationsPerSecondPerInstance is the number of invocations per second that one instance can take, which you measure with a load test of your model, instance type, and typical payload. MaxCrossRegionPercentPerEndpoint is the share of that capacity that other Regions might use. SageMaker AI multiplies the per-instance rate by the instances in service and applies the percentage, so the cap follows autoscaling. For example, with 50 invocations per second per instance, a 20 percent cap, and 4 instances in service, the endpoint accepts up to 40 requests per second from other Regions. When autoscaling adds 2 instances, the cap rises to 60 requests per second.
Only requests from other Regions count against the cap. Requests from the endpoint’s own Region, including direct InvokeEndpoint calls and calls from a router in the same Region, are never throttled by it. When cross-Region requests exceed the cap, the endpoint rejects the extra requests before your model runs, and the router retries each one once on a different destination. If no other destination can take the request, your application gets a throttling error.
The cap applies to real-time endpoints, and all inference components on an endpoint share it. For an endpoint that hosts inference components, load test one instance with its usual mix of inference components and payloads to measure MaxInvocationsPerSecondPerInstance, and run the test again when that mix or your payloads change. If you leave out CrossRegionTrafficConfig, the endpoint accepts any amount of cross-Region traffic.
Get started: One model in two Regions
In this example, we deploy Qwen3-4B with the vLLM container as an inference component in US East (Ohio) and US West (Oregon), in one account. Because the inference router doesn’t support response streaming, the application sends non-streaming requests, and each request must complete within about a minute, the same limit as InvokeEndpoint. We then create a router in US East (Ohio) with one routing target that lists both:
Run DescribeInferenceRouter and confirm that each destination’s RoutingStatus is Routable before you send traffic.
The application invokes the router with the routing target name and the same payload it would send to InvokeEndpoint, and reads the serving destination and routing reason from the response:
What we observed
| Step | RoutingStatus in DescribeInferenceRouter (us-east-2 / us-west-2) | Served by | Routing reason | 
| Both inference components running | Routable / Routable | us-east-2 | local-preferred | 
| us-east-2 inference component removed | Unroutable / Routable | us-west-2 | only-healthy | 
| us-east-2 inference component restored | Routable / Routable | us-west-2 | only-healthy | 
| Traffic back in us-east-2 | Routable / Routable | us-east-2 | local-preferred | 
Traffic stayed in US East (Ohio) while its inference component ran, moved to US West (Oregon) with no change to the application when we removed it, and came back after we restored it.
The complete notebook for this example is available on GitHub.
Tip: Use instance pools and cross-Region inference routing together. With a capacity-aware instance pool, SageMaker AI can use another instance type in the same Region at creation and during scale-out. The router moves new requests to another Region when the local endpoint as a whole can’t serve. For details, see Capacity-aware inference: Automatic instance fallback for SageMaker AI endpoints.
See where each request went
The inference router gives you two views of routing: a record on every real-time response and metrics in CloudWatch.
Per-request routing record
Every real-time response includes the ARN of the destination that served the request in InvokedRoutedResourceArn, and the routing reason in RoutingReason. The routing reason is one of the following:
- local-preferred – Served by a healthy destination in the router’s Region.
- capacity-available – Served by a destination with available capacity.
- failover – Moved away from a destination that couldn’t serve reliably.
- only-healthy – Served by the only eligible destination that was healthy.
We recommend logging both values with your application’s own request logs.
Asynchronous responses don’t include the serving destination. Router metrics in CloudWatch show where asynchronous requests were placed.
Router metrics in CloudWatch
The router publishes OpenTelemetry metrics to CloudWatch in its own account and Region, labeled with the router, routing target, and destination:
- aws.sagemaker.inference_router.invocations – Requests per destination, with an error.type label on failures (invocation_4xx, invocation_5xx, or invocation_model_error).
- aws.sagemaker.inference_router.destination.duration – Time at the destination, including your model.
- aws.sagemaker.inference_router.overhead.duration – The router’s own work plus network time to and from another Region.
- aws.sagemaker.inference_router.destination.status – Each destination as healthy, overloaded, or degraded.
Alarm on destinations that aren’t healthy and on the error rate across all error types. See Monitor an inference routers with Amazon CloudWatch and AWS CloudTrail.
Each destination endpoint keeps publishing its existing SageMaker AI metrics in its own account and Region. To view them in one place, use CloudWatch cross-account observability and cross-account cross-Region dashboards.
AWS CloudTrail records the router’s API calls (create, update, delete, describe, and list) as management events and router invocations as data events. You enable data events on your trail as you do for other SageMaker AI data events.
Plan your deployment
Keep the following in mind when you design with the inference router:
- Put the router in the Region where most of your traffic originates. The router always prefers destinations in its own Region.
- Size each Region for its own traffic plus the overflow you want it to absorb. By default, a receiving endpoint accepts any amount of cross-Region traffic, so configure autoscaling with headroom for the overflow you expect. To protect an endpoint’s local callers, set a cross-Region traffic cap, as described in Protect a receiving endpoint with a cross-Region traffic cap. If every remote destination reaches its cap, requests beyond the combined caps return throttling errors.
- Keep a low-cost standby Region. You can register an inference component in another Region and keep its cost low, but plan for how it gets capacity. A remote inference component with zero copies receives only a small share of traffic during failover, and those requests fail until it has copies. Keep at least one copy running, or configure autoscaling on copies and confirm that it scales out before you rely on the standby Region.
- Plan for resilience at the entry point. A router is regional, so if its Region is impaired, calls to it fail. Create routers in two Regions and switch between them on the client side.
- Register only destinations where your data might be processed. A request can be processed in the router’s Region or in any Region where you’ve registered a destination. For data that must stay in one geography, use a separate router, for example one for US data and one for EU data. You are responsible for configuring your routers to align with your data residency and compliance obligations.
- Keep your own retries modest. A throttling error means every destination was busy, and a service-unavailable error means no destination could take the request. A service-unavailable error after about a minute means the request timed out and the model might have run, so don’t retry it automatically.
- Remove deleted destinations from the router. Traffic already avoids a deleted endpoint, but the router never removes a destination on its own.
- Call the router privately. Applications in a virtual private cloud (VPC) can call the router through an interface VPC endpoint (AWS PrivateLink), which supports IPv4 (IPv6/dual-stack not supported).
Also note the following limitations:
- Response streaming isn’t supported.
- A real-time request that the destination doesn’t respond to within about a minute fails with a service-unavailable error.
- Each router holds up to 20 routing targets, each routing target holds up to 10 destinations, and real-time payloads can be up to 6 MB. For default quotas, such as routers per account and request rates, and how to request an increase, see Service Quotas in the Amazon SageMaker AI documentation.
Conclusion
Cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI gives your application one invocation path across the endpoints and inference components you already run, in multiple AWS Regions and AWS accounts. The router prefers its own Region, shifts new requests when a destination can’t serve reliably, returns traffic gradually after recovery, and shows you where each request ran and why. Your endpoints, models, containers, and autoscaling policies don’t change.
Cross-Region inference routing is generally available starting today in most commercial AWS Regions (except me-south-1 and me-central-1), for real-time and asynchronous inference.
There is no additional charge for cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI. You pay for the SageMaker AI endpoints and inference components that serve your requests at standard SageMaker AI pricing, whether a request reaches them directly or through an inference router. The inference router publishes metrics to Amazon CloudWatch in the router’s account, and you pay standard CloudWatch rates for those metrics and any queries you run on them. For details, see Amazon SageMaker AI pricing.
To get started, see the Amazon SageMaker AI documentation on cross-Region inference routing and explore the sample notebook on GitHub.

articles.title: Son pedigree est déjà bien chargé : c’est quoi ARTEX, l’outil de piratage chinois utilisé contre la Commission européenne ?
articles.text:
Le voici sur le devant de la scène médiatique… européenne.
Le 19 novembre 2026, Politico a révélé que le service de cybersécurité des institutions européennes avait détecté l’utilisation d’ARTEX dans une campagne de cyberattaques visant la Commission européenne.
Depuis plus de dix jours, cette attaque perturbe plusieurs services internes de la Commission, de la plateforme RH aux services de traduction en passant par l’outil de remboursement des frais médicaux.
L’outil n’a pourtant rien d’un inconnu dans l’écosystème cyber. Le CERT-EU lui avait consacré une note technique dès le 5 novembre, le FBI a publié une alerte le 13, et les grands éditeurs de cybersécurité suivent sa diffusion depuis la fin de l’été.
Qu’est-ce qu’ARTEX ?
Sur le papier, l’intention était bonne. ARTEX a en effet été conçu comme un outil de test d’intrusion (pentest), qui simule des attaques pour qu’une organisation découvre ses failles avant les pirates. S’il est présenté comme un outil d’IA, ARTEX n’est pas un modèle en lui-même. C’est une surcouche qui se branche sur des modèles existants, de Claude à DeepSeek, ou sur n’importe quel service compatible avec l’interface d’OpenAI.
Il fait travailler ensemble plusieurs agents, entre lesquels un module de planification répartit les tâches de l’intrusion, et chacun consigne ses découvertes dans un journal commun. Un opérateur humain les dirige et reprend la main aux moments décisifs. Ces agents scannent le réseau visé, exploitent les failles trouvées, installent des portes dérobées et récupèrent des identifiants, en changeant de piste dès qu’une voie est bloquée.
Sur le fond, ARTEX n’invente donc aucune technique d’intrusion. Il passe toujours par des identifiants volés ou des systèmes non mis à jour ou mal protégés.
Reste qu’il crée une sérieuse bascule dans la vitesse d’exécution, et c’est l’une des principales sources d’inquiétudes lorsqu’il tombe entre de mauvaises mains.
Publié en open source en juillet 2026, ARTEX n’est resté que quelques mois sur GitHub. Le 8 octobre, son développeur chinois, un certain « Autumn-27 » a annoncé qu’il ne le mettrait plus à jour et le passerait en code fermé « compte tenu des abus ».
Un retrait qui n’a pas fait disparaître l’outil pour autant. Selon le FBI, des copies archivées, des versions dérivées et une édition commerciale baptisée ARTEX PRO circulent toujours, et début novembre la société Censys recensait près de 1 500 consoles ARTEX accessibles publiquement sur Internet.
La Commission européenne n’est pas la première victime d’ARTEX
C’est une affaire antérieure à celle de la Commission européenne qui a poussé son créateur à le retirer. Fin septembre, au moins neuf établissements financiers sud-coréens ont été visés par des cyberattaques destinées à voler les données personnelles de leurs clients. Selon l’entreprise de cybersécurité CrowdStrike, l’attaquant se serait appuyé sur ARTEX et sur Claude Code, l’outil de programmation d’Anthropic.
Réputé pour laisser de nombreuses traces sur son passage, les usages malveillants d’ARTEX avaient même été repérés avant l’affaire coréenne. D’après les équipes de sécurité de Google, des groupes d’extorsion l’utilisaient déjà à la fin du mois d’août, et en septembre, l’institut néerlandais DIVD a été piraté par un agent qui, selon lui, s’appuyait sur l’outil.
Depuis, des groupes liés à Pékin s’en seraient emparés. Toujours selon CrowdStrike, le groupe APT VAPOR PANDA a visé à partir du 17 octobre plus de 200 organisations dans 14 pays en moins de deux semaines, parmi lesquelles des ministères et des opérateurs télécoms, et en a compromis au moins neuf. Microsoft impute de son côté la compromission du service ConnectWise Cloud Backup à Storm-0940, un autre groupe aligné sur la Chine.
Dans le cas de la Commission européenne, le rôle exact d’ARTEX reste à déterminer. Les enquêteurs ne savent pas encore si l’outil a permis l’intrusion ou s’il a seulement servi à repérer des failles, ni si des données du personnel ont été consultées ou volées, et aucun attaquant n’a été nommé.

articles.title: Los nacidos entre 1960 y 1970 pueden cobrar el 100% de la pensión, pero necesitan haber cotizado estos años
articles.text:
Quienes han nacido entre 1960 y 1970 ya no tienen tan lejos la jubilación, y por eso es un buen momento para repasar cuánto aspiran a cobrar y los años cotizados que necesitan para llegar al 100% de la pensión. El número de años cotizados es uno de los factores que más pesan, porque marca tanto la edad a la que puedes retirarte como el porcentaje de la base reguladora que te corresponde.
Si vemos los datos de la edad de jubilación, durante 2026 hacen falta 36 años y seis meses de cotización para cobrar ese 100%, y a partir de 2027 el listón sube a 37 años. Pero cobrar la pensión máxima también depende de las bases por las que hayas cotizado a lo largo de tu vida laboral.
Cuántos años hacen falta para el 100% y para jubilarse a los 65
La pensión se calcula combinando los años cotizados con la base reguladora, que a su vez se obtiene a partir de las bases de cotización del trabajador durante un periodo concreto. Según las tablas de la Ley General de la Seguridad Social, los primeros 15 años cotizados dan derecho al 50% de la base reguladora, y a partir de ahí cada mes adicional va sumando un pequeño porcentaje hasta completar el 100%.
Otra cosa que cuenta es la edad ordinaria de jubilación, que el calendario de la reforma de las pensiones va subiendo poco a poco hasta llegar a los 67 años en 2027 para quienes no acrediten suficiente cotización. Durante 2026 pueden jubilarse a los 65 años los trabajadores que hayan cotizado al menos 38 años y tres meses, mientras que para el resto la edad ordinaria es de 66 años y diez meses.
A partir de 2027 los requisitos quedan así: 65 años para quien acredite al menos 38 años y seis meses cotizados, y 67 años para quien no llegue a ese periodo. Vamos, que hay que distinguir entre los años que te dan el 100% de la base reguladora y los que te permiten jubilarte a los 65, porque son dos requisitos diferentes y cumplir uno no garantiza cumplir el otro.
El nuevo cálculo de la base reguladora y las otras formas de jubilarse
Lo que acabes cobrando depende también de las bases de cotización que hayas ido acumulando. Hasta 2025, el cálculo tenía en cuenta los últimos 25 años de cotización, pero desde 2026 tenemos un sistema dual: la Seguridad Social calcula la base reguladora con las dos fórmulas y aplica de oficio la que resulte más favorable para el trabajador.
¿Y cómo es la fórmula nueva? En 2026 toma las 302 bases más altas de los últimos 304 meses, y ese periodo se va ampliando poco a poco hasta 2037, cuando ya se contarán las 324 mejores bases dentro de un periodo de 29 años, de manera que se podrán descartar los dos años con las cotizaciones más bajas.
Este cambio puede beneficiar a las personas que han tenido etapas con ingresos más bajos o interrupciones a lo largo de su trayectoria laboral, porque esos meses peores pueden acabar quedándose fuera del cálculo.
Otra cosa a tener en cuenta es que llegar al 100% de la base reguladora significa que tienes derecho a cobrar todo el porcentaje que te corresponde según el cálculo de la Seguridad Social, pero no garantiza que vayas a recibir la pensión máxima. Esta depende de las bases de cotización y está sujeta a un límite legal que se actualiza cada año. Por eso dos personas que hayan cotizado exactamente los mismos años pueden acabar cobrando cantidades diferentes.
También hay distintas modalidades de jubilación. Por una parte tienesla jubilación anticipada que te permite dejar de trabajar antes a cambio de reducir permanentemente tu pensión final. Y luego tienes la jubilación parcial, que combina una reducción de la jornada laboral con el cobro de una parte de la prestación.
Existe también la jubilación activa, que permite seguir trabajando mientras se cobra una parte de la pensión, y la jubilación demorada, pensada para quienes deciden alargar su vida laboral más allá de la edad ordinaria y que, según la guía del CSIF, da derecho a incentivos económicos. Para los nacidos entre 1960 y 1970, revisar el historial laboral y las bases de cotización es especialmente importante a la hora de planificar esta etapa, porque de esos años y de esas bases depende tanto cuándo podrán jubilarse como cuánto van a cobrar.

articles.title: Fuite de données chez Chargemap : des millions de conducteurs sont touchés par une cyberattaque
articles.text:
Chargemap prévient tous les conducteurs concernés par mail. Consulté par 01net, le courriel révèle que l’application a été « la cible d’une attaque informatique » le 8 novembre 2026. Une personne non autorisée « a pu accéder à certaines données de comptes utilisateurs ». Pour ceux qui ne connaissent pas, Chargemap est une application française très utilisée par les conducteurs de véhicules électriques. Elle permet de localiser les bornes de recharge, de préparer ses trajets et de payer toutes ses recharges grâce au badge Chargemap Pass. La plateforme revendique plus de 3,5 millions d’utilisateurs. Le nombre de comptes touchés n’a pas été communiqué par l’entreprise originaire de Strasbourg.
À lire aussi : Fuite de données géante à La Poste – « 22 millions de personnes sont concernées » par une cyberattaque massive
Une faille sur une ancienne interface
D’après Chargemap, le pirate a exploité « une faille de sécurité sur une ancienne interface technique de Chargemap pour extraire certaines données de comptes utilisateurs ». Les équipes de l’entreprise ont repéré « une activité anormale » le 10 novembre, soit deux jours après le début de l’attaque. La faille a ensuite été corrigée dès le 12 novembre, quatre jours après la cyberattaque.
Conformément à la loi, Chargemap a ensuite prévenu la CNIL, le gendarme français des données personnelles. L’entreprise a aussi « engagé une procédure de dépôt de plainte » et « déploie des ressources et des mesures de sécurité supplémentaires pour se prémunir contre toute nouvelle attaque de ce type ».
Quelles données ont été volées ?
Pour tous les comptes concernés, le pirate a mis la main sur « votre adresse email, votre nom d’utilisateur et la langue de votre application ». D’autres informations sont touchées, mais « uniquement si vous les aviez renseignées lors de votre inscription », comme le prénom et le nom, le numéro de téléphone, la date de naissance, la ville et le pays, la photo de profil et la date de dernière connexion.
Pour les comptes créés avec un mot de passe, le pirate a pu récupérer « une empreinte ou une version chiffrée de votre mot de passe, et non le mot de passe lui-même ». Concrètement, le mot de passe a été transformé en une suite de caractères illisibles, par mesure de sécurité. Avec l’aide d’algorithmes, les pirates peuvent ensuite récupérer le mot de passe, même si l’opération est incertaine, fastidieuse, et prend du temps. : si votre mot de passe était retrouvé, « son décryptage pourrait aussi permettre à des tiers malveillants de se connecter à vos autres comptes ».
Chargemap reconnaît par ailleurs que les mots de passe des personnes qui ne se sont pas connectées depuis avril 2019 étaient conservés « dans un ancien format, moins robuste ». Même les anciens utilisateurs, qui ont supprimé leur compte, peuvent être concernés par la fuite de données.
L’entreprise se veut toutefois rassurante. L’incident « ne concerne ni vos moyens de paiement, ni votre adresse postale, ni vos recharges (historique, lieux, montants), ni vos factures, ni le numéro (RFID) de votre badge Chargemap Pass ». Néanmoins, Chargemap précise qu’une vingtaine de badges ont bien été touchés. Les détenteurs de ceux-ci seront prévenus individuellement dans les plus brefs délais.
« Quelqu’un pourrait utiliser ces données pour vous envoyer des messages frauduleux qui paraissent crédibles », prévient Chargemap.
Chargemap vient rejoindre la liste des entreprises piratées en France cet automne. Début novembre, le spécialiste de l’entretien automobile Auto Planning a confirmé le piratage de 14 millions de plaques d’immatriculation. Quelques jours plus tard, une filiale de La Poste a été frappée par une cyberattaque massive, touchant 22 millions de personnes.
À lire aussi : Cyberattaque contre Engie – une fuite de données touche les clients en France
Que faire si vous utilisez Chargemap ?
Chargemap recommande de modifier immédiatement votre mot de passe, surtout si vous recyclez celui-ci sur d’autres services. Profitez-en pour choisir un bon mot de passe, composé d’une suite aléatoire de chiffres, de lettres et de caractères spéciaux. Si vous vous connectez uniquement avec Google, Facebook ou Apple, vous n’avez rien à changer.
Restez aussi très « vigilant face aux emails, SMS ou appels se présentant comme Chargemap ». L’entreprise rappelle qu’elle ne vous demandera « jamais votre mot de passe ou vos coordonnées bancaires par email, SMS ou téléphone ». Par ailleurs, les messages émis par l’application proviennent toujours d’une adresse en « @chargemap.com ». Enfin, on vous recommande de consulter régulièrement votre historique de recharges à la recherche de la moindre session recharge inconnue.

articles.title: TSMC Reportedly Reviews Customer Finances, Asks Some Chip Buyers to Pay Upfront
articles.text:
Thursday, November 19th 2026
TSMC Reportedly Reviews Customer Finances, Asks Some Chip Buyers to Pay Upfront
TSMC is reportedly seeking to audit its customers' ability to finance chip allocations, as the company aims to secure funding for its production runs. The report states that TSMC is going as far as obtaining data on customers' financial situations, data center construction stages, and other factors that influence demand assessments. These assessments are then used to propose credit lines based on each company's balance sheet. This evaluation includes collecting information on past debt defaults, the company's position in the industry, and its liquidity. For any orders that exceed the TSMC-imposed credit limit, TSMC requires cash payments for its production runs, with some customers even needing to make upfront payments to secure production capacity. Those who cannot secure a good credit line may pre-pay their production runs to ensure allocation.
With NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang now out of the loop, TSMC is conducting checks with customers to ensure that, in the event of a broader industry shakeup, its production remains well-funded. The reported AI circular financing scheme that the entire industry has been engaging in is net positive for valuations, but TSMC wants to ensure it gets paid first, regardless of the situation. Many chipmakers and startups have been raising capital to access more cash to fund operations, and a significant portion of that will go to TSMC for its production lines. It is important to note that TSMC isn't changing the way it allocates supply. The company is simply protecting the way that allocation is settled, and the old rule of "first come, first served" remains in practice for securing allocation on any node, including leading-edge and upcoming ones.For example, TSMC has been making demand projection estimates based on data center buildouts, so it knows how many wafers its facilities need to produce. For instance, NVIDIA's supply chain commitments include $390 billion in spending through Fiscal Year 2030, and a large portion of that will go to TSMC. This way, TSMC knows that its biggest customer will pay for orders in the years to come, but it also needs reassurance from smaller customers.

articles.title: NASA's new Moon plans have a problem: Orion wasn't designed to fly this way
articles.text:
NASA recently announced a significant shakeup to the Artemis program that will land humans on the Moon.
The moves were designed to give the agency’s lunar lander providers—SpaceX with its Starship vehicle, and Blue Origin with Blue Moon—more flexibility in reaching the Moon. For Starship, this means docking with Orion in Earth orbit, and then traveling to the Moon in tandem. For Blue Moon, it shifts the rendezvous with Orion all the way to low-lunar orbit.
These changes benefit the lunar landers, but in turn impose more of a burden on the Orion spacecraft, which is built for NASA by Lockheed Martin. To understand the implications for the spacecraft, Ars spoke with Kirk Shireman, Human Spaceflight Exploration and Orion program manager at Lockheed.
Starship challenges
For Starship, the evolved plan has SpaceX fueling a Starship lunar lander in low-Earth orbit before docking with Orion in high-Earth orbit. The crew will fly to the Moon on board Orion before two of the four astronauts transfer into Starship for a landing on the Moon.
Due to the docking configuration with Starship, Orion must now fly backward to the Moon, with its Service Module at the top of the stack. This is a fundamentally different flying posture than Orion was designed for, Shireman said, and creates issues for Orion’s propulsion system.
As a result, the Service Module, which is provided by the European Space Agency, will require modifications to its propellant tanks. This is because liquid propellant would move toward the gas inlet side of the tanks, rather than settling in the direction expected during normal operation.
“When you push it the other way, the liquid goes to the gas end of the tank, and you don’t want the liquid in the gas part,” Shireman said. “Bad things can happen to you.” To address this, he said, the European Space Agency and its main contractor, Airbus, are modifying the vehicle’s tanks for Starship lunar missions.

articles.title: 100 Millionen Euro: Telekom investiert in das wertvollste KI-Startup Europas
articles.text:
Telekom steigt bei Mistral ein: 100 Millionen Euro für Europas Antwort auf OpenAI
Die Deutsche Telekom steigt beim größten europäischen KI-Unternehmen Mistral AI ein. Die Konzerntochter T.Capital Tech Fund habe bei einer neuen Finanzierungsrunde 100 Millionen Euro in das französische Startup investiert. Das teilte die Telekom auf Nachfrage mit und sprach von einem ersten Schritt zu einer strategischen Partnerschaft. Zuerst hatte der Spiegel darüber berichtet.
Laut Mitteilung planen die Telekom und Mistral, gemeinsam Unternehmen und den öffentlichen Sektor in Deutschland bei der Einführung passgenauer KI zu unterstützen. Die Zusammenarbeit stütze sich auf Investitionen der Telekom in souveräne KI-Infrastruktur in Deutschland und die wachsende Präsenz von Mistral.
„Die europäische Wettbewerbsfähigkeit hängt davon ab, ob wir leistungsstarke KI entwickeln und einsetzen können“, sagte Telekom-Vorstandsmitglied Ferri Abolhassan. Unternehmen müssten dieser Technologie vertrauen und gleichzeitig die Kontrolle über ihre Daten behalten können.
Telekom verdoppelt KI-Rechenleistung in München
Die Telekom nahm im Februar in München eine KI-Fabrik in Betrieb. Wegen der hohen Nachfrage baut der Konzern den Standort aus. Die Telekom investiert knapp eine weitere Viertelmilliarde Euro in die Fabrik und verdoppelt so die Rechenleistung der Anlage.
Zu den Nutzern zählen namhafte Industrieunternehmen wie Siemens und Daimler Trucks. Die Infrastruktur dient unter anderem dem Training von KI-Sprachmodellen, der Robotik-Entwicklung und der Simulation komplexer Produktionsabläufe.
Mistral sammelte 3 Milliarden Euro für KI-Expansion ein
Erst im September hatte sich das französische KI-Startup Mistral in einer Finanzierungsrunde drei Milliarden Euro gesichert. Die Bewertung des 2023 gegründeten Unternehmens stieg auf über 21 Milliarden Euro – die bislang größte Eigenkapitalfinanzierung eines europäischen Technologieunternehmens überhaupt. Mistral positioniert sich als europäischer Gegenentwurf zu US-Unternehmen wie OpenAI, Google und Anthropic.
Das Startup ist nach eigenen Angaben mittlerweile in 20 Ländern aktiv und unterstützt mehr als 125 Großkunden bei unternehmenskritischen KI-Projekten, darunter Airbus, der niederländische Halbleiterausrüster ASML und die Großbank HSBC. ASML hatte im vergangenen Jahr rund 1,3 Milliarden Euro in Mistral investiert und wurde damit größter Anteilseigner.
Im Juli kündigten der US-Technologiekonzern Microsoft und Mistral an, ihre strategische Allianz auszubauen. Mit einer neuen Vereinbarung über mehrere Milliarden Euro wollen die Partner die europäischen Infrastrukturkapazitäten für Künstliche Intelligenz erweitern und hochmoderne KI-Modelle in sensiblen Unternehmen und Behörden verankern.

articles.title: Pakistan undersea cable fault causes internet failure near Strait of Hormuz — fault detected offshore weeks after Iran threatened infrastructure in the region
articles.text:
Pakistan undersea cable failure causes internet outage near Strait of Hormuz — fault detected offshore weeks after Iran threatened infrastructure in the region
Pakistan's telecommunications authority says that Transworld Associates is looking into what caused the issue and when it expects it to be fixed, but traffic has been rerouted for now.
Pakistan's telecommunications authority, the PTA, has confirmed that internet connectivity issues affecting the country's residents are related to the failure of an international submarine cable. SEA-ME-WE 5 is located almost seven miles off the coast of Pakistan, near the Gulf of Oman and the Strait of Hormuz, and connects the region with European networks via the Middle East. The TWA says that the outage may have caused intermittent connectivity issues and a decline in service quality, with Transworld Associates (TWA) working to identify the cause of the issue. No timeframe has been provided for when a fix will be available yet, but for now, internet traffic has been rerouted to minimize the impact of the outage.
The outage comes weeks after the Islamic Republic of Iran described several undersea fiber cables that run through the Strait of Hormuz as "legitimate new targets" in the ongoing tensions in the area. February's start of military action by the United States, Israel, and others has made the Strait of Hormuz a household name in recent months. General Hossein Mohebbi, a spokesman for Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, pointed out that as many as seven "large cables pass beneath the Strait of Hormuz, and all internet and commercial data pass through them," going on to say they are "legitimate" targets for the group.
Notably, the SEA-ME-WE 5 cable does run through the Strait of Hormuz, although it should be stressed that there is currently no indication that this outage was caused by any act of sabotage. However, that is no doubt something that the TWA investigation will seek to confirm before it can apply whatever fix is necessary to fully restore services for those in the region.
Undersea cables are vital for maintaining connectivity between nations and continents, and Iran isn't the only one to have taken note. A Russian ship was chased from British waters by a Royal Navy attack helicopter earlier this year after it was found less than a mile from five undersea cables. The ship was in the area for 14 hours, and the cables it was near happened to connect the UK with Spain, Portugal, Canada, and the United States.

articles.title: Elegoo's 9K resin 3D printer with AI camera makes miniature printing easy
articles.text:
Elegoo Mars 5 Ultra resin 3D printer deal drops to $259 for Black Friday
A fantastic choice for miniatures and models, and now it’s more affordable
Elegoo's 3D printer line has consistently impressed us during our workshop testing. And when it comes to models and miniatures, its resin 3D printers are worth considering. One I'd recommend is the Elegoo Mars 5 Ultra. It's a good budget to mid-range pick for new starters.
Now, as part of its early Black Friday sale, the company has cut the price of the Elegoo Mars 5 Ultra resin 3D printer to $259 (was $338). That price drop makes the Mars 5 Ultra well worth considering if you want a compact, versatile unit that can handle detailed miniature printing.
The printer uses a 7-inch 9K monochrome LCD, with 18-micron XY resolution and a build volume of 153.36 x 77.76 x 165mm. It also features tilt-release technology and automatic leveling. It produces models at speeds of up to 150mm/h, and includes an AI monitoring camera to improve its automation credentials.
Today’s best Elegoo printer deal
The Mars 5 Ultra is specifically engineered for model and miniature 3D printing. Print speeds are high, as is the 9K resolution, which Elegoo bills as "true-to-life". Features include a smart mechanical sensor and camera monitoring with time-lapse recording to track your printing progress.
Why we recommend the Elegoo Mars 5 Ultra
We've reviewed a number of Elegoo's multi-filament and resin 3D printers, and they've all scored 4 stars and above. While we haven't tested this model, our sister site Tom's Hardware awarded it 4.5 stars and an Editor's Choice award.
The review praised its excellent 9K resolution, built-in camera, and tilt release features, noting that Elegoo had “knocked it out of the park” with an affordable model that’s “practically plug and play”.
Price context and historical value
At $259, you’re saving $79 against the advertised $338 price. The 23% discount is part of Elegoo’s Black Friday promotion, and ends in three days. That's a fair discount
Also note that lots of discounts are available on bundles that add accessories, like resin, post-processing devices, and build plates.
Should you buy it?
✅ Buy the Mars 5 Ultra if… you want an affordable resin printer for miniatures and models that’s easy to use without much hassle
❌ Skip the Mars 5 Ultra if… you need a larger build volume or want to avoid the extra cleaning, curing, and handling involved with resin printing.

articles.title: A “headless Slack”: Vercel’s new message board lets Claude Code and Codex agents work together
articles.text:
A “headless Slack”: Vercel’s new message board lets Claude Code and Codex agents work together
For AI agents to work together effectively, they need a way to communicate and divvy up tasks — much as humans already do through a swath of digital collaboration tools.
Vercel is tackling this with Board, an experimental shared message board through which agents can claim tasks, exchange findings and track progress across different tools and environments, while allowing developers to follow and intervene in the work.
In a blog post published on Wednesday, Vercel says it developed Board for its own engineering operations, first using it to coordinate security agents investigating vulnerabilities and submitting fixes. It then rebuilt v0’s software factory around Board, which Vercel says now “merges over 50% of PRs.”
“It packages what we’ve learned about coordinating work across agent fleets.”
“It packages what we’ve learned about coordinating work across agent fleets and builds towards a future where multiple teams of humans and agents orchestrate swarms, software factories, and other agentic workflows,” the company writes.
The coordination conundrum
OpenAI demonstrated the importance of multi-agent communication in September when it announced that its agents had solved the Navier–Stokes problem, a longstanding mathematical challenge concerning the behavior of fluids.
The company said some 10,000 agents operated concurrently in the group that produced the result, exchanging information as they worked.
“In the process of resolving the Navier–Stokes problem, the agents sent 2.7 million messages and used approximately 130 billion output tokens,” the company wrote.
The need to manage multiple agents in parallel is becoming increasingly apparent in software development. Just last week, Google and Cursor introduced competing approaches to coordinating coding agents, with Google focusing on agents working on behalf of a single developer and Cursor enabling agents belonging to different teammates to communicate.
Then on Tuesday, Replit introduced Missions, bringing multiple agents together to tackle larger development projects.
Elsewhere, companies are also turning to existing collaboration platforms to bring humans and AI agents together. Devin Bots, which Cognition launched on Tuesday, uses Slack to connect agents with their human teammates.
In an X post published on Thursday, Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff says more than 226,000 custom agents have been deployed to Slack from across the major agent-building platforms. Notably, he says that he hadn’t anticipated this use of Slack when Salesforce acquired it back in 2021, acknowledging that companies are now using the platform as “trusted agent infrastructure.”
Vercel itself added its Agent to Slack code channels in August, allowing teammates to follow its work, give instructions and review proposed changes.
With Board, Vercel provides channels and threaded discussions where agents can pick up assignments, exchange findings, monitor dependencies and record completed work. It also maintains a history of activity, allowing developers to follow what their agents have been doing.
Crucially, Board is designed to accommodate agents built on different technologies. Vercel explicitly lists Claude Code, Codex, Pi, OpenCode, eve, fx, Mastra and LangChain, as tools that can work together through Board.
“This is an important building block for software factories, self-optimizing systems, and scientific research.”
In an X post published on Wednesday, Vercel CEO Guillermo Rauch described the technology as a “message board infrastructure primitive.” Or, a “headless Slack” for agents.
“This is an important building block for software factories, self-optimizing systems, and scientific research, where the human prompting is just the seed of the system, and millions of agents can operate in a decentralized fashion,” Rauch writes, adding that Board is designed to work independently of any particular model, agent harness or hosting provider.
“Just bring your agents, give them our CLI, and watch magic happen,” he adds.
Keeping humans in the loop
Board also connects agents to the tools developers already use, including Slack, GitHub and Linear. For example, a developer can submit a request through Slack, which an agent can then pick up and break into smaller assignments for other agents to complete.
The ensuing discussion, task ownership and progress updates are maintained in Board.
As work progresses, Board can synchronize information with GitHub, allowing agents and developers to follow changes to pull requests and review feedback, without having to manually relay information between systems. It also supports event-driven triggers, so agents can resume work when new messages arrive or task statuses change.
It’s worth noting that human oversight remains a crucial part of the process. Agents can report findings and wait for developers to approve changes before proceeding, while Board also provides channel-level permissions that determine which people and agents can access information or perform particular actions.
The security question
The ability of agents to communicate independently raises key questions about who controls those conversations and what information they can exchange.
Indeed, Rauch points to the OpenAI/Hugging Face cybersecurity incident from July as another high-profile example of message boards facilitating agent coordination. During the breach, agents repurposed an internal software repository to exchange findings and coordinate their activities.
“A core part of why we built Vercel Board was to fulfill our own needs for security and auditability.”
Thus, security and oversight are key considerations for systems such as Board. Vercel says it built access controls and activity logs into the service, allowing teams to restrict which agents can interact with particular channels and track their actions.
“A core part of why we built Vercel Board was to fulfill our own needs for security and auditability,” the company writes.
The accompanying documentation also warns that agents may “read messages as instructions,” making it important to control who can post in channels where agents receive tasks. By default, channels are accessible to team members, project deployments and installed apps unless administrators restrict access. Vercel recommends creating private channels or restricting permissions where necessary, and keeping sensitive information such as API keys and tokens off Board entirely.
Vercel Board is available now as an experimental feature on all Vercel plans, accessible through the Vercel CLI or JavaScript SDK. It’s free during the experimental period, though Vercel says it may introduce charges later.

articles.title: Telus Buy One, Give One promo returns for Black Friday
articles.text:
Telus is bringing back its Buy One, Give One promo for Black Friday.
The Vancouver-based national carrier will give a phone through its Mobility for Good program for every phone purchase between Nov. 27 and 29, helping connect youth aging out of government care and others in need.
To qualify, phones must be purchased on a two-year Telus financing plan with a postpaid activation. Like last year, Telus pledged to give up to a maximum of 5,000 phones through the Buy One, Give One program.
In its sixth year, Telus says the Buy One, Give One initiative helps Canadians “shop with purpose,” adding that people can know their purchase helps “bridge digital divides” and keep vulnerable youth, low-income seniors, and families in need connected through free or subsidized rate plans and devices.
To add some context, Mobility for Good is part of Telus’ larger Connecting for Good programs, a series of initiatives launched in 2016. They’re designed to provide connectivity and technology for “those who need it most” by supplying used phones (Mobility For Good), internet (Internet For Good), tablets and computers (Tech For Good), and access to health services (Health for Good) to individuals like in-need families, low-income seniors, and the previously-mentioned youth aging out of care.

articles.text:
Motorola Edge 70 Fusion reaparece por menos da metade do preço na Black November
Edge 70 Fusion tem tela AMOLED 144 Hz e câmera frontal de 32 MP que o destacam entre os celulares abaixo dos R$ 2 mil; desconto é de 53% no Mercado Livre
O Motorola Edge 70 Fusion 5G de 256 GB está saindo por apenas R$ 1.889,10 no Pix na Black November no Mercado Livre. Este desconto de 53% frente ao preço original é quase idêntico a uma oferta boa que encontramos na sexta-feira (dia 13), mas havia acabado.
O Edge 70 Fusion traz como destaques a tela fluida e brilhante, o processador Snapdragon e a câmera de selfies de 32 MP, que o destacam como uma boa opção custo-benefício para um celular nessa categoria de preço.
O Motorola Edge 70 Fusion conta com uma tela AMOLED de 6,78 polegadas que tem como principal destaque a taxa de atualização de 144 Hz, que torna a experiência fluida na troca entre aplicativos e nos gráficos em jogos. Além disso, seu brilho forte de 5.200 nits garante boa visibilidade mesmo luz solar intensa.
No kit de câmeras, a principal de 50 MP conta com estabilização óptica, o que significa fotos nítidas e vídeos sem tremores, mesmo em ambientes escuros. Já a lente para selfies oferece 32 MP, um número grande para um celular abaixo dos R$ 2 mil, e que garante boa qualidade para a edição de fotos e vídeos.
Equipado com o processador Snapdragon 7s Gen 3 e 8 GB de RAM, o celular da Motorola é capaz de rodar jogos e aplicativos de multitarefa sem travamentos. Porém, o sistema operacional só será atualizado até o Android 19, que gera uma desvantagem em relação ao Galaxy A57 na mesma faixa de preço, por exemplo.
A bateria de 5.200 mAh deve garantir uma longa autonomia, e o suporte ao carregamento de 68 W é um diferencial que deve garantir bastante carga mesmo com poucos minutos na tomada. Lembrando que nesta oferta, o Edge 70 Fusion sai por apenas R$ 1.889,10, um bom preço pela ficha técnica.
