articles.title: How Amazon ECS handles blue/green, canary, and linear deployments
articles.text:
How Amazon ECS handles blue/green, canary, and linear deployments
Deploying containers safely at scale can mean assembling your own system: traffic-splitting logic, alarm evaluation, rollback automation, approval gates. It’s infrastructure that exists solely to protect the deployment itself. AWS has built all of those capabilities directly into Amazon Elastic Container Service (ECS), so you don’t have to.
“Deploying containers safely at scale can mean assembling your own system: traffic-splitting logic, alarm evaluation, rollback automation, approval gates. It’s infrastructure that exists solely to protect the deployment itself.”
You can access all these tools through a single API endpoint. AWS built them to work out of the box when you use Amazon ECS as your container orchestration platform with the Amazon ECS deployment controller. As a result, you don’t have to build your own abstractions or learn a new framework to get the deployment behavior you want. Instead, you pick and choose the features you want through a service deployment configuration and update it as your needs change.
How the building blocks map to ECS
If you’ve run progressive delivery on Kubernetes with Argo Rollouts or Flagger, you know the shape of the stack: a controller you install and keep current, analysis wired to your metrics backend, and a traffic provider for weighted canaries. Argo Rollouts approximates canary weights with replica counts and uses an ingress controller, service mesh, or Gateway API for precise percentages. Flagger uses a service mesh or ingress controller for weighted canaries, and plain Kubernetes Services for blue/green. Both are mature open-source projects and a great fit when you want to own and tune every layer. ECS takes a different approach and builds the same capabilities into the service. Here’s a comparison of the different deployment controllers:
| What you need | With Argo Rollouts or Flagger (Kubernetes) | Built into ECS | 
| Deployment strategies | Rolling updates come with Kubernetes Deployments; blue/green and canary come from a controller you install and keep current | Rolling, blue/green, linear, and canary, set in the service’s deployment configuration | 
| Traffic shifting | Argo Rollouts: replica-count weighting by default, or an ingress controller, service mesh, or Gateway API for precise percentages. Flagger: a service mesh or ingress controller for weighted canaries | ECS shifts traffic through your ALB, NLB, ECS Service Connect, or VPC Lattice, or calls your own logic through lifecycle hooks | 
| Health and metric analysis | Analysis templates or built-in checks against your metrics provider (Prometheus, Datadog, CloudWatch, and others) | Deployment circuit breaker plus CloudWatch alarm monitoring | 
| Automatic rollback | The controller aborts and shifts traffic back to the stable version when analysis fails | ECS rolls back on circuit breaker or alarm, and you can pull the cord yourself with the StopServiceDeployment API | 
| Custom checks and approval gates | Webhooks, custom analysis steps, or manual promotion | Lifecycle hooks with Lambda or pause targets, resumed with the ContinueServiceDeployment API | 
When are rolling deployments not enough?
Rolling deployments are where ECS started, and they’re still the right default for most customers. In a rolling deployment, ECS replaces tasks running the old version with tasks running the new one, a batch at a time. New tasks start receiving production traffic as soon as they pass health checks, and ECS stops old tasks as the new ones take over. Two settings, minimumHealthyPercent and maximumPercent, control how many tasks can be replaced at once and how much extra capacity the deployment can use. Rolling deployments work with both the deployment circuit breaker and CloudWatch alarm-based automatic rollback, which we’ll cover below.
So, where’s the gap? Let’s say you have an API service running on ECS behind an ALB. You ship a large refactor. A bug surfaces, but it takes time because of metric emission and alarm-processing delays. By the time your alarm fires, a large share of your tasks (maybe all of them) are already running the new version and serving production traffic. ECS rolls back for you, but in a rolling deployment, rollback means another rollout of the previous task definition: ECS must launch new tasks, pass health checks, and replace the bad ones. Your application’s availability will be exposed for some time.
“There’s a limit to how fast a rolling deployment can roll back, which increases customer impact (measured by failed requests per unit of time) from the new, bad application version.”
So, there’s a limit to how fast a rolling deployment can roll back, which increases customer impact (measured by failed requests per unit of time) from the new, bad application version. Blue/green deployments can shorten the duration of the impact. With ECS’s built-in blue/green strategy, the old version stays running alongside the new one for a configurable bake period (up to 24 hours). All production traffic routes to the new version, but the old version’s tasks remain registered and ready to take traffic with a flip of a switch. If something goes wrong, rollback is a simple traffic shift, and not a complete redeploy.
The tradeoff is that you’re doubling compute capacity during the deployment window. For services where a bad release serving 100% of traffic for even a few minutes is costly, that tradeoff is worth it.
How does ECS know something went wrong?
How would Amazon ECS know when to flip traffic back? There are several ways to perform a service deployment rollback, and they’re all configurable through an ECS service’s deployment configuration:
- Task launch and health state monitoring during a deployment through circuit breaker
- Amazon CloudWatch alarm(s) monitoring and auto-rollback
- Controls to roll back an ongoing service deployment through the StopServiceDeployment API
- Service deployment lifecycle hooks (Lambda or pause target type)
For API server failures, you can set up Amazon CloudWatch alarms to monitor server response codes and trigger a rollback when a high volume of 4xx or 5xx codes is detected. But what if your application monitoring constructs are outside of Amazon CloudWatch and stored on another service like Datadog, Splunk, or Grafana? With service deployment lifecycle hooks, you can implement your own automation that polls these data sources for alarm data by implementing that logic in a Lambda function and configuring a Lambda target type. The primary consideration is configuring the lifecycle hook for the POST_PRODUCTION_TRAFFIC_SHIFT stage.
If you can’t use Lambda functions, then implement an Amazon EventBridge trigger with a pause hook target type instead. Amazon ECS will send an Amazon EventBridge event when the service deployment reaches the lifecycle stage configured for the lifecycle hook. The trigger should fire a process you own that runs the same polling loop to monitor an alarm or metric. Once the monitoring condition succeeds, call the ContinueServiceDeployment API to allow the service deployment to progress.
In addition to alarms and lifecycle hooks, the service deployment circuit breaker monitor can stop a bad deployment from progressing. This deployment monitor looks for failed or unhealthy tasks during a service deployment and compares the sum against a threshold. With configurable circuit breaker settings, you can customize the counter algorithm to ignore intermittent task launch or health failures. You can also customize the failure threshold based on your application’s needs.
Advanced deployment strategies
The example above is just one way to use built-in ECS features to customize your service deployment. If a one-step traffic shift isn’t suitable for your application, linear and canary deployments are also alternatives.
Linear and canary deployments are like blue/green deployments in that they use well-defined traffic-shift steps to isolate application traffic between versions. Linear deployments move traffic in equal increments based on your configuration. Canaries are a little different in that there is a two-step migration in application traffic as opposed to n number of incremental shifts.
Not advanced enough? There’s more!
All the deployment tools we talked about today apply to all deployment strategies that ECS supports. Similarly, all deployment strategies are compatible with ECS Service Connect and VPC Lattice network integrations. The only caveat is that lifecycle hooks can be applied to only two stages for a rolling deployment, since that lifecycle is inherently simpler than blue/green, linear, or canary deployments.
“All deployment strategies also work without a load balancer, ECS Service Connect, or VPC Lattice integration! That’s right, even blue/green, linear, and canary deployments.”
All deployment strategies also work without a load balancer, ECS Service Connect, or VPC Lattice integration! That’s right, even blue/green, linear, and canary deployments. We developed these service deployment lifecycle hooks with customization in mind, so we created specific integration points to shift your application traffic. You can control the behavior by writing your own logic, and Amazon ECS invokes a lifecycle hook at the production traffic-shift stage. Just note that this stage takes a Lambda target, since pause hooks can’t be configured there.
Which strategy should you pick?
Here’s the short version of everything above:
| Your situation | Reach for | What you get | What it costs | 
| Most everyday changes, or cost-sensitive services | Rolling with circuit breaker and alarms | Automatic rollback on failed tasks or alarms, and you can tune minimumHealthyPercent and maximumPercent so you’re not paying for a second copy of your service | Rollback is a redeploy, so the bad version serves traffic until it’s replaced | 
| A bad release is expensive, and you need an instant way back | Blue/green | Old version stays warm through the bake period; rollback is a traffic shift | Double compute capacity during the deployment window | 
| You want production signal from a small slice before full exposure | Canary | A small share of traffic hits the new version first, then the rest moves in a second step | Same capacity tradeoff as blue/green, and a slower rollout | 
| You want exposure to grow steadily and catch load-dependent issues | Linear | Traffic moves in equal increments, with a chance to roll back at each step | Same capacity tradeoff, and the longest rollout | 
| Your monitoring lives outside CloudWatch (Datadog, Splunk, Grafana) | Blue/green, linear, or canary, plus lifecycle hooks at the post-production traffic shift stage (rolling supports hooks too, at fewer stages) | Your own checks gate the deployment through Lambda or pause targets | Code you write and own | 
| You don’t use a load balancer, Service Connect, or VPC Lattice | Blue/green, linear, or canary, plus a Lambda lifecycle hook at the production traffic shift stage | ECS calls your logic to shift your own traffic | Code you write and own | 
Pick a strategy
Whichever deployment strategy you choose, the guardrails (alarms, circuit breaker, lifecycle hooks, and rollback) come with the service. Configure them once, and spend your engineering time on your product, not your pipeline.
Pick one service, turn on blue/green with a CloudWatch alarm, and see for yourself. The Amazon ECS lifecycle hooks guide is a good next step once you want custom checks.

articles.title: Protect agent tool calls with Skyflow and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Protect agent tool calls with Skyflow and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway
In this post, we show how Skyflow and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway keep sensitive data out of the tools your AI agents call, and out of the model context those tools feed. We add Skyflow Detect to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway as a request and response interceptor. The Skyflow interceptor de-identifies data before it reaches a tool, restores it before the agent reads the result, and replaces documents with clean copies before the agent opens them. Your agents and tools don’t change.
Skyflow is available in AWS Marketplace, and the interceptor is open source on GitHub.
Agents act through tools, and tools move data
Agents have moved from answering questions to taking action, and they take action through tools: Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, SaaS APIs, document stores, and web search. Every agent tool call is a data flow. Most enterprise controls cover what goes into and comes out of the model. Far fewer cover what an agent sends to its tools or what those tools send back.
That gap shows up in three ways:
- Sensitive data leaves through tool arguments. The model writes the arguments from everything in its context, including details the tool doesn’t need. Ask an agent about a customer, and the customer’s name, account number, or email goes straight into a query to a third-party server. That server sits outside your AWS account and your compliance scope.
- Sensitive data comes back in tool results. Scraped web pages, CRM records, and case notes land in the model’s context, memory, traces, and logs. This happens even when the task never needed them.
- Documents bypass text inspection. Document tools such as Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), Box, and Google Drive return a signed URL, not text. A filter that inspects strings sees a link and lets it through, and the agent then opens the original file.
Patching each agent doesn’t scale across teams and frameworks, and it can’t reach third-party tools. The controls need to sit where every tool call passes, so authorization, content safety, and data protection apply the same way to every agent and tool.
AgentCore Gateway is that place. It fronts every tool an agent uses, whatever framework or model the agent runs on. It does more than route that traffic. With AgentCore Gateway interceptors, you can run your own code, as an AWS Lambda function, on every call that passes through it. A request interceptor sees each call before it reaches a tool, and a response interceptor sees each result before it reaches the agent. Either one can inspect the payload, rewrite it, or block the call. That makes the gateway a natural place to add data protection alongside Policy and Guardrails. This single control, attached once, covers every agent and every tool behind the gateway, without any change to agent or tool code.
Example: A dispute-resolution agent at a large European bank
Consider a large European bank with retail and corporate banking operations and strict data-residency obligations. Its operations teams are adopting agents to investigate card disputes.
An analyst asks the agent to look into a disputed transaction. The agent searches the web for the merchant, then pulls the dispute case note from Amazon S3 to summarize it. Without protection, three things happen:
- The model builds the search query from everything in context. The search provider receives ‘Mateo Jackson dispute AnyCompany Electronics London’. That’s the customer’s name, sent to a third party, for a search that only needed the merchant.
- Scraped merchant pages bring unrelated personal data into the model’s context.
- The agent reads the original case note, with the customer’s full name, email, phone number, and card details.
With the Skyflow interceptor on the gateway, the same workflow plays out differently:
- The search provider receives ‘[NAME_AJbrIud] dispute AnyCompany Electronics London’, where [NAME_AJbrIud] is a reversible vault token. The merchant results come back the same, the provider never learns who the customer is, and the analyst still sees the real name in the agent’s answer.
- Web content reaches the model already de-identified.
- The agent only ever receives a link to a de-identified copy of the case note.
Solution overview
The Skyflow interceptor is a single AWS Lambda function attached to both of the AgentCore Gateway interception points:
- REQUEST runs before the gateway calls a tool.
- RESPONSE runs after the tool answers and before the agent sees the result.
At each point, it calls Skyflow Detect to find sensitive entities such as names, email addresses, phone numbers, government IDs, card numbers, dates of birth, and locations. It replaces them with tokens, or restores the originals. Skyflow Vault stores the original values so authorized systems can reverse the tokens.
The Skyflow gateway configuration decides, for each tool, which of three protection modes applies: Shield the tool, Shield the model, and Shield the document.
| Mode | What happens | Who sees real data | How it works | Typical use | 
| Shield the tool | Sensitive values are stripped from arguments on the way out and restored in results on the way back | The agent and user, not the tool | Uses reversible vault tokens, so values the tool echoes back are restored before the agent reads them | Web search, enrichment, and third-party APIs that don’t need customer identity to do their job | 
| Shield the model | Prompts, history, files and tool results are de-identified before the model reads them. The answer is re-identified on the way back | Agent and user, not the model | Model calls go through the gateway’s inference endpoint. On the way back, only the tokens minted for that call are restored | Customer conversations, scraped web content, cross-Region or third-party models | 
| Shield the document | The file’s signed URL is swapped for one pointing to a de-identified copy | No one on the agent side | Skyflow Detect v2 (preview) fetches the file, cleans it and stores the copy in an approved Region. The file never passes through Lambda, so payload limits don’t cap file size | Case notes, statements, contracts in Amazon S3, Box, Google Drive | 
Four properties matter in production:
- No change to agents or tools. Agents discover the gateway and sign requests with their AWS Identity and Access Management (AWS IAM) role as before. To shield the model, the agent points its model client at the gateway’s inference endpoint. The interceptor is otherwise invisible to them.
- Configuration without redeploys. The policy sets the direction, entity types, and token type (reversible vault tokens or one-way tokens) per server and per tool. It lives in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store, and changes take effect without redeploying.
- Fail closed. If de-identification can’t complete, the call is withheld rather than sent in the clear. The interceptor fetches files only from allowlisted locations, and it blocks traffic it can’t inspect rather than passing it silently.
- Operations built on AWS. The Skyflow API key lives in AWS Secrets Manager. Every decision is logged to Amazon CloudWatch, with metrics for alarms, and the interceptor never logs credentials or original values.
Architecture
The reference architecture shows where each component sits. The three walkthroughs after it follow a single tool call through the Shield the tool and Shield the document modes.
The following diagram shows how the interceptor sits between AgentCore Gateway and your tools.
The flow:
- The agent calls a tool through AgentCore Gateway, signed with its IAM role.
- The REQUEST interceptor matches the tool against the policy and, where required, de-identifies the arguments with Skyflow Detect.
- The gateway calls the tool, which receives tokens instead of sensitive values.
- The RESPONSE interceptor re-identifies the result, de-identifies it, or swaps a document URL, as the policy requires.
- The agent receives the result.
The agent runs on AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Alongside that flow, the interceptor reads its policy from Parameter Store and its Skyflow API key from Secrets Manager, and it logs each decision to Amazon CloudWatch. It calls Skyflow Detect and Skyflow Vault in an approved Region to de-identify and re-identify data. The targets sit outside the gateway: a third-party web search MCP server, a case-note store in Amazon S3, and a model in Amazon Bedrock that the gateway reaches through an inference target. For model calls, the interceptor keeps a short-lived record in Amazon DynamoDB of which tokens each call minted, so it restores only those. The record holds no original values. For documents, Skyflow Detect fetches the file directly through a presigned URL, so the file bytes never pass through Lambda.
Walkthrough: Shield the tool
This is the web search from the dispute example, step by step. The customer’s name leaves as a token and comes back as the real value, so the search provider never sees it and the analyst still does.
Walkthrough: Shield the model
This is the analyst asking the agent to draft a reply to the customer. The customer’s name and email address reach the model as tokens, and the draft comes back with the real values in place.
Walkthrough: Shield the document
This is the case-note request. The interceptor never handles the file itself. It checks the presigned URL and hands it to Skyflow Detect, which returns a link to a clean copy.
Here is the case note as stored in Amazon S3, beside the copy the agent receives:
A token like [NAME_AJbrIud] is a vault token, which an authorized user can reverse through Skyflow. A token like [NAME_1] is a one-way counter that nothing can reverse.
The following video shows Shield the document end to end. The agent asks for the dispute case note and receives a link to a de-identified copy instead of the original.
Video 1: Shield the document in action. Without Skyflow, the agent reads the original case note. With Skyflow on the gateway, it reads a de-identified copy.
How it fits with the rest of AgentCore
The interceptor complements the controls AgentCore and Amazon Bedrock already provide:
- Policy in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore authorizes what agents can do, using Cedar and Dogwood. It goes beyond deciding whether a principal can call a tool. It can base decisions on earlier actions in the agent’s trajectory, control access to agents and models, stop specific arguments from being sent to specific tools, and check the data passing through the gateway using Amazon Bedrock Guardrails. Skyflow works alongside Policy. When Policy allows a call, Skyflow swaps the sensitive values in it for reversible tokens, so the call goes through without exposing real data to the tool or model. Policy decides what an agent may do, and Skyflow controls how sensitive data is handled when it does.
- Amazon Bedrock Guardrails handle content safety and sensitive information redaction for model interactions. Skyflow adds vault-backed tokenization and document de-identification to the same gateway. Use them together for layered protection across every model and tool call.
- AgentCore Identity, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and AWS IAM stay as they are. The interceptor adds no credentials for agents to manage.
- AgentCore Observability, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and Amazon CloudWatch record interceptor decisions alongside gateway traces.
Deploying the solution
The Skyflow interceptor is open source in the agentcore-skyflow repository on GitHub under the MIT license. Skyflow is available in AWS Marketplace. To add the interceptor to a gateway you already run:
- Subscribe to Skyflow in AWS Marketplace, create a vault, and store its API key in AWS Secrets Manager.
- Deploy the interceptor stack from the repository with the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK). It creates the Lambda function, its policy parameter, a DynamoDB table for model-call records, and the Amazon CloudWatch metrics and alarms.
- Attach the interceptor to your gateway at both interception points. A script in the repository does this and grants the gateway role permission to invoke only that function. If you manage the gateway with AWS CloudFormation or the AWS CDK, declare the interceptor there instead, so later stack updates keep it.
- To shield the model, add an inference target to the gateway and point the agent’s model client at the gateway’s inference endpoint.
The repository also contains the complete reference deployment from this post, including the agent, the gateway, and its targets, which you can deploy with the AgentCore CLI, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.
There are five ways in:
- Existing gateways. Attach the interceptor to a gateway you already run. Agents and tools stay as they are.
- New agents. Put tools behind AgentCore Gateway from day one.
- MCP servers outside AWS. Front them as gateway MCP server targets so their traffic passes through the interceptor.
- Document stores. Tools that return signed URLs are covered by adding their location to the policy’s allowlist.
- Model calls. Add an inference target and send the agent’s model calls through the gateway.
Skyflow offers several vault deployment models and Region choices to meet residency requirements. See Skyflow deployment models.
Considerations
- Formats. Text and Office formats (TXT, JSON, CSV, XML, JSONL, DOCX, XLSX, and PPTX) keep reversible vault tokens. PDFs and images are fully de-identified but receive one-way tokens, so the original values can’t be restored from those files.
- Availability. String de-identification and re-identification are generally available. Document de-identification through signed URLs uses Skyflow Detect v2, which is in preview. AgentCore Gateway availability varies by AWS Region. Before you deploy, check Supported AWS Regions in the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore documentation.
- Document size and latency. Document de-identification is bounded by design. The interceptor checks file size before submitting, so a file above your configured limit is refused immediately rather than timing out. Files within the limit complete within the connection window AgentCore Gateway allows. De-identification time scales with document size, so set the size limit to match your documents. Skyflow Detect v2 is in preview. Validate latency against your own workloads and Region during a pilot, before you widen the rollout.
Conclusion
Agents are only as trustworthy as the data they move. With AgentCore Gateway and the Skyflow interceptor, you can enforce a privacy control at the one place every tool call passes through. It works in both directions, covers documents and text, and needs no change to agent code.
Where to start
- Pick one agent workflow that touches customer data and calls at least one tool outside your account.
- List the entity types that must never leave, and the tools allowed to see them.
- Deploy the interceptor from the GitHub repository and attach it to that workflow’s gateway.
- Start with Shield the tool. Then add Shield the document for your document store, and Shield the model once the agent’s model calls go through the gateway.
- Watch the interceptor’s CloudWatch metrics for a week before widening the rollout.
- If you have further questions, see the Skyflow SDK documentation.

articles.title: Anthropic hits Nasdaq exchanges at $111, 33% above IPO price | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Shares of Anthropic are now trading on the Nasdaq exchange, as the company successfully executes its initial public offering. In the early minutes of availability, shares were trading at $111.50, a 33% premium over the $83 IPO price.
Set on Wednesday, the IPO price was already higher than the projected range set by the company, which anticipated a price between $70 and $78 per share. All told, the offering will raise over $81 billion, directed to a combination of employees and the company’s own coffers.
The IPO funding, together with existing fundraising and new private offerings timed to coincide with the company’s public market debut, will leave Anthropic with an expected $220 billion in cash reserves. As one analyst told TechCrunch, “Anthropic’s going to have more cash on hand than any company has ever had.”
The share price continues to fluctuate, but the opening price would put the company’s market cap over $2 trillion, making it more valuable than Meta, Tesla, or Walmart. Only five companies boast a higher valuation by market cap: Apple, Amazon, Alphabet, Nvidia, and Microsoft.
In a speech before the opening bell, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei emphasized the company’s commitment to safety. “Today puts the company in a stronger financial position, and in doing so, only strengthens our resolve to do the right thing,” Amodei said. “If we can show it’s possible to make the right choices on safety and still build an incredibly successful company, others in our industry will be inspired to do the same. We call this a race to the top.”

articles.title: AI infrastructure economics favor Vultr's global footprint - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Sovereignty is the AI story everyone mentions and few have planned for ahead of 2027
AI infrastructure economics are entering a more sober phase as enterprises move past standing up AI factories and start asking how to run them profitably. Durability, real demand and long-term value are now the tests separating lasting providers from the froth.
That shift rewards cloud providers with an operating track record rather than a single speculative wager. Vultr has extended its global cloud to AI with chips from Nvidia Corp. and Advanced Micro Devices Inc. Enterprises are now making a flight to quality toward stable, cost-efficient platforms, according to Kevin Cochrane (pictured), chief marketing officer of Vultr.
“We’re seeing now not speculative bets in the buildout of AI infrastructure. We’re seeing real bets based on proven economics, proven ROI that people are looking to achieve,” Cochrane said. “What I think is going to wind up happening is a maturation of our industry leveraging this open stack.”
Cochrane spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how AI infrastructure economics favor a global footprint and why sovereignty requirements reach well beyond national governments. (* Disclosure below.)
AI infrastructure economics favor a global footprint
Vultr now operates 34 cloud data center regions, the latest a new region in Chennai, India. That footprint was built to keep cloud-native applications close to users, and inference follows the same logic, Cochrane explained. Agents make fast turns back to reasoning models, so CPUs and GPUs must sit together near the edge, he noted.
“This is kind of what Vultr was built for, which is one global platform, not isolated islands of data centers that are serving a bespoke customer. It is a true global cloud platform,” Cochrane said.
Sovereignty adds another constraint, and it reaches well beyond national governments. A global insurer tuning an open-source model for credit risk needs training clusters in each country because the underlying data cannot cross borders, Cochrane noted. Regulators are already tightening the rules, as the U.S. Commerce Department’s new curbs on remote chip access show.
“The way you have to post-train a model for credit risk in the U.K. versus Germany versus Singapore versus the United States, it’s going to be different,” Cochrane said. “It uses different data.”

articles.title: How to tell a cyberattack from a plain old outage
articles.text:
Yet there’s still no evidence that any one of these clustered technological failures were related, much less caused by hackers. Their improbable, sequential timing left Americans anxiously doomscrolling for signs of foul play. But in cases like these, it’s the job of cybersecurity analysts (and reporters at WIRED) to determine—vibes aside—whether the latest tech outage was actually an accident or the result of a cyberattack.
The baseline for that fact-finding, as anyone tasked with investigating these incidents will tell you, is that the vast majority of these digital breakdowns are not the result of malicious intent but rather casualties of IT admins’ constant war to keep computer systems from collapsing under the weight of their own complexity.
“I’ve just seen enough times where we thought maybe it’s a cyberattack and it turns out it’s not. Sometimes it will be, but typically not,” says Matthew Prince, CEO of the Internet infrastructure company Cloudflare. “Right now, most of what we’re seeing is the standard background noise. Stuff breaks, and that’s just the nature of complex systems.”
So in the interest of soothing the country’s rattled nerves and helping us all find ground truth amid seemingly endless tech catastrophes, we at WIRED present our general guide to determining whether a tech outage is the result of a cyberattack. So take a breath—maybe open the bunker door to let in some fresh air—and read on.
1. Start with a presumption of innocence–or negligence
The process of determining the cause of an IT service outage should begin with the assumption that it was an accident, says cybersecurity researcher Doug Madory.
As the head of Internet analysis at the network security firm Infoblox, Madory says he monitors as many as a dozen network outages a day. Only around “one in a thousand,” he says, turns out to have been caused by hackers. “One’s default position should be that it isn’t a cyberattack,” he says, “unless there is some concrete evidence to the contrary.”
Given the rarity of cyberattacks compared to outages as a whole, it’s wise to look at other potential causes first. “Most big outages that look like attacks are self-inflicted,” says João Tomé, the Internet research editor at network data company IPinfo. (In response to WIRED’s questions, Tomé also wrote his own guide for distinguishing outages from cyberattacks.) The usual suspects, he says, include “a bad update, a configuration change, a cable cut, or a power failure.”
2. Look at status updates from organizations that might be involved
In the scramble to understand what’s really happening with a given outage, it can sometimes be difficult to tell which sites and services are actually down. And there can be a few reasons for this muddled picture. Sometimes, an outage occurs within a foundational service like a big cloud provider. Major downtime within Amazon Web Services, for example, can cause a cascade of other failures among the company’s customers, who are all dependent on that infrastructure.
In other cases, multiple services can seem to be having outages and producing errors but are functioning normally and only having problems when they interact with an entity that’s down. This appears to have been the case in this week’s bank outage: Multiple banks appeared to be having issues, but they all seem to have been linked to certain inter-institutional transactions that involved JPMorgan Chase. Another good example of this scenario is situations where it may appear that multiple wireless carriers are struggling, but all of the failed calls actually involve one network that’s having an outage.
On top of these, there are also scenarios where one or more large services are down, and false (typically accidental or anecdotal) reports of additional outages create further confusion and opacity.
It can all feel overwhelming, even impossible, to attempt to parse these situations yourself—but there is a concrete place to start. If you think a website or service from a major tech company may be down, look for acknowledgment of the situation on their verified social media accounts or in the “newsroom” press release section of their websites. And keep in mind that you can find these pages and social media accounts through search engines, so you definitely don’t need to be familiar with every company’s communications strategy. Use this same approach for government agencies and other institutions.
Another concrete and vital source of information that you can find through search engines is what’s often known as “status dashboard” pages. Large digital platforms specifically offer these informational pages to provide transparency into whether different components of their service are functioning normally or dealing with issues. In a major incident, companies often thread incremental updates about system restoration on the status dashboard. AWS, Google Cloud Platform, and Microsoft Azure all offer these landing pages, and there are similar ones for other services like Meta business products, Google Workspace, telecom companies, AI companies, and so on.
3. Check trusted sources of network data
When a cascading tech failure causes outages across many services at once, and the point of failure isn’t clear, sources of network data that monitor the Internet at a broad scale can also help determine the underlying issue. Amanda Meng, a research scientist at Georgia Tech who helps run its Internet Outage Detection and Analysis service, or IODA, points to not only IODA’s own data—and its social media accounts on BlueSky and Mastodon—but also tools like Cloudflare Radar and Watch the Net. Infoblox’s Madory also posts his own findings about network outages on his socialmediaaccounts.
When IODA sees evidence of a network disruption, “we’ll look at the timing of it, the start, the end, the network affected, anything we can find out about it, and then try and connect it with what we see from reporting,” Meng says. That scope, location, and timing of an outage can help determine a suspected cause, whether it’s a single network that might be the victim of a buggy update, a region cut off by damage to a fiber optic cable or, in rarer instances, a cyberattack or even a government purposefully cutting off Internet access to its citizens to stifle protests.
Even with those network clues, however, Meng advises returning to step two: Once an affected service is identified, its actual owners are often the best source to monitor for updates. “Usually the operators have the most information about what’s actually going on,” she says.
4. Look for claims of responsibility
Most often, mea culpa updates from companies or government agencies confirm an outage is caused by a tech mishap. In the rarer cases when that downtime results from an actual cyberattack or hacker breach, however, the hackers responsible often claim responsibility in some form.
Ransomware gangs, perhaps the most common source of serious malicious Internet disruption, publicize their breaches on dark web pages that list their targets for the purposes of extortion, sometimes with a countdown timer designed to pressure victims to pay before they leak stolen information. In other cases, like the NotPetya or WannaCry worms—two of the worst cyberattacks in history—the hackers’ self-perpetuating code left behind ransom messages on machines that quickly spread on social media as the attacks unfolded. Ideological “hacktivist” groups—or state-sponsored hackers working for military or intelligence agencies but posing as hacktivists—also often take credit for their cyberattacks on platforms like X, Telegram, or their own websites. These messages then quickly spread to social media and through news reports.
Even these statements, however, should be taken as just another significant data point: Hacker groups exaggerate, misdirect, or lie when it serves their purposes. And some significant mass hacking incidents—such as the Mirai attack on the Internet infrastructure company Dyn in 2016 that took down thousands of websites—have been accompanied by no public message at all from the hackers responsible.
In cases where neither the perpetrator of a hacking incident nor its target has confirmed the attack, confirmation can sometimes come first from a government agency—such as the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency—or even from threat intelligence researchers at private cybersecurity firms. Government and industry investigators sometimes post their findings to their websites or share them with media, but it often takes days, weeks, or even months to come to confirmed conclusions. Hence, step five.
5. Sit tight and reserve judgment
If all these other measures of determining the cause of an outage don’t offer a clear understanding of the situation, the best approach may be patience. “It’s going to get a little conclusive at some point,” Madory says. “Sometimes you just have to just sit and wait.”
Aside from the time it takes for companies to admit to their screwups—or hackers to claim a win—the length of an outage can also sometimes offer a clue to its cause. A faulty update, power outage, or cascading bug can often be resolved quickly. Determined hackers who have maximized their damage, who shift tactics to outsmart defenders, or who may still be in a network they’ve breached can cause far longer and more severe outages. “A rollback takes minutes or hours,” Tomé says, referring to reverting to older code as a fix for a faulty update that introduces a bug. “Ransomware takes days or sometimes even weeks.”
In other words, as with all breaking news, when facts are in short supply, it’s better to maintain skepticism about early rumors or conspiracy theories and wait for more concrete evidence.
In the information vacuum that precedes that evidence, it can be easy to see connections between events that may just be coincidences. What are the odds, you may ask, that five major IT outages occurred on a sequential Thursday, Friday, Monday, and Tuesday?
For Doug Madory, who tracks those network outages every day of the week, that string of failures may just be a sign of the increasing complexity of technology—and how fundamentally our civilization has come to depend on it. “For better or worse, modern society is completely mediated through Internet-based services. They have outages from time to time. And that’s a reality I don’t think we’ll ever completely eliminate,” Madory says.
“If you’re immersed in that world of looking at outages for years on end, then they don’t really surprise you,” he adds. “You just try to understand what’s different about each one. And maybe what we can learn from it.”

articles.title: Silicon Motion demos SM8466 PCIe 6.0 SSD controller, expected to ship by 2028 — controller boasts improved quality of service, samples imminent
articles.text:
Silicon Motion demos SM8466 PCIe 6.0 SSD controller, expected to ship by 2028 — controller boasts improved quality of service, samples imminent
SM8466 taped out, sampling imminent.
Silicon Motion is showing off its PCIe 6.0 SSD controller for data center applications for the first time at the SC26 conference in Chicago. The final iteration of Silicon Motion's SM8466 controller was taped out recently, and drives based on the chip are due in late 2027 or early 2028. However, the new controller also has a secret weapon designed to ensure consistent performance of SSDs under concurrent workloads that may set it apart from competitors.
The new controller
Silicon Motion introduced its high-end MonTitan SM8466 enterprise SSD controller designed for next-generation data center and hyperscale storage applications at FMS 2025. The controller features a PCIe 6.x x4 host interface and 16 NAND channels to enable sequential transfer speeds of up to 28 GB/s, random performance of up to 7 million 4K IOPS, and capacities of up to 512 TB and beyond as newer 3D NAND devices emerge. Just like other high-end data center-grade SSD controllers released in recent years, the SM8466 complies with NVMe 2.0 and OCP NVMe 2.5 SSD specifications.
To improve performance and reduce latency, Silicon Motion has developed its Separate Command Architecture (SCA), which separates command and address transmission paths within the NAND interface to improve parallelism and increase effective throughput. Additionally, the controller supports Silicon Motion's 2nd Generation PerformaShape technology, which enables programmable performance limits and predictable quality of service (QoS) across concurrent workloads, which is arguably its most important differentiator against rivals who rely on different methods of guaranteeing performance.
In addition to its performance chops, the MonTitan SM8466 incorporates advanced error correction, virtualization, data protection, and security features. The controller's error correction engine supports low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes with 4KiB codewords and Silicon Motion's 16KiB Collaborative Codeword (CoCo) technology to improve data integrity and reliability with advanced NAND flash memory. The controller also supports Single Root I/O Virtualization (SR-IOV), MPF virtualization, SMART diagnostics, and comprehensive data protection mechanisms. Security capabilities include Secure Boot, AES-256 encryption, TCG Opal compatibility, and firmware attestation. Together, these features make the SM8466 suitable for high-capacity data center drives that are expected to deliver high performance, predictable latency, and reliable operation under demanding data center workloads.
The tactical advantage
Silicon Motion's 2nd Generation PerformaShape technology builds upon the original PerformaShape architecture introduced with the company's PCIe 5.0-based MonTitan SM8366 enterprise SSD controller several years ago. The 1st Generation implementation uses dedicated hardware accelerators and two-stage leaky-bucket regulators to control read and write performance in terms of IOPS and throughput, both for individual workloads and for the SSD as a whole. This approach enables data center operators to prevent one workload from monopolizing SSD resources at the expense of others.
PerformaShape 2 retains these capabilities but doubles the number of supported quality-of-service (QoS) sets from 256 to 512 and introduces more sophisticated performance controls to accommodate a larger number of concurrent workloads with different requirements. One of the key additions to PerformaShape 2 is Multi-Dimensional Shaping, which enables the controller to coordinate performance limits across multiple I/O characteristics rather than enforce each limit independently. This gives data center operators greater flexibility when allocating SSD resources among applications with different performance requirements.
Another important enhancement of PerformaShape 2 is support for NVMe TP4176, a proposed extension to the NVMe specification that aims to standardize performance management and QoS controls. Whereas the original PerformaShape relies on Silicon Motion's vendor-specific NVMe commands and a dedicated host driver, TP4176 could eventually enable compatible host software to configure performance policies through a standardized mechanism. The technology is particularly relevant for cloud environments where SSDs serve numerous virtual machines, containers, and applications whose storage requirements can change considerably over time, according to the company.
Anton Shilov is a contributing writer at Tom’s Hardware. Over the past couple of decades, he has covered everything from CPUs and GPUs to supercomputers and from modern process technologies and latest fab tools to high-tech industry trends.

articles.title: Your small business could lose out on Black Friday business if your website isn’t resilient enough — here's what you need to know
articles.text:
Your small business could lose out on Black Friday business if your website isn’t resilient enough — here's what you need to know
Is your business ready for Black Friday?
- Many small retailers are not equipped to handle traffic spikes on Black Friday, study claims
- Network Solutions finds over 60% of US business websites crashed during a sale in the past year
- 31% haven’t begun preparations for the extra traffic likely during Black Friday 2026
Black Friday could turn out to be a damp squib for smaller business websites – or worse, according to new research from Network Solutions.
Its survey of 507 online store owners has found that while 61% saw their sites crash during a sale or traffic spike in the past year, 31% still haven’t made preparations for Black Friday 2026, or the possibility of a repeat (under) performance.
A site slowdown doesn’t just make it difficult to browse the catalogue and add items to your cart. These issues – often due to inadequate or unsuitable hosting – can prevent a successful checkout, leaving businesses missing out on valuable orders.
Traffic surge
The research has uncovered where the failures occurred, and how long it took for the sites to recover, exploring the impact of a traffic surge on a small business website with an attached store. These are typically built using Woocommerce, although in-house options are also in use. But the end-product is typically the same – sites load too slowly (50%), and crash (21%).
Further exploration into the reasons for the crashes yields few surprises. Owners blamed too much traffic (64%), and hitting the limits of their hosting (19%). Responses that indicated a subject with better awareness of their web host’s capabilities believed the site itself was out of date (11%). Interestingly, 60% believed their site was able to handle a traffic surge, but 56% actually reported their site failing during one.
Some surveyed for the research felt that the hosting plan or the server was responsible for their site’s crash (31%). Only 22% blamed the payment gateway, although multiple factors typically affect these platforms.
Reduce the load
While a popular site might seem like a positive, traffic surges during sale periods can have an immediate financial impact. Payment can fail (25%) and errors occur at checkout (20%). While shopping cart software and web hosting has become more resilient over the years, these risks still exist.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
Immediate solutions include exploring what hosting upgrade options are available. A modern hosting platform will typically offer short-term upgrades to plans, affording more performance and accommodating traffic spikes. But other options may already be available within hosting plans, such as enabling caching to reduce load on the server’s resources.
Any business concerned about the impact of Black Friday traffic surges on their ability to trade during the popular sale period should be taking steps to ensure their store remains online.

articles.title: Teilt Metas KI-Agent Muse Informationen aus fremden Chats?
articles.text:
Sicherheitsprobleme bei Metas KI-Agent: Teilt Muse Informationen aus fremden Chats?
Anfang September 2026 hatte Meta mit Muse einen persönlichen KI-Agenten vorgestellt. Der Start erfolgte zunächst nur in den USA. Die App verzeichnet mittlerweile mehr als zehn Millionen Downloads. Intern sorgt der KI-Agent aber für Unruhe.
Muse liest private Nachrichten
Wie von Reuters ausgewertete Berichte von Meta-Mitarbeiter:innen zeigen, soll sich Muse unerlaubt Zugriff auf Nachrichten des Ende-zu-Ende-verschlüsselten Messengers Signal verschafft haben. Außerdem soll der KI-Agent ungefragt Buchungen vorgenommen und – ebenfalls ohne entsprechende Anweisung – angebliche Kontostände der Nutzer:innen genannt haben.
Große Besorgnis ausgelöst haben zudem Muse-Aktionen, in denen der KI-Agent Nutzer:innen Antworten zu Anfragen geschickt haben soll, die sie selbst nicht gestellt hatten. In einem Fall teilte Muse mit, dass eine Anfrage bezüglich der Kontrolle über den Datenschutz eines Kindes nicht übermittelt werden konnte.
Gibt es ein Datenleck bei Metas KI?
Der betroffene Meta-Mitarbeiter zeigte sich laut Reuters überrascht, da er mit dem KI-Agenten nie über das Thema gesprochen und auch nichts getan habe, was diese Nachricht hätte auslösen können. Muse ließ auf eine entsprechende Nachfrage hin wissen: „Ich habe keine wirkliche Erklärung dafür, außer dass es nichts mit unserem Gespräch zu tun hatte“.
In einem anderen Fall soll die Meta-KI einem Mitarbeiter angeboten haben, eine Nachricht bezüglich der Abholung eines Couchtisches zu verfassen. Der Mitarbeiter hatte allerdings weder einen Tisch gekauft noch einen solchen Kauf geplant. Die Erklärung laut KI: „Ich habe Kontextinformationen zur Abholung eines Couchtisches abgerufen, die offenbar gar nicht zu dir gehören“.
KI könnte Kontexte vermischt haben
Und: Es habe sich „nicht um mein Gespräch“ gehandelt, wie der Mitarbeiter aus dem entsprechenden Chat zitiert. Bedenken, dass es zu einer „möglichen Vermischung von Kontexten zwischen verschiedenen Konten“ gekommen sein könnte, versuchte Meta allerdings auszuräumen.
Die KI scheine Nachrichten zu halluzinieren, hieß es intern. Auslöser sei wohl, dass der Agent angehalten sei, auch zwischen den eigentlichen Sitzungen mit den Nutzer:innen zu interagieren.
Meta nennt die Vorfälle Einzelfälle
Demnach seien sowohl das zugrundeliegende KI-Modell als auch die Software von dem Problem betroffen. Das zuständige Meta-Team arbeite schon an der Behebung. Meta-Sprecher Daniel Roberts bezeichnete die von Reuters beschriebenen Beispiele gegenüber der Nachrichtenagentur als „Einzelfälle“. Meta führe interne Tests durch, um seine Produkte zu aktualisieren und den Schutz zu verbessern.
Neben dem befürchteten Datenleck steht auch der oben erwähnte Signal-Zugriff im Fokus externer Beobachter:innen. Signal-Präsidentin Meredith Whittaker forderte von Meta verbindliche technische Barrieren, damit App-Entwickler:innen ihre Programme vor dem Zugriff von KI-Agenten besser schützen könnten.
Apple-Update soll KI-Agenten beschränken
Wie Reuters mit Expert:innen nachvollziehen konnte, ist Muse in der Lage, auf Android-Geräten Nachrichtentexte aus Push-Mitteilungen zu lesen. Auf dem Mac nutzt der KI-Agent Bedienungshilfen und Bildschirmaufnahmen. Auf dem iPhone scheiterte derweil der Versuch, sich Zugriff zu verschaffen. Apple hat mittlerweile ein Update ausgeliefert, das den Zugriff von Agenten beschränken soll.

articles.title: Le Xiaomi Redmi Note 17 5G mise sur son écran AMOLED 120 Hz, sa batterie et son prix en baisse de 37% pour séduire pendant le Black Friday — Frandroid
articles.text:
Le Redmi Note 17 5G est un smartphone qui peut très bien faire office de premier modèle pour un adolescent. Il sait plaire avec sa grande taille, et son endurance importante est un atout, surtout quand on a tendance à oublier de brancher son smartphone régulièrement. Ce n’est pas le modèle le plus puissant du marché et il y a quelques petits compromis à connaître avant de l’acheter. Mais Amazon fait baisser son prix de près de 130 euros pendant le Black Friday, de quoi fermer un peu plus facilement les yeux.
Pourquoi se tourner vers le Redmi Note 17 5G ?
- Son grand écran AMOLED de 6,99 pouces bien calibré
- Sa batterie de 7 700 mAh avec charge filaire de 45 watts
- Sa certification IP65 et son port microSD
Lancé à 353 euros en septembre 2026, donc il n’y a pas si longtemps que ça, le Redmi Note 17 5G profite de son premier Black Friday pour passer à 223,97 euros dans sa version 6+128 Go.
Si, par la suite, l’offre mentionnée dans cet article n’est plus disponible, merci de jeter un coup d’œil ci-dessous afin de dénicher d’autres offres concernant le Xiaomi Redmi Note 17 5G. Le tableau s’actualise automatiquement.
Le Black Friday est lancé sur l’univers Apple. Sur Back Market, profitez de promotions sur les iPhone, MacBook, iPad, AirPods et Apple Watch. Chaque appareil est soumis à jusqu’à 100 points de contrôle qualité et est livré avec une garantie de 12 mois. De quoi profiter de performances comparables à celles d’un produit neuf.
L’écran et la batterie : deux atouts de taille
Le Xiaomi Redmi Note 17 5G mise sur son grand format et c’est ce qui frappe en premier chez lui : sa dalle AMOLED de 6,99 pouces affiche de la Full HD+ de 2 396 x 1 080 pixels pour un taux de rafraîchissement de 120 Hz. L’ensemble offre une image fluide et surtout, même en mode Standard, les couleurs sont bien calibrées. Il est aussi assez lumineux pour rester lisible en extérieur. Mais voilà, il faut accepter son gabarit imposant. Avec ses 225 grammes et ses 8,45 millimètres d’épaisseur, le Redmi Note 17 5G n’est ni discret dans une poche, ni très confortable à une main.
L’autre argument de ce Redmi Note 17 5G est sa batterie de 7 700 mAh, généreuse sur le papier, qui permet de tenir une journée complète et même plus selon votre usage. Il ne faut pas attendre de miracles toutefois, parce que malgré cette capacité importante, l’autonomie mesurée dans notre test ne dépasse pas celle de son prédécesseur, le Redmi Note 15 5G, qui n’avait pourtant qu’une batterie de 5 520 mAh. La charge filaire de 45 watts est assez lente : il faut compter quasiment deux heures pour refaire le plein. Mais Xiaomi a quand même conservé quelques arguments appréciables, comme la certification IP65, le verre Gorilla Glass 7i à l’avant et le port microSD pour le stockage.
Pas mal de concessions sur les performances et la photo
Il faut quand même prendre en compte les limites du Redmi Note 17 5G, et il y en a quelques-unes. À commencer par son processeur, une puce Snapdragon 4 Gen 4 avec, ici, 6 Go de RAM. Cette configuration suffit pour les usages courants, mais elle manque de répondant. L’interface peut connaître quelques ralentissements et les applications n’ont pas toujours la fluidité attendue. Le jeu vidéo n’est pas non plus son terrain de prédilection : les titres 3D exigeants demandent de baisser les réglages graphiques. C’est d’autant plus regrettable que le Redmi Note 15 5G faisait mieux avec son Snapdragon 6 Gen 3 et ses 8 Go de RAM. Il progresse sur l’écran, mais recule sur la puissance.
La partie photo subit aussi plusieurs coupes, avec un capteur principal qui passe de 108 à 50 mégapixels et perd la stabilisation optique. Que dire de l’ultra grand-angle, qui disparaît purement et simplement ? En plein jour et avec beaucoup de lumière, ça reste correct, mais dès que le soleil baisse, c’est beaucoup plus compliqué. Autre régression : le smartphone abandonne les haut-parleurs stéréo pour un mono qui manque forcément de basses et de richesse. Il conserve heureusement un suivi logiciel de 4 ans de mises à jour d’Android et 6 ans de correctifs de sécurité, ce qui est appréciable. L’interface HyperOS 3 est en revanche bardée d’applications préinstallées, et un petit ménage s’impose à l’allumage.
Vous pouvez en apprendre bien plus sur le Xiaomi Redmi Note 17 5G en lisant notre test complet de ce grand smartphone, qui recule sur plusieurs points face à son prédécesseur.

articles.title: Los expertos en limpieza coinciden: "Para que la calefacción dé más calor y gaste menos, nosotros colocamos las láminas reflectantes detrás de los radiadores"
articles.text:
Cuando empieza a hacer frío y enciendes la calefacción, lo haces pensando en más calorcito sin que la factura sufra mucho. Para conseguirlo hay un par de trucos que te pueden venir muy bien, y uno de ellos es colocar láminas reflectantes detrás de los radiadores. ¿Por qué? Es una solución súper sencilla que es todavía más interesante cuando están instalados en paredes que dan al exterior.
Es probable que no lo sepas, pero cuando enciendes un radiador una parte termina calentando la pared que tiene detrás y, si esta da a la fachada del edificio o a una zona sin calefacción, parte de esa energía se puede perder. Justo ahí entran en juego estas láminas (fabricadas con aluminio u otros materiales metalizados) y, en algunos casos, incorporan una capa de espuma aislante.
Cómo aprovechar mejor el calor de tus radiadores
Lo que consigues con estos paneles es reflejar parte del calor hacia el interior de la habitación, reduciendo así las pérdidas que se producen a través de la pared. Según explica Energy Saving Trust, este recurso puede ayudarte a ahorrar energía, sobre todo si tu vivienda tiene paredes exteriores poco aisladas. Eso sí, el resultado dependerá del aislamiento de tu casa y de dónde estén colocados los radiadores.
A todo esto debes sumar otra cuestión que seguramente hayas visto alguna vez en casa: las manchas oscuras que aparecen encima de algunos radiadores. El aire caliente mueve partículas de polvo que pueden terminar acumulándose en la pared y, aunque las láminas no eliminan por completo este problema, sí pueden proteger la superficie que queda detrás del aparato. Además, dependiendo del material, puedes limpiarlas pasando una bayeta de microfibra ligeramente humedecida.
Y lo mejor es que colocarlas tampoco exige grandes complicaciones. Lo primero que debes hacer es medir el radiador y cortar la lámina para que no sobresalga por los lados. Después, con el aparato apagado y frío, conviene que retires el polvo de la zona antes de instalarla. Algunos modelos se fijan con adhesivos o clips, mientras que otros se pueden deslizar directamente detrás del radiador, así que lo más recomendable es que sigas las instrucciones del fabricante para que el panel quede bien colocado.
De esta forma, puedes reducir parte del calor que se pierde por las paredes exteriores sin necesidad de hacer obras. Eso sí, no debes olvidarte del mantenimiento habitual: revisar los radiadores, purgarlos cuando sea necesario y mantener sus rendijas libres de polvo también ayuda a que el aire caliente circule correctamente por la habitación.

articles.title: PolyAI Dialog-RSN-1 is now on Amazon SageMaker JumpStart | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
PolyAI Dialog-RSN-1 is now on Amazon SageMaker JumpStart
Dialog-RSN-1, a reasoning model built for real-time complex dialog, is available today on AWS Marketplace and Amazon SageMaker JumpStart. It powers frontier dialog: agents that hear a live call, reason about it, and act in real time.
As an AWS customer, you can subscribe to Dialog-RSN-1 through AWS Marketplace and deploy it as a SageMaker endpoint inside your own AWS environment. You can also deploy directly from Amazon SageMaker Studio following the steps in Deploy and evaluate models with Amazon SageMaker JumpStart. That means the model designed to handle your customer conversations can be deployed like other Amazon SageMaker models with an AWS Marketplace subscription.
Deploying Dialog-RSN-1 inside AWS
Dialog-RSN-1 is the first PolyAI model available through AWS Marketplace. It runs inside your own AWS environment on the same AWS cloud that powers PolyAI’s compute and model training and serving.
All in a single pass, Dialog-RSN-1 perceives a caller’s audio directly, reasons about what they need, and responds in real time. On SageMaker, it deploys as an endpoint like other models you run there. It is reachable from your own architecture, billed through your AWS account, and covered by the same virtual private cloud (VPC), AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles, and monitoring you already have in place.
You keep ownership of orchestration, telephony integration, and business logic. Dialog-RSN-1 takes off your plate the hardest part to build yourself: understanding a live call and responding to it in real time. The endpoint speaks the OpenAI Realtime protocol, so an existing Realtime client connects through PolyAI’s bridge by changing its base URL. Audio in is 16-bit PCM mono at 16 or 24 kHz (transcode G.711 or Opus first). Connections last up to 30 minutes, and the model is English-only today.
To get started, find Dialog-RSN-1 on AWS Marketplace, then deploy it straight into an Amazon SageMaker endpoint in your own account. Or you can deploy directly from Amazon SageMaker JumpStart.
With Dialog-RSN-1 now onboarded to SageMaker JumpStart, deploying Dialog-RSN-1 takes one click. From the Amazon SageMaker AI console, open the Model Hub, select Dialog-RSN-1 from the JumpStart catalog, and choose Deploy. SageMaker JumpStart then spins up a real-time inference endpoint on a serving stack it has already tuned for you. No containers to wrangle, no instance types to second-guess, and no manual benchmarking. For automated workflows, the same one-click deployment also runs in a few lines of the SageMaker Python SDK.
The Dialog-RSN-1 endpoint runs entirely within your own AWS account. It is deployed in your VPC, accessed through your IAM roles, and monitored with the same Amazon CloudWatch logging and metrics you use for every other workload. Because inference happens inside your account, your callers’ audio and transcripts stay within a boundary you control. For a model handling live customer conversation, this helps support your data residency and auditability requirements.
Built for speed and accuracy
Models built for live calls may make you choose between speed and understanding. And models built for speed may miss the meaning, and ones built for reasoning may lead to wait time for callers. Dialog-RSN-1 avoids the tradeoff.
With PolyAI, you can build dialog agents that hear and handle calls the way your human agents would. These agents catch hesitation, hear frustration before it escalates, and know when to speak.
Real-time customer conversation is the job PolyAI’s Dialog-RSN-1 is built for, and it is already handling live calls in production today. Because the model reasons directly over the caller’s audio, it picks up tone, hesitation, and timing, the signals a plain transcript loses, and decides for itself the right moment to respond.
A model that hears calls the way humans do
Dialog-RSN-1 is a model focused on real-time conversations. There is no separate speech-to-text step and no reasoning model on the appropriate moment to talk, so thereby no multiple handoffs.
In practice, that means the callers get responses faster:
- Barge-in keeps working even when call volume spikes, instead of getting switched off to protect performance.
- Responses keep pace, so the model is not lagging behind the conversation while it reasons through what to say.
- Transcription is produced from the audio itself, because Dialog-RSN-1 is reading the actual audio, not someone else’s best guess at it.
Dialog-RSN-1 on Amazon SageMaker JumpStart
Amazon SageMaker JumpStart is the machine learning hub inside Amazon SageMaker AI, and it exists to collapse the distance between choosing a model and running it in production. For Dialog-RSN-1, that means the frontier of real-time dialog is a few clicks away. You can discover it, prove it on your own data, and ship it to a secure endpoint, all in one place. Here is what you get.
The code path using the SageMaker Python SDK is explained in our GitHub repository: Deploy PolyAI Dialog-RSN-1 on Amazon SageMaker AI.
Discover and evaluate before you commit
Dialog-RSN-1 shows up in the SageMaker JumpStart catalog with overview and sample notebooks in one place, so your team can understand the model before spending a dollar on infrastructure. To try the model on your own calls, deploy the endpoint and run PolyAI’s sample notebook, which streams recorded caller audio and prints the model’s turn decisions, replies, and transcripts.
One-click deploy and optimizations for your workload
From the same model card you choose Deploy, and Amazon SageMaker JumpStart stands up a real-time inference endpoint with a pre-configured serving stack. There is no manual container selection or instance guesswork. The real convenience is the named optimization profiles: instead of hand-tuning infrastructure, you pick the target that matches how you run Dialog-RSN-1. Latency optimized minimizes Time to First Token for interactive, real-time calls. Throughput optimized maximizes tokens per second for high call volumes. Cost optimized minimizes infrastructure cost per request. Balanced is an even tradeoff for general-purpose use.
Because Dialog-RSN-1 is built to respond in real time, you can use the latency-optimized profile to carry that responsiveness straight to your own endpoint. Before you deploy, SageMaker JumpStart surfaces the key performance metrics: P50 latency, Time to First Token, and throughput. This lets you right-size the ml.* instance for your traffic instead of benchmarking dozens of combinations by hand. You can run the whole flow from the console, or script it through the SageMaker Python SDK to wire deployments into continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD).
Deployed in your account, governed by your controls
The endpoint runs inside your own account boundary: in your VPC, under your IAM roles, with the CloudWatch logging and metrics you already have in place. For a model handling live customer conversations, that means your call audio and transcripts stay in an environment you control, which keeps data residency and auditability straightforward.
The result is a frontier voice model that deploys like the other workloads your machine learning team already runs, using the same hub, the same discovery and evaluation tools, and the same security posture. The hard part is the conversation Dialog-RSN-1 handles, not the infrastructure behind it.
For more detail on the architecture behind our frontier dialog model and the evaluation results behind our benchmarks, read our Dialog-RSN-1 launch post.
