articles.title: At Nasdaq opening bell, Anthropic CEO recommits to pacing AI development | TechCrunch
articles.text:
As Anthropic made its Wall Street debut on Thursday in the largest IPO in history, CEO Dario Amodei reaffirmed the company’s commitment to developing AI responsibly. In his speech ahead of the Nasdaq opening bell, Amodei vowed that the AI company would not bend to either business or political pressure and would “remain under human control.”
Reading the speech from a printout, the CEO began by talking about Anthropic’s origins as a way to build powerful technology to help humanity — something that he said was inspired by the loss of his father to a disease that became curable just a few years later.
He acknowledged that while human intelligence had made diseases like the plague, smallpox, and polio history for most of the world, there were still too few scientists with too little time to make progress in other areas of disease. AI, he said, could help with this by working in concert with humans to further medical progress.
It’s telling that Amodei began with a story highlighting AI’s potentially lifesaving applications, since he’s warned repeatedly about the risks of advancing the technology too quickly. In September, Amodei drew headlines when he outlined a plan to pace AI development, which included things like coordinating with other leading companies on safety standards and embedding evaluators from third-party organizations to verify that companies were following their safety commitments.
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Google DeepMind chief Demis Hassabis, and xAI owner Elon Musk said they agreed with Amodei’s position, although few concrete commitments have been made.
In this morning’s speech, Amodei again stressed the need to progress AI technology and the safety required in doing so. He referred to the “very real risks” of AI in the hands of bad actors, whether those were individuals or nation-states, and the potential for things like “economic disruption” and “losing control of AI systems.”
Anthropic believes these risks are avoidable, he noted, as long as there are safeguards in place. Amodei said the company would continue to be invested in the work of AI alignment and testing, and developing new ways to understand AI behavior so it could remain under human control.
“There is much work still to be done, and the most difficult safety work lies ahead of us,” he said. “The incredible talent of the company that has enabled us to build the most capable AI systems will need to be directed more so than it has already towards double and triple checking that those AI systems are safe and remain under human control.”
“And to state it unequivocally, we will pace the training and deployment of AI systems, taking as long as is necessary to have confidence that they are safe and will remain under human control,” Amodei concluded.
His sister, Anthropic co-founder Daniela Amodei, echoed these sentiments in an interview with CNBC on Thursday, noting that while the risks were real, the promise of AI was also “incredible.”
“We were really founded on this idea that it is our job to mitigate those risks, and I think we have to date done an incredible job doing that. We obviously have more work ahead of us, but we are deeply committed to safety,” she added. 
The full text of Dario Amodei’s opening speech is below:
Thank you, Daniela. My co-founders and I started Anthropic because we believe that the most powerful technology of our time should be built for the benefit of humankind. Daniela and I lost our father to a disease that just a few years later became curable. I started my career in biology, hoping to help future cures come sooner. In the lab, I saw the vast thicket of complexity that scientists face when they’re trying to understand disease and develop new treatments. So many of the scientific tools that can cut through that thicket — tools for gene editing, tools for gene synthesis, tools for controlling brain cells with light — started as pure ideas. In other words, they came from thinking, from intelligence.
Human intelligence has already made diseases like plague, smallpox, and polio history for most of the world. But progress in other diseases has been too slow for so many patients and their families. Going from a great idea to a treatment can take decades. It took many years from the first discovery of a strange repeating pattern in DNA to the approval of the first treatment for a disease using CRISPR. Nature is full of these patterns, but we’ve had too little intelligence to decipher most of them. Too few scientists with too [little] time. Now we can build that intelligence. Whether it’s protein folding, drug design, cancer genetics, or clinical trial administration, scientists across many areas of biology and medicine are finding Claude can help them do their research in a fraction of the time it would have taken just a couple of years ago. I believe sufficiently powerful AI, working in concert with humans, could compress a century of scientific and medical progress into a decade.
I don’t want to get ahead of myself. At this point, all we have are early results. Experiments and clinical trials will still take time, and although they involve slow and ponderous processes, I believe these processes can be substantially accelerated by AI. We hope that in the future fewer families miss a cure by a few years. Medicine is just a particularly vivid example, but there are many other applications of Claude. Our customers, the world’s most ambitious companies, nonprofits, and individual people, are already applying the intelligence we’ve built to stimulate economic growth, lift people out of poverty, protect democracy and free societies, even make everyday services like the DMV work better. We’re proud to work alongside them, and I’m extremely optimistic about what we can do together in the future.
At the same time, we’ve always been honest that this technology has very real risks. These range from misuse of the technology by individuals or by nation-states to economic disruption to losing control of AI systems. We discuss these risks not because we think they are inevitable and we are building anyway, but because we think they are avoidable and we can avoid them. Avoiding them depends on the choices made by the people building AI. There is a gigantic difference between how AI will go if we pay little attention to safety versus how it will go if we are obsessed with safety. And an obsession with safety and public benefit has been built into Anthropic’s DNA from the start, from safeguards against biological and cyber risks to alignment training and testing to looking inside our models like an X-ray, Anthropic has pioneered methods for understanding and steering the behavior of AI and keeping it under human control. There is much work still to be done, and the most difficult safety work lies ahead of us, the incredible talent of the company that has enabled us to build the most capable AI systems will need to be directed more so than it has already towards double- and triple-checking that those AI systems are safe and remain under human control.
And to state it unequivocally, we will pace the training and deployment of AI systems, taking as long as is necessary to have confidence that they are safe and will remain under human control, we will not bend to either business nor political pressure. Today puts the company in a stronger financial position, and in doing so, only strengthens our resolve to do the right thing. If we can show it’s possible to make the right choices on safety and still build an incredibly successful company, others in our industry will be inspired to do the same. We call this a race to the top.
When the race to the top is working properly, it doesn’t matter which company has the best models. Everyone wins because everyone is building safely. The race to the top works best when driven from the front of the pack, and we fully hope and expect to do so. But the goal is to make the whole industry better, regardless of whether Anthropic is winning or losing at any given time. The advent of machine intelligence is one of the seminal moments in human history, and we have a rare opportunity to shape it for the better. Thank you.

articles.title: Scientific simulation meets AI sovereignty and the CLOUD Act - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Enterprises fear AI success more than failure, because success means lock-in they can’t escape
The supercomputing world built its reputation on scientific simulation, but the artificial intelligence infrastructure now filling the same data centers raises a harder question. When models turn data into revenue, control over that data and the intelligence it produces becomes a board-level concern few companies discuss publicly.
A new buyer’s guide sets out to measure that control provider by provider. Sovereignty is not a single checkbox but a stack of control layers that buyers have to examine one at a time, according to Amit Eyal Govrin (pictured), lead analyst for sovereign AI at theCUBE Research and chief executive officer of Agentcy Labs.
“When it comes to sovereignty, it’s all about control,” Govrin said. “And when we have to look at control, there’s a lot of layers to go into it. And the first one is, are you in fact comfortable … ceding that control to somebody else? Are you comfortable being in somebody else’s jurisdiction where they can potentially compel your data if ever required?”
Govrin spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how sovereignty pillars, the U.S. CLOUD Act and incoming European regulation are reshaping the way enterprises choose AI infrastructure. (* Disclosure below.)
Beyond scientific simulation: The five pillars of AI sovereignty
The guide rests on five pillars — territorial, operational, technological, legal and financial. Territory, meaning where data centers sit and where data is hosted, is the pillar most providers get right easily, Govrin explained. The operational layer is murkier, and he pointed to Amazon Web Services Inc. as one example while noting that AWS does run a sovereign region in Brandenburg, Germany, covered by EU citizens.
“You’re in the AWS Frankfurt region as a German customer. Perfectly fine. Are you sovereign because you’re in that region?” Govrin said. “If that region goes down, that PagerDuty may not necessarily go to somebody out of Germany. It may go somewhere else. It may go into Seattle or to Hyderabad for all you know.”
To build the guide, Govrin and his team graded seven hyperscalers across 40 offerings and handed out 117 grades in five regions. The scoring framework uses 17 yes-or-no tests, with legal assessed separately because local laws make it a poor fit for pass or fail, drawing on more than 300 sources and hundreds of buyer interviews. Google LLC’s air-gapped offerings scored relatively well, but the finding that surprised Govrin most applied to every provider.
“No hyperscaler across the board had an answer to the U.S. CLOUD Act,” Govrin said. “Now imagine you’re a European entity or anywhere else outside the world, and now there’s a production order from a U.S. court system that states that this hyperscaler needs to turn over your data. At that point, there is no contest. Your data becomes Uncle Sam’s data.”
Furrier compared the stakes with the General Data Protection Regulation, a privacy rule he viewed as less operationally relevant. Sovereignty is more consequential because AI models running where data sits produce intelligence that drives revenue, according to Furrier.
“When money’s on the table, you know what happens,” Furrier said. “Everyone fights for it or argues for it. So I think this is a tinderbox moment where one match could blow everything up.”

articles.title: PM Mark Carney says oligopolies 'can lead to more competition'
articles.text:
Amid this week’s announcement that Quebecor is seeking to acquire Telus, Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canada’s telecom market could become more competitive with fewer major companies under certain conditions.
Speaking at a Nov. 18, 2026 press conference in Shenzhen, China, during his visit for the APEC CEO Summit, Carney declined to endorse the proposal or say whether the federal government should permit a telecom market with three major national wireless providers — down from the current four.
Quebecor, the Montreal-based owner of Videotron, Freedom Mobile, and Fizz, publicly unveiled its proposal to buy Vancouver-based Telus on Nov. 16. The deal is valued at approximately $31 billion, excluding debt, based on the stock prices used in Quebecor’s announcement.
When asked by media about the proposal, Carney suggested the effect on competition would depend on how the market is organized.
Discussing markets dominated by a handful of large companies, known as oligopolies, the prime minister said that “depending on the market structure, the form of oligopoly can lead to more competition with fewer players under certain circumstances.” He acknowledged that he would likely face some criticism for suggesting this.
However, Carney repeatedly stressed that he was not passing judgment on the Telus-Quebecor combined company proposal and pointed to the responsibilities of the Canadian Radio-Television and Telecommunications Commission and federal competition regulators.
“Again, I’m not going to make a direct comment about the number of players in the market, which would necessarily imply a conclusion about any specific transaction,” he said.
A Telus-Quebecor merger would put two of Canada’s four major national telecommunications companies under the same owner, leaving Rogers, Bell, and the combined company.
Carney was also asked whether growing competition from foreign satellite provider Starlink, owned by Elon Musk, called for a different approach to the industry. He said the federal government is reassessing telecommunications policy as technology and the market change, while emphasizing the need for companies to keep investing in better services.
He pointed to recent rule changes allowing providers to sell broadband services using other companies’ networks, saying that opening up access helps increase competition and lower prices. He maintained that affordability, service quality, and investment would guide the federal government’s decisions.
“You need a competitive market structure that provides that competition. We have seen the costs, for example, of broadband come down significantly over the last years, but technological developments, including some of the ones you referenced, has the potential to further that progress,” said the prime minister.
When asked about Canadians continuing to face high telecommunications bills, Carney acknowledged that more needs to be done.
“There has been improvement, but we need more improvement,” he said.
The federal NDP is calling for Carney’s administration to reject the acquisition outright.
“We don’t need bigger telecom empires. These companies are already charging us way too much — they don’t need even more power,” said NDP leader Avi Lewis in a statement on Nov. 18. “The Liberal government must not allow this deal to go through.”
The NDP leader warned that combining the companies would give a smaller number of owners greater control over the industry and put upward pressure on phone bills.
The NDP is also calling for a publicly owned telecommunications option to compete with private companies. Lewis pointed to SaskTel — Saskatchewan’s provincially owned provider — as a model for other parts of Canada.
“Only a public telecom option can permanently lower bills and give Canadians a real alternative to corporate price-gouging,” continued Lewis.
“Saskatchewan has done it for generations with SaskTel, offering some of the lowest prices in the whole country. It’s time to take that proven model to Quebec and the rest of Canada.”
Quebecor argues that combining its networks and resources with Telus would give it more money to improve services and compete with foreign technology and satellite companies. It has also promised to keep Telus’ brands and Vancouver headquarters.
The proposal would face intense scrutiny given the federal government’s previous efforts to establish a fourth major national wireless competitor.
When Rogers acquired Shaw in April 2023, Shaw’s Freedom Mobile was sold separately to Quebecor’s Videotron. The federal government had refused to let Freedom Mobile’s wireless spectrum licences — the rights to use airwaves for cellphone service — pass to Rogers, instead approving their transfer to Videotron under conditions intended to strengthen competition against Rogers, Bell, and Telus.
Quebecor’s new proposal would bring that fourth competitor together with one of the three companies it was meant to challenge.
Telus has not accepted the proposal. Its board has raised major concerns about the price, debt, shareholder voting rights, and the likely difficulty of securing regulatory approvals.
Header image credit: Shutterstock

articles.title: Frapper n'importe quelle cible depuis l'espace : l'Europe a désormais son projet d'arme orbitale avec MBDA et Atmos
articles.text:
Bombarder la Terre depuis l’espace. Voilà, en somme, ce qu’est le concept de frappe orbitale de précision en profondeur, ou PODS (Precision Orbital Deep Strike). Et c’est justement une capacité qui pourrait prochainement se développer en Europe, et plus particulièrement en Allemagne, dans le cadre d’un rapprochement entre deux sociétés.
Atmos Space Cargo a en effet annoncé ce mercredi 18 novembre, dans un communiqué commun, avoir signé avec MBDA Deutschland (la branche allemande du missilier MBDA, l’un des géants de la défense en Europe) un accord pour concevoir, développer et tester un projet de Precision Orbital Deep Strike.
Pour Atmos, c’est un développement notable de son activité : jusqu’ici, la startup faisait plutôt de la logistique spatiale. Fondée en 2021 à Lichtenau, en Allemagne, cette jeune entreprise développe Phoenix, une capsule équipée d’un bouclier thermique gonflable, qui doit ramener sur Terre des expériences menées en orbite.
De son côté, MBDA est un poids lourd, spécialisé dans la fabrication de missiles et de systèmes hybrides, comme ce drone-missile conçu pour saturer les défenses aériennes adverses – les fameuses munitions téléopérées, qui se développent tous azimuts. Le groupe compte plus de 21 000 salariés et appartient à Airbus, BAE Systems et Leonardo.
Pour l’Europe, la capacité de frappe de précision lancée depuis l’espace est relativement inédite. Jusqu’à présent, ce terrain a plutôt été exploré par l’URSS, puis par la Russie et la Chine. Les États-Unis aussi ont mené des recherches dans cette direction. Désormais, c’est donc au tour du Vieux Continent de s’y mettre.
Il s’agit, selon Thomas Gottschild, directeur général de MBDA Deutschland, d’offrir aux forces armées « une capacité européenne souveraine et hautement innovante ». Sebastian Klaus, patron d’Atmos, voit dans l’aller-retour vers l’orbite une nouvelle couche d’« infrastructure stratégique », capable selon lui de renforcer la « dissuasion conventionnelle » de l’Europe.
À quoi ressemblerait une frappe orbitale ?
Le communiqué évoque d’abord des études sur l’architecture du système, sa faisabilité technique et l’intégration de charges militaires, avec de possibles démonstrations technologiques. Selon Zone Militaire, Atmos tirerait de Phoenix un véhicule de transfert et de retour orbital, capable de rester des mois en orbite grâce à sa propre propulsion et à son alimentation électrique. MBDA se chargerait de l’explosif et du guidage.
On aurait donc un engin placé en orbite basse, à quelques centaines de kilomètres d’altitude, qui plongerait dans l’atmosphère sur ordre pour frapper une cible spécifique. Les deux partenaires précisent que PODS sera un système militaire séparé des capsules Phoenix civiles. À ce stade, l’accord porte sur des études de faisabilité, et rien ne garantit que la technique fonctionne.
L’arme devra en effet supporter un long séjour dans l’espace, puis la chaleur extrême de la rentrée dans l’atmosphère.
Or, à ce stade, Atmos n’a qu’un vol à son actif. En avril 2025, Phoenix 1 a décollé sur une fusée Falcon 9 de SpaceX et a bien déployé son bouclier gonflable. Mais sa trajectoire a dû être modifiée pour les besoins de la charge principale du lancement, et la capsule est tombée dans l’Atlantique Sud, à environ 2 000 kilomètres des côtes du Brésil, sans pouvoir être récupérée.
Depuis, l’entreprise a levé des fonds pour construire d’autres capsules Phoenix 2, qui auront leur propre moteur pour choisir où elles retombent.
Des armes légales sur le papier, mais vulnérables ?
Sur le plan juridique, le Traité de l’espace de 1967 interdit de placer des armes de destruction massive en orbite, mais il ne dit rien des armes conventionnelles. Le projet profite donc d’une « zone grise », comme le relève Zone Militaire. En revanche, le même traité et la Convention de 1972 sur la responsabilité internationale pour les dommages causés par des objets spatiaux rendent l’Allemagne responsable de ce que feraient Atmos et MBDA dans l’espace.
C’est sans doute pour cela que le communiqué insiste autant sur le respect du droit et des autorisations nécessaires.
Sur le plan militaire, un engin en orbite basse ne peut pas rester au-dessus d’une cible : il défile autour de la Terre selon une trajectoire prévisible, que l’adversaire peut suivre. Pour rester au-dessus d’un point fixe, il faudrait orbiter à la même vitesse que la rotation de la Terre, ce qui se fait sur une orbite géostationnaire, qui se trouve beaucoup plus loin, à près de 36 000 kilomètres d’altitude.
En orbite basse, l’engin resterait à la portée d’une arme antisatellite à ascension directe, c’est-à-dire un missile tiré depuis le sol pour aller détruire un objet en orbite – cela générerait assurément un nuage de débris, mais le pays menacé préférerait sans doute pulvériser le PODS, jugeant que c’est un moindre mal face à une frappe orbitale réussie.
Atmos et MBDA n’ont donné ni calendrier ni budget, et précisent que les développements concrets feront l’objet d’évaluations et d’accords séparés.

articles.title: 4.250 neue Millionäre? Der Börsengang macht Anthropic-Mitarbeiter reich
articles.text:
Anthropic: Das sind die großen Gewinner des Rekord-Börsengangs
Wenn die Anthropic-Aktie am 19. November in den Handel startet, gehören neben frühen Investoren und Big-Tech-Konzernen auch viele Mitarbeiter zu den großen Gewinnern. Sie dürfen schon am ersten Handelstag bis zu zehn Prozent ihrer Aktien verkaufen.
Andere Investoren müssen sich länger gedulden. Für sie gelten gestaffelte Lockup-Fristen: Erste Aktienpakete werden 27, 48, 62 und 76 Tage nach dem Börsengang handelbar. Die sieben Gründer verkaufen beim IPO zwar kleine Pakete, dürfen den Großteil ihrer Anteile aber erst nach Veröffentlichung der Zahlen für das erste Quartal 2027 oder spätestens nach 180 Tagen verkaufen.
Anthropic bringt 980 Millionen Aktien zu je 83 Dollar an die Börse und nimmt damit 81,3 Milliarden Dollar ein, mehr als SpaceX mit 75 Milliarden. Voll verwässert wird das Unternehmen mit rund 1,5 Billionen Dollar bewertet. Weitere 26 Milliarden Dollar kommen über eine Privatplatzierung bei Tech- und Chipkonzernen hinzu.
Anthropic-IPO: Big Tech gewinnt
Die größten Gewinner sind zwei Big-Tech-Konzerne, die Anthropic zugleich mit Rechenleistung beliefern. Laut der letzten Fassung des Börsenprospekts hält Amazon nach dem IPO rund 1,92 Milliarden Aktien, Google rund 1,79 Milliarden. Zum Ausgabepreis entspricht das etwa 159 Milliarden Dollar für Amazon und 147 Milliarden für Google. Eingesetzt hat Amazon nach Berechnungen von Reuters rund 18 Milliarden Dollar, Google 33,3 Milliarden.
Anthropic machte zuletzt knapp die Hälfte seines Umsatzes über die Cloud-Plattformen der beiden Konzerne. Umgekehrt hat Anthropic zugesagt, über zehn Jahre mindestens 110 Milliarden Dollar bei AWS auszugeben und bis 2033 mindestens 114 Milliarden Dollar bei Google Cloud.
Über die Privatplatzierung steigen jetzt weitere Lieferanten ein: Neben Google kaufen Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft und TSMC zusammen für 26 Milliarden Dollar Aktien zum Ausgabepreis.
Milliardengewinne auf Raten
Zu den frühen Investoren bei Anthropic gehören außerdem Skype-Mitgründer Jaan Tallinn, Facebook-Mitgründer Dustin Moskovitz und der frühere Google-Chef Eric Schmidt. Forbes schätzt Tallinns Paket zum Ausgabepreis auf rund 15,6 Milliarden Dollar, etwa das 260-Fache seines Einsatzes.
Laut Daten von PitchBook haben seit 2021 mehr als 300 Geldgeber Anteile bei Anthropic investiert. Zuletzt hatten Altimeter Capital, Dragoneer, Greenoaks und Sequoia Ende Mai eine Finanzierungsrunde angeführt, bei der Anthropic noch auf eine Bewertung von 965 Milliarden Dollar kam.
Viele dieser Investoren dürfen erst ab dem 15. Dezember verkaufen und zunächst nur bis zu sechs Prozent ihrer Aktien. Großaktionäre mit mehr als 0,5 Prozent müssen noch länger warten, für sie endet die Sperrfrist erst nach einem Jahr.
Ein früher Investor geht dagegen leer aus: Im Jahr 2021 steckte der wegen Betrugs zu 25 Jahren Haft verurteilte Gründer der Kryptobörse FTX Sam Bankman-Fried 500 Millionen Dollar in das damals kaum bekannte Startup.
Der FTX-Insolvenzverwalter verkaufte die Anteile aber bereits 2024 für insgesamt rund 1,3 Milliarden Dollar. Zum IPO-Preis wäre das Paket nun etwa 37 Milliarden Dollar wert gewesen.
Anthropic-Börsengang: Tausende Millionäre auf dem Papier
Nach einer Schätzung der Privatmarkt-Plattform Hill könnten bei der Bewertung von mehr als 1,5 Billionen Dollar rund 4.250 der etwa 5.300 Anthropic-Mitarbeiter jetzt zumindest auf dem Papier zu Millionären werden. Das sind rund 80 Prozent der Belegschaft. Das Analysehaus Sacra kommt auf rund 2.800 aktuelle und frühere Beschäftigte mit mindestens einer Million Dollar.
Anders als bei den meisten Börsengängen dürfen Mitarbeiter schon am ersten Handelstag bis zu zehn Prozent ihrer Aktien verkaufen und weitere 35 Prozent, nachdem die Jahreszahlen für 2026 veröffentlicht wurden.
Die sieben Gründer geben beim IPO jeweils Aktien im Wert von rund 280 Millionen Dollar ab. Der Großteil ihrer verbleibenden Anteile bleibt jedoch bis zu einem Jahr gesperrt.

articles.title: InPrime Finserv raises Rs 101 Cr in Series B round led by FMO
articles.text:
InPrime Finserv raises Rs 101 Cr in Series B round led by FMO
InPrime will use the funding to expand its reach and improve its technology stack, especially in AI use cases.
InPrime Finserv, a tech-led NBFC, has raised Rs 101 crore in a Series B funding round led by FMO, the Dutch entrepreneurial development bank. This round also saw participation from existing investors Z47 and Pravega Ventures.
InPrime will utilise the capital to expand the reach of existing products and diversify into micro-mortgage products, in line with its segment-focused lending approach. The NBFC will also deepen its investments in AI-driven use cases, across agentic AI and co-pilots.
“From the beginning, we have believed that prime customers are not limited to the formal economy. We have been building around the evolving needs of India’s informal prime customers by combining engineering, local presence and relevant financial products.,” said Rajat Singh, Co-founder and CEO, InPrime Finserv.
InPrime operates 46 area offices across Karnataka, Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan, Haryana, Uttarakhand and Madhya Pradesh. It has served 27,000+ households and has disbursed Rs 516.92 crore to date. As of September 30, 2026, its assets under management stood at Rs 332.8 crore, with gross non-performing assets of 0.80%.
Founded in 2021 by Sneh Thakur, Manish Raj and Rajat Singh, InPrime is focused on customers who do not fall under the category of formal employment. This NBFC believes that despite the credit worthiness of this segment, they are unable to raise loans due to the traditional practices of lenders.
According to InPrime, its technology stack allows it to effectively do the task of credit underwriting, which requires interpreting unstructured data, understanding customers beyond conventional financial metrics, and delivering services at scale in vernacular languages.
“Expanding access to finance for underserved entrepreneurs and households is closely aligned with FMO’s aim of making finance more inclusive and accessible. InPrime’s combination of technology, data-driven underwriting, and local presence provides an opportunity to reach customers who are often overlooked by traditional lenders,” said Peter Byrde, Director Private Equity at FMO.
Edited by Swetha Kannan

articles.title: Windows 11 : Microsoft va tuer son application To Do
articles.text:
Microsoft To Do vit ses derniers mois. L’application de gestion de tâches de Microsoft baissera le rideau à compter du 30 juin 2027. Microsoft vient de l’annoncer officiellement sur une de ses pages de support repérée par Windows Lastest. Si la firme de Redmond suggère aux utilisateurs professionnels de migrer vers Planner (aucune migration automatique n’est prévue), elle n’offre aucune solution de secours aux utilisateurs grand public. Microsoft To Do ne sera pas remplacé.
Microsoft tue Wunderlist une deuxième fois
La fin annoncée de Microsoft To Do va laisser, encore une fois, un goût amer aux utilisateurs. Car l’application de gestion de tâche de Microsoft était la digne héritière de Wunderlist, une application que Microsoft avait rachetée courant 2015, avant de supprimer celle-ci au profit de sa remplaçante, Microsoft To Do, qui avait été développée par l’équipe de Wunderlist.
La mort annoncée de Microsoft To Do pose désormais un sérieux problème aux utilisateurs, qu’ils soient grand public ou professionnels. Microsoft n’a en effet prévu aucune solution de remplacement pour les premiers. Le grand public devra en effet impérativement se tourner vers une solution tierce, Microsoft n’ayant prévu aucun transfert vers Planner, même pour les abonnés payants à Microsoft 365 Personnel ou Famille.
Les utilisateurs professionnels quant à eux auront la possibilité de transférer leurs tâches dans Microsoft Planner, mais la migration vers cet outil ne se fera pas automatiquement. Microsoft, qui a néanmoins promis qu’elle fournirait un outil permettant d’exporter les données To Do avant le retrait des différentes applications, tout en assurant que cet export n’assurait pas la possibilité de réimporter les données dans Planner.
Une régression majeure pour les utilisateurs professionnels
Les professionnels qui devront faire la transition entre Microsoft To Do et Microsoft Planner risquent de l’avoir mauvaise. Car les différences fonctionnelles entre les deux applications sont a priori conséquentes.
À titre d’exemple, Planner ne dispose d’aucune application de bureau native. Pour l’utiliser, il faudra donc soit passer par le Web ou par Microsoft Teams. Aucun accès hors ligne, comme c’est le cas avec Microsoft To Do, n’est prévu.
Par ailleurs Planner ne permet pas de configurer des rappels individuels programmables comme To Do. L’outil n’utilise en effet que des notifications basées sur les dates d’échéance des tâches. À noter également que Planner ne prend pas en charge les pièces jointes sur les tâches des plans privés.
Les futurs naufragés de Microsoft To Do dont vous faites peut-être partie ont encore quelques mois devant eux pour trouver une solution de remplacement. Il en existe plusieurs équivalentes à Microsoft To Do, comme Google Tasks, Super Productivity ou encore Vikunja.
