articles.title: ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini réunis dans un mini PC, le tout sans abonnement
articles.text:
| Systeme d'exploitation | Windows | 
| Processeur | Nvidia RTX Spark N1X (20c) | 
| Chipset graphique | Blackwell 6144 cores | 
| Dimensions (h x l x p) | 57 x 152 x 147 mm | 
| Connectique | 4 x USB-C, x USB-A, Ethernet | 
| Norme Wi-Fi | Wi-Fi 7 | 
L’EdgeMesa N AI+ est le mini-PC dédié à l’IA locale sous Windows de MSI. Super compact, il s’adresse aux créateurs de contenus et aux personnes souhaitant multiplier les agents IA en local grâce à sa puce Nvidia RTX Spark, et à qui le format PC portable ne conviendrait pas.
Après la présentation des PC portables de la plateforme Nvidia RTX Spark, c’est au tour des mini-PC d’être disponibles. Ces derniers ne sont déclinés qu’avec la version la plus performante de la puce, celle dotée de 20 cœurs CPU et 6144 unités Cuda. Les partenaires peuvent se démarquer sur les configurations 64 ou 128 Go de mémoire vive et des unités de stockage s'étendant de 1 à 4 To. Le NSI EdgeMesa N AI+ suit donc le cahier des charges à la lettre en enveloppant le tout d’un boîtier en aluminium perforé sur sa face avant.
Il embarque une puce N1X avec ses 20 cœurs et 6144 unités Cuda. Notre modèle de test est équipé de 128 Go de mémoire vive et d’un SSD de 4 To, histoire d’accumuler les modèles et agents sans avoir à se poser de questions. Il est proposé à 8199 €.
Le MSI EdgeMesa N AI+ bénéficie d’un boîtier tout en aluminium de 15,6 x 14,6 x 5,3 cm, donc à peine plus grand que le Mac mini M6. Il est surtout bien plus petit qu’un Mac Studio, qui paraît tout simplement énorme à côté de ce minuscule boîtier.
Sa façade est perforée sur les deux tiers de sa partie inférieure, tandis que le tiers supérieur est un simple bandeau qui rappelle les tiroirs de lecteurs CD. Une fois le boîtier allumé, une simple led blanche s’illumine dans le coin inférieur gauche, derrière les perforations.
Le reste du boîtier arbore une finition sablée assez proche de celle des Mac. MSI a relevé les chanfreins avec une finition brillante, tout comme le logo de la marque qui trône à gauche du faux tiroir de lecteur CD.
La connectique se compose de quatre ports USB 4, dont un réservé au connecteur d’alimentation. Le constructeur fournit un bloc de charge de 240 W avec un câble secteur, tandis que chez Apple, l’alimentation est directement intégrée dans les Mac. Un port HDMI et une prise Ethernet à la norme 10 Gb/s complètent la connectique.
On regrette le manque de diversité au niveau des ports disponibles pour une machine censée servir aux créateurs de contenus. Il n’y a pas de lecteur de cartes SD, ni même de simple port USB-A pour y brancher un dongle clavier/souris. Le passage par un hub USB-C est donc indispensable pour diversifier la connectique.
Notez que si vous pensiez chaîner plusieurs MSI EdgeMesa pour démultiplier les performances, l'opération n'est pas permise. En effet, si le DGX Spark (la version Linux du RTX Spark) possède deux ports QSFP offrant une bande passante de 200 Gb/s, ceux-ci sont absents de la déclinaison Windows. Il est probable que l'envolée des prix de la RAM ait eu raison de la puce ConnectX-7 nécessaire au fonctionnement de ces ports très haut débit.
Si vous souhaitez toutefois répartir la charge sur vos différentes machines RTX GeForce ou Spark, vous pouvez opter pour la solution logicielle Nvidia PAIR. Cela ne remplacera pas une connexion à 200 Gb/s, mais assurera un équilibrage d'exécution sur votre parc matériel.
La partie réseau sans-fil est gérée par la puce MediaTek MT7925, déjà croisée sur de nombreux PC portables gaming AMD. Bien que compatible wifi 7, elle ne prend pas en charge la largeur de bande de 320 MHz sur la fréquence des 6 GHz. On se retrouve donc quasiment avec des débits du wifi 6E. Une économie de bouts de chandelles pour une machine frôlant les 8000 €, d'autant que l'on est souvent amené à télécharger des modèles d’IA pesant plusieurs dizaines de gigaoctets.
Un mot sur la dissipation thermique, puisque le MSI EdgeMesa N AI+ se destine à tourner quasiment 24 h/24 et se doit d'embarquer un système de refroidissement à toute épreuve.
D’après notre démontage, deux ventilateurs de type blower aspirent l’air frais par la façade perforée et recrachent l’air chaud à l’arrière après avoir traversé un radiateur sur une chambre à vapeur.
En plein travail (Hermes + CineBench), notre caméra thermique relève un peu moins de 38 °C sur le boîtier en aluminium. À l’arrière, l'extraction souffle à près de 46 °C, et bien plus haut dans le radiateur. À l’intérieur, c’est une autre histoire. HWMonitor, qui affiche les températures des sondes internes de la puce RTX Spark, nous donne une moyenne de 93,75 °C pour le CPU et 84 °C pour le GPU. Côté consommation électrique, ce même logiciel indique 92 W (max) pour la partie CPU/RAM et 192 W (max) pour la puce N1X complète.
Au niveau des nuisances sonores, le MSI EdgeMesa N AI+ atteint 40,3 dB sur notre sonomètre, ce qui correspond à un souffle audible, mais inférieur aux 47 dB de l'Asus ProArt P16. Soulignons d’ailleurs que le bruit perçu est moins, car les ventilateurs sont plus gros et les fréquences émises moins gênantes que celles des ventilateurs très fins des PC portables.
Le MSI EdgeMesa N AI+ mis à notre disposition par Nvidia embarque la plus grosse configuration disponible : puce N1X 20 cœurs CPU avec 6144 unités Cuda, accompagnée de 128 Go de mémoire vive et un SSD 4 To à la norme PCIe Gen5.
Ainsi, sur notre indice de performance uniquement dédié à la partie CPU, le MSI EdgeMesa N AI+ obtient exactement le même score (95), calculé selon les résultats obtenus sur sept logiciels, que l'Asus ProArt P16 testé il y a quelques semaines.
Le constat est donc le même : la partie CPU de la RTX Spark suffit amplement à jouer son rôle de chef d’orchestre pour piloter le vrai point fort de la puce, son GPU. Notons encore une fois que la puce RTX Spark est basée sur l’architecture ARM et que notre protocole possède encore quelques logiciels non optimisés utilisant l’émulation, ce qui représente à l'heure actuelle le paysage Windows.
Le véritable atout de la puce RTX Spark reste les 6144 unités Cuda qui accélèrent les calculs effectués par la partie graphique. Ainsi, dans Premiere, Photoshop et Blender, les temps de traitement sont drastiquement réduits par rapport à un rendu sur le CPU : pour Blender, le temps de rendu est divisé par 10, pour Premiere par 5,8 et pour Photoshop par 6,3.
En jeu, le MSI EdgeMesa N AI+ obtient le même nombre d'images par seconde (FPS) dans Shadow of the Tomb Raider que l’Asus ProArt P16. Toutefois, ce titre étant fortement limité par les performances du processeur, il n’est pas forcément représentatif de l’augmentation de l’enveloppe thermique accordée à la puce N1X sur les mini-PC (140 W).
Dans Cyberpunk 2077 sur l’ensemble de nos mesures, le framerate est en hausse de 9 % sur le MSI EdgeMesa N AI+ face au PC d'Asus.
Sur notre benchmark d’IA Procyon, la puce RTX Spark intégrée au mini-PC se montre 6 % plus performante que son pendant dans l’Asus ProArt P16, pourtant équipé exactement de la même puce.
Évidemment, avec 128 Go de mémoire vive, le MSI EdgeMesa N AI+ offre la possibilité de charger des modèles d'IA plus lourds, donc plus précis, voire de faire tourner plusieurs agents simultanément en choisissant des modèles moins imposants.
Un mot sur le SSD en provenance de chez Samsung : les débits obtenus sont de 14,7 Go/s en lecture et 13 Go/s en écriture. Nous n’avons pas noté de ralentissement durant le transfert des 160 Go de données nécessaires à nos tests. Les débits sont donc conformes à ceux attendus pour un SSD à la norme PCIe Gen5. Surtout, ce composant assure un ralentissement moins important des tâches IA si ces dernières saturent la mémoire vive et se déchargent donc sur le SSD
Celui-ci est par ailleurs facilement accessible. Il suffit de retirer les quatre vis au niveau des patins antidérapants pour faire coulisser la structure interne vers l’avant. Le stockage se trouve sur la face inférieure, au dos de la carte mère. On regrettera son format peu conventionnel, mais il a au moins le mérite d'être remplaçable.
Pour aller plus loin :
Le MSI EdgeMesa N AI+ s'impose comme une station de travail de choix pour les créateurs et technophiles exigeants. Sous son format ultracompact aux finitions soignées, il abrite une puissance de calcul importante grâce à l'association de la puce N1X (plateforme Nvidia RTX Spark) et de 128 Go de mémoire vive. S'il pèche par une connectique trop chiche nécessitant l'ajout d'un hub, il remplit parfaitement son contrat en faisant tourner les modèles d'IA locaux les plus lourds avec une fluidité redoutable.
Face à la concurrence, l’Apple Mac mini M5 Pro étant limité à 64 Go de mémoire vive, on se tournera logiquement vers le Mac Studio équipé de la puce M5 Max qui, à configuration équivalente, s'avère moins cher (7830 € contre 8199 € pour le MSI). Sous Windows, le choix est au final très restreint, puisque la puce AMD Ryzen AI Halo est introuvable en France. Seul le Framework Desktop reste disponible avec 192 Go de mémoire vive, mais avec des performances brutes en retrait, le tout pour un tarif de 8379 €.
1

articles.title: Orange veut remplacer le premier téléphone de vos enfants par une montre à 68 euros
articles.text:
Après Bouygues Telecom et SFR, Orange se lance à son tour sur le marché de la montre connectée pour enfants avec SaferKids, couplée à un forfait bloqué. L'opérateur propose un prix d'appel plus bas que ses concurrents.
Orange a dévoilé ce mercredi 19 novembre l'offre SaferKids, qui est vendue sous la forme d'une montre connectée pour enfants, avec un forfait bloqué sans engagement. L'opérateur historique rejoint ainsi Bouygues Telecom et SFR, qui proposent déjà ce type d'alternative au premier téléphone portable. Avec une montre européenne, un prix cassé à son lancement et une gamme SaferPhone enrichie d’un forfait 100 Go pour les lycéens, la nouvelle offensive familiale d'Orange est plutôt intéressante.
Une montre connectée pour enfants pilotée depuis le téléphone des parents clients d'Orange
Là où Bouygues et SFR ont misé sur les fabricants chinois TCL et Honor, Orange a préféré une marque espagnole, SaveFamily, et son modèle SaveWatch Plus 2. Ici, la montre sert d'abord à appeler ses proches et à être joint par eux. Les parents décident quels contacts sont autorisés, et un bouton SOS permet à l'enfant de joindre un numéro favori en cas de problème.
Tout se gère depuis l'application SaveFamily, sur le téléphone d'un parent. C'est là qu'on consulte la position de la montre, qu'on définit la liste des contacts autorisés et qu'on programme des plages de déconnexion. À l'école, pendant les devoirs ou à l'entraînement, elle se fait oublier. Pour la prise en main, Orange propose des tutoriels et une assistance au 3900, ainsi que des conseils aux parents sur son site Bien vivre le digital.
Concernant les tarifs, Orange marque de gros points, en tout cas pour le moment. Jusqu'au 2 décembre, la montre affichée à 139 euros prix fabricant tombe à 68 euros, avec une formule de 15 % de remise immédiate, puis 50 euros remboursés, à demander soi-même après l'achat. Après le 2 décembre, il faudra compter 89 euros, remboursement déduit. Ces prix supposent de souscrire le forfait SaferKids de 2 Go proposé par Orange, sans engagement. Comme il est bloqué, aucun hors-forfait n'est possible. Il coûte 4,99 euros par mois aux abonnés Internet Orange et 9,99 euros aux autres.
Bouygues, SFR, Orange : quelle montre pour enfants coûte vraiment le moins cher ?
Orange refait son retard sur ses concurrents. Bouygues Telecom a tiré le premier en juin 2025 avec sa Kids Watch signée TCL, remplacée en octobre par le modèle MT48. SFR a suivi le 18 août avec son Pack Kids Protégés, bâti autour de la Honor Choice Kids Watch Plus. Sur le forfait, Orange et Bouygues s’alignent, avec 4,99 euros par mois pour leurs clients box (chez Bouygues, il faut aussi un forfait mobile maison), 9,99 euros pour les autres. SFR facture le sien 11,99 euros, avec une remise pour ses abonnés box qu’il ne chiffre plus sur sa page, mais se montre plus large en data, avec 5 Go contre 2 Go chez ses rivaux.
La principale différence se fait sur le prix de la montre. Orange profite du Black Friday pour être le moins cher avec ses 68 euros, mais d'une courte tête, on va dire. SFR demande 69 euros, payables comptant ou en quatre fois. Bouygues réclame 97 euros pour sa nouvelle MT48 (1 euro, puis 4 euros par mois pendant deux ans). Pour un foyer sans box qui garde le forfait 24 mois, la facture atteint environ 308 euros chez Orange pendant la promotion et 329 euros ensuite, contre 337 euros chez Bouygues et 357 euros chez SFR. Pour les abonnés box, Orange descend à 188 euros pendant le Black Friday, puis 209 euros, contre 217 euros chez Bouygues. Chez SFR, tout dépendra de la remise appliquée au forfait.
Enfin, pour les ados, Orange étoffe sa gamme SaferPhone. Le forfait 5 Go est proposé à 5,99 euros par mois pour les clients Internet. Un nouveau forfait de 100 Go, taillé pour les lycéens, arrive à 13,99 euros par mois pour ces mêmes clients. Les deux donnent droit, sur demande, à un pack Protection Enfant adapté à l'âge, qui comprend le contrôle parental, la géolocalisation du téléphone, l'aide à l'installation et l'alerte anti-cyberharcèlement sur WhatsApp et les réseaux sociaux. Cette alerte, assurée par SafeBear, est offerte un an d'ailleurs. Ensuite, il faudra décider de la garder, pour 10 euros par mois ou 48 euros par an, au choix.

articles.title: Agent security is product security, and your marketing site counts
articles.text:
Agent security is product security, and your marketing site counts
A marketing site used to have two kinds of visitors: people and search crawlers. Now an agent can build a page, a second agent can scrape it, a third can summarize it for a potential customer, and a fourth can optimize it overnight after studying yesterday’s traffic.
“The ones that you do not control make the marketing site a product with agent users, and products need product security.”
You control some of these agents but not all the data they ingest and train on. The ones that you do not control make the marketing site a product with agent users, and products need product security. A marketing site is usually public with no login required to view or break. Adversaries go after whether the site still says what you wrote, serves what you built, and reports what real visitors did. This article calls those content integrity, delivery integrity, and signal integrity, and looks at where each kind of agent touches them.
Five agents, three kinds of integrity
Five agent roles show up on a marketing site today, agents that:
- build,
- read or scrape,
- analyze its visitor data,
- optimize the site from that data,
- adversarial agents that attack
Each role touches at least one of three things worth protecting the integrity of:
- Content – what the site says and links to.
- Delivery – how that content reaches a browser, including DNS, redirects, third-party scripts, hosting, and the publish pipeline.
- Signal – the visitor and behavior data the site produces, plus every decision made from it.
Because the content is public, the checks that matter are integrity checks. An agent with write access can be talked into making unapproved changes, so you need governance over what it may touch and logs that show what it did.
Agents that build sites
Builders are usually the first agents a team adopts, so they set the pattern for every agent that follows. A builder agent writes pages, config, scripts, and redirects. The risk sits in what it reads before it writes. A doc, a ticket, a scraped competitor page, or a CMS field can carry instructions, and an agent can follow them.
Recent incidents show the shape of this. In July 2025, someone slipped a destructive prompt into a pull request for the Amazon Q Developer extension for VS Code, and it shipped in a production version. AWS removed it and said no customer resources were affected, and reports indicate a formatting error kept the prompt from running. The same month, a Replit coding agent reportedly deleted a production database during a code freeze, despite instructions not to change anything. Replit’s response was to separate development and production databases automatically. The causes differ from provenance checks to agents stepping outside their boundaries.
The incidents above failed at different stages of Figure 2. Amazon Q failed at the input and review stages, where untrusted text in a pull request reached a trusted release. Replit failed at the harness, where an instruction to freeze changes was the only barrier between the agent and a production database. A marketing site has the same exposure, and three layers around the agent carry those controls.
- The agentic SDLC is the process – where agents act across plan, draft, review, and publish, and which stages need a human decision.
- The agent harness is the control layer – the code around the model that decides which tools the agent can call, with which credentials, and what gets logged or approved.
- The sandbox is the containment layer – an isolated runtime with no standing credentials, restricted network egress, and no path to production data.
For a marketing site, that translates into a few working rules.
- Give builder agents draft access and keep publishing behind a person.
- Review a diff of content, scripts, and redirects. A summary written by the agent describes what it believes it did.
- Treat every input as untrusted, including your own docs and tickets, because anyone who can edit them can steer the agent.
- Add provenance records – which agent changed which page, from which inputs.
Webflow’s AI site builder drafts a multi-page site and design system from a prompt. The Webflow MCP server connects AI tools like Claude to a site, so an agent can design, build, and manage it through natural conversation or agentic workflows.
“Treat every input as untrusted, including your own docs and tickets, because anyone who can edit them can steer the agent.”
Webflow’s controls map to the rules above. Agent Instructions give an agent your design system, voice, CMS, and policies as skills and rules stored with your site, and agents should read them before they act. They guide an agent but don’t enforce anything, and an agent follows them as an input, so edit access matters: only Site managers and Designers can change them, and new ones stay off until someone reviews and turns them on. To see what an agent is doing, agent presence shows where any agent connected through the Webflow MCP server is working on the canvas, the same way you’d see a teammate. For the record afterward, the Site Activity Log for enterprise labels each change as Human, Webflow AI, or MCP.
Site roles do the enforcing. They let a team give a builder a narrow role, such as a Marketer with publishing switched off. That role can build pages from components but can’t publish, create API tokens, or open custom code. On Enterprise plans, design approvals go further. A role without the “Edit main site without approval” permission works in page branches, and its changes reach the main site only after required reviewers approve them.
Source by Webflow, now in research preview, is a new platform purpose-built for teams and agents to drive growth on the web, together. Source’s site-building agents work directly on your codebase. It’s designed to let teams decide how much autonomy those agents have, from requiring human approval for every change to giving agents more freedom for lower-risk work, and to hold agent actions to the same roles, permissions, and review systems as human work, with a record of what changed and which agent changed it.
Agents that read and scrape the site
Search is turning into answers, and answers are built from your pages. Agents read page text as context, and a page can contain text no visitor sees. In August 2025, Brave researchers hid instructions behind a spoiler tag in a Reddit comment. When a user asked Perplexity’s Comet browser to summarize the page, Comet followed them and exfiltrated a one-time password. Perplexity patched the issue. Any field attackers can write to on your site, such as comments, reviews, form-fed content, or CMS entries, can carry the same kind of payload to every agent that reads it.
The agent also might not see the same page you do. Researchers at SPLX showed that a site can check the user agent and serve AI crawlers different content than it serves browsers. The same technique works against you if an attacker gains write access to your site: they can change what AI systems say about you while every human check looks clean. Monitor what agents see, not only what browsers see.
Before you can control which agents read your site, you need to see them. AI bots don’t show up in standard visitor analytics, so most teams have no record of which ones visit or what they request. Webflow’s LLM bot insights fills that gap with data from your site’s server logs, so it covers the bots it tracks whether or not visitor tracking is on. It groups each bot by purpose: agentic bots that fetch pages live to answer a user’s question, training bots that collect content for model development, indexing bots that map pages for retrieval, and bots with more than one purpose. You can view activity for the whole site or a single page, filter by provider or category, and export the data as a CSV.
That gives you a baseline. Bots often focus on different pages than human visitors do, and a jump or drop after you publish is easy to spot. A page that agents fetch heavily is also a page where tampered content or injected text reaches the most readers, which makes it a good place to start the integrity checks below. The view covers named LLM bots. It doesn’t flag traffic as hostile, and it doesn’t show a user’s original query or whether a page was cited.
Visibility tells you who is there. What to do about them is a separate decision, because scrapers differ in intent. An indexer that maps your pages for retrieval and a collector that copies them for training both read public content, and you may want to allow one and not the other. Scrapers that hit your endpoints at volume add hosting cost and can slow the site for real visitors, and they count as traffic in your analytics unless something classifies them. A robots.txt file states your preference but doesn’t enforce it. Set a policy for each purpose, enforce it with rate limits and bot rules, and carry the classification into analytics so scraper traffic is reported separately from human visitors.
Agents that analyze visitor data
Analysis agents work with the most sensitive data on the site: behavior tied to real people. Webflow shows what this looks like in practice. Webflow Analyze records click events, sessions, bounce rate, time on page, and audience attributes such as traffic source, region, and device. Teams can connect an AI tool to the Webflow MCP server and ask about their site’s traffic and engagement, including page-level data, goals, and filtered results, without opening Analyze. That connected tool is an analysis agent.
The shape of the data limits what the agent can expose. Analyze uses anonymous identifiers and, according to Webflow, collects no personally identifiable information, and it relies on local storage instead of cookies. This is the setup the controls below call for: an agent that reads an anonymized dataset, not raw visitor records. If you build your own analysis agents, keep sensitive identifiers out of their context, run them in a sandbox, and give them read-only access.
Two things still need your attention. The first is consent. Analyze lets you choose always-on, opt-in, or opt-out tracking, and the opt-in and opt-out methods need a consent management solution to work properly. The tracking method decides which visitors are in the data, so the consent choices you apply belong in the dataset before an agent reads it. The second is signal quality. An analysis agent reports what the site counted, and it learns from the same signal that attackers can pollute. Label automated traffic before it reaches the agent, so it can report human and agent traffic separately. Blended answers describe bots as much as people.
Optimization agents close the loop
Optimization agents turn signal into action. They rewrite headlines, reorder sections, and adjust audiences from traffic data. That makes signal integrity a content integrity problem. If an agent learns from poisoned traffic, it ships a confident change based on bad data, and the changed page produces more skewed data for the next round.
A person who sees a conversion spike from a country you don’t sell in asks questions. An agent ships the variant. The fix is to make the loop checkable: validate the signal before an agent acts on it, hold out traffic the agent can’t tune, and require approval and rollback for changes to live pages.
“If an agent learns from poisoned traffic, it ships a confident change based on bad data, and the changed page produces more skewed data for the next round.”
Webflow Optimize shows where this loop exists in a product. An optimization has a target goal, and its variations can be tested with a traditional A/B/n split, shown by personalization rules, or handled by an AI-optimized mode that uses machine learning to serve the best-performing variation and adapt as visitor behavior shifts. That last mode is the loop in Figure 3: whatever counts as a conversion becomes the signal the system learns from, so automated traffic that completes the goal action can push a weaker variation forward. A variation can also redirect a visitor to a different page, which puts redirect destinations in scope for the delivery checks above. For teams using these features, treat the target goal as a security decision. Pick goals that bots find hard to fake, separate automated traffic from human results, and have a person review results before an AI-optimized variation becomes the default.
Agents that attack the site
A marketing site does not require a login to view its public content. Attackers go after integrity: they attempt to change what the site says, hijack what it serves, or corrupt what it reports. Automation already does this at scale, and agents lower the cost further. In testing by hCaptcha’s threat group, browser agents run against 20 common abuse scenarios attempted nearly every malicious request without any jailbreaking. Most block attempts failed because the tool lacked the capability.
Content
Content attacks change what visitors read, or send them to a copy of your site. In July 2025, Okta reported that attackers were using Vercel’s v0, a tool that builds web pages from natural-language prompts, to clone sign-in pages for brands including Microsoft 365 and cryptocurrency companies. Okta’s researchers reproduced the attack with a single prompt asking for a copy of their own login page, and Axios reported it can take as little as 30 seconds. Vercel restricted access to the sites Okta identified. The same approach can reproduce a marketing site.
Agents that run on your site raise a related problem, and the attacker doesn’t have to be an agent. In December 2023, a visitor talked the chatbot on a Chevrolet dealership’s site into agreeing to buy a new Tahoe for $1 and calling it a legally binding offer. In February 2024, a Canadian tribunal ordered Air Canada to pay $812.02 after its chatbot gave a customer wrong bereavement fare information. The tribunal wrote that “it makes no difference whether the information comes from a static page or a chatbot.” It treated the chatbot’s words as the company’s words.
Platforms carry part of the response. Webflow’s Acceptable Use Policy prohibits using the platform for impersonation, fraud, malware, and content altered to mislead people, and Webflow’s Trust and Safety team removes sites that break it. Removals come from automated detection and from reports, and ~1000 sites are taken down each day. If you find a site impersonating yours on Webflow, you can report it through the form linked in the policy or at abuse@webflow.com.
Delivery
Delivery attacks hijack the path between your content and the visitor’s browser, and they don’t need to touch your page. In 2024, a company acquired the polyfill.io domain and changed the script it served, which redirected mobile visitors on more than 100,000 sites to scam pages. The site owners hadn’t changed a line of code, and Google began warning advertisers whose landing pages loaded the script. A week after the disclosure, Censys still counted nearly 385,000 hosts referencing the domain, including 182 government sites.
DNS follows the same pattern. Guardio Labs found more than 8,000 domains and 13,000 subdomains tied to well-known brands hijacked through dangling CNAME and SPF records, then used to send about five million emails a day under those brands’ names. Open redirects borrow a trusted domain’s reputation the same way. Cofense found that every US .gov domain abused in phishing campaigns between November 2022 and November 2024 was used for an open redirect, and KnowBe4 documented a 2025 campaign against finance and healthcare organizations that relied on open redirects in legitimate services.
Agents make the search for these cheaper. Finding a dangling record or a redirect parameter is a scanning problem, and agent tooling can follow a hit through to a tailored phishing page faster than a script could.
Signal
Signal attacks corrupt what the site reports. Fake form fills, synthetic sessions, and scripted browsing pollute analytics, attribution, and audiences. The scale is real: Imperva’s 2025 Bad Bot Report found that automated traffic reached 51% of web traffic in 2024, and bad bots accounted for 37%. Forms are the most direct path from a bot into a marketing team’s CRM, so they are a good place to start. Webflow’s form spam protection offers four methods that you can combine. The reCAPTCHA field asks visitors to identify themselves as human before they submit, although Webflow notes that it can hurt user experience and that more advanced bots can get around it. A site-level bot blocking setting uses AI to analyze mouse movements, inputs, and other signals, and blocks submissions from bots on every form on the site. A second site-level setting, spam filtering, checks all the form data sent on your site and filters out spam submissions. The honeypot technique adds a hidden field that real visitors never fill in, so a filled field marks the submission as spam. Because the CAPTCHA can be circumvented, none of these should carry the load alone.
The damage reaches visitors too. A visitor’s history is the record that drives what they see next. When synthetic sessions merge into real audiences, or identities get stitched together wrongly, retargeting and personalization act on the wrong history, and real visitors get irrelevant offers.
How to secure your marketing site against agents
The controls differ by layer, but the first step is the same for all three: list every agent that touches your site, including the ones you don’t operate. You can’t protect a layer from an agent you haven’t counted.
Content. Review agent-authored changes like code. Keep a record of which agent changed what and from which inputs, and alert on diffs nobody requested. Fetch key pages with common AI crawler user agents and compare the result to what a browser gets.
Delivery. Allowlist redirect destinations, and remove any endpoint that redirects to an arbitrary URL. Audit DNS for dangling CNAME records and SPF includes that point at services you no longer use. Keep an inventory of third-party scripts, and apply Subresource Integrity or serve them from your own origin where you can. The polyfill.io incident is the case for it.
Signal. Classify automated traffic before it reaches analytics. Rate-limit and validate form submissions, and layer the protections your platform offers, such as bot blocking, spam filtering, and a honeypot field. Tag agent-originated sessions so they stay out of human audiences and human-focused tests, and report on them as their own segment.
Across all of it. Apply least privilege to every agent, keep logs you can query, and put a person in front of the publish step.
Your marketing site now has more kinds of visitors, and some of them can edit it.
If an agent changed what your site says tonight, would you know which one it was, what it read first, and who approved the change?
This article was originally published on November 10, 2026, on webflow.com.

articles.title: Intel says its graphics-free D270 GPU beats Nvidia's RTX Pro 6000 by up to 5.9x in benchmarks
articles.text:
In context: Intel first teased Crescent Island over a year ago as a data center GPU that can't even render graphics. It has none of the 3D or ray-tracing hardware you'd find on a regular graphics card; instead, the chip – now sold as the GPU D270 – spends that space on AI and scientific work. Until this week, though, Intel hadn't really shown how fast it is. That changed at the SC26 supercomputing show in Chicago.
In a post, Intel put the D270 up against Nvidia's RTX Pro 6000 Blackwell Server Edition. Instead of games or AI models, Intel went with something a little more niche. It picked four workloads that banks rely on to put a price on financial contracts.
Across those four, the D270 delivered between 1.92 and 5.9 times the performance of Nvidia's card. Its biggest win showed up in a European Monte Carlo simulation. Intel's card also did all of this at just 350W, compared to the 600W that Nvidia's card is rated for.
All four tests rely on double-precision, or FP64, calculations. Intel's Xe3P architecture handles those calculations at full speed, so the D270 barely slows down when a task needs that extra accuracy. That full-speed FP64 support is where most of the D270's lead over Nvidia's card comes from.
The RTX Pro 6000, on the other hand, uses the same chip as the GeForce RTX 5090. That silicon only handles FP64 at a tiny fraction of its usual speed, so by sticking to FP64-heavy workloads, Intel chose the kind of tests where Nvidia's card was likely to fall behind.
Of course, these are Intel's own numbers from pre-production chips. On top of that, the two cards didn't even run in matching systems, since Intel put the D270 in a single-socket server but gave Nvidia's card a bigger dual-socket machine.
Intel only claims modest gains in its AI tests, though, such as a 12% throughput edge on one language model. That's a little surprising, since AI is what the D270 was designed for in the first place.
Picking FP64 workloads also lets Intel poke at a sore spot for its rival. Nvidia's newest Blackwell Ultra chips offer only about a teraflop of double-precision compute, as HPCwire pointed out last December. So Nvidia has been nudging scientists toward software that emulates FP64 on its Tensor Cores, though it has promised more FP64 muscle in future chips.
As for the D270, customers are already testing it ahead of a 2027 launch, but Intel still hasn't said a word about how much it will cost.

articles.title: .NET 11 : ASP.NET Core: Union Type Support, OpenAPI 3.2 by Default and Blazor AI Components
articles.text:
Last week, Microsoft shipped ASP.NET Core in .NET 11 as part of the wider .NET 11 release. The update spans Minimal APIs, OpenAPI, SignalR, Blazor, authentication, and the Kestrel server. As stated in the announcement, .NET 11 is a Standard Term Support release with two years of support.
On the API side, developers can now use C# 15 union types in JSON request and response bodies across Minimal APIs and MVC. The release notes limit the feature to JSON bodies, so route, query, header, and form values cannot bind to a union.
Minimal API validation also runs asynchronous validators, which keeps threads free while a rule waits on a database lookup or a remote call. The framework can now localize validation messages and display names itself, and endpoints can skip the remaining middleware pipeline through a new [ShortCircuit] attribute.
Developers who generate OpenAPI documents now get version 3.2 unless they select an earlier one for tooling that has not caught up. As described in the release notes, the framework depends on Microsoft.OpenApi 3.3.1 for this, and the notes label that update a breaking change.
With 3.2, endpoints that stream server-sent events are documented with a schema for each event's payload, and the generator emits an anyOf schema for unions. Generated documents can also describe endpoints that use the HTTP QUERY method, and APIs that carry the [Obsolete] attribute show up as deprecated.
SignalR adds authentication refresh, so a long-lived connection no longer has to close when its access token expires. As reported, server developers enable it per hub, while the .NET client refreshes automatically by default and the TypeScript client can do the same. Blazor passes the refreshed identity on to Interactive Server components while the circuit stays connected.
Blazor receives the longest list of changes, and many of them target static server-side rendering. With the new CacheView component, developers can cache the rendered markup of a component subtree, and the child components do not run when a cached copy is served. Blazor now ships client-side validation for static SSR forms, enabled by default.
Developers can also carry data between requests with TempData or session values. According to the release notes, the Blazor Web App template drops its app.UseAntiforgery() call, because a middleware for CSRF protection is now added by default.
For Interactive Server apps, an opt-in package pauses the circuit of a hidden browser tab after a delay, two minutes by default, to free server memory. Lists built with Virtualize may now mix items of different heights, and Microsoft raised the default OverscanCount from 3 to 15. Page and sort state in QuickGrid now lives in the URL query string, with sortable headers and pager controls rendered as links instead of buttons.
The release notes flag this as a CSS breaking change, because custom styles written for the buttons also have to target the links. The release also includes Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.AI, a set of components for chat and agent interfaces. According to the announcement, Microsoft treats that package as experimental and will keep it in prerelease throughout .NET 11.
On the security and server side, an experimental package adds Device Bound Session Credentials, a protocol that ties session refresh to a private key held by the browser. Response compression and request decompression gain Zstandard support, which is on by default.
Kestrel's HTTP/1.1 parser no longer throws exceptions on malformed requests, a change that is reported to raise throughput by up to 20 to 40 percent under heavy invalid traffic. The shared framework libraries of ASP.NET Core are now compiled with runtime-async, described in the release notes as an internal change with no public API impact.
Two older APIs are on the way out. The Microsoft.AspNetCore.Grpc.Swagger package is now deprecated, and Kestrel's TlsClientHelloBytesCallback option is obsolete in favor of the new UseTlsClientHelloListener extension.
Other changes in this release are native OpenTelemetry tracing attributes, client-side cancellation of SignalR hub invocations, scrolling to a specific item in Virtualize and QuickGrid, passkey display names inferred from the authenticator, and TimeProvider support in ASP.NET Core Identity.
For interested readers and developers, the full release notes are available in the What's new in ASP.NET Core in .NET 11 article on Microsoft Learn.

articles.title: Cómo activar los controles para adolescentes en Instagram, TikTok y YouTube
articles.text:
Instagram, TikTok y YouTube ofrecen herramientas para que los padres limiten el tiempo, las notificaciones y las recomendaciones de los adolescentes, pero la mayoría exige que el padre o la madre vincule su cuenta con la del joven y que este acepte. Estos son los pasos, según las páginas de ayuda de cada aplicación.
Las tres aplicaciones activan por defecto ajustes protectores para los usuarios de 13 a 17 años. Esos ajustes funcionan sin intervención de los padres, que solo necesitan la vinculación de cuentas para cambiarlos, endurecerlos o recibir información sobre el uso del adolescente.
La vinculación es voluntaria y requiere el consentimiento de ambas partes. En Instagram, el joven puede cortarla, pero el adulto recibe un aviso inmediato; en YouTube, cualquiera de los dos puede desactivarla. Las guías corresponden a lo publicado por cada plataforma al 19 de noviembre de 2026 y los menús varían según el país.
Antes de empezar conviene acordar con el adolescente qué se va a activar, porque sin su aceptación la vinculación no se completa.
Cómo usar las cuentas de adolescentes de Instagram
Las cuentas de adolescentes de Instagram nacen privadas, solo reciben mensajes de personas que ya siguen o con las que tuvieron contacto, y tienen el modo de sueño activado de 22 a 7, según el Centro de ayuda de Instagram. Durante ese horario se silencian las notificaciones. A los 60 minutos diarios aparece un recordatorio para cerrar la aplicación.
Los menores de 16 años necesitan permiso de un padre o tutor para volver menos restrictivos esos ajustes. Los de 16 y 17 pueden cambiarlos solos, salvo que su cuenta esté supervisada. Para fijar un límite de tiempo propio, aprobar o rechazar cambios o ver con quién chatea el joven, la supervisión es obligatoria.
Para activarla, el adulto entra en el Centro de Familias de Meta, toca “Empezar”, elige el perfil del adolescente y selecciona “Enviar invitación”, según el Centro de ayuda de Meta. La invitación vence a los siete días. Cada adolescente puede tener un solo adulto supervisor, que a su vez puede supervisar hasta cinco cuentas.
Una vez aceptada, el padre puede fijar un límite diario, programar horas sin Instagram y ver a quién sigue el joven y quién lo sigue. Meta aclara que Explore y Reels no se pueden personalizar por completo y que el supervisor no ve el historial de búsqueda ni el contenido de los chats.
Qué opción tiene TikTok para menores de edad
En TikTok, las cuentas de 13 a 17 años son privadas por defecto, tienen un límite diario de 60 minutos y no reciben notificaciones push por la noche: desde las 21 para los de 13 a 15 años y desde las 22 para los de 16 y 17, según la Guía para tutores de la plataforma.
La herramienta de control es Family Pairing. El adulto abre en su perfil el menú, entra en “Configuración y privacidad”, toca “Family Pairing” y elige su rol de padre. La aplicación muestra un código QR o un enlace que el adolescente debe escanear o abrir para confirmar.
Con la cuenta vinculada, TikTok permite fijar un límite diario de tiempo, programar horas de ausencia, filtrar publicaciones por palabras clave en el feed “Para ti”, restringir comentarios y definir quién puede escribirle al joven. Cuando se agota el tiempo, el adolescente necesita un código de acceso de un solo uso que le da el padre.
Internet Matters indica que el límite más corto que se puede fijar es de 40 minutos. Sin Family Pairing, cualquier usuario puede ajustar el tiempo diario desde el perfil, en Configuración y privacidad, Tiempo de pantalla, según la ayuda oficial de TikTok.
Cuáles opciones vienen desactivadas en YouTube para cuidar a los menores
En YouTube, la reproducción automática, que pasa sola al siguiente video, viene desactivada para los usuarios de 13 a 17 años, según su ayuda oficial. Un blog de la plataforma indicó que los recordatorios de descanso y de hora de dormir vienen activos para adolescentes, con un aviso cada 60 minutos.
Para una cuenta supervisada, el padre inicia sesión en YouTube con su cuenta vinculada, toca su foto de perfil y entra en Configuración. Allí baja hasta Centro de Familias y elige “Administrar perfiles de niños y funciones para adolescentes”. Después selecciona al hijo y activa “Desactivar reproducción automática”, con lo que el joven ya no podrá volver a encenderla.
La supervisión de adolescentes se crea desde el mismo Centro de Familias. Tanto el padre como el joven deben aceptar y cualquiera de los dos puede desactivarla cuando quiera. Los padres pueden fijar recordatorios de descanso y de hora de dormir, un tiempo máximo para desplazarse por los Shorts (videos cortos) y el nivel de contenido que puede ver.
Con la supervisión activa, el padre ve cuántos canales tiene el adolescente, cuántos videos y transmisiones en vivo publicó, cuántos comentarios escribió en otros videos y a cuántos canales está suscrito, según la ayuda de YouTube.

articles.title: Intel Diamond Rapids shows signs of life in SC26 demo running live server
articles.text:
Intel Diamond Rapids shows signs of life in SC26 demo running live server — next-gen Xeon 7 CPU breaks cover at partner booths, no showcase from Intel
Diamonds Rapids is set to launch next year.
Intel’s next-gen Xeon Diamond Rapids CPUs appeared at Supercomputing 2026 (SC26) in two separate booths, but neither was from Intel directly. Most interesting was a running server at the CXL booth, showcasing a demo with a Diamond Rapids CPU. The server ran for the first day of the show, and upon returning to the booth, we were informed that it had been shut down due to noise complaints (it’s hard to mistake a running server). Elsewhere at Bull’s booth, a Diamond Rapids CPU was shown installed in a server behind a glass case. Notably, Intel didn’t have a Diamond Rapids demo, instead focusing most of its booth on Xeon 6+ and its new D270 GPU, otherwise known as Crescent Island.
The demo in question is for Montage’s CXL MXC, or Memory eXpander Controller. If you’re unfamiliar, memory expansion via CXL is an increasingly common tactic to give multi-host environments access to a large pool of memory, breaking free of an individual server’s capacity via CXL. In the demo, Montage is showing off its memory expansion controller running across a Xeon 6 and a Diamond Rapids server, each sharing a pool of memory over CXL. CXL is an open standard, built atop PCIe.
Of course, the demo doesn’t say much about Diamond Rapids performance, but it’s the first time we’ve seen a chip running in the wild. The 256 GB memory capacity shown doesn’t provide any hints, either. Intel has announced that Diamond Rapids will support 16-channel memory, with RDIMM support up to 8,000 MT/s and MRDIMM support up to 12,800 MT/s, matching AMD’s recent EPYC Venice CPUs. However, Intel hasn’t revealed capacity, though we anticipate the maximum capacity will be far above 256 GB – for context, last-gen Granite Rapids-AP supports up to 3 TB per socket.
Bull is a French server designer focused on HPC and AI infrastructure, and it showed off two Xeon 7 Diamond Rapids chips installed in the Bullsquana XH31600 server. As expected for a 2P Diamond Rapids server, it supports 32 channels of DDR5 memory, and it’s designed for a liquid-cooled deployment.
As you can see from the image, these aren’t production chips. They’re labeled with “Intel confidential,” and the code starts with “Q,” revealing that this is a sample. Originally, we expected to see Diamond Rapids in the second half of this year, perhaps around this time. However, in August, Intel revealed that Xeon 7 chips would launch in 2027.
Based on the various servers we saw and the live demo, it seems Intel is targeting a launch earlier in the year, likely in Q2; we expect a larger consumer focus in Q1. It could slip later into the year, though that seems very unlikely given that Diamond Rapids was already pushed back, and the insatiable demand for CPUs in AI data centers doesn’t appear to be drying up.
Also pointing to a relatively quick release are the various servers we saw on the floor at SC26. Several partners showed off their next-gen servers built for Diamond Rapids CPU, sporting the LGA 9324 socket, including Dell and Asus (pictured above). However, Bull was the only vendor we could find that had an actual chip on display.
Diamond Rapids is Intel’s true next-gen CPU, following up on the E-core-only Xeon 6+ range that launched earlier this year. Diamond Rapids packs up to 256 P-cores, and it’s built on Intel’s performance-enhanced 18A-P node. The most interesting aspect of the chip is its topology, with Intel breaking from its previous layout and building something much similar to an EPYC CPU. The package features centralized memory and I/O, which were pushed out to the edges of the package with Granite Rapids. You can read more about the design of the chip in our Diamond Rapids recap from Hot Chips on Tom’s Hardware Premium.
Jake Roach is the Senior CPU Analyst at Tom’s Hardware, writing reviews, news, and features about the latest consumer and workstation processors.

articles.title: Bell's Black Friday sale gives you more for smartphone trade-ins
articles.text:
Bell’s Black Friday deals are here with discounts on phones, devices, and more.
Smartphones

articles.title: Balance Theory acquires CISO decision intelligence platform VectorBlack - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Balance Theory acquires CISO decision intelligence platform VectorBlack
Cybersecurity investment management company Balance Theory Inc. today announced that it has acquired VectorBlack, a decision intelligence platform for chief information security officers developed by ThreatShare.ai, for an undisclosed sum.
Developed by Jason Lewis, Gerry Eaton and Wayne Schepens, VectorBlack is designed to provide CISOs with timely decision support on emerging threats, industry developments and market trends. The artificial intelligence-driven platform is aimed at anticipating the issues most likely to catch the attention of chief executives and boards, allowing security leaders to raise them before the questions are asked.
Rather than simply aggregating information, VectorBlack is said to show security leaders what has changed in the cybersecurity landscape and why it matters to their organization. Its focus as what the company calls a CISO Strategic Intelligence Platform was shaped by input from security executives, including Ryan Clarque, CISO at Black Rifle Coffee Co. Clarque said having a strategic view ahead of a renewal, budget decision or board discussion “can make all the difference.”
Lewis began developing the underlying technology before teaming up with Eaton, an industry analyst, and Schepens, a cybersecurity entrepreneur who founded public relations firm LaunchTech Communications in 2015.
As part of the deal, Schepens will join Balance Theory as chief cyber market analyst to help shape market strategy and product adoption. Lewis is taking on the role of principal data engineer, leading the continued development and integration of VectorBlack’s technology. Eaton will focus on applying the platform to targeted research and sector-specific intelligence for cybersecurity leaders.
At the core of Balance Theory’s offering is an AI-native platform for cybersecurity investment decisions and execution. Combining program context, proprietary market intelligence and AI agents, the platform is used by security teams to manage more than $1 billion in cybersecurity spending. It claims customers average a first-year return on investment of more than 300%.
VectorBlack’s technology will be integrated into the Balance Theory platform, adding to the market intelligence that already informs customer investment decisions. By tracking market developments, competitive dynamics, emerging technologies and real-world experience with security products, the combined teams are aiming to show CISOs how their own investments are performing, what others in the industry are seeing and where the market is headed.
“VectorBlack will take Balance Theory’s capabilities a step further by delivering tailored intelligence across the security product categories our customers invest in,” said Greg Baker, co-founder and chief executive of Balance Theory. “This creates a powerful new level of insight to inform smarter technology investments and long-term security strategy.”
The company said details on integration and availability will be announced at a later date.
Balance Theory is a venture capital-backed company that raised $19 million in a Series A round led by SYN Ventures in July, with existing investors DataTribe and the Maryland Technology Development Corp. also participating. The round coincided with Accuvant Inc. founder and former Optiv Security Inc. Chief Executive Dan Burns joining Balance Theory as executive chairman. Including a $3 million seed round in 2022, Balance Theory has raised $22 million to date.

articles.title: DDR6 memory modules could be 44% shorter than DDR5 while delivering over 50% more bandwidth
articles.text:
Forward-looking: JEDEC is looking forward to a point when buying DRAM doesn't require selling a kidney and DDR6 is available. In an early preview of the next-gen memory standard, the organization noted that not only would it bring several upgrades, but the proposed modules would also be around 44% shorter than DDR5 versions.
As VideoCardz notes, a full-size DDR5 stick measures just over 133 mm from end to end. The design JEDEC has in mind for DDR6 measures 74 mm, putting it within a few millimeters of those little SO-DIMMs found in laptops. Unfortunately, you can probably guess who stands to benefit most from being able to squeeze more memory into the same amount of motherboard space.
Sure enough, JEDEC singles out AI inference and agentic AI as two workloads that could use more memory close to the CPU. The speed figures it gives are for registered DIMMs, the kind typically found in servers. DDR6 RDIMMs are expected to start at 12,800 MT/s, up from the 9,200 MT/s ceiling for DDR5 RDIMMs, with 14,400 MT/s and higher speeds to follow.
That works out to a roughly 39% increase in the transfer rate right from the start. There's also the data bus, which goes from 64 bits wide to 96 bits, allowing the module to move more data with each transfer. JEDEC expects those two changes to deliver more than 50% additional bandwidth at launch. It's also developing low-power modes specifically for use in data centers.
As for how much memory you could get on one of those shorter sticks, DDR6 is expected to support 128-gigabit dies. That's 16GB on a single die, and manufacturers will be able to stack several of them in the same package. Micron offered some idea of where that could lead last month when it outlined plans for a 1TB server module.
The big question now is when DDR6 might make its way into your next build. Don't expect it anytime soon. JEDEC lists the unbuffered DIMMs used in desktop PCs and the low-profile CAMM design among the formats under consideration, though it hasn't put a date on any of them.
Back in May, we heard that Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron were already working with substrate suppliers on DDR6, with the first commercial modules expected in 2028 or 2029. Whether those first modules will include a reasonably priced kit for a gaming PC is another matter, but here's hoping.

articles.title: ID. Up : Volkswagen mise sur un nom culte pour son électrique à 20 000 euros — Frandroid
articles.text:
Volkswagen traverse actuellement une période particulièrement troublée. La firme est dans une situation en demi-teinte en Chine et a dû prendre plusieurs décisions difficiles. Parmi elles, la mise en pause du développement de l’ID. Golf ainsi que de la modernisation de son usine de Wolfsburg. En parallèle, le constructeur prévoit de réduire fortement sa gamme d’ici 2035. Le groupe poursuit tout de même son électrification avec quatre nouvelles citadines électriques abordables : les Volkswagen ID. Polo et ID. Cross, le Skoda Epiq et la Cupra Raval.
Après l’ID. Polo, Volkswagen prépare également le lancement d’une autre citadine encore plus abordable. Il s’agit de la version de série du concept ID. EVERY1, qui avait été dévoilé en mars 2025. Attendue pour 2027, la voiture ne devrait pas s’appeler ID.1, comme on l’a longtemps cru. Volkswagen abandonne en effet les noms à chiffres au profit de noms de modèles connus, comme pour l’ID. Polo (ex-ID.2) et l’ID. Tiguan, qui succède à l’ID.4.
Volkswagen a déposé le nom ID. Up le 22 octobre 2026 auprès de l’EUIPO, l’office de l’Union européenne chargé des marques, ainsi qu’auprès de son équivalent allemand, le DPMA. Bien sûr, un dépôt ne signifie pas forcément que l’appellation sera utilisée. C’est toutefois probable, et le calendrier va dans ce sens. Selon le magazine portugais Razão Automóvel, les premières voitures de présérie sont déjà sorties de l’usine Volkswagen de Palmela, au Portugal, et la production en série doit démarrer au dernier trimestre 2027. Le nom ID. Up circulait d’ailleurs déjà fin août, comme le rapportait Electrive.
Environ 20 000 euros pour la citadine
Le nom Up n’est pas nouveau chez Volkswagen. Il est apparu en 2011 sur une petite citadine abordable de la marque. Celle-ci était également déclinée en une version e-Up!, lancée quant à elle en 2013. La production de la e-Up! a pris fin en 2023. Elle avait alors pour cousines les Citigo et Mii chez Skoda et Seat.
La future ID. Up n’aura en revanche pas de cousine chez Skoda, Seat ou Cupra. Kai Grünitz, directeur du développement de Volkswagen, l’a confirmé à Autocar en mars 2025, sans exclure d’y revenir si la demande suit. L’ID. Polo, elle, partage sa plateforme MEB+ avec l’ID. Cross et les nouveaux Epiq et Raval. Volkswagen a encore peu détaillé la fiche technique de sa petite citadine, annoncée à partir d’environ 20 000 euros. Le concept ID. EVERY1 reçoit un nouveau moteur électrique de 70 kW (95 chevaux), pour une vitesse maximale de 130 km/h. La marque n’a en revanche communiqué ni la capacité ni la chimie de la batterie.
D’après Electrek, la citadine devrait reprendre le pack LFP (lithium-fer-phosphate) de 37 kWh de l’ID. Polo, qui offre jusqu’à 329 kilomètres d’autonomie WLTP à cette dernière. Volkswagen promet de son côté au moins 250 kilomètres pour le concept, ce qui laisse la porte ouverte à une batterie plus petite. À bord, la présentation devrait être reprise du concept, avec un poste de conduite très épuré. Celui-ci laisserait tout de même la part belle aux boutons physiques, comme l’avait laissé entendre la firme quelques mois plus tôt.
Avec 3,88 mètres de long, quatre places et 305 litres de coffre pour le concept, la future ID. Up se placera sous l’ID. Polo, vendue à partir de 24 995 euros. Elle visera surtout la Renault Twingo E-Tech, affichée à 19 490 euros avec 263 kilomètres d’autonomie WLTP, et la future Dacia Spring, que Dacia promet sous les 18 000 euros. Avec une production en série prévue fin 2027, Volkswagen arrivera plus d’un an après la Twingo.

articles.title: Marre des miles dans GTA 6 ? On peut changer les unités de mesure
articles.text:
GTA 6 est un jeu vidéo qui se déroule dans un monde ouvert immense et garni de détails, se situant à Leonida, un État inspiré de la Floride. Par conséquent, on y retrouve les unités de mesure utilisées aux États-Unis. Les distances sont exprimées selon le système impérial (pouces, pieds, yards et miles), les températures en degrés Fahrenheit, le poids en livres tandis que le système horaire se base sur des cycles de 12 heures.
Quand on habite en France, ces unités de mesure ne sont pas forcément très parlantes. Prenons l’exemple d’une longue distance à parcourir en voiture. Dans GTA 6, elle s’affiche par défaut en miles (un mile équivaut à environ 1,6 kilomètre). Si on n’a pas cette conversion en tête, savoir que notre futur point d’intérêt se trouve à 5 miles (environ 8 kilomètres) n’aidera pas beaucoup à se rendre compte du temps que cela prendra. Heureusement, on peut passer au système métrique.
Comment changer les unités de mesure dans GTA 6 ?
Rien ne vous oblige à vous coltiner des unités de mesure qui ne vous parlent pas dans GTA 6. Dans les paramètres, on peut tout modifier. Depuis le menu pause et l’onglet Paramètres, on se rend dans le sous-onglet Interface (quatre appuis sur le bouton de tranche droit, R1 sur PS5 ou RB sur Xbox) et on descend tout en bas. L’onglet compte 70 réglages et ceux dédiés aux unités sont à la fin. On peut donc facilement passer à côté en parcourant les menus.
On peut indépendamment changer chaque élément :
- Les distances selon le système impérial (États-Unis) ou métrique (France) ;
- Le poids en livres (États-Unis) ou en kilogrammes (France) ;
- La température en degrés Fahrenheit (États-Unis) ou degrés Celsius (France) ;
- Le système horaire au format 12 heures (États-Unis) ou 24 heures (France).
Les changements s’appliquent tout de suite à la partie en cours, sans avoir à relancer le jeu.
Vous pouvez mélanger les différentes unités, si vous le désirez.
Rockstar Games se montre plus souple que dans GTA 5. Sur l’épisode précédent, un seul réglage, rangé dans l’onglet Affichage, faisait passer tout le jeu d’un bloc du système impérial au système métrique.

articles.title: Filtrado el Razr Flex, la respuesta de Motorola al Galaxy Z Fold 8 y el iPhone Duo
articles.text:
El segmento de plegables con formato wide está pronto a sumar un nuevo contrincante a modelos como el Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8, el iPhone Duo y el Xiaomi 18 Fold. Se trata del Motorola Razr Flex, cuyas imágenes se han filtrado para revelar las principales características de su diseño.
Que Motorola está preparando un plegable de las citadas características no es una novedad. La compañía ya había dejado ver su silueta en un primer teaser, luego de que Apple diera el salto al mercado de móviles con pantallas flexibles. No obstante, ahora sí podemos verlo en todo su esplendor y con sus opciones de colores.
El material filtrado revela que el Motorola Razr Flex tiene un formato de libro como el del Razr Fold, pero con un diseño más ancho y retacón. Este dispositivo expandirá el catálogo de la marca posicionándose como una alterativa más compacta y que busca sacar provecho del concepto de "tablet de bolsillo".
Los móviles plegables con relación de aspecto 4:3 destacan por permitir mayor maniobrabilidad al usar la pantalla exterior con una sola mano. Asimismo, la pantalla interior suele destacar por brindar un formato optimizado para el consumo multimedia y la productividad; esto último, gracias a que permite una mejor ejecución de dos apps lado a lado.
Así es el Motorola Razr Flex
Las imágenes filtradas por SammyGuru presentan al Motorola Razr Flex en dos colores: verde y marrón. Los nombres oficiales de los dispositivos estarían vinculados con referencias oficiales de PANTONE, como ya es costumbre de la marca. En el caso de la versión verde, la parte trasera presentaría un acabado tipo tela, mientras que en la marrón sería similar al cuero. En ambos casos, los marcos metálicos estarían pintados con tonos acordes.
El material de marketing también permite apreciar al Motorola Razr Flex abierto en posiciones intermedias. Esto permitiría darle funcionalidades adicionales, más allá de lo que se puede hacer con el equipo totalmente abierto o cerrado. En la parte trasera también se observa que el fabricante abandonaría el módulo de cámaras que caracteriza a sus demás smartphones y que incorporaría un bloque tipo píldora, centrado y en horizontal.
Las especificaciones técnicas definitivas del Motorola Razr Flex son todavía un misterio. Sin embargo, filtraciones previas indican que será más pequeño que el Galaxy Z Fold 8. La pantalla exterior podría ser de 4,97 pulgadas, mientras que la interior alcanzaría las 6,92 pulgadas. Ambas medidas son bastante inferiores a las del plegable de Samsung, que cuenta con paneles de 5,5 y 7,6 pulgadas.
Sobre precio y fecha de lanzamiento, todavía no hay novedades. Se especula con que Motorola podría presentar el Razr Flex a comienzos de 2027, durante el CES. Aunque también se rumora un posible anuncio antes de finales del corriente año, con miras a lanzarlo el que viene.

articles.title: Newly Patched VMware vCenter Flaw Exploited as Zero-Day by Chinese APT
articles.text:
A China-linked espionage group exploited a VMware vCenter zero-day vulnerability for more than two months before Broadcom released a patch on Thursday, according to Google.
Tracked as CVE-2026-123890 (CVSS score of 9.8), the bug resides in the VMware Directory Service and could let remote, unauthenticated attackers obtain an authenticated session with administrator privileges.
Mandiant, which reported the bug to Broadcom, has linked its exploitation to Armory Castle, a suspected Chinese threat actor formerly tracked as UNC5221 and also known as Warp Panda.
According to Mandiant, the hackers gained initial access through CVE-2026-102764, a recently patched BeyondTrust Remote Support zero-day. They then pivoted to Linux appliances on the internal network and targeted vCenter in early September.
They used a custom tool called Bonesaw to exploit CVE-2026-123890, steal the Lightning Memory-Mapped Database (LMDB), extract SAML signing material, and create a single sign-on (SSO) administrator account.
Next, the attackers deployed a second tool to forge SAML tokens and installed backdoors. They also took the vCenter master encryption key and database credentials, then moved to an ESXi host and extracted additional information.
“Mandiant has evidence that Armory Castle had knowledge of CVE-2026-123890 prior to the disclosure of CVE-2026-59309 on July 29, 2026,” Google notes.
Bonesaw was used against a vCenter server already patched for CVE-2026-59309, a separate vCenter authentication bypass disclosed in July.
Charles Carmakal, CTO at Mandiant, said on LinkedIn that the company investigated multiple incidents involving Armory Castle’s exploitation of CVE-2026-123890.
Broadcom has released fixes in vCenter versions 9.1.1.0200, 9.0.2.0200, and 8.0 U3m. According to Mandiant, Bonesaw works against vCenter 7.x and 8.x. However, there is no public patch for version 7.0, which reached end of general support in October 2025.
Broadcom’s advisory, which also resolves four SDDC Manager and VMware Tools flaws, does not mention in-the-wild exploitation.
“Organizations should both apply the patches and examine their systems for evidence of compromise,” Carmakal said.

articles.title: Es un gesto casi absurdo, pero es una forma práctica de abrir y guardar los paquetes de espaguetis en la despensa
articles.text:
Los paquetes de espaguetis son largos, estrechos y poco cómodos de guardar cuando ya están abiertos. Sacar una ración por el extremo superior es sencillo, pero después hay que recoger el plástico que sobra y buscar la manera de sujetarlo antes de devolverlo a la despensa. La forma de abrir el envase puede facilitar ese segundo paso.
El truco consiste en cortar el paquete a lo largo, siguiendo la dirección de los espaguetis. Así puedes acceder a la pasta por un lateral y utilizar el propio envoltorio para recoger lo que quede después de cocinar. Basta con unas tijeras y una goma o un trozo de celo para el cierre.
Cómo hacer el corte y volver a cerrar el paquete
Primero, tumba el paquete sobre una superficie y haz un pequeño corte en una de las puntas del plástico. Desde ahí, continúa hasta el extremo contrario. La abertura debe recorrer la longitud del envase, de modo que puedas separar sus bordes y sacar los espaguetis con la mano.
Retira la cantidad que necesites y deja el resto sobre el envoltorio. El plástico abierto queda alrededor de la pasta, como un estuche desplegado. Para cerrarlo, vuelve a envolver los espaguetis que han sobrado y sujeta el paquete con una goma. Si prefieres usar celo, puedes fijar con él el borde del plástico.
Guardarlo bien también depende del lugar y del cierre
Para conservar la pasta seca, Barilla recomienda un lugar fresco y sin humedad, tanto si el envase está abierto como si sigue cerrado. La marca señala una despensa o un armario como sitios adecuados y aconseja consumir sus productos dentro de la fecha de consumo preferente indicada en el paquete.
Barilla también desaconseja guardar las cajas de sus productos de pasta seca en la nevera o en el congelador, porque la pasta puede absorber humedad. Esta indicación se refiere expresamente a la pasta envasada en cajas, estén abiertas o cerradas.
Si buscas un cierre hermético, la Asociación Nacional de la Pasta de Estados Unidos recomienda guardar la pasta seca en un recipiente o caja herméticos. Sujetar el envoltorio con una goma sirve para recogerlo, pero no permite dar por hecho que el envase haya quedado sellado herméticamente.
La misma asociación aconseja terminar primero los paquetes que llevan más tiempo guardados antes de abrir otros nuevos. Puedes aplicar esa pauta al organizar la despensa y reservar para el siguiente uso el paquete de espaguetis que ya tienes empezado.
