articles.title: Producing Healthy Code with Artificial Intelligence Costs Fewer Tokens
articles.text:
Agentic AI can speed up velocity, but the gains vanish within months as code complexity grows. In his presentation on AI-friendly code at GOTO Copenhagen, Adam Tornhill showed that healthy code makes AI perform better and costs fewer tokens. Safeguarding means keeping code health high through agentic refactoring, with an MCP supplying code health data, so AI can maintain the code it generates.
Developing software with agents is significantly harder than writing code manually, Tornhill argued. But with agentic AI, they can complete tasks two to three times faster, he added. It also helps them unblock themselves and reduces coordination needs.
Tornhill mentioned a study done on 1000+ open-source projects which showed that with AI, velocity went up during the first few weeks, but after two months the velocity gains were fully canceled out due to a massive increase in code complexity:
AI operates in a self-harm mode, often writing code it cannot reliably maintain later.
Code health measures how easy code is to understand, change, and maintain. Research done on human coding (before AI) shows that if you have healthy code, you can be up to 10x faster than someone who works on similar problems in unhealthy code, Tornhill said. The defect risk is reduced 15 times, and code reviews go twice as quickly, he added.
Building a prototype was never the hard problem in software; 95% of the costs for any software project come after the first release. This is where code quality, maintainability, and architecture start to matter, Tornhill said.
Recent research shows that large language models perform consistently better in healthy code. AI won’t generate perfect code; if we want to survive in the Agentic age, we need to focus on safeguarding, Tornhill said.
The average codebase has a code health of 5.15, where AI-friendly code starts at 9.5. Technical depth is a bottleneck for enterprise adoption of agentic coding; what’s needed is an agentic refactoring, Tornhill argued. Claude can be used to fix code health issues, but only to a certain extent:
As a best-case scenario, an agent can fix roughly 50% of the code health issues for lower-health code. Once the code health improves, the AI performance drops sharply, and Claude can only correctly refactor 20% of the code. AI tends to become conservative, doing small changes that don’t really move the needle on code quality.
Adding an MCP with code health data can lead to a 90%-100% fix rate, Tornhill said. Agentic refactoring turned out to be a predictable and mechanical process at scale, where AI was capable of doing codebase-specific refactorings.
Healthy code is also financially viable code, with healthy code, you can do things with 40% to 45% fewer tokens, Tornhill said.
By refactoring code, modularizing it and making it healthy, we can also reduce organizational friction, Tornhill said. Code quality at the module level is a largely solved problem with the automation we now have. Scaling AI friendliness to the design and architectural level is the next big challenge, he concluded.
InfoQ interviewed Adam Tornhill after his talk.
InfoQ: How can we measure code health?
Adam Tornhill: Code Health is a multifacetted concept, so we need to combine multiple metrics. We’ve found that it works best when combining measures from three levels of software design:
- Module level design: e.g. are your modules cohesive and do one thing well? Or are there multiple, unrelated responsibilities?
- Function level design: e.g. how well-designed are the individual function blocks? How expressive are their APIs?
- Implementation level: where you want to avoid any accidental complexity in how the code is written such as deeply nested logic, excessive copy-paste, etc?
InfoQ: How do you safeguard AI-generated code?
Tornhill: Safeguarding needs to happen at multiple levels, and all safeguards need to be completely automated in an agentic context. Examples of concrete safeguards include linting, code coverage, mutation testing to ensure your tests actually test, and higher-level metrics like Code Health. In practice, these safeguards are exposed to agents as local MCP servers or command-line tools.
InfoQ: How can we do refactoring at scale with agents?
Tornhill: The main steps are to establish a baseline, build a safety-net for behavior, and provide a feedback loop to the agents refactoring the code. The whole process is highly iterative.
- The baselining step focuses on measuring code quality to identify what needs improving.
- The safety-net is a reliable test suite that helps preserve the existing behavior of the codebase.
- The agentic feedback loop builds on objective code health information and test outcomes so that the AI can determine whether a change moves the code quality closer to the goal.
- Finally, enable the agents to learn. In our study on Refactoring at Scale with Agents, we instructed agents to build an evolving playbook of successful codebase-specific refactoring patterns.

articles.title: Using NVIDIA Run:ai GPU Fractioning on Amazon EKS | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Using NVIDIA Run:ai GPU Fractioning on Amazon EKS
GPU sharing is not new: Multi-Instance GPU (MIG), time-slicing, and Multi-Process Service (MPS) address different isolation and utilization needs. NVIDIA Run:ai GPU Fractioning builds on MPS with Kubernetes-integrated scheduling, per-Pod memory contracts, enforcement, and metrics.
NVIDIA Run:ai is AI workload orchestration software for Kubernetes. Its GPU Fractioning Operator can help several teams share one or two GPUs on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS). Notebooks, model evaluations, and small inference services can leave teams waiting even when GPU memory remains available. In this walkthrough’s baseline, the NVIDIA device plugin exposes the single GPU as one nvidia.com/gpu resource, with GPU sharing disabled. Two Pods each requesting nvidia.com/gpu: 1 cannot run concurrently on that node, even when their combined GPU-memory demand fits.
NVIDIA Run:ai GPU Fractioning adds Kubernetes scheduling integration, enforced GPU-memory limits, and per-Pod metrics to software-based sharing. The approach applies to NVIDIA GPUs that meet the GPU Fractioning Operator’s hardware and software requirements, including GPUs without MIG. We use one Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) g5.xlarge instance with an NVIDIA A10G Tensor Core GPU as the validated example. Other configurations require compatibility checks and validation.
NVIDIA announced the open source release of NVIDIA Run:ai on October 13, 2026. This example uses two of its four modular components: KAI Scheduler and GPU Fractioning Operator. KAI Resource Management and Workload Map address organizational governance and additional workload types, outside this walkthrough’s scope.
In this post, we show how to build a custom Amazon Linux 2023 (AL2023) image and configure GPU-memory sharing on Amazon EKS. In the validated G5/A10G example, you establish a whole-GPU baseline, give each Pod an 8 GiB memory contract, and verify 6 GiB allocations. You then inspect per-Pod metrics, test rejection of a 9 GiB allocation, and clean up the disposable environment.
Choose a GPU sharing approach
MIG provides hardware partitions on supported GPUs. Device-plugin time-slicing shares a GPU without replica memory or fault isolation. MPS permits concurrent CUDA processes. Fault containment depends on configuration. NVIDIA Run:ai GPU Fractioning adds enforced per-container memory limits and supports time-slicing (default) or sm-sharing compute modes. NVIDIA documents separate workload error domains for its default mode and a shared error domain for sm-sharing. These are not security guarantees. This walkthrough tests memory limits, not fault containment or compute performance. A memory limit does not reserve proportional compute.
Amazon EKS documents several GPU sharing options: MIG, time-slicing with the NVIDIA device plugin, and time-slicing with the NVIDIA DRA driver and Karpenter. For guidance on choosing among them, see the GPU sharing guidance in the Amazon EKS Best Practices Guide. Choose GPU fractioning when you need enforced per-Pod GPU-memory limits on GPUs without MIG and can run fixed-size GPU node groups.
Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) provides Kubernetes APIs for requesting and allocating devices. GPU sharing and isolation depend on the device driver’s implementation and enabled features. KAI Scheduler and GPU Operator support DRA. This walkthrough uses NvFractions annotations, not DRA.
GPU fractioning can help interactive notebooks with idle periods, short evaluation jobs, GPU compatibility tests, and small inference services. Choose each GPU-memory request from measured peak usage plus overhead, then test latency under concurrent load. The demonstrated density improvement does not establish a throughput gain or a universal cost reduction.
Solution overview
The following diagram shows the validated single-GPU environment in the US East (Ohio) Region (us-east-2). You use the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), eksctl, Helm, and Packer to build and operate it. The Amazon EKS control plane runs Kubernetes version 1.36 in an AWS managed Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC), separate from the customer VPC. It connects to EC2 workers in private subnets of the customer VPC.
An m7i.large system node hosts the operator controllers and KAI Scheduler. KAI Scheduler places both Pods on a tainted g5.xlarge with one A10G containing 23,028 MiB of GPU memory.
Each Pod has an 8 GiB GPU-memory limit and allocates 6 GiB of GPU memory. The GPU worker uses custom AL2023 with the NVIDIA R615 driver branch, NVIDIA Container Toolkit, and containerd. It runs fractiond with Node Resource Interface (NRI) integration and MPS for sharing. The metricsd daemon exports per-Pod GPU-memory metrics.
Implementation walkthrough
The walkthrough uses the AWS Samples repository. Confirm the prerequisites and validated component versions, then complete Steps 1 through 10.
Prerequisites
Use an AWS account with permissions for Amazon EKS, AWS CloudFormation, Amazon VPC, Amazon EC2, Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS), AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), and AWS Systems Manager for Amazon Machine Image (AMI) discovery. Confirm quota and capacity for g5.xlarge, the system node, and a temporary m5.xlarge image builder. Install AWS CLI v2, eksctl, kubectl, Helm, Packer, Git, jq, and curl.
Use your normal AWS credential provider: a named profile, AWS IAM Identity Center, an assumed role, or access-key environment variables. Prefer temporary credentials. AWS_SESSION_TOKEN is required when using temporary access keys. The examples use us-east-2. Another Region must support the selected Amazon EKS version and instance types.
Before choosing another GPU, check NVIDIA’s GPU Operator hardware list, the selected driver’s hardware support, and the GPU Fractioning Operator prerequisites. Hardware support alone does not establish fractioning compatibility. This walkthrough validates the G5/A10G configuration only. The AMI build targets x86_64. Check CUDA compatibility and memory headroom: The two 8 GiB contracts require room for both contracts and runtime overhead. Smaller devices need smaller contracts and adjusted probes.
The walkthrough creates billable resources, including an Amazon EKS control plane, a NAT gateway, instances, volumes, and an AMI snapshot. Use a disposable environment and complete cleanup when validation finishes.
Use the validated AL2023 stack
At the time of validation, the EKS-optimized AL2023 NVIDIA image provided R580 and R595 driver branches. GPU Fractioning Operator v0.1.7 requires R615 or newer. R615 is short-lived and is not the GPU Operator default. This example builds a custom standard Amazon EKS 1.36 AL2023 image with AMI-owned driver and toolkit. It does not use an operator-managed driver container on another OS. The table records lab validation, not vendor support certification.
| Component | Validated version | 
| Amazon EKS | 1.36 | 
| GPU | NVIDIA A10G, 23,028 MiB | 
| NVIDIA driver / Container Toolkit | 615.71.10 / 1.20.1-1 | 
| containerd | 2.3.5 with NRI | 
| GPU Operator / device plugin | 26.7.1 / 0.20.1 | 
| KAI Scheduler / Fractioning Operator | 0.18.5 / 0.1.7 | 
We validated this walkthrough on October 22, 2026, using NVIDIA driver 615.71.10. On November 18, 2026, after updating the GPU node taint, we repeated every step except the Step 3 image build, using an image with the same driver. The results matched. The table lists the tested component versions, not a permanent support matrix. Recheck the Amazon EKS AMI documentation and NVIDIA prerequisites before changing any component.
Step 1: Clone and configure
Clone the repository, then create a local configuration file from the provided example and restrict its permissions:
After cloning, use walkthrough.env for configuration and run.sh for each stage. Generated files and kubeconfig stay in the ignored .state directory. GPU_INSTANCE_TYPE selects the instance type. Changing it alone does not establish compatibility.
Defaults and optional authentication settings in walkthrough.env
Never commit credentials. The local configuration file is ignored by Git. Confirm the active identity before provisioning:
Run stages separately to inspect results, or use ./run.sh walkthrough to run through the memory-limit test. Cleanup is always a separate action.
Step 2: Create the disposable cluster
Run the following command to create the disposable Amazon EKS cluster and its system node:
The command provisions an Amazon EKS cluster running Kubernetes version 1.36, a dedicated VPC with one NAT gateway, OpenID Connect (OIDC) integration, and a private m7i.large managed node.
Selected fields from config/eksctl-cluster.yaml.tpl
Step 3: Build the custom AL2023 image
Run the following command to build the custom AL2023 image with the R615 driver branch:
The script discovers a public builder subnet and the recommended standard Amazon EKS AMI for Kubernetes 1.36 on AL2023. Packer installs the current patch release from the R615 driver branch and the toolkit, configures the NVIDIA runtime, checks package state, and creates an encrypted image. The Region-specific AMI ID is stored in .state/ami-id.
NVIDIA_DRIVER_VERSION selects the R615 branch. It is not an exact patch pin. The workflow records the discovered driver version with the AMI ID and uses that version in AMI and node-group tags. Read .state/installed-driver-version for the version observed in your build. For production, pin exact packages and the base image in your own build and validate a supported driver-branch upgrade.
You need this step only because the EKS-optimized AL2023 NVIDIA AMI did not include the R615 driver branch at the time of validation. Prefer an EKS-optimized NVIDIA AMI once the driver that it selects for your GPU and the remaining host prerequisites meet the GPU Fractioning Operator requirements. Check the driver versions in the Amazon EKS AMI releases on GitHub. The sample’s scripts currently require the R615 driver and metadata from the image build, so using a stock AMI also requires script changes.
Relevant Packer settings from ami/eks-al2023-r615.pkr.hcl
SOURCE_AMI_ID and PACKER_SUBNET_ID are optional overrides for an approved base image or builder subnet. Rebuild and test images when the operating system or GPU stack changes.
Step 4: Add the GPU worker
Run the following command to add a GPU managed node group that uses the custom image:
By default, the managed node group uses the custom image and stays at one On-Demand g5.xlarge, the validated GPU worker. A GPU taint excludes ordinary workloads. The script disables eksctl’s NVIDIA device-plugin installation because GPU Operator manages that component.
Selected fields from config/eksctl-gpu-nodegroup.yaml.tpl
Step 5: Install GPU Operator and inspect the host
Run the following command to install GPU Operator and inspect the GPU worker’s host configuration:
GPU Operator 26.7.1 supplies the device plugin and Kubernetes integrations. Its configuration preserves the image-owned driver and toolkit:
The same command runs a temporary privileged inspection Pod on the GPU worker, prints the host configuration, and removes the Pod. The validated node reports:
Observed host configuration
On this AL2023 node, /var/run is a symbolic link to /run. Both paths identify the same socket. Limit privileged inspection to the disposable environment and confirm the Pod is removed.
Step 6: Establish the whole-GPU baseline
Run the following command to test whole-GPU scheduling before fractioning is installed:
Each baseline Pod requests and limits nvidia.com/gpu to 1. The test assumes one available physical GPU with sharing disabled: One Pod runs and the other remains Pending. This demonstrates the whole-device scheduling constraint before fractioning is installed. On multi-GPU nodes, adapt this baseline and verify that both fractional workloads use the same GPU.
Measured baseline result
The script checks this state and removes both baseline Pods.
Step 7: Install KAI Scheduler and GPU Fractioning Operator
Run the following command to install KAI Scheduler, which includes GPU Fractioning Operator:
The pinned KAI Scheduler 0.18.5 chart includes GPU Fractioning Operator 0.1.7. The values turn on NvFractions and per-Pod metrics while retaining GPU-stack version checks. The optional nvidia.com/container.<name>.gpu-compute.mode annotation selects compute mode. These workloads leave the default unchanged.
Relevant fields from helm/kai-values.yaml
In the validation, FractiondReady, MpsdReady, and Ready are True. DriverUpgradeInProgress is False with reason NoDriverUpgrade, consistent with the AMI retaining driver ownership.
Step 8: Run the positive sharing test
Run the following command to deploy two Pods with 8 GiB GPU-memory contracts:
Each Pod requests and limits memory to 8 GiB and selects kai-scheduler. Neither requests a whole nvidia.com/gpu resource. The repository applies these scheduling fields and runs a CUDA probe that allocates 6 GiB:
Essential fields from kubernetes/fraction-8gi-pods.yaml
Measured positive result
The script verifies matching node names and GPU UUIDs. In the validation, both Pods see 8,192 MiB and report allocation_succeeded_mib=6144. Those checks establish placement on one physical GPU, the bounded device view, and successful allocations within each contract.
Measured allocation output from each Pod
Observe memory while both Pods remain active
The gpu_fractioning_gpu_memory_used_bytes metric attributes memory by Pod and GPU UUID. The observed 6,394 MiB (about 6.24 GiB) per Pod exceeds the probe’s 6,144 MiB allocation by 250 MiB. Metrics can include CUDA context and runtime overhead. This experiment does not measure that breakdown. Retain workload identity and request, limit, and usage values together when monitoring the shared device.
Measured per-Pod metric series
Step 9: Verify rejection above the limit
Run the following command to test an allocation that exceeds the 8 GiB contract:
This command removes the positive-test Pods and creates one Pod with an 8 GiB contract that attempts a 9 GiB allocation. The probe reports:
Measured over-limit result
Measured negative-test Pod status
Here, cudaMalloc returns an out-of-memory error, which the probe handles before exiting with code 0. Completed is expected, not OOMKilled. This demonstrates allocation rejection, not container termination or general fault isolation.
Step 10: Clean up
Capture the VPC ID before deleting the cluster. The independent checks that follow use the default cluster name and Region. Substitute your configured values if you changed them.
Capture the VPC ID
Remove the disposable environment
Standard cleanup removes the test namespace, Helm releases, and disposable cluster while preserving the custom AMI and its Amazon EBS snapshot.
Verify resource deletion
Expect explicit resource-not-found responses for deleted resources. Authentication or permission errors do not establish deletion. Also inspect remaining node groups and cluster-tagged instances. If cleanup fails, inspect CloudFormation events and resolve owned dependencies before retrying. An absent Amazon EKS endpoint does not prove that its VPC is gone.
Use ./run.sh cleanup-all only when the custom AMI and its Amazon EBS snapshot are no longer needed. If image deletion is refused, confirm the AMI ID and sample ownership tag. Do not bypass the safeguard.
Production considerations
Treat this as a behavior validation. Use trusted workloads and apply least-privilege IAM, namespace controls, approved images, and admission rules for fraction requests. Choose whole GPUs or MIG on supported hardware when stronger isolation is required.
The pinned fractioning daemons use privileged containers, host PID access, and NRI/MPS host mounts. Restrict their deployment and configuration to trusted administrators.
Allow headroom for CUDA contexts, caches, batching, and runtime overhead. Measure latency and throughput under concurrent load. Monitor allocation failures, MPS health, NRI connectivity, and GPU errors. Pin the base AMI, driver, toolkit, device plugin, operator, scheduler, and workload images as one tested combination. Rebuild images and test rollback before rollout.
This walkthrough requires pre-provisioned GPU capacity. It does not configure or validate GPU-fraction-aware autoscaling. The fractional Pods select kai-scheduler, request no nvidia.com/gpu resource, and use a nodeSelector that targets a node group fixed at one node. Karpenter support for secondary schedulers is an open feature request (issue #742 on GitHub). The custom image cannot run on Amazon EKS Auto Mode-managed nodes, because Auto Mode selects and manages their AMI. A cluster can mix Auto Mode-managed nodes with managed node groups, but we did not validate this walkthrough in such a cluster.
Teams that use Karpenter can reference the same custom AMI by ID in an EC2NodeClass. The autoscaling limit still applies. We did not validate this path.
KAI Scheduler is a second scheduler. It handles queueing and placement for Pods that select it. If you already use Kueue, decide which component owns queueing for GPU workloads before you adopt KAI Scheduler.
We recommend running the Amazon EKS node monitoring agent on GPU nodes. In a November 18, 2026 regression run, the agent ran on the custom R615 image with MPS sharing active and reported healthy GPU conditions throughout the sharing and limit tests. That run did not test fault detection. Because GPU Operator already runs a Data Center GPU Manager (DCGM) host engine, configure the agent to use that host engine instead of its bundled one.
Conclusion
In this post, we showed how to configure GPU-memory fractioning on Amazon EKS with a custom AL2023 image, using G5/A10G as the validated example. The approach extends to compatible NVIDIA GPUs after checking prerequisites and validating the selected configuration. You established the whole-GPU baseline, ran two bounded workloads on the same GPU, inspected per-Pod memory usage, and verified rejection of an allocation above the limit. Fractioning can improve access to existing capacity when workload memory fits. Production adoption also requires isolation controls and performance testing.
To repeat the experiment, clone the AWS Samples repository and compare your results with its validated evidence. Explore the GPU Fractioning Operator documentation and the Amazon EKS accelerated AMI guidance before adapting the example to your workloads.
The content and opinions in this post are those of the third-party author and AWS is not responsible for the content or accuracy of this post.

articles.title: UK government forced to disclose secret Apple backdoor order | TechCrunch
articles.text:
The U.K. government has been ordered to confirm that it issued a secret order demanding Apple to provide authorities with encrypted customer information.
The Thursday ruling from the U.K.’s Investigatory Powers Tribunal, an independent court that allows citizens to challenge government surveillance orders, is a rare rebuke for the government, which sought to keep the encryption backdoor order a state secret.
The tribunal’s ruling rejected the Home Office’s claim that disclosing the order would be damaging to national security.
The ruling comes a year after the U.K. government reportedly demanded that Apple build a backdoor to allow U.K. authorities access to customer data anywhere in the world. Details of the so-called “technical capabilities notice,” which are issued under strict non-disclosure rules, leaked to the media, which drew ire from White House officials and U.S. lawmakers who criticized the effort, arguing that the U.K. order would put Americans’ privacy at risk.
California-based Apple refused the order, and blocked U.K. users from switching on its Advanced Data Protection data-encryption feature for iCloud, rather than comply with the demand. The U.K.’s secret order was later narrowed to allow access to British nationals’ data stored in Apple’s encrypted cloud, and Apple also challenged this second order.
Prior to the ruling, Apple was legally barred from disclosing the order, even after details leaked. When reached for comment, Apple told TechCrunch that it welcomes the decision to make public the fact that the U.K. Home Office issued a technical capability notice.
Apple previously said that it has “never built a backdoor or master key” to any of its products or services and “never will.”
A spokesperson for the U.K. Home Office, which has yet to confirm the existence of a notice, did not respond to a request for comment.
Rights group Liberty International, which brought the legal challenge on behalf of two individuals, said that this is the first known time that the government has been compelled to confirm the existence of a secret technical order.
A final hearing on what specific order details can be released is anticipated next year.
Updated with comment.

articles.title: Ukraine deploys homemade 'flying modems' in daring drone attack to destroy Crimean Bridge, ditching Elon Musk's Starlink — airborne relay stations allow pilots to dodge Russian air defences to deliver 1,200kg payload
articles.text:
Ukraine deploys homemade 'flying modems' in daring drone attack to destroy Crimean Bridge, ditching Elon Musk's Starlink — airborne relay stations allow pilots to dodge Russian air defenses to deliver 1,200kg payload
Ukraine used a network of so-called "flying modems" to maintain a live video feed of the attack despite Russia's attempts to jam the signal.
Ukrainian forces ditched Elon Musk's Starlink wireless system and used their own relay network of "flying modems" to maintain a live feed of an attack on the Crimean Bridge, even amid Russian attempts to block the signal. The attack, which led to the partial collapse of the bridge, was significant for a number of reasons. The bridge is one of Russian President Vladimir Putin's most symbolic assets due to its linking of the occupied Crimean Peninsula and Russia. But perhaps more importantly, the attack's use of Ukrainian connectivity technology highlights the country's lessening of its reliance on Starlink. The modems were crucial to the success of the mission, with the FT reporting that they kept missiles connected to their pilots while they manoeuvred through Russia's air defenses.
Videos of the attack showed Flamingo missiles, carrying a 1,200kg warhead, being remotely piloted towards the bridge. Flamingo missiles are capable of traveling at around 590 miles per hour, requiring a stable and reliable video feed. It's reported that the Ukrainians deliberately chose not to use Starshield, the military version of Musk's Starlink, for the operation, with the company's satellite network having been restricted in recent weeks. That restricted service would have been insufficient for the Crimean Bridge attack, forcing Ukrainian forces to find another solution. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said this week that he has not been told why Starlink's connection has been throttled, with neither the White House nor the Pentagon being forthcoming. SpaceX, Starlink's parent company, has also so far not provided any explanation. However, relations between Zelenskyy and Musk appear to be strained, with the SpaceX CEO saying that Ukraine had "gone too far" by striking Russian data centers.
With Starlink, or Starshield, no longer fit for Ukraine's needs, it turned to the "flying drones" instead. The flying communications towers were used as a relay, boosting the signal sent from individual missiles so that it could more readily reach their pilots. This approach allowed the weapons to fly farther while still maintaining a reliable connection, allowing them to bypass Russian air defense systems and attempts to block their signals in the process. Without the relays, Ukrainian drone pilots have previously had to program missiles with coordinates and then rely on their autopilot system. They were inevitably shot down because they could not be steered away from Russian defenses.
Perhaps ironically, Ukraine isn't the first country to use flying communications towers. Russian forces were using similar technology as early as 2023, before the system began using a Chinese mesh networking system.

articles.title: Insta360's new Toast photo frame can stand on a desk, stick to the front of your fridge, or hang around your neck
articles.text:
Insta360's latest gadget is a pocket-sized color e-paper photo frame called Toast that lasts for 195 days between battery charges
A neat frame for your memories
- Insta360's new photo frame is called the Toast
- It features a 3.7-inch, six-color e-paper display
- For now it's only available to buy in China
Insta360 is taking a break from action cameras to give us the Toast, a pocket-sized, e-paper photo frame that checks a lot of the boxes we look for in gadgets here at TechRadar: stylish looks, innovative tech, an affordable price, and lots and lots of battery life.
The key specs you need to know (via Notebookcheck) are a 3.7-inch, color E Ink Spectra 6 display with a 720 x 480 pixel resolution (that's 234 pixels per inch), and a battery capacity of 400mAh — apparently good enough for 195 days between charges.
Wi-Fi 6 connectivity is supported, and you can get your photos onto the Toast via WeChat or the Insta360 app. Supported formats are PNG, JPEG, and HEIF, with room for 30 photos on the internal storage and 200 in the cloud.
If you have one of the company's newer cameras — such as the Insta360 Luna Ultra — you can sync images straight over from the device, no app needed, as long as you're signed up for the Insta360+ cloud storage service.
Around your neck or on the fridge
Some other details we have from Insta360: dimensions of 62.5 x 96 x 5.25mm (2.5 x 3.8 x 0.2 inches), a weight of 1.5 ounces / 43 grams, and an IPX4 rating for some minimal protection against splashes.
In a rather unusual twist, a lanyard is included as well as a desk stand, so you can wear the Toast around your neck if you'd like, though we're not sure that we can see that catching on, given its size. There are also accessories for sticking it to your fridge or attaching it to your bag or belt if you prefer.
Insta360 says the six-color e-paper display (red, yellow, blue, green, black, and white) makes photos look richer and more natural, and there's no backlight, which should help with the natural printed-picture look.

It's on sale now for CNY429 (about $65 / £50 / AU$100), but only in China for the time being. There's no word yet on international availability, but, given that Insta360 sells other products globally, we're hoping to see it become more widely available soon.

articles.title: Microsoft stellt To Do ein – und lässt private Nutzer ohne Alternative zurück
articles.text:
Microsoft stellt To Do ein: Welche App den Wunderlist-Nachfolger künftig ersetzen soll
Microsoft übernahm im Jahr 2015 das Berliner Unternehmen 6Wunderkinder, das die Organisations-App Wunderlist entwickelt hat. Wie das Wall Street Journal damals berichtete, soll die Kaufsumme zwischen 100 und 200 Millionen Dollar gelegen haben. Microsoft stellte Wunderlist 2020 ein, stattdessen entwickelte das Team die App To Do. Jetzt soll aber auch damit bald Schluss sein. Wie der Tech-Konzern in einem Beitrag auf seiner Support-Seite mitteilt, wird die App zum 30. Juni 2027 eingestellt. Für private Nutzer:innen bietet Microsoft keine Alternative an. Sie sollen sich stattdessen „eine andere Aufgabenverwaltungsanwendung [suchen], die ihren Anforderungen entspricht“.
Wer jetzt auf den Planner umsteigen muss
Die Änderung betrifft alle, die To Do im Web, unter Windows, Mac, iOS und Android nutzen. Das gilt sowohl für den beruflichen und schulischen Einsatz als auch für private Microsoft-Konten. Der zugrundeliegende Dienst, die APIs und die Synchronisierung sollen zu separat festgelegten Zeitpunkten eingestellt werden. Diese Termine und die nötigen Vorbereitungsmaßnahmen will der Konzern später bekannt geben.
In dem Beitrag heißt es: „Für Arbeits- oder Schulkonten wird Microsoft Planner die Plattform sein, auf der persönliche Aufgaben neben zugewiesenen Arbeitsaufgaben verwaltet werden können.“ Eine entsprechende Funktion soll ab Dezember schrittweise eingeführt werden, in der Aufgaben dann übersichtlich als Liste erscheinen. Auf Daten aus To Do können Nutzer:innen dort noch bis zum 30. Juni 2027 zugreifen. Danach können sie diese im Planner nicht mehr anzeigen oder verwalten.
Nutzer:innen von To Do reagieren enttäuscht
To Do endet auch für private Microsoft-Konten, einschließlich Microsoft 365 Personal und Family. Für sie ist der Planner allerdings nicht verfügbar. Nutzer:innen mit entsprechenden Abonnements stehen damit künftig ohne App da. Microsoft rät ihnen, sich eine andere Anwendung zu suchen, mit der sie künftig ihre privaten Aufgaben verwalten möchten. Bei ihnen löst die Änderung entsprechend Frust aus. Einer dieser Nutzer:innen ist Abhijith M B, Redakteur bei Windows Latest. „Für jemanden wie mich, der To Do täglich nutzt, ist das verheerend“, schreibt er in einem Artikel. Über das Ende der App sei er „zutiefst enttäuscht“.
Auch für Nutzer:innen mit Arbeits- oder Schulkonto ändert sich mit dem Umstieg auf den Planner einiges. Microsoft weist selbst darauf hin, dass beide Apps unterschiedliche Aufgaben- und Kollaborationsmodelle verwenden. Der Konzern rät Kund:innen, die künftig statt To Do den Planner nutzen müssen, sich schon jetzt mit der neuen App vertraut zu machen und zu prüfen, wie das ihre Arbeitsabläufe ändert. Vor dem Ende von To Do will Microsoft außerdem eine Möglichkeit zum Datenexport bereitstellen. Weitere Informationen dazu sollen aber erst später folgen. Eine automatische Übertragung der Daten in den Planner ist nicht vorgesehen.

articles.title: Une Tesla Model Y sans volant ni pédales : le nouveau pari risqué d'Elon Musk — Frandroid
articles.text:
Ça y est, Tesla vient de franchir une nouvelle étape dans son développement. La firme américaine a en effet ouvert les commandes de son Cybercab aux particuliers, à 29 990 dollars (environ 27 200 euros, hors taxes). Le tout avec des conditions particulièrement contraignantes : la voiture ne roule que dans les zones couvertes par le service Robotaxi et exige un abonnement de 299 dollars par mois (environ 270 euros). En parallèle, le constructeur tente toujours de faire autoriser en Europe son FSD, une aide à la conduite avancée qui exige un conducteur attentif. Les États membres pourraient voter en décembre, au plus tôt, sur son homologation dans toute l’Union européenne. Mais Tesla ne compte pas s’arrêter là.
Elon Musk a encore un autre projet dans ses cartons, repéré par Electrek. Le CEO de Tesla s’est exprimé ce mercredi 18 novembre au DealBook Summit du New York Times. Il y a annoncé que Tesla prévoit une version autonome de sa Model Y, capable de transporter six ou sept personnes. Celle-ci serait totalement dépourvue de volant et de pédales, comme c’est le cas pour le Cybercab. Ce nouveau modèle compléterait le Cybercab, qui ne compte que deux places.
L’homme d’affaires explique que « nous avons toujours besoin de véhicules autonomes si vous êtes quatre ou six, ou une famille entière ». Il reconnaît ainsi la principale lacune de son robotaxi, qui manque cruellement de places disponibles. Avec six ou sept places, le projet vise logiquement la Model YL, la version allongée à trois rangées du SUV électrique, ou la Model Y classique avec l’option sept places, selon Electrek. C’est un revirement pour Elon Musk, qui jugeait encore récemment ce grand SUV inutile.
Encore quelques obstacles à surmonter
En août 2025, au lancement de la Model YL en Chine, Elon Musk avait indiqué qu’elle pourrait ne jamais arriver aux États-Unis, à cause de l’arrivée de la conduite autonome. Il estimait qu’une grande voiture familiale serait inutile. Tesla a pourtant lancé la Model YL aux États-Unis en juillet 2026, à 61 990 dollars (environ 56 000 euros, hors taxes), et la produit au Texas. Elon Musk en veut désormais une version sans conducteur. Pour Electrek, c’est la preuve que les familles ont toujours besoin d’une grande voiture, avec ou sans conducteur. Plusieurs obstacles se dressent encore avant une arrivée massive du SUV électrique sans pédales ni volant.
Tesla doit d’abord prouver que sa conduite autonome est sûre et aboutie. Or, son FSD (Full Self-Driving), rebaptisé TAD (Tesla Assisted Driving) en Europe, a récemment été épinglé pour ses excès de vitesse. Il permettait de rouler jusqu’à 50 % au-dessus de la limite, une marge que Tesla vient de ramener à 10 %. Côté réglementation, le dossier n’est pas bouclé non plus. Tesla a auto-certifié son Cybercab conforme aux normes de sécurité fédérales américaines, alors que la norme FMVSS 135 exige au moins la présence d’une pédale de frein.
Elon Musk n’a d’ailleurs donné ni calendrier, ni prix, ni lieu de production. Il faudra du temps avant que la Model YL sans pédales arrive sur les routes. Encore faut-il que la demande suive. Electrek cite l’étude 2026 de Cox Automotive sur les véhicules autonomes. Seuls 10 % des Américains interrogés choisiraient une voiture entièrement autonome, sans commandes (niveau 5), contre 17 % en 2016. Le niveau 4 arrive en tête avec 28 % des réponses : une conduite autonome qui laisse toujours la possibilité de reprendre le volant.
Quoi qu’il en soit, rien ne dit que ce projet verra réellement le jour. Tesla n’a toujours pas livré son nouveau Roadster, présenté en 2017 avec une production promise pour 2020. Elon Musk vise désormais 2028.

articles.title: L'écran du nouveau MacBook Pro fait mal aux yeux de certains de ses utilisateurs
articles.text:
Avec ce MacBook Pro Oled tout juste sorti, Apple s’est essayé pour la première fois aux dalles Oled sur ses ordinateurs portables. Un écran magnifique, mais Apple semble n’avoir pas réussi un point : le taux de scintillement de la dalle. Tant et si bien que certains clients se plaignent de cet écran qui leur causerait des douleurs aux yeux.
Maux de tête, yeux qui brûlent…
Certains acheteurs du tout dernier MacBook se plaignent en ligne. Par exemple l’un d’eux nommé pelzo0711 s’est exprimé sur le forum de MacRumors : « je me demande ce qui arrive à mes yeux. Ils me brûlent constamment et sont fatigués. Parfois, ma vision se dégrade ou je ressens simplement une douleur derrière les globes oculaires ». Même ressenti pour un certain HD4kAI sur Reddit : il explique ressentir des vertiges et que « ça rend la lecture de texte presque nauséabonde. » Dans les réponses, un autre internaute l’assure : « J’ai dû retourner mon 16 aujourd’hui pour cette raison. Écran magnifique, mais fatigue oculaire et nausées après utilisation. »
En bref, les symptômes sont multiples, mais tous ces témoignages convergent sur un point : ces gênes ne sont pas immédiates pour tous, mais surviennent souvent après une utilisation prolongée. C’est particulièrement le cas lorsqu’on lit du texte ou qu’on travaille sur des fonds sombres. La plupart de ces témoignages parlent d’une sensation de brûlure oculaire, les yeux qui piquent, une vision qui fatigue. D’autres parlent de maux de tête, de vertiges ou encore de nausées.
Pourquoi cet écran Oled peut faire mal aux yeux
Le point commun est le PWM, pour Pulse Width Modulation, une technique qui règle la luminosité de l’écran de ce MacBook en allumant et en éteignant les pixels à très haute fréquence. Grâce à la persistance rétinienne, en général cela ne pose pas de problème aux yeux, puisque ces derniers perçoivent une luminosité moyenne. Sur son dernier ordinateur, Apple est obligé d’utiliser cette technique puisque sur un écran Oled, il n’y a pas de rétroéclairage : pour ajuster la luminosité, il faut allumer et éteindre chaque pixel à une fréquence suffisamment élevée.
Le problème sur ce MacBook Pro Proled XDR, c’est que selon les mesures de Notebookcheck, le scintillement est réglé à 240 Hz dès que la luminosité n’est pas au maximum. Un taux extrêmement faible par rapport à d’autres écrans de smartphones ou d’ordinateurs, y compris chez Apple. Il faudrait plutôt monter à 3 125 Hz, un taux au-delà duquel on considère qu’on ne peut pas voir le scintillement à l’œil nu.
Il n’y a pas grand-chose à faire pour régler ces désagréments, mais si vous pensez acheter cet ordinateur, nous vous conseillons de l’essayer en magasin avant de vous décider. Apple n’a pour le moment pas réagi publiquement à ces plaintes : aucun correctif logiciel n’a été annoncé. Pourtant, il est possible de corriger ce problème : Google l’avait fait sur ses Pixel 10 l’année dernière.

articles.title: The bottleneck just moved: why African startups should care about MCP - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Earlier this year, our four-person studio cleared a 126-item product backlog in a single 48-hour stretch. A few weeks later, an AI edited a 268,000-word manuscript overnight — coordinating a dozen sub-agents while the author watched from a terminal, writes Barrett Nash, former-founder of Rwandan startup SafeMotos and now CEO of InfiniteUp.
Neither happened because AI suddenly got smarter. Both happened because of a quiet piece of plumbing called MCP, and it deserves more attention from African founders than it’s getting.
What MCP actually is, in plain language
MCP — the Model Context Protocol — is an open standard, introduced by Anthropic in late 2024 and since adopted across the industry, that lets AI assistants operate software rather than just talk about it.
Think of any piece of software as having a front desk: a published list of requests it will accept. MCP lets an AI walk up to those front desks itself. Before MCP, you described a problem and the AI described a solution — then you did the work. With MCP, it does the work. Type “make the button on the contact page green,” and in your website builder, the button turns green.
That’s the entire idea. Everything interesting is downstream of it.
Why this matters more in Africa than almost anywhere
African tech has a long habit of turning constraints into architecture. M-Pesa didn’t wait for branch banking; it leapfrogged it. The constraint MCP erases is headcount.
A four-person team that restructures its work around these tools can genuinely outproduce a much larger one that has bolted a chat window onto an unchanged process. We know because we are one: 40+ production apps, users in 117 countries, including DOER Business, a product we built specifically for African small businesses. Meanwhile, the cost side has collapsed — our own AI bills fell roughly 100× in three years. Intelligence stopped being a premium feature and became affordable infrastructure, priced for markets where every dollar of runway counts.
For startups that could never afford a twenty-person engineering floor, that combination — AI that does the work, at prices that keep falling — is not an efficiency gain. It’s a different game.
What it looks like in practice
Real examples from our own workshop this year:
- Operations that run themselves. Connect an AI to your inventory, your payment provider and WhatsApp, and “check stock, reorder, notify the customer” stops being someone’s job and becomes a sentence.
- Localisation as market-building. Asked to translate our site for Gulf markets, the AI didn’t translate it — it deployed sub-agents that rebuilt every page’s argument for a different audience. The same approach applies to Swahili, Amharic or Lingala: not your words in another language, but your business argued to a different room.
- Grounded strategy. We fed our raw search data straight into the model and let evidence, not opinion, set our content strategy. Organic traffic responded within weeks.
- Finishing what AI started. A wave of founders have “vibe-coded” apps to 80% in tools like Lovable and Bolt — then stalled at the last, hardest 20%. Rescuing those apps is now real engineering work, and the demand is continental.
The honest caution
MCP hands AI a pair of hands, not judgment. We once watched an agent of ours report five consecutive rounds of “improving results” while measuring nothing at all — the numbers were real, the link to reality had quietly broken. Our rule since: more AI throughput means more human verification, not less. The teams that win with this won’t be the ones that automate everything; they’ll be the ones that know exactly what to supervise.
Where to start
You don’t need a research budget. Pick one painful, well-documented workflow — documentation quality is the real fuel here — connect an AI to the systems it touches, and supervise the first runs closely. If you want a shortcut: we’re offering a free 30-minute MCP consultation to any company that wants a concrete map of what this could do for their business — no pitch, just the map. The tools are the easy part. The reorganization is the work, and it’s the most interesting work in software right now.
Barrett Nash is the CEO of InfiniteUp, a four-person software studio in Nanaimo, Canada that has shipped 40+ apps to users in 117 countries — including DOER Business, built for African small businesses, and HearWB, the National Acoustic Laboratories’ Team of the Year for 2024. He previously co-founded SafeMotos in Kigali, Rwanda. African companies can book a free 30-minute AI consultation here.

articles.title: Disseqt AI raises $8M to build enterprise AI safeguards
articles.text:
Disseqt AI raises $8M to build enterprise AI safeguards
The funds will support the expansion of Disseqt’s enterprise customer base globally. The company is also hiring in India across sales, operations and technology, with plans to expand into London.
Disseqt AI, a Dublin-headquartered AI assurance company with a significant presence in India, has raised $8 million in a round led by Gresham House Ventures, the growth equity arm of investment manager Gresham House.
Other investors include Sure Valley Ventures, an AI-focused venture fund; Delta Partners, an Irish early-stage investor; and Enterprise Ireland, the Irish government’s enterprise development agency. Angel backers include senior leaders from OpenAI, Palo Alto Networks, Salesforce and Meta, alongside cricket legend Rahul Dravid, who invested in his individual capacity.
The funds will support the expansion of Disseqt’s enterprise customer base globally. The company is also hiring in India across sales, operations and technology, with plans to expand into London.
Disseqt helps organisations test and oversee AI agents, software systems that can take actions, access company data and work across business applications. Its platform tests systems before launch, enforces company policies once they are live, monitors behaviour, blocks outputs that breach rules and maintains audit records.
“Every enterprise is handing real work to AI agents, but very few can prove those agents are safe, fair and within policy,” said Apoorva Kumar, chief executive and co-founder.
Disseqt claims it improved the safe-response rate of a global sports league’s fan-engagement agent, used by 80 million fans, from 80% to 99% in tests covering safety, bias and privacy.
Founded in late 2025 by Kumar, Manish Atri and Cyril Treacy, whose backgrounds include senior roles at Microsoft, AWS and Salesforce, Disseqt is entering a market where businesses are increasingly moving from AI chatbots to agents capable of performing tasks within company systems.
McKinsey’s 2026 survey found that 40% of respondents at companies with annual revenue exceeding $1 billion were scaling AI agents in at least one business function, compared with 27% a year earlier.
The risks associated with their deployment are also becoming clearer. OpenAI disclosed in October that two internal coding agents had weakened monitoring safeguards during separate tasks.
Gresham House Ventures partner Rohit Mathur said companies needed “tools that sit apart from the model providers they rely on”.
Investment is also reaching adjacent areas of the sector. Bengaluru-based Karta AI raised $3 million in October to develop voice agents for financial services, while AI infrastructure company Simplismart secured $14 million in a Series B round to expand its technology for running AI models more efficiently.

articles.title: ASUS warns of critical hard-coded key flaw in Control Center Express
articles.text:
ASUS released Control Center Express v1.7.29 to fix three critical vulnerabilities that could let remote attackers gain administrative control of the management console and the devices it manages.
Of the three, one is a maximum-severity vulnerability (CVSS score: 10.0) tracked under CVE-2026-114202, arising from a hard-coded cryptographic key used in the product.
The flaw lets an unauthenticated remote attacker forge an authentication token and gain administrator privileges, without requiring any privileges or user interaction.
The second flaw is CVE-2026-114204, also a hard-coded key problem, which lets a remote attacker with low privileges forge a session token for a recently logged-in account.
The third is CVE-2026-114205, an authorization flaw that lets a low-privileged user create an administrator account.
ASUS Control Center Express is a central dashboard that IT administrators use to monitor and remotely manage fleets of PCs.
ASUS markets it to businesses and IT service providers and lists support for more than 200 of its business, workstation, and Corporate Stable Model motherboards.
While all three vulnerabilities are rated critical, CVE-2026-114204 has a recent-session prerequisite, and CVE-2026-114205 requires a low-privileged account, whereas CVE-2026-114202 enables remote administrative access with no prerequisites.
ASUS’s security bulletin says versions earlier than v1.7.29 are affected. However, the CVE records only list affected versions through v1.7.27, leaving the status of v1.7.28 unclear.
Impacted users are advised to install v1.7.29, then update the agents on managed devices through Select Function → Client Agent Updater, and verify their versions.
Also yesterday, ASUS released security updates for Control Center Enterprise, its centralized IT management platform, and Armoury Crate, a hardware configuration utility.
Specifically, ASUS patched CVE-2026-126574, a critical authorization flaw that lets a remote user with the low-privileged Viewer role change an administrator’s password and take over the account.
The flaw affects Control Center Datacenter 4.0.0.2 and earlier and Control Center Enterprise 3.1.0.8 and earlier.
The Armoury Crate update addressed CVE-2026-112115, a high-severity privilege escalation flaw.
The flaw affects all versions up to and including 6.7.2 and could allow a low-privileged local user to trick an elevated process into loading a malicious library.

articles.title: Ce robot de piscine repasse sur les débris qu'il a oubliés
articles.text:
AquaSense 3 et Sora Neo R : Beatbot renouvelle ses robots de piscine sansfil
Chacun son bassin
À l'occasion du salon Piscine Global Europe, Beatbot a dévoilé deux robots sans fil. L'AquaSense 3 mise sur la détection des débris, tandis que le Sora Neo R associe nettoyage et diffusion de pastilles de traitement.
Au salon Piscine Global Europe de Lyon, Beatbot présente deux nouveaux robots de piscine sans fil. Séparés par 1100 €, l'AquaSense 3 et le Sora Neo R ne s'adressent pas tout à fait aux mêmes bassins, mais partagent une fonction appréciable au moment de les sortir de l'eau : tous deux remontent et restent à flot en fin de cycle.
AquaSense 3 : un dernier coup d'oeil au fond
Avec l'AquaSense 3, Beatbot cherche à limiter les oublis. Le robot établit une carte 2D du fond pour organiser ses déplacements et utilise une caméra afin de repérer les débris. La marque affirme que son système de reconnaissance peut identifier plus de 40 types de déchets.
Après un nettoyage complet du fond, la fonction AI Final Check effectue un nouveau passage pour détecter les débris restants et les cibler. Un mode rapide se concentre quant à lui sur les saletés visibles, sans lancer de cycle complet.

Ses deux pompes assurent un débit de 18,9 m³/h. Le robot nettoie le fond, les parois, la ligne d'eau et les plages immergées à partir de 30 cm.
Son compartiment accueille jusqu'à deux pastilles de chlore compatibles ou de clarifiant Beatbot. Elles se dissolvent dès l'immersion et sont diffusées dans l'eau pendant le déplacement. Ce dispositif vient en complément du traitement principal de la piscine.

articles.title: Disney's new Star Wars robots use AI to react to guests in real time
articles.text:
First look: Walt Disney Imagineering R&D has built three small Star Wars robots that watch and listen to visitors and choose their own responses without a hidden puppeteer. The Audio-Animatronics prototypes are modeled on the Anzellan aliens from this year's film The Mandalorian and Grogu, and they send camera and microphone data to several AI models running on Amazon Web Services. Those models decide in the moment what each character says and how it moves, but every line and gesture they can pick from was written ahead of time by Disney's Imagineers.
The characters are named Vilo Vele, Kado Bre'a and Jibu Bre'a. Their first public appearance will be at AWS re:Invent in Las Vegas later this month, where conference attendees can interact with them. Disney has not committed to a park debut. However, the characters and the technology behind them could eventually show up in Star Wars: Galaxy's Edge and other attractions.
The project changes how Disney's animatronics have worked for decades. Since the first Audio-Animatronics figures sang in Disneyland's Enchanted Tiki Room, the company's figures have mostly performed choreographed shows that run the same sequence every time. Even the most lifelike recent figures either follow predefined routines or rely on an operator out of view. The Olaf robot Disney introduced recently is an example of the second approach, since a handler drives it with a Steam Deck.
The Anzellans have no handler. Each figure carries hidden cameras and microphones that capture what guests do and say. That input goes to AWS cloud servers, where the processing is divided between models of different sizes.
A fast-decision model handles split-second reactions, such as making a character lock eyes with a guest who has just walked up, so the figure appears to be paying attention. Larger models work more slowly and plan longer exchanges by weighing the wider context of the interaction.
That split addresses the hardest problem for any interactive character: timing. If a guest waves and the robot reacts a second late, the illusion falls apart. Disney says each part of the system has been tuned for latency so the characters respond fast enough to feel natural.
Running the heavier reasoning in the cloud while a lightweight model covers immediate reactions lets the figures seem responsive while still drawing on more compute for decisions that can wait.
The characters also respond to each other, not just to guests. In one scenario Disney describes, a visitor approaches and all three figures turn at once. One speaks in a mix of English and the Anzellan language, another blinks and tilts its head, and the third studies the guest before saying, "we have something special for you."
What the system does not do is just as important as what it does. The AI never generates new speech or motion. Instead, it selects from prerecorded audio clips, which are played back alongside dynamic animations. Imagineers wrote every line of dialogue and designed every movement, including personality quirks that make each Anzellan distinct. The models decide which piece of material to use and when, but they cannot step outside the script.
That design keeps the characters on-brand and predictable for the people who built them, which matters for a company protective of its intellectual property. Disney summed up the goal this way: "The result is a set of characters that surprise the guest, without surprising its creators or artists." The approach also avoids the risks of open-ended generative AI in a family theme park, where an unscripted line from a Star Wars character could become a public relations problem.
The prototypes build on an existing business relationship. AWS already serves as a public cloud infrastructure provider for Disney+, and the Anzellan project takes that partnership from streaming into physical, guest-facing entertainment. AWS supplies the cloud and AI capabilities that handle each character's sensing and decision-making, while Disney controls the creative content the system draws on.
The re:Invent demonstration will be the first chance to see how well the system performs with real crowds. A conference floor is noisy and unpredictable, and it will test whether the fast-decision layer can keep reactions feeling immediate when many people are competing for the characters' attention. If it works, Disney will have a template for park characters that behave differently with each visitor while performing only material its artists have approved.

articles.title: L’Ukraine détruit un pont russe avec des drones relais contournant les limites de Starlink
articles.text:
Dans la nuit du 15 au 16 novembre, des vagues de drones et de missiles ukrainiens ont fait s'effondrer une arche du pont de Kerch. Pour guider ses armes à plus de 250 km, Kiev a monté son propre réseau de communication aérien, sans passer par Starshield.
Le dispositif repose sur des drones équipés de radios maillées, qui jouent le rôle de relais entre les opérateurs et les munitions. Une réponse technique directe aux limites imposées à la version militaire de Starlink.
D'après Ars Technica, l'opération reprend une innovation russe : Moscou a d'abord utilisé ces drones relais pour ses frappes à longue portée sur des villes ukrainiennes. L'Ukraine a retourné la méthode contre l'un des symboles de Vladimir Poutine, ce qui donne au contournement de Starlink une portée bien plus large qu'une simple astuce de télécommunications.
Black Friday : -40 % sur la Samsung Q995H
Pour le Black Friday, la barre de son premium Samsung et ses 23 haut-parleurs passent à 890€
Des drones en maillage plutôt qu'un satellite
Le principe ressemble à celui d'un réseau Wi-Fi maillé domestique : au lieu de passer par un point central, chaque nœud transmet les données au suivant. Ici, les nœuds sont des drones équipés de radios mesh, qui prolongent la liaison entre les opérateurs humains, les missiles pilotés à distance et les drones d'attaque. Cela a permis à des opérateurs situés à plus de 250 kilomètres de guider les armes, tout en évitant les défenses aériennes et en visant les points faibles de la structure.
Pourquoi renoncer à Starshield ? Des restrictions américaines empêchent son usage sur des appareils dépassant 161 km/h (100 mph). Volodymyr Zelensky affirme qu'elles n'ont pas été levées, SpaceX nie leur retour. Un missile de croisière file bien au-delà de cette vitesse : le satellite était donc inutilisable pour ce type de frappe. Pour le contexte, nous avions déjà évoqué le ralentissement de Starlink en Ukraine.
Reste que le message est limpide : quand un fournisseur privé américain peut brider vos outils, mieux vaut avoir une alternative maison.
Quatre vagues pour une arche
Des centaines de drones d'attaque ont d'abord saturé les défenses russes. Une deuxième vague a installé le relais radio. Puis sont arrivés les missiles de croisière Flamingo, conçus en Ukraine, capables d'emporter 1 000 kg d'explosifs. Des semaines de frappes préalables avaient déjà dégradé radars, défenses antiaériennes et moyens de guerre électronique autour du pont. L'attaque du 15 novembre a coïncidé avec la plus grosse attaque nocturne de drones ukrainiens sur la Russie depuis le début de l'invasion.
Le bilan matériel : une des deux arches d'acier supportant la chaussée s'est effondrée, la partie ferroviaire n'étant que modérément touchée. Des trains semblent d'ailleurs circuler de nouveau. Prudence toutefois face aux images : France 24 a identifié plusieurs vidéos virales de destruction générées par IA, qui exagèrent les dégâts. Les frappes sont réelles, pas ces séquences-là.
Le contournement de Starlink ne relève plus de la rustine : c'est une doctrine en construction. Reste à voir si Washington, SpaceX ou Moscou auront une réponse à un réseau qui ne dépend de personne.

articles.title: Beyond Pass/Fail: Characterizing Silicon Margin With PVTW
articles.text:
Determining not only whether a device meets specification, but how far it is from the boundary, helps inform product robustness and future design decisions.
Production test is necessarily built around decisions. PASS. FAIL. Bin 1. Bin 2. Ship. Do not ship. Characterization has a different objective. It asks not only whether the device meets specification, but how far it is from the boundary.
That distinction becomes increasingly important as processors integrate compute, memory, high speed interfaces, multiple power domains and advanced packaging into increasingly complex systems.
Suppose five devices all pass the product specification, but under the same controlled workload their minimum stable operating voltages are:
0.70 V | 0.71 V | 0.73 V | 0.76 V | 0.79 V
Production test sees five passing devices. Characterization sees five different levels of margin. That changes the engineering question from “Why did this device fail?” to something potentially much more useful:
What is consuming product margin?
PVTW (process, voltage, temperature, workload) gives us a framework for exploring that question.
Take the same device and establish its voltage and frequency boundary using conventional ATE content. Then establish another boundary while running a deterministic compute workload. Repeat with SRAM, memory, PCIe and combined workloads. We may discover that the boundaries are different.
That difference can tell us which workload is exposing the limiting condition and where deeper characterization should begin.
Rather than testing at one nominal operating point, deliberately approach the boundary. Sweep voltage at fixed frequency, temperature and workload. Sweep frequency while the other conditions remain fixed. Repeat across temperature. Then manipulate individual power domains.
A compute workload may be characterized while the core rail is swept and memory and I/O rails remain fixed. A memory-intensive workload can be characterized while a memory-related rail is swept. PCIe traffic can be maintained while relevant electrical and thermal conditions are changed.
Now we are not simply determining whether a subsystem functions. We are measuring how much margin it has under a defined workload.
Population analysis makes this more powerful. Take known good devices and devices showing reduced SLT margin. Characterize both populations under identical PVTW conditions. Instead of asking only which devices fail, compare the shapes of their operating envelopes.
Does the marginal population show a consistent voltage shift? Does the difference emerge only at high temperature? Does it appear only under simultaneous compute and memory activity? Is there a particular rail or frequency transition where the two populations separate?
The shape of the margin distribution can provide clues to the physical mechanism.
Suppose a particular system workload requires 45 minutes before marginal devices begin generating errors. That is useful for learning, but expensive as a production screen.
PVTW characterization can help determine why that workload exposes the problem. Once the mechanism is better understood, the ATE capability can search for a shorter electrical, structural or functional signature correlated with the same marginality.
Perhaps a voltage and frequency corner exposes it in seconds. Perhaps a targeted functional pattern reproduces the condition. Perhaps a particular power rail response or interface measurement predicts it.
If the correlation is strong enough, the shorter test can potentially move into Final Test or even Wafer Sort. The learning flow becomes:
SLT discovers → PVTW characterizes → ATE correlates → Production test screens
The goal of deeper SLT characterization is therefore not necessarily more SLT. In some cases, its greatest value may be teaching us how to screen the risk earlier and faster.
This is why I believe we should preserve margin data rather than reducing everything immediately to PASS and FAIL. Minimum operating voltage, maximum stable frequency, thermal margin, interface margin, power margin and workload margin can all become continuous characterization parameters. Those measurements can be compared across device populations, process corners, assembly conditions and eventually manufacturing history.
A device with 100 mV of margin and a device with 10 mV of margin may both satisfy the production specification today. But they may tell us very different things about process variation, product robustness and future design decisions. Characterizing those differences can help answer a more fundamental question:
Where is the product operating boundary, and what moves it?
That question does not end at the silicon. The package surrounding the silicon has its own manufacturing history, materials and process variation.
In Part 3, I will explore how 2D ID and unit level traceability could connect PVTW margin all the way back to wafer X,Y and substrate panel X,Y.
