articles.title: Groundcover Investigations lets engineers steer AI SRE agents
articles.text:
Groundcover Investigations lets engineers steer AI SRE agents
Groundcover, the eBPF-based observability startup, has introduced Investigations, giving agents and engineers one place to collaborate on incident response in real time.
In the shared workspace, groundcover’s investigator and moderator agents work with on-call engineers and their preferred coding agents to investigate production incidents together, analyzing behavior across applications and infrastructure to create a shared record of evidence.
Rather than handing full control to agents, the idea is to help engineers and agents work together on incident investigations.
“Most AI SRE tools ask engineers to step back and let the agent take over. We built Investigations for engineers to step in.”
Shahar Azulay, CEO and co-founder at groundcover, tells The New Stack that “Most AI SRE tools ask engineers to step back and let the agent take over. We built Investigations for engineers to step in.”
Everyone has their favorite agent. That’s a problem
AI agents are flooding daily software engineering workflows. Already, Salesforce reports that organizations use an average of 12 agents — a number that’s expected to grow by 67% within two years. But half of those agents are working in silos.
This presents a particular problem in incident response. Individual agents, like Claude Code or Codex, may be able to troubleshoot on their own, but how can engineers aggregate their findings? They don’t — or at least, it’s very tricky. More often than not, Azulay says agents’ varying conclusions are spread across chats and tickets.
As he describes it: “Every engineer now has an agent, but each of those agents investigates on its own and findings end up in a chat window.”
How groundcover wants engineers and agents to work together
With its Investigations, groundcover aims to eliminate fragmented incident response and create a single source of truth for every engineer and agent. Here, agents can lead collaborative, evidence-driven investigations, testing hypotheses against production data, validating findings, and backing every conclusion with evidence. Engineers, for their part, get real-time visibility into the investigation and can step in to steer it as they see fit.
It all starts when a monitor issue fires and an engineer opens an investigation from groundcover or Slack. groundcover says automatically opening an investigation when a monitor fires is coming next.
The investigator agent builds a graph with a question (e.g., Why is checkout latency spiking in the US?) and then opens several hypotheses to explain it. From there, it turns to production telemetry to query the traces, logs, metrics, and Kubernetes events the groundcover eBPF sensor is already collecting, testing each one and recording what it finds as evidence.
Importantly, Azulay tells The New Stack, “the investigator can’t mark its own work as correct. When it thinks a hypothesis is supported, it submits a proposal that cites specific findings, and a separate agent, the moderator, acts as an LLM-as-a-judge and checks whether that evidence backs up the claim. No findings, no closure.”
“Separating the agent that does the work from the agent that judges it gives you a conclusion you can trust without redoing every step.”
Given the speed at which agents reach conclusions — and the risk that they act beyond scope — Azulay says this separation of hypothesis and conclusion is crucial to arriving at a trustworthy conclusion: “Separating the agent that does the work from the agent that judges it gives you a conclusion you can trust without redoing every step.”
According to groundcover, the investigator agent also learns from each investigation so it can understand which hypotheses tend to hold up and where to look first when similar problems arise.
External coding agents are invited to the party, too
While groundcover’s investigator and moderator agents lead investigations, the startup recognizes that most engineers already bring a slew of third-party agents to the table, whether for business intelligence, coding, product roadmapping, etc. Those agents are welcome in Investigations, too.
Using groundcover’s MCP server, engineers can connect Claude Code, Codex, and other agents to the shared workspace to read and add to the same investigation. That builds on groundcover’s October launch, which let outside coding agents query its telemetry over MCP and hand off investigations to groundcover’s own agent.
For Azulay, this lets each agent shine in what it does best. As he tells The New Stack:
“Coding agents and groundcover’s agents are good at different things. Our agents know your telemetry and how to query it fast. Your coding agents know your code. Neither has the full picture.”
Working together, then, via Investigations, the different agents can lean on each other depending on the task at hand. If a hypothesis points to a code problem, for example, the investigator agent may bring in Claude Code or Codex to check it. When engineers’ coding agent needs telemetry, groundcover’s agent fetches the data.
“Our agents know your telemetry and how to query it fast. Your coding agents know your code. Neither has the full picture.”
What matters is that every agent publishes its findings in the same investigation tree, preventing engineers from going on a wild goose chase trying to connect the dots across five different private chat sessions.
“Everyone can see what’s been checked, what’s still open, and why anyone believes what they believe,” says Azulay. “Every contribution is attributed, so you know a finding came from a specific engineer’s Claude session at a specific time.”
Does this mean agents and engineers are on even footing?
Not quite. Per Omer Mayer, senior product manager, groundcover, engineers can “watch each hypothesis get supported or ruled out in real time” — and they can “step in and steer it” at any time.
In other words, engineers can immediately see what groundcover agents are investigating. If they think the agents are off the mark, they can easily take over.
Azulay offers The New Stack an example: Suppose a checkout latency monitor fires, and an automated investigation kicks off, generating three hypotheses, one of which is a slow query from a recent deploy.
But the on-call engineer knows something the investigator agent doesn’t: The deploy was rolled back 10 minutes earlier and latency didn’t recover. Easy — they can stop that hypothesis, which closes everything under it and tells the agent to stop spending time and tokens there.
“The engineer might also add context the agents don’t have, like ‘the payments team changed their retry policy this morning,’” adds Azulay. “That opens a new line of inquiry nobody would have found in the telemetry alone.”
What’s also important is engineers’ right to override where agents can’t. Remember, the investigator agent is forbidden from closing anything without the moderator agent’s okay. But engineers don’t need the moderator’s permission to steer the investigation, Azulay says.
“The moderator is there to keep the agents honest, not to slow down the people responsible for the incident,” says Azulay.
More agents are teaming up
Earlier this year, more vendors made moves to bring individual agents out of isolated workflows and into a shared space.
On the coding side, Cognition, Microsoft, and Augment Code all launched team-layer coding agent platforms, pushing coding agents past the single-developer loop.
Last month, Harness acquired select Augment Code assets, including Cosmos, to link AI coding agents to its delivery platform. This way, teams writing code in Cosmos will have context from across the software development lifecycle available to the agent as it works.
Now, groundcover’s Investigations brings a similar shared-space principle to incident response. More work is happening elsewhere, too. Slack Code has given coding agents their own temporary channels for plans, diffs, and live previews, which Katie Steigman, vice president of product at Slack, told The New Stack is already being used for incident response.
Other companies are also building tools for collaborative incident investigations, including shared workspaces for engineers and agents and handoffs to coding agents over MCP.
So far, conversations have focused on agents’ individual prowess and what they can do. But as agents move deeper into software engineering workflows, agent-engineer teamwork looks like what will make incident response work best.

articles.title: En 1974, Stephen King entró en la habitación 217 de un hotel vacío buscando una cama. La pesadilla que tuvo aquella noche dejó una leyenda para toda la vida
articles.text:
La noche del 28 de septiembre de 1974, un joven escritor y su esposa llegaron a un hotel de Colorado que estaba a punto de cerrar por el invierno. No había otros huéspedes y los pasillos parecían interminables. Lo que sucedió durante aquellas horas acabaría convirtiéndose en una de las historias más rentables de la literatura de terror, aunque nadie podía imaginar hasta dónde llegaría el negocio.
Una pesadilla de 1974 de 400 millones. El 15 de mayo de 2025, el histórico Stanley Hotel de Estes Park, Colorado, protagonizó una operación financiera de casi 400 millones de dólares para cambiar de manos y financiar una ambiciosa transformación. La propiedad, famosa por haber inspirado El resplandor de Stephen King, pasó a manos de una entidad vinculada a la autoridad de financiación cultural y educativa de Colorado.
El objetivo era ampliar sus instalaciones y convertirlo en un gran destino turístico y cultural dedicado, entre otras cosas, al cine de terror. La ironía es que buena parte de su fama nació de una sola noche que King pasó allí 51 años antes.
Un hotel de lujo que se quedó sin huéspedes. El Stanley Hotel había abierto sus puertas el 4 de julio de 1909, impulsado por F. O. Stanley, empresario relacionado con los automóviles de vapor Stanley Steamer. Situado junto a las Montañas Rocosas, ofrecía lujo, aislamiento y vistas espectaculares, pero en septiembre de 1974 estaba preparando su cierre invernal.
Stephen King, que acababa de publicar Carrie, llegó con su esposa Tabitha y descubrió que eran los únicos huéspedes. Se instalaron en la habitación 217 y el escritor comenzó a recorrer unos pasillos desiertos que parecían diseñados para una historia de fantasmas.
La noche en que una manguera creó un monstruo. Mientras dormía, King tuvo una pesadilla en la que su hijo de tres años corría aterrorizado por los pasillos del hotel, perseguido por una manguera contra incendios. Despertó sobresaltado, encendió un cigarrillo y se sentó a contemplar las montañas desde la ventana.
Según explicó posteriormente en su web oficial, antes de terminar aquel cigarrillo ya tenía prácticamente concebida la estructura de la novela. Tres años después, en enero de 1977, publicó El resplandor, la historia de Jack Torrance, un escritor que acepta cuidar durante el invierno un hotel aislado mientras una presencia siniestra comienza a apoderarse de su familia.
Kubrick convirtió el hotel en inmortal. En 1980, Stanley Kubrick llevó El resplandor al cine con Jack Nicholson y Shelley Duvall, creando algunas de las imágenes más reconocibles del terror cinematográfico. Sin embargo, el Stanley Hotel no fue el escenario principal del rodaje: el director utilizó otros establecimientos y decorados, y cambió la habitación 217 de la novela por la 237.
King criticó duramente la adaptación porque consideraba que había eliminado buena parte de la evolución psicológica de Jack Torrance. Paradójicamente, aquella película que disgustó al escritor ayudó a convertir el hotel que lo había inspirado en un lugar de peregrinación para los aficionados al género.
El hotel descubrió que los fantasmas eran un negocio estupendo. Con el paso de los años, el Stanley Hotel dejó de limitarse a ofrecer alojamiento y comenzó a explotar su conexión con El resplandor. Organizó recorridos paranormales, visitas a sus instalaciones y festivales de cine de terror, mientras los huéspedes podían ver la película de Kubrick en sus habitaciones.
Según contó CBS News en 2014, solo durante 2012 unas 81.000 personas participaron en las visitas guiadas del establecimiento. La habitación 217 se convirtió en uno de sus grandes reclamos, alimentada además por una leyenda anterior a King: una explosión de gas ocurrida en 1911 que había dejado herida a una empleada del hotel. La ficción y el pasado real del edificio terminaron mezclándose en una maquinaria turística extraordinariamente eficaz.
De habitación maldita a museo del terror de Hollywood. La operación de mayo de 2025 permitirá ampliar el complejo, que ocupa unas 41 acres de terreno, equivalentes a 16,6 hectáreas. Según el anuncio oficial, el proyecto contempla 65 nuevas habitaciones, un centro de eventos de unos 6.000 metros cuadrados, un auditorio para 864 personas y un museo de cine de terror diseñado con la colaboración de Blumhouse Productions, responsable de franquicias como Paranormal Activity e Insidious.
También se prevén exposiciones renovadas periódicamente y actividades culturales durante todo el año. La operación incluye financiación pública y privada, entre ella hasta 46 millones de dólares procedentes de un programa estatal de promoción turística. La idea es convertir un hotel famoso por una novela en un centro permanente de entretenimiento.
Los 400 millones tienen truco. Porque la cifra de aproximadamente 395 millones de dólares no representa los beneficios obtenidos gracias a El resplandor, ni tampoco el presupuesto exclusivo del museo. Se trata de una emisión de bonos destinada a financiar la adquisición del complejo, refinanciar obligaciones anteriores y acometer las nuevas instalaciones. Por supuesto, gracias a su reconocimiento mundial por aquella pesadilla del escritor.
La operación ilustra hasta qué punto la leyenda creada alrededor del Stanley ha terminado formando parte de su valor comercial. Stephen King pasó allí una sola noche en 1974 y salió con la semilla de una novela que cambiaría su carrera. 51 años después, el hotel consiguió financiación cercana a los 400 millones para reinventarse alrededor de una identidad que aquella pesadilla ayudó a construir. Probablemente, pocas noches de insomnio han resultado tan productivas.

articles.title: Tesla n'est plus la seule lanterne rouge du contrôle technique allemand, une électrique chinoise l’y rejoint
articles.text:
C’est devenu un marronnier dont les détracteurs de Tesla se régalent. Chaque fin d’année, le TÜV-Verband (la fédération des organismes TÜV, qui réalisent une grande partie des contrôles techniques outre-Rhin) dresse le bilan des véhicules les plus recalés (ainsi que les plus fiables). Comme les années précédentes, les Tesla Model 3 et Model Y figurent parmi les pires scores de la catégorie des véhicules récents.
Le rapport 2027, qui porte sur les contrôles réalisés du 1er juillet 2025 au 30 juin 2026, vient de paraître le 19 novembre 2026 sur le site de l’ADAC. Avec 18,5 % de contre-visites pour des défauts majeurs, le Tesla Model Y termine une nouvelle fois bon dernier, mais il est rejoint en bas de classement par la MG4 qui affiche 16 % de recalage à la première présentation du véhicule.
Comme souvent, des histoires de frein
Si ces voitures électriques échouent massivement, ce n’est pas parce que leur batterie flanche ou que leur moteur rend l’âme. Ce n’est de toute façon pas ce que vérifie le contrôle technique, qu’il soit allemand ou français. Le mal dont ces modèles souffrent est bien plus banal.
Dans le cas de la MG4, les inspecteurs allemands pointent un coupable majeur : les disques de frein. Sur plus d’une MG4 sur dix (10,3 %), les disques sont signalés comme défectueux ou piqués par la rouille, un chiffre dix fois supérieur à la moyenne des voitures de cet âge.
C’est le grand paradoxe de la voiture électrique : grâce au freinage régénératif, le conducteur ne sollicite plus assez le freinage mécanique. Sauf qu’à force de ne jamais pincer les disques, ces derniers rouillent, s’encrassent et finissent par perdre en efficacité, jusqu’à se faire recaler au contrôle. Un défaut qu’un simple freinage très appuyé sur une voie rapide de temps en temps suffirait souvent à éviter.
L’absence d’entretien régulier des Tesla les pénalise toujours
Pour les Tesla, le problème des freins sous-exploités s’ajoute à une usure prématurée des suspensions. Le Model Y et le Model 3 sont des véhicules particulièrement lourds et puissants, ce qui met les rotules et les triangles de suspension à rude épreuve sur les routes bosselées. En l’absence de révision par le constructeur qui constaterait ce défaut avant le passage au TÜV, beaucoup de propriétaires de Tesla se rendent directement au contrôle technique sans jamais être passés par un atelier de la marque depuis l’achat de la voiture.
Au contrôle technique, ces propriétaires se font alors recaler pour un phare mal réglé ou un triangle fatigué, obtiennent la liste exacte des défauts sur procès-verbal, et retournent chez Tesla pour réparer uniquement ce qui est nécessaire. Cette façon de faire gonfle mécaniquement le chiffre des véhicules recalés, l’ADAC le reconnaît lui-même, et maintient la marque en bas du classement.
Un chiffre joue en revanche en faveur de Tesla : les Model Y contrôlés affichaient 58 000 km en moyenne, soit 11 000 km de plus que la moyenne de leur classe d’âge. De quoi peser aussi sur l’usure des rotules et des triangles.
Le client y gagne, puisqu’il économise le prix des révisions. Sur le papier, en revanche, les statistiques de la marque virent au carnage. Les autres électriques du classement, choyées par des révisions annuelles chez leur concessionnaire (comme le Mazda MX-30 ou l’Audi Q8 e-tron), affichent d’excellents scores : 3,0 % de défauts importants pour le Mazda, troisième sur 109 modèles, et 3,2 % pour l’Audi, cinquième. Les révisions y sont sans doute pour quelque chose, une partie des défauts étant corrigée en amont par le garagiste.

articles.title: RIIIR: Rewrite It In *Idiomatic* Rust (with AI)
articles.text:
Transcript
Niko Matsakis: My name is Nicholas Matsakis. I am one of the lead designers of the Rust programming language. I've been working on it since 2011. I also am a senior principal engineer at Amazon. I started there about five years ago, in part because Amazon has been adopting tons of Rust, and I wanted to see it firsthand, see how it was going. I'm going to just show my whole cards with you and just tell you all the things I'm going to tell you. Step one, I'm going to try to convince you that Rust and AI is a really great combination, perhaps better than some of the alternatives out there. I have a project I'm curious to get feedback on that I think makes it even better, which I call Symposium, and covers up some of the gaps I see. Next, that actually, if you look at how Symposium works, what you'll find is it reveals something about the way we're currently building all our development tools here, which is that individual vendors, like Anthropic or OpenAI or whatever, everyone's trying to build a complete tool that solves all the problems, and I want to see us do more of an extensibility story where people can plug in and add things and you have a whole bunch of extensions. I think we're only scraping the surface of what is possible, but it's very difficult to do with the way the tools are set up now. Then I'll talk to you about Agent Client Protocol, which is an interesting way to get past that and get to a more extensible model.
Rust + AI
How many have heard of Rust? Rust is all about having a language that can go as low-level as you want, as efficient, give you as much control over the hardware. Low-level enough to be used in a kernel, but be productive. High-level enough that you can write application-level software in it, and it's not too bad. It may not be the minimum line count or what have you, but it's not too bad. Low-level enough for a kernel, I mean that quite literally. We are the only language apart from C, not even C++, that's allowed in the Linux kernel, just C and Rust. Also, we're being used in the Microsoft's kernel and elsewhere. That's been pretty cool. In terms of high-level enough for an application, just to give you some idea, this is a library called ratatui, which is a text user interface library, and they have all kinds of neat little demos.
You're seeing more and more of this user-facing software where performance may not be the number one criteria, but it works really well in Rust, and then it does scale up to crazy things like this oscilloscope or whatever that is. I've been giving a lot of talks on Rust for the last 15 years. I was at QCon in Brazil, in Sao Paulo in 2019 giving a talk like this. What I would say is it's sometimes a bit of a tough sell, because Rust's whole premise is like this eat your spinach thing. You know where your parents were like, eat it, it's good for you. We're telling you, Rust is going to make your code faster, it's going to make it more efficient, but it is going to take you a month and a half or three months or however long it's going to be to learn how it works and incorporate those new style of development into your workflow.
People are like, I would like it to go fast, but I want to ship tomorrow, so actually I'm going to stick with TypeScript. I can hire all the people I need. That makes a lot of sense. What I try to tell them is, yes, it is spinach, but it's like Popeyes spinach. You're going to eat it, and then you're going to be stronger, you're going to go faster. It's going to be great. Usually it doesn't win over, but that's changed a lot. What's happened is, if the agent's doing the coding, the agent already learned Rust in its training, its reinforcement learning stages and whatnot. It already passed that stage, so you just get to skip to the Popeyes stage, to the part where you've got this type system that's giving the agent guardrails and helping it stay on track and get programs that are more likely to be correct. You don't have to take it from me. You can take it from Greg Brockman, co-founder and president of OpenAI, who said Rust is a perfect language for agents, given that if it compiles, it's approximately correct.
In terms of this range of applications, another thing pulling people in is, like I said, Rust is low-level enough for a kernel, but usable enough for an application. It covers a wide space. You have things like codex-rs, which used to be in TypeScript, being ported over. That's something that's pulling people in. Then, of course, there's the old standby, which is efficiency. If you're building network services or whatnot, where you're paying per load, or maybe you're building a mobile app or something that's going to take your user's battery, then it becomes a really big consideration. You can save quite a bit of money. That's, of course, what's driving Rust at Amazon. We run things at really large scale. It's been fascinating, though, to watch the shift. When I first got there, it's the same as what I told you, people are thinking, Rust is maybe going to take me some time to learn.
I'm only going to use it in the critical data paths. S3, EC2, Lambda, those are the first adopters where the real heavy workloads are driving. Then people get used to it, and they started to use it in more and more places. There's an interesting blog post talking about DSQL, which is this serverless SQL database, and their story where they went through that whole trial. They started with just one narrow part, wound up using Rust in the data plane and the control plane and in their Postgres bindings and the whole thing. What's happening lately, it's really different, except I didn't actually get cleared to talk about all the cool things. Let me tell you about something else, and then we'll come back, where Microsoft is saying we're maybe going to try to do AI-driven rewrites of a million lines of code by one engineer. This is just a research project.

As agentic coding becomes more mainstream, we're going to need to have some standards that let us build on top of it and build more complex workflows. One of the places we're seeing a lot of interest, actually, is in enterprise applications and so on, where they want to build integrations for their employees to offer a better experience than just a CLI.
Recap
You should use Rust for your next project, especially if you're using AI. If you've tried it and bounced, give it another try because it feels different now. Second, when you do it, use Symposium, cargo agents init. Easy. Third, portability sucks, but I hope it will get better.
Questions and Answers
Participant 1: For teams that are not familiar with Rust, what's your recommendation on how to start with it? Because with AI, you can really start along with building immediately, and we do, but the fear is that you don't understand the language completely, but then it may end up in production. What's your recommendations for teams that are just starting and they want to ship faster or something like that?
Niko Matsakis: How do you avoid digging yourself into a hole? That is exactly what battery packs are meant to answer, but I'm still trying to make them a real thing. First off, I worry a little less these days because it's so much easier to make changes. Even if you've built stuff, refactoring it is easier. Secondly, what I found really helpful when I'm learning new things is to just really aggressively ask the LLM about its choices. Like it made some choices. You could ask it why. Often, it will give you a good answer. Sometimes it'll say, you're right, that was a bad choice. I'm like, I didn't mean to imply that actually, but ok, go ahead, refactor it. It can go both ways. You don't just have to take the code. You can ask it all about the code and so forth. I think that's the best that I know of. Of course, what I've seen within Amazon, the old advice is still true. Hire someone who knows Rust. That's the surefire way. If you can't do that, then as you get experience, of course, you'll start to have homegrown experts of your own.
Participant 2: I think a lot of us have noticed when writing skills and however much stuff you put in place to try and ensure that the LLM actually uses it or uses it as intended, and so on, sometimes it will just not do it or ignore it. That kind of skills are too loose, hooks are too hard. How do you make it deterministically actually use this stuff? Have you found through this Symposium project any ways to do that better or make sure it actually does the right thing?
Niko Matsakis: How do we nudge the LLM to be more deterministic? This is exactly why I'm so interested in ACP, actually. I'll give you an example, that retcon thing I showed you, it began as just a giant LLM script where I told it how to rebase and do stuff. What I found was it worked like 90%. Usually, it would forget some parts of the branch. It just would be like, I'm done. I'm like, no, you're not, you've left off a whole thing. Or it wouldn't check that the test pass and everything else. Now when it's written in Rust, like I'm guaranteed every commit passes the test, every commit is formatted because it's got a deterministic backing. I have been toying with similar things for skills where I had experiments where I would detect with some various heuristics and things that I thought a skill was probably good and give it some extra hints to avoid that problem.
I've backed off from a lot of that, partly because models get better, but also because I think we need telemetry first. I feel we need deterministic stuff, and I feel we need a way to measure, are we actually helping or not? Because what I noticed is a lot of times it's a little unclear. I want some better infrastructure where I can actually measure, how often is a skill being used? If I do give it some nudges, am I actually making people's lives better? Like I could do A/B tests, stuff like that. I think it's a real concern, and I don't think there's a great answer right now.

articles.title: PHP Patches Seven Critical RCE Vulnerabilities
articles.text:
PHP on Thursday rolled out a fresh set of security patches as part of its four-week update schedule, including fixes for seven critical-severity remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities.
First in line is CVE-2026-115560, which was publicly disclosed last month, two days after PHP2Shell patches landed. Residing in the session upload progress feature, it could be triggered to write attacker data using one session serialization format and then read it using another.
“A mismatched decoder can interpret part of a session key as serialized object data. An application with a suitable object gadget chain can then execute code with the privileges of the PHP worker,” PHP’s advisory reads.
Next in line is CVE-2026-129481, described as a use-after-free that occurs after a session shutdown has been interrupted, and which PHP describes as an incomplete fix for CVE-2026-109619, one of the two PHP2Shell flaws fixed in October and now widely exploited.
“An attacker who can cause an application’s session cleanup to fail in this way may corrupt memory or crash a reused PHP worker. The use-after-free could potentially lead to remote code execution, but code execution through this specific field has not been demonstrated,” PHP notes, adding that PHP 8.2 is not affected.
Another use-after-free, CVE-2026-129182, covers additional exploitation scenarios for CVE-2026-109619, an RCE via stale global state. According to PHP, however, RCE via these scenarios has not been demonstrated.
Impacting PHP 8.5 and later, CVE-2026-129474 is a use-after-free weakness that could allow an unauthenticated attacker to cause a fatal error and achieve RCE. “Exploitation depends on the application and requires control over enough request data to influence memory allocation, a reachable magic method call, and a fatal error at the relevant point,” PHP says.
Attackers able to influence session contents and interrupt the write of serialized data to a session file may trigger the deserialization of attacker-controlled content when the session is next opened. Tracked as CVE-2026-126714, the flaw could lead to RCE via a suitable object gadget chain in the application.
PHP also patched CVE-2026-129289, a PHP-FPM request smuggling issue caused by PHP reading a request-body stream lazily, treating a request body as handled during request shutdown and skipping the normal cleanup that discards unread input.
“PHP can fail to discard unread bytes from an HTTP request body before reusing a persistent PHP-FPM or LSAPI connection. In PHP-FPM, an unauthenticated attacker can make those bytes form a separate FastCGI request, bypass front-end routing and execute attacker-controlled PHP code with the privileges of the worker,” PHP explains.
The seventh critical-severity vulnerability patched today, CVE-2026-129496, resides in the timezone cache. PHP can retain a reference to it when writing a diagnostic to a PHP error log file during process startup, and a later diagnostic can access the freed cache before it is reset.
“On affected configurations, a remote attacker can trigger memory corruption, cause a worker to crash, and potentially execute arbitrary code with the privileges of the PHP worker,” PHP explains.
PHP 8.6.0 and PHP 8.5.13 were rolled out with fixes for all critical bugs and for 10 high and medium-severity flaws. Patches for most issues were also included in PHP 8.4.28, PHP 8.3.37, and PHP 8.2.36. More information is available on PHP’s news archive page.
Related: PHP Readies Critical Security Updates to Patch Another RCE Flaw

articles.title: Coinbase frenó con IA una estafa de criptomonedas con un falso Elon Musk que prometía duplicar el dinero
articles.text:
Coinbase señaló que su sistema de inteligencia artificial (IA) impidió que USD 4,7 millones salieran de las cuentas de sus clientes hacia estafadores. Los ciberdelincuentes usaron un deepfake (video falso hecho con IA) de Elon Musk en una transmisión de YouTube que prometía duplicar las criptomonedas que los espectadores enviaran.
La empresa lo detalló el 17 de noviembre de 2026 en su blog, dentro de una serie semanal sobre protección al consumidor. Según Coinbase, el sistema detuvo cerca del 91% del dinero que sus clientes intentaron enviar, sin intervención humana.
Los estafadores armaron una transmisión en vivo que imitaba la del evento de Tesla sobre su “auto volador”. Incluía el deepfake de Musk, direcciones de billeteras digitales en pantalla y un código QR, y ofrecía devolver el doble de cualquier cantidad enviada.
Más de 500.000 personas vieron la transmisión, según Coinbase. En unas dos horas, cientos de sus clientes intentaron enviar millones de dólares a esas direcciones.
Nadie hackeó las cuentas de los espectadores del video en YouTube
Coinbase subrayó que no hubo intrusión: ninguna cuenta fue vulnerada, ninguna contraseña robada y ninguna credencial obtenida por engaño. Los clientes, muchos de ellos usuarios de larga data, decidieron por su cuenta enviar dinero a un desconocido.
La empresa explicó que ese es el obstáculo principal. Las defensas habituales buscan movimientos no autorizados, pero aquí el cliente había iniciado sesión y confirmó la operación. Sus sistemas detectan señales de riesgo, dijo, pero no la intención de quien envía el dinero.
Por eso el sistema intenta interrumpir la decisión. Primero, modelos de aprendizaje automático puntúan en tiempo real los envíos riesgosos, por ejemplo los vinculados a sorteos, a la suplantación de marcas o a billeteras recién creadas.
Luego, un agente de IA conversa con el cliente, le nombra el tipo de estafa y le hace preguntas que desarman la historia. Cada respuesta recibe un puntaje de confianza antes de llegar al usuario.
Coinbase afirmó que el agente nunca había visto esta modalidad, un sorteo con deepfake atado a un lanzamiento en vivo. Aun así reconoció la promesa de multiplicar fondos, la urgencia de un evento de pocas horas y una transferencia irreversible.
Lo que Coinbase no dijo que fue revelado al público
El cálculo inverso muestra un límite. Unchained, un medio especializado en criptomonedas, estimó a partir de las cifras de Coinbase que los clientes intentaron enviar unos USD 5,2 millones y que cerca de USD 460.000 sí salieron de sus cuentas. La empresa no dijo cuánto llegó a los estafadores ni la fecha de la transmisión falsa.
The Block y Unchained coinciden en que las cifras provienen solo del blog de Coinbase. No hay una auditoría independiente ni datos por transacción que permitan comprobar la pérdida final.
Coinbase sostuvo que los deepfakes abaratan este tipo de fraude: antes armarlo requería un equipo y semanas, y ahora basta una transmisión en vivo y un modelo de IA. La empresa dijo que invierte en IA para detectar nuevos formatos de estafa en horas y no en semanas.
Cómo reconocer el engaño
La compañía sugirió no enviar criptomonedas a una dirección o un código QR mostrado en un video en una plataforma streaming o enviado a través de aplicaciones, porque cualquiera puede poner una billetera en pantalla. Pidió verificar en la cuenta oficial o el sitio de la empresa, y no en enlaces de la publicación.
Coinbase señaló que ninguna oferta legítima duplica el dinero que se envía, y que nunca pedirá enviar criptomonedas para reclamar un premio ni presionará para actuar antes de que termine una transmisión. Quien sospeche que fue blanco de un engaño debe escribir de inmediato al soporte de la aplicación.

articles.title: Anthropic's IPO puts AI's circular financing boom to the test | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Arriving at public markets today, Anthropic’s IPO is poised to raise billions for the company and its investors. But the biggest surprise may be just how much of that money will end up going to supplier-investors.
Amazon and Google, two of Anthropic’s largest infrastructure partners, hold stakes valued around a combined $307.9 billion at the company’s updated IPO price of $83 per share. Amazon, which invested $18 billion into the AI startup, would see its 14.7% stake hit upwards of $159 billion, while Google’s 13.7% stake is valued at nearly $149 billion, according to share ownership figures disclosed in Anthropic’s IPO prospectus.
A handful of other AI infrastructure providers are also positioned to benefit. Nvidia, AMD, Microsoft, Broadcom, Micron, and TSMC have joined Google in committing $26 billion to Anthropic at its IPO price in a private placement.
In total, Google has invested $12.3 billion into Anthropic since 2023, with another promised $30 billion dependent on Anthropic meeting certain performance milestones. And with the exception of TSMC, Anthropic has announced multibillion-dollar strategic partnerships with its other infrastructure supplier investors — including Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom, Microsoft, and Micron — that would see Anthropic purchasing their products.
This is the circular financing that has made some observers so skeptical of the AI boom. These companies are not just investors; they’re also Anthropic’s biggest suppliers. It might look like Amazon and Google are putting billions into Anthropic, but they get that money right back when Anthropic needs to train a model or serve Claude to users. From afar, it looks like unprecedented revenue growth for cloud companies and unprecedented fundraising from Anthropic — but it’s just the same money passing from one pocket to another.
Today’s IPO marks a critical change in that financing system, the moment it might just become self-sustaining. Those investments appear to have paid off, and are now liquid. Anthropic is still operating at a net loss of tens of billions of dollars each quarter — but it will no longer be suppliers and private investors footing the bill. Now, capital will come from a mix of public-market investors and corporate bonds, neither of which have the conflicts-of-interest that caused concerns before.
And critically, the company’s new bottom line looks pretty good.
Once it debuts, Anthropic is expected to have about $220 billion in cash, cash equivalents, and short-term investments, including proceeds from its IPO and the $26 billion private placement. Anthropic also has the ability to pay for future commitments in stock.
Joey Brookhart, who leads the Tokenomics team at SemiAnalysis, estimates that Anthropic needs roughly $280 billion in cumulative revenue over the next four years to pay for its compute bill, which Brookhart said is “achievable given where they will be next year from a revenue perspective.”
“The ownership stake is very worthwhile, and those companies no longer need any more support from [suppliers],” Brookhart told TechCrunch. “Amazon doesn’t need to prop them up anymore. The revenue is all coming from other customers.”
That doesn’t mean the server bills are going down, though. Anthropic has already committed to spend $900 billion, primarily for compute and infrastructure, according to a regulatory filing. Certain agreements have termination provisions, but Brookhart thinks the company is in a strong position to pay up.
On the other side, Anthropic generated $17 billion in third-quarter 2026 revenue, putting the company on pace for a $68 billion annualized rate for the year. If Anthropic continues to grow at its current trajectory, Brookhart believes it could easily cover the gap needed to fund its compute.
Gil Luria, head of technology research at D.A. Davidson, agreed.
“By the time the IPO is done, Anthropic’s going to have more cash on hand than any company has ever had,” Luria told TechCrunch, noting that the firm raised around $141 billion in capital and will take home around $91.7 billion in net proceeds at $83 per share. “And they’re not burning cash. They’re just going to have a war chest.”
A public listing will make Anthropic a more credible borrower, making it easier to raise money outside of public markets, says Brookhart. That’s despite recent reports that creditors might not see Anthropic as “investment-grade” material.
Luria distinguished between Anthropic’s supplier investments and neoclouds like CoreWeave, which he sees as more purely supported by circular financing. “CoreWeave wouldn’t exist if Nvidia didn’t prop them up, and it probably won’t exist if Nvidia doesn’t bail them out,” Luria said.
Brookhart also pushed back on describing Anthropic’s financing as purely circular, saying it was still “additive to the ecosystem.”
For both analysts, the biggest risk to Anthropic is simply that it will lose the AI race. Right now, the company’s growth is fueled by its status at the frontier of generative AI — but if it’s overtaken by OpenAI, Google DeepMind, or even cheap open-weight models, that could change fast. As Luria put it: “If we’re all using other people’s models, then Anthropic’s not worth a trillion and a half dollars. It’s worth nothing.”
But regardless of who wins the frontier, compute suppliers will likely be just fine. Neither Brookhart nor Luria believe Anthropic’s growth is at risk, despite some arguments that cheaper tokens and more competition will directly affect the AI company’s bottom line.
“For Amazon and Google, the risk isn’t actually that high because in that scenario, we’re using other models,” Luria said. “I’m arguing we’re going to use a lot more AI. I don’t know if it’s all Anthropic’s AI…. That’s still going to come from a data center managed by Amazon, Google, and Microsoft.”

articles.title: Three 'e-waste' Nvidia V100s hit 100 tokens per second on Qwen 3.6 35B in a $1,042 homelab rig — decommissioned GPUs outpace a $5,399 M5 Max Mac Studio at long contexts
articles.text:
Three 'e-waste' Nvidia V100s hit 100 tokens per second on Qwen 3.6 35B in a $1,042 homelab rig — decommissioned GPUs outpace a $5,399 M5 Max Mac Studio at long contexts
An M5 Max Mac Studio is slightly faster at short context, but the V100s pull ahead at 64K and longer.
A homelab builder benchmarked three used Nvidia V100s on Qwen 3.6 35B, achieving about 100 tokens per second in a custom setup costing $1,042 with just “e-waste” GPUs. The smaller, dense Qwen 3.6 27B manages about 24 tokens per second on the same platform, and the V100s use about half the energy of the same number of P100s for a given job.
The blog post, “Scaling ‘E-Waste’: LLMs on Multiple Decommissioned GPUs,” compares nine different builds — one to three K80s, P100s, or V100-16GB cards — on a single Supermicro dual-Xeon board. The test uses llama.cpp and covers more than 130 LLM tests, including Qwen 2.5, Gemma 4, and, of course, Qwen 3.6, at Q4/Q8/F16 precisions and from 4K to 128K context sizes. GPU energy per run is also recorded. The builder is “daily driving Qwen 3.6 35B” on the V100s and notes that scaling decommissioned GPUs will only get you so far.
“E-waste,” in this case, refers to decommissioned enterprise GPUs, which are a popular but somewhat underpowered option when compared to very expensive modern alternatives. The Nvidia Tesla V100s in question are tested as a follow-up to a July round which tested 15 “e-waste” GPUs, and this time the board and CPUs stay the same for every build — the Supermicro X10DRG-Q with two Intel Xeon E5-2687W 12-core CPUs, powered by the Corsair HX1500i PSU.
Performance is judged based on what is considered “realtime interaction” which, here, is 70 tokens per second. As to why the number of GPUs is three: Qwen 3.6 35B, the primary tested model, fails on just one or two at Q8, or 8-bit quantization.
Here are the given prices, with the note that they aren’t “100% reflective of what you could find on eBay today,” although the totals count only one of the two CPUs and omit RAM, storage, the case, and any cooling.
| What the builder paid for each three-card build |  |  |  | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Part | 3x K80 | 3x P100 | 3x V100-16GB | 
| Three GPUs | $270 ($90 each) | $403.50 ($134.50 each) | $655.16 ($436.77 per pair) | 
| Board | $211 | $211 | $211 | 
| PSU | $147.70 | $147.70 | $147.70 | 
| One CPU | $28.20 | $28.20 | $28.20 | 
| Builder’s total | $657 | $790 | $1,042 | 
| With 2nd CPU | $685 | $819 | $1,070 | 
The older cards are relatively inexpensive because they “run hot and ship without cooling,” which required the builder to 3D print one blower duct per card and has led to the development of a standalone cooler.
The bench itself involves 10 runs of 512 generated tokens per test with context pre-filled to 4K, 32K, 64K, or 128K. Qwen 3.6 35B is a mixture-of-experts (MoE) model, which only activates about 3 billion out of its 35 billion total parameters per token. The numbers that immediately follow are at Q8.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
The token goal was easily reached…when the context window was small, or 4K. The 100.8 tokens per second there fell to 72.7 at 128K, still usable by the 70 tokens per second goal. The 27B model, which is not MoE, fared much worse, at 24.3 at 4K, 21.6 at 32K, 18.7 at 64K, and just 14.2 at 128K. The MoE ends up about four to five times faster, depending on the context size.
| Qwen 3.6 35B generation speed by context length (tokens per second) |  |  |  |  | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Setup | 4K | 32K | 64K | 128K | 
| 3x V100, Q8 | 100.8 | 89.4 | 83.5 | 72.7 | 
| 2x V100, Q4 | 105.4 | 96.2 | 89.5 | 77.1 | 
| 3x P100, Q8 | 55.2 | 50.9 | 47.5 | 40.2 | 
| M5 Max Mac, 8-bit | 105.5 | 91.1 | 78.5 | 61.3 | 
Also tested were other dense models of about 30B parameters. At 4K, Gemma 4 31B achieved 20.9 and Qwen 2.5 32B 21.0, while the MoE Gemma 4 26B cleared the 70 tokens per second bar with just two V100s at Q8. If you move down to Q4, or 4-bit quantization, two V100s can run Qwen 3.6 35B at 77.1 to 105.4 tokens per second, between 128K and 4K context size. This is where it’s claimed that adding more cards gives you more memory, which enables larger models to be run, but not speed.
The P100s, for comparison, only hit 40.2–55.2 tokens per second in the same context range with Q8 Qwen 3.6 35B, and the target 70 only with Qwen 2.5 3B. If we compare to more modern hardware — the Nvidia DGX Spark, MSRP $4,700, and the M5 Max Mac Studio, which starts at $2,499 but costs $5,399 with the tested 40-core GPU, 128GB of memory, and a 1TB SSD — the 3x V100 build holds its own, using sourced data.
The Mac comparison comes from the oMLX benchmark page for the M5 Max with 40 GPU cores and 128GB of unified memory, and that hits 43.9 tokens per second with a ~195K-token prompt on the Qwen 3.6 35B model. The Mac is slightly ahead at 4K and 32K, while the V100s pull ahead at 64K and 128K, by 19% at the longest context. These numbers have to be taken loosely, as the machines use different runtimes.
The Spark run came from Kleybrink’s dgx-spark-bench, using Ollama in thinking mode with short prompts. Its 45.8 tokens per second is less than half the V100s’ 4K figure.
Going further to modern GPUs, which “destroy our decommissioned equivalents,” as the builder puts it, you get about 315 tokens per second on two H100s and about 455 on one B200 at 128K, the B200 roughly six times the V100 box, even though the hosted cards ran the full 16-bit model against the V100s’ 8-bit. Parasail, an inference provider, sponsored that comparison with dedicated H100 and B200 deployments.
As for energy, the V100 setup came out to about 0.02 kWh for a 128K 35B run, with the P100s taking twice that much and two or three K80s as much as 0.35 to 0.45 kWh. The V100-16GB simply “[puts] up better scores while consuming less energy,” in comparison to the P100s. These numbers are for the GPUs and not from the wall.
There’s more to come. The builder wants a benchmark that “maps to ‘software factory’ performance,” a term for models being prompted constantly, around the clock, where instant speed matters less. Then there’s the cooler, which is “almost ready for release,” with beta testers to be recruited from the mailing list, although no date has been given. From the Reddit thread, the builder mentions the intention to compare inference backends and use speculative decoding to improve performance.

articles.title: Bell considering its own Telus proposal, held preliminary talks
articles.text:
Bell Canada Enterprises (BCE) reportedly held preliminary talks with Telus and is assessing what a potential Telus transaction would include in the wake of Quebecor’s push to acquire the Vancouver-based national telecom.
Three sources spoke to the Globe and Mail about Bell’s reaction to the Quebecor bid, which included preliminary discussions, hiring financial and legal advisors, and more. Bell is now considering possible next steps, including possible remedies Ottawa might require should Bell move ahead with a formal proposal. However, the considerations are still in the early stages.
The news comes after Quebecor, which owns Freedom Mobile, Videotron, and Fizz, made a roughly $31 billion proposal to acquire all of Telus’ shares. Quebecor first proposed the idea to Telus in June, and then published a revised proposal on Nov. 9.
If a deal were to go through, it would see Canada drop from four major carriers to three. The proposal sparked concerns from critics and politicians over the impacts on competition and affordability. Quebecor CEO Pierre Karl Péladeau, however, said in a recent interview that combining Quebecor and Telus would enable the companies to better fend off foreign competition, such as from satellite provider Starlink.
Telus is currently reviewing Quebecor’s proposal and considering its options. Telus’ special committee director Lisa de Wilde told the Globe that “all options are on the table” when asked about deals from other telecoms.
Notably, this isn’t the first time Bell and Telus have considered combining. The two carriers looked into it in 2007 but didn’t move ahead. However, some in the industry consider the companies to be good potential partners, given that they already have a network sharing agreement. Some made a similar argument for Telus and Quebecor, noting that Telus has a stronger footprint in Western Canada where Quebecor is more limited.
Regardless of the possible synergies Telus has with other telecoms, any combination will inevitably be bad for Canadians. Just look at the Rogers-Shaw merger from a few years ago. Since the companies merged, we’ve seen higher internet and TV costs, worse service, increased customer complaints, and significant cuts to Canadian jobs.
Source: The Globe and Mail

articles.title: Lo nuevo de Windows te avisará si un programa o componente tiene una vulnerabilidad grave (y ayudará a solucionarlo)
articles.text:
Microsoft prepara una nueva capa de seguridad para Windows 11 que intentará resolver uno de los problemas más comunes de los usuarios y empresas. Conocida como Emerging Risks (riesgos emergentes), la función detectará si hay aplicaciones, controladores o componentes de firmware que tengan una vulnerabilidad grave. La nueva característica se integrará al sistema operativo como parte de sus próximas mejoras de seguridad.
Aprovechando el inicio de su conferencia Ignite, Microsoft realizó múltiples anuncios de las funciones que llegarán a Windows 11 en los próximos meses. Si bien este evento se enfoca en desarrolladores y empresas, muchas de las características son de interés general y terminan implementándose en las versiones de consumo del sistema operativo. Una de ellas es Emerging Risks, que ya comenzó a probarse en las versiones preliminares de Windows 11 Insider.
De acuerdo con WindowsLatest, el objetivo de esta capa de seguridad es identificar fallos en el software y hardware del ordenador y avisarle al usuario. Microsoft define como "riesgos emergentes" a las vulnerabilidades graves en aplicaciones, drivers o firmware que requieren atención inmediata. Cuando Windows detecte alguno de estos problemas, mostrará una alerta acompañada de los pasos a seguir para reducir el riesgo.
Cómo funciona Emerging Risks, la función de Windows que evitará que te hackeen
Los programas, controladores o componentes desactualizados son un mal que enfrentan todos los usuarios de Windows. Fuera de los parches mensuales que corrigen los fallos del sistema, rara vez instalamos actualizaciones del software o drivers. Los usuarios se quedan con la primera versión que instalaron o la que venía de fábrica cuando compraron el equipo, algo que puede dejar vulnerable al equipo si alguno de ellos tiene un agujero de seguridad.
Emerging Risks funciona como un panel que analiza el software y los componentes del PC y coteja la información con bases de datos de vulnerabilidades. En caso de que detecte una anomalía, el sistema sugerirá instalar la versión más reciente que corrige el problema. Pero si no existe un parche disponible, Microsoft podría recomendar que desinstales la aplicación o el controlador, o en casos más extremos, desactivar el componente vulnerable para que los riesgos no escalen.
La herramienta podrá clasificar el nivel de riesgo detectado, de modo que los usuarios sepan qué problemas requieren atención urgente y cuáles pueden esperar. Emerging Risks también añadirá información de cada vulnerabilidad usando los datos de Microsoft y de fuentes externas.
Hasta ahora todo suena muy bien, excepto por el hecho de que Emerging Risks no solucionará automáticamente los problemas. La nueva función no es un antivirus, por lo que los usuarios deberán seguir las indicaciones para evitar un hackeo. Otro detalle es que su alcance se limita a las vulnerabilidades en los programas de Microsoft, ya que el software de terceros utiliza sus propios sistemas de actualización y notificaciones.
¿Cuándo estará disponible la nueva capa de seguridad de Windows 11?
Microsoft confirmó que Emerging Risks llegará a todos los ordenadores compatibles con Windows 11 dentro del panel de Windows Security. La función no exige requisitos adicionales y puede usarse en equipos que desactivaron el arranque seguro o la integridad de memoria. Por ahora solo se encuentra disponible en las versiones preliminares de Windows 11 Insider.

articles.title: Giving public sector ICT teams the space to deliver digital change
articles.text:
Giving public sector ICT teams the space to deliver digital change
Technology needs to deliver more efficient services to the public
Ask the provider of vital public services what they want from technology and the answer is unlikely to be more IT management. Technology needs to help people do their jobs, generate value and, ultimately, deliver more efficient services to the public.
The challenge is securing the time, resources and expertise needed to make that happen. Internal ICT teams still have to keep essential, secure services running every day, while demands for technology adoption continue to grow.
Digital transformation projects cannot simply wait until there is a lull in the workload of day-to-day service operations. For most public services organizations, that day may never come.
Head of IT Managed Services at Telent, part of M Group.
This is where a managed service approach can help balance the conflicts of day-to-day operations and major new initiatives that have the potential to transform service delivery.
There can still be a concern that bringing in a managed service provider means handing over control. Yet long-term partnerships across the public sector organizations show that the approach can work very differently.
Internal teams stay close to the organization and its strategic priorities, while drawing on specialist expertise, service management discipline and additional capacity when they need it.
Keeping ICT decisions close to the organization
Working with a managed service provider does not require an organization to distance itself from its ICT. Internal teams still understand their organization, its people and its operational priorities. That knowledge matters. The role of the provider is to work alongside it and bring in specialist support, governance and service management capability where it can make a difference.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
For public sector organizations, retaining control should not automatically mean maintaining every capability in-house. It is about making informed decisions over how technology supports the service, manages risk and delivers value, with the right expertise available to turn those decisions into practical improvements.
Finding the capacity to plan ahead
That becomes harder when an ICT team's attention is constantly being pulled towards immediate operational demands.
Technology keeps changing, which means the expertise required to implement it as well as support it changes too. A managed service can give an organization access to specialist knowledge when it needs it, while providing additional resources to support transformation, service transition and ongoing improvement work.
That can create much-needed space for internal teams. Rather than every new project and business requirement competing with the daily workload, there is more capacity to plan ahead, manage risk and align technology decisions to organizational outcomes.
And there will always be a daily workload.
Public sector organizations cannot put existing services on hold while they transform them. For emergency services in particular, technology supports people doing critical work every day. Systems need to remain available, secure and resilient, and users still need responsive support, regardless of what technology transformation is happening in the background.
Digital change is also much easier when the day-to-day ICT service operations underpinning it are stable, secure and well managed. If teams are constantly reacting to problems in the existing environment, it becomes much harder to devote attention to improving it. Keeping the day-to-day service running well creates the breathing room needed to introduce change without losing sight of the people already relying on that technology.
Planning for a service that will change over time
One mistake public sector organizations can make is thinking too much about what they need from a managed service on day one.
The immediate requirements obviously matter. But technology, cybersecurity threats and service expectations will move on during the life of a contract, and the organization will change with them. Priorities shift and different skills are needed. Technology that works well today may also reach a point where replacing it makes more sense than continuing to maintain it.
Flexibility needs to be part of the relationship from the start. A provider should bring ideas, service performance insight and relevant expertise into the conversation, while looking for ways the service could add additional value over time. This also gives internal teams an opportunity to look ahead and consider whether their technology is keeping pace with the organization.
That becomes even more important when there are wider digital transformation plans. Change rarely happens in one big leap. Organizations need the freedom to introduce new technology when it makes sense, adjust their approach, maintain good governance and respond to priorities that may not have existed when the original contract was signed.
For public sector leaders, it is worth looking beyond the immediate requirements when choosing a provider. Think about where the organization could be several years from now and whether the relationship has enough flexibility, governance and continual improvement focus to support that journey.
Giving ICT teams more time to make a difference
The purpose of all this is to give the people delivering public services technology that works for them. The ICT teams supporting those services need the same consideration. When immediate operational demands take up most of their time, there is inevitably less capacity to focus on the changes the organization wants to make.
A managed service can provide extra capacity and specialist knowledge while internal teams remain closely involved in the decisions that affect their organization. That gives them more time to consider what needs to change and how technology can better support the service.
The results should be visible in the day-to-day work of public services. Frontline staff get the information and systems they need when they need them, while ICT leaders have more time to plan what comes next. For the communities relying on those services, technology simply helps the people serving them get on with the job.

articles.title: Mots de passe : les internautes privilégient toujours la simplicité
articles.text:
NordPass publie la huitième édition de son classement des 200 mots de passe fréquents, sur 44 pays. On y retrouve les traditionnelles suites de chiffres mais aussi des références à Minecraft, à Pantera ou à LeBron James.
Les données viennent de fuites publiques et de campagnes de malware, entre septembre 2025 et septembre 2026. Au niveau mondial, le trio de tête ne change décidément pas : "123456", »admin« et "12345678".
Lebron0319, P@ssw0rd : une touche perso ne rend pas un mot de passe solide
"123456" reste en pôle position pour la septième fois en huit ans, avec plus de sept millions d’occurrences sur la période. Aux États-Unis, il reprend la première place à "admin", avec "password" en troisième place. On retrouve également des variantes qui occupent cinq places du top 20. Les réflexes se ressemblent d’un pays à l’autre : beaucoup traduisent simplement "password", d’où "motdepasse" en français et "contraseña" en espagnol. Les pays à alphabet latin préfèrent les mots, les autres les chiffres. Bref, de toute évidence, il reste encore beaucoup de chemin à faire en termes de sensibilisation…
On retrouve par ailleurs plusieurs éléments de pop culture et l’étude relève par exemple "minecraft", "sasuke20", "Slayer@666", "Pantera1234", "skibiditoilet" ou "Tiktok2002". La star incontestée du basket a elle aussi influencé les mots de passe des internautes avec "Lebron0319". C’est aussi le cas de Messi, Lampard et Lewandowski.
Rajouter un symbole ne change pas grand-chose à la faiblesse des mots de passe. Le top 200 compte 39 mots de passe avec des caractères spéciaux, soit sept de plus qu’en 2025, comme "P@ssw0rd" ou "Admin@123". NordPass juge que tous ces mots de passe tomberaient en quelques secondes face à un logiciel qui teste des combinaisons à la chaîne.
Alors, que faire ? Choisir un mot de passe unique par compte, avec majuscules, minuscules, chiffres et symboles. Une phrase de passe (des mots sans rapport entre eux) fait aussi l’affaire. Fin 2026, l’authentification multifacteur n’est plus une option à ignorer. Bien entendu, pour Nord, la publication de cette étude vise surtout à mettre en avant son gestionnaire de mots de passe. L’usage d’un tel service est bien évidemment recommandé, tout comme l'adoption des clés d’accès permettant de se connecter avec son empreinte, son visage ou le code PIN de l’appareil, sans rien taper ni retenir. Microsoft, Facebook, Apple et Google poussent déjà très largement les passkeys.

articles.title: BYD actualiza su coche más vendido con mejoras muy interesantes: así es el SEAL U DM-i Model Year 2027
articles.text:
BYD sigue apostando por traer nuevas opciones para los que buscan un coche y lo hace esta vez con una nueva versión de su SUV familiar SEAL U DM-i que llega bajo el nombre del Model Year 2027. Este modelo, perteneciente al segmento D, llega con más potencia y mayores prestaciones, un salto cualitativo muy interesante frente al estándar.
Destacan, sobre todo, una mayor autonomía gracias a su nueva batería de mayor capacidad y algunos cambios muy interesantes para hacer más cómoda la conducción, como la tracción total y la suspensión trasera y dirección totalmente renovadas.
La base es la del SEAL U DM-i que la compañía lanzó al mercado en 2024 y que se convirtió en el modelo más vendido tanto de Europa como en España dentro de los híbridos enchufables en tan solo un año, siendo uno de los modelos referentes de 2025. Ahora, esta actualización para el modelo 2027 busca mantener ese puesto, pero ofreciendo una mejora en la mayoría de sus aspectos clave.
En este sentido, una de esas grandes mejoras está en lo que esconde bajo el capó; ahora las versiones del SUV incorporan un motor de gasolina renovado de 1,5 litros turboalimentado de 130 CV (96 kW) en sustitución del anterior bloque atmosférico en las versiones de tracción delantera, lo que supone un salto en potencia, prestaciones y eficiencia. No obstante, llega en tres versiones diferentes.
Por un lado, el acabado Boost, que es el de acceso a la gama SEAL U DM-i, combina el motor de gasolina con un motoreléctrico de 204 CV (150 kW) para entregar una potencia total conjunta de 238 CV (175 kW); una versión Comfort, que mantiene su batería de mayor capacidad con 130 km de autonomía en modo 100% eléctrico y una combinada de 1.030 km; y el Design, que cuenta con un motor adicional de 204 CV (150 kW) en el eje trasero para ofrecer una potencia total máxima de 374 CV (275 kW) y una aceleración de 0 a 100km/h en solo 5,1 segundos.
Otro aspecto interesante es que ahora todas las versiones del SEAL U DM-i disponen de carga rápida en corriente continua (CC) de hasta 55 kW, que reduce a la mitad el tiempo de recarga del 30% al 80%:15 minutos en el acabado Boost y 20 minutos en los acabados Comfort y Design.
Y, como es habitual en la marca, vienen cargados de tecnología en su apartado de infoentretenimiento, con dos tamaños de pantalla según el acabado. Por un lado, en Boost cuenta con una pantalla central de 12,8” (32,5 cm), mientras que Comfort y Design disponen de una de 15,6” (39,6 cm). Los tres modelos integran Google Built-in, con Google Maps, Google Assistant y acceso a Google Play Store.
Este nuevo SEAL U DM-I ‘Model Year 2027’ estará disponible en Burgundy Red y Graphite Blue, que se suman a los Polar White, Time Grey, Obsidian Black y Boundless Cloud, con llantas 19” de serie.
Sobre los precios, arranca desde los 39.300€ en el Boost y pueden llegar hasta los 48.500€ en el caso del SEAL U DM-I Design. También hay una versión 100% eléctrica, el SEAL U, disponible en acabados Comfort y Design por 44.290 y 48.290, respectivamente.

articles.title: Nigeria’s Payaza secures Central Bank of Kenya licence - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Nigerian payments infrastructure company Payaza has been authorised by the Central Bank of Kenya (CBK) to provide payment gateway services, just weeks after getting regulatory approval in Zambia.
Payaza offers payment collection, payout and merchant tools to businesses in Africa and international markets. It handles card, mobile money and bank payments in more than 40 currencies and operates in more than 27 countries.
The CBK approval allows Payaza to operate as a licensed payment service provider in Kenya. It can now serve local merchants directly with online checkout and payment acceptance. The licence does not cover deposit-taking or customer wallets.
It comes after the Bank of Zambia gave Payaza a Certificate of Designation of a Payment System. The company has also recently picked up payment licensing milestones in China, Pakistan and Bangladesh.
“Kenya is the heartbeat of East Africa’s digital economy, and we are entering it the right way: fully licensed,” said Seyi Ebenezer, Payaza’s group CEO. “Coming so soon after our Bank of Zambia approval, this licence from the Central Bank of Kenya connects East, West and Southern Africa on one regulated platform.”
Payaza says it will now speed up merchant onboarding, build closer ties with banks and mobile money operators, and seek more licences across Africa, especially in East Africa. Nigeria makes up about 35 per cent of its revenue.

articles.title: When agents go out of bounds: How Lasso is helping enterprises secure the AI agents they build and use
articles.text:
NetApp Excellerator
View Brand Publisher
When agents go out of bounds: How Lasso is helping enterprises secure the AI agents they build and use
Enterprises are deploying AI agents faster than they can track them, and not every agent stays within the boundaries it was given. Lasso, part of NetApp Excellerator, is changing that.
An AI agent handling a refund request starts a funds transfer that no one asked for and no one approved. Would the company notice before the money moved?
This is the problem Lasso is addressing. Part of the NetApp Excellerator program, it protects the AI agents enterprises build and use, wherever they run, by learning what each agent is meant to do and checking every action it takes against that purpose.
Enterprises are putting AI agents to work faster than they can keep track of them. These agents plan their own steps, call tools and MCP servers on their own, and act without a person approving each move. That autonomy is the reason companies deploy them, and it is also how an agent ends up outside the boundaries it was given.
Two challenges make this hard to control.
The challenges of securing AI agents
Agents are everywhere, and each one has its own purpose. AI agents now run in every part of the enterprise. Developers use coding assistants on their endpoints and connect them to MCP servers and skills. Engineering teams build custom agents that run in code and in the cloud, and business teams create their own agent using low-code no-code builder platforms.
Each of these agents are set up for a different purpose, and each one works toward it autonomously. With this many agents running in this many places, it becomes difficult to track what any single agent is meant to do, and without that there is no reliable way to tell when one has gone off task or gone rogue.
Context windows are large, and attacks hide inside them
Each agent gathers the context it needs for a task by calling models, MCP servers, tools, and data sources, and everything it gathers goes into its context window. For a single task, that context can reach hundreds of thousands of tokens. A prompt injection can be one sentence hidden in an email, a web page, or a tool response, and inside a context that large it becomes the needle in the haystack. Most detection models were built for short prompts. On inputs of this size, they slow down or miss the attack, and an agent that reads the injected instruction may act on it as if it came from the user.
How Lasso does it
Lasso’s AI security platform protects the AI agents enterprises build and use, wherever they run, whether that is on an endpoint, in code or in the cloud.
It works from each agent’s intent. Its Intent Security Engine learns what each agent is meant to do from its configuration and its history, and it checks every action the agent takes against that purpose.
An action that does not fit, such as a support agent starting a funds transfer in the middle of a refund conversation, is flagged, masked or blocked inline in under 50 milliseconds, with 98.6% detection accuracy. Because the check is made against the agent’s purpose, it catches an agent that has gone off task even when nothing in the request looks like a known attack.
Lasso’s detection is built for the size of agentic inputs. It holds the same accuracy and latency as the context grows toward a million tokens, so an injection hidden deep in a long input is found before the agent acts on it.
The Lasso platform
The platform covers the full path from finding an agent to protecting it in production.
- Discovery finds every AI agent, model and component in use across SaaS tools, code, cloud and agent builder platforms.
- AI-BOM gives each agent a bill of materials listing the models, MCP servers, tools and components it depends on, so a vulnerable component can be traced to every agent that uses it.
- AI-SPM maps each agent’s connections in a visual graph that shows its blast radius, checks configurations against NIST, OWASP and MITRE, and limits use to approved models and components.
- Automated AI Red Teaming tests agents the way an attacker would. Reconnaissance of each agent shapes static, dynamic and high-agency attacks drawn from more than 300,000 payloads, and the tests run in CI/CD on every deployment.
- Runtime Protection and AI Detection and Response enforce policy per agent at the SDK, API or AI Gateway layer and detect prompt injection and other OWASP and MITRE risks. Each alert explains what happened, which agent was targeted and what to do next.
- Rogue Agent Protection uses the Intent Security Engine to detect goal misalignment, intent drift and behavioral anomalies, and it stops an agent’s action when it moves outside its purpose.
Customer success stories
A European insurance group runs Lasso on the production agents that process its internal claims, where prompt injection attempts arrive embedded inside the claims documents themselves. Lasso blocks them before the agents act. The company has since moved the application to production and is adding hundreds of new agents.
A global hospitality company uses Lasso to secure the agents it built for employee-facing logistics workflows. Intent-based guardrails enforce each agent’s behavior in real time, and the company’s internal MCP-based use cases were secured without code changes.
A global automotive manufacturer runs Lasso’s runtime protection across its customer-facing systems to stop jailbreak attempts and sensitive data exposure. A red teaming engagement on a separate chatbot found more than 15 vulnerabilities that had gone undetected, and all of them were fixed before they could be exploited.
Lasso Security is part of the NetApp Excellerator program. If you’d like to learn more about Lasso, book a demo today.

articles.title: Transport for London breach exposes 265,000 Oyster card users' data
articles.text:
Transport for London (TfL) has announced that around 265,000 Oyster photocard customers may have had their account details exposed in a data breach.
TfL is London's public transport authority, operating the Underground, Overground, buses, trams, and the Elizabeth line. It recorded 3.53 billion passenger journeys in 2025/26, including 1.78 billion bus journeys and 1.20 billion Tube journeys.
Oyster photocards are travel smartcards with the holder's photo that give eligible passengers free or discounted travel.
The organization discovered the security incident on November 16, 2026, after receiving customer reports about emails requesting them to create an account, which came directly from TfL's mail systems as a result of a compromise.
The Oyster photocard website has now been taken offline and the organization is sending impacted individuals data breach notifications.
Oyster photocards remain valid for travel, and customers who need to renew their cards or check their journey history can still do so by contacting TfL's Customer Services.
These notifications, with one shared on Reddit, state that the following customer data may have been exposed:
- Full names
- Phone numbers
- Email addresses
- Home addresses
- Dates of birth
- Security questions and answers
TfL's current assessment is that passwords, bank and payment card details, journey information, and the names and dates of birth of children with Zip Oyster cards were not compromised.
The transportation organization also said it has found no evidence so far that the affected data has been misused.
TfL estimates that around 265,000 photocard customers may have been impacted, up from an estimated 250k previously, but the investigation is not yet complete and the figure may increase further.
TfL says it has now contained the incident and contacted affected customers. It has also notified the UK's Information Commissioner's Office (ICO).
Those who received the previous email urging them to create an account on the platform should ignore it.
The leak of security questions and answers is particularly concerning, as those may be used in account access restoration, so customers should remain vigilant for suspicious activity and report it to the organization as soon as possible.
Once the Oyster photocard portal is restored, all photocard customers will be prompted to change their password, security question, and answer.
However, if those same security questions are used at other sites, they should be rotated to new questions and answers.
It is also recommended to change passwords on other services where the same information was used.
In 2024, Scattered Spider members breached TfL's network and stole customer data and disrupted online services, including Oyster refunds.
The attack cost the agency £29 million in losses and recovery costs, while two of the hackers pleaded guilty in June 2026 and were sentenced to five years and six months in prison.

articles.title: Fontaneros expertos sobre la situación en España: "Antes cambiar la ducha salía por 800 euros, ahora pasa de 1.900"
articles.text:
Cambiar la bañera por un plato de ducha es la reforma más solicitada en los baños españoles, y su precio ha cambiado mucho en los últimos años. Según fontaneros expertos con más de 25 años de experiencia: “antes salía por unos 800 euros, ahora pasa de los 1.900 si se hace bien”. Pero esa comparación parece mezclar dos obras diferentes.
Dos presupuestos diferentes. Esos 1.900 euros coinciden con la guía de precios de reformas de baño de Habitissimo, según la cual cambiar la bañera por un plato de ducha y alicatar la zona de la ducha ronda esa cantidad, con el desescombro, el alicatado, el plato y la mampara incluidos. Eso sí, la misma plataforma mantiene en su guía sobre el cambio de bañera por ducha precios de entre 700 y 900 euros para la sustitución básica con mampara de cristal, y una horquilla general de 900 a 2.300 euros.
Vamos, que lo que acabes pagando entre 800 y 1.900 euros suele depender ya no solo de los materiales escogidos, sino en lo que incluya estos presupuestos.
Por qué ha subido. La subida se debe a los materiales, a los salarios y a una mayor exigencia en impermeabilización y seguridad. Hay datos que lo respaldan: la Asociación Nacional de Constructores Independientes (ANCI) señala que el índice de costes de la construcción del Ministerio de Transportes subió más en el bienio 2021-2022 que en los quince años anteriores, y que la mano de obra siguió la misma tendencia desde 2021.
Lo que se queda fuera. El precio de partida tampoco suele ser el que acabas pagando, porque los presupuestos iniciales dejan fuera a menudo imprevistos como nuevas tuberías o desagües o la retirada de escombros. Para una reforma integral, la guía de reformas de Habitissimo calcula unos 3.500 euros en un baño de unos 5,4 metros cuadrados.
Cómo contener la factura. Para reducir la factura, puedes recurrir a platos cerámicos en lugar de los de resina de gama alta, mamparas correderas estándar, conservar lo que esté en buen estado y limitar el alicatado a la zona de la ducha.
Las ayudas públicas también pueden rebajar el gasto cuando la obra mejora la accesibilidad. En Bilbao, el programa Helduak-Mayores Renove Vivienda de la sociedad municipal Surbisa cubre en su edición de 2026 hasta el 50% del presupuesto protegible, para mayores de 70 años y personas con movilidad reducida o discapacidad sensorial.
