articles.title: GTA 6 en PS5: la actualización obligatoria que todos deben hacer antes de abrir el juego
articles.text:
Sony exige una actualización de PS5 para que los jugadores puedan entrar a GTA 6 desde el primer minuto de su estreno. La medida llegó desde antes de su lanzamiento y generó dudas entre quienes ya tenían el juego preinstalado en la consola.
La compañía no presentó el paso como una mejora opcional, sino como un requisito ineludible. Sin el firmware correspondiente, la consola simplemente no permite iniciar el título de Rockstar Games.
Qué actualización exige Sony para jugar
La cuenta de soporte de PlayStation en Estados Unidos advirtió que los usuarios de PS5 deben instalar la actualización de software del sistema 26.07-14.23.00 antes de jugar Grand Theft Auto VI.
Rockstar Games amplificó el mensaje entre sus seguidores, con lo que convirtió una actualización de sistema en un requisito inmediato para quienes esperaban jugar desde el día del lanzamiento. La compañía publicó el comunicado de Sony en su cuenta de X y pidió descargar el paquete antes de la medianoche previa al estreno.
Las notas de parche de esa versión fueron breves: solo mencionaron “correcciones de seguridad”, sin precisar qué vulnerabilidades corrige. Una actualización previa, la 26.07-14.22.00, reportada el 17 de noviembre, sí fue descrita con un tamaño de 1,267 GB y correcciones de seguridad, aunque no hay base para atribuir esas mismas características a la versión 14.23.00 exigida para GTA 6.
Por qué Sony refuerza la seguridad de la consola
El requisito se produce en medio de avances recientes en la escena del jailbreak de PS5, que desarrolla herramientas para modificar el software de la consola. A finales de septiembre, un jailbreak compatible con firmwares de la versión 7.00 a la 13.60 sacudió esa comunidad, con un alcance que incluyó incluso a las PS5 Pro que no se habían actualizado.
Después de ese episodio, algunos juegos de PS5 comenzaron a requerir el firmware 14.00 para descargar actualizaciones, lo que renovó los intentos de la escena homebrew por encontrar un jailbreak para versiones más recientes. Un investigador de seguridad identificado como Gezine afirmó haber extraído binarios de juegos en firmwares anteriores, aunque no compartió públicamente un jailbreak junto con esa afirmación.
La información disponible no confirma que el requisito de actualización para GTA 6 responda de forma directa a ese volcado de binario, ni que exista una vulnerabilidad explotable contra el juego. Tampoco está confirmado que Sony haya bloqueado de forma general el acceso a PlayStation Network desde firmwares anteriores, aunque esa posibilidad se menciona como una explicación plausible del endurecimiento.
El temor a la piratería y a la inteligencia artificial
La inquietud por la seguridad de GTA 6 también llegó a Take-Two, la compañía matriz de Rockstar Games. Su director ejecutivo, Strauss Zelnick, dijo en una entrevista que la empresa toma en serio la seguridad y que reforzaría sus defensas técnicas y acciones legales de manera apropiada ante los riesgos de piratería.
Zelnick explicó que el negocio de los videojuegos había sido en gran medida inmune a la piratería por el tamaño de los archivos, la complejidad técnica y la conexión con servidores. Sin embargo, reconoció que el fenómeno podría convertirse en un desafío mayor, en parte por el uso de inteligencia artificial para acelerar procesos de ingeniería inversa.
El directivo sostuvo que la piratería afecta, en alguna medida, a todas las compañías de entretenimiento y que probablemente también alcanzará al negocio de Take-Two. No detalló qué herramientas específicas desplegaría ni anunció una acción judicial concreta contra un actor determinado.
Cómo instalar la actualización en PS5
El proceso de actualización no exige demasiado tiempo ni pasos complejos. Quienes tengan habilitadas las actualizaciones automáticas solo deben esperar a que el sistema complete la descarga y reiniciar la consola para que el cambio se aplique.
Para quienes prefieran hacerlo de forma manual, el camino es ingresar a los ajustes del sistema, buscar la opción de software del sistema y seleccionar la alternativa para actualizar. Desde ahí, la PS5 descarga e instala la versión 26.07-14.23.00 sin pasos adicionales.

articles.title: South Korea uses nationwide emergency alert to catch exam cheats, exposes 22 students with hidden phones
articles.text:
Facepalm: South Korea has resorted to extreme measures to catch students sneaking phones into their university entrance exam: authorities sounded the country's highest-level emergency alert on handsets nationwide. The plan worked, too. The first alarm caught 22 students who hadn't handed over their devices.
Half a million people took South Korea's annual College Scholastic Ability Test (CSAT), known as the suneung, at 1,312 centers across the country on Thursday. The five exams take place over eight hours in a single day, and the results can determine which university a candidate gets into and what they can study.
There's been a lot of focus on cheating this year after the top scorer in South Korea's professional tax accountancy exam got a suspicious 159 out of 160 questions right. He later admitted to using a microcamera and generative AI to cheat.
At 8:30 am, just before the first exam began, authorities triggered the Extreme Emergency Alert, a 10.5-second alarm designed to sound at full volume even on phones set to silent. Officials say it caught 22 people across nine cities and provinces who had failed to surrender their smartphones. A second alert went off at 2:21 pm, while proctors were collecting the test papers and answer sheets after the third exam.
Given the tensions between North and South Korea, it's understandable that a nationwide emergency alert gave some people a fright. One Seoul resident said their first thought was that war had broken out. Two Japanese visitors at a café in central Seoul had to translate the message before they realized what had interrupted their morning coffee.
The alarm may also have caught a few people its organizers hadn't intended. According to the Korea JoongAng Daily, posts appeared online claiming that several soldiers had their second phones confiscated after the alert gave them away.
Then there was the civil servant who finished a night shift at around 8 am and was trying to get some sleep. A third alarm at 2:57 p.m. brought the day's total to three, prompting the understandably tired worker to complain that he "couldn't get a wink of sleep."
Authorities had originally planned to keep the timing of the afternoon alerts a surprise, but decided to give the public a heads-up. So at 2:45 pm, people received a message warning them that in 12 minutes they'd get another message telling them there was nothing to worry about.

articles.title: Kuda cuts jobs for the second time in 2026
articles.text:
Kuda, the Nigerian digital bank, will cut about 7.5% of its workforce across seven countries in its second round of job cuts this year as it restructures operations to reach group profitability in 2027.
In March, the company laid off hundreds of employees across several units after a company-wide review. The latest cuts will affect roles in Nigeria, the UK, South Africa, Canada, Tanzania, Uganda and Ghana, Kuda said in a statement shared with TechCabal on Thursday.
Affected employees will go through a consultation period before any final decisions, and Kuda said it would offer them “a comprehensive support package.” In March, employees expected up to seven months of pay.
The redundancies are part of Kuda’s push to cut costs as it pursues profitability. Kuda said its March job cuts were not linked to financial performance. This round, Babs Ogundeyi, Kuda’s co-founder and CEO, said, will help the company achieve group profitability by 2027 and meet the capital rules for its banking licence.
Kuda’s Nigerian branch is already profitable, Ogundeyi told TechCabal on a call on Thursday, though he declined to share figures. Investors are still backing the company, he said, but “they are not putting in money as charity. At some point they expect a return beyond valuations.”
In January, the Central Bank of Nigeria upgraded Kuda’s microfinance bank to a national licence, which requires at least ₦5 billion ($3.9 million) in paid-up capital. Ogundeyi described that money as “idle capital” and said Kuda now has to hold more of it as it grows.
“That requires us to be more efficient than we would need to be at the earliest stage of our journey,” he said. “For our 8 million customers, nothing changes. Their money is safe, and we’ll keep building products that help them do more with it,” Ogundeyi said in the statement.
Kuda joins a growing list of African tech companies that are cutting staff as AI and better software change how many people they need. African tech companies cut a record 2,574 jobs in the first half of 2026, according to TechCabal Insights, which named restructuring and AI adoption as leading causes.
In May, Jumia said it would cut about 200 jobs as it brings AI into operations, logistics, finance and marketing. In October, Moniepoint began reorganising its engineers and product managers into smaller teams, a setup it said “requires fewer roles in some areas.”
“You can see a few companies in the industry doing this, so I do not think it comes as a surprise in an era of better technology and better tools for managing companies,” Ogundeyi said.
Kuda’s statement did not say how many people would lose their jobs. On the call, Ogundeyi said the company has “about 500 people” and put the number at risk at “around 40.”
The company tied both rounds of 2026 job cuts to the same plan. The changes “build on the Kuda 2.0 programme the company began in March 2026, which focused the business on its core products and customers,” it said.
Kuda’s push for profitability follows a period of rapid customer growth that came with high operating costs. Kuda’s loss narrowed to $5.83 million in 2024, from $35.11 million the year before, and staff costs fell 46% to $6.31 million, according to its financials. Group revenue, reported in dollars, fell 15% to $18.34 million, which management blamed on the weaker naira. Measured in naira, revenue at the Nigerian bank nearly doubled to ₦21.2 billion ($13.8 million). Customer deposits fell to ₦83.2 billion ($54.2 million) from ₦96 billion ($105.8 million).
Kuda’s future
To reach profitability, Kuda said it is taking a bigger bet on lending.
This week, some Kuda customers posted on X that the amounts they owed on overdue loans had been reduced. Kuda said the reductions are part of a campaign by its credit team that gives customers with long-overdue loans “a brief window between now and December 23” to settle.
Today, Kuda’s main loan product is its overdraft, a short-term loan that Oyegun said suited users who were running low “in the last two weeks of the month.” Now Kuda wants to sell the kind of loans big banks offer, like GTBank’s QuickCredit, to customers whose needs have grown.
“As I have grown older, my needs have changed. I want to buy a car or a house,” Nosa Oyegun, Kuda’s chief operating officer, said, describing his time as a Kuda user. The overdraft and other current products will stay, but new loans will be built on top of them.
“We have just offered the overdraft and some other loans here and there, but we have not built the product around credit,” he said. “Kuda 1.0 is done and dusted. It worked. Kuda 2.0 is for us to go deeper into what it means to bank a customer beyond transactions.”

articles.title: Scientists tracked kids for 8 years. What they found about screen time was surprising
articles.text:
Scientists tracked kids for 8 years. What they found about screen time was surprising
- Date:
- November 17, 2026
- Source:
- University of Jyväskylä - Jyväskylän yliopisto
- Summary:
- A surprising Finnish study found that children who spent more time using screens tended to have better cognitive processing abilities as teenagers, challenging the assumption that screen time is always harmful. Researchers suggest that what children do on screens may matter more than how much time they spend using them.
- Share:
An eight-year study of children in Finland has revealed a surprising connection between screen time and brain function. Researchers found that children who spent more time using screens tended to have better cognitive processing abilities as teenagers, challenging the widespread assumption that screen time is necessarily harmful to developing brains.
The findings suggest that the amount of time children spend in front of screens may be less important than how they use that time. Activities that encourage learning, creativity, and problem-solving could be particularly valuable. Researchers emphasize that the goal should not be to eliminate screen time, but to balance it with physical activity and mentally stimulating experiences.
The discovery comes amid growing concerns about insufficient physical activity among teenagers. A sedentary lifestyle has been linked to poorer academic performance, while regular exercise is known to support brain function, particularly in adults. However, scientists still have much to learn about how physical activity, sitting, and screen use during childhood influence thinking abilities later in adolescence.
These questions are especially important because childhood and adolescence are critical periods of brain development. Changes in attention, memory, and learning during these years can have lasting consequences, potentially influencing educational opportunities and career paths well into adulthood.
To investigate these relationships, Finnish researchers examined how screen time, physical activity, and sedentary behavior from childhood through adolescence were associated with cognitive performance in teenagers. They also explored whether the connections differed between boys and girls and whether the intensity of physical activity made a difference.
More Screen Time Linked to Better Thinking Skills
One of the study's most unexpected findings was that greater screen time throughout childhood was associated with better cognitive processing in adolescence.
Cognitive processing refers to the mental abilities people use to take in information, pay attention, remember details, learn new things, and solve problems. These abilities play an important role in school performance and everyday decision-making.
The findings challenge the idea that all screen time should be viewed as harmful. However, the researchers caution that the relationship may depend on what children are actually doing while using digital devices. Watching videos, playing games that require strategic thinking, and engaging in educational activities may involve very different levels of mental effort.
"The findings suggest that screen time can support children's and adolescents' cognitive processing. Presumably, the essential point here is what kind of things they do in their screen time. Teachers and parents should encourage children to use devices and screens in such ways that promote active thinking, problem-solving, creativity, and learning," states Doctoral Researcher Petri Jalanko from the University of Jyväskylä.
"We should not regard screen time solely as harmful but seek balance between physical activity and screen time that promotes active thinking," Jalanko summarizes.
Exercise Affects Boys' and Girls' Brains Differently
The researchers also uncovered a more complicated picture of how physical activity relates to thinking and memory.
Among girls, spending more time engaged in light-intensity physical activity since childhood was associated with better working memory during adolescence. For boys, greater participation in guided physical activity over the same period was linked to stronger working memory.
Working memory is the brain's ability to temporarily hold and use information. It allows someone to remember instructions while completing a task, keep track of numbers during mental calculations, or follow a conversation while processing new information.
Light-intensity physical activity generally includes relatively gentle movements that do not substantially increase breathing or heart rate. Guided physical activity refers to exercise carried out with some form of instruction or supervision, such as organized sports or structured exercise sessions.
The differences between boys and girls suggest that the relationship between exercise and brain health may depend on more than simply how much a person moves. The type of activity, how it is organized, and the individual's sex could all play a role.
Another Surprising Finding About Physical Activity
The study produced another counterintuitive result. Teenagers who reported spending less time in unsupervised physical activity tended to perform better on measures of cognitive processing.
Yet when researchers used wearable sensors to objectively measure movement and heart rate, they found no association between overall physical activity or sedentary time and cognitive performance.
One possible explanation is that wearable devices measure movement without revealing what a person is actually doing. For example, a sensor may record periods of sitting or physical activity, but it cannot determine whether someone is solving a difficult problem, studying, participating in an organized activity, or simply resting.
This distinction could help explain why questionnaire responses revealed relationships that were not apparent in the sensor measurements.
"Our study indicates that the connections of physical activity and sedentary behavior to cognitive processing are complex and depend on the sex, the type and assessment method of physical activity and sedentary time. Moreover, boys and girls may benefit from different types of physical activity in view of brain health," Jalanko adds.
"However, we need more intervention studies to find out causal relations and sex differences in this respect. Moreover, it is important to examine more specifically the effects of the intensity of physical activity on changes taking place in cognitive processing."
What the Eight-Year Study Revealed
The findings come from an eight-year follow-up conducted as part of the PANIC study, a long-running Finnish research project investigating children's physical activity and nutrition.
The current analysis included 260 participants, consisting of 124 girls and 136 boys. Their average age at the adolescent assessment was 15.8 years.
Researchers collected information about physical activity and sedentary behavior using both questionnaires and wearable devices that combined heart rate monitoring with movement measurements. This approach allowed them to compare participants' reported activities with data collected by sensors.
To evaluate cognitive abilities, the researchers used the CogState test battery, a collection of computerized assessments designed to measure aspects of mental performance. The tests examined learning, attention, and working memory.
Importantly, the findings show associations rather than cause and effect. They do not establish that increasing screen time will improve a child's thinking abilities or that reducing certain types of exercise will produce cognitive benefits. Intervention studies, in which researchers deliberately change participants' activities and measure the results, are needed to determine whether these relationships are causal.
Nevertheless, the results offer an important perspective on the continuing debate over children's screen use. Rather than treating all time spent with digital devices as equally harmful, the researchers suggest paying closer attention to whether those activities encourage active thinking and learning.
The research also highlights the importance of considering different forms of physical activity rather than focusing exclusively on the total amount of exercise children receive.
Together, the findings suggest that supporting healthy brain development may require a more nuanced approach, one that combines physical activity with opportunities for learning, creativity, and mental engagement, including those that take place on screens.
The study was published in the scientific journal Pediatric Exercise Science.

articles.title: Discord Rewrites Desktop and Mobile Clients in Rust Using Zed's GPU-Accelerated Rendering Framework
articles.text:
Discord’s CTO Stanislav Vishnevskiy recently announced rewriting its desktop and mobile clients in Rust, moving away from Electron and React Native. The project (codenamed Phoenix) eliminates layers of abstraction to directly leverage the device’s GPU, native mobile views, and a Rust core shared across platforms. Early results hint at a significant reduction in RAM usage and boot time for chat, voice, and streaming.
Vishnevskiy expanded on the rewrite on X:
We’ve been early adopters of Rust since 2018 and a lot of our infra, voice tech, and even some of the current client is already Rust, the holy grail was getting the whole client there. That means Electron goes away, and so does React Native, mobile keeps native UI but shares app code with desktop via Rust. We hope to get it into testing with users soon™. (And it’s not Tauri, it’s GPUI, so good guess everyone.)
The desktop app thus drops Chromium/Node.js for GPUI, the open-source, GPU-accelerated Rust UI framework built by the Zed team for the Zed editor. Zed is an open-source code editor written in Rust for macOS, Linux, and Windows by a team including the creators of GitHub’s Atom code editor, which was sunsetted in 2022, four years after Microsoft’s acquisition of GitHub. Zed touts a narrow focus on performance and user (i.e., developer) experience:
VS Code won by being good enough for everyone. Zed wins by being excellent for developers who refuse to compromise on speed.
Discord’s mobile app rewrite drops React Native, instead directly leveraging native iOS and Android views and reusing a common Rust core.
The browser client keeps rendering HTML with the application logic layer compiled to WebAssembly. Embedded web surfaces (e.g., YouTube videos and Activities), however, invoke an OS webview, with Electron’s built-in browser no longer available.
Vishnevskiy signals decreasing RAM usage, startup time, and latency as key motivations behind the rewrite:
The new Discord client using less RAM is just part of the story. Clicking around feels instant, I can’t go back. Check out the boot time.
Early internal builds for the desktop app reveal RAM usage at around 290 MB (measured with two accounts logged in simultaneously) and a near-instant cold start versus 5.5 s on Electron.
Vishnevskiy showcased similar improvements on mobile with a load time under 2 seconds for the rewrite versus approximately 5 seconds for the legacy app.
Elias Floreteng, in his master’s thesis at KTH this year (An Empirical Study of React Native’s New Architecture), reported performance gains across several metrics for native Swift and Kotlin over React Native, even with its new architecture. The controlled benchmark involves a 1,000-row scrollable image list using stock list and image components, with identical assets and row geometry across all binaries. Floreteng concludes that Swift beats React Native across every comparable runtime metric on iOS. On Android, the gap to native is small and runs in both directions, with native ahead on memory and CPU.
On desktop, Zed proved that leveraging GPUI could provide better performance over Electron and alternative frameworks reusing the device’s native webview (e.g., Tauri).
While Tauri also uses a Rust backend, it leverages the operating system’s native webview. This has the advantage of letting web developers reuse their knowledge of HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, while also avoiding the bundling of Chromium. Executable size is, as a result, generally smaller. Tauri apps’ RAM usage on Windows, however, tends to be similar to that of their Electron counterparts, as the same core, resource-hungry browser technology is used. Webview behavior may also be inconsistent across operating systems.
GPUI replaces the browser engine with a hybrid immediate and retained mode, GPU-accelerated UI framework that targets 120-frames-per-second rendering without garbage-collection pauses. In exchange for the reported performance gains, developers give up many rendering and accessibility features that come baked into the browser (e.g., text layout, input method integration, screen-reader accessibility hooks, right-to-left support). While miscellaneous Rust libraries exist to address some of these issues (e.g., Parley for text layout), developers still have to wire them into a consistent user experience.

articles.title: Un fallo en un registro de pruebas convirtió 178 webs enormes en trampas para robar tarjetas y criptomonedas
articles.text:
Que alguien ataque una web cualquiera y logre inyectar código parece algo relativamente sencillo, que esto ocurra con webs como la de la BBC, Ikea o Zoom se antoja casi imposible. Pero no, ocurrió. Aunque con una estrategia distinta: en lugar de atacar las páginas principales, los atacantes han logrado hackear a un proveedor. Su nombre es Optimizely.
Qué ha ocurrido. El pasado lunes 16 de noviembre un proveedor de pruebas A/B, ese tipo de tests que las empresas utilizan para comprobar qué versión de un cambio funciona mejor, se vio comprometido. Los atacantes lograron inyectar código malicioso en ese proveedor aprovechando un fallo en el proceso de alta de cuentas, según la propia Optimizely. Y dicho código terminó en las webs que contrataron el servicio de pruebas.
El ataque tuvo lugar el lunes y se prolongó por espacio de unas 17 horas. Al principio nadie se dio cuenta de que el servicio que ofrecía Optimizely estaba comprometido: el código llegó a la BBC, Ikea, CNN, Fox News, Zoom, Air France-KLM... Y permitía robar datos de tarjetas bancarias, cargaba exploits para aprovecharse de iPhone y iPad sin actualizar y hasta cambiaba las direcciones de las carteras cripto. Todo sin que las empresas que servían las páginas se dieran cuenta.
La raíz del problema es que el código salía de cdn.optimizely.com, el servidor oficial de la empresa, con su certificado válido. Para el navegador era un script auténtico, así que las webs y sus visitantes se lo comieron sin sospechar. Lo detectó Scott Helme, de Report URI: tras analizar 1.611 scripts de Optimizely, encontró 188 infectados, de 178 organizaciones.
Quién es Optimizely. Es una empresa que casi nadie conoce y que, sin embargo, se encuentra en muchas webs que usamos a diario. Su especialidad son las pruebas A/B (A/B testing). Por ejemplo, una prueba de este tipo enseña a la mitad de los usuarios un botón verde y a la otra mitad uno azul: el que más clicks saque es el que mejor funciona. Así pueden descartar el menos efectivo.
Optimizely se ha especializado en ofrecer A/B testing a otras empresas para que ellas no tengan que hacer los desarrollos ni la implementación. Para obrar la magia, las webs cargan un pequeño programa (script) en cada visita con un campo que las empresas rellenan con su propio código. Para quienes contratan a Optimizely es muy cómodo, porque les permite cambiar la web sin tocar sus propios servidores. Es justo por donde entraron los atacantes.
El agujero de confianza. La cadena mantiene los eslabones unidos, pero no todos poseen la misma fuerza. Como usuarios, confiamos en las páginas web que aportan autoridad, porque resulta inconcebible que Ikea quiera robar nuestros datos bancarios. A su vez, estas páginas confían en otras empresas para aportar valor a sus propios servicios. Y la cadena de subcontratas va creciendo hasta que falla un eslabón.
Por mucho que confiemos en una página o app, siempre existe el riesgo de que un código que carguen de otro sitio pueda venir infectado. Y si las empresas no auditan todo aquello que contratan estamos vendidos: el incidente de Optimizely demuestra que nuestros datos privados nunca van a estar completamente asegurados.
El robo. El script malicioso estuvo sirviéndose a las webs de al menos 178 organizaciones de enorme relevancia hasta que se dieron cuenta de la inyección y Optimizely le puso remedio. Durante ese tiempo, y según los datos preliminares de Report URI, las carteras del atacante recibieron unos 7.000 dólares en cripto, aunque algunas ya tenían actividad antes del ataque. No hay constancia de que los iPhone y iPad resultaran vulnerados por el código malicioso ni tampoco de la cantidad de tarjetas o cookies que los atacantes pudieron llevarse. 
Optimizely todavía no explicó cómo funcionaba el fallo, cuántos visitantes recibieron el código ni quiénes son los atacantes que se encuentran por detrás. Y no es su primer susto del año: en febrero ya confirmó una intrusión tras un ataque de phishing por teléfono. Para una empresa cuyo producto vive dentro de las webs de sus clientes, son demasiadas preguntas abiertas.

articles.title: The Download: a living liver, a billion-dollar battery deal, and AI hype
articles.text:
The Download: a living liver, a billion-dollar battery deal, and AI hype
Plus: Anthropic has raised $81 billion in the biggest-ever IPO.
This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
A human liver has been kept alive outside the body for a record seven weeks
Researchers in Australia claim they’ve kept a human liver alive on life support outside the body for seven weeks, smashing the previous record of about two weeks.
They achieved the feat by connecting a donated liver to a system of automated pumps and sensors that fed the organ nutrients, supplied it with blood, and whisked away waste.
The approach could open up new possibilities in biomedical engineering, from repairing damaged organs to growing new ones. Some researchers are even exploring artificial wombs.
Take a closer look at the technology keeping human organs alive.
—Antonio Regalado
What a billion-dollar deal says about the US battery market
After a tough few years littered with high-profile failures, there’s some positive news for next-generation batteries in the US: Sila has signed a deal with battery maker Panasonic Energy to supply silicon-carbon anode material that could be worth more than $1 billion.
The agreement will help Sila scale production, potentially bringing smaller, lighter batteries to market. But it also reveals how battery politics have shifted. The factory is backed by a $1.4 billion loan from the Trump administration’s Defense Department—and the industry is increasingly focused on geopolitics rather than the energy transition.
Find out what this deal reveals about the US battery industry.
—Casey Crownhart
This story is from The Spark, our weekly climate tech newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Wednesday.
The AI Hype Index returns
Separating AI reality from hyped-up fiction isn’t always easy. That’s why we’ve created the AI Hype Index—a simple, at-a-glance summary of what’s shaping the industry right now.
The latest edition tracks AI’s spread across everything from literary prizes and cyberattacks to a Grok-ified version of The Odyssey. See where it all landed on this month’s index.
The must-reads
I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.
1 Anthropic has raised $81 billion in the biggest-ever IPO
It eclipsed SpaceX as the largest stock-market debut. (Bloomberg $)
+ Its stated mission could conflict with shareholders’ interests. (NYT $)
+ The IPO comes amid new safety fears about its AI advances. (FT $)
+ Its performance will test the strength of the AI boom. (BBC)

Beijing is trying to circumvent US export controls. (CNBC)
+ Alibaba tapped Nvidia to support a military-linked lab. (NYT $)
+ When the US military implemented AI, civilian deaths rose. (Intercept)
+ “Humans in the loop” in AI war is an illusion. (MIT Technology Review)
3 Elon Musk has joined Silicon Valley’s retreat from Trump
He called his midterm spending “foolish” and broke with MAGA. (FT $)
+ OpenAI and Palantir leaders have also struck new tones. (Gizmodo)
+ Silicon Valley got the midterms badly wrong. (MIT Technology Review)
4 Ukraine used relay drones to strike Putin’s bridge without Starlink
The strike showed how it’s learning to fight without SpaceX. (Ars Technica)
+ Musk has denied Kyiv’s claims about restrictions on Starlink. (CNBC)
5 A major cyberattack has hit the European Commission
It may have exposed large amounts of staff personal data. (Politico)
+ Trump has blamed Minnesota for water system hacks. (ABC)
6 Trump may force US firms to disclose their use of Chinese AI
The proposal aims to discourage reliance on Chinese models. (Reuters $)
7 The US has slashed funding for biomedical science abroad
It’s also weakened oversight of foreign grants. (Economist $) 
8 AI datacentres are set to drive a 70% rise in emissions by 2030
The US and China are turning to fossil fuels to power AI. (Guardian)
+ The climate case for AI has not been made. (MIT Technology Review)
9 Grand Theft Auto 6 has become the best-reviewed game ever
It scored 99 out of 100 on review aggregation site Metacritic. (BBC)
+ Schools and businesses are bracing for “GTA Flu” season. (NYT $)
10 A new underwater research station aims to protect coral reefs
Aquanauts there will monitor struggling ecosystems. (New Scientist $)
Quote of the day
“Here are some of the smartest people on the planet being completely idiotic.”
—Thomas Nagel, a philosopher and professor emeritus at NYU, tells Wired why he objects to Anthropic giving Claude more independence, just as the company makes its record-breaking stock-market debut.
One more thing
China has approved the world’s first invasive brain-computer chip—here’s what’s next
Sitting in the courtyard of his house in China’s Henan province last October, Dong Hui decided to try holding a pen. Six years after a car accident left him paralyzed from the neck down, he slowly wrote his name, “Thank you,” and the date.
The breakthrough was made possible by a brain implant called NEO. In March, it became the world’s first invasive brain-computer interface approved for use beyond clinical trials. The approval is expected to accelerate China’s push to become a global leader in brain implants.
Here’s how China reached the milestone—and what it means for the future of BCIs.
—You Xiaoying
We can still have nice things

articles.title: Why groundcover's CEO says agents are the power users of observability
articles.text:
Why groundcover’s CEO says agents are the power users of observability
An AI coding agent can write a patch in minutes. Ask it whether that patch slows down the API endpoint your customers hit most, and suddenly it needs something that lives outside the repository. It needs to see how the software runs.
That’s the premise behind groundcover, an observability platform that wants to put production telemetry in the hands of developers and their coding agents. Yes, you read that correctly.
In a conversation with The New Stack’s Frederic Lardinois at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon this month in Salt Lake City, groundcover CEO and co-founder Shahar Azulay explained why he thinks the same data engineers use to troubleshoot an incident can help an agent write and test a better change in the first place.
Your new observability user is an agent
“Now agents are the power users of observability,” Azulay told TNS.
Groundcover exposes telemetry through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), giving coding agents a way to query it while they work. An agent investigating a slow API, for example, could use traces to see which service accounts for most of the latency. A developer writing a test could use observed application behavior to pick a scenario customers actually encounter.
Groundcover uses that approach internally. Its coding agents pull context from the company’s own telemetry, and agents involved in code review can look at measurements from staging deployments. It’s a way to give a reviewer something concrete to check when a patch looks perfectly reasonable in a diff.
Agents also give engineers something new to monitor. Azulay contrasts a familiar application trace that follows a request across several microservices with an agent run that can span hours and thousands of tool calls. A trace that long can make a Kubernetes incident look like light reading.
Developers may need to inspect prompts and tool calls or use evaluations to judge whether a run behaved as intended. A completed run tells you the agent stopped. The trace can help you figure out what it did along the way.
Less instrumentation work, more room for detail
Groundcover uses an eBPF sensor to collect application and infrastructure telemetry without requiring developers to add an SDK to every service. It also supports OpenTelemetry, so teams can keep sending the signals they already collect and add custom instrumentation where they need more detail. That gives developers a baseline for a new service and a way to get more specific when a particular path or business operation warrants it.
Where the data runs is part of the pitch. Groundcover’s bring-your-own-cloud model keeps telemetry and groundcover’s agent operations in the customer’s cloud environment, Azulay said. Customers pay for the underlying infrastructure, and groundcover manages the deployment.
For teams weighing how much telemetry to retain, the model puts the infrastructure bill in their own account. It also matters when prompts or tool calls may contain sensitive customer data and teams want to keep that information under their control.
We also ask what happens when the platform starts acting on what it sees. Azulay points to groundcover’s move into Kubernetes optimization, where the immediate work centers on cost and resilience. He sees a path from there to agents that can help address an incident on both sides of the deployment, proposing a code change and adjusting infrastructure configuration. The conversation also gets into the practical work of switching observability platforms, including what happens to the dashboards and monitors engineers have spent years building.
Watch the full KubeCon interview on The New Stack’s YouTube channel to hear how groundcover uses its own telemetry in code reviews and why Azulay thinks the next generation of coding agents will be a regular part of the observability stack.

articles.title: Nvidia Responds to Gentlemen Ransomware Claim
articles.text:
Nvidia says it has found no indication that its systems or networks were affected after the Gentlemen ransomware group named the company on its data leak website.
The group’s listing includes Nvidia’s logo and a general description of the chipmaker. It offers no explanation of the alleged attack, with the section about stolen information indicating that details will be provided later.
The company has acknowledged that it is investigating a possible security incident, but its statement points to a third party rather than Nvidia’s own infrastructure.
“Nvidia is investigating an incident that may have affected a third-party partner. We have found no indication that Nvidia systems or networks were affected. We continue to monitor the situation,” an Nvidia spokesperson told SecurityWeek.
The statement does not identify the partner or describe the nature of the incident. It also does not specify whether any Nvidia-related information may have been exposed.
The ransomware group’s listing does not establish that Nvidia was breached or that any of its data was stolen.
The Gentlemen ransomware operation emerged around mid-2025, initially operating as a closed group before launching an affiliate program later that year. Microsoft tracks its operators as Storm-2697.
The group uses a double-extortion model in which attackers steal data and encrypt systems, threatening to publish the stolen information to pressure victims into paying. Its affiliates have targeted organizations in numerous sectors, including manufacturing, healthcare, transportation, and financial services.
The Gentlemen has become increasingly active, with its leak website now listing more than 1,100 alleged victims.
According to Sophos, Gentlemen affiliates have used compromised credentials and legitimate administrative tools during intrusions. In one investigated incident, ransomware was deployed less than 24 hours after the earliest identified post-compromise activity.

articles.title: Superhuman pushes its Go assistant everywhere | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Productivity apps are simultaneously trying to feed more context to their AI tools while also making those AI assistants available in every nook and corner of their products. Superhuman (formerly Grammarly) is going in the same direction with the rollout of features, including a personalized Go assistant, making agents available in Docs, and third-party agent integrations.
While some of the company’s AI features have faced criticism, Superhuman started pushing its Go assistant after its rebranding last year. With the new rollout, it is making Go learn context across different apps and give better personalized suggestions for prompts. Superhuman is revamping its onboarding flow to let users connect their preferred tools and load context about their work upfront.
The assistant works inline with the cursor — just like Grammarly — and also manages other agents. Superhuman is also making the agent proactive, which means it looks for your schedule, keeps an eye on your email, and even drafts responses. The updated Go agent also learns users’ writing styles and responds accordingly in email and Docs.
The productivity company is adding 20 new connected agents, including DeepL, Legora, Amplitude, Databricks, and Blackboard, through its Go SDK.
The company is also thinking about adding AI to different products, including Docs and Superhuman Mail. In Docs, all Go agents work natively, and you can set them off to work on different tasks in the background. Users can also set routines to trigger workflows based on events.
Until now, Mail has used AI as its central tool, which is being replaced by Go. Users can also do enterprise search by using data from the company knowledge base and connected tools. Go also uses this context to form drafts and organize the inbox across Google and Outlook accounts.
Superhuman acquired notetaker Fathom in September to add more context to its suite. The company is now rolling out live collaborative notetaking, which would be shared across the team. Plus, Go can now make decisions post-meeting, like forming an initial draft of a proposal.
The company’s CEO, Shishir Mehrotra, said that Go has had good momentum with over 1 million active users. There are a host of agents now that are vying for users’ attention on both the personal and professional front. Mehrotra thinks that while Go is more work-focused, it can help with personal emails and schedules.
“One of the reasons why these assistants have been popular is that they treat you as a whole person and recognize that we need to cover both extremes. Go is definitely more work-focused than some of the tools coming out of the pure consumer ecosystem. It doesn’t mean we draw the boundary at helping you with your personal tasks or helping you with your calendar or all of your email,” he told TechCrunch over a call.
While Go might not directly compete with the likes of Instinct, Muse, and Fo, Superhuman wants users to choose its assistant over something like OpenAI’s Dots or Claude Duet.

articles.title: Vercel brings on Toronto team behind AI developer platform Traces | BetaKit
articles.text:
The Toronto team behind Traces is joining Vercel less than a year after releasing its flagship product.
The news: Traces founder Tarun Sachdeva announced this week that his Toronto-based company, a collaborative platform for coding with AI agents, is being acquired by US cloud and web hosting platform Vercel. All four Traces team members started work at Vercel this week as part of the deal, Sachdeva told BetaKit. Financial details were not disclosed. Vercel did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Existing Traces users can continue using the app and will retain access to their data, Traces said in an email to users, but the creation of new communities, or “orgs,” is paused. The deal does not give Vercel access to users’ data, the company said.
From the source: Sachdeva explained in a video with The Other Stuff podcast that Traces grew out of a desire to learn from other developers about how they were coding with AI agents.
“I wanted to keep that data, because I felt like it was so useful to keep those decisions that we make when we’re building products,” Sachdeva said.
The context: Sachdeva told BetaKit in a direct message that he launched the Traces developer platform in February after founding the company a few years ago. It had raised an undisclosed amount of funding from Canadian VCs Golden Ventures and Northside Ventures, as well as US VC Signalfire and angel investors from Shopify and Wattpad. Sachdeva is a longtime Canadian tech operator who worked in senior product management roles at Research in Motion and Wattpad.
Valued at $9.3 billion USD ($13.3 billion CAD) as of its Series F round in September 2025, Vercel has connected to the Canadian tech scene in other ways, too; this summer, its COO Jeanne DeWitt Grosser joined Shopify’s board.
Final thought: This deal is another indication that Silicon Valley’s developer community is paying attention to Canadian talent. It’s the second time this month that a Canadian-founded AI-native platform has been acquired by a high-profile US tech company within a year of its product launch. AI travel agent startup Odessia, led by former Sonder co-founder Francis Davidson, joined OpenAI last week.
Feature image courtesy Tarun Sachdeva via X.

The Samsung 990 Pro 4TB is among the fastest Gen 4 SSDs available thanks to read and write speeds of up to 7450/6900 MB/s, almost maxing out the Gen 4 bandwidth. This M.2 NVMe drive comes in the 2280 form factor and holds enough capacity to store a large selection of your favorite games or files.
Random reads/writes come in at 1.6 million and 1.55 million IOPS, respectively, while endurance is rated for a respectable 2,400 TBW.
For this 4TB drive, Samsung used 236-layer TLC V-NAND while also using a single-sided design, making it a good option for installation in a PC where physical space is at a premium. Our own tests at the time saw it score above the competition in almost every test we ran, with the lowest latency in 3DMark's storage test. That's a particularly good result for gamers, hopefully giving you faster load times. You're also getting a drive with sustainable performance, even while writing to the drive, maintaining speeds of 6.2 GB/s for 75 seconds during our IOMeter tests, thanks to that 10GB of pSLC cache.
While newer Gen 5 drives can best it on speed and performance, we've not tested a faster Gen 4 SSD. This is a high calibre drive, but it's important to focus on the capacity here, too. 4TB is a huge boost for most PCs that will ensure that, once you've installed your OS, you're left with a vast amount of extra storage for games, photos, and important documents.
AI might have forced SSD prices to shoot through the roof, but the $699 sale price on this 4TB Samsung 990 Pro is a good option in the current market. The $100 price drop compared to last week, let alone from its high of $1,099, means you can secure fast, vast storage for a price we've not seen in months. Expect to see this deal sell out fast.

articles.title: 'The risks of AI spread faster': Report finds workers are handing over logins and even passwords to AI to make their jobs easier
articles.text:
'The risks of AI spread faster': Report finds workers are handing over logins and even passwords to AI to make their jobs easier
Should you be trusting AI with passwords?
- Dashlane study finds concerning lack of security awareness among workers using AI
- Many workers admit they're happy giving AI logins or passwords
- This is despite growing worries over AI-boosted cyberattacks
Nearly one in five UK employees has shared a password, API key or other login credential with an AI tool, potentially giving it access to sensitive business systems, new research has claimed.
Almost half (48%) of workers surveyed by Dashlane said they had allowed AI to carry out at least one task without prior approval, including handling email, company files and customer information; one in ten allow AI to process payments.
Dashlane's report also found more than a third (37%) of UK workers would be willing to give their login credentials to a new AI tool after using it for just a week - and 45% say they would comply if an AI tool asked them to confirm their credentials every day, potentially exposing them to credential theft or impersonation.
AI safety
Overall, 44% of workers said they had used AI for work without prior approval in the past year, and 46% started before workplace rules were in place - and worryingly, only a quarter of workers say they always consider security risks when using an AI agent at work.
This includes 15% who had given an AI tool access to a file, system or account and later discovered it should not have had that access - with nearly half (43%) admitting they believe the access is still active.
Nearly one in four have also pasted confidential or proprietary information into AI that they would not normally share with a colleague or another work system. Perhaps most concerningly, nearly half (42%) of workers say they have never received guidance on what information is safe to share with AI.
Despite these shortcomings, security leaders appear more confident than employee behavior suggests - as while 92% of UK IT security executives say they know about every AI agent in their organization - a quarter of employees admit using tools their employer does not know about.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
This is despite 72% of UK security executives say their organization experienced an incident involving an AI agent’s credentials or access in the past 12 months. A third report an agent accessing data, systems or credentials without authorization, while 32% say an agent took an unauthorized action.
The pressure to deploy quickly may be contributing, as more than two-thirds (68%) of security executives said they feel caught between accelerating AI adoption and protecting their organization. Among those facing pressure, 54% say deployment moved faster with less security review.
“The risks of AI spread faster, appear inside already approved tools, and unfold often without any further action from employees," noted Dashlane chief product officer Christophe Frenet.
"This raises the stakes for organisations when employees grant access and expose sensitive data to AI tools or, as we’re seeing in our data, trust their new AI colleagues more than they would their human coworkers.”

articles.title: A human liver has been kept alive outside the body for a record seven weeks
articles.text:
A human liver has been kept alive outside the body for a record seven weeks
Technology called “machine perfusion” is creating the chance for more transplants—and daring new science.
Researchers in Australia claim they’ve kept a human liver alive, on life support, outside the body for seven weeks, opening up speculative new possibilities in biomedical engineering.
The feat, whose details are pending publication, was carried out in Sydney after a team led by surgeon and inventor Carlo Pulitano connected a donated liver to a system of automated pumps and sensors that fed the organ nutrients, supplied it with blood, and whisked away waste.
In an interview, Pulitano, a transplant surgeon at the Royal Prince Alfred Hospital and a professor at the University of Sydney, likened the life support system to “an artificial body.” Its official name is the Extended Organ Perfusion System.
“Our group is the only one in the world to have maintained a human liver under fully normothermic, physiological conditions for seven weeks,” he says.
Normothermic means body temperature, or about 37 °C. The previous record for keeping an internal organ alive outside the body was set in Switzerland several years ago. That organ—also a liver—lasted around two weeks.
Most organs destined for transplant survive only a few hours in special ice buckets and need to be raced to their destination. Over the last decade, however, surgeons have been switching to perfusion systems, which pump warm or cold fluids into an organ. This can double the time it can be held before it must be transplanted.
Pulitano says the key to breaking the record was to automate the systems used to keep the organ thriving. During a meeting in Switzerland earlier this year, the Sydney team described perfusing 55 human livers, one after the other. Some were connected to a system that needed to be adjusted manually, but for those placed on the automated system—which produced the seven-week survivor—the average survival time tripled, to about four weeks.
Perfusion has already enabled doctors to restart hearts from dead people and keep them beating outside the body. Paulo Martins, a transplant doctor at the University of Oklahoma, says about half the kidneys he transplants are now perfused, even though the process can add $100,000 to the cost of a transplant.
While the research awaits formal publication, the eventual goal is what Pulitano and colleagues call “time-unlimited liver preservation.”
Scientists have already discovered possible medical benefits to keeping organs on life support longer than usual. One, they say, is that perfused organs apparently start to repair themselves and become stronger after a day or so. That’s what led a Swiss team, in 2022, to transplant a damaged liver that had been kept on perfusion for three days—the longest time any internal organ had remained outside the body before a successful transplant, says Waldemar Hoffmann, the CEO and cofounder of Apersys, a startup formed to commercialize the technology.
Pulitano says his own startup, Aeternum Life Technologies, will be helping with a planned trial in Sydney to transplant low-quality livers kept on perfusion for four days.
What’s less clear, says Hoffmann, is whether any transplant surgeon would ever want, or need, to use an organ kept alive for nearly two months. He says people in the field believe Pulitano’s record is real, but they don’t know how healthy the organ was at the end or even what so much extra time is likely to achieve. “The key question is what the purpose for a seven-week perfusion would be,” he says.
Yet that’s where things could start to get interesting, says Martins, the Oklahoma surgeon. Long-term life support could enable far-out concepts like artificial wombs, new types of organ manufacturing, and the chance to experiment directly on human organs outside the body for extended periods.
For his part, Pulitano says long-term machine perfusion could help grow new organs. In living donations, surgeons commonly take half of a person’s liver to give someone else. After about two months, both parts will have grown back almost to their full volume. Pulitano says he’s tried dividing a liver and then attaching the sections to the machine. If that works, he says, it could be a way to multiply one donor liver into several full-size organs.
“It’s important to have people thinking outside the box and pushing the limits and creating possibilities for things that, right now, sometimes we don’t even have a need for but are going to be needed in the future,” says Martins. “That’s how science moves.”
He’s not the only one who thinks so. For instance, a US company, Bexorg, has been reanimating human brains using perfusion pumps. The idea is to study what effects experimental drugs have on them. That company perfuses brains for about a day but has said it wants to extend the time to two weeks.
Similar experiments can be done on livers, says Pulitano, who has already tried adding gene therapies to the organs. “It gives us a living human organ model for translational research that no animal system can match, because the biology, the immunology, and the drug responses are human from the outset,” he says.
Meanwhile, in Silicon Valley, patents filed by Altos Labs, a billionaire-backed longevity startup, describe attempts to introduce reprogramming genes into animal livers maintained outside the body. Eventually, Altos scientists have speculated, they might temporarily disconnect a failing organ while it’s still in a person’s body, connecting it to a perfusion machine in order to douse it with ultra-powerful genetic treatments without risking the rest of the body.
Doctors probing the limits of organ life support have now formed two new scientific societies to explore the concept. One, founded by Martins and called the International Society for Organ Preservation and Perfusion Therapy, will hold its inaugural meeting this year in Italy. The other, based in China, was launched in August to advance what doctors at the First Affiliated Hospital of Sun Yat-Sen University have termed “organ medicine”: research at the level of whole organs kept alive by “bionic maintenance.”
“What is exploding is the idea of this technology that clearly goes beyond simply organ preservation,” says Pulitano. “Basically, that’s a concept that’s entirely new.”

articles.title: Google's Gemini 4 Neon tripled its coding score without changing the model
articles.text:
Google’s Gemini 4 Neon tripled its coding score without changing the model
Google’s new Gemini 4 Neon resolved 12.8% of the SWE-sweep coding benchmark using the mini-SWE harness, but that score jumped to 39.0% when the same model ran inside Antigravity.
The more-than-threefold improvement raises questions about how much coding-agent performance comes from the underlying model and how much depends on the harness…
Both results were reported Wednesday as part of the Neon launch. The more-than-threefold improvement raises questions about how much coding-agent performance comes from the underlying model and how much depends on the harness managing its tools, context, and execution.
A day earlier, a FrontierHarness benchmark found that running the same open model could cost up to five times more depending on the harness
Same model, different scores
Google’s Gemini 4 Neon model card compares three frontier models on SWE-sweep using their respective provider harnesses and a shared mini-SWE baseline.
Neon and Opus performed substantially better with their providers’ harnesses, but Sol did not.
Claude Opus 5.5 climbed from 3.6% with mini-SWE to 10.1% with Claude Code, while GPT-6.2 Sol went the other way, falling from 11.6% with mini-SWE to 8.3% with Codex. Neon and Opus performed substantially better with their providers’ harnesses, but Sol did not.
Google tested each model in two harness configurations, though the comparison does not isolate which changes account for the differences or whether the results would hold up across other benchmarks and repositories.
The harness does the work
Antigravity’s harness was co-trained with Gemini, and Neon has been updated to make fewer unnecessary file reads and better manage context during long coding sessions. Antigravity can also run subagents in separate Git worktrees and verify their changes.
Google only tested Neon against mini-SWE, so there’s no data yet on how it performs with other harnesses.
It’s unclear which of those changes contributed most to the SWE-sweep improvement, since they weren’t tested separately. Google only tested Neon against mini-SWE, so there’s no data yet on how it performs with other harnesses.
Neon plans, Hydrogen builds
Neon is joining the model-switching system Google introduced with Gemini 4 Hydrogen. It handles planning and harder coding problems, leaving routine work to Hydrogen, and can run multiple Hydrogen subagents in parallel using the /swarm feature introduced with Carbon.
Google hasn’t said how much this setup affects Neon’s SWE-sweep results or what it means for the cost of completing a task.
Counting the cost per task
The company reports that Neon scored 65.2% on Terminal-Bench 4.1 and 46.2% on FrontierCode 2.0 at its default high reasoning setting. It also topped the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index with a score of 58.6.
At its default high thinking level, the model costs 32% less per task than Gemini 4 Carbon, according to Google’s comparison using the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index. API pricing is $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens, with cached input at $0.15 per million tokens and a 1 million-token context window.
Neon is available through the Gemini API, Google AI Studio, and Gemini for Business. Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers can also access it through Antigravity.
