articles.title: Africa’s AI adoption numbers are only as good as the counting
articles.text:
Kenya came first in a global ranking of ChatGPT use last year. In a survey published by DataReportal in July 2025, 42.1% of Kenyan Internet users aged 16 and above said they had used ChatGPT in the previous month—the highest share among the markets surveyed. South Africa came in at 34.3% and Nigeria at 27.9%.
Microsoft’s ranking put the three countries in the opposite order. In the first quarter of 2026, it estimated that 23.1% of South Africans aged 15 to 64 had used a generative artificial intelligence (AI) tool, followed by 10.1% of Nigerians and 8.7% of Kenyans. The next quarter brought modest gains in all three countries, with South Africa reaching 23.9%, Nigeria 10.4% and Kenya 8.9%.
The reversal can be confusing—and consequential—because AI adoption figures shape how investors size a market or how governments decide to deliver services. Yet if you look at the numbers closely, the two rankings describe different things.
One shows how popular ChatGPT is among people who already use the internet. The other estimates how far a range of generative AI tools has reached across the working-age population. Then there is a third question, which neither headline figure answers: how many people have found a use for AI that brings them back?
The people surveys leave out
DataReportal’s ChatGPT figures come from GlobalWebIndex (GWI), which surveys internet users. Imagine two countries with 100 adults each. In the first, 40 are online, and half of them use ChatGPT. In the second, 80 are online, and a third use it.
The first leads among internet users. The second has more ChatGPT users across the adult population. The ranking changes simply because the share of people who are online differs.
The difference in access between Kenya and South Africa is substantial. In its Digital 2027 country reports, DataReportal puts Internet penetration at 40.6% in Kenya and 79.5% in South Africa. Nigeria sits at 47.5%.
Those figures cover the whole population and come from a different period from the original ChatGPT survey. They show why connectivity matters, but multiplying them by the ChatGPT percentages would mix age groups and timeframes, yielding a misleading national estimate.
The denominator becomes even more important as the definition of AI widens. In its more recent global AI report, DataReportal says 97.3% of Kenyan internet users aged 16 and above reported using some form of AI in the previous month. In Nigeria, the figure was 96.6%.
“It’s critical to stress that these figures represent the share of Internet users,” the report says. This time the survey was asking about AI broadly. The figures cannot be read as evidence that ChatGPT use has doubled, or that almost everyone in either country uses AI.
Who gets online also affects the comparison. DataReportal found that, across the markets surveyed, 93.3% of internet users aged 16 to 24 said they had used AI in the previous month, compared with 52.2% of those aged 65 and above.
If one country’s online population skews younger than another’s, that alone could lift its adoption rate. The published rankings leave open the question of how much of Kenya’s lead reflects the ages of the people surveyed and how much reflects differences in behaviour among people of the same age.
What Microsoft can see
Microsoft starts with a wider population—everyone aged 15 to 64, whether they work, study or have internet access. It also counts activity across generative AI products. However, the data it observes directly are “primarily originating from users on Windows desktop (PC/tablet) platforms,” according to its technical paper.
People can opt out of sending diagnostic data, and Microsoft uses other sources to estimate usage beyond Windows and account for activity on mobile devices. “These assumptions are difficult to validate,” the researchers write of their mobile adjustment.
That matters when someone’s first encounter with generative AI may be through a chatbot on their phone. A survey can capture that person’s experience if they remember and report it; a model anchored in desktop activity has to estimate how much use it misses.
Both approaches make assumptions, and the two headline figures offer little basis for saying exactly how much of the gap comes from internet access, the mix of products counted, or the way each study collects its data.
Microsoft’s tables also give reason to be cautious about drawing fine distinctions between countries. Its technical paper notes that it sometimes pools markets with limited data to produce regional averages. Nigeria shares its 10.4% second-quarter estimate with several countries, including Ghana, Benin, and Togo.
The table alone offers little basis for treating Nigeria’s 1.5 percentage-point lead over Kenya as a precise measure of how differently people in the two countries use AI. South Africa’s much wider lead is the more striking result.
Relying on chatbots
For a startup selling an AI writing tool to small businesses, familiarity with ChatGPT could make it easier to explain what the product does. Pricing it calls for a different kind of evidence. How often do those businesses need help writing? Do they already get enough from a free chatbot? Would a tool that works in the languages they use with customers be worth paying for?
A high adoption rate among internet users tells a founder where to look for customers. It takes more to work out what those customers will buy.
For a government, the cost of getting the denominator wrong is different. If a ministry puts an AI assistant on its website to explain how to apply for a permit, a high rate of ChatGPT use among connected Kenyans may suggest some applicants will find it familiar.
The ministry still needs to know how many applicants can reach the site, whether they can follow the instructions on a phone and how often they manage to complete the application. Even Microsoft’s wider estimate excludes people aged 65 and over, who may also need the service.
A student who asks ChatGPT to summarise one reading and a trader who uses it every week to draft replies to customers both count in a monthly survey. The distinction starts to matter when the trader changes how they handle enquiries because of the tool. Knowing how many people have reached that point would tell us more about what AI is changing in Africa than knowing which country came first.

articles.title: Robots can do backflips but can't hold a gaze or press piano keys, and scientists think they've fixed that
articles.text:
What just happened? Engineers at the University of Pennsylvania have built an artificial muscle fiber that tracks its own temperature and corrects itself, so it can hold a precise position instead of slowly drifting back to its resting shape. The fiber pairs a rubber-like liquid crystal elastomer with graphene and an ultrathin copper coil that works as both a heater and a sensor. In lab tests, the muscles let a robot hand strike piano keys with different amounts of force and let a pair of robotic eyes hold a steady gaze.
The work, published in Advanced Functional Materials, is modeled on the small muscles that move human fingers and eyes. Those muscles make fine, controlled movements, and that kind of control has been hard to get from the hardware inside most robots today.
Large humanoid robots usually run on bulky, rigid motors and mechanical parts. That setup is good enough for walking and lifting, but not for small, careful motions. It's a familiar problem in robotics. Machines that can dance or do acrobatic flips still struggle with jobs people find easy, like folding laundry or keeping their eyes fixed on one spot.
Moving to soft materials brings its own trade-off. "Soft robotic muscles need to be both strong and flexible to mimic human movements, but these properties are rarely found in the same material," said Shu Yang, a University of Pennsylvania engineer and co-author of the study, in a statement.
The team's answer was a composite fiber in which each material has its own job. The liquid crystal elastomer, or LCE, is the part that moves. It contracts and stretches when heated, much like a muscle. Graphene mixed into the elastomer makes it softer and tougher, so the fiber holds up when an opposing muscle pulls the other way. That's important in any system where muscles work in pairs.
Even so, the elastomer and graphene alone couldn't hold a position. Heat makes the fiber move, but the fiber cools quickly and creeps back toward its original length. For a steady gaze or a light, constant press on a piano key, that drift is a serious problem, because the muscle has to stay in one place over time.
A copper coil fixed the drift. The researchers built it into the fiber so it would act as a temperature gauge, showing when the muscle was losing heat and starting to move back. With that reading, the system could add heat little by little to keep the fiber where it was supposed to be.
"We used the resistance of the embedded copper coil as a feedback signal and adjusted the heating power in real time to keep the resistance near a target value," said Xuelin Wu, a University of Pennsylvania Ph.D. student and co-author of the study. "Because the coil served as both a heater and a sensor, we did not need a separate sensor for feedback."
Because one part does both jobs, the design stays simple. There's no separate sensor to add or wire up, which helps as the muscles get smaller and are packed closer together.
The team tested the fibers in two setups. In the first, the muscles were fitted into a 3D-printed robot hand built to mimic how fingers move. The fingers pressed piano keys with varying amounts of force and at different speeds, and sensors under the keys measured how hard each note was struck. The hand isn't a skilled pianist, but it varied its touch on command.
In the second setup, the researchers put two robotic eyeballs on freely rotating ball joints inside 3D-printed shells. They attached the fibers in opposing pairs around the edges of each eye, much like the muscles that turn a human eye. The eyes shifted their gaze when commanded, and the movements were controlled and repeatable.
The Penn project is one of several efforts by labs and companies to replace standard motors with muscle-like actuators. Other researchers have stretched lab-grown human skin over robot faces and built synthetic hydrogel skin that lets robots sense burns and cuts. In 2025, the Polish startup Clone Robotics released a video of a faceless, human-sized robot hanging from a ceiling and twisting. The company said the robot was driven by synthetic muscles and a hydraulic system designed to copy human muscles and blood vessels, and it called the machine the world's first "musculoskeletal android." The video looked more like an early proof of concept than a finished prototype.
The Penn team's next step is to combine many of its fibers into larger systems, where dozens of small muscles have to work together to produce natural-looking expressions. Further out, the researchers want to explore using AI computer vision to coordinate those muscle groups. Their long-term goal is robots that look and move more like people.
"I'm excited about the possibility of using this approach to create robots that move with the same subtlety and expressiveness we see in human faces," said Ziyun Zhang, a University of Pennsylvania engineer and co-author of the paper.

articles.title: Elon Musk acusó a Zelenski de mentir sobre la velocidad limitada del internet satelital en Ucrania
articles.text:
El dueño de SpaceX, Elon Musk, acusó al presidente de Ucrania, Volodímir Zelenski, de mentir sobre las restricciones de velocidad que afectan a la red satelital militar Starshield. Lo mencionó en la cumbre DealBook de The New York Times, en Nueva York, ante el periodista Andrew Ross Sorkin.
Sorkin le preguntó por la afirmación de Zelenski de que la velocidad fue reducida. “Eso es falso”, respondió Musk. “No quiero sorprenderte, pero Zelenski no siempre es veraz”. Cuando Sorkin insistió, repitió que el presidente ucraniano miente.
Según Musk, lo que Kyiv pide en realidad es usar Starlink, el servicio comercial de internet por satélite de SpaceX, para operaciones militares ofensivas. “Nos hemos negado desde el comienzo de este conflicto”, dijo.
Zelenski había dicho horas antes, el miércoles 18, que los límites seguían vigentes y que dificultaban interceptar misiles y drones rusos. “Lo estamos hablando con la parte estadounidense”, afirmó, según CNBC.
Starlink y Starshield, dos redes distintas
Musk explicó que Starlink es una red civil y Starshield una versión militar que opera el gobierno de Estados Unidos. Las decisiones sobre Starshield corresponden al Departamento de Guerra y, en última instancia, al presidente, no a él, afirmó. “No me pidan, como individuo privado, que tome decisiones de matar”, afirmó. Según su relato, la presión para que cambie esa regla es constante, pero no la modificará.
En Starlink existe un tope de velocidad equivalente al límite más alto de las rutas de Ucrania, que Musk calculó en unas 100 millas por hora (cerca de 160 km/h). Un terminal que se mueve más rápido que ese umbral queda inutilizable para guiar un dron.
El presidente ucraniano había descrito en octubre otro límite: según Engadget, cualquier terminal que se desplace a más de 161 km/h pierde la conexión con la red. Zelenski dijo entonces que eso ayudaba a Rusia a atacar con más precisión.
Musk también defendió su historial. Mencionó que ninguna persona privada ayudó más a Ucrania que él y que, si SpaceX apagara Starlink, “todo el frente ucraniano colapsaría de inmediato”. Aseguró que las reglas de uso son las mismas desde el inicio de la guerra.
Versiones enfrentadas sobre quién dio la orden
La última reducción de velocidad ocurrió el 14 de octubre, según Engadget. SpaceX y la Casa Blanca se atribuyeron mutuamente la decisión y nunca se confirmó cuál de las dos la tomó. Reuters informó, citando a funcionarios estadounidenses, que la orden vino de la Casa Blanca. The Wall Street Journal publicó el 20 de octubre, con fuentes cercanas al caso, que fue el propio Musk quien ordenó el recorte.
Por entonces, Musk escribió en X que los sistemas Starshield pertenecen al gobierno de Estados Unidos y que cualquier límite de velocidad o uso lo decide el ejército y, en última instancia, el presidente Donald Trump.
También en octubre, Musk afirmó en su red social que Ucrania había violado los términos de servicio de Starlink al usarlo en ataques con drones. Un funcionario ucraniano respondió que las restricciones previas hacían “físicamente imposible” ese uso, según Engadget.

articles.title: Quantum computers are getting too powerful to check. Scientists have a solution
articles.text:
Quantum computers are getting too powerful to check. Scientists have a solution
- Date:
- November 16, 2026
- Source:
- University of Innsbruck
- Summary:
- Scientists have developed a new way to determine whether quantum simulations can be trusted, solving a growing problem as quantum computers become too powerful for conventional machines to check. Demonstrated on a 51-qubit system, the technique measures uncertainty and provides verifiable error margins that could help unlock the full potential of quantum computing.
- Share:
As quantum computers grow more powerful, researchers face a troubling question: How can they know whether the results are correct when conventional computers can no longer verify them? Scientists have now developed a promising new method that could help overcome this challenge by measuring the accuracy of quantum simulations and identifying how much uncertainty their predictions contain.
The technique uses experimental measurements to reconstruct how a quantum system behaves, then calculates how uncertainties in that reconstruction affect the results. Researchers successfully demonstrated the approach using a quantum simulator with up to 51 qubits in Innsbruck, Austria.
Quantum systems are expected to become capable of solving increasingly complex problems that traditional computers struggle with or cannot handle at all. However, this progress creates a verification problem. When a simulation is small enough, scientists can compare its results with calculations performed on a conventional computer. As quantum systems grow beyond those limits, that direct comparison becomes impractical, making alternative ways to assess their reliability essential.
A New Way to Measure Quantum Computing Accuracy
The breakthrough comes from an international research team led by Tristan Kraft at the Technical University of Munich and Peter Zoller at the University of Innsbruck and the Institute for Quantum Optics and Quantum Information of the Austrian Academy of Sciences, working alongside Barbara Kraus of the Technical University of Munich. The researchers developed a method for experimentally determining how a quantum simulator operates and translating uncertainties in its behavior into measurable limits on the accuracy of its results.
Quantum simulators are specialized physical systems designed to reproduce the behavior of other quantum systems. They are especially useful for investigating situations involving large numbers of interacting particles, where the calculations required can quickly overwhelm even powerful conventional computers.
But quantum experiments are never entirely free from errors. "But no real experiment is perfect," says Tristan Kraft. "Interactions may turn out differently than expected, the system is influenced by its environment, and measurements are also subject to uncertainties."
Rather than assuming a quantum simulator behaves exactly as intended, the new approach examines experimental data to determine what is actually happening inside the system. This allows researchers to identify important interactions and account for disturbances such as fluctuations and noise.
"From this data, we determine the relevant interactions as well as key influences from fluctuations and noise. We then calculate how the uncertainties in this model affect the simulation results," explains Tristan Kraft. "The quantum simulator thus provides not just a single value, but a result with error margins that quantify its accuracy."
Successfully Tested on a 51 Qubit Quantum Simulator
To evaluate the method, the researchers began with a relatively small quantum system containing ten trapped ions. Because conventional computers can still calculate the behavior of a system of this size, the team could test its reconstructed models and calculated error limits against independent measurements.
After this initial validation, the researchers expanded their experiments to a chain of 51 trapped ions. The larger demonstration, carried out by a team led by Manoj Joshi and Christian Roos using an ion trap quantum simulator, showed that the technique could also work with substantially more complex quantum systems.
This represents an important step toward establishing how trustworthy quantum simulation results are, particularly as quantum devices advance into territory where direct verification with traditional computing methods becomes increasingly difficult.
Extending the Breakthrough to More Complex Quantum Systems
The next challenge is to bring the technique to two-dimensional quantum simulators. These systems can model more complicated interactions among particles, making them valuable for exploring quantum physics. At the same time, their growing complexity makes their results particularly difficult to confirm using conventional calculations.
"This is particularly important because classical calculations for such systems become significantly more difficult as the number of particles increases," explains quantum computing pioneer Peter Zoller. "This also makes independent verification of the results increasingly complex, making the question of experimentally determined error limits all the more important."
The researchers are now adapting their method for the newest generation of two-dimensional quantum simulators, which offer improved precision and can investigate systems containing larger numbers of particles.
Looking further ahead, the approach could help scientists establish a more meaningful way to measure quantum advantage, the ability of quantum systems to outperform conventional computers. Instead of comparing machines based only on their processing speed or the size of the problems they can handle, researchers could also examine how accurately each system produces its answers.
"After all, when a classical computer and a quantum simulator tackle the same problem, it's not just a matter of which one delivers a result faster. What's also crucial is which one can solve the problem with a smaller, verifiable margin of error," says Peter Zoller.
This shift could change how progress in quantum computing is evaluated. Future breakthroughs may be judged not simply by how many particles a simulator can model or how quickly it performs calculations, but by its ability to solve increasingly difficult problems with demonstrably reliable results.
The findings were published in Physical Review X. The research received support from the Austrian Science Fund (FWF), the German Ministry of Research, Technology and Space, the European Union, BMW, and other funding organizations.

Materials provided by University of Innsbruck. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

articles.title: Hackers Exploit Cisco Expressway Vulnerability Soon After PoC Release
articles.text:
Hackers exploited a critical Cisco Expressway vulnerability to breach a Russian organization soon after proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit code was released publicly, according to cybersecurity firm F6.
Expressway gateways allow remote employees, partners, and third-party users to securely connect to an organization’s collaboration services, including video calls, voice calls, and instant messaging.
Tracked as CVE-2026-76466 (CVSS score of 9.8), the flaw can be exploited without authentication by remote attackers with network access to a device, allowing them to execute commands as root. It affects virtual and appliance versions of Expressway Core and Expressway Edge, but only when the devices are clustered.
Cisco, which disclosed the issue on October 21, said it resides in the Expressway database service feature and stems from persistent cookies.
An attacker possessing the persistent cookies could reach the database service and issue certain remote procedure call (RPC) commands, gaining the ability to run root-level commands on the underlying operating system.
Expressway X15.5.20 resolves the vulnerability. There are no workarounds, and customers on X14 or earlier releases need to move to a fixed release, Cisco says.
The advisory has not been revised since its initial release and still states that Cisco is unaware of public announcements or malicious use of the flaw. However, a PoC exploit has since been posted on GitHub, and F6 says the attack it investigated came shortly after.
According to F6, the attackers first breached two Expressway X15.5.3 devices exposed to the internet. They then pivoted from one of them to two other cluster nodes sitting on the organization’s internal network.
After securing root privileges, the attackers prepared tools for lateral movement. These included custom Python scripts designed to scan the network, locate SMB resources, interact with SQL Server and WinRM, and search GitLab repositories, aiming to exfiltrate credentials and other sensitive information.
F6 determined that the attackers modified the scripts on the fly, during the attack. “The source code contained characteristic comments and descriptions of fixes indicating the use of an AI assistant,” the company says.
F6 did not name the victim or attribute the attack to a known threat actor.
To detect exploitation, F6 points to the Erlang system log on Expressway devices. The security firm has also published IP addresses and file paths associated with the attack in a Russian-language press release.
Although Cisco lists no workarounds, F6 recommends that organizations unable to patch immediately block connections to TCP ports 4371–4372 at the firewall, except from the IP addresses of trusted cluster nodes.
SecurityWeek has reached out to Cisco for comment on F6’s findings and will update this article if the company responds.

articles.text:
There’s a patient who’s stuck in Dr. Bijan Teja’s head. He calls him “Bob.”
Last year, Bob was sitting in his hospital bed talking with his family and joking with his nurse as he recovered from surgery. Sure, his heart rate rose, and his blood pressure fell a bit throughout the day, but nothing dramatic happened. Everything seemed to be going well. But by midnight, Bob was back on a breathing machine and rushed into surgery. By morning, he was dead.
“The worst feeling as an intensivist is when the alarms only ring when it’s too late and you lose a patient.”
Dr. Bijan Teja,
AI Compass
“The worst feeling as an intensivist is when the alarms only ring when it’s too late and you lose a patient,” Teja, an ICU doctor at St. Michael’s Hospital in Toronto, said.
Teja has been working with Dr. Michael Sklar, his best friend at the hospital, on a new tool that might have been able to save Bob’s life: AI Compass. It will be fed data on tens of thousands of ICU patients to identify imperceptible patterns that emerge in patients’ health before they take a turn for the worse, potentially giving doctors more time to save a life.
“Bijan and I, as ICU doctors, think we know the patterns that exist when someone may deteriorate, and alternatively, when someone may be improving,” Sklar said. “Is it possible that there are signs in the data that we’re collecting that we just don’t know yet … that could signify deterioration?”
AI Compass isn’t in any ICUs yet, and it may sound theoretical right now, but Teja and Sklar have a reason to believe it will work. St. Michael’s Hospital already uses a similar tool called ChartWatch, which monitors patients in wards and provides an early warning if they need to head to the ICU. A hospital study found the tool led to a 26-percent reduction in unanticipated deaths in the general medicine ward, where there is much less data to work with than in the ICU. While wards collect a set of vital signs every four hours, and maybe labs once a day, Teja explained that the ICU collects data every minute, giving AI Compass even more to find patterns in.
“The volume of data is enormous, and on many more things too, including ventilator settings and life support, … many more parameters, and it’s predicting something different,” Teja said. “ChartWatch predicts who needs to go to the ICU; AI Compass predicts who in the ICU is at risk for deterioration and death.”
RELATED: Getting old is hard. This age-tech housing aims to make it easier.
AI Compass has a multidisciplinary team within St. Michael’s of 30 people, including Dr. Amol Verma, who led ChartWatch’s development. Teja and Sklar, who say they bring complementary skill sets to the project, have been working on AI Compass since roughly 2024. However, they didn’t feel like they were actually “getting it off the ground” until earlier this year, Teja said, when they started preparing to pitch for the St. Michael’s Hospital Foundation’s Angel’s Den competition. Angel’s Den claims to be Canada’s biggest medical research competition; earlier this month, it had $700,000 up for grabs, of which AI Compass secured $200,000 under the Mitchell Award for Health System Innovation.
The award is just a start for AI Compass. It buys the team time to train its AI model and get it ready for testing, but Teja stressed he’s “fighting hard” to secure even more because he knows they’ll need it. His ultimate dream is that this St. Michael’s-led project ends up in hundreds of ICUs across Canada and beyond.
“We want to see, looking retrospectively at St. Mike’s patients, would [AI Compass] have caught those patients like Bob earlier and given us more time?” Teja said. “We’ll need more support, but to get it at least to that proof-of-concept stage, already this $200,000 starts to move us toward [it].”
Feature image courtesy St. Michael’s Hospital Foundation.

articles.title: Ubisoft lays off 166 employees in Quebec
articles.text:
Ubisoft has laid off 166 employees at its Montreal and Quebec City studios.
“As our portfolio evolves, our production needs are changing, requiring us to adjust the size of some teams to ensure our resources are aligned with current production priorities and business needs,” a Ubisoft spokesperson said in a statement to MobileSyrup. “We deeply value the contributions of these teams and recognize the impact this may have on our colleagues. We are committed to supporting them through this process with care and respect.”
The company added that affected staff are being provided with severance, extended health care benefits, career transition services and other resources.
Ubisoft Montreal is the French gaming giant’s flagship studio with around 4,000 employees, leading development on marquee franchises like Assassin’s Creed, Rainbow Six, Far Cry, Prince of Persia and Watch Dogs. Outside of this year’s Rainbow Six Mobile, though, the studio has largely been supporting development on other Ubisoft titles while working on various other new projects, including an upcoming Assassin’s Creed codenamed “Hexe.”
Ubisoft Quebec, meanwhile, staffs around 600 and was behind last year’s hit Assassin’s Creed Shadows, the latest mainline Assassin’s Creed game, not counting this year’s remake of Black Flag. It’s unclear what the studio has been working on since the release of Shadows outside of various updates to the game.
These layoffs come as Ubisoft has been struggling in recent years, leading to a studio co-ownership venture with Tencent that led to a company restructuring. Amidst all of that, Ubisoft has laid off hundreds of employees, including 70 last month at its Singapore team and 40 in Toronto earlier this year, as well as closed multiple studios, including those in San Francisco, Osaka, Stockholm, Belgrade, and Finland. Here in Canada, it also closed Halifax (following unionization efforts) and Winnipeg. Ubisoft’s next release is Rayman Legends Retold, a Ubisoft Montpellier- and Milan-led remake of 2013’s Rayman Legends that hits consoles and PC on Dec. 3.
It should be noted that the timing of this news is certainly questionable. After all, today is the long-awaited launch of Grand Theft Auto VI, which has understandably dominated the news cycle. Therefore, it seems as though Ubisoft is looking to try to bury the latest rounds of layoffs under the shadow of GTA.
The string of cuts and closures in Canada, especially, has garnered renewed scrutiny in recent months due to the significant government subsidies Ubisoft has received. As The Walrus noted earlier this year, Ubisoft has been given as much as $2 billion in Canadian incentives since the ’90s, yet it’s been reducing significant portions of its workforce here.
Update: 19/11/2026 at 3:08 p.m. ET — This news also comes alongside Ubisoft’s announcement of a GenAI subsidiary because AI slop will certainly help cut costs in the long-term.

articles.title: ¿A qué hora se estrena 'Percy Jackson y los dioses del Olimpo' temporada 3?
articles.text:
La temporada 3 de Percy Jackson y los dioses del Olimpo por fin regresa a los hogares de todo el mundo. La serie seguirá adaptando los icónicos libros de Rick Riordan y abriendo a los jóvenes las puertas a la mitología griega. El título se ha convertido en una de las sagas de aventuras más queridas de la actualidad. Pero, ¿a qué hora y dónde se estrena la temporada 3 de Percy Jackson y los dioses del Olimpo?
En esta nueva aventura, Percy deberá enfrentarse a la repentina desaparición de Annabeth y a la inminente Gran Profecía revelada por el Oráculo de Delfos, de la que depende el destino del Olimpo. Según la profecía, uno de los hijos semidioses de los Tres Grandes está destinado a elevar el Olimpo a una nueva era de esplendor o sumirlo en la ruina, mientras su propia vida pende de un hilo.
Acerca de dónde podrá verse, a diferencia de otros títulos, aquí no depende para nada del territorio. En Estados Unidos, España, Latinoamérica y en el resto del mundo, Percy Jackson y los dioses del Olimpo temporada 3 estará disponible en Disney+. La plataforma alberga los derechos exclusivos de toda la serie, por lo que contará de nuevo con su tercera entrega en el catálogo.
Hora de estreno de Percy Jackson y los dioses del Olimpo temporada 3
En cuanto a la hora de estreno de Percy Jackson y los dioses del Olimpo temporada 3, en Estados Unidos se emitirá el viernes 20 de noviembre a las 12:00 am P.T. En España y Latinoamérica, llegará a Disney+ en la conversión horaria de cada país:
- España: 9:00 h.
- México, Guatemala, Honduras, El Salvador, Nicaragua, Costa Rica: 2:00 h.
- Perú, Colombia, Panamá, Ecuador: 3:00 h.
- Chile, Venezuela, Bolivia, República Dominicana, Puerto Rico: 4:00 h.
- Paraguay, Argentina, Brasil, Uruguay: 5:00 h.
Date de alta en Disney+ ahora y ahorra gracias a la suscripción anual, con la que podrás disfrutar de todo su catálogo de series y películas. Acceso a los últimos estrenos, al catálogo de Star y ESPN* y a los mejores documentales de National Geographic.
*ESPN solo está disponible en Latinoamérica. Ahorro respecto a 12 meses de suscripción mensual.
A partir de ese momento, los dos primeros episodios de la temporada 3 de Percy Jackson y los dioses del Olimpo. Desde entonces, la serie seguirá una estrategia de estreno semanal semejante. Es decir, habrá dos nuevos episodios disponibles cada semana hasta llegar al séptimo y octavo el viernes 11 de diciembre. Será entonces cuando esta entrega llegue a su fin y los fans tengan que armarse de paciencia a la espera de una cuarta.

articles.title: Meta’s Muse Charm might cost $300
articles.text:
Meta is planning to price the Muse Charm, a little gadget with a screen that lets you chat with your Muse AI agent, at $300, according to The Information. CEO Mark Zuckerberg revealed the gadget earlier this year and said the company expected to ship the Charm “in time for the holidays in December,” but he didn’t provide a price at the time.
Meta’s Muse Charm might cost $300
The Information has reported a potential price for the Muse Charm, which is expected to ship in time for the holidays.
When he announced the Muse Charm, Zuckerberg said that the company had “packed the whole Muse experience,” including real-time voice and avatar technology, into the gadget. It has a fingerprint sensor, and you can tap it to be able to talk to a Muse AI agent without unlocking a phone or opening an app. The Information reports that the Muse Charm will come with a free 12-month 5G data plan from Verizon.
Spokesperson Tyler Yee wrote to The Information that “We’re charmed by the interest in our AI devices, and we’ll have more to share soon.” When reached for comment by The Verge, Yee provided the same statement.
The company is also working on a smartwatch, The Information says, but a launch for that has been pushed to 2027 as Meta tries to get Muse Charm out the door.
Meta also open sourced code to let users make their own Muse gadgets, which my colleague Sean Hollister used to make his own DIY Muse Charm.
Update, November 19th: Noted statement given by Meta spokesperson Tyler Yee.

articles.title: Critical Java vulnerability puts millions of sites, services, and devices at risk of remote code execution — triggers with 64 As and an '=' sign, OpenJDK optimization bug lets an attacker trigger it just by inputting repeated text
articles.text:
Critical Java vulnerability puts millions of sites, services, and devices at risk of remote code execution — triggers with 64 As and an '=' sign, OpenJDK optimization bug lets an attacker trigger it just by inputting repeated text
The Winds of Winter have arrived — just not written by G.R.R. Martin.
We've just had a few high-stakes security vulnerabilities making systems administrators run around with their heads on fire, and the deluge doesn't look like it's stopping any time soon. Java, the programming language that Oracle has always claimed is on billions of devices, has a critical security vulnerability that allows for remote code execution (RCE), often without even needing to log in to the application. The consequence is that an attacker can gain access to the target system, read user and internal data, and have a launch point for further shenanigans, including database access and potential system takeover.
The flaw was dubbed Java4Shell by Calif Research, the lab that found the vulnerability. The researchers say it rates 9.2 on the newer CVSS 4.0 scale, though individual reports from companies like Oracle itself and Red Hat give it their own ratings, but they're all in the 8 to 9.8 range depending on the vendor. The root cause is a bug in OpenJDK, the library that nearly every distribution of Java, whether Oracle's or anyone else's, derives their implementations from.
You can see an exploit of the bug in action below across multiple software services.
The actual bug is a flaw in an optimization for Base64 decoding, functionality that's ubiquitous in any programming language. Base64 is a format to allow for easy transformation of binary data into plain text. In the modern day, it's used to embed files in the middle of text, like inserting image data in the middle of HTML or CSS, attaching files to emails (internally they're all text-based), or simply representing data as text for visual inspection, like file checksums or cryptographic key fingerprints.
Oracle has already fixed the bug and issued updated versions of its wares. However, much like digital certificates, operating systems and even individual programs include their own copy of a Java executable, meaning that the potential blast radius is far wider than you'd expect at first glance. Calif listed many such common applications: at the time of the post, Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Jenkins, and PingFederate all had full unauthenticated RCE, while Apache Kafka Broker, Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit, and Spinnaker have RCEs after authentication.
Because Java is so darn widespread, most every company has to issue security advisories and updates for their wares, including IBM, Red Hat, Siemens, and Broadcom. Because so many containers also use Java-based applications in some form, those too are vulnerable, and the count of individual vulnerable container images across registries everywhere is likely a high figure. This is likely not a bug that will be easily eradicated.
There is a condition to trigger the exploit, but it's not too difficult to fulfill. The Java instance in question must be running on an x86-64 CPU with AVX-512 support and the VBMI extension. In practice, that means chips from the Intel Ice Lake and AMD Zen 4 families, from 2021 and 2022 respectively, for their server variants. Older CPUs are not affected, as the code optimization that contains the bug is specific to VBMI.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
The specific bug is in a hand-written assembly optimization that fails a simple bounds check. If an attacker inputs 64 As and an "=" sign as padding, they can overwrite neighboring memory, and then weaponize that corruption, similar to how Heartbleed worked. As usual these days, Calif says that the vulnerability was found by an AI bot, with $200 worth of tokens. Though unlike many other examples, this one was actually fairly deep, and it wasn't low-hanging fruit that illustrated poor code or network security hygiene.
Bruno Ferreira is a contributing writer for Tom's Hardware. He has decades of experience with PC hardware and assorted sundries, alongside a career as a developer. He's obsessed with detail and has a tendency to ramble on the topics he loves. When not doing that, he's usually playing games, or at live music shows and festivals.

articles.title: Don't buy cheap old stock this Black Friday; these top-end headphone makers just released stunning new products
articles.text:
Forget Black Friday for headphones: meet two new wired and (oddly) wireless headphones and IEMs from the audiophile world’s heavy-hitters
Meet the premium audio experience (no, they're not on sale)
- Campfire Audio unveils Cascara Mk2 premium IEMs
- Grado shows off GW200 open-back headphones
- Neither company lets Black Friday slow them down
With Black Friday scheduled for next week, everyone's lining up to find good deals on consumer-grade audio kit. Some brands aren't letting the sales season ruin a good thing, though, with two major companies unveiling fresh new products — which almost certainly won't be seeing any seasonal discounts.
I'm talking about Grado and Campfire Audio, two of our favorite premium audio makers, which have spent years making great-sounding devices that we're able to heap rare praise upon. And both have dropped exciting new products in the last few days.
One's a pair of premium IEMs (In-Ear Monitors), while the other is a pair of open-back headphones that, in a twist for the form factor, are wireless.
Campfire Audio Cascara Mk2
Let's start with the smaller product: the Campfire Audio Cascara Mk2, which are on sale right now for $549 / £549 (about AU$1,100). As you can tell, they're the successor buds to the original Cascara from 2024.
These earbuds come with a 10mm Dual-Magnet dynamic driver, seemingly carried over from the original pair, and it's designed to offer a rich and textured sound. That doesn't mean the buds sound the same though, and one of the upgrades here is a variety of tuning refinements and a better focus on smooth high-frequency.
The other change is in the design, with the Mk2 designed to better fit in your ear and feel comfortable for hours of listening. It looks a little more funky too thanks to that blue pebbling.
One extra detail about the Cascara Mk2 I appreciate, is that Campfire Audio is offering you more in the box. It's giving you a loads of cleaning tools, a carry pouch and a little wallet to tote them about in, as well as multiple eartip sizes. It's something we've seen with all Campfire Audio products (see the company's Grand Luna, Chimera, Clara or Trifecta for more) but still, it's good to see at this slightly more affordable level.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Grado GW200
Next up, we have some on-ear open-back headphones. The Grado GW200 are the eight-years-later follow-up to the Grado GW100, though they seem more similar to the point-five model, the Grado GW100x.
The GW100 were the first open-back wireless headphones, and Grado is continuing that with its new model. These cans bring new tech specs to the wireless audiophile experience, using Bluetooth 5.4 as connection.
You're getting an upgraded version of the 44mm S driver seen in the GW100x, using a paper-composite diaphragm to offer a natural sound profile. There are also tuning refinements from the earlier pair, but it sounds like functionality is the main change.
That's to say, these have a 60 hour battery life and are designed to be comfortable to wear for long periods of time. They don't weigh any more than your average pair of over-ear headphones at 235g, and use custom-designed cushions to help with the fit and the tuning.
The Grado GW200 are due to go on sale in December, for $329 / £329 (about AU$660) so they're cheaper than the Campfire Audio. Believe me though, I hope I get to test both for sound-per-pound value — but even just the one pair would be a delight…

articles.title: What a billion-dollar deal says about the US battery market
articles.text:
What a billion-dollar deal says about the US battery market
The deal between Sila and Panasonic Energy is a bright spot for the industry, and it shows how politics have shifted recently for batteries.
After a tough few years littered with some high-profile failures, there’s some positive news for next-generation batteries in the US.
Sila just signed an agreement with Panasonic Energy, a global battery manufacturer, to supply silicon-carbon anode material, a possible key to smaller, lighter batteries. It’s a deal that Sila says could be worth more than $1 billion over time.
This arrangement also shows how much the politics of batteries have shifted lately. A major part of the financial backing for this factory’s production is a $1.4 billion loan from the Trump administration’s Defense Department. While batteries can be a major tool to help drive the energy transition and cut emissions, right now much of the industry is more focused on geopolitics.
Founded in 2011, Sila makes silicon-based anodes for lithium-ion batteries. The big selling point here is the potential to improve energy density—Sila’s anode weighs a fifth as much as the graphite used in anodes today and cuts the volume in half, according to the company. So using this new material enables batteries to pack more energy into the same weight and volume, allowing longer range for EVs, for example. The material can also deliver more power and recharge faster, compared with conventional chemistry.
We’ve been following Sila (and its competitors) for years. My colleague James Temple covered the company when its battery first appeared in Whoop fitness wearables in 2021.
Things have gotten a lot bigger since then. In 2022, Sila announced plans for a factory in Moses Lake, Washington, and received $100 million from the US Department of Energy, part of a multibillion-dollar round of grants under the Biden administration to support the US battery supply chain.
The company opened its factory in September 2025, and it’s already operating. But the deal with Panasonic will help it scale to at least 10 times more production than current levels, says Gene Berdichevsky, the company’s cofounder and CEO.
Panasonic has committed to buying tens of thousands of tons of material, Berdichevsky says, though Sila isn’t sharing specific numbers on the total commitment or the price Panasonic is paying.
This agreement is Sila’s first mass-market deal and a big one for the United States’ next-generation battery market, which has largely been on the ropes over the past few years. Two billion-dollar battery companies, 24M and ESS Tech, have declared bankruptcy and shut down just in the last year.
The glimmer of hope here is tied up with something I’ve been noticing about this industry: the shifting politics. While batteries used to be firmly considered a climate technology, we’ve seen a lot of companies move away from messaging around the clean energy transition and lean into geopolitics.
China dominates the battery world and particularly the battery anode market, controlling over 90% of graphite production today. For years, the US has been trying to curb reliance on Chinese batteries, battery materials, and other materials used in crucial technologies, like rare earth metals. But the Trump administration has ramped things up, and earlier this year the US Defense Department committed a $1.4 billion loan to Sila aimed at helping the US face a “significant technology sovereignty challenge,” as a press release put it.
Sila’s announcement of the Panasonic deal does mention EVs—but not climate, emissions or the energy transition. Rather, it’s all about American industrialization. (And, of course, a mention that a North American battery supply chain can also help power the AI market.)
I asked Berdichevsky about this shift and whether the company holds decarbonization as a priority.
“I think the politics of it has shifted around us much more than our motivations have shifted,” he said. “It’s really the energy efficiency that motivates engineers like myself and technologists at our company. And I still think that that’s still at the heart of it.”

articles.title: Inside MS Dhoni’s startup playbook: 13 companies backed by Captain Cool
articles.text:
Inside MS Dhoni’s startup playbook: 13 companies backed by Captain Cool
From Garuda Aerospace to SolarSquare, explore 13 startups backed by MS Dhoni across fintech, electric mobility, gaming and clean energy.
MS Dhoni's retirement from the Indian Premier League (IPL) as a player marks the end of an important chapter in his cricketing career. On November 17, 2026, Chennai Super Kings (CSK) announced that Dhoni would take up the role of team mentor from the 2027 season.
However, cricket is not the only field where Dhoni has built a presence. Over the years, the former Indian captain has invested in several Indian startups through personal investments and his family office, Midas Deals.
His investment portfolio spans fintech, drone technology, electric mobility, food, gaming, digital entertainment and renewable energy.
Here are 13 startups and companies backed by MS Dhoni.
1. Garuda Aerospace
Founded in 2015 by Agnishwar Jayaprakash, Chennai-based Garuda Aerospace develops drones for agriculture, defence, infrastructure and industrial applications. Dhoni invested in the company in June 2022 and became its brand ambassador. In February 2024, he acquired a 1.1% stake for Rs 4 crore.
2. Khatabook
Founded in 2018, Bengaluru-based Khatabook is a fintech platform that helps small businesses and merchants manage digital bookkeeping and daily transactions. Dhoni invested in the startup in March 2020 and also became its brand ambassador. The investment amount was not disclosed.
3. CARS24
CARS24 is a Gurugram-based online marketplace for buying and selling pre-owned vehicles. Founded in 2015, the company uses technology to simplify vehicle valuation, inspection and transactions. Dhoni invested in the startup in August 2019 as part of its Series D funding round.
4. HomeLane
Founded in 2014, HomeLane is a Bengaluru-based home interior design company that helps homeowners plan and customise their living spaces. Its services include modular kitchens, wardrobes and complete home interiors. Dhoni invested in the company in August 2021, although the investment amount was not disclosed.
5. EMotorad
Pune-based EMotorad manufactures electric bicycles for urban commuting and recreational use. Founded in 2020, the company aims to make electric mobility more accessible. Dhoni invested an undisclosed amount in the startup in April 2024 in exchange for equity and also became its brand ambassador.
6. Shaka Harry
Shaka Harry is a plant-based protein and alternative meat brand based in Bengaluru. It develops plant-based food products for consumers looking for alternatives to conventional meat. Dhoni invested in the company in 2022, although the financial details of the investment were not disclosed.
7. 7InkBrews
Mumbai-based 7InkBrews operates in the food and beverage industry. Dhoni became a co-founder, shareholder and brand ambassador of the company in April 2021. Its consumer brand, Copter7, offers chocolates and beverages inspired by Dhoni's iconic helicopter shot and jersey number seven.
8. Tagda Raho
Tagda Raho is a fitness startup that combines traditional Indian exercise techniques with modern fitness practices. Based in Bengaluru, the company promotes indigenous workout methods and fitness equipment. Dhoni invested in the startup in November 2023.
9. ACKO
ACKO is a digital-first insurance company offering products across motor, health and travel insurance. The company uses technology to simplify insurance purchases and claims. In July 2025, Dhoni joined ACKO as an investor and brand ambassador through his family office.
10. Kuku
Kuku is a Bengaluru-based digital storytelling platform operating across audio entertainment, educational content and short-form video. Its products include Kuku FM, Kuku TV and Guru. In March 2026, Dhoni invested in the company and became the brand ambassador for its microdrama platform, Kuku TV. The investment amount was not disclosed.
11. LightFury Games
LightFury Games is a gaming startup developing cricket-based gaming experiences for digital audiences. In 2025, the company raised $11 million in a funding round involving investors such as Blume Ventures, V3 Ventures, MIXI and Times Internet. Dhoni participated as a strategic investor alongside cricketers Jasprit Bumrah, Hardik Pandya and Ravindra Jadeja.
12. SolarSquare
SolarSquare is a rooftop solar company that provides residential solar installation and related services. Founded in 2015, the company helps households adopt solar energy solutions. In July 2026, Dhoni invested in the startup through his family office, Midas Deals, and joined as its brand ambassador as part of its $53 million Series C funding round.
13. BluSmart
BluSmart was an electric mobility startup that operated an all-electric ride-hailing service and EV charging infrastructure. Dhoni's family office invested in the company during its pre-Series B funding round in June 2024. However, the company suspended its ride-hailing operations in 2025 following financial and regulatory challenges.
Final thoughts
MS Dhoni's investments reflect his growing involvement in India's startup ecosystem beyond professional cricket. His portfolio spans businesses working in financial technology, electric mobility, drone manufacturing, digital entertainment and clean energy.
While the investment amounts and ownership details remain undisclosed for several companies, his involvement demonstrates how sports personalities are increasingly participating in India's entrepreneurial ecosystem.
As Dhoni transitions from an IPL player to a mentor, his business interests offer another perspective on his journey beyond the cricket field.

articles.title: EEUU busca desesperadamente tarjetas de memoria de los años 90 para su caza furtivo más sofisticado. El problema es que ya nadie las hace
articles.text:
Hay máquinas tan avanzadas que parecen adelantadas a su tiempo. Pero mantenerlas funcionando durante décadas puede convertirse en una batalla contra la obsolescencia, especialmente cuando sus componentes dejan de fabricarse y la tecnología que utilizan desaparece del mercado. Estados Unidos acaba de encontrarse con una de esas paradojas en uno de los aviones más sofisticados de su arsenal.
Un caza de 150 millones buscando tarjetas de los años 90. Sí, la Fuerza Aérea de Estados Unidos está buscando proveedores de tarjetas de memoria similares a las que utilizaban los ordenadores portátiles y las cámaras digitales hace casi tres décadas. Lo extraordinario es su destino: el F-22 Raptor, uno de los cazas furtivos más avanzados del mundo, capaz de superar Mach 2 y diseñado para dominar el combate aéreo.
El 16 de noviembre de 2026, la oficina responsable del programa publicó una solicitud oficial para localizar empresas estadounidenses capaces de suministrar tarjetas con una capacidad mínima de 256 megabytes. Una cantidad diminuta comparada con la memoria de cualquier teléfono actual, pero que sigue siendo necesaria para mantener operativos estos aviones.
La tecnología que sobrevivió a los ordenadores que la utilizaban. La Fuerza Aérea busca dos formatos concretos: tarjetas PC Card de tipo II, también conocidas como PCMCIA, y tarjetas CompactFlash con adaptadores compatibles. Las primeras eran habituales en los portátiles de los años 90 y tenían aproximadamente el tamaño de una tarjeta de crédito. Las segundas se popularizaron en las cámaras digitales de principios de los 2000.
Ambas han quedado prácticamente relegadas a equipos especializados, pero siguen siendo compatibles con los sistemas originales del F-22. El problema no es que Estados Unidos desconozca alternativas modernas, sino que cambiar el formato implicaría modificar equipos militares diseñados y certificados alrededor de una arquitectura informática antigua.
Una tarjeta diminuta con una misión gigantesca. Estos dispositivos forman parte del sistema conocido como Data Transfer Cartridge, una especie de cartucho que conecta la planificación de misiones en tierra con los ordenadores del avión. Antes del despegue, permite introducir rutas de vuelo, frecuencias de radio, coordenadas e información sobre amenazas enemigas.
Después de aterrizar, los técnicos pueden recuperar registros del vuelo y datos de diagnóstico para comprobar el estado del aparato. Es decir, una tecnología que hoy parece propia de un museo informático continúa desempeñando funciones esenciales en la preparación y el mantenimiento de un caza furtivo.
El problema de construir un avión para varias décadas. El F-22 realizó su primer vuelo en septiembre de 1997, entró en servicio en 2005 y su última unidad fue entregada en 2012. Estados Unidos construyó 195 ejemplares de un avión cuyo coste de fabricación rondaba los 143-150 millones de dólares por unidad. Sus prestaciones siguen siendo extraordinarias: alcanza aproximadamente 2.414 kilómetros por hora, puede operar a casi 20.000 metros de altitud y tiene un alcance de unos 2.960 kilómetros con depósitos adicionales.
Sin embargo, buena parte de su electrónica fue concebida cuando las tarjetas PCMCIA eran una tecnología corriente. El resultado es que una aeronave diseñada para seguir volando durante décadas depende de componentes comerciales que dejaron de ser habituales hace mucho tiempo.
Algo peor que quedarse sin tarjetas: comprar falsificaciones. La solicitud estadounidense dedica buena parte de sus requisitos a garantizar la procedencia de los componentes. Los proveedores deberán identificar al fabricante original, especificar el país de fabricación de cada pieza, señalar dónde se realizó el ensamblaje final y documentar toda la cadena de suministro.
También tendrán que presentar medidas para evitar productos falsificados y explicar cuándo dejarán de fabricar las tarjetas, incluyendo posibles oportunidades para realizar una última compra antes de su desaparición. La preocupación es comprensible: un componente aparentemente insignificante puede comprometer la fiabilidad de un sistema militar extraordinariamente caro.
Una flota que envejece, que Washington no quiere jubilar. El suministro de tarjetas es solo una parte de los problemas logísticos del F-22. En 2020, un alto mando estadounidense reconoció que la flota sufría escasez de motores porque los aviones habían acumulado más horas de vuelo de las previstas.
Aun así, el Raptor continúa participando en operaciones y ejercicios internacionales: en octubre de 2026, unidades desplegadas desde Alaska participaron en unas maniobras estadounidenses y japonesas en el sur de Japón. Paralelamente, la Fuerza Aérea está probando nuevos sensores y depósitos de combustible para mantener estos cazas operativos durante la década de 2030.
El futuro de un caza furtivo depende también de su pasado. Por ahora, Estados Unidos no ha comprado ninguna tarjeta: la solicitud publicada en el portal federal SAM.gov es una consulta al mercado, abierta hasta el 1 de diciembre de 2026, para conocer qué empresas pueden suministrarlas, si es que hay alguna. Tampoco se han especificado cantidades ni presupuesto.
Sea como fuere, el caso ilustra una contradicción habitual en la tecnología militar: desarrollar sistemas extraordinariamente avanzados es solo la primera parte del desafío, mantenerlos durante treinta o cuarenta años puede resultar igual de complicado. El F-22 puede volar a más de 2.400 kilómetros por hora y operar con tecnología furtiva de última generación pero, ironías del destino, para seguir haciéndolo necesita que alguien continúe fabricando tarjetas de memoria como las que utilizábamos cuando todavía no existían los smartphones.

articles.title: Microsoft is experimenting with open-source AMD code to give Xbox up to 16% performance boost
articles.text:
Something to look forward to: Microsoft is testing an experimental open-source AMD shader compiler in the Xbox Game Development Kit, marking a major change in the way game consoles are optimized. Redmond believes that the update will improve game performance by 2% to 16% on current-gen Xbox consoles.
The open-source AMD compiler at the heart of the updated GDK is based on ACO, a shader compiler from the Mesa project that is used by the RADV Vulkan driver for AMD GPUs on Linux. It converts high-level shader instructions into machine code optimized for RDNA 2 GPUs powering Xbox Series X|S, Steam Deck, and other gaming handhelds.
Developed by the open-source Linux community in collaboration with Valve and independent developers, the compiler will replace the older LLVM-based architecture, enabling much faster shader compilation and yielding smoother runtime performance in Vulkan games on the Steam Deck and Linux PCs.
 – Xbox_Serious_X|S 🧬 🇺🇸 (@Xbox_Series_XS) November 15, 2026
By integrating technologies from multiple platforms, the new compiler is expected to eliminate existing shader bottlenecks and boost gaming performance. Microsoft noted that, following an initial evaluation, developers testing the updated GDK reported a performance improvement of between 2% and 16% depending on the game engine and graphics content.
The AMD compiler is an experimental addition that enables developers to optimize their upcoming games to perform better on Xbox consoles, but it does not automatically apply any optimization to existing games. Microsoft has yet to announce which titles will support the new compiler or when the changes will translate to tangible benefits for gamers.
The new compiler is part of Microsoft's latest Xbox GDK released in October. The updated kit also includes a new Xbox Test Account CLI that can be used to block player privileges based on account activity and a new command-line tool called ConvertPevt that converts .pevt offline timing captures from Xbox Series X|S consoles into .xpix captures without opening PIX.
The latest GDK also introduces AMD's machine learning-based FSR 4.1.2 upscaling to Xbox Series X|S, adding support for the existing Full INT8 model and a new Lite INT8 model, which is half the size and has a significantly lower computational cost. Developers will be able to pick between the two models to optimize either frame rates or visual quality, depending on the game.

articles.title: Black Friday 2026: 10 Tricks, mit denen du wirklich Geld sparst
articles.text:
Black Friday 2026: 10 Tricks, mit denen du wirklich Geld sparst
Es zeichnet sich bereits seit Tagen ab, dass nahezu alle Onlinehändler mit den Zauberwörtern Black Friday und Black Week um Aufmerksamkeit kämpfen. Immer mehr Kund:innen in Deutschland gehen an Black Friday und Cyber-Monday gezielt auf Schnäppchenjagd, wobei Studien ergeben haben, dass auch schon vor den Schnäppchentagen Ende November attraktive Rabatte drin sind.
Dabei ist der Black Friday stets auf den Freitag nach dem US-amerikanischen Thanksgiving festgelegt und erzielt in den USA seit vielen Jahren Umsatzrekorde. In diesem Jahr fällt der Black Friday auf einen relativ späten Termin, den 27. November.
Der Black Friday ist längst kein einzelner Aktionstag mehr. Viele Onlinehändler beginnen schon Wochen vorher mit ihren Angeboten und verlängern die Rabattaktionen über das Wochenende bis zum Cyber Monday. Wer erst am eigentlichen Black Friday mit dem Preisvergleich anfängt, kann deshalb schon zu spät dran sein und riskiert zumindest, einen Teil der Angebote auszulassen.
Eine Untersuchung hat außerdem ergeben, dass immer noch das Gros der Menschen in Deutschland Weihnachtsgeld erhält – Tarifbeschäftigte häufiger als außertarifliche und Menschen im Osten häufiger als im Westen (diese im Schnitt dafür etwas mehr). Und die Händler:innen bemühen sich folglich immer früher und vehementer darum, dass das zusätzliche Budget möglichst umfassend bei ihnen ausgegeben wird. Nicht nur Amazon, sondern auch einige andere Händler:innen haben die Frist, in der die Ware gegebenenfalls zurückgeschickt werden kann, bis in den Januar pauschal erweitert, um frühe Weihnachtseinkäufe nicht zu behindern.
Was ist beim Black Friday 2026 anders?
Interessante Preisnachlässe und Rabattaktionen gibt es auch 2026 – nur sollte man sich von den Prozentzahlen nicht blenden lassen. Die Preissuchmaschine Idealo hat die Preise von 10.000 besonders gefragten Produkten untersucht. Am Black Friday 2025 waren demnach 79 Prozent günstiger als im Oktober. Die durchschnittliche Ersparnis lag allerdings bei lediglich acht Prozent. Nur etwa jedes achte untersuchte Produkt war um mindestens 20 Prozent reduziert. Bei Smartphones fiel die durchschnittliche Ersparnis sogar noch kleiner aus.
Das bedeutet aber auch, dass ein Preis, der mit „40 Prozent Rabatt“ beworben wird, noch lange nicht deutlich günstiger sein muss als anderswo. Denn die Rabatte beziehen sich häufig auf Vergleichspreise, etwa eine unverbindliche Preisempfehlung. Auch wenn Händler bei der Werbung mit eigenen Preisermäßigungen bestimmte Vorgaben einhalten müssen, ersetzt das keinen unabhängigen Preisvergleich. Dazu gehört aber auch eine Regel, die in Deutschland vorsieht, dass Händler als Vergleichspreis im Sinne der Transparenz aufzeigen müssen, wie der Artikel in den letzten 30 Tagen bepreist war.
Online-Marketing-Expert:innen erklären, dass es durchaus in diesem Jahr ähnlich gute Angebote geben wird, wie die Kund:innen es gewohnt sind – und das deckt sich auch mit unseren Beobachtungen im Handel und in den einschlägigen Foren. Denn die Erwartungshaltung der Kund:innen, die immer häufiger Kaufentscheidungen aufschieben, sorgt dafür, dass rund um die Black Week viele Shops besonders offensiv um die Kundschaft kämpfen.
Diese 10 Tipps können dir helfen, um Sonderangebote zu finden
Was kann man als Kunde oder Kundin tun, um sich auf Black Friday, den Cyber Monday und die Cyber Week vorzubereiten? Auch in diesem Jahr heißt es: Preise langfristig beobachten, Angebote vergleichen und sich nicht aus der Ruhe bringen lassen. Mehr Hilfestellung liefern unsere 10 Black-Friday-Tipps:
1. Vorab entscheiden, was du wirklich kaufen willst
Am Black Friday selbst ist bekanntermaßen nicht unbedingt das beste Angebot interessant, sondern das beste Angebot für ein Produkt, das du ohnehin haben möchtest. Du solltest daher vorab eine Wunschliste machen und festlegen, was die Geräte oder Artikel höchstens kosten dürfen. Gerade bei Technik lohnt es sich außerdem, vorher Tests und Kundenbewertungen zu lesen und die Unterschiede zwischen den Modellen zu verstehen.
Allerdings musst du dich nicht auf jede Eigenschaft festlegen. Eine andere Farbe, weniger Speicher oder das Vorjahresmodell können den Preis deutlich drücken, ohne dass du im Alltag viel davon merkst. Dagegen ist ein vermeintlich billigeres Gerät mit zu wenig Speicher oder einer schwächeren Ausstattung dann kein guter Kauf, nur weil ein großes Rabattetikett daran hängt. Auch wer flexibel ist und das Vorjahresmodell akzeptiert, kann reichlich Geld sparen.
2. KI-Assistenten als persönliche Schnäppchenscouts einsetzen
Insbesondere seit diesem Jahr können ChatGPT, Gemini und andere KI-Assistenten eine gute Anlaufstelle für die Recherche sein. Ähnlich wie du dich früher mit einem Verkäufer ausgetauscht hast, kannst du jetzt dialogbasiert recherchieren. Und die KI-Assistenten verfügen teilweise über bessere Waren- und Sortimentskenntnis als dies ein Verkaufsberater leisten kann. Lass dir etwa technische Alternativen zu einem teuren Wunschgerät nennen, die Unterschiede zwischen zwei Modellreihen erklären oder eine Liste von Angeboten nach Preis, Ausstattung und Folgekosten sortieren. Gerade wenn es zahlreiche unterschiedlich ausgestattete Produktvarianten eines Gerätes gibt, kannst du so schneller den Überblick gewinnen und erstaunlich viel Recherchezeit sparen.
Bei der Preisrecherche waren wir allerdings noch nicht immer mit den Ergebnissen der KI zufrieden. Bedenke auch, dass KI-Systeme Angebote verwechseln oder Produkte empfehlen können, die gar nicht mehr lieferbar sind. Kontrolliere Preis, Händler und Verfügbarkeit daher immer auf der tatsächlichen Shopseite – insbesondere unmittelbar vor dem Kauf.
3. Auch einen Blick auf Refurbished werfen
Lange Jahre war es verpönt, Gebrauchtware zu kaufen, doch spätestens seit der Entdeckung der Nachhaltigkeit als Wert im E-Commerce hat es sich bewährt, den Lebenszyklus von Produkten zu verlängern – und dabei gutes Geld zu sparen. Sowohl bei hochwertigen Smartphones (insbesondere aus dem Apple-Kosmos) als auch bei Notebooks und IT-Equipment kann es durchaus auch lohnenswert sein, sich ein Premium-Gerät mit entsprechend guter Verarbeitung in Refurbished-Qualität zu sichern.
Diskutieren kann man, ob solche Produkte gebraucht etwas für unter dem Weihnachtsbaum sind, für den eigenen Gebrauch passt das aber allemal – und gibt das gute Gefühl, gleichzeitig etwas fürs verantwortungsvolle Handeln und die Umwelt getan zu haben.
4. Produktherkunft überprüfen
Viele Händler:innen wissen inzwischen die Vorteile der Globalisierung für sich zu nutzen. Oftmals werden günstigere ausländische Varianten eines Gerätes importiert. Nicht nur bei kleineren Händler:innen findet man derartige Tricks. Während die sich in manchen Fällen überhaupt nicht vom deutschen Modell unterscheiden oder bestenfalls die Voreinstellungen (etwa bei Sendern) andere sind, ist es in anderen Fällen durchaus problematisch, etwa wenn Antennensysteme, Frequenzbereiche (Stichwort 5G-Bänder) oder die Firmware auf andere Gegebenheiten ausgerichtet sind. Auch kann es dann Probleme bei der Wahrnehmung der Garantie (nicht aber der Gewährleistung) geben.
5. Die 30-Tage-Regel kennen – und Streichpreise richtig lesen
Ein durchgestrichener Preis sieht zunächst eindrucksvoll aus, ist aber nicht automatisch der Betrag, den Kund:innen zuletzt tatsächlich bezahlt haben. Entscheidend ist daher, worauf sich die Rabattwerbung bezieht. Bei einer angekündigten Preisermäßigung muss ein Händler in Deutschland grundsätzlich den niedrigsten eigenen Gesamtpreis der letzten 30 Tage angeben. Das schreibt Paragraf 11 der Preisangabenverordnung vor. Für bestimmte Fälle gelten Ausnahmen.
Vergleiche diesen 30-Tage-Preis mit dem Aktionspreis und achte darauf, ob daneben eine unverbindliche Preisempfehlung (UVP) steht. Eine Ersparnis gegenüber der UVP kann riesig aussehen, obwohl das Produkt anderswo schon seit Monaten deutlich günstiger verkauft wird. Die 30-Tage-Regel bezieht sich zudem auf den betreffenden Händler, nicht auf den besten Preis im gesamten Markt. Den findest du weiterhin nur mit einem Preisvergleich heraus.
6. Nicht unter Druck setzen lassen
Bei Weitem nicht jedes Angebot ist attraktiv. Selbst an einem der Schnäppchentage lassen sich oft noch bessere Angebote finden. Als Kund:in solltest du dich nicht unter Druck gesetzt fühlen, sondern trotz des Hypes vergleichen, ob der gebotene Preis gut ist. Helfen können hier neben den bereits genannten Preisvergleichen von Idealo bis Geizhals auch Schnäppchenportale wie Mydealz, wo ausführlich über die jeweiligen Angebote diskutiert wird. Speziell an Amazon-Kund:innen richtet sich die Suchmaschine Camelcamelcamel, die gezielt Preisverläufe bestimmter Waren aufschlüsselt. Außerdem solltest du dir das Tool Keepa ansehen, mit dem du mit etwas Übung viel über Preisverläufe herausfinden kannst.
7. Angebote reservieren
Du willst dir einen guten Preis für ein paar Tage reservieren? Das geht in den meisten Fällen, wenn die Händler:innen Vorkasse etwa per Überweisung anbieten. Dann kannst du nämlich das Angebot kaufen und gegebenenfalls wieder per Widerruf freigeben, falls du doch noch ein besseres Angebot findest – und das, ohne dass die Händler:innen die Ware verschicken mussten. Unfair ist es dagegen, sich Ware „auf Halde“ schicken zu lassen und gleichzeitig auf die teilweise lange Rücksendemöglichkeit zu bauen. Das verursacht den Händler:innen unnötige Kosten (und ist schlecht fürs eigene Schnäppchenjäger:innenkarma).
Weiterer Nachteil: Du musst schlimmstenfalls nach Rücksendung auf dein Geld warten. Denn bei Bezahlung auf Rechnung läuft auch dann die Frist, wenn du die Ware wieder zurücksendest – und die Frist ist in der Regel nur 14 Tage, auch wenn du aufgrund der verlängerten Rücksendefrist deutlich mehr Zeit für deine Entscheidung hast.
8. Unbekannte Shops auf Fakes prüfen
Vor allem wenn ein Preis deutlich unter allen anderen Angeboten liegt, solltest du misstrauisch werden und genauer hinschauen. Denn Betrüger:innen locken mit täuschend echten Onlineshops und kassieren Geld für Ware, die dann geliefert wird. Ein professionelles Design, ein deutsches Impressum oder ein Gütesiegel allein sind kein Beweis für Seriosität. Übrigens nimmt das Problem gerade im KI-Kontext noch zu. Es sind bereits Fälle bekannt, in denen Fakeshops auch von LLMs empfohlen wurden. Besonders perfide ist dabei, dass die KI ja solche Angebote sehr überzeugend zu präsentieren weiß. Wer hier nicht genauer hinschaut, kann schnell ein Problem haben.
Kontrolliere deshalb Internetadresse, suche nach unabhängigen Erfahrungen und schaue nach, wer hinter dem Angebot steht. Hilfreich ist dafür auch der kostenlose Fakeshop-Finder der Verbraucherzentralen. Und wenn in der Kassenzone dann plötzlich nur noch Vorkasse per Überweisung möglich ist, ist besondere Vorsicht geboten. Du solltest daher generell bei unbekannten Anbietern möglichst eine Zahlungsart mit Käuferschutz einsetzen und sicherstellen, wohin die Ware gegebenenfalls zurückgesandt werden muss. Bei Auslandsshops kann ein vermeintlicher Bestpreis wertlos sein, wenn du das Geld am Ende nicht wiederbekommst oder erst mit hohen Kosten für den Rückversand in Vorleistung gehen musst.
9. Alternative Vertriebswege überprüfen
Ein Angebot ist beim Händler oder der Händlerin selbst ausverkauft? Das kann schnell gehen, gerade wenn Angebote stark beworben oder auf Angebotsplattformen wie Mydealz diskutiert werden. In vielen Fällen gibt es aber auch alternative Vertriebswege, etwa Ebay. So haben etwa auch viele große Handelsketten ihre Sonderangebote gleichzeitig auch bei Ebay verfügbar, um andere Kund:innenschichten anzusprechen. Schlechter fährst du dort übrigens auch nicht in Sachen Service – sondern hast sogar zusätzliche Bewertungsmöglichkeiten gegenüber dem oder der Händler:in.
Gerade bei den (ausverkauften) Angeboten größerer Ketten oder Händler:innen kannst du außerdem über Preisvergleichsportale prüfen, ob andere Händler:innen hier mitgehen. Hier kann sich auch der Gang zum Laden vor Ort lohnen, denn oftmals ziehen diese mit, wenn ein Angebot entsprechend vorgelegt werden kann.
10. Zusätzliche Rabatte erhalten
Zusätzlicher Rabatt gefällig? Das geht oftmals in Form von Kickback- und Cashback-Programmen aus dem Affiliate-Bereich, etwa via Shoop, oder beim Sammeln von Payback- und sonstigen Punkten. Diese lassen sich entweder gegen Sachpreise tauschen oder im besten Fall einfach als Geldprämie auszahlen. Du solltest daher vorab prüfen, welche Händler:innen entsprechende Affiliate-Programme unterstützen. Manchmal gibt es auch einen Neukund:innengutschein, den du bei einer Anmeldung vorab bekommst. Das geht übrigens nicht nur, wenn du dort noch nicht Neukund:in warst, sondern in manchen Fällen auch, wenn du dort länger nichts bestellt hast (oder über eine andere E-Mail-Adresse oder Kontoverbindung verfügst).
Prüfen solltest du auch, ob der Hersteller in bestimmten Zeiträumen eine Cashback-Aktion hat. Diese gelten zumeist für bestimmte Modellreihen oder Warengruppen, oftmals mit weiteren Bedingungen wie dem Upload des Kassenbelegs oder der Rechnung. Prüfe auch, ob bestimmte Händler:innen ausgeschlossen sind.

articles.title: Tech, defence, and life sciences are driving Edmonton’s economy: report | BetaKit
articles.text:
Tech, AI, life sciences, and defence and aerospace industries are outpacing the growth in Edmonton’s legacy industries, a new economic report from the Edmonton Chamber of Commerce shows.
The news: The Chamber of Commerce unveiled its 2026 State of the Economy Report on Wednesday, naming the tech, life sciences, and defence and aerospace industries as some of the city’s emerging economic drivers. The report credits those industries—which account for one in 50 jobs and just two percent of Edmonton’s overall GDP—as emergent for high wages, fast growth, and a sustainable path toward expansion.
From the source: “Every other cluster in this report earns its place by scale: hundreds of thousands of jobs, billions in output … the emerging three earn their place differently,” a portion of the report reads. “For industries this young, the more useful questions are how fast they’re moving and what’s pulling them forward. Measured that way, these three are the most dynamic part of the regional economy.”
The context: The Chamber’s state of the economy report is an annual economic analysis and policy report that evaluates performance, growth, and challenges to Edmonton’s regional economy. The 2026 report looks at the period between 2019 and 2025 and finds that wages across the three sectors average out around $94,480—much higher than the regional average of $67,784. Job growth and output also outpace the region’s other sectors, with jobs predicted to rise at a rate of nearly 10 percent against a wider seven-percent regional forecast.
Despite a rosy outlook on the future of tech in Edmonton, the report also finds that the city lags behind its peers in Calgary and the national average. The report calls these emerging sectors the region’s “least-claimed opportunity,” citing that the Edmonton region has less than half the concentration of these industries than does the rest of Canada. 
Final thought: Edmonton’s tech sector has its foundations in academic and research institutes like the University of Alberta or the Alberta Machine Intelligence Institute (Amii). It has historically been pigeonholed as a place where IP and technology is developed rather than commercialized. That dynamic is also at play in the Chamber’s report, where findings show that while talent has grown in the City, senior-level roles and business headquarters remain largely anchored elsewhere. In recent years, the City’s tech ecosystem has deliberately focused on trying to close the commercialization gap with programs designed to take research from the lab to the market. 
BetaKit’s Prairies reporting is funded in part by YEGAF, a not-for-profit dedicated to amplifying business stories in Alberta.
