articles.title: AI discovers a hidden heart signal that could predict sudden death
articles.text:
AI discovers a hidden heart signal that could predict sudden death
- Date:
- November 14, 2026
- Source:
- University of California - Berkeley
- Summary:
- Scientists have uncovered a hidden warning sign in routine heart scans that could predict sudden cardiac death before it strikes. The AI-powered discovery outperformed conventional screening methods, potentially revealing thousands of people at risk of a fatal heart malfunction that doctors might otherwise miss.
- Share:
More than 300,000 people in the United States die from sudden cardiac arrest each year. This deadly emergency occurs when the heart's electrical system suddenly fails, causing the heart to stop pumping blood. It can strike older adults with known heart conditions as well as seemingly healthy young athletes. Although implanted defibrillators can prevent some of these deaths, doctors have long struggled to determine which patients need them most.
Now, researchers at UC Berkeley have identified a previously overlooked warning signal in routine heart scans that could make it easier to recognize people at risk before a fatal event occurs.
The discovery was made using artificial intelligence trained on more than 440,000 electrocardiograms, or EKGs, collected in Sweden. By comparing the electrical patterns recorded in these scans with information from death certificates, the researchers taught an AI system to recognize subtle differences between healthy individuals, patients with known heart risks, and people who eventually died from sudden cardiac causes.
The team then evaluated the technology using thousands of additional patient records from the United States and Taiwan, testing whether the patterns could reliably identify people at heightened risk in different populations.
AI Detects Hidden Heart Risks That Standard Tests Miss
The results suggest that AI can identify vulnerable patients more effectively than the conventional tests doctors typically rely on. Current screening methods largely focus on how much blood the heart pumps with each contraction, a measurement used to assess whether someone might benefit from an implanted defibrillator.
Using these traditional measurements, doctors can identify a group of patients with an annual sudden cardiac death rate of 4.6%. The AI system, however, identified a group with an annual death rate of 7%, demonstrating a greater ability to distinguish patients facing serious danger.
Importantly, the algorithm also recognized a broader population of people at elevated risk, including thousands who would not normally raise concerns under existing medical guidelines. Most of these individuals would have been classified as relatively low risk using conventional methods.
Another major advantage is that the AI system works with ordinary EKG images, which are already routinely collected in hospitals and medical centers around the world. This means the technology could potentially improve screening without requiring an entirely new type of medical test.
The findings, published in Nature, could eventually help physicians make more informed decisions about who should receive an implanted defibrillator. They also raise an intriguing scientific question about what changes inside the heart produce the electrical patterns that AI has learned to recognize.
"Medical decisions are really hard, and I think that's why AI is so exciting for me," said Ziad Obermeyer, an associate professor at UC Berkeley's School of Public Health and the study's lead author. "We can not only make better decisions, but also start to understand what's actually going on with these patients before their heart stops."
Why Sudden Cardiac Death Is So Difficult to Predict
Sudden cardiac arrest is different from a heart attack. A heart attack happens when blood flow to part of the heart becomes blocked or severely restricted. Cardiac arrest, by contrast, results from a failure of the electrical signals that coordinate the heartbeat.
Immediate CPR and an electrical shock from an automated external defibrillator can sometimes restore the heart's rhythm. However, roughly 90% of people who experience sudden cardiac arrest outside a hospital die within minutes, making early recognition of those at risk especially important.
For Obermeyer, an emergency physician whose research combines artificial intelligence, medicine, and health policy, sudden cardiac death remains one of medicine's most frustrating unsolved problems.
Because victims often die without warning, researchers have limited opportunities to observe what happens inside the heart immediately before it stops. An autopsy may uncover blocked blood vessels, hardened tissue, or other structural abnormalities, but it cannot fully reveal how the heart was functioning in the moments leading up to death.
"One thing that makes the problem very tragic, but also very well suited for AI, is that we have the cure for this problem," Obermeyer said. "If you knew you were one of the people who was going to drop dead, you would go to a cardiologist and you'd get a defibrillator implanted. The problem is that doctors can't figure out who needs one before it's too late."
The Problem With Current Heart Risk Screening
Doctors currently rely heavily on a measurement of how effectively the heart pushes blood out with each beat. Patients whose hearts pump below a specified threshold may be considered candidates for an implantable cardioverter defibrillator, a device that can deliver an electrical shock when a dangerous heart rhythm develops.
But obtaining this measurement generally requires a more extensive medical evaluation. Many people who eventually experience sudden cardiac arrest never receive such testing because they have no obvious reason to suspect they are in danger.
The approach also has limitations for patients who are identified as high risk. About two-thirds of implanted defibrillators in these patients never need to deliver a shock. As a result, many individuals undergo expensive, invasive procedures for potentially fatal emergencies that may never occur.
At the same time, thousands of people who are not recognized as being at risk die unexpectedly each year.
"In some fraction of those people, we could have prevented those deaths if we had just known it in time," Obermeyer said. "There are a lot of lives being lost from people who are dropping dead of sudden cardiac death that are preventable if we just had better AI tools to find these things."
The researchers hope that identifying more accurate warning signs could help doctors direct preventive treatments toward the patients most likely to benefit.
How Researchers Trained AI to Recognize Deadly Heart Patterns
Developing the algorithm required three independent collections of medical data gathered from different parts of the world.
The researchers began with six years of EKG recordings from Sweden's unified healthcare system. By linking these scans to death certificates, they could examine the electrical patterns of patients who later experienced sudden cardiac death and compare them with those of other patients.
The AI learned to identify combinations of spikes, waves, and other characteristics in the recordings that appeared to be associated with increased risk. Once the system had been trained, the team tested it against two additional datasets: two years of anonymized EKG records from a San Diego hospital system and a separate collection of patient data from Taipei.
This international testing helped researchers evaluate whether the algorithm's predictive abilities extended beyond the Swedish population used to develop it.
"Good AI starts with good data," said Obermeyer, who is also part of the joint UCSF-UC Berkeley Computational Precision Health program. "Unfortunately, data like the ones we used for this study are incredibly hard to access. It's a big part of why there's so little clinical AI in use today."
Obtaining and organizing the information was itself a massive undertaking. According to Obermeyer, assembling the datasets took approximately 10 years and involved contributions from two organizations he helped establish, Dandelion Health and Nightingale Open Science. Both organizations work to advance medical research through better access to data and artificial intelligence.
"It's one of the tremendous luxuries of being at Berkeley," Obermeyer said. "You can pursue these projects that just are a slow burn and then have -- hopefully -- a big return when they get over the finish line."
From Hidden Heart Signals to Lifesaving Treatments
The researchers have already begun exploring how the system might be used in actual healthcare settings.
Obermeyer is collaborating with medical systems in Sweden, Taiwan, and the United States to introduce the algorithm into hospital EKG databases. The goal is to examine existing heart scans for signs of elevated risk and identify patients who may benefit from additional monitoring.
Under the proposed approach, physicians would contact patients whose EKGs receive a high-risk assessment and offer them the opportunity to wear a patch that continuously records their heart's electrical activity.
These longer recordings could provide valuable clues about the biological processes responsible for the warning signals detected by the AI. Understanding those processes could help researchers explain why certain hearts are more vulnerable to suddenly developing fatal electrical disturbances.
For some patients, the additional information might ultimately support a recommendation to receive an implanted defibrillator, potentially preventing a sudden and otherwise unexpected death.
Obermeyer has also created a website where people interested in learning about their own risk can provide basic personal information and an email address. The research team can then contact them about EKG analysis when the technology becomes more widely available.
Could AI Reveal New Secrets About the Human Heart?
Beyond its potential to improve the prevention of sudden cardiac death, the discovery highlights how artificial intelligence could help scientists investigate medical mysteries that have resisted conventional approaches.
Rather than simply identifying patients who might need treatment, the algorithm has uncovered patterns in heart activity that researchers do not yet fully understand. Studying those signals could lead to new insights into the electrical disturbances responsible for sudden cardiac death and potentially reveal additional opportunities for prevention.
Obermeyer believes this ability to uncover previously unrecognized biological patterns could become one of AI's most important contributions to medicine, opening new directions for research while helping physicians make better decisions.
"There is also going to be a new way of doing science that comes out of these tools," Obermeyer said, "and it's fun to think about how that starts happening."

articles.title: StepSecurity Secures $20 Million to Expand Supply Chain Protection
articles.text:
Supply chain security startup StepSecurity has raised $20 million in a Series A funding round, which brings the total raised by the company to $23 million.
The new investment round was led by Elephant, with additional support from Runtime Ventures, Inner Loop Capital, and SaaS Ventures.
Founded in 2021, Seattle-based StepSecurity has built a platform that combines developer-machine protection, repository checks, a hosted upstream proxy and policy gate, and a CI/CD security agent to identify and block malicious components.
According to the company, its platform can secure every stage of the software development process, including developers’ systems, AI coding agents, repositories, package registries, and CI/CD runners.
The startup offers a free community tier of its CI/CD runtime security agent Harden-Runner, already used by over 20,000 open source projects, which now also integrates a free Secure Registry proxy and policy gate tier to help open source maintainers block compromised packages.
StepSecurity will use the fresh funding to accelerate the development and distribution of its platform by growing its engineering team, enhancing the security research team’s capabilities, and expanding go-to-market efforts.
“We believe independent controls at all control points in agentic software pipelines are the strongest defense for agentic software development,” said StepSecurity co-founder and CTO Ashish Kurmi.
“We have seen our customers adopt one product, find value, and ask us to protect the next part of their development process. This funding gives us the resources to respond faster,” Kurmi added.

articles.title: Brasil concentra ataque que roubou dados de um milhão de cartões
What Canadian startups risk when they rely on a single AI provider | BetaKit
articles.text:
As Canadian startups race to integrate AI into their products and services, many are relying on third-party models and infrastructure to power their businesses.
These technologies can help companies develop products faster and with fewer upfront costs, but they also introduce risks that may become difficult to manage as those businesses grow.
“A lot of startups are wiring their entire product to one AI provider and treating that as a permanent decision.”
LSP, Zoho Canada
AI model providers can raise prices, change their terms of service, or introduce competing products of their own. For startups that have built their businesses around a particular provider, those decisions can threaten profit margins, undermine their competitive advantage, and leave them facing costly technical challenges.
Chandrashekar Lalapet Srinivas Prasanna, known as LSP, the managing director of Zoho Canada, worries that startups are becoming increasingly vulnerable to decisions made by their technology suppliers.
“You end up competing against the company that supplies a core part of your product,” LSP said. “That’s difficult if most of what you offer is an interface or a light workflow on top of their model, because they can often ship something similar with better economics.”
According to LSP, startups building products around third-party AI models risk losing control over their operating costs and product development. He believes founders need to consider those dependencies before they become too expensive to undo.
When the supplier calls the shots
A June report from RBC noted that three US tech companies now account for 85 percent of Canada’s cloud infrastructure spending. In its National Artificial Intelligence Strategy, Canada’s federal government warned that Canadian businesses building on technology largely controlled outside the country are “competing on infrastructure they do not own, govern, or meaningfully influence.”
“A lot of startups are wiring their entire product to one AI provider and treating that as a permanent decision,” LSP said. “It feels smart in the moment because you move faster and spend less on engineering. The problem shows up later.”
LSP’s concern is vendor lock-in, where a company becomes so dependent on one technology supplier that switching to another becomes difficult or expensive. As startups develop their products, their prompts, data retrieval systems, and methods for evaluating AI performance can become closely tied to the requirements of a particular model.
“If your context structures, evaluation tests, and tool abstractions are already locked to one provider’s formats, you will only discover how expensive it is to leave when you actually need to leave,” he said.
Vendor lock-in also carries financial risks. LSP warned that higher supplier costs could erode a startup’s profit margins, particularly if switching would be prohibitively expensive. He also questioned how startups can protect their competitive advantage when their core technology can be accessed by competitors.
“An interface that just calls the same model everyone else can call is hard to defend,” LSP added. “Investors notice when the core capability can be replicated by competitors or by the model provider itself.”
The price of true independence
Zoho has taken a relatively expensive route to technological independence. The company, which offers a suite of cloud software applications for businesses, operates data centres in multiple regions, including Canada, and has invested in developing its own AI models rather than relying entirely on third-party providers. The strategy gives Zoho greater control over its infrastructure and the direction of its products.
“Owning the relevant parts of the stack gives us the ability to adapt without being forced into someone else’s timeline or terms,” LSP said.
But operating data centres requires significant investment in physical infrastructure and technical staff. Zoho also accepts that competitors using external models can sometimes introduce new capabilities faster.
“The biggest trade-off is the sustained investment in capital, people, and time,” LSP explained.
What to own, what to outsource
Most startups don’t have the resources to build their own technology stacks, and LSP acknowledged that total independence is unrealistic even for established software companies. His advice is to identify which parts of a product are worth retaining control over, and which can be outsourced without creating an excessive dependence on a single supplier.
For Canadian startups, Zoho offers one way to reduce that dependence without having to build their own infrastructure. According to LSP, Zoho’s ownership of its AI models and underlying infrastructure makes customers less vulnerable to disruptions when outside providers change their pricing, policies, or access terms.
“The point isn’t to avoid external technology. It’s to make sure you still own the knowledge and the decision rights that let you adapt while the models keep changing.”
LSP, Zoho Canada
“Controlling where your data is stored is no longer enough,” LSP said. “Businesses also need to know who controls the models and infrastructure that process it. Zoho owns both layers and has never sold customer data.”
For startups developing their own products, LSP believes external AI models and infrastructure can still play an important role, provided their software is designed to accommodate another provider. Still, he encouraged founders to calculate the cost of switching while they still have the ability to do so.
LSP suggests starting by considering what would happen if their provider changed its terms tomorrow. Could they continue operating and improving their products? Could they move their data retrieval systems and AI performance tests to another provider, or would doing so require extensive engineering work?
He also encouraged startups to consider what information they’re sharing with their suppliers, including usage patterns and corrections that help improve AI systems. Retaining control over that knowledge, he argued, is essential to building a business that can adapt as the underlying technology changes.
“The point isn’t to avoid external technology,” LSP said. “It’s to make sure you still own the knowledge and the decision rights that let you adapt while the models keep changing.”

articles.title: DDR6 RAM shrinks by 44% while delivering 4X DDR5's baseline bandwidth — JEDEC previews 12.8 GT/s modules with up to 1 terabyte of capacity per slot
articles.text:
DDR6 RAM shrinks by 44% while delivering 4 times more bandwidth than DDR5 — JEDEC previews 12.8 GT/s modules with up to 1 terabyte of capacity per slot
Today's best RAM will look huge compared to upcoming DDR6 memory. JEDEC has just released a preview of the DDR6 specification, confirming that next-generation memory modules will be 44% shorter than DDR5. That is only the physical aspect, though. From a performance perspective, DDR6 will debut at 12.8 GT/s, more than double DDR5's baseline transfer rate, while also quadrupling the memory bandwidth per memory module thanks to a new design.
JEDEC's DDR6 preview highlights improvements in various areas, including performance, capacity, reliability, and power efficiency. These advancements align with the upgrades DDR5 brought to the table when it launched.
One of the most notable differences is that DDR6 memory modules will measure just 74mm in length, 44% shorter than DDR5’s 133mm memory modules. This makes DDR6 only 6% longer than DDR5 SO-DIMM modules, which you commonly find in laptops and mini-PCs.
JEDEC has maintained the pin count for many years, sticking to 288 pins for DDR4 and DDR5. However, DDR6 may finally break that mould. Given the substantial reduction in length with DDR6 and the data bus width upgrade, it is reasonable to assume that DDR6 will have a completely different pinout and density. Sadly, JEDEC has not revealed the pin count for DDR6.
Early rumors suggested that DDR6 may be limited to CAMM form factors to feed the AI boom. However, JEDEC's announcement at least does not rule out other form factors. It appears JEDEC is still determining which form factors DDR6 will use. Potential options include RDIMM, UDIMM, and CAMM formats, just like DDR5.
DDR6 Specifications
| Header Cell - Column 0 | DDR6 | DDR5 | DDR4 | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Baseline JEDEC Transfer Rates (MT/s) | 12,800 | 4,800 | 1,600 | 
| Baseline JEDEC Bandwidth Per Module (GB/s) | 153.6 | 38.4 | 12.8 | 
| Peak JEDEC Transfer Rates (MT/s) | 14,400 | 9,200 | 3,200 | 
| Peak Baseline Bandwidth Per Module (GB/s) | 172.8 | 73.6 | 25.6 | 
| Channels | 4 x 24-bit | 2 x 32-bit | 1 x 64-bit | 
| Burst Length | ? | BL16 | BL8 | 
| Banks | 64 | 32 | 16 | 
| Nominal Operating Voltage (V) | ? | 1.2 | 1.1 | 
| Pins | ? | 288 | 288 | 
| Length (mm) | 74 | 133 | 133 | 
Notably, JEDEC has increased the data bus width in DDR6 to 96 bits, a 50% boost over DDR5's 64 bits. The channel architecture for DDR6 will also change substantially. While DDR4 and DDR5 leveraged a single 64-bit channel and two 32-bit sub-channels, DDR6 takes a different approach. JEDEC will implement a design with four 24-bit sub-channels.
Using the baseline for comparison, DDR6 offers up to 153.6 GB/s of total module bandwidth, compared to DDR5's 38.4 GB/s. That is a 4X uplift in bandwidth. If we compare DDR5-9200 RDIMMs, which max out at 73.6 GB/s per module, with DDR6-12800 RDIMMs, the uplift is a little more than double.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
At least on the server side, DDR6 RDIMMs will start at DDR6-12800, whereas DDR5 RDIMMs topped out at DDR5-9200. JEDEC anticipates DDR6 reaching DDR6-14400 and beyond. This is for the server and enterprise market, though. It remains to be seen which DDR6 speed will launch in the consumer market. DDR5 commenced at DDR5-4800.
DDR6 may be shorter than DDR5, but it makes up for it by having 2X the bank count. This will help push higher data rates and capacities. DDR6 will support 128Gb (16GB) dies, which represents a massive leap. We are looking at 4X the density of early DDR5 memory modules. Instead of placing chips side by side on the PCB, DDR6 enables die stacking, allowing manufacturers to place multiple dies on top of each other via Through-Silicon Vias (TSVs).
Consumer DDR5 memory modules currently sit at 64GB per module, while server RDIMMs have reached 512GB. DDR6 could raise module capacity to 128GB or 256GB and potentially scale RDIMMs to 1TB or more per slot.
DDR6 has no official launch date. Many believe 2029 is a realistic target for commercialization. However, in the current state of things, it would be a miracle if DDR6 had no setbacks.
Download the Tom's Hardware app for up-to-the-minute updates on iOS and Android. Also follow Tom's Hardware on Google News, or add us as a preferred source, to get our latest news, analysis, & reviews in your feeds.
Zhiye Liu is a news editor, memory reviewer, and SSD tester at Tom’s Hardware. Although he loves everything that’s hardware, he has a soft spot for CPUs, GPUs, and RAM.

articles.title: I'm find the coolest GTA 6 secrets, tips and reactions live on launch day — for people like me who have to work instead of playing
articles.text:
Live
GTA 6 secrets, tips and reactions live on launch day — auto save confusion, surprising animal encounters, alternative ways to play, and funny videos
It's finally here — here are the most interesting things people are discovering already
GTA 6 is here, after a decade of waiting and high expectations — and (thankfully) it's absolutely awesome. Millions of people have been diving into Vice City since midnight, but obviously not everyone is actually able to spend all day playing right away.
So I'm here to help you live GTA 6 vicariously — I'm going to collect the most interest launch day reactions from people around the internet. I'll highlight easter eggs, secrets, early tips, fun videos and anything else to ease the pain of people who can't visit Leonida yet.
And because it's Black Friday, I've also picked out a bunch of deals on accessories to elevate your GTA 6 experience.

LIVE: Latest Updates
Yes, there are easter eggs
Some are quite literal. If you don't want to be spoiled just know that to get see the easter egg below you need to climb a radio tower. If you're happy to just see what's there, then here you go.
Get the most from your fancy TV
Screen technology expert (and occasional drinking buddy of mine…) Vincent Teoh has some advice on making sure the game looks as good as it can on your TV, and it's all about how the smart processing on the latest sets handles HDR.
It's easy to accidentally set the HDR output of the game in a way that causes things to look washed out once the TV then attempts to compensate for what it things the HDR should look like. But there's a solution…
A bunch of good tips
This thread on X has a bunch of good tips. The summary is:
1. You can always find your next mission using the mission list on the Map screen, so don't panic if doesn't show up automatically.
2. You can use the RydeMe app on the phone to instantly travel around the map (or you can actually watch the ride).
3. You lose the cash you're carrying if you get Wasted or arrested, but you can use the baking app on the phone to find an ATM and deposit it, which keeps it safe.
4. You can play non-lethally, which can affect how the game plays out.
5. Hold down on the d-pad to choose nearby locations and objectives super-quickly, so you don't always have to dive into the map.
6. If you get stuck miles away from your favorite car, you can use the Scooter Bros. app on the phone to get it delivered to you.
7. GTA fans will obviously guess this already: but if you steal a cool car you want to keep, you can 'Register' it at a Pay 'N' Spray.
The saving situation
There seems to be some confusion over how saving works in GTA 6, so if you haven't started playing yet, it's probably worth getting a grip on what to expect.
GTA 6 uses a mix of sporadic auto saves (ie, don't just rely on them), and manual saving. It'll auto save after every mission, or when you have some kind of big encounter in the open world (including if you get Wasted, or get arrested).
But that's it. Otherwise, you need to manually save, and you only have 15 slots, so you won't be able to just constantly branch out into a new save slot so you can go back to any point.
Oh, and most importantly, you can't save during missions. It seems that Rockstar wants you to have a fully immersive experience. It should support the console's Rest mode, saving where you are as long as no one else turns it on to play on their accounts, so that's your best bet if you need to take a break during a big scripted mission.
Surprise attack
I'm not really sure how many cars to expect will have cats in, but it'll certainly an extra thrill to a tense getaway…
An early loot tip
This video gives a recommendation on a early impressive haul you'll want to pick up — including a collectible card that's worth loads a pawn shop. Something to keep in mind if you haven't started playing yet…
Games on film
Unsurprisingly, given the graphical fidelity, it looks like people are really enjoying the game's Photo Mode.
Be careful what you press on piers
An innocent bird-watching day may rapidly turn into an altercation.
Avoiding arrest
You perhaps don't have to shoot your way out of every single encounter with the police. This video shows that stashing your guns away can diffuse the situation, if you want to go in more a simulation direction when you're playing.
Of course, none of that matters if the plane is simply too stubborn to explode…
Explosive opinions
It seems like people are torn over plane explosions. One poster is shocked at the size of them, one is disappointed in the realism. Personally, I think they look a little too fireworky, but I doubt I'll care if I'm in the middle of doing the coolest stuff I've ever done in game.
Paint the town beige
You know, I wasn't expecting to see a wall painting simulation outside of, like, WarioWare. I guess if you find games as boring as watching paint dry, then this won't change your mind…
Now that's what I call doggy paddle
Videos with silly stuff are starting to appear, and this is easily one of my favorites. The good stuff lands about 18 seconds in.
Crash course
Someone did a comparison of a car crash in GTA 6 with a similar crash in GTA 4. I gotta say, I'm not against the zaniness of the GTA 4 physics! Sometimes you just want to exit the car really fast.
Let us know if you're seeing the framerate dips
If you've been playing, are you experiencing the framerate dips? Let us know below!
Avoid the dead zones
One of the comments on the last tip says there's a much more pressing option to change if you want the game to feel more responsive: change the dead zones in the controller settings.
Games tend to ignore the first little bit of motion you apply to the thumbsticks, because if they didn't, you'd get loads of annoying twitching when your thumbs move a little, and small mistakes while you correct your movement. This is the dead zone, and the larger the dead zone is, the more motion is ignored.
Some people are saying the dead zone is too big by default in GTA 6, so you have to move the sticks a lot before the game responds, so it feels sluggish. You can change it, though, so maybe it's worth giving it try!
This isn't the same as the framerate dropping, but could be mistaken for it: one Reddit user says they stopped some choppiness by changing a few settings on their PS5. (Though I should note that if you turn off HDCP, you won't be able to use your PS5 for streaming or Blu-rays.)
PC vs console
The performance question has even divided the PC community. Some are saying they're glad PC players will be getting a later more optimized version (they hope…), but others are pushing back and saying that it's not really a big concern given how revolutionary the world is.
Framerate frustrations?
Speaking of motion, there is generally a bit of negative feedback early on to the game around the framerate dips. We knew Rockstar Games was aiming for 30fps even on PS5 Pro, but it looks like the game is regularly dipping below that on the base PS5 when there's action on-screen. And the action is the juice here, right?
To blur, or not to blur
The first big tip: disable motion blur! Or… maybe not? This seems like it's going to be a debate early on. Quite a few people are recommending disabling motion blur to really be able to see the beauty of the game — but others are saying that keeping it on is essential on OLED TVs (which have pixels that refresh in a different way to LCD screens).
Hello folks! Welcome to the first day of a post-GTA 6 world. People have had hours overnight to play the game and start to find its many quirks and secrets — but not all of us. I sit here in an office, far away from my PS5, so this blog is for people in the same situation who want to see all the cool things people have been doing.

articles.title: FCC greenlights rule allowing prisons to jam cellphone signals
articles.text:
The Federal Communications Commission voted unanimously to allow state and local prisons to jam cellphones. In an announcement on Thursday, the FCC argues the rule will help combat an “influx of contraband cellphones” used to carry out crimes from prison.
FCC greenlights rule allowing prisons to jam cellphone signals
The FCC passed the rule despite warnings that jammers could block lawful communications, like 911 calls.
Jammers are generally banned under Section 333 of the Communications Act of 1934, though they’re used at some federal facilities. FCC Chair Brendan Carr claims that giving correctional facilities access to this technology will help prevent prisoners from using phones for illegal activity. “These devices [phones] are being used by inmates to order hits, run drug operations, traffic women and children, and unleash mayhem on our communities from behind bars,” Carr says.
In the months leading up to the vote, trade groups and human rights advocates have raised concerns about the risks of blocking cellphone signals in prisons. The US Chamber of Commerce and the CTIA, a wireless association representing the nation’s biggest carriers, have both warned in letters to the FCC that jamming technology could disrupt lawful communications outside prisons, including 911 calls. Meanwhile, the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) has long argued that cellphones can keep prisoners safe by allowing them to document safety and human rights issues that the outside world may not see.
FCC Commissioner Anna Gomez, the sole Democrat on the Commission, voted for the measure despite the risk of “potential unintended consequences,” according to the Associated Press. “I want to make sure that we don’t harm public safety in the name of helping public safety,” Gomez added.
The FCC says prisons that choose to jam cellphone signals will need to obtain a license, adhere to “technical standards and testing requirements,” and ensure that the jamming technology doesn’t interfere with communications outside the facility. Prisons must also notify nearby communities of testing and when the technology is being deployed.

articles.title: What Is Driving Silicon Wafer Demand Recovery?
articles.text:
The high number of new and upcoming production lines is a unique factor influencing this particular cycle.
Global silicon wafer shipments are forecast to grow 11.8% in 2026, according to the Q3 2026 SEMI Silicon Wafer Market Monitor. This increase is primarily due to strong demand for AI, which is projected to drive shipments through 2029.
Alongside AI, rising process material sales are also supporting recovery. The positive correlation between material sales and silicon wafer demand not only reflects growth in manufacturing complexity, but it also points to greater material consumption per wafer.
Finally, increases in memory demand, precautionary inventory building, and global fab capacity expansions are boosting silicon wafer shipments as well.
To better understand today’s landscape, it’s helpful to revisit past silicon wafer demand curves. From 2018 to 2019 and from 2022 to 2023, silicon wafer shipments rose ahead of major increases in memory work-in-process (WIP) inventories, or unfinished memory chips undergoing fabrication. However, shipments lagged at the same time WIP inventory peaked. Because fabrication lines were already producing at full capacity, their need for silicon wafers slowed.
While this pattern provides historical context for today’s demand recovery, the high number of new and upcoming production lines is a unique factor influencing this particular cycle.
Silicon Wafer Shipments and Memory WIP: Historical Lead–Lag Pattern. Both series use four-quarter moving averages. Sources: SEMI SMG and financial disclosures from Samsung Electronics, SK hynix, and Micron. Data for 3Q26–2Q27 are forecasts.
SEMI’s fab investment outlook predicts continued growth in planned equipment spending beyond 2026. So long as investment plans remain broadly on track, ongoing equipment installation and capacity ramps are likely to support silicon wafer demand. The report also demonstrated a widening gap between YoY growth rates for semiconductor fab equipment spending and silicon wafer manufacturing equipment spending, suggesting that investment support for wafer demand may persist longer than initially expected.
This also helps explain why the historical relationship between wafer shipments and WIP does not necessarily imply an imminent slowdown. Wafer procurement momentum can moderate before WIP inventories peak, although investment support may slow if moderation becomes visible in wafer shipments.
Investment Spread: A Signal of a Later Wafer-Cycle Slowdown. Spread between the YoY growth rates of semiconductor fab equipment spending and silicon wafer manufacturers’ equipment spending, compared with silicon wafer shipment trends. Sources: SEMI Silicon Wafer Shipment Statistics and SEMI WWSEMS. Shipment data are updated through 2Q26, while equipment spending data are updated through August 2026.
SEMI projects continued wafer shipment growth in 2027, although growth will likely be more moderate than it was in 2026. As inventory stockpiles subside, ongoing production will be important for sustaining demand. If planned capacity expansions continue and customers buy the resulting chips, semiconductor companies can gradually reduce their wafer inventories while also maintaining their purchase rate. However, investment delays or weaker demand for semiconductors would slow this absorption and increase the risk of declining silicon wafer orders.
While AI-related investment is a critical source of support, broader semiconductor recovery is still uneven. Because of this, the key to maintaining demand growth will be how quickly fabs can use wafers purchased in advance. Doing so will help shape the duration of this recovery period and the depth of any subsequent wafer inventory adjustments.

articles.title: Nvidia Reports $115.8B in Quarterly Revenue Under Interim CEO - EE Times
articles.text:
Nvidia reported third-quarter revenue of $115.8 billion on Tuesday, more than twice its revenue in the same period last year. Cloud providers and tech giants kept buying its AI processors at a strong pace.
This was the first financial report under interim CEO Colette Kress, who took over after co-founder Jensen Huang resigned. The results show demand for Nvidia’s enterprise computing systems remains strong, even as the company faces leadership changes, a board investigation, and growing national security questions from Washington.
Rise in data center revenue
Nvidia’s third-quarter revenue rose 20% from the previous quarter and 103% from the $57.0 billion reported in the same period last year.
Most of the growth came from Nvidia’s Data Center business, which brought in $107.6 billion in sales, up 21% from the last quarter and 110% from a year ago. Gross margins stayed high, with a GAAP gross margin of 74.8% and a non-GAAP margin of 74.9%.
Operating income was $77.5 billion on a GAAP basis, up 115% from $36.0 billion a year ago. Net income grew to $65.3 billion, or $2.70 per diluted share, compared to $31.9 billion, or $1.30 per share, a year earlier. On a non-GAAP basis, net income was $64.9 billion, or $2.68 per diluted share. Nvidia generated $43.8 billion in free cash flow for the quarter, up from $22.1 billion in the same period last year.
Nvidia returned $28.1 billion to shareholders through share buybacks and dividends during the quarter. In September, the board had increased the company’s share repurchase authorization by $150 billion. At quarter-end, $227.3 billion remained available under the authorization. The board declared a quarterly cash dividend of $0.25 per share, payable on Dec. 23 to shareholders of record on Dec. 2.
Kress, who has served as Nvidia’s executive VP and CFO since 2013 and became interim CEO last week, said in the earnings release: “Our momentum is real. Nvidia is an exceptional technology leader, powered by the relentless innovation of our people. Vera Rubin is off to an explosive start, our roadmap is on track, and our ambition has never been greater.”
Vera Rubin ready for market adoption
The financial results came as Nvidia began ramping production of its next-generation Vera Rubin NVL72 rack-scale AI computing system and started shipping units to customers.
Nvidia said systems were already running at cloud providers including CoreWeave, Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, and Nebius. An installation was also underway with SpaceXSI.
Nvidia expanded its product lineup by shipping Vera CPUs, marking its first fully custom CPUs for data centers. Cloud platforms and AI developers such as Meta, OpenAI, Anthropic, AWS, and Verda have been using these custom processors with graphic accelerators to handle inference processing and automated agent tasks. For high-performance computing and complex simulations, Nvidia also introduced the Rubin HPC GPU.
The DSX POD reference design standardized how physical deployments are built, letting partners put together containerized data center modules that need less water cooling.
In networking, Nvidia rolled out more Spectrum-X Ethernet switches and BlueField-4 data processing units. The company also worked with Cisco on a new, higher-density optical transceiver called USFP.
Beyond hardware, Nvidia announced a deal to acquire Hugging Face, an open-source platform popular with AI researchers and software engineers.
Edge computing, PCs, and robotics
Outside of central data centers, Nvidia’s Edge Computing business brought in $8.2 billion in revenue for the quarter, up 14% from the previous quarter and 42% year over year.
RTX Spark laptops began shipping through partners including ASUS, Dell, HP, Lenovo, Microsoft Surface, and MSI.
For desktop software, Nvidia launched DLSS 5 graphics software for games. It also released a 64-GB DGX Spark personal system, supporting local execution of models from Liquid AI, Qwen, and Black Forest Labs locally.
Nvidia’s automotive and robotics segments had more deployments this quarter. Mercedes-Benz and Volvo Cars expanded their partnerships using Nvidia’s automated driving systems, and European logistics companies started testing commercial fleets built on the Hyperion vehicle platform.
The robotics division updated its Isaac platform tools to support human-sized robotic prototypes powered by Jetson Thor chips. It also worked with Nokia and T-Mobile on wireless infrastructure trials that use accelerated computing in cellular networks.
Jensen’s departure and reinstatement campaign
The company reported these results during a major management crisis. Huang resigned suddenly after internal investigations into extramarital relationships with a subordinate and an executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed International, which is under federal investigation for possibly diverting regulated semiconductor hardware.
On Nov. 17, Huang made his first public remarks since stepping down, expressing remorse while leaving the door open to a return as an executive. “I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at Nvidia, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life,” Huang said in a published statement. “If the board of directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”
A public petition called “Stand with Jensen” has collected over 202,000 signatures, including support from thousands of Nvidia employees. Industry leaders such as Elon Musk and Tim Sweeney have publicly backed Huang’s return, and shareholder groups led by Brad Gerstner of Altimeter Capital and Gavin Baker of Atreides Management sent open letters asking the board to keep all leadership options open.
As of Nov. 19, the Associated Press reported that Nvidia’s board had unanimously rejected Huang’s offer to return as CEO. Board chairman Harvey Jones said the company “unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.” Jones added, “We want to install the permanent CEO as quickly as possible, but we won’t expedite the CEO before finding exactly the right person.”
Governance and outlook
Governance experts noted that reversing his termination could cause compliance problems with upcoming government proceedings.
Huang has agreed to appear before congressional committees on Dec. 1 to answer inquiries concerning foreign interactions and export compliance, with Nvidia’s general counsel, Tim Teter, scheduled to appear the following day.
In response to the controversy, Nvidia’s board set up a special committee to oversee national security and export rules. The company has also started looking for a new permanent chief executive.
Looking ahead, Nvidia expects revenue of $130.0 billion, plus or minus 3%, for the fourth quarter of fiscal 2027, which includes an extra working week. Gross margins are expected to fall to between 71.0% and 72.0%, and operating expenses should be about $11.0 billion.
Because of current export controls, Nvidia’s guidance assumes no data center revenue from China.

articles.title: Black Friday: Warum die Rabattschlacht schon jetzt tobt
articles.text:
Warum der Black Friday mittlerweile schon Anfang November startet – und welches Kalkül der Händler dahintersteckt
Wir schauen auf den Kalender und reiben uns verwundert die Augen: Der Black Friday ist erst am 27. November – und doch wirbt gefühlt schon die halbe Branche mit dem Schnäppchen-Schlagwort, das die preisbewussten Kund:innen in Wallung bringen soll. Und die Geschäfte sind erfinderisch: Pre-Black-Friday-Angebote, Early-Black-Friday-Deals und Black Weeks sind nur ein paar der kreativen Wortschöpfungen, die allesamt nur eins suggerieren sollen: Billiger wird’s so schnell nicht mehr.
Man könnte fast glauben, der Handel hätte Angst, den Black Friday zu verpassen. Doch in Wahrheit laufen vor allem die Händler dem Geld ihrer Kund hinterher. Dass sie damit seit Jahren immer früher anfangen, hat einen Grund, der insbesondere in diesem Jahr eine große Rolle spielen könnte: Die Kund:innen können ihr Weihnachtsgeld, so sie es überhaupt noch bekommen, schließlich nur einmal ausgeben.
Und wer hier früher dran ist als die anderen, so das Kalkül, hat größere Chancen darauf. Wer also sein Budget bereits Anfang November bei Händler A gelassen hat, fällt Ende November womöglich als Kunde für Händler B aus.
Die Angst, zu früh gekauft zu haben
Doch gerade in wirtschaftlich angespannten Zeiten überlegen Verbraucher:innen genauer, wofür sie ihr Erspartes ausgeben. Schon länger beobachten Marktforscher:innen gar nicht mal so sehr eine Kaufzurückhaltung, wohl aber, dass die Verbraucher:innen bis zum November mit wichtigen Anschaffungen warten – wohl wissend, dass in dieser Zeit das Rennen um die Rabatte besonders ausgeprägt ist.
Eher neu ist hier aber neben der verlängerten Rückgabefrist bis in den Januar, mit der Amazon schon seit Jahren den Markt zum Mitziehen motiviert, ein weiterer Faktor: Immer mehr Händler:innen bieten automatisch oder auf Anfrage eine Bestpreis-Garantie für all jene, die sich jetzt für einen Kauf entscheiden. Die Idee dahinter: Wer heute kauft, soll sich in zwei Wochen nicht ärgern, wenn das gleiche Produkt am eigentlichen Black Friday plötzlich noch günstiger angeboten wird.
Dabei lohnt sich dennoch ein Blick ins Kleingedruckte, denn nicht bei allen Händlern bedeutet das, dass man automatisch davon profitiert. In einigen Fällen müssen Kund:innen selbst aktiv werden, den günstigeren Preis entdecken und die Differenz beim Kundenservice beantragen. Eine weitere Einschränkung: Während die Preisgarantie in vielen Fällen branchenweit gilt, bezieht sie sich manchmal auch lediglich auf die Preise beim selben Händler.
Aus Sicht der Logistik ein gutes Geschäft
Dass viele Händler:innen den Black Friday entzerren wollen, hat aber auch noch einen weiteren, durchaus vernünftigen Grund: die Logistik. Denn die letzten Jahre haben gezeigt, dass innerhalb weniger Tage Lager, Versanddienstleister und Kundenservice übermäßig strapaziert wurden. Auch können die Händler:innen so ihre Ads-Kampagnen über einen längeren Zeitraum ziehen, anstatt an einem einzigen Wochenende mit allen anderen um die Aufmerksamkeit der Kund:innen zu buhlen.
Aus dem Black Friday wird so eine Art vorweihnachtliche Dauerschleife der Kaufverführung. Noch sieht es nicht danach aus, dass die Händler:innen das Thema überreizt hätten, auch wenn das Risiko durchaus besteht, dass dabei die Aufmerksamkeit irgendwann auf der Strecke bleibt.
All das ist aus Sicht vieler Händler nachvollziehbar. Denn wer abwartet, bis die Mitbewerber ihre Rabattaktionen starten, muss nicht nur gegen deren Preise ankämpfen, sondern riskiert auch, dass viele potenzielle Kund:innen längst eingekauft haben und aus dem Rennen sind.

articles.title: Google offre YouTube Premium Famille à ses abonnés AI Ultra, mais il y a une condition
articles.text:
C’est Noël avant l’heure chez Google : le géant de la Tech inclut désormais YouTube Premium Famille dans les forfaits AI Ultra.
Que de changements pour les abonnements Google cette année ! La firme a entièrement revu ses tarifs au printemps dernier, au point d’en perdre plus d’un. Ses forfaits se sont dotés de Gemini Spark cet été, mais l’Europe ne faisait, hélas, pas partie des chanceux. Un peu plus tard, Gemini 4 Argon, qui était jusqu’alors réservé aux abonnés AI Ultra, est devenu disponible pour les membres AI Pro.
Cette semaine, Google était à nouveau d’humeur généreuse. On vous explique.
Les forfaits AI Ultra comprennent désormais YouTube Premium Famille
Jusqu’ici, AI Ultra proposait la version individuelle de YouTube Premium, ce qui était, avouons-le, un peu radin pour l’abonnement le plus onéreux du catalogue. Mais Google s’est enfin décidé à corriger le tir : « Nous sommes ravis d’annoncer que tous les nouveaux et anciens membres de Google AI Ultra des pays éligibles bénéficient d’une mise à niveau gratuite vers l'abonnement YouTube Premium Famille ! », annoncé le géant de la Tech dans une annonce parue il y a quelques heures.
La formule Famille de YouTube est donc disponible sans surcoût, et ce, sans que les abonnés n'aient rien à faire. Les nouveaux venus bénéficieront eux aussi automatiquement de ce beau geste.
Concrètement, si vous possédez un forfait AI Ultra, vous allez pouvoir faire profiter jusqu’à 5 personnes de votre foyer de YouTube, sans aucune annonce publicitaire. À eux donc les fonctionnalités premium, téléchargements hors connexion et lecture en arrière-plan compris. Ils devront cependant avoir plus de 13 ans pour profiter des largesses de Google.
Une condition essentielle à respecter
La formule Famille de YouTube Premium coûte aujourd’hui 29,99 € par mois et une hausse de prix est dans les tuyaux. En permettant à ses abonnés AI Ultra d’en faire profiter leurs proches, Google veut probablement fidéliser un peu plus ses utilisateurs, dans un contexte où la concurrence est particulièrement féroce. C’est aussi l’occasion pour la firme de se faire bien voir des familles.
- Grande diversité de contenus
- Monétisation pour les créateurs
- Accessibilité sur toutes les plateformes
Il y a toutefois une petite subtilité qui mérite d’être soulignée : « l’abonnement YouTube Premium Famille ne peut être partagé que si l’abonné Google AI Ultra est le gestionnaire de la famille », peut-on lire en bas de l’annonce. Tout le monde n’aura donc pas la main sur l’abonnement : si votre conjoint a créé le groupe et que vous souhaitez prendre sa place en tant que gestionnaire, il faudra réorganiser le groupe familial. Rappelons que Google impose une restriction de 12 mois pour créer ou rejoindre un nouveau groupe après la suppression du précédent.
Ceci étant dit, difficile de bouder un tel cadeau. Ce petit bonus devrait ravir les abonnés AI Ultra mais aussi inciter plus d’un utilisateur à sauter le pas.

articles.title: From pattern matching to governing intent: How Semantic DLP is securing enterprise Gen AI
articles.text:
NetApp Excellerator
View Brand Publisher
From pattern matching to governing intent: How Semantic DLP is securing enterprise Gen AI
Legacy DLP was built to catch patterns. It was not built to understand what employees paste into AI. Wald.ai, part of NetApp Excellerator’s Cohort 15, is teaching security to read intent.
A quiet tug-of-war is playing out in nearly every enterprise today. On one hand, engineers, financial analysts, legal teams, and operations staff are turning to generative and agentic AI to debug code, summarize contracts, and automate tasks and decision-making. On the other side, security and compliance leaders are racing to prevent proprietary source code, financial projections, and regulated customer records from leaking into unauthorized models.
For most Chief Information Security Officers (CISOs), the question is no longer whether employees are using AI; it is what they are pasting into it. Yet the security tools most organizations rely on to police this boundary were built for a completely different era.
Why legacy DLP fails in the GenAI era
Traditional Data Loss Prevention (DLP) systems were designed for structured data moving across predictable channels such as emails, file transfers, and cloud storage. They rely heavily on regular expressions (regex), keyword lists, and static rules. If a document contains a 16-digit credit card number or a government ID, legacy DLP flags it.
Generative AI breaks this model entirely. AI interactions happen in unstructured natural language, where data sensitivity is defined by context and intent rather than fixed formatting. Consider two scenarios:
- A software engineer pastes a snippet of proprietary authentication logic into an LLM and asks it to optimize the code.
- A strategy analyst uploads a paragraph describing an upcoming, unannounced product roadmap or M&A target to draft an executive summary.
Neither prompt contains a credit card number, a Social Security number, or a flagged keyword. To a regex-based DLP system, both interactions look completely benign. Conversely, when security teams tighten keyword rules to catch more nuances, false positives skyrocket, triggering alert fatigue for security teams and frustrating employees who are simply trying to do their jobs.
Faced with this visibility gap, many organizations initially defaulted to blunt-force bans on public AI tools. However, blocking AI only drives usage underground onto personal devices and unsanctioned accounts, multiplying “Shadow AI” risk while starving the enterprise of productivity gains.
The shift to semantic, context-aware security
As generative AI evolves from simple chat interfaces to complex, autonomous workflows including Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool calls and agent-to-agent communications, the enterprise attack surface is expanding across every endpoint and application. Securing this environment requires moving from pattern matching to semantic understanding.
At Wald.ai, we built our platform around a simple premise: to secure AI, your security layer must understand language as well as the AI itself.
Instead of scanning for static patterns, Semantic DLP evaluates the meaning, context, and intent behind every prompt and file upload. By deploying a specialized Small Language Model (SLM) directly on the employee’s endpoint, Wald.ai inspects and classifies AI interactions locally in milliseconds before sensitive data ever traverses the network or reaches an external AI server or provider.
This on-device, context-aware approach solves three critical enterprise challenges simultaneously:
1. Catching what Regex misses: Semantic models distinguish between an engineer pasting harmless open-source boilerplate and one exposing proprietary algorithms, or between general market research and confidential corporate strategy.
2. Eliminating alert fatigue: By disambiguating context in real time, organizations drastically reduce false positives, allowing security teams to focus on genuine exposure risks.
3. Enabling safe productivity at the endpoint: Rather than a binary “allow or block” posture, enterprises can enforce granular, real-time guardrails, automatically redacting, masking, or sanitizing sensitive entities within a prompt while preserving the context needed for the LLM to return a useful answer.
Real-world impact across regulated sectors
We are already seeing this playbook transform how regulated industries such as financial services, healthcare, and legal practices adopt AI. For instance, financial institutions and credit unions using Wald.ai have transitioned from restrictive AI policies to sanctioned, company-wide adoption.
Scaling enterprise AI governance with NetApp Excellerator
As enterprises mature in their AI journey, the boundary between data infrastructure and AI security is disappearing. Participating in Cohort 15 of the NetApp Excellerator program has been a pivotal milestone for Wald.ai as it scales contextual intelligence architecture for large enterprise environments.
Working alongside NetApp’s technology leaders and deep-tech ecosystem provided insights into how global enterprises architect, govern, and manage massive data estates across hybrid and cloud environments. Combining robust data infrastructure practices with real-time, endpoint semantic guardrails ensures that data remains protected from the storage layer all the way to the AI prompt.
The road ahead
The next wave of enterprise competitiveness will not be won by the companies that restrict AI, nor by those that deploy it recklessly. It will be won by organizations that build trust into their AI stack, replacing outdated, reactive compliance checks with intelligent guardrails that operate at the speed of conversation. When security understands context, enterprises no longer have to choose between innovation and data privacy.

articles.title: La reflexión del actor Maxi Iglesias sobre el trabajo: “Trabajamos para pagar cosas que no necesitamos”
articles.text:
Durante la promoción de una de sus películas ha habido una reflexión que me ha llamado la atención. Se trata de cuánto tiempo invertimos en nuestro trabajo y qué hacemos con el dinero obtenido. “Trabajamos para pagar cosas que no necesitamos”, dice Maxi Iglesias. Porque en este modo de gestionar nuestra vida siempre parece haber algo más que conseguir.
En la conversación, él mismo lo asocia a un problema de consumismo. Y para explicarlo utiliza la película “El club de la lucha” (David Fincher, 1999), protagonizada por Brad Pitt y Edward Norton.
Y en ella se asocia el hecho de ganar dinero con el de comprar cosas. De tal forma que si nuestras ambiciones materiales van en aumento, también tenemos que trabajar para ello. Es importante pararse a pensar en estas metas.
La obligación de sentirse productivo
Por otro lado, es relevante dejar claro que no hablamos de la vivienda. “Dejando el tema de la vivienda a un lado, somos muy autómatas en ese sentido, seguimos lo que el sistema nos ha dicho que hay que hacer: generar, producir, sentir que somos productivos, que hacemos y generamos”.
Hay que destacar esta idea de que tenemos que estar haciendo algo. Además de añadir metas a las anteriores. También es importante destacar que el problema está en que esperamos seguir creciendo sin saber dónde está el límite. “¿Hasta dónde se va a engordar la lista? ¿Hasta dónde se va a crecer?”, plantea.
Por otro lado, se puede reflexionar sobre el papel que tiene el trabajo en nuestra vida personal. Es importante repensar nuestras prioridades e incluso el tiempo que dedicamos a otras actividades sin recompensa económica inmediata.
Con el trabajo podemos satisfacer nuestras necesidades. Además, nuestro objetivo puede ser avanzar en nuestro ámbito profesional. Sin embargo, hay que tener cuidado con caer en el problema de ir añadiendo requisitos de manera inercial sin pararnos a pensar para qué sirven. “Lo llevo diciendo muchos años: esto en algún momento va a explotar”.

articles.title: Drupal patches critical RCE flaw, warns exploits may surface quickly
articles.text:
The Drupal Security Team has patched a critical remote code execution vulnerability that can let attackers take over vulnerable sites.
This content management system (CMS) is commonly used by large organizations that manage multi-site installations and massive data structures, including government entities, educational organizations, major research universities, and high-profile enterprise and media organizations.
The security flaw (tracked as CVE-2026-132165) was discovered by Anthropic's OSS Scanner, and anonymous users can exploit it to reinstall the Drupal CMS.
"Drupal core ships with an install.php file for installing Drupal core. Under specific conditions, an attacker can use the installer to attempt to reinstall Drupal. This can lead to a site takeover or remote code execution," the Drupal Security Team warned in a Wednesday advisory. "Some exploit paths are mitigated if the web server cannot write to or change permissions on settings.php."
Admins whose websites use the paid Drupal Steward Web Application Firewall (WAF) service are already protected from known attack vectors, but should still upgrade to Drupal 10.6.22, 11.3.22, or 11.4.13 in case other attack vectors are discovered.
Those who can't immediately upgrade should secure the Drupal installer by blocking access to /core/install.php in the web server configuration or the .htaccess file in the web root.
On Wednesday, Drupal also addressed a moderately critical gadget chain vulnerability (CVE-2026-132166) that attackers with admin privileges can exploit to gain remote code execution on a targeted site if the application deserializes untrusted data due to another security flaw.
"The Drupal Security Team urges you to reserve time for core updates at that time because exploits might be developed within hours or days," the security team said in a Monday advance warning. "The vulnerabilities are currently rated as critical and at least one can be exploited by anonymous users."
In May, Drupal also confirmed that attackers were actively exploiting an SQL injection vulnerability (CVE-2026-9082) in the database abstraction API that could let them escalate privileges, access sensitive information, or achieve remote code execution on unpatched servers.
More recently, Drupal warned that a critical access bypass vulnerability (CVE-2026-118539) in the Commerce Core module is being abused in attacks.
The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has flagged 5 Drupal vulnerabilities as exploited in the wild since November 2021, two of which have also been abused in ransomware attacks.

articles.title: Tiny flaws in diamonds could unlock a quantum computing revolution
articles.text:
Tiny flaws in diamonds could unlock a quantum computing revolution
By treating qubits like individual molecules, scientists can now predict their behavior faster and more accurately
- Date:
- November 13, 2026
- Source:
- Princeton University
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered a faster way to identify diamond-based materials that could power quantum computers and sensors at room temperature. The breakthrough has already revealed promising new quantum building blocks that could help unlock computing capabilities far beyond those of today's supercomputers.
- Share:
A new computational technique could accelerate the search for diamond materials capable of powering future quantum computers and highly sensitive sensors. Developed by a researcher at the U.S. Department of Energy's (DOE) Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory (PPPL), the method makes it much easier to identify promising materials for quantum technology, potentially opening the door to advances across many areas of science.
The approach has already revealed new candidates for quantum computing and sensing applications. The findings were recently published in ACS Central Science and have attracted attention from other researchers in the field.
One of the biggest challenges in developing quantum technology is finding materials that can maintain delicate quantum states under practical conditions. Many candidates require extremely low temperatures to function reliably. Diamond materials stand out because certain quantum properties can remain useful even at room temperature.
This capability could help advance technologies that are important to national research priorities and the development of next-generation computing. Quantum sensors promise levels of sensitivity and precision beyond those of conventional instruments, while quantum computers could eventually solve certain extraordinarily complex problems much faster than today's most powerful supercomputers.
Why Imperfect Diamonds Could Be the Key to Quantum Computing
Although diamonds are made of carbon atoms, a flawless diamond crystal is not enough to create a useful quantum computing system. The key lies in tiny irregularities within the crystal structure.
These imperfections, known as defects, can occur when a carbon atom is absent from its normal position, when another element replaces a carbon atom, or when both changes occur together. The atoms surrounding these defects can form qubits, the basic units used to store and process quantum information in quantum computers and sensors.
Finding the most useful defects, however, has been difficult. Accurately modeling their quantum behavior traditionally requires enormous computational resources, making it challenging to evaluate large numbers of possible candidates.
A Simpler Way to Discover Better Diamond Qubits
Mark Martirez, a staff research scientist at PPPL, developed a way to dramatically reduce the complexity of these calculations. Instead of simulating a much larger diamond structure, he isolates a small region containing just 16 to 30 atoms around a defect.
By "carving out" this tiny atomic cluster and treating it like a separate molecule, Martirez can use powerful computational methods that chemists have spent decades refining. These established techniques make it possible to analyze the quantum properties of diamond defects much more efficiently without sacrificing the high level of accuracy needed for the calculations.
"Because we're treating the qubits as molecules, the cost of calculating these defects is equivalent to the cost of just modeling a simple molecule," Martirez said. "This method really opened the floodgates" in terms of how qubits can be assessed.
The new technique allows researchers to calculate how different qubits respond to laser light and microwave pulses far more quickly than before. Using this approach, the team identified promising defects involving boron and oxygen that could serve as new types of qubits.
New Diamond Defects Reveal a Spectrum of Quantum Colors
Light plays an important role in how scientists interact with diamond qubits. Researchers use lasers and microwave pulses to manipulate their quantum states and retrieve stored information.
Much of the previous work in this area has centered on a defect known as the nitrogen-vacancy center. This structure forms when a nitrogen atom takes the place of a carbon atom in a diamond crystal, while an adjacent position that would normally contain another carbon atom remains empty.
Under laser illumination, this type of defect can emit red light when it occupies a particular quantum state.
The newly investigated defects offer different optical properties. Oxygen defects can produce blue light, while those involving boron emit ultraviolet light.
These differences could make it possible to combine several types of qubits within a single quantum device. Because each type responds differently to light, researchers might be able to interact with one group of qubits without disturbing another.
"One could imagine, then, combining different qubits of different responses, so you can basically probe one qubit but not the other," Martirez said.
Beyond identifying new candidates, the findings suggest a broader change in how researchers approach quantum technology. Diamond qubits have traditionally been studied primarily through physics, but understanding their underlying chemistry could provide additional ways to design them.
Martirez believes that researchers could eventually engineer qubits for particular functions using principles similar to those applied when chemists create specialized molecules, including compounds designed for new medications.
How Quantum Chemistry Could Transform Future Research
The potential benefits extend well beyond the development of quantum computers themselves. Martirez sees an intriguing possibility in which advances made possible by quantum chemistry eventually lead to quantum technologies that help improve the field of chemistry.
In other words, quantum chemistry could develop the very tools needed to "enrich itself" in the coming decades.
A practical quantum system containing multiple qubits could make molecular calculations substantially more accurate. That would allow scientists to study increasingly complex chemical structures, including large biological molecules and proteins, with a level of detail that is difficult to achieve using conventional methods.
"We could describe larger molecules, biomolecules, proteins and everything like that in a more accurate way, and that could improve all the chemical-adjacent industries, such as pharmaceutical science and materials science. Even our fundamental understanding of molecular systems could be enriched."
Such improvements could have far-reaching implications for pharmaceutical development, materials research, and the fundamental study of how molecules behave.
Martirez also hopes the research will encourage more chemists to explore solid-state physics. Although building advanced quantum computers is often viewed as a challenge primarily for physicists, he argues that chemistry offers valuable expertise that could help accelerate progress.
"At this moment in time, there's a great emphasis on building the first state-of-the-art qubit computer," he said. "But it's not just physicists who should be participating in this research. Chemists have decades of developed intuition about chemical systems that could be easily translated into understanding defects in solids as well."
By bringing these disciplines together, scientists may be able to develop more effective ways to discover, understand, and eventually engineer the quantum materials needed for future technologies.
The research was funded through PPPL's Laboratory Directed Research and Development program under prime contract number DE-AC02-09CH11466, with additional support from the DOE Office of Science, Office of Fusion Energy Sciences.

articles.title: Welcome to GTA VI day!
articles.text:
Well, it's finally here. After 13 years, countless rumors, trailers, delays, and a level of anticipation few games have ever experienced, Grand Theft Auto VI is officially launched.
The hype has translated into extraordinary sales, too. GTA VI is estimated to have generated more than $1.5 billion in preorders. Early reviews have been overwhelmingly positive, with critics praising Rockstar's ridiculously detailed recreation of Vice City, its living, breathing open world, and the story of Jason and Lucia.
Of course, there's plenty to debate beyond the hype. GTA VI is launching exclusively on PS5 and Xbox, with no PC version in sight. And despite all the visual wizardry, Rockstar has settled on a 30 fps target across consoles, including the PS5 Pro. For some, that's a reasonable trade-off. For others, going back to 30 fps in 2026 is a tough sell.
So, who's jumping into Vice City today or over the weekend? Which console are you playing on? Did you buy new hardware just for GTA VI?
Anyone taking a day off work or skipping class for the occasion? And if you've already spent a few hours with it, what are your first impressions? If you're waiting for the PC release, a discount, or simply don't understand the hype, we'd like to hear from you, too.
Consider this our GTA VI launch-day hangout. Share your experiences, discoveries, and hot takes below. Just keep the story spoilers out of the comments for now.

articles.title: Kenyan businesses to pay Chinese suppliers in yuan under WapiPay, Alipay deal
articles.text:
WapiPay, a Kenyan cross-border payments fintech, has partnered with Alipay to enable local merchants pay suppliers in mainland China, allowing importers to send shillings while suppliers receive yuan through the Chinese payments app.
The partnership gives WapiPay a second route into China after its earlier work with WeChat Pay. Alipay described the agreement as a first for the company in Africa. The service starts in Kenya, with the two companies looking to serve businesses that buy from suppliers elsewhere in Asia.
Most Kenyan businesses that buy from China pay through their banks, which usually convert the money into dollars on the way. That pushes up transaction costs, a burden for importers working on thin margins. WapiPay is offering a direct shilling-to-yuan route that skips the dollar.
“Our work with WeChat Pay helped lay the groundwork,” Paul Ndichu, WapiPay co-founder, said in a statement. “With Alipay, we’re opening another payment route and positioning WapiPay to serve a market with an estimated $300 billion in annual flows.”
Kenyan importers are heavy buyers of Chinese currency and have little yuan income to offset it, meaning every payment has to be funded by selling shillings, directly or through the dollar. A service that can source yuan cheaply and settle it without a bank in the middle could, in theory, pass on savings.
Kenya’s biggest trading partner
China’s exports to Africa rose almost 26% to $225 billion in 2025, and two-way trade hit a record $348 billion, according to Chinese customs data compiled by Nanyang Technological University’s Centre for African Studies. Machinery, electronics, and clean energy equipment were among the main goods.
China is Kenya’s largest source of goods, and imports from it rose by KES 93.31 billion ($717.4 million) to KES 671.25 billion ($5.1 billion) in 2025, driven by machinery, manufactured goods, and electronics. That was 24.2% of Kenya’s total import bill. Kenya, on the other hand, exported just $130.8 million.
Wapi Pay told TechCabal it has processed more than KES 40 billion ($307.5 million) in cross-border payments across its network, but only Rmb2.5 million ($374,936.25) in transfers from Africa to China. The initial service covers only payments from Kenya to the mainland.
“Trade moves on roads, through ports, and across oceans. Money needs a route of its own,” said Eddie Ndichu, WapiPay co-founder. “For a business owner, that means a simpler way to pay for the next shipment and keep goods moving.”
Nairobi has been moving some of its dealings with Beijing out of dollars. Kenya has been in talks with China, its biggest bilateral lender, to convert dollar-denominated debt into yuan. Chatham House, the London think tank, said the loan conversion also aligns with China’s stated ambition to promote the internationalisation of the yuan.

articles.title: Critical Apache Roller, Axis Vulnerabilities Exploited in Attacks
articles.text:
Two critical vulnerabilities in Apache software are being exploited in attacks, and CISA added one of them to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on Wednesday.
Apache Axis vulnerability exploited in attacks
CVE-2026-90436, disclosed on November 6, is an unsafe reflection vulnerability in Apache Axis 1.x, an end-of-life Java-based SOAP implementation. The flaw has a CVSS score of 9.8 and can allow unauthenticated attackers to execute arbitrary code on vulnerable systems.
Rapid7 detected exploitation on November 13 in a customer environment running Atlassian Confluence Data Center. The attacker executed hundreds of commands, accessed Confluence’s database using the application’s credentials, and searched for sensitive information.
Within four hours of the initial exploitation, the attacker had obtained a service account credential and was querying a production cloud data warehouse. Roughly twelve hours after the first exploit request, the attacker signed in to Microsoft 365 using an integration service account.
Rapid7 also cited N-able’s report of attacks against N-central involving a vulnerability strongly correlated with CVE-2026-90436. Both Confluence and N-central require non-default configurations to be vulnerable.
Separately, Previdian reported detecting 50 exploitation attempts from 14 IP addresses between November 12 and 19. Its sensor data does not establish whether those attempts succeeded.
Apache does not plan to release a fixed Axis 1.x version and recommends migrating to another SOAP engine or applying its published patch.
Confluence Data Center users can upgrade to version 9.2.28 or an unaffected 10.x release. N-central 2026.4 HF3 disables the Legacy API functionality that exposes the vulnerable Axis component.
CISA has added CVE-2026-90436 to its KEV catalog, instructing federal agencies to address it by November 21.
Apache Roller vulnerability also exploited
Apache has also confirmed active exploitation of CVE-2026-129448, a CVSS 9.8 vulnerability affecting versions 4.0.0 through 6.1.4 of its Java-based blogging platform Roller. The flaw allows unauthenticated remote code execution.
“This issue is being actively exploited,” Apache said in its November 17 advisory, without providing further information about the attacks.
The vulnerability stems from unsafe deserialization in Roller’s XML-RPC interface, which processes malicious data before authentication. Disabling XML-RPC through the application’s administration interface does not prevent exploitation.
Apache initially disclosed the same underlying vulnerability in September as CVE-2026-82384.
“This is the same vulnerability as CVE-2026-82384, which listed only Apache Roller 6.1.5 as affected,” Apache explained.
The flaw was fixed in Roller 6.1.6. Apache recommends upgrading to that version or later. Version 6.1.7, released on November 11, addresses another 15 vulnerabilities.
