articles.title: Detachable Fiber Connectors Pose New Challenges For Photonics
articles.text:
Multiple designs are emerging for CPO and NPO, but standardization and high-volume manufacturing are still not ready.
Key Takeaways:
As photonics shifts from pluggable optical transceivers toward near- and co-packaged optics (NPO, CPO), engineers are devising new ways to attach fibers to the photonics chips on a board. Several different designs exist today, but so far there is no common interface.
With pluggable photonics, lasers and connections are attached at the server faceplate, with the board itself housing only electronic components. Yet long electrical connections to the faceplate mean higher power and longer latency. Fibers would need to move onto the interior of the board to solve that. That eliminates the need for pluggables, but it requires new solutions.
“With the rapid growth of generative AI, AI data centers are required to process enormous volumes of data faster and more efficiently than ever before,” said Yoshimasa Bando, principal scientist at Mitsubishi Chemical. “To meet this demand, further improvements in communication speed and energy efficiency have become critical challenges.”
The goal of CPO and NPO is to reduce reliance on long electrical connections.
Long lines
One reason for maintaining faceplate pluggables is that lasers are not always reliable. Using a pluggable module makes it easy to replace the laser.
“What we are focused on has the laser on the faceplate, because the laser is the highest reliability risk,” said Vishal Chandrasekar, director of product management at Ayar Labs.
All connections, whether they have a laser or not, happen in pluggable modules today. That means the signals those fibers carry must travel electrically from their origin to the edge of the board. Bandwidth necessitates serial lines driven by serializer/deserializer (SerDes) circuits. Driving those signals over that distance requires high power.
CPO aims to reduce system power by eliminating those long electrical lines and bringing fiber into the processor or switch packages. “CPO unlocks the token economics that everyone cares about,” said Chandrasekar. “The major bottlenecks are compute, memory, and moving data back and forth. If you’re trying to make step changes in hardware every one or two years, the way you make 5× or 10× kinds of improvements is by having new hardware. How do you use that hardware intelligently? How do I ensure that whatever hardware I have, I’m using it for the most important problem so my utilization is good?”
Fig. 1: With co-packaged optics, an optical engine is placed inside a package along with other chiplets. The laser remains outside the package for thermal reasons, and in the near term it will remain pluggable. Source: Bryon Moyer/Semiconductor Engineering
Photonics plays a key role in this effort. “You’re trying to reduce copper, so you’re trying to bring the PIC [photonic integrated circuit] closer to the processor or the switch,” said David Harame, COO at AIM Photonics, which operates with NY Creates (New York Center for Research, Economic Advancement, Technology, Engineering, and Science). “The industry is still very much using pluggables; you plug in the front panel. So there’s a lot of copper going between this [and the processor]. The next step is to move the optical transceiver closer to the switch by putting it on the PCB and reducing the copper line length to the switch. This is called near-packaged optics. Essentially, it moves the optical pluggable connector further inside the box on the PC board, so the optical-to-electrical connection takes place closer to the switch.
CPO is yet another variant of advanced packaging. “And all the challenges in advanced packaging are the same for co-packaged optics, except for fiber coupling and getting the PIC closer to the target chip,” noted Harame.
CPO receives the bulk of the near-term optical development efforts.
Fig. 2: In near-packaged optics, the optical components lie on the board near where their signals originate. Lasers will remain pluggable for now. Source: Bryon Moyer/Semiconductor Engineering
Unknown fiber length
Both CPO and NPO share the need to connect fiber directly to components on the board. One straightforward way is to attach a nominal length of fiber to the chip package and ship it that way, with the system integrator connecting the other end of the fiber directly to the destination.
The challenge there is that chip producers have no way of knowing how long that fiber will need to be. If it’s long enough for designs that require long runs, it will be too long for the many designs that don’t. That said, there are ways of dealing with extra fiber.
“The fiber goes into a fiber management tray, and there are spool points on the board,” said Nick Harris, CEO of Lightmatter. “They’re neatly managed for airflow.”
Others agree. “Usually, you’ll have some kind of excess fiber management,” explained Obie Roy, vice president, strategic commercial development at Senko. “But depending on the system that you’re building, you could cut it to length and terminate it once you know the exact application.”
Some engineers see this as a non-issue, which may be true if one is fusing the fibers or having the integrator attach a connector. “The fiber length is irrelevant,” said Professor Amr Helmy at the University of Toronto. “You connect a strand of fiber to the chip. With the other end, you can connectorize it, cut it, or fuse it with another fiber to make it longer. Fusing is one approach, but each one of these fibers can come with a connector depending on the amount of loss appetite you have.”
For ease of assembly, some means of attaching and detaching a fiber would also be helpful, such as a fixture or clip on the end to which another fiber can attach. But several considerations make this decision about more than simply adding wire connections as shown in the figures above.
Moving beyond the die edge
Today, fibers typically are placed using well-established V-groove technology, where the fibers exit out the side of a photonic chip. This attachment method works at low volumes and low total fiber counts, but it lacks the modularity and convenience needed for high-volume automation.
“The V-groove is a great concept, but the fibers are attached,” explained Gerard John, senior director, chiplets/FCBGA business unit at Amkor. “When being assembled onto a board, if one of them breaks, there’s no rework. People are generally thinking in terms of detachables and moving away from V-grooves.”
In addition, attachment space is bound by shoreline, which is essentially the real estate on the edge of the die. With metal connections, it might include the first few rows of bumps on the package, but fiber footprint is bigger and can chew up a lot of shoreline.
“The fiber diameter is 10 µm, but you have all the cladding around it, making it 125 µm,” John said. “So if you’re putting, let’s say, 16 cables like that, even if it’s staggered you will use a lot of real estate.”
Nevertheless, this is the predominant approach today. For example, Senko has put together a LEGO-like connector, with one part glued to the chip and the other attached to a fiber. This is one of many approaches underway at different companies.
There are three configurations for bringing fiber out (see figure 3, below). One takes the light from a waveguide, reflects it upward 90°, and sends it horizontally to a connector. These connectors would be situated around the periphery of the die.
Another is simply to run the waveguide to the edge of the die and have a connector butt up to the die to capture the light and route it to a fiber. The number of such connections is also determined by the perimeter.
A third approach moves the light vertically but then connects to the top surface rather than going out horizontally. This makes the entire area of the chip available for connections, providing more “shoreline” than the other two schemes.
“You have the waveguide shooting out laterally, and then it hits a mirror at a 45° angle,” said John. “It shoots upward, and once you get it upward, you put a connector with all the fibers on it.”
Fig. 3: The three ways of getting a waveguide signal into a fiber — horizontal-to-vertical-to-horizontal, fully horizontal, and horizontal-to-vertical. Source: Bryon Moyer/Semiconductor Engineering
But vertical approaches must avoid any heat sinks or other elements attached to the top. “When you send it vertically, you may get in the way of your thermal solution,” said Ravi Mahajan, fellow at Intel Foundry. “So if you have a solution that does both vertical and lateral, then you have more flexibility. In cases where thermal is a potential problem, go horizontal. In cases where you don’t worry about it, you can go vertical.”
The problem with pigtails
As depicted above, these connectors could be short pieces of fiber — pigtails — that are affixed firmly to the die and with some sort of clip connector at the end. A matching connector clip could then be plugged in to make the connection. Such a clip would likely cause some insertion loss, but if managed well, it can work. And it can be made to be sturdy.
“We have taken a part with a pigtail and banged it on the desk to convince a VP that it doesn’t come off,” said Mahajan. “We expose it to temperature cycles, to a little bit of moisture, and bake it for a long time, and it doesn’t come off.”
But the greater concerns are the high-volume manufacturing implications. Even without considering how the fiber attaches to the die, a more immediate question is how these chips would be packaged in bulk for test and delivery. The same issue holds for shipping a longer fiber and cutting it to order during integration.
Today, chips go into trays, and automated handling equipment can pick and place them onto boards or into test heads or anywhere else they’re needed. What happens if it’s no longer just a chip in the tray pocket, but potentially a chip wrapped with pigtails?
“If you have a pigtail, it’s very difficult to wrap that pigtail around and put it in a tray, and you probably won’t have many parts on the tray,” said John. “So our choice is to have a detachable connector, and it also makes sense from a manufacturing perspective.”
In addition, it is inconvenient to try to place a chip with pigtails into such a tray in an orderly, repeatable way. And then, when pulling the chip out of the tray, it will have dangling pigtails floating about, potentially interfering with whatever operation the equipment is attempting. Then, presumably, those pigtails would be manually connected.
This arrangement, while suitable at low volumes, may not work in high-volume production.
“I understand people being worried about a pigtail dangling off the edge, so we decided, ‘Why not just bring it to the edge of the die,’” said Mahajan. “Then an integrator just attaches it [to the fiber].”
Fig. 4: A fiber plugs into the side of a package. Source: Intel Foundry
Old habits change slowly, however. “Pigtails are probably still more common because people are trying to make incremental changes,” noted Sanjay Gangadhara, senior architect at Synopsys.
Scaling volumes also must address the assembly of any connector on the package. “Terminating a fiber is complex,” said Badri Gomatam, CTO of STL. “You’ve got to make it low cost, high yield, and repeatable. You’ve got hundreds of connections. No speck of dust can be allowed, and the assembly has to survive high-temperature reflow and all the other growth steps.”
Alignment concerns
One of the unique and challenging characteristics of photonics is that where two conductors meet, as much light as possible must get from one to the other. That applies to assembly and test.
Today, this is done through active alignment, where a tool measures the light exiting a waveguide and positions a fiber to maximize the captured light. This is a six-degree-of-freedom problem, where the aligner must be able to move in three linear dimensions as well as three angles of approach. It can take time.
With the pigtail configuration, presumably the clips would be designed to provide the alignment, but you still need to affix the stationary end of the pigtail during assembly. Given the downsides of pigtails, an alternative is to build the connector into the package itself. That way, nothing is hanging off the package, and it can be handled like other chips.
But alignment is still necessary. One method places a lens over the optical TSV to focus the light into an attached fiber while the other connection hardware aligns.
“One of the advantages when you have a lens is that, even if you do have some misalignment, the lens can correct for some of that because it’s focusing the light into a common region,” said Synopsys’ Gangadhara. “So this idea of using micro-optics, whether in a vertical-coupling or an edge-coupling architecture, is becoming more and more common.”
The Senko technique, for instance, provides passive mechanical fine alignment and restraint when snapped together. Roy explained that the snap-on structure provides the fine alignment, but you need something to hold it down. “We have screws and a structure that pushes it down into the fine alignment. This is the mechanical latching.”
It’s one thing to perform alignment during assembly, but it’s another to require it when attaching system fibers to the chip. Magnetic connectors, such as those used by Apple on iPhones, are being considered. Once the receiver end is built into the package, someone (or an automated handler) attaching the fiber must first align it roughly in place. From there, the magnet pulls it into the necessary precise location.
Unfortunately, some magnetic connectors are easily damaged. Any acceptable CPO fiber connection must be firm.
Stronger magnets could help, and this is an active area of development, possibly along with a mechanical restraint (such as Senko’s screws). What’s unclear, however, is how strong that magnetic field would be and whether it may adversely affect surrounding components such as MRAMs.
“When you design your system board, are you going to put sensitive memory close to these devices?” mused John.
As a result, any mechanical alignment would likely also be supplemented with a latch.
Serviceability and testability are critical
One way to connect fibers, common in long-haul optical applications, is to literally fuse them together. This permanent attachment method does not allow detachment, so it provides poor serviceability if a photonics chip fails.
“People have this concern about any kind of failure,” said Gangadhara. “How do you replace it? That serviceability part of the RAS requirement becomes a challenge.”
Serviceability, reliability, and availability make up the RAS feature that’s in high demand these days. It means components at greater risk of failure must be easy to replace, so you don’t have to throw out an entire expensive module or server.
“Once you attach a pigtail, if it gets damaged during shipment, the whole thing needs to be thrown out,” said John.
Roy agreed. “You need to make it detachable because if you permanently attach it and the fiber breaks, you have to fail the entire module out, which is very expensive,” he said.
Testing is heavily affected by these connector types, especially without standards. “An important aspect is making sure your solution is testable in real life,” noted Roy.
Addressing testability, especially for future high-volume manufacturing, means collaborating with test-equipment manufacturers. “We worked with Advantest and developed a test connector made out of tungsten carbide,” explained Roy. “It has the same bumps [as the LEGO-like connector] on the other side, and so it can come down, align precisely, and test very quickly. And you can scale it to test one at a time or a row of these things.”
Critically, the connection doesn’t require active alignment, saving test time. “We demonstrated 10,000 matings with very little variation in the loss [through the connection],” said Roy.
The connectors themselves must be reliable enough, but only up to a point. “Ideally, you’re not detaching and reattaching frequently,” noted Gangadhara. “If these things are up and running and working, then they’re running for thousands or tens of thousands of hours. Meta published a study last year where they had done serviceability/reliability analysis of some CPO devices, and they showed 10,000 hours of constant usage without any degradation of signal integrity or performance.”
Settling on a common design
Connector attachment is a textbook case of a development that needs standards so that any user can plug into anyone else’s photonics chip. At present, there are numerous pigtail-based designs and no standards. Likewise, no magnetic (or other) pigtail-less approach has been standardized or proven in high volumes. Customer requirements also appear to vary in ways that may make standardization difficult.
Consider the mechanical latching of Senko’s solution, for example. “Each of these parts is custom, depending on the ganging requirements and the mechanical sizes that are important to avoid — cooling plates and thermal elements and such,” Roy said. “Our vision is to take the receptacle part [that gets attached to the package], make that a common interface of the chip, and then sell the cover plate to any FAU manufacturer.”
For that to become an actual standard, however, typical licensing will presumably need to be reasonable and non-discriminatory (RAND). That’s a situation where different connector companies will work closely with photonics companies to find an approach that works functionally and is suited to high-volume manufacturing. That means compatibility with handling equipment.
These efforts will likely continue until standards (or at least multi-source agreements, or MSAs) are put in place, removing one major photonics volume barrier once the solution is established.

articles.title: PesaLink’s bank owners remain split on what it should cost
articles.text:
Gituku Kirika runs a payments network owned by Kenya’s banks, but he cannot dictate what they charge customers.
This constraint defines PesaLink’s efforts to win everyday payments from mobile money services. Launched in 2017, PesaLink allows customers to send up to KES 999,999 ($7,700) instantly between bank accounts at different financial institutions. The network is operated by Integrated Payment Services Limited (IPSL), which Kirika leads. The Kenya Bankers Association (KBA), the industry body representing the country’s lenders, is its sole shareholder.
PesaLink says it processes an average of KES 4 billion ($30.8 million) daily, up 24% from 2025. Monthly transaction value has reached KES 110 billion ($846.5 million), up 41% year on year. The company reports a transaction success rate of about 98%.
This year, IPSL has been encouraging banks to adopt a common transfer fee: free for transactions of KES 1,000 ($7.70) or less, and a flat KES 20 ($0.15) for larger transfers, up to KES 999,999 ($7,700). Sending KES 50,000 ($384) between bank accounts costs just KES 20, compared with KES 108 ($0.83) through M-PESA or Airtel Money.
KCB, Co-operative Bank, NCBA, Absa and Stanbic have adopted the flat-fee model. Equity Bank, Standard Chartered and I&M have not, leaving their customers on tiered pricing, where transfer fees rise with the amount sent.
Kirika says PesaLink can only recommend a price, not impose one, but he expects all banks to switch before the end of 2027.
He spoke to TechCabal on Wednesday in Balaclava, Mauritius, a day before the AfricaNenda Foundation, a non-profit that helps African central banks build instant payment systems, released its annual report. He discussed PesaLink’s bank ownership, the lenders yet to adopt its proposed pricing model, competition from M-PESA, merchant payments, and the network’s plans to move beyond bank-to-bank transfers.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
PesaLink is owned by the banking industry, but could its owners also be its biggest constraint?
PesaLink was established by the banking sector. All the banks set it up under the Kenya Bankers Association, so the KBA holds sole ownership of IPSL. PesaLink is available across all banks today. Different banks use the platform differently, based on their strategies and customer segments. As we support more use cases, you will see PesaLink more across the banking world.
If PesaLink transfers can be cheaper than mobile money, why hasn’t the platform pushed that advantage more aggressively?
At PesaLink, we champion lower payment costs, inclusivity, and affordability, and we are passionate about seeing payment costs come down. But we don’t dictate prices to our customers. Banks, microfinance banks, Savings and Credit Cooperative Organisations (SACCOs), and telcos. We do share with them what we believe is the right approach to pricing instant payments. The banks make decisions based on their strategies and budgets. We’ve seen most banks adopt the new KES 20 ($0.15) price this year, and I’m confident many more will do so next year. I expect that before the end of next year, all banks will have changed their price.
Mobile money has built customer habits, merchant acceptance and an extensive distribution network. What is PesaLink doing to make customers choose it without their banks having to push them towards it?
We are a mobile money-native country when it comes to instant payments, and PesaLink also offers instant payments through its different participants. We still need much more work to build awareness of PesaLink. People already have mobile money as an option, but we believe it’s important to have different options. We are working on awareness together with the PesaLink participants who are on board.
As we increase the use cases PesaLink supports, people will learn more about it. Everyday use cases such as person-to-merchant payments will help drive that. The more relevant PesaLink becomes day to day, the more awareness will grow, and next year you will see a huge change.
More participants with large consumer bases are also coming on board. Airtel Money, for example, has now joined PesaLink, so a lot more people will see and hear about it. We look forward to a significant increase in awareness.
Can PesaLink become a payment option at shops and supermarkets?
First, 50% of the payments we process today either terminate at a business or originate from one, so person-to-business payments are already happening. What you’re asking about, though, is person-to-merchant payments. That will follow the approach we’re all familiar with: a merchant number, which we call a till number or paybill, or a QR code. We have now gone live with that use case. As we speak, we are live with Equity Bank and SBM at Quickmart, and we look forward to scaling across other merchants and PesaLink participants.
As PesaLink extends its reach through SACCOs, fintechs, telcos and agent networks, is its ambition to become Kenya’s underlying payment infrastructure, including for transactions that do not originate from bank accounts?
Our agenda is simplifying life through instant, affordable payments for everyone, everywhere, every time. For payments to be affordable, our own costs have to be affordable. And for payments to reach everyone, everywhere, every time, we have to break down the silos created by closed-loop ecosystems.
If you are with your bank, your mobile money operator, or your SACCO, and you can’t use or access that money without moving it to another ecosystem, we consider you in a closed-loop ecosystem. For example, if you’re in the mobile money world and you come across a merchant served by a bank, where you have to pay by card, you’re in a closed loop.
We’re working to reduce barriers to moving money by breaking down those silos and ensuring real interoperability. One way to do that is to reduce the effort it takes for two parties to move money between each other. Today, for a bank, a telco or a SACCO to move money to one another, they have to go through lengthy, time-consuming and expensive arrangements, from technology work to contract negotiations. PesaLink can cut all of that out if every participant is a member.
Can PesaLink become a gateway for cross-border payments into Kenya?
PesaLink is integrated with the Pan-African Payment and Settlement System (PAPSS), so people can now send money into Kenya from other PAPSS-enabled countries. We’re happy to be powering inbound remittances through PAPSS. But we’ve been doing this for a long time: many international money transfer operators, both banks and non-banks, use PesaLink for last-mile delivery of money into the country. We look forward to powering many more of these transactions.

articles.title: Mikel Oyarzabal, Bruce Springsteen y José Luis Rebordinos, entre los nominados al Tambor de Oro de San Sebastián
articles.text:
Imagina el cartel de una final donde tienes a un campeón del mundo en fútbol, un tipo que lleva décadas llenando estadios y el director de un festival de cine. No es un amistoso de verano, sino la lista de aspirantes al Tambor de Oro 2027 de San Sebastián. Y para quien se pregunte cómo se compara a un futbolista con un compositor, la respuesta honesta es que no se compara: se celebra.
Qué es el Tambor de Oro. Es el galardón que el Ayuntamiento entrega cada 20 de enero, día de San Sebastián, durante la tamborrada infantil. Existe desde 1967 por el Centro de Atracción y Turismo. Según el reglamento, premia a quien más haya contribuido a dar a conocer Donostia y a proyectar una imagen positiva fuera. O sea, no hay criterio artístico: no se premia al mejor libro, al mejor gol ni a la mejor croqueta, sino al mejor embajador.
Puedes acceder al reglamento en DonostiaKIN, el trámite de elección y el proceso de elección: la Junta de Portavoces selecciona hasta tres finalistas. Si hay mayoría cualificada, dos tercios con representación ponderada del pleno (no un voto por grupo), se otorga directamente. Si no, vota la ciudadanía, que vota desde hace una década. Y al principio solo podían ganarlo quienes habían nacido en la ciudad. En 1986 cambiaron la norma, y los donostiarras ya pueden ser embajadores. Aunque deberíamos recordar que un vasco, de facto, nace donde quiere.
El criterio: “lo que sea, pero que se note”. El listado de premiados incluye al cocinero Pedro Subijana, la escultora Cristina Iglesias, un nadador paralímpico elegido por voto popular, una activista contra los desahucios, la artista Esther Ferrer y el CEO de una biotecnológica. También se ha premiado a eventos, como la Clásica ciclista. Las últimas ediciones fueron para la productora Moriarti, elegida entre 98 candidaturas, y para el tenor Xabier Anduaga, “por llevar el nombre de la ciudad allá donde actúa”. Un tambor, al fin y al cabo, es instrumento de ritmo y ruido y el premio es para quien más ruido haga fuera de casa.
Quién decide. Los ciudadanos proponen, los servicios municipales filtran y el 1 de diciembre se reúnen los cinco grupos políticos del Ayuntamiento. Necesitan dos tercios de los votos, y si no los logran sale una terna y vota la ciudad. Como el que ha intentado elegir restaurante en un grupo de WhatsApp de cinco personas, el reto es sumar sin que nadie imponga veto.
Cuando no cuaja, pues se queda sin dar. En 1984 el pleno rechazó que fuera para los Duques de Alba y quedó desierto; en 2017 pasó lo mismo. En 1981 se concedió a un periodista y, dos años después, el pleno le retiró el galardón por un artículo polémico. Es el único caso conocido de “devuélvame el tambor”. En 2003 el alcalde directamente retiró la candidatura de La Oreja de Van Gogh.
Los candidatos. Parece la quiniela más rara del año:
- Fútbol: Oyarzabal y Zubimendi, campeones del mundo (este último ya en el Arsenal, lo que complica lo de “vecino”), además de Xabi Prieto y el presidente del club.
- Cultura: Ane Gabarain y Elena Irureta, que repiten, y José Luis Rebordinos, director del Zinemaldia hasta fin de año, con la maleta casi hecha.
- Cocina: Arzak, que ya tiene bien merecida la Medalla de Oro, y la tarta de queso de La Viña. Un campeón del mundo contra un postre.
- Los habituales: Bruce Springsteen y David Bisbal. No sabemos si El Jefe está al tanto de que compite. Ojalá la llamada, a ambos, arranque con un “Cómo están los máquinas”, lo primero de todo.
Eso sí, de los 46 aspirantes, solo once son mujeres (si bien hay una edición femenina). Las propuestas son de la ciudadanía, no del Ayuntamiento, pero para ser un torneo con tantos campeones, conviene mirarse la banda. Las candidaturas han bajado de 98 en la edición que ganó Moriarti a 56, hasta los actuales 46.
El trofeo. Tomás Hernández Mendizabal, pintor, hizo el dibujo y las letras durante unos 50 años. Colgó los pinceles en 2020. Tomó el testigo Iñigo Arístegui, artista donostiarra de 57 años con tienda de arte en la calle Mari. Pinta sobre un círculo de cuero de 25 centímetros, además de ser un prestigioso escultor.
Premios de consolación. Existe además la Medalla al Mérito Ciudadano, de la que se dan hasta cinco al año entre 65 candidatos y con otra lógica: agradecer lo que se aporta a la convivencia, no lo que se proyecta fuera. Oyarzabal, Rebordinos y el club Arraun Lagunak juegan en las dos ligas, por ambas bandas, con doble ficha. Mientras llega el 1 de diciembre, la lista de apuestas sigue abierta, aunque el favorito, como siempre, es el consenso.

articles.title: Inside this quantum computer, memory vibrates like a guitar string
articles.text:
Inside this quantum computer, memory vibrates like a guitar string
- Date:
- November 11, 2026
- Source:
- ETH Zurich
- Summary:
- Researchers have created a quantum computer that stores information in microscopic vibrations, potentially making quantum machines smaller, more powerful, and better at preserving information. The breakthrough successfully demonstrated advanced quantum calculations and could help overcome major barriers to practical quantum computing.
- Share:
A quantum computer might seem to have little in common with a guitar, but researchers at ETH Zurich have found a surprising connection. Physicist Yiwen Chu and her team have developed a system that uses microscopic mechanical vibrations to store and manipulate quantum information, much like the vibrating strings of a guitar produce musical notes.
Unlike the sounds produced by a musical instrument, these vibrations occur at frequencies far beyond human hearing. They take place within a tiny quantum chip, where they serve as a new form of computer memory.
By harnessing these vibrations, the researchers have created a way for quantum computers to process information efficiently while accessing a flexible working memory. "The interaction between the quantum processor and the quantum memory provides a crucial foundation with a view to establishing quantum computers as a powerful and reliable way to perform computations that are not feasible with conventional computers," says Yiwen Chu.
The breakthrough, described in the journal Science, introduces a different approach to quantum computer design. Instead of closely integrating information processing and storage, as many existing systems do, Chu's team has developed an architecture that gives these functions more distinct roles.
Quantum Memory Inspired by Conventional Computers
The researchers drew inspiration from the basic design of everyday digital computers. In a conventional machine, the central processing unit (CPU) carries out calculations while information is held separately in working memory, commonly called random access memory (RAM). The arrangement of these components plays an important role in determining how efficiently a computer operates.
Chu's quantum system follows a similar principle. A superconducting qubit acts as the processing and control unit, performing a role comparable to that of the central processing unit (CPU). Meanwhile, a separate quantum memory temporarily holds the information needed during calculations, allowing the processor to retrieve and modify it as necessary.
The major difference lies in how that information is stored.
"In our quantum working memory, however, information is not stored electromagnetically -- as is usually the case today -- but rather in the form of mechanical vibrations," explains Chu.
Quantum computers take advantage of unusual properties of quantum physics, including superposition, which allows quantum systems to exist in combinations of different states, and entanglement, which creates powerful connections between quantum states. These effects could eventually enable quantum machines to tackle certain extremely complicated calculations much faster than conventional computers, including some problems that are currently beyond their practical capabilities.
Why Vibrating Quantum Memory Could Be Better
One of the greatest challenges in quantum computing is maintaining precise control over quantum information. The states used for calculations are delicate, and even small disturbances can cause information to be lost. To perform calculations reliably, the processor and memory must interact closely enough to transfer and manipulate quantum states with high precision.
In the new system, microscopic structures called mechanical resonators hold information in particular patterns of vibration. When the superconducting qubit needs that information, it accesses the stored vibrational state, performs the required operation, and returns the modified information to memory.
Many existing quantum computers instead use electromagnetic memory alongside superconducting qubits. Researchers understand these technologies well, and they can be combined to provide extremely accurate control over quantum states, including reading, changing, and manipulating stored information.
However, electromagnetic memory systems have a significant disadvantage. They can occupy considerable space, making it difficult to expand experimental quantum devices into the larger, more capable computers that researchers and industries ultimately need.
Mechanical resonators offer several potential advantages. They are substantially smaller, allowing more compact designs. They can also support numerous different patterns of vibration, providing opportunities to store more information simultaneously than conventional electromagnetic memory.
Another important benefit is that mechanical vibrations can preserve quantum states for longer periods before the stored information begins to fade. Longer storage times could make it easier to carry out complicated calculations that require information to remain available throughout multiple processing steps.
New Quantum Computer Passes Major Tests
The research published in Science provides the first experimental demonstration that mechanical resonators can work together with superconducting qubits to carry out quantum computations. The results establish that vibration-based memory is a feasible alternative to electromagnetic storage.
The achievement goes beyond simply storing information. Chu's team demonstrated that its architecture can handle both relatively straightforward calculations and more demanding quantum operations.
To evaluate the system, the researchers tested two important computational techniques: the quantum Fourier transform and period finding. Both are fundamental tools in quantum computing and require a computer to coordinate multiple quantum states with considerable precision.
"The Quantum Fourier Transform is a fundamental computational procedure required for many quantum algorithms. The period-finding algorithm we implemented served as a demonstration of how this procedure can be used," explains Igor Kladaric, doctoral student in Chu's team and co-author of the publication.
Successfully completing these tasks requires the system to store, control, and maintain coherent relationships among multiple quantum states at the same time. The experiments showed that the new architecture can meet these requirements, providing strong evidence that it can support genuine quantum computation rather than simply function as a memory device.
A Promising Step Toward Powerful Quantum Computers
One of the most significant findings is that the new system can, in principle, carry out all the fundamental operations needed for arbitrary quantum computations. This means the architecture has the essential capabilities required for a programmable, general-purpose quantum computer.
However, demonstrating those capabilities in an experimental chip is only the beginning. The next major challenge is scaling the technology to larger systems with greater processing power while preserving the precision and reliability demonstrated in the laboratory.
Chu and her colleagues are continuing to investigate how their approach can be developed further. Its long-term success will depend on whether mechanical quantum memory can remain effective as more components and increasingly complex computations are added.
Practical quantum computers powerful enough for widespread scientific and industrial applications are still some distance away. Nevertheless, by showing that tiny mechanical vibrations can serve as compact, capable quantum memory, the ETH Zurich team has demonstrated a promising new route toward making those machines a reality.
Story Source:
Materials provided by ETH Zurich. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Yu Yang, Igor Kladarić, Martynas Skrabulis, Michael Eichenberger, Stefano Marti, Simon Storz, Jonathan Esche, Raquel García Bellés, Max-Emanuel Kern, Andraz Omahen, Arianne Brooks, Marius Bild, Matteo Fadel, Yiwen Chu. Mechanical resonator–based quantum computing. Science, 2026; 392 (6801): 972 DOI: 10.1126/science.aef4139

articles.title: Splunk Patches Nearly 140 Flaws Across Three Core Products
articles.text:
Splunk on Wednesday announced patches for nearly 140 vulnerabilities in its Enterprise, Enterprise Security, and SOAR products.
Enterprise received fixes for 38 security defects, including two critical and 13 high-severity flaws that could allow unauthenticated attackers to bypass authentication, inject arbitrary code, and cause denial-of-service (DoS) conditions.
The critical bugs, tracked as CVE-2026-76536 and CVE-2026-76535, could allow attackers to read and modify clustering configuration using an empty clustering shared secret, or read or modify data and configurations by running arbitrary Search Processing Language (SPL) searches.
Fixes were included in Splunk Enterprise versions 10.6.1, 10.4.5, 10.2.9, 10.0.12, and 9.4.17.
Splunk released Enterprise Security and Splunk App for PCI Compliance version 8.7.0 with patches for 42 vulnerabilities, including a critical flaw (CVE-2026-131202) leading to remote code execution (RCE). It can be exploited by an attacker with the ‘ess_admin’ role by combining lookup file upload and Configuration Checker functionality.
The security updates also resolve 11 high-severity code injection and privilege escalation issues leading to data tampering, service disruption, and command execution with elevated privileges.
Splunk SOAR version 8.8.0 arrived on Wednesday with fixes for 59 security bugs, including two critical flaws leading to remote code execution (CVE-2026-131253 and CVE-2026-131287). Both require authentication.
The SOAR refresh also resolves 27 high-severity information disclosure, missing authorization, RCE, path traversal, XSS, improper authorization, improper access control, and privilege escalation weaknesses.
On Wednesday, Splunk also announced fixes for three vulnerabilities in App for Stream, four flaws in AI Assistant, and nearly 160 bugs in third-party packages for Enterprise, Enterprise Security, and SOAR.
The company makes no mention of any of these security defects being exploited in the wild. More details are available on Splunk’s security advisories page.

articles.title: Community-Focused Academic Brings AI Tools to Colorado Farmers
articles.text:
Many farmers and ranchers in eastern Colorado are curious about artificial intelligence, but they don’t have a local tech-savvy person to show them how to use it. Xue “Alice” Dong has made that her job.
Dong, an IEEE senior member, is an extension regional specialist with the Colorado State University Extension, CSU’s outreach arm. She works in Logan County and serves a 10-county farming area in Colorado’s northeast corner. Her job is to turn university research into practical help for the people who live there.
Xue “Alice” Dong
Employer
Colorado State University Extension in Logan County
Title
Extension regional specialist
Member grade
Senior member
Alma maters
Inner Mongolia Normal University, in Hohhot; Beijing Normal University; State University of New York College of Environmental Science and Forestry, in Syracuse; Colorado State University Global
She built the AI-Powered Agritourism Chatbot (AgriTourismAI.com), which helps farmers and ranchers launch and run “agritourism” businesses. Agritourism is when farmers open their property to visitors for fun, education, or shopping events. Familiar examples include pick-your-own fruit orchards, lessons on how to grow vegetables, and sales of handmade products.
Dong also teaches workshops where she shows farmers and ranchers how they can use AI tools to help grow and manage their business.
She says she sees herself as a link between the university and the countryside.
“We [extension specialists] act as a bridge,” she says. “We bridge our campus to the rural communities we serve.”
Many farmers and ranchers are older, and they typically have no technical training. Often their children and grandchildren have left the farm to work in a city or otherwise aren’t around to teach them about new tools. Without help, the benefits of AI could pass the farmers by. Dong’s workshops give them a way in.
Dong was named a finalist in the 2026 GenAI for Good Challenge for her AgriPivot AI Agent. The challenge was organized by IEEE Humanitarian Technologies and theU.N.’s International Telecommunication Union, and her project was selected from 318 teams across 79 countries. She also won the 2026 Award for Innovation from the National Extension Technology Community (NETC), and both the 2025 national and Western regional Educational Technology Awards from the National Association of Community Development Extension Professionals (NACDEP).
She has secured seven competitive grants totaling more than US $250,000 as principal investigator or co-principal investigator, including funding supported by the Department of Agriculture’s National Institute of Food and Agriculture.
An early love of design and problem-solving
Dong was born in Beijing. Both her parents are doctors.
As a child, she liked drawing new and inventive things. Sketching, she says, lets her picture solutions to problems in her head and put them on paper as practical designs.
That habit grew into a way of relating to her surroundings.
“I’ve always had a passion to create something tangible that can solve problems in the real world,” she says.
She doesn’t credit a single mentor for the direction her life has taken. Instead, she says all her teachers helped lay the groundwork for her career.
She attended the Inner Mongolia Normal University, in Hohhot, an institution that trains teachers. She earned two bachelor’s degrees there in 2013—one in geographical science and one in education.
She then earned a master’s degree in curriculum and instruction from Beijing Normal University in 2016.
That year, she moved to the United States to continue her graduate studies at the State University of New York College of Environmental Science and Forestry, in Syracuse. She earned a master’s degree in environmental biology in 2020.
From outreach to extension work
After earning her second master’s degree, she joined Paul Smith’s College, in Paul Smiths, N.Y., as an education and outreach coordinator.
She managed several national watershed projects to protect rivers, lakes, and aquifers. Watersheds are areas of land from which water drains into bodies of water.
She also undertook invasive-species-prevention projects, wrote grants to secure project funding, and designed two educational websites and several outreach publications. One website, Maintain the Chain, helps lake residents, boaters, and visitors from around the world keep invasive species out of the Fulton Chain of Lakes in New York’s Adirondack Park.
In 2022, she joined Stewards of the Coast and Redwoods as program manager. The nonprofit, based in Guerneville, Calif., works with California State Parks to protect, restore, and educate the public about the parks along Sonoma County’s coast and the Russian River area. The region is known for its redwood forests, wineries, and resort towns.
She left in 2023 to join the CSU Extension as a regional specialist, a title she still holds.
Her employer is part of the Cooperative Extension System, a nationwide network run by land-grant universities, schools founded with federal grants to teach farming and other practical subjects. Extension faculty and staff share what researchers at their universities learn with the citizens of those states.
The cooperative system operates on three levels. It is overseen federally by the Department of Agriculture’s National Institute of Food and Agriculture, managed statewide through land-grant universities, and delivered locally by county offices and Extension agents across more than 3,000 counties.
The work goes well beyond farming, Dong says, also covering community and economic development, health initiatives, and the 4-H program, which teaches children hands-on skills in agriculture, science, leadership, and citizenship.
Extension faculty members’ performance is judged on their research, teaching, and service to the community, Dong says—similar to the way professors in academia are evaluated. The difference, she says, is the audience: Professors teach students; most extension specialists teach adults, including farmers, ranchers, and community leaders. The setting is different, too. Dong doesn’t commute from the campus to the countryside; she lives and works in it. Her office is in Sterling, a small rural town. But her projects serve the whole state, and many of the people she helps live one to four hours’ drive away. So, most of her work with farmers and ranchers happens by email, phone, and virtual meetings. County fairs, farmers markets, and agricultural events give her chances to meet large groups of them in person.
She can’t just hand Colorado residents research findings and expect them to figure out the information they need, she says.
“We need to translate that research into something more practical, and easier to use, that farmers and ranchers can understand immediately,” she says.
Dong also focuses not on only on whether people use AI, but also on how they use it. In 2026, she and Paul Hill from Utah State University Extension published “From Access to Governance: Generative AI Literacy for Extension Professionals and Small Businesses, and a Governance-Aware Design Framework” in the journal AI. The paper offers a framework for helping Extension professionals and small businesses adopt generative AI responsibly.
How her AI chatbot helps farmers and ranchers
In 2025, Dong earned a third master’s degree, in artificial intelligence and machine learning, from CSU Global.
She immediately put those skills to work on agritourism, she says. She built the chatbot in Python, a popular programming language. It answers typed questions, and its user interface looks much like ChatGPT’s, but it works differently. Under the hood, it uses retrieval-augmented generation, a technique that has the AI look up information in a set of trusted documents before it answers. Dong curated that collection from Extension publications, so the chatbot’s answers rest on authoritative sources and are less likely to be made up. She presented the project at NeurIPS 2025 (Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems). The code is openly available on GitHub, so other Extension offices can adapt it.
The bot runs in a web browser rather than as a phone app. Many farmers she works with don’t own a smartphone, Dong says, but nearly all have a computer, tablet, or other gadget that can connect to a website. The bot works on any of them, with no app to download.
Extension specialists “act as a bridge. We bridge our campus to the rural communities we serve.”
Farmers often ask the bot how to attract visitors and how to write a business plan. A farmer thinking about opening a corn maze, for example, can ask how to price admission, what kind of insurance to carry, and which permits to get. The bot also gives advice on managing risk.
One of her test sites was Prairie Ridge Buffalo Ranch, in eastern Colorado. Dong documented how the ranch put AI to work in a peer-reviewed case study, “Revolutionizing Agritourism with AI and Machine Learning: A Case Study of Prairie Ridge Buffalo Ranch in Colorado,” published in 2025 in CABI Tourism Cases.
Surveys and interviews she conducted with other users showed that people find it’s easy to use the bot, learn from it, and act on its advice, she says. She is preparing the full results for publication.
Her work extends beyond agritourism. In 2026, she contributed an AI assistant to Project Pythia, an open-science program funded by the U.S. National Science Foundation and led by the National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR). The AI assistant turns raw airport weather report data into plain-language guidance for farmers and other non-technical users, and it tells users when data is missing rather than guessing.
She also teaches workshops on AI tools such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini. She has taught her workshop 20 times to more than 200 entrepreneurs and business owners, who came from 32 Colorado counties. In follow-up surveys, 90 percent of participants reported trying at least one new AI task in their business. Some of the workshops take place at a community center run by the Logan County Economic Development Corp., in Sterling. She has also co-hosted the workshops with the Rural Community Assistance Corp., Colorado Startup Week, and Boulder Startup Week. And she occasionally presents them as webinars, so people don’t have to travel.
Her outreach has taught her that many farmers are eager to try new tools, she says. She shows them how simple her chatbot is to use.
She also offers advice to high school students drawn to the field. Extension specialists each have a specialty, such as livestock, natural resources, food systems, or 4-H. Students should pick one based on their passion, she says.
Land-grant universities offer related programs at the bachelor’s and master’s levels. For graduate students, she adds, Extension offers a third career path beyond academia and industry: “You apply advanced skills directly to the communities that need them.”
How IEEE membership supports her career
Dong joined IEEE in 2025 and soon was elevated to senior member. Her professional home is the IEEE Society on Social Implications of Technology. She also serves as vice treasurer of the IEEE Denver Section’s Young Professionals group.
IEEE supports all three parts of her job, she says. For research, she presented “Entrepreneur AI Agent: Empowering Small Businesses and Bridging the Digital Divide through Context-Aware Generative AI” at the 2026 IEEE Global Humanitarian Technology Conference (GHTC). For teaching, she has offered to bring her AI workshop to Denver Section members and local entrepreneurs. For service, she reviews papers for IEEE conferences.
IEEE conferences matter most to her, she says: “Through them, I can present my research and network with other researchers in the field.”
She attended the IEEE World Forum on Public Safety Technology in Boulder, Colo., in September 2026. The event, she says, opened her eyes to many new projects underway across IEEE.
Still, she says, her work always points back to the farms and ranches of eastern Colorado. Its people are curious, she says, but they can’t make the leap to new technology alone.
“They really need this kind of a bridge,” she says.

Willie Jones is an associate editor at IEEE Spectrum. In addition to editing and planning daily coverage, he manages several of Spectrum's newsletters and contributes regularly to the monthly Big Picture section that appears in the print edition.

articles.title: Float to open Montréal office, invest $5 million in Québec expansion | BetaKit
articles.text:
Fresh off closing its Series C round, Float is expanding its presence in Québec with a new office.
The news: Toronto-based FinTech company Float Financial, which provides banking and AI-powered financial management services for small and medium-sized businesses, announced on Thursday that it’s committing $5 million to grow its Québec presence and open an office in Montréal, its first outside of Toronto. Float said it plans to hire a general manager for the region and expand its team in sales, product support, and customer success.
From the source: The news comes as a growing share of Float’s customer base leans into AI. An August study of its business customers found that monthly AI spending has increased by more than twelvefold over the past two years, while 47 percent of businesses buy at least one AI product, up from 27 percent.
The context: Founded in 2019, Float got its start offering Canadian small and medium-sized businesses corporate cards and expense management software to simplify their spending. It has since grown to serve more than 10,000 customers, including Cohere and Clutch. It has roughly 1,000 customers in Québec, including medtech company Puzzle Medical Devices.
The company recently released its AI intelligence layer, which can automate tasks for finance teams, like tracking down receipts, data entry, and payment reconciliation. It also just brought on Jack Fraser as its first CFO; Fraser invested in Float while he was at BDC Capital.
Final thought: Float is part of a cohort of FinTech companies that joined the non-profit national organization Payments Canada as members this year, setting the stage for it to build on top of national payment infrastructure like the new Real-Time Rail. This week, CEO Rob Khazzam said Float can now directly facilitate pre-authorized debit requests from third-party financial institutions without a “middleman,” which wouldn’t have been possible without its new Payments Canada designation.
Feature image courtesy Float.

articles.title: Report finds workers are staying around at their jobs — but many say that's because they feel stuck
articles.text:
Report finds workers are staying around at their jobs — but many say that's because they feel stuck
Is AI affecting stability?
- Workday study finds workers feel "stuck" in their roles due to lack of prospects
- European markets have higher two-year retention job rate than the global average
- But many workers say they feel less supported by their employers
Despite widespread promises that AI is going to make workers happier and more productive, new research has found many are feeling less confident in their future.
Workday's European Workforce Report found that across the continent, retention rates are rising, and in fact are higher than the global average - but AI may be having a more negative effect than leaders might think.
Although retention rates seem encouraging, the report found workers feel less supported by their employer, with many saying they feel underappreciated and even stuck in their current role with no chance of moving forward.
Work work work
Workday's report found every European market it analyzed has a higher two-year retention rate than the global average of 69.6%, with Germany leading the way at 78.8%.
Yet more than a third (34%) of workers in key markets including the UK, France, and Germany say they feel stuck in their current role due to a lack of prospects in a weak job market.
Many of these workers also said they feel less supported by their employers, with just over half (54%) saying they feel their employer cares about them as a person, compared with 59% globally.
Despite three-quarters (75%) of workers saying they know which skills they need to succeed, a much lower number (62%) say their employer is actually helping them build the skills they will need next.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
And despite most workers admitting they have received AI training from their employer, fewer than four in 10 in the UK (37%), France (36%), and Germany (39%) expect AI to create new opportunities in their careers.
Ironically, the study also found many job seekers are now using AI tools to look for a new role - with 84% admitting so - but only 34% said AI led them to apply for more jobs.
“Europe’s companies are holding on to their people, and on paper that looks like a strength,” said Angelique De Vries-Schipperijn, president, EMEA, Workday.
“But when a third of workers say they’re staying because they feel stuck, leaders should hear that as a warning. AI is hanging many jobs, and the people who stay need to see where they fit in what comes next.”

articles.title: Why AI-enabled scientific research is a double-edged sword
articles.text:
OpenAI has sparked a backlash in the mathematics community by apparently using AI to solve more than 700 longstanding maths problems in a short space of time. A recent open letter signed by 28 recipients of the Fields Medal (one of the highest honours in maths) goes some way to explaining why.
Mathematicians who have gone through some of the solutions offered by AI say they are opaque in their reasoning. As the open letter explains: “Solving problems is only a tool and proxy for achieving the primary goal of conceptual understanding and insight.”
As famed mathematician and Fields Medal winner Terence Tao put it: “These companies are dumping carcasses of raw meat onto our communal village table and saying: ‘Here you go, I solved your food problem.‘”
OpenAI said it had consulted with the community prior to announcing the latest three results, one of which was in my own field of computer science.
Nevertheless, mathematicians are having to adapt fast to the disruptive arrival of AI in their field. This challenge extends far beyond mathematics and into all other disciplines of science and research.
The impact AI has had on software development through tools such as Claude and Codex, is undeniable. Industry software teams are now routinely using AI tools in their work.
But now, AI is already having a major impact on the practice of science itself. Academic journals and conferences are dealing with exponential increases in submissions from researchers, in a system largely based on volunteer effort for reviewing and editing.
Breaking peer review?
This year, the International Conference on Learning Representations, a leading academic meeting on AI, received 60,000 submissions. This has increased from 490 in 2017. One researcher, commenting on the figures, said: “AI is breaking traditional academic peer review.”
This doesn’t seem to be a special case. In 2024, Mark A Hanson, from the University of Exeter, and colleagues, published a paper titled: “The strain on scientific publishing”. In it, the authors note that the total number of available academic articles has grown exponentially in recent years.
This is in part the result of a decades-long trend, predating modern generative AI, with many factors playing a role – including pressure on researchers to publish large numbers of academic articles, known as “publish or perish”. In 2022, just before ChatGPT launched, the number of papers published was about 47% higher than in 2016. The increase has occurred while the number of practising scientists has seen little growth. But AI is undoubtedly accelerating the process.
Yet this raises questions about whether the current trajectory is sustainable – and whether the quality of science will suffer. One academic conference has been testing whether AI could be part of the solution as well as the problem. This year, the NeurIPS meeting, which focuses on AI and machine learning, introduced a voluntary AI-assisted review for those submitting conference abstracts.
Afterwards, scientists evaluated the quality of the review and how helpful it was. But some in the field believe this could compound current problems.
Protecting critical thinking
Anecdotal evidence suggests some members of the public who are not professional scientists are using AI to produce and submit their own academic papers and write books on science. Citizen scientists make valuable contributions in areas such as biodiversity monitoring and astronomy.
But AI should not be viewed as a substitute for the formal training, daily research work, critical thinking and expert input from colleagues that academia offers. While AI and related technologies are powerful tools for democratising knowledge, it took me 13 years from my PhD to write my first book (the only one I have written so far), whereas now the same can apparently be done in weeks. But, as with peer review and maths proofs, humans have to check and interpret these.
As this story plays through and repeats, we may need to resort to new modes of scientific dissemination to deal with the new methods of creating research.
This brings me to the critical thinking that research requires. Currently, I provide the ideas, but increasingly rely on my AI assistant to do a lot of the work of thinking for me, or at least appear to. But the results of AI-enabled research can be obtuse, as the Terence Tao quote above illustrates, or even plain wrong. They can only be sorted out with human time and domain expertise.
I increasingly wonder what this means for the role of the researcher and for training the future generation of scientists, mathematicians and engineers. I am finding that a challenging, long term student project that would normally take several months to complete is at risk of being able to be almost completely automated through providing judicious prompts to an AI agent.
If I am guiding the student while they provide the prompts to an AI system, what do they learn from the process? And in my own research, where AI enables me to undertake projects I would not otherwise have the resources to, if I am providing the ideas but the AI is doing a lot of the “thinking” for me, am I even doing my own research anymore?
This could have an impact on the future generation’s ability to generate novel research questions, as well as their capacity for critiquing AI’s attempts to answer them.
One of my favourite sci-fi short stories is Profession, by Isaac Asimov. In it, the author imagines a future where young adults are educated by direct upload into their brains using technology known as magnetic tapes – which could be seen as a stand-in for AI. At one point, the main protagonist, George, tries to convince another character that humans can learn in other ways – by reading books, for example.
The other person is baffled, seeing this only as an unnecessary expense. Through the narrative, Asimov reveals the risks in the “direct upload” approach to learning. He also explores what is needed for society to progress when some forms of knowledge can be gained so easily.
We seem to be arriving at the science fiction future I once looked forward to where, like a science officer on a starship exploring unknown corners of the universe, or a billionaire genius tech superhero, I can just provide the ideas while getting the computer to do the heavy lifting. Like others, I am exhilarated by this, but also concerned about what it means for the practice and future of my discipline.

articles.title: Some creators are skeptical of Instagram’s new affiliate program
articles.text:
For years, influencers have come up with workarounds on social media to figure out how to share affiliate links with followers. A new integration between Instagram and Amazon was announced earlier this month as a way to make it easier for influencers to make money from affiliate links — but some content creators are suspicious about who really benefits.
Some creators are skeptical of Instagram’s new affiliate program
Influencers are now able to link their Amazon and Instagram accounts to promote products. Some are concerned about what they’re opting in to.
The new integration allows creators to connect their Instagram and Amazon accounts and automatically tag products with their affiliate links, from which they earn a commission when followers make purchases. Influencers will be able to embed up to 30 product links in a Reel or 20 in a feed post, but a permissions setting has led to concerns about what creators are actually agreeing to.
In connecting an Amazon account, creators must agree to allow the retailer and its brand sellers to create ads from “any public content” that includes a related affiliate link. Influencers must also agree to acknowledge that brands can edit their content and use their “testimonial, caption or media” for ads.
The wide-ranging permissions are giving creators pause. Some have urged peers not to connect their accounts without reviewing the permissions and understanding how the feature would affect earnings. People making money on social media spend years tweaking their content and strategy to maximize reach, engagement, and, by extension, their bottom line. For some, it appeared that they would be giving Amazon and its sellers the ability to use their content under unclear terms. On Instagram head Adam Mosseri’s post announcing the feature, influencers complained about the lack of clarity, questioned whether using the feature would decrease their reach (which some creators say happens when they link to outside products), and demanded answers to whether their commission rate would stay the same when Amazon or brands use their content for ads.
Linking products through the new integration won’t reduce reach, Jimmy O’Keefe, Instagram’s director of product marketing, said in an email to The Verge. O’Keefe also noted that creators will continue to earn commission through affiliate links when Amazon boosts their posts, and that they can stop the boosting in settings or disconnect the integration entirely. There’s also a separate, manual way to add products without linking accounts, if a creator wants to opt out of having their content made into ads.
Amazon has an enormous influencer program that reaches across social media platforms. It is so lucrative that some content creators are able to make a living almost exclusively by hawking products for sale on Amazon, building empires on the shopping habits of their followers. When it comes to putting those links in front of followers, though, social platforms have historically been a roadblock, hence the cottage industry of link-in-bio tools meant to circumvent limits. Slowly but surely, though, platforms like Instagram, Facebook, and YouTube — perhaps chasing the success of TikTok Shop — have added more and more shopping features. The result is that shopping and social media begin to feel more and more like the same thing.

articles.title: Así está el mercado laboral de tecnología: una de cada seis ofertas pide IA, solo uno de cada 60 programadores la pone en su currículum
articles.text:
Así está el mercado laboral de tecnología: una de cada seis ofertas pide IA, solo uno de cada 60 programadores la pone en su currículum
Los puestos de trabajo en España para desarrolladores muestran el crecimiento rápido de la inteligencia artificial y las dificultades para encontrar puestos júnior
El 98% de los programadores españoles usa ya la IA cada día y el 86% dice que así es más productivo. Esa presencia cotidiana inunda inexorablemente el mercado laboral tecnológico: una de cada seis ofertas ya pide IA, pero solo uno de cada sesenta perfiles tiene algo de IA en su currículum. La aparición de la IA es la que más crece en las ofertas, ya aparece en el 15,7%, y las que mencionan agentes de IA se han multiplicado por ocho. La IA también provoca ya la creación de roles propios, como el “ingeniero de IA”, que reúne varios perfiles anteriores y que tiene 20 veces más demanda que en 2023.“Para la gran mayoría de profesionales tech del país, incluir la IA en su currículo va a ser prácticamente una obligación si quieren encontrar oportunidades”, destaca el nuevo informe de Manfred, del que salen los datos citados.
La empresa Manfred, que reúne una comunidad de más de 125.000 programadores, aborda en su último trabajo las ofertas y profesionales del sector en los últimos 12 meses con datos de TheirStack, plataforma que rastrea el sector y ha reunido más de 165.000 ofertas. Este crecimiento en el uso de la IA ya provoca que el mérito no sea solo usarla, sino revisar el código que escribe. “El cuello de botella ahora está en la revisión”, dice un directivo en el informe. Amazon acaba de añadir este detalle en una guía interna para ingenieros: el puesto no se define por cuánta IA uses, sino por el impacto y por saber explicar dónde no ayuda.
Además de mucha IA, el informe detecta otra tendencia: la dificultad para acceder al mundillo de la gente con menos de dos años de trabajo en el sector. Uno de cada cinco apenas tiene experiencia, pero este grupo solo recibe un 4,4% de las ofertas. La mediana en salario de esas ofertas (25.500 euros) es muy parecida a la mediana general en España. El mejor campo para entrar en el sector es la ciberseguridad, más de moda ahora por los posibles ataques usando precisamente modelos de IA. También hay ofertas junior buenas para analistas de datos.
Los puestos más tradicionales para desarrolladores que acaban de empezar casi han desaparecido. La IA tiene obviamente parte de responsabilidad: “Si antes contratabas 10 y ahora contratas uno, me voy a uno que sea senior”, dice un directivo anónimo en el informe. “La IA no va a cerrar la puerta junior: la va a cambiar de sitio”, dice el propio informe. “Con asistentes [de IA] que escriben el código de base, lo que vale de un junior ya no es picar rápido, sino entender pronto el negocio. Las empresas que lo entiendan antes tendrán cantera; las demás, una guerra por seniors cada vez más caros”, añade.
Los salarios, un misterio
Los salarios concretos suponen uno de los grandes misterios. Solo una de cada 10 ofertas publica una horquilla del sueldo. En los que hay ese dato, el informe comprueba que las compensaciones están casi congeladas desde 2023. Un programador ha pasado de 39.000 a 37.500 euros en esos años. Solo suben las que piden IA. En la diferencia de sueldos hay un detalle clave: cuenta mucho qué tipo de empresa contrate. Las start-ups en crecimiento o las big tech globales tienen sueldos internacionales. Las consultoras o las enormes empresas nacionales juegan en una liga menor.
El informe también incluye datos interesantes sobre la distribución geográfica de las ofertas y la brecha de género. Si eres ingeniero, te conviene vivir en Madrid o, un poco menos, en Cataluña. En Madrid viven el 28% de los profesionales y tienen la mitad de las ofertas. Si unimos Cataluña, entre ambas reúnen la mitad de los profesionales y cuatro de cada cinco ofertas. Aunque sigue habiendo mucho trabajo remoto, el híbrido (donde hay que ir algún día a la oficina) aumenta. Así que quienes viven fuera de los dos motores económicos, lo tienen más complicado. En Andalucía, Galicia y Comunidad Valenciana viven el 28% de profesionales, pero solo tienen el 13% de las ofertas. En cambio, Málaga ya es la tercera ciudad nacional por número de ofertas.
Las mujeres, que son aproximadamente el 15% de profesionales, solo logran la paridad en un tipo de trabajo: diseño de producto y experiencia de usuario. En la mayoría del resto de perfiles no llega al 10%. Su brecha salarial crece con la experiencia: es del 0,4% con menos de dos años de experiencia, pero del 13,4% a partir de 10 años, unos 8.300 euros anuales.
Otro de los grandes cambios son las entrevistas o pruebas para contratar: la IA ha llegado para quedarse. Entre las empresas con las que habló Manfred, el 46% ha rediseñado su prueba técnica por la IA, y de ellas el 67% ha eliminado la prueba en casa. Los formatos nuevos de entrevistas consisten en programar en directo con un asistente de IA o retocar código generado.
Además de la IA, hay otro gran ámbito que está superando a todos los ingenieros que se formaron con la web: la nube. En Kubernetes, un sistema que gestiona de forma automática las aplicaciones que funcionan en la nube, la demanda duplica la oferta. Algo similar ocurre con Azure y Google Cloud, las nubes de Microsoft y Google, y Terraform, que permite crear y configurar infraestructura en la nube. En cambio, sobran ya JavaScript, que lo usa el 45% de programadores y lo pide solo el 16% de las ofertas, CSS o React, tres tecnologías web. Las ofertas de IA piden sobre todo Python, un lenguaje de programación, pero luego ya en seguida exigen saber manejar agentes de IA.

articles.title: Las dos oleadas de nerviosismo global por el lanzamiento de GTA VI: así se sufrieron las caídas más importantes de la PlayStation Network
articles.text:
Las dos oleadas de nerviosismo global por el lanzamiento de GTA VI: así se sufrieron las caídas más importantes de la PlayStation Network
El número más alto de problemas se reporta poco antes del estreno en India y el segundo pico coincide aproximadamente con el lanzamiento en EE UU, pero no coincidiendo con las medianoches, hora del estreno
Justo a la medianoche, cuando miles de personas estaban frente a su consola contando los minutos para poder jugar GTA VI, la red de PlayStation presentó problemas para concretar la conexión. La caída no se ha dado de manera simultánea en todo el mundo, sino que se ha registrado en momentos diferentes, según ha reportado el portal DownDetector. Ha empezado poco antes de que iniciara oficialmente el 19 de noviembre, fecha de estreno del nuevo videojuego que ha desatado la locura de jóvenes y adultos, y ha acabado horas después, ya durante la madrugada.
A nivel mundial, según un análisis de los datos de esta página, se distinguen dos oleadas de avisos de problemas en PlayStation Network y no siguen las medianoches locales: la primera oleada se produce poco antes del estreno en India y la segunda coincide aproximadamente con el lanzamiento en Estados Unidos.
La caída de PlayStation Network, según el reporte de los usuarios ansiosos por probar las novedades del último lanzamiento de Rockstar North, no coincidió con la medianoche local; sin embargo, la caída del propio videojuego sí. En España, según los mismos datos de DownDetector, los incidentes iniciaron a las 17.16 de ayer, se intensificaron a las 22.31 y llegaron a su punto máximo a las 00.01 de este 19 de noviembre. Los problemas más notificados han tenido relación con la conexión al servidor, en un 38%; con el inicio del juego, en un 13%; y con el videojuego en sí, en un 50%.
En otros países, como el Reino Unido, los problemas de conexión directamente con el videojuego, y no con la red de conexión, se han replicado casi en la misma franja horaria, pero con 60 minutos de retraso, por el huso horario del territorio británico. En este caso, los incidentes empezaron a llegar de manera masiva a las 18.18 (británicas), pero alcanzaron su punto máximo exactamente dos horas después, a las 22.18. Para la medianoche, a diferencia de España, los reportes de caídas fueron bajando, de 134 a 88 incidentes registrados, y se normalizaron cerca de las dos de la madrugada.
Además de los incidentes recogidos por DownDetector, Sony también reconoció los problemas en sus servicios de juegos y funciones, con dificultades para ejecutar aplicaciones y utilizar herramientas online. El incidente alcanzó a distintas generaciones de consolas, desde la PlayStation 3 hasta la 5, además del PS Vita (una consola portátil) y el acceso desde la web, según el aviso de la compañía recogido por Android Authority. El portal de PlayStation Network explicaba que, si se intentaba iniciar sesión, los usuarios podrían encontrarse con dificultades para acceder a las funciones de la red.
Para el mediodía, hora peninsular española, los servicios se encontraban funcionando casi con normalidad, con algunos reportes mínimos que fueron llegando a DownDetector a lo largo de la mañana.

articles.title: Microsofts KI-Framework verteilt Malware: So konnten sich Angreifer Zugang verschaffen
articles.text:
Microsofts KI-Framework verteilt Malware: So konnten sich Angreifer Zugang verschaffen
Erst in jüngster Vergangenheit musste Microsoft einen großen Ausfall der Microsoft-365-Dienste verkraften, jetzt folgt schon der nächste Schlag für das Unternehmen. Wie mehrere Sicherheitsforscher:innen berichten, wurde Malware im Agent-Framework des Konzerns eingeschleust. Mit dem Framework können User:innen ihre eigenen KI-Agenten in Python, .NET und Go bauen.
Wie landet Malware in Microsofts KI-Framework?
Laut den Expert:innen von Ox Security steckt die Malware in den Versionen 1.26.1 und 1.26.2 des KI-Frameworks. Die Tools, die Microsoft Entwickler:innen an die Hand gibt, werden im Schnitt etwa 200.000 Mal im Monat heruntergeladen. Es könnten also eine Reihe von User:innen von dem Schadcode betroffen sein. Die Malware hat es dabei auf Logindaten von diversen Diensten abgesehen.
Ist der Infostealer erst einmal im System, kann er Anmeldedaten von Diensten wie Azure, Git, Docker, Hugging Face und anderen für Entwickler:innen relevanten Webseiten und Apps auslesen und an die Hinterleute schicken. In dem Paket für Python findet sich die Datei „agent_framework_meta.pth“, die eine Zeile enthält. Darin steht „import agent_framework_meta“. Diese Zeile wird immer dann ausgeführt, wenn ein Programm Python ausführt. Sobald sich die Malware festgesetzt hat, verteilt sie sich also über eine Reihe von Python-Projekten hinweg.
Laut OX Security könnten sich die Angreifer:innen Zugang zu Microsoft-Logins verschafft haben, um die Malware in das Framework einzubetten. Demnach wurde die zunächst infizierte Version 1.26.1 von Microsoft auf die sichere Version 1.26.0 zurückgestuft. Danach konnten die Cyberkriminellen aber noch eine weitere infizierte Version, 1.26.2, hochladen. Dieses Update enthielt einen anderen Weg der Malware-Aktivierung, führte aber schließlich zum selben Infostealer.
Gegenüber The Register betonte Microsoft, dass das Unternehmen den Angriff untersucht. Um die Untersuchungen umfassend durchführen zu können, wurden einige Microsoft-Repositories auf GitHub vorübergehend auf „privat“ gestellt. Wie Opensource Malware schreibt, die den Schadcode ebenfalls entdeckt haben, müssen Betroffene, die das KI-Framework genutzt haben, handeln.
Zunächst sollten alle aktiven Projekte gestoppt und möglicherweise infizierte Systeme isoliert werden. Ferner sollten alle Zugänge, die auf dem System genutzt wurden, erneuert werden. Bei den betroffenen Diensten sollten User:innen die Aktivitäten genau im Blick behalten, um zu sehen, ob sich jemand Zugang verschaffen konnte.
