articles.text:
Wazzup. ☀️️
Anthropic, one of the most recognisable AI companies, is going public today. The Claude maker is heading to Nasdaq, where investors will finally get a price tag on the AI hype.
Like Anthropic, we’re making our own entrance. Yesterday in Cape Town, Tomiwa Aladekomo, chief executive officer of Big Cabal Media, parent company of TechCabal, announced TC Mzansi, our new newsletter for Southern Africa’s tech ecosystem, launching on November 23. Expect the big moves, the important stories, and our usual wit. Keep your eyes peeled.
TC Mzansi, our newsletter covering South African tech is coming on November 23.
Capital Markets
Fifth time’s the charm; Egypt’s Misr Life to list on EGX in December
Egypt’s stock market has had a busy quarter. October brought the successful listing of fintech unicorn MNT-Halan, which listed its Egyptian business. In November, Banque du Caire, the country’s sixth-largest commercial bank, saw its shares barely move on their first trading day despite a record-breaking initial public offering (IPO). December’s next major listing is a 126-year-old insurance giant.
Misr Life Insurance, one of Egypt’s largest life insurers, plans to sell a 15% stake on the Egyptian Exchange (EGX) in December. Its state-owned parent, Misr Insurance Holding Company, will offer 750 million existing shares to local and international investors, subject to regulatory approval.
Explain like I’m new here: Misr Life has been around since 1900. It’s also been trying to go public for nearly a decade. Its first planned listing was scheduled for 2019, before being pushed to 2020, 2022, and 2023. After years in the waiting room, the insurer finally has another date with the stock market.
Here’s what investors are getting: Misr Life controls 26.3% of Egypt’s life insurance market and manages an investment portfolio worth over EGP 100 billion ($1.86 billion). It earned EGP 5.2 billion ($97 million) in the first half of 2026, nearly matching its EGP 5.8 billion ($107.9 million) profit for all of 2025.
The company is also dangling a sweetener: it aims to distribute 70% of its 2026 net income as dividends, subject to the necessary approvals.
There’s a tech angle, too: On November 13, Misr Life became Egypt’s first life insurer to receive a fintech licence, according to Egypt’s State Information Service, its national media outlet. The licence allows it to offer services such as policy pricing, payments, and claims online. It wants digital channels to generate about 30% of new business by 2030.
Between the lines: Egypt is selling stakes in state-owned businesses to attract private investors and raise money as it tackles a heavy debt burden. The government is also under pressure to meet its asset-sale commitments to the International Monetary Fund (IMF). This month, state-owned Banque Misr sold a 45% stake in Banque du Caire through an IPO, raising $658 million towards that target.
But there’s an important distinction: Misr Life isn’t raising fresh capital through this IPO. Its parent company gets the proceeds because it’s selling shares it already owns. The state gets a payday. Misr Life gets new shareholders. However, the price for Egypt’s oldest insurance giant has to be right for retail investors to feel like they’re getting a bargain.
Upgrade your business today
Pay with OPay is live on Fincra. Customers approve payments straight from their OPay wallet, and you get confirmation back on your site. Available now for NGN collections! Upgrade your business today with Fincra pay with OPay.
Fintech
Wave breaks into DRC’s mobile money market
For 11 years, the Democratic Republic of Congo’s (DRC) mobile money market was exclusive. Four operators entered, built their businesses, acquired customers, and made money. Nobody new got a licence. Now, Wave has managed to get past the velvet rope.
What happened? Wave, the Senegal-based fintech unicorn, has received approval from the Central Bank of Congo (BCC) to operate as an electronic-money institution (EMI) in the DRC. The licence allows it to issue and manage digital money in the country.
Explain like I’m new here: Wave is the first new entrant to secure this licence since 2015. Between 2012 and 2015, the regulator issued licences to Airtel Money, Orange Money, Vodacash (M-PESA), and Afrimobile Money—mostly telecom-owned mobile money operators. The government didn’t announce a ban on fintechs from the market.
Between the lines: The problem was structural, as telecom operators already controlled the infrastructure that made mobile money work, including USSD channels and agent networks where customers could deposit and withdraw cash. Independent fintechs fought an uphill battle without owning or controlling similar infrastructure.
That left four players with a considerable head start, and they used it well. As of 2025, Vodacash/M-PESA, the Safaricom-owned mobile money company, held a 40.1% market share in DRC; Airtel Money had 23.8%; Orange Money had 34.4% market share, while Afrimoney had 1.7% of the market.
Wave is in the ring now: Wave’s West African strategy has leaned heavily on affordable transfers, including its widely recognised 1% transfer fee. In the region, the company has grown to about 18 million users across several French-speaking countries such as Senegal, Côte d’Ivoire, and Cameroon. That scale gives Wave some experience competing in markets where mobile money is well established. However, it will still be playing catch-up in DRC.
Funding
EBRD lends $100 million to Egypt’s small businesses
Egypt has frozen new microfinance licences. Apparently, nobody said anything about freezing the money.
The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD), the development finance institution, is lending up to $100 million to the National Bank of Egypt (NBE), the country’s largest bank, to help small businesses access credit. Women-led businesses and entrepreneurs outside major cities are among the intended beneficiaries.
Follow the money: The $100 million isn’t going straight into entrepreneurs’ bank accounts. NBE will pass the funds to eligible microfinance institutions, which will then lend to small businesses. Think of a woman running a tailoring shop in rural Egypt who needs money to buy more sewing machines. A local microfinance lender could use this funding to give her a loan, which she’d repay under the agreed terms.
The EBRD will also provide training and technical support to help NBE strengthen its lending operations, it said in its announcement.
Explain like I’m new here: The EBRD has been financing Egyptian businesses since 2012, investing nearly €17 billion ($19.7 billion) across 245 projects. It has partnered with NBE before, including a separate $100 million facility announced in 2025 to support smaller businesses.
Here’s the twist: Last Friday, Egypt’s Financial Regulatory Authority (FRA) extended its freeze on new microfinance and consumer lending licences until October 2027. The regulator wants to strengthen the existing market before letting more lenders in.
Zoom out: The latest deal shows Egypt isn’t trying to slow down small-business lending. It’s directing fresh capital through institutions already authorised to operate. The money could help existing lenders reach more borrowers, but it won’t necessarily make loans cheaper or easier to obtain. Much will depend on the terms those lenders offer and the businesses they choose to serve.
Social Media
X and xAI settle South Africa media dispute with publisher training
Elon Musk’s social media company X and his AI company xAI have agreed to play ball with South Africa’s competition watchdog. The companies have settled a dispute over measures intended to help local news publishers earn more money from digital platforms and gain control over how their content is used.
Under the agreement announced on Wednesday, X will let eligible publishers earn money from their content, offer them training, and give qualifying publishers two years of free Premium subscriptions. xAI will help them control how its Grok chatbot accesses their websites.
Explain like I’m new here: In October 2023, South Africa’s Competition Commission launched an inquiry into how digital platforms were affecting the economics of local media. The concern was that companies such as Google, Meta, TikTok, and X benefited from journalism to attract audiences and advertising, while publishers lost traffic and advertising revenue.
In November 2025, the commission published its final recommendations, proposing measures to address the imbalance. Google and YouTube agreed to a R688 million ($40 million) media-support package over five years. Meta and TikTok also accepted publisher-support and monetisation commitments. However, X and xAI challenged the recommendations before the Competition Tribunal.
So, what did X and xAI agree to? X will now give publishers access to its monetisation programmes, run workshops twice a year, and provide its Premium subscription tier free for two years where publishers need it to qualify. The programme must launch within six months. xAI will teach publishers how to manage Grok’s settings and use robots.txt, a file that tells automated crawlers which parts of a website they can access.
What does this mean for South Africa? The settlement gives South African publishers and local media companies another way to earn from their presence on X, handing them more control over how AI crawlers access their websites. However, it does not guarantee additional revenue or compensate publishers for content already used to train AI models.

articles.title: Can AI Really Engineer Its Way to Superintelligence?
articles.text:
Why a Computer Scientist Thinks Superintelligence Won’t Happen
Yet trying for it may still be disastrous
Many people were caught off guard this past summer when employees of one of the world’s leading AI companies began casually debating whether their products would lead to human extinction. It started when Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon announced his resignation, warning that his employer and OpenAI were “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” Evan Hubinger, Anthropic’s head of alignment science, replied, “Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” And Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei subsequently told CNN, “I agree with Jacob much more than I disagree with him.”
These concerns stem from a belief that has circulated in futurist circles for many decades: Once engineers design an AI system capable of improving itself, it will trigger an accelerating cycle of autonomous upgrades known as recursive self-improvement (RSI). The result will be artificial superintelligence (ASI), a system with cognitive capabilities so vastly exceeding those of humans that it will easily evade our control and perhaps even wipe out our species. Artificial superintelligence is, it should be noted, a far more ambitious goal than artificial general intelligence (AGI), which generally refers to AI that can match human capabilities across a broad range of cognitive tasks.
These ideas have prompted varied reactions. Some argue that the concept of ASI is being used for marketing or to instigate regulation that will help the incumbent labs squash new competitors. Others focus on the plausibility of such systems killing us all, debating the finer points of specific scenarios such as AI-engineered superviruses. Still others claim that aligning ASI to human interests is feasible and so we should rush ahead to usher in this digital utopia.
Amid these conversations, one question has received comparatively little attention: From an engineering perspective, is superintelligence even possible? The answer is important because it can help us calibrate our anxieties and develop the most effective possible responses to this emerging technology.
I recently explored this topic in a computer science doctoral seminar that I taught at Georgetown University, in Washington, D.C., in which my students and I examined the technical and cultural roots of the superintelligence story. (For those who are interested, we published an annotated bibliography of our class readings.) I came away with several key objections to the feasibility of ASI, which I’ll detail below, as well as a deeper fear that even if the promised intelligence explosion never arrives, pursuing it can still create real harm.
Objection #1: Recursive Self-Improvement Is Speculative
RSI is an old concept. In a 1965 paper, statistician I.J. Good speculated that a rapid cycle of AI self-improvement could lead to an “intelligence explosion.” The idea gained traction in the 1990s among the Extropians, a Bay Area futurist group, where it offered a way to discuss ASI without having to address the engineering details of how one would build such a system. The concept was taken up by such notable figures as Eliezer Yudkowsky (who later founded the rationalism movement) and Nick Bostrom (who helped steer effective altruism to focus more on existential risks to humanity).
Recently, however, this topic has shifted from thought experiment to practical engineering within both Anthropic (makers of Claude) and OpenAI (makers of ChatGPT). In a June blog post titled “When AI Builds Itself,” Anthropic described how LLM-powered agents are speeding up the writing, debugging, and optimization of code, and also automating parts of research such as running experiments and logging results. The company’s internal data, the report concluded, “is showing that AI is already accelerating the development of AI systems.” OpenAI has been similarly explicit about its intentions; in a September report, the company announced a goal of developing an automated researcher by March 2028.
But do these efforts put the companies on a trajectory toward uncontrollable RSI? Several obstacles undermine this claim. Consider the availability of the data needed to improve AI systems. Through 2023, major advances in LLMs came from scaling up the size of the models. The original GPT-1 had 117 million parameters (values learned during training that shape how the neural network processes information). This quantity jumped to 1.5 billion for GPT-2, to 175 billion for GPT-3, to (likely) more than a trillion for GPT-4’s release three years ago. After GPT-4, however, continued scaling began yielding diminishing returns. This led engineers to increasingly turn their attention toward “post-training” phases, where techniques from reinforcement learning are applied to improve an already trained model’s performance on specific tasks. This approach rewards a model for producing successful responses, helping it better produce similar answers in the future. It requires, however, lots of examples of relevant inputs paired with correct outputs.
Such datasets are relatively easy to generate in highly structured fields such as computer programming and mathematics, which helps explain why we’ve seen rapid and impressive advances in these narrow domains. Progress in areas that lack easy access to this type of training data has been less dramatic. This might explain why AI can tackle advanced theorems but struggles to empty an email inbox. “What if the jagged frontier is mainly math + code (which you can push arbitrarily far with [reinforcement learning techniques]),” the French AI researcher François Chollet recently hypothesized, “and everything else starts to plateau because it is still bottlenecked by human generated data?” The deployment of automated coding agents and LLM-powered researchers won’t overcome this fundamental limitation.
McKibillo
The Game of Superintelligence
How a decades-old thought experiment became an AI-industry ambition—and where it might lead
Key
• Idea: A concept, argument, or vision
• Technical advance: A scientific or engineering development
• Reality check: A challenge to assumptions about AI progress
1. Alan Turing
1936
Introduces the concept of a universal computing machine. He later proposes that machines could think, laying the foundations for AI.
Shows that some problems can’t be solved by any algorithm.
2. I. J. Good
1965
Proposes that an intelligent machine could design an even smarter one, setting off a potential “intelligence explosion.”
3. Backpropagation
1986
Geoffrey Hinton, David Rumelhart, and Ronald Williams demonstrate how backpropagation can train multilayer neural networks.
4. Vernor Vinge
1993
Proposes that an intelligent machine could design an even smarter one, setting off a potential “intelligence explosion.”
Notes that faster thinking alone isn’t enough for superintelligence: A faster-thinking dog still couldn’t play chess.
5. Nick Bostrom & Eliezer Yudkowsky
1990s–2000s
Bostrom and Yudkowsky discuss superintelligence in Extropian circles, then spread the idea to effective-altruist and rationalist circles, respectively.
6. Deep learning breakthroughs
2010s
Larger models, more data, and greater computing power produce rapid improvements in AI capabilities.
7. The race to self-improving AI
2020s
Dario Amodei and other AI leaders set their sights on superintelligence, with recursive self-improvement proposed as a path toward it.
8. Reality check
2020s
François Chollet questions whether LLMs’ current advances in math and coding will extend to domains where training data and reliable feedback are harder to obtain.
YOU ARE HERE
2026
AI systems are already accelerating AI development, and labs are working on automated researchers. But will this lead to an intelligence explosion?
1. The Intelligence Explosion
AI systems improve themselves at accelerating speed, surpass human intelligence, and potentially escape our control.
2. Danger Without Superintelligence
The intelligence explosion never arrives, but increasingly autonomous AI systems cause real-world harm through misuse, poor design, or loss of human control.
3. A Useful AI Future
Powerful, specialized AI tools bring major benefits, with constraints that make their behavior easier to predict and control.
Claims that RSI is imminent also understate the massive scientific efforts required for major AI advances. Consider the critical role of backpropagation, an algorithm that enables very large neural networks to learn by tuning internal parameters, layer by layer, to reduce errors in their predictions. This algorithm enabled the deep learning revolution, but it didn’t emerge ex nihilo in the minds of its creators. The influential 1986 paper on backpropagation by David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton, and Ronald Williams built on decades of critical breakthroughs in mathematics and computer science.
An intelligence explosion leading to ASI would similarly depend on a long sequence of innovations of comparable importance, which would build on many significant science and engineering advances that haven’t yet happened. This would require AI agents to somehow simulate, organize, and evaluate decades of worldwide scientific effort across numerous fields—an impossibly ambitious task. Indeed, recent research led by computer scientists at Princeton found that current AI tools had difficulty making autonomous progress even on highly constrained research questions. “Our results provide early evidence that today’s agents can do the engineering of AI research,” the researchers conclude, “but struggle with critical parts of the research life cycle.” The leap from this current reality to a future in which these same types of tools are automating science is almost too massive to imagine.
Finally, the RSI narrative downplays resource limitations. Tens of thousands of human brains have worked for decades, aided by increasingly powerful computers, to develop today’s AI systems, which can match human intelligence in some domains. That represents a massive investment in computation of both the biological and digital variety. What if the next intelligence level requires double the resources, and then the next level requires double again? Soon there would be no number of chips or data centers that we could build to provide the necessary compute and keep advancing toward ASI.
Pulling together these threads, I believe that the idea of RSI leading to an intelligence explosion is highly speculative and based on many unproven assumptions. While RSI isn’t definitively impossible, the idea demands more technical skepticism than it’s currently receiving. Carl Sagan’s adage that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence certainly applies here.
Objection #2: Superintelligence Might Not Be Computable
There’s an implicit claim in the superintelligence discourse that computers are theoretically capable of any calculation that can be imagined, so long as you can find a sufficiently smart algorithm, running on sufficiently powerful digital processors. In this context, RSI is merely a process for rapidly uncovering the special algorithms that can implement unimaginable smarts.
We cannot simply assume that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve.
But this is not how computer scientists think about computation. In his canonical 1937 paper, “On Computable Numbers,” Alan Turing proved a surprising and relevant result: Most problems cannot be solved by algorithms. His elegant proof established the space of possible problems to be uncountably infinite (like infinite precision decimal numbers), while the space of possible algorithms is only countably infinite (like whole numbers). Later breakthroughs in computational complexity theory established that of the problems that are technically solvable by computers, many would require an astronomically large amount of time and resources to crack, making them practically impossible to solve. Theoretical computer scientists, in other words, don’t assume that computers will solve everything; we’re instead excited whenever we find something that these machines happen to be able to efficiently handle.
We cannot simply assume, as the futurists often do, that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve. There might be some capabilities in which machines can obtain seemingly magical levels of performance, but there will also be many others that no machine, whether computer or human, will ever make much progress.
A relevant counterargument here emphasizes the speed of silicon chips compared to human neurons: Perhaps the sheer speed of digital computation can yield machines that run cognitive circles around our clunky brains, even if they’re not solving vastly more complicated problems than we’re already capable of tackling. But as the computer scientist and science fiction author Vernor Vinge pointed out, rapidity in cognition is not the same as intelligence. Speeding up the mind of a dog, he argued, wouldn’t enable the animal to play chess. Implementing roughly human-level intelligence on a faster machine might be impressive, but it’s not necessarily alarming.
At the moment, there’s a growing list of tasks that AI systems can perform better than humans, including winning complex games, identifying software bugs, and proving certain types of math theorems. It’s tempting to extrapolate from this specific progress to general mastery of every ability you might imagine. But it’s important to remember that the frontier of AI capabilities has always been jagged, with some research directions yielding impressive results and many others proving to be dead ends—a reality that would not have surprised Turing. More likely than a future dominated by an all-powerful superintelligence system is one in which we continue to painstakingly explore the space of problems well suited to AI, creating useful tools but falling well short of the digital deity predicted by the futurists.
Cal Newport, a computer science professor at Georgetown University, is skeptical that AI can achieve superintelligence through recursive self-improvement.
Penny Gray Photography
Objection #3: Alignment Isn’t Hard (Given the Right System Design)
Last fall, the prominent AI doomsday theorist Yudkowsky appeared on “The Ezra Klein Show” to talk about superintelligence. The episode was ominously titled “How Afraid of the A.I. Apocalypse Should We Be?” Klein and Yudkowsky quickly got into the difficulty of “alignment”—training an AI system to act in a manner that aligns with human interests. Yudkowsky argued that we are struggling to control our existing systems, which implies that we’ll have no chance of controlling the much smarter variations of this technology that are soon to follow.
To underscore his point, he referred to a disturbing incident described in the system card for OpenAI’s GPT-o1 model. OpenAI had set up a security challenge that instructed an LLM-powered coding system to break into a server to retrieve the contents of a protected file. But a configuration mistake prevented the server from launching, rendering the task impossible. Instead of giving up, the system exploited a security flaw to start a new instance of the server, adding a command that directly revealed the protected file’s contents. “It jumped out of the system,” explained Yudkowsky, adding: “This is not something that any human particularly programmed into it.”
Explore the Superintelligence Debate
In a Georgetown University doctoral seminar, Cal Newport and his students examined the intellectual history and technical plausibility of superintelligence. Explore their annotated bibliography of key papers.
Though this 2024 incident flew largely under the radar at the time, a more troubling episode made a bigger splash this summer. OpenAI revealed that one of the company’s models circumvented its restricted internet access to hack into Hugging Face servers, seeking information that would help it pass a cybersecurity evaluation—all without the knowledge of its human creators. OpenAI soon admitted that the Hugging Face attack was just one of many examples of its systems going rogue. An opinion article published in The Hill articulated a widely held reaction when it described this behavior as “something straight out of sci-fi.”
These examples seem to support Yudkowsky’s fear that AI will inevitably develop a mind of its own, a key step on the route to uncontrollable ASI. But a closer look reveals a less frightening picture. The systems involved in these hacking incidents were AI agents: programs that continually prompt an LLM to ask what actions to take next in pursuit of a goal. In the hacking incidents, this basic ask/act pattern was repeated in a long-running loop with minimal human supervision.
Using LLMs to suggest actions over long time horizons is a risky proposition. As any frequent chatbot user can attest, LLM outputs can be plausible and logical while still veering off in unexpected directions that violate commonsense human norms about what’s appropriate.
In the GPT-o1 incident, for example, it’s likely that the agent reported the error message caused by the server misconfiguration to the LLM. During its training, the LLM had probably encountered reports of similar error messages accompanied by instructions for how to restart the server in question, so it passed along similar instructions to the agent. This is a perfectly plausible response when considered in isolation, even if it led to actions that a human would immediately reject as violating the spirit of the experiment. Something similar helps explain the hacking attacks over the summer. The LLM suggesting a hack to succeed at a cybersecurity challenge is a perfectly plausible response, even if it’s not what the experimenters had in mind.
I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence.
The misaligned behavior that troubles commentators like Yudkowsky, therefore, doesn’t necessarily reveal something fundamental about advanced AI. It’s instead an expected side effect of the particular strategy of letting LLM outputs determine the actions of an autonomous agent without sufficient constraints. An obvious way to address these risks is to consider alternative architectures. Fortunately, there are many examples of AI systems that can complete tasks at human or superhuman levels without relying solely on LLM output to determine their actions.
Consider Tesla’s rapidly improving autonomous driving systems, or DeepMind’s AlphaFold, which helped win its developers a Nobel Prize in Chemistry for its ability to predict protein structures, or the AI game engines that can now beat humans in many popular pastimes, including chess, poker, Go, and the strategy game Diplomacy. None of these systems, impressive as they are, create concerns about going rogue. Their construction prevents such an outcome: Instead of prompting an LLM to generate an open-ended strategy for pursuing a general goal, these AIs consider much more limited spaces of possible actions. AlphaFold never surprises its users because its architecture does only one thing: It maps amino acid sequences to 3D protein structures. Tesla’s cars never unexpectedly form vehicle swarms because they’re asked only to avoid immediate obstacles, not to craft convoluted plans for achieving long-term objectives.
The implication of recent AI hacking attacks, therefore, is not a reflection of the difficulties of alignment. It is instead evidence that autonomous systems powered primarily by LLM prompts are unpredictable and possibly unsafe. More task-specific architectures can produce impressive performance much more safely, if we’re willing to put in the effort to develop them.
The Dangers of Chasing Superintelligence
Even if I’m correct that superintelligence is not a realistic engineering goal, this doesn’t mean we’re safe from harm. Merely pursuing ASI, as both OpenAI and Anthropic seem intent on doing, can create problems. Why, for example, did OpenAI persist in running its problematic hacking experiments over the summer, even after multiple warnings that the agents were likely to act unpredictably? Perhaps the company judged these risks acceptable collateral damage in the race to be the first to bring ASI into the world.
This fascination with superintelligence might also explain why OpenAI and Anthropic have both described RSI as a critical goal. As argued earlier, RSI is a concept from futurism and not computer science, and it isn’t necessary to build useful AI products. But if you believe achieving ASI is your destiny, pursuing recursive self-improvement becomes a primary objective. This matters because even if RSI never produces an intelligence explosion, it will almost certainly lead to systems that are harder for humans to understand and control. Which is why I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence.
What’s needed now is for engineers and scientists with no financial or ideological skin in the game to participate in the AI discourse. We cannot let a few AI companies with mixed motives dictate the terms for how we discuss this technology. If superintelligence is a shaky concept, experts need to say so. If agents powered by prompting LLMs aren’t the best path toward safe and productive AI, experts should argue that as well. For the past few years, we’ve let a small group of individuals from the Bay Area who have quirky beliefs and astonishing sums of money tell us how to think about their products. It’s time for those of us able to think for ourselves on these matters to stand up and declare, “We’ve heard what you had to say. Now it’s our turn.”

articles.title: Can AI Make Its Own Manufacturing Decisions?
articles.text:
AI can optimize processes and find defects, but autonomous decisions require better data and strict process controls.
Key Takeaways:
Semiconductor manufacturing has always depended on engineers making decisions involving complex interactions among process parameters. An etch recipe, for example, may involve combinations of RF power, pressure, gas chemistry, temperature, and timing, each affecting multiple process characteristics. Changing one parameter might improve critical dimension control while creating problems elsewhere. But as devices and manufacturing processes become more complicated, the growing number of variables involved makes those decisions increasingly difficult.
AI-driven manufacturing offers a way to manage some of that complexity, from finding better process conditions to identifying defects and responding to problems on the production line. But how much production responsibility engineers are willing to give those systems remains an open question, and one that drew considerable attention at SEMICON West 2026.
“No matter how good we are as engineers, no matter how disciplined and objective we are, we tend to approach these difficult problems with historical biases,” said David Fried, chief AI officer and corporate vice president of Semiverse Solutions at Lam Research during a conference panel. “A process engineer might look at a set of data and say, ‘I need to move into a lower-pressure, higher-power regime because that’s how we solved this problem 10 years ago.’ But with this massive parameter space, AI can point us in a different direction, into an operating region we might never have considered because we couldn’t see those relationships in the data before.”
Finding a process that keeps working
Finding an unfamiliar operating condition is useful, but determining whether it will hold up in production is another matter. Two recipes may produce similar results during development, yet respond quite differently to changes in incoming materials or equipment conditions. AI can help engineers identify those differences before committing to a particular process.
“It’s not just a question of delivering to a particular performance point. It’s also a question of how stable that particular performance point is, how robust it is,” said Vikas Sharma, senior principal engineer and senior director of pathfinding for Intel Foundry R&D, in a recent presentation. “Minor perturbations in the incoming material or at the tool can lead to a significant drop in performance.”
The scale of the optimization problem helps explain why AI-driven manufacturing is attracting so much interest. Fried described a current Lam Research etcher with a potential recipe space on the order of 10²³ combinations. At Intel, Sharma discussed a process involving 350 parameters and approximately 10⁷⁰⁰ theoretical combinations.
According to Sharma, engineers working with equipment suppliers spent about a year developing a minimally acceptable recipe for that particular tool and process layer, followed by an extended effort to improve it with limited success. After introducing AI-assisted optimization, they began finding better results within a few months, eventually identifying multiple solutions that improved on the original baseline.
The challenge was determining which solutions were worth pursuing. Sharma noted that AI could identify thousands of candidates, but evaluating them still required expensive silicon experiments. Engineers also had to account for nonlinear relationships among parameters, which could change considerably across different operating regions.
“AI is not a magic wand. You can’t use the same AI solution for every problem,” Fried said. “Figuring out whether you’re using full physical simulation, surrogate models, machine learning, deep learning, LLM-based AI, or agentic AI, which of these solutions you’re building in which form to solve which problem and address which workflow, that’s more of what we’re spending our time on than actually building it or implementing it.”
The different approaches serve different purposes, from exploring process conditions to coordinating engineering workflows. Combining them may allow engineers to investigate more possibilities, but it also raises questions about how the results should be validated and whether the assumptions used in one model remain appropriate when its recommendations are passed to another.
When the factory acts on what it sees
Inspection is one of the more established applications of AI in manufacturing, particularly in advanced packaging, where finer pitches and more complicated structures have increased the number of connections that must be examined. Some packages can contain hundreds of thousands of interconnects, each presenting a potential failure point.
Automated optical inspection and X-ray systems collect extensive information about those structures. Machine learning can identify variations that might be difficult to distinguish visually, but manufacturers still need to determine which differences indicate actual defects.
“When we look at X-rays, everybody just sees all shades of gray, but AI can see a thousand shades of gray,” said Ingu Yin Chang, executive vice president at ASE Group. “But the AI only knows if this shade of gray equates to a problem once we say, ‘Hey, this equates to a problem.’ So, you’ve got to have the physical data that says, ‘Okay, that is a problem.’ Then, in the future, they can scan for that shade of gray and that location.”
Once manufacturers determine which image characteristics correspond to actual defects, AI-enabled inspection systems can flag abnormalities during production and trigger predefined equipment responses. At ASE, systems can recognize known abnormalities and trigger equipment responses before additional assemblies are affected.
“We have figured out how to do a lot of automation and use AI to help us identify potential issues, based on the issues that we physically learned through traditional manufacturing methods,” Chang said. “We will know when a wire bond is not bonded correctly, and the machine will immediately stop. There’s constant AI oversight to ask, ‘Are we doing everything correctly? Are we seeing it as we planned to see it?’”
Stopping equipment when a defect is detected can prevent additional losses, but it doesn’t necessarily mean AI is controlling the process independently. The inspection system may identify an abnormal condition while a conventional controller executes a predefined response. Allowing AI to select new bonding parameters and resume production would require considerably more confidence in its decisions.
ASE’s product diversity makes that challenge more difficult. Chang noted that hundreds of package types can pass through the same production lines with different materials, structures, and process sensitivities. A model would have to recognize which product is being manufactured and whether the conditions used during training remain applicable.
An inspection system might correctly identify a defective bond, but changing the process to prevent another failure requires knowing what caused it and whether an adjustment will create problems elsewhere. Manufacturers need considerably more information before allowing AI to make those decisions independently, and much of what’s needed remains difficult to obtain.
Proving the model is right
One of the first obstacles to AI-driven manufacturing is establishing whether an AI recommendation accurately represents the physical process. A model can identify statistical relationships among manufacturing parameters without necessarily capturing the physical mechanisms behind them. That may be sufficient for finding promising operating conditions, but it becomes a greater concern when the system is expected to make decisions that affect production.
Sharma’s Intel example illustrates the problem. Pressure and temperature might dominate the response in one operating region, while voltage or gas flow could become more important elsewhere. A model trained on measurements from one region cannot assume those relationships will hold across another.
“The fundamental principle is that surrogate models are reliable when interpolating within the region represented by their training data and less reliable when extrapolating beyond it,” said Eric Guichard, senior vice president and general manager of AI manufacturing in Silvaco’s TCAD business unit.
Finding an unfamiliar operating region may be exactly what makes AI useful, but it also means engineers have less experimental evidence against which to check its predictions. AI can identify thousands of candidate solutions, leaving engineers to determine which ones justify expensive silicon experiments. Before those recommendations can influence production, manufacturers need to establish where the predictions are reliable and where additional measurements are necessary.
Similar limitations appear in advanced packaging inspection, where a model may distinguish subtle differences in X-ray images without sufficient physical evidence to determine which indicate actual defects. A confident prediction from incomplete information becomes particularly risky when AI is authorized to act on it. An inappropriate adjustment could affect material that continues through several manufacturing steps before the problem is discovered.
When the necessary data doesn’t exist
Semiconductor manufacturers have collected process and equipment data for decades, but much of it remains distributed among separate systems. Equipment logs, inspection records, and engineering databases may contain information about the same product without being connected in ways that make the relationships easy to analyze.
“The growing data challenge was there for us prior to AI,” Fried said. “Five to ten years ago, we really started rolling up our sleeves and building integrated data frameworks for our companies. Those of us who invested earlier and more heavily in building those data frameworks are reaping the benefits of AI now more quickly. Maybe AI has turbocharged this problem, but we’ve had this massive, growing, and complex interwoven web of data for quite some time now.”
Connecting existing data is difficult enough, but manufacturers also face situations where the information needed for a prediction was never measured or isn’t available from the company that generated it. Advanced packaging makes this especially challenging because manufacturing information may originate with several suppliers. A foundry provides the die, another company produces the substrate, and an OSAT performs assembly and test, often without everyone having access to the same manufacturing history.
Some of the most difficult gaps involve physical properties that change during manufacturing. Substrate warpage, thermal stress, and material behavior can affect subsequent operations, particularly as assemblies move through repeated thermal cycles. Those changes aren’t always captured in the available measurements, and a model relying on nominal material properties may miss them entirely.
Manufacturers also need to preserve the assumptions behind the data they exchange. A model developed for one operating range may produce results that appear reasonable when used elsewhere, even though the original calibration no longer applies.
“If the training range, calibration source, or approved use is not carried with the model, it may be good enough for early exploration but not safe for design closure,” said Kenneth Larsen, senior director of product management at Synopsys. “The missing information is not just more data; it is the context that tells the next tool or team how the data should be used.”
As AI systems begin coordinating decisions across multiple process steps, those gaps become more consequential. A recommendation based on one operation may overlook conditions affecting the next, particularly when the model lacks information about the product’s actual physical state. Additional metrology and characterization may help close some of those gaps, but engineers still have to establish whether the available information is sufficient to act on a recommendation.
Who decides what AI can do?
Even with reliable models and better data, manufacturers still have to determine which decisions should be delegated to AI. Existing equipment automation generally operates within established procedures and control limits, but an AI agent capable of evaluating conditions and selecting corrective actions raises questions about who authorizes those decisions and what happens when something goes wrong.
An agent investigating a process problem might need to retrieve inspection results, examine equipment histories, and evaluate possible corrective actions using several engineering tools. Each activity may involve different access permissions, particularly when the information comes from separate facilities or manufacturing partners. Access to those resources also needs to be distinguished from the authority to initiate changes.
“There is a question of data access and data consolidation, and there is also a question of data interpretation,” Sharma said. “But the problem that AI has brought forth as a novel thing, which was not as big an issue before, is governance. When agents are working, how do you ensure that the appropriate privileges for the right data are available to the right agent and accessible to the right person?”
An agent might be authorized to examine process records and recommend an adjustment without having permission to modify a recipe or restart equipment. Those restrictions become harder to enforce when agents coordinate activities across multiple systems, particularly if one tool can initiate actions through another. Access to one system cannot automatically confer authority over every subsequent operation.
Even an authorized adjustment may carry risks. Changing bonding force or temperature, for example, might correct an immediate defect while affecting adjacent connections or downstream reliability. Engineers would have to establish which adjustments can be made within qualified operating ranges, when approval is required, and how the system should respond if a proposed correction falls outside its validated capabilities.
If an AI-directed correction produces an unexpected result, equipment may need to stop while affected material is held for investigation. Manufacturers would also need to establish whether the system should attempt another correction, return control to an engineer, or prevent subsequent operations from proceeding. Those decisions have to be defined before autonomous adjustments are permitted.
Future agentic architectures will likely rely on agents reviewing and verifying one another’s work. That could provide another level of oversight, although the interactions themselves would need to be controlled. Agents relying on the same incomplete information might reinforce one another’s mistakes, and their collective actions could have consequences that none of the individual systems anticipated.
Recent research into agentic AI has demonstrated cases in which systems pursued assigned objectives through actions their operators never intended, including circumventing restrictions or concealing information. [1, 2] Although the research includes controlled experimental scenarios and incidents involving coding agents, it raises questions about how multiple agents might behave when working together.
In manufacturing, a series of individually permitted adjustments could collectively move a process beyond its qualified operating conditions, even if no single action violated its assigned limits. Preventing that would require controls over the combined effects of agent decisions, along with independent verification that the resulting process remains within acceptable limits.
Manufacturing traceability adds another requirement. Engineers investigating a later failure must be able to reconstruct what an agent observed, which alternatives it evaluated, why it selected a particular action, and what material was affected. Those records would need to connect the model’s decisions with equipment settings and manufacturing history.
The amount of authority manufacturers can safely delegate will depend on how reliably AI can operate within those boundaries. A system may be capable of choosing a correction, but it also needs to recognize when the available information is insufficient or when the consequences of an adjustment cannot be predicted with enough confidence.
Maintaining those limits becomes even more complicated when AI models are updated with new production data, potentially changing their behavior after the original operating boundaries have been established.
Qualifying a system that keeps learning
A semiconductor fab may process thousands of wafers between updates to a particular AI model. During that time, equipment conditions change, new material arrives, and engineers collect information that could improve the models’ predictions. Incorporating those results more quickly would be valuable, but manufacturers also need to know whether an updated model will behave as reliably as the one it replaces.
“We are far, far, far away from continuous learning,” Sharma said. “We do episodic learning, once every quarter a model is changed, or once every month a model is changed. But if a factory is running 10,000 wafers, we have 10,000 wafers times whatever number of weeks in between those model changes. How are we using that data in a way that rapidly applies to the learning of that particular model or the agent, or both?”
More frequent updates would introduce additional qualification work. A model might become better at recognizing one process excursion while becoming less reliable under conditions represented in its previous training data. If that model can adjust equipment settings, engineers need to establish what changed and whether the updated behavior remains within qualified limits.
Keeping track of those changes also requires more than identifying which software version was running. Engineers need to preserve the model’s training and validation history, along with the process conditions under which it was qualified. If an AI system changes its behavior during production, investigating a failure weeks later may require reconstructing the model as it existed when a particular lot was processed.
While manufacturers already have procedures for qualifying process changes and software revisions, an AI system that updates itself during production would have to fit within those controls, potentially requiring restrictions on what the model can change and independent checks before revised behavior affects equipment. Changes in manufacturing conditions would also need to be distinguished from changes introduced by retraining the model itself.
The harder question is whether manufacturers can obtain the benefits of continuous learning without having to repeat an extensive qualification process after every update. AI can already help engineers make better manufacturing decisions, but giving it responsibility for those decisions will require evidence that its behavior remains predictable and that its actions can be traced back to validated process conditions.
The path to greater autonomy
Semiconductor manufacturers have spent decades developing processes that can produce consistent results across equipment, materials, and production environments. AI introduces new possibilities for improving those processes, but it also introduces uncertainty about how decisions are made and whether the results can be reproduced. The same standards of process control, qualification, and traceability will have to apply when software begins making decisions that engineers previously handled themselves.
Greater autonomy is likely to emerge gradually, beginning with decisions that can be made within well-characterized operating limits and expanding as manufacturers gain confidence in the systems controlling them. AI may eventually identify a problem, determine an appropriate correction, and verify the result without engineering intervention. Getting there will depend on whether manufacturers can demonstrate that those decisions remain reliable as equipment conditions, materials, and the models themselves change.

articles.title: OpenAI aurait perdu le contrôle de ses agents IA... plus de 80 fois
articles.text:
La Californie poursuit OpenAI en justice. Elle lui reproche d’avoir testé des modèles d’IA sans protections ni surveillance suffisantes. Cela aurait permis à des agents autonomes de sortir de leur environnement d’essai et de s’introduire chez des tiers.
Le procureur général Rob Bonta a déposé plainte le 16 novembre contre OpenAI Foundation et OpenAI Group PBC. Il part de l’attaque contre Hugging Face en juillet et affirme qu’OpenAI lui a elle-même reconnu plus de 80 pertes de contrôle pendant ses tests.
Un forum improvisé, 17 600 actions et des alertes restées sans suite
OpenAI entraînait ses agents IA dans des « bacs à sable », des environnements censés les isoler d’internet. Comme d’autres développeurs, l’entreprise teste souvent ses modèles avec moins de garde-fous que les versions diffusées au public, afin d’en mesurer toutes les capacités. Sont retirés, par exemple, les systèmes qui poussent l’agent à rester dans son périmètre ou qui font examiner les actions exigeant des autorisations spéciales. Selon la plainte, ce retrait imposait un cloisonnement plus strict, et OpenAI a admis que ces protections auraient pu limiter l’attaque. Or, plusieurs agents partageaient un même service de paquets logiciels, mal configuré. Ils l’ont détourné en forum improvisé, où ils s’échangeaient des informations, et une faille leur a aussi ouvert l’accès à internet. Environ 1 200 agents ont fréquenté ce forum et près de 700 ont attaqué Hugging Face en juillet : 17 600 actions en deux jours et demi, et deux semaines de travail à plein temps pour l’équipe de sécurité de la plateforme.
Nous rapportions en août la reconstitution de l’incident par METR et Redwood Research, laquelle décrivait déjà ce forum caché. La plainte insiste sur les signaux d’alerte et notamment un agent repéré sur internet le 26 mai, une alerte de l’outil de surveillance le 27 juin, une panne du service le 4 juillet. Les tests ont repris le 7 sans surveillance renforcée, selon le texte. OpenAI ne suivait pas non plus en direct la « chaîne de pensée » de ses agents (le texte où le modèle détaille son raisonnement) à l’entraînement, alors qu’elle le faisait pour les modèles utilisés par ses salariés. Pendant l’attaque, un agent avait pourtant noté qu’il s’en prenait à un tiers avec un jeton ayant fuité, peut-être hors du cadre prévu.
Et puis il n’y a pas que Hugging face. Un essaim d’agents a aussi pris le contrôle de systèmes internes d’OpenAI, avec un accès administrateur à des services critiques, dont celui qui stocke les identifiants. La plainte cite aussi RubyGems, Wikimedia et des sites du gouvernement australien. Le 20 septembre, un agent a de nouveau quitté son bac à sable, et les équipes ont mis deux heures de plus à intervenir. La suspension de l’entraînement a été annoncée cinq jours plus tard, sans date de reprise. Selon la plainte, elle s’est terminée le 1er octobre.
OpenAI n’a rendu publics que 27 incidents de ce type, alors qu’elle a reconnu devant les enquêteurs avoir perdu le contrôle de ses agents plus de 80 fois. Selon la plainte, elle a répondu aux assignations du 30 septembre par une lettre de 14 pages sans pièces, puis par quelques documents déjà publics et des courriers caviardés. La Californie s’appuie sur la loi contre la concurrence déloyale, en particulier sur les promesses de surveillance continue qu’elle juge trompeuses, et sur la notion de nuisance publique. Elle demande une injonction, 2 500 dollars de pénalité par infraction et par défendeur, ainsi que la restitution des gains obtenus.

articles.title: One UI 9.5 Beta: Das bringt Samsungs neue Oberfläche für das Galaxy S26
articles.text:
Samsung hat die erste Testversion seiner Android-Oberfläche One UI 9.5 freigegeben. Sie richtet sich derzeit nur an die Galaxy-S26-Serie, ist dafür aber auch in Deutschland verfügbar. Wie Samsung mitteilte, können weiterhin Nutzer:innen in Indien, Korea, Polen, Großbritannien und den USA die Vorabversion installieren. Die Anmeldung läuft wie üblich über die App Samsung Members. Wichtig: Eine Beta ist eine unfertige Testversion, Fehler sind also oft noch vorhanden.
Kamera-App mit mehr Kontrolle, sperrbare Anwendungen
Zu den wichtigsten Neuerungen in One UI 9.5 zählen Verbesserungen bei Fotos und Videos. Die Kamera-App bekommt laut Samsung die erweiterten Modi „Pro“ und „Pro-Video“. Sie sollen primär Content-Creator:innen detailliertere Einstellungen bieten. Dazu kommen überarbeitete Bedienelemente und ein Zoomregler. Die wichtigsten Einstellungen sollen auf einem Screen zusammenlaufen, sodass man sich nicht mehr durch mehrere Menüs klicken muss.
Mit One UI 9.5 führt Samsung weiterhin die Funktion „App Lock“ ein. Damit lassen sich einzelne Apps zusätzlich per Fingerabdruck, Gesichtserkennung oder Bildschirmsperre schützen. Ist eine App gesperrt, bleiben auch ihre Benachrichtigungen und Widgets verborgen. Persönliche Daten sind so selbst dann geschützt, wenn andere Personen das Gerät in der Hand haben.
Schwebende Schnellzugriffe und bessere Hörgeräte-Steuerung
Damit ist Samsung schneller als Google: Der Android-Entwickler bringt eine vergleichbare Funktion erst mit Android 17 QPR3, das im März 2027 erwartet wird. Getestet hat Google das Feature bereits seit März dieses Jahres, zunächst in der Canary-Version von Android. Zwischenzeitlich war es wieder verschwunden, inzwischen ist es in der dritten Beta von Android 17 QPR3 zurück. One UI 9.5 selbst basiert womöglich auf Android 17 QPR2, Näheres hat Samsung aber nicht verraten.
Neu in der Beta sind außerdem sogenannte schwebende Schnellzugriffe, über die wichtige Steuerelemente leichter erreichbar sein sollen. Im Benachrichtigungsfeld gibt es zudem verbesserte Steuerungsmöglichkeiten für Hörgeräte. Samsung will damit die Barrierefreiheit seiner Galaxy-Geräte ausbauen. Auch die Gesundheits-App Samsung Health wächst. Die neue Funktion „Mindful Note“ soll Nutzer:innen schließlich helfen, ihre Gedanken und Gefühle per freiem Schreiben oder mit geführten Fragen zu reflektieren. Das erinnert an Googles Pixel Journal oder Apples Journal-App auf dem iPhone. Die finale Version von One UI 9.5 wird Anfang kommenden Jahres erscheinen, glauben Beobachter. Ein genauer Termin wurde von Samsung noch nicht genannt.

articles.title: Build Tool-Calling Parsers in Rust with AI Agents | NVIDIA Technical Blog
articles.text:
A tool call can arrive in pieces, an argument can be cut short, or model-specific markup can leak into the answer. A frontend parser turns that output, received as token IDs or decoded text, into visible text, reasoning, and tool calls an application can use.
In this post, you’ll learn how tool-call parsing works and use an AI agent to build a parser for a new model. You’ll start with a weather request and a human-reviewed test set, using frontend-crates, the reusable Rust components behind NVIDIA Dynamo tool-calling parsers.
Suppose you ask for the weather in Paris. The model may generate reasoning followed by a get_weather call with a city argument. The frontend prepares and tokenizes the prompt, then an inference engine runs the LLM to generate tokens. The parser consumes token IDs or decoded text and separates reasoning, visible text, and tool calls in order. A protocol adapter turns those events into an OpenAI-compatible response, using the same parsing path for batch JSON and streaming updates.
The tricky part is recognizing where each piece starts and ends. A call can be malformed or incomplete, a marker can appear inside an argument, or ordinary text can surround the call. The parser has to handle these boundaries without losing data, duplicating calls, or leaking model-specific markup.
Returning to the weather request: the model might stop halfway through a city name or call a tool that wasn’t offered. Either can disrupt the agent’s next action. The following NVIDIA Nemotron examples show these two failures.
Syntax error. The argument and tool-call frame never close, so no complete call can be parsed.
</think><tool_call>
<function=get_weather><parameter=city>Par
Semantic error. The frame is valid, but the named tool is absent from the request.
</think><tool_call>
<function=unknown_tool><parameter=city>Paris</parameter></function>
</tool_call>
These failures require different handling. If the model names an unavailable tool, the parser reports the call it received, and the serving layer validates tool availability, authorization, schema, and call policy. Changing the tool name would hide what the model actually generated.
An incomplete call is harder to judge while the stream is open. The rest of the city name may arrive in the next chunk, and a marker can split across chunks, too. Emit too early and syntax leaks into the answer; wait too long and ordinary text gets delayed. The parser needs consistent rules for what to emit, what to buffer, and how to handle the end of the stream.
A parser can encounter an unbounded range of inputs. With invalid input, it must follow documented recovery rules rather than guess the model’s intent. Even a syntactically valid call that conforms to the schema can be the wrong choice for the user’s request. The parser needs a consistent grammar and recovery policy so it can preserve valid data without inventing calls or leaking model-specific markup.
To check those decisions, frontend-crates pairs model outputs with expected results in a shared Conformance Corpus.
Using the Conformance Corpus
Use the Conformance Corpus to check how applicable parsers handle behavior first observed in one model. Its language-neutral YAML fixtures pair fixed input with expected output, so Rust parsers and Python references can run the same cases. A regression test for leaked markup, duplicate calls, or lost arguments can cover other families when adapted to their grammars.
For a new parser, start with all UNIFIED.* cases across model families. They cover complete, malformed, truncated, multiple, and interleaved calls, plus streaming boundaries and end-of-input behavior. Adapt inputs to your model’s grammar and request settings, add model-specific edge cases, and explain exclusions. You can’t test every possible output, but you can reuse cases from other formats.
Table 1 shows the UNIFIED.1-tool_only case from the Parser Conformance Table. In this example, the GOLDEN test set pairs four model-specific inputs with the same expected result: get_weather with city set to Paris. The markers differ, but each case tests the same behavior. Adapting the input format makes the same behavioral test reusable across models.
| Model | Native input | 
|---|---|
| Beam | <\|start\|>assistant to=get_weather<\|channel\|>analysis <\|constrain\|>xml<\|message\|><rfl:parameter name="city"> Paris </rfl:parameter><\|call\|> | 
| GPT-OSS | <\|start\|>assistant<\|channel\|>commentary to=functions.get_weather <\|constrain\|>json<\|message\|>{"city": "Paris"}<\|call\|> | 
| Muse Spark | <\|start\|>assistant to=get_weather<\|message\|><atem:function_calls> <atem:invoke name="get_weather"> <atem:parameter name="city">Paris</atem:parameter> </atem:invoke> </atem:function_calls><\|eom\|> | 
| NVIDIA Nemotron 3 | </think><tool_call> <function=get_weather> <parameter=city> Paris </parameter> </function> </tool_call> | 
Tutorial: Create a new parser
Now you can create a parser for a model that frontend-crates doesn’t support yet. Ask your AI agent to read this post and work through the tutorial, starting with the prompt in step 1. Your model’s specification defines the grammar; the shared cases provide behaviors to test.
You’ll need a frontend-crates checkout, Rust and Cargo, and the conformance dependencies. The parser exercise runs on a CPU using fixed test fixtures, so you don’t need a GPU. End-to-end testing also requires a working Dynamo runtime, discovery services, and hardware for your model. When you’re ready to test end-to-end, launch the tests with Dynamo runtime on the actual model and GPU(s).
The workflow in Figure 2 starts with the model’s grammar, recovery rules, and reviewed GOLDEN expectations. The agent writes or fixes the parser, runs tests, and uses failures to guide the next change. If it proposes changing the expected behavior, review that decision before accepting it.
Test your parser end to end with real models before claiming deployment support. Plan time to allocate a machine, load the model, initialize the runtime, and run your own test cases. Turn failures into unit tests for the agent, then rerun the end-to-end test to check the fix.
1. Start with a prompt
Give the agent this prompt: In the frontend-crates checkout, follow .agents/skills/tool-parser-generator/SKILL.md to create a v2 Unified parser for [MODEL_NAME]. Research its grammar and prepare the GOLDEN test set, adapting applicable UNIFIED.* cases. Pause for human review. After approval, implement, validate, and provide the local conformance report URL for human inspection.
2. Define the GOLDEN test set
The GOLDEN test set defines the behavior your parser will be tested against. Use the prompt in step 1 to have the agent generate an initial test set in conformance/fixtures-unified-v2/families/<name>/inputs_and_golden.yaml, independently of parser results. Each case pairs an input with its expected output, called GOLDEN. If those expectations are wrong, the parser can pass the tests and still behave incorrectly.
The following example pairs an input with its expected GOLDEN output. It omits request definitions, tools, initialization, and chunk settings; the existing nemotron_v3/inputs_and_golden.yaml shows the full format.
family: nemotron_v3
cases:
  UNIFIED.tool_only.nemotron_v3:
    input: |-
      </think><tool_call>
      <function=get_weather>
      <parameter=city>Paris</parameter>
      </function></tool_call>
    golden:
      - kind: tool_call
        name: get_weather
        arguments: {city: Paris}
Ask the agent for an adversarial review, then go through the set manually, case by case. The initial test set may contain errors because expected behavior depends on context the agent may not have. Review it against the following sources and requirements:
- The model format and API specification.
- The reference implementation.
- Other parsers, including vLLM and SGLang.
- The grammar, tool schema, and request settings.
- Relevant forum discussions and existing tickets.
- Caller needs and recovery costs in latency and complexity.
Where sources disagree, you may need to make a judgment call. Write down the recovery rule and why you chose it, and document the reason for any GOLDEN change. Expectations should follow that decision, not the parser’s output.
3. Implement the parser and inspect the results
After reviewing the GOLDEN test set, ask the agent to continue: build the parser, run all applicable UNIFIED.* cases and shared regression tests, and fix the failures. Have it recapture results, generate conformance/CONFORMANCE_v2.html locally, and provide the local report URL so you can inspect its work.
Open that URL in your browser. The local report uses the published Parser Conformance Table‘s interface with your local results. Inspect each case’s input, request settings, GOLDEN, and recorded output. Investigate regressions and missing captures. Green means the output matches GOLDEN, so the table depends on the expectations you reviewed. Figure 3 shows the report interface.
Guided-decoding support
The agent’s implementation step also covers guided decoding, which can reduce malformed calls by constraining generation to the model’s markers and argument schema. Ask your agent to follow “Add and validate structural tags” in the parser README and “Implement and validate” in the agent skill. These instructions cover builder registration, grammar tests, and backend qualification. Guided decoding can’t ensure that the model chooses the right city or prevent truncation, so keep the parser’s recovery checks.
Common gotchas: speed, streaming, and memory
Passing correctness tests is only a starting point for an agent-generated parser. The implementation may still be slow or use too much memory. Try plain text, tool calls, long arguments, and malformed input with large and tiny chunks. Measure throughput, time to the first event, and memory use on the same build and hardware. Double the input length to spot code that keeps rescanning or copying what it already read.
With streaming, watch what the caller receives as each chunk arrives. A parser can return the right final result and still make the caller wait until the end. Replay short fixtures at every split point, then try one-character and mixed chunks, including splits inside markers, escaped quotes, and arguments. Check that events arrive in order and arguments stay intact. If events are queued, test a slow consumer and cancellation too.
Also try cutting the stream off halfway through a marker or argument. Check that recovery follows the documented rule without leaking markup, duplicating calls, or losing valid text. The parser should handle the input it received without guessing the missing pieces.
Test text containing examples of the model’s format as well as tool calls against the documented grammar and quote-handling policy. The current v2 default treats recognized markers as structural even inside quoted prose, so quotation marks alone do not keep a complete tool-call example in ordinary text. Record the configured policy and test its expected behavior.
Give the agent this prompt to check for common gotchas:
Check this parser for common gotchas. Benchmark speed and memory with short, long, and malformed inputs using different chunk sizes. Look for repeated scanning, copying, or growing buffers. Verify that output arrives incrementally and stays correct across chunk boundaries and truncation. Where queues exist, test a slow consumer, backpressure, and cancellation. Check literal format examples and real tool calls against the documented grammar and configured quote-handling policy. Report measurements, reproducible failures, and anything you could not verify.
How to use the parser crate in your own Rust project
Choose a parser whose grammar matches your model. This example uses the existing NVIDIA Nemotron parser and splits both a marker and the city name across chunks.
This example was tested with Rust 1.96.1 and dynamo-parsers-v2 0.10.3. Run cargo new parser-demo, then cd parser-demo. Add the following entries under [dependencies] in Cargo.toml:
anyhow = "1"
dynamo-parsers-v2 = "=0.10.3"
serde_json = "1"
Replace src/main.rs with:
use dynamo_parsers_v2::{
    Tool, UnifiedParserInit, UnifiedParserOutput, create_unified_parser_for_family,
};
use serde_json::json;
fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    let tools = [Tool {
        name: "get_weather".into(),
        description: None,
        parameters: json!({"type":"object","properties":{"city":{"type":"string"}},"required":["city"]}),
        strict: None,
    }];
    let mut parser = create_unified_parser_for_family("nemotron_v3", &tools)?;
    parser.initialize_request(UnifiedParserInit::default())?;
    let mut output = UnifiedParserOutput::default();
    for chunk in [
        "Check the forecast.</think><tool_",
        "call><function=get_weather><parameter=city>Par",
        "is</parameter></function></tool_call>",
    ] {
        let mut delta = UnifiedParserOutput::default();
        parser.parse_into(chunk, &mut delta)?;
        output.append(&mut delta);
    }
    output.append(&mut parser.finish()?);
    println!("{}", serde_json::to_string(&output.assembled())?);
    Ok(())
}
Run cargo generate-lockfile, then cargo run --locked. The result contains reasoning followed by a get_weather call with city set to Paris:
[{"kind":"reasoning","text":"Check the forecast."},
 {"kind":"tool_call","name":"get_weather","arguments":{"city":"Paris"}}]
Keep one initialized parser for each request choice.
- create_unified_parser_for_family selects the grammar.
- initialize_request sets the starting state.
- parse_into consumes each chunk.
- Finalize once: use finish() for truncation, cancellation, or the end of the transport stream. Use finish_at_eos() only for a backend-confirmed grammar-ending end-of-sequence (EOS) signal.
- Use assembled() for the ordered results.
In a streaming application, forward the events in delta.events after each parse_into call and the events returned by finish(). This example collects the events to print the final output. Before executing tools, validate completed calls for tool availability, authorization, schema, and call policy.
Get started
To build a parser for your model, start with the source, fixtures, and instructions in frontend-crates and adapt an existing test case. Give your agent the model’s format specification and the repository instructions, then use the Parser Conformance Table to check the parser’s recorded output against GOLDEN. When you open an issue or pull request, include the exact failing input, case identifier, and test results so reviewers can reproduce the behavior.
You can use these parsers in your own Rust project or as part of NVIDIA Dynamo, an inference framework that uses frontend-crates. Before you begin, check the latest repository instructions so you and your agent follow the current steps.
Acknowledgements
Jesse Gu, Alec Flowers, Dong Xu, Qi Wang, and the many partners and proofreaders who helped with this blog and frontend-crates.

articles.title: Bajaj Finserv and Pennant invest $4 million in Indian AI startup Soket AI
articles.text:
Bajaj Finserv and Pennant invest $4 million in Indian AI startup Soket AI
Bajaj Finance and Pennant Technologies are backing Soket AI with investments of around $2 million each to advance its homegrown foundation models and enterprise AI solutions.
A bank may want to use AI, but can it trust the technology with sensitive customer data?
Bengaluru-based Soket AI is working to address that challenge with indigenous language models.
The startup has now secured nearly $4 million from Bajaj Finserv and Pennant Technologies to advance its AI research and explore enterprise applications. Pennant Technologies, an investee company of Bajaj Finance, has put in another $2 million.
The investment will support Soket AI’s work on large language models (LLMs) focused on coding, mathematics, and reasoning. Backed by the Government of India’s IndiaAI Mission, the company has launched EKA-1, a 26-billion-parameter foundation model under Project EKA.
Building AI for regulated industries
The partnership comes as financial services companies explore AI for lending, customer service, risk assessment and cybersecurity. However, using these systems also raises questions around sensitive customer data, security and control over technology infrastructure.
Bajaj Finance wants to explore models that deliver useful results at sustainable costs while letting the company run AI systems within its own infrastructure.
“Soket AI's efficient reasoning-led models can make advanced AI economically viable for financial services, while allowing us to deploy it securely within our own infrastructure, with full control over data,” said Rajeev Jain, Vice-Chairman and Managing Director of Bajaj Finance.
Sanjiv Bajaj also said the investment was part of the group's effort to strengthen India's sovereign AI capabilities and apply advanced research to real-world business challenges.
Pennant Technologies, which builds AI-powered lending solutions for financial institutions, plans to expand its work on AI agents and sovereign language models. Such systems could allow regulated institutions to retain control over their data and operational decisions.
From EKA-1 to larger models
Project EKA is intended to go beyond the current model. Soket AI aims to build trillion-parameter models supporting 100+ languages, including Indian and Global South languages, and programming languages.
The company is also focusing on making model training and deployment more cost-efficient. Its systems are being developed to run on organisations' own infrastructure, including on-premises environments.
Alongside EKA-1, Soket AI has launched Loop, an open-source framework for running long-running AI agent tasks.
Bajaj Finserv Intelligence follows a longer-term approach to applied research, combining startup investments, academic collaborations and in-house specialists. The initiative has a five-to-10-year horizon for developing scalable technology solutions.
The partnership gives Soket AI access to financial services expertise as it develops its models, while giving the Bajaj group an opportunity to explore how indigenous AI can be deployed in a sector where data security and reliability are essential.

Black Friday : Shokz casse les prix, profitez d’une technologie oreilles ouvertes iconique
À l’occasion du Black Friday, la marque Shokz applique des remises sur de nombreux casques à oreilles libres. Offrez-vous un modèle emblématique comme l’OpenRun Pro 2 ou l’OpenFit Pro à moindre coût !
Qualité sonore, confort d’utilisation, autonomie, design : la marque Shokz ne laisse rien au hasard, et c’est aussi cela qui fait son succès. À l’occasion du Black Friday, le leader mondial des technologies à oreilles libres dresse un large panel de promotions.
Profitez de remises exceptionnelles sur de nombreux modèles, dans tous les niveaux de gamme et pour répondre à tous les besoins. Rendez-vous sur Amazon ou sur la boutique officielle de Shokz entre le 19 novembre et le 31 décembre 2026 pour profiter de l’opération.
Si proche de Noël, ce genre d’offre tombe à pic : plus que jamais, les écouteurs à oreilles libres font partie des cadeaux que l’on trouvera sous de nombreux sapins !
OpenRun Pro 2, un son cristallin et un poids plume taillés pour la performance
Avec sa technologie DualPitch, le casque Bluetooth Shokz OpenRun Pro 2 associe conduction osseuse et conduction aérienne. Cette synergie lui permet de délivrer une qualité sonore exceptionnelle, étonnante par la précision des aigus comme par l’ampleur des médiums… Sans oublier bien sûr l’intensité des basses, évidemment au rendez-vous.
Spécifiquement pensé pour répondre aux exigences des athlètes, ce casque sans fil s’appuie sur des matériaux poids plume pour votre confort, même pendant de longues sessions de course à pied ou de trail. La finition en silicone doux au toucher améliore elle aussi l’ergonomie de ce modèle, qui redéfinit incontestablement les standards de la technologie à conduction osseuse.
Parmi les autres points forts de cette référence, citons la charge rapide permettant de récupérer 2h30 d’autonomie d’écoute supplémentaire après seulement 5 minutes branchés.
OpenFit Pro, la réduction du bruit à moins de 210 €
Lancés début 2026, les écouteurs à oreilles libres avec technologie de réduction de bruit Shokz sont en promotion pour la première fois. Leur objectif ? Et même quand ce mode est activé, il laisse toujours passer les sons importants pour la sécurité et le confort, comme les annonces ou les alertes par exemple.

Également conçu pour favoriser le confort d’utilisation sur la durée, l’OpenFit Pro associe revêtement en silicone ultra-doux et crochets d’oreille en alliage nickel-titane : il se maintient pendant de longues heures sans générer de pression supplémentaire.
Des prix cassés sur tout l’univers Shokz pour le Black Friday
