articles.title: Sonos is taking up to 30 percent off speakers and soundbars right now
articles.text:
Sonos speakers and soundbars aren’t exactly cheap, but thankfully the company’s Black Friday sale has already begun, making everything a little easier to afford through November 30th. Most notably, you can pick up the Arc Ultra soundbar for a new low of $849 ($250 off) from Sonos, Amazon, and Best Buy, or the newfangled Sonos Play for $239 ($60 off) from the same retailers (Sonos, Amazon, Best Buy).
Sonos is taking up to 30 percent off speakers and soundbars right now
Whether you want a portable speaker or a new home theater setup, Sonos is offering great deals through November 30th.
If you’re looking to give your home theater setup a big upgrade, the Arc Ultra is an excellent soundbar. It supports Dolby Atmos and delivers more immersive sound than the original Arc, while adding Bluetooth connectivity. Dialogue also sounds noticeably clearer, and the new Quick Tune feature automatically adjusts the soundbar’s audio to suit your room using built-in microphones, so you no longer need an iPhone to fine-tune the sound for your environment. For more powerful bass, you can also pair it with a compatible Sonos subwoofer, like the Sub 4, which is also available from Sonos as part of a discounted bundle for $1,499 ($499 off).
If you’re looking for a more affordable soundbar, the second-gen Sonos Beam has also hit a new low price at Amazon, Best Buy, and Sonos’ online storefront, where you can buy it for $339 ($160 off). The sound isn’t quite as immersive as that of the Arc Ultra, but the latest Beam can still fill a room with rich, clear audio. It also supports Dolby Atmos; however, unlike the newer Beam Ultra, it lacks side- and upward-firing speakers and instead relies on software to replicate surround sound effects. It also supports HDMI eARC, providing high-quality audio from a compatible TV.
If you’re shopping for a smart speaker instead of a soundbar, the Era 100 SL is available for an all-time low of $149 ($40 off) from Sonos, Amazon, and Best Buy (the standard Era 100 is also down to $179 at Amazon and Best Buy). The feature-packed speakers are nearly identical, but the SL model lacks a built-in mic, and thus voice controls. Both offer excellent stereo sound and rich bass, with dual tweeters and a large woofer that delivers clear, detailed audio despite its small size. They also support Bluetooth and Apple’s AirPlay 2, and you can connect a wired audio source like a turntable using an optional USB-C adapter. For a more immersive experience, you can even pair two for stereo sound or use them as rear surrounds with a compatible Sonos soundbar.
If you want a speaker you can take on the go, the newer Sonos Play is available from Sonos, Amazon, and Best Buy for $239 ($60 off), which is the first notable discount we’ve seen. The portable speaker delivers clear, detailed sound that can fill both larger rooms and outdoor spaces. It also offers up to 24 hours of battery life and an IP67 rating for water and dust resistance, making it a great companion for long days at the beach or other outdoor adventures. Plus, its removable carrying loop makes it easy to bring along, and you can even use it to top off your phone. Like other Sonos speakers, it supports both Wi-Fi and Bluetooth, and you can also group it with other Sonos speakers over Bluetooth when you’re outdoors and away from Wi-Fi.
Last but not least, you can also buy the Sonos Ace for $229 ($120 off) at Amazon, Best Buy, and directly from Sonos, which marks a new low price. The newer Ace Ultra offer better sound and improved noise cancellation, but the Ace is still a solid option, especially if you already own a Sonos soundbar. The gorgeous headphones deliver powerful, detailed sound, solid noise cancellation, and an exceptionally natural-sounding transparency mode, along with up to 30 hours of continuous playback on a single charge. Unlike the newer Ultra, though, they can’t transfer music from your other Sonos speakers to your headphones. However, their TV Audio Swap feature still lets you transfer audio from a compatible Sonos soundbar to your headphones, so you can watch movies or listen to music playing on your TV without disturbing anyone else.

articles.title: NVIDIA and Microsoft Expand Accelerated Computing From Azure to Windows PCs
articles.text:
NVIDIA and Microsoft are extending their full-stack collaboration to help organizations build, customize and deploy intelligent applications — from next-generation infrastructure on Azure to industrial systems and Windows PCs.
At Microsoft Ignite, the companies are expanding access to Azure virtual machines powered by NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 systems, as well as adding customer availability to NVIDIA open models and customization capabilities through Microsoft Foundry, and new options for running AI at the edge, where businesses generate and use their data.
Microsoft is also using NVIDIA technologies to accelerate its own models and services, including NVIDIA Dynamo inference software for post-training and NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs for Bing search models.
NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 Running in Azure
NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 systems are running in Azure data centers, providing infrastructure designed for demanding reasoning, agentic applications, and large-scale model training and inference.
Microsoft and NVIDIA are also collaborating to extend confidential computing to bare-metal and rack-scale AI infrastructure. The work will help protect sensitive models and data while they are being processed, supporting organizations that need to work with proprietary or regulated information.
NVIDIA Confidential Computing and attestation help customers verify the computing environment before releasing sensitive models, data or keys. As AI workloads span more interconnected accelerators, the companies are working to extend those protections across the AI factory infrastructure.
To help data centers get more performance from available power, NVIDIA and Microsoft are also collaborating on power efficiency using NVIDIA MaxLPS.
Azure’s Vera Rubin preview builds on NVIDIA and Microsoft’s codesign and performance optimization, underscored in the latest NVIDIA Blackwell-based MLPerf results. In MLPerf Training v6.1, Azure scaled to 10,240 NVIDIA GPUs with GB200 NVL72 systems on the DeepSeek-V3 model, the largest scale in the round. In MLPerf Inference v6.1, Azure’s NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 systems led cloud submissions on DeepSeek-R1 interactive throughput by over 10%, per Signal65.
Helping Enterprises Customize and Deploy Open Models
Enterprise AI agents need to reason through complex tasks, find relevant company information and understand business documents. NVIDIA and Microsoft are expanding the models and services available through Microsoft Foundry to help developers bring these capabilities into business applications.
Microsoft’s serverless Programmed Training offering gives developers control over post-training workflows while Foundry manages the underlying infrastructure. Enterprises can focus on their business data, evaluating model responses and improving model behavior.
Foundry Managed Compute adds support for deploying custom model weights, helping connect model customization with deployment through Microsoft’s managed services.
EY used Programmed Training in Microsoft Foundry to adapt NVIDIA Nemotron open models for classifying corporate purchasing records, improving accuracy on its evaluation dataset by 55% and lowering cost by 15x compared with proprietary frontier models. The work demonstrates how enterprises can customize open models for specialized business tasks.
The expanded NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 lineup on Foundry Managed Compute supports different requirements across enterprise applications. Nemotron 3.5 Super is designed for long-running agents working across coding, research and business workflows, while Lightning supports applications that need fast responses and tool use.
Complementary models help agents find relevant information with Nemotron Embed and Rerank, extract structured information from documents with Nemotron Parse and detect harmful content with Nemotron Content Safety. Nemotron 3.5 Bolt — designed for high-throughput, low-latency reasoning — and Transcribe, for speech recognition, are coming soon.
Bringing AI Closer to Enterprise Data
NVIDIA and Microsoft are expanding deployment options beyond the cloud, helping organizations run models and agents closer to their data while maintaining control over their infrastructure and operations.
Expanded support for Nemotron 3.5 in Foundry Local brings capabilities for reasoning, coding and tool-using agents to Azure Local environments. Retrieval models help applications find evidence across text, document images, charts and tables.
Azure Local will also support NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs from hardware partners, giving organizations additional options for deploying AI on premises.
Azure Local is expanding to NVIDIA Jetson Thor and Jetson Orin edge AI platforms to support industrial applications such as machine vision, robotics and autonomous operations. NVIDIA physical AI models, including Cosmos, are also being brought to Foundry Local.
On Windows PCs powered by NVIDIA RTX Spark, NVIDIA and Microsoft will showcase local large language model experiences at Ignite, demonstrating how developers can run AI applications directly on devices.
For organizations using Cloud PCs, the companies are bringing Direct Stream capabilities to GPU-accelerated Windows 365 Cloud PCs. These capabilities support demanding graphics applications with up to two 4K streams at 60 frames per second and low latency, even over challenging networks. A limited preview is open for sign-ups, with public preview planned for early 2027.
Connecting Scientific AI With Microsoft Discovery
For scientific research, NVIDIA BioNemo Agent Toolkit and NVIDIA ALCHEMI Toolkit are expanding into the Microsoft Discovery catalog, bringing models for life sciences, drug discovery and materials and chemical science into Microsoft’s agentic research platform.
BioNeMo Agent Toolkit helps scientists use natural language to run computational biology workflows in Microsoft Discovery, with agents coordinating the tools and model calls needed to carry out the work.
An initial integration uses the RFD4-Proteina model, developed in collaboration with the University of Washington’s Institute for Protein Design, to generate candidate protein structures and amino acid sequences for further evaluation and laboratory validation.
Accelerating Microsoft’s Models and Services
Alongside expanding customer access to NVIDIA technologies, Microsoft is using NVIDIA software and accelerated computing in its own AI development and services.
Microsoft AI uses NVIDIA Dynamo to support reinforcement learning rollout inference during post-training. This computationally intensive process generates the experiences used to improve models.
Dynamo coordinates inference across a large GPU fleet, optimizing performance, as well as helping manage requests, model updates and recovery from failures. The deployment builds on joint engineering between Microsoft AI and NVIDIA.
Visit NVIDIA at Ignite for demonstrations spanning enterprise applications, robotics, accelerated data processing and local computing, with hardware including an NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 rack and RTX Spark devices. View NVIDIA sessions, hands-on labs and booth theater presentations.

articles.title: El GTA VI desata la locura: vuelos a Nueva Zelanda para probarlo antes, ausencias laborales y hasta días libres en el ejército
articles.text:
El GTA VI desata la locura: vuelos a Nueva Zelanda para probarlo antes, ausencias laborales y hasta días libres en el ejército
Los expertos alertan del peligro de entablar relaciones amorosas con personajes de videojuegos y de los comportamientos dañinos que pueden derivar en una adicción
La fiebre por el estreno del GTA VI —que llega este jueves, 13 años después de su última edición— ha alcanzado su punto más alto en las últimas horas. Streamers con millones de seguidores, como El Rubius, han viajado hasta la otra punta del mundo, a Nueva Zelanda, para experimentar antes que el resto el nuevo juego de Rockstar North. La elección del destino no ha sido aleatoria: el lanzamiento está previsto para la medianoche de cada país, lo que ha permitido a los jugadores neozelandeses adelantarse 12 horas al estreno en España.
El Rubius no ha sido el único en cometer este tipo de locuras. Algunos docentes de universidades españolas han decidido adelantar deberes, suspender sus clases y postergar los exámenes previstos para permitir que sus alumnos tengan más horas para disfrutar del videojuego que trae gráficos imponentes, detalles hiperrealistas, el “superpoder” de la concentración para los personajes y hasta la posibilidad de entablar una relación amorosa entre los dos protagonistas principales, Jason Duval y Lucía Caminos.
Otros directamente han optado por faltar al trabajo —aunque no existen cifras que permitan cuantificar las personas que se han decantado por esta alternativa— o pedir vacaciones con antelación para asegurar tener toda la jornada libre. Es el caso de Pol Faz Arias, un auxiliar administrativo de 26 años que vive en Barcelona, que cuenta que este nuevo lanzamiento le permitirá saldar “una deuda con su niño interior”. Según explica por teléfono, ni él ni su hermano han tenido la posibilidad de disfrutar del “juego del año” durante su etapa de adolescentes por motivos económicos. Ahora la situación es completamente diferente: es un adulto que trabaja y que puede permitirse comprar cualquiera de las versiones disponibles, la edición estándar, de 79,99 euros, o la Ultimate, que incluye tiendas o vehículos exclusivos y que cuesta unos 99,99 euros.
Y, aunque el trabajo le ha permitido hacerse con el videojuego en cuanto estuvo disponible para su compra, ha tenido que pedir unos 10 días de vacaciones a su jefe para poder concretar su plan. Al principio, no estaba seguro de poder conseguir la autorización, porque otros compañeros suyos tenían la misma intención de solicitar el día libre. Al final, recibió el visto bueno, junto a los otros dos interesados, y podrá pasar el día con sus amigos y familia para probar las novedades del juego. “Que traigan una tele y una consola, es la condición que he puesto para quien venga a mi casa. La idea es salir de trabajar el miércoles a las tres, comer y subir al pueblo. Dejar el juego instalado, preparar un par de comidas para no cocinar en dos o tres días y, a las 12 de la noche, estar frente a la pantalla para poder empezar a jugar cuanto antes”, apunta el barcelonés.
Muchos empleados han pedido libranzas, pero algunas empresas han ido más allá y no han esperado a que sus trabajadores pidan días libres o llamen para intentar justificar sus ausencias con supuestos síntomas de alguna enfermedad. Por ejemplo, la firma tecnológica Logitech ha otorgado un día libre a sus 7.000 empleados para que jueguen y “reconozcan formalmente los beneficios cognitivos y profesionales de los videojuegos”, según indican en un comunicado en el portal oficial de la compañía suiza.
Pero este tipo de iniciativas no se ha quedado dentro de los límites de las empresas privadas. En Estados Unidos, el propio ejército ha ofrecido cuatro días libres a los que se reenlisten por un periodo de dos a seis años. Según han reportado medios locales, como ABC News o NBC News, un memorando interno de la base Fort Stewart indicaba que “todo soldado que firme un contrato, entre el 1 de agosto de 2026 y el 14 de noviembre de 2026, tendrá derecho a un pase específicamente diseñado para coincidir con el esperado lanzamiento del videojuego Grand Theft Auto VI”.
El revuelo por el lanzamiento es tan grande que algunas plataformas de gestión de recursos humanos han realizado seguimientos en diferentes países. En Australia, Employment Hero ha analizado el comportamiento de más de 870.000 empleados y ha registrado un aumento del 29% en los pedidos de vacaciones para el 19 de noviembre, respecto al mismo día del 2025.
En Estados Unidos, BambooHR, que trabaja con más de 3,4 millones de empleados, ha recibido un 13% más de solicitudes en comparación con los mismos datos de 2024 y 2025. En Reino Unido, BrightHR, que cubre a más de 1,2 millones de empleados en 70.000 empresas, descubrió que Grand Theft Auto se mencionaba en el 4,63% de las solicitudes de vacaciones anuales para el día del lanzamiento. En España, según los datos de Remote, las peticiones de días libres han aumentado un 44% respecto al tercer jueves de noviembre de 2025.
Pérdida del control de impulsos
Para Marc Masip, licenciado en Psicología por la Universidad de Barcelona y experto en adicción a las nuevas tecnologías, este furor generalizado que está impulsando a las personas a faltar al trabajo, al colegio o a la universidad puede ser una señal de alerta. “Cuando es una decisión tan drástica, vemos que hay una pérdida de control de impulsos, una evasión total de la realidad; sería comparable al que está consumiendo drogas [...] La base de la adicción para mí sería el síndrome de abstinencia, la sustitución de actividades necesarias o positivas, como hacer deporte, trabajar, estar con la familia, tener relaciones interpersonales. Si dejas de hacer esto por estar jugando, ya es un claro signo de que algo no está funcionando bien”, explica.
El experto en adicciones critica también a las personas que intentan justificar la fiebre por los videojuegos y compararlos con los fanáticos que acampan por días para ver a su artista favorito. “No es lo mismo un videojuego, en el que matas a la gente, que una película o algo de arte, no tiene nada que ver. Tú puedes acampar tres días para ver un concierto o una película que te haga mucha ilusión, pero una vez la hayas visto, sigues con tu vida. En cambio, estos seguirán jugando, jugando y jugando. No es comparable”, insiste.
Respecto a la novedad que ofrece GTA VI de poder establecer una relación amorosa entre los dos protagonistas del juego, Masip señala que puede generar una dependencia y afectar las relaciones sociales en un futuro. “Me parece penoso y muy peligroso. Una relación interpersonal, amorosa, sexual, afectiva, de ninguna manera se puede entender a través de una pantalla. Aquí lo que estamos haciendo es disociar. Una pantalla siempre va a ser mucho más complaciente y no tendrá esa parte real, sino que va a tener un algoritmo, y eso puede generar estragos en la sociedad actual y del futuro, y en las relaciones interpersonales de la misma”, zanja.
Aunque algunos estudios científicos aseguran que los videojuegos tienen un efecto positivo en la salud mental y la satisfacción vital de las personas, el especialista es tajante. Para él, no hay manera de jugar videojuegos obsesivamente de manera sana. De hecho, hace un paralelismo con los cigarrillos. “También puedes fumar sin tener cáncer de pulmón o beber sin morir por problemas con el hígado. Puedes ser adicto, drogarte cada día y tener una vida funcional. Pero no es lo que deseamos y menos para nuestros hijos”, concluye.

articles.title: Internet traffic and attacks during the 2026 U.S. midterm elections
articles.text:
Internet traffic and attacks during the 2026 U.S. midterm elections
Visitors to government election websites surged 363% on November 3, the date of the 2026 midterm elections in the United States. Across Cloudflare's election protection programs, we also detected a significant shift in the types and timing of cyberattacks throughout 2026.
Unlike what we saw in other recent elections, attackers focused on gaining access to internal systems and data, rather than knocking websites offline. Government election websites faced website vulnerability attempts 180 times more often than denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks, and at roughly ten times the rate of Cloudflare's broader customer base. We also found evidence of at least one attempt to exploit a recently disclosed critical PHP vulnerability on a state government voting website in the Western United States.
These attacks peaked in late October, several weeks before the election. Vulnerability exploit attempts climbed steadily throughout 2026: from 200,000 per day in January, to 2 million per day in October. However, on Election Day in the U.S., Cloudflare detected no escalation in attack volume and zero major DDoS incidents across protected election sites, marking a sharp contrast to other recent elections, such as in Moldova last year.
Our data regarding cyberattacks on election institutions came from organizations participating in Cloudflare's free cybersecurity programs: the Athenian Project, Cloudflare for Campaigns, and Project Galileo. Together, these initiatives helped protect more than 1,400 election-related websites during the 2026 U.S. midterm elections, including those belonging to state and local governments, candidates, political parties, voting-rights advocates, journalists, and civil society groups.
Cloudflare launched its first election protection program in 2016 after widespread reports of cyberattacks targeting the U.S. elections. A decade later, it is remarkable to see how far governments and campaigns have come in securing their digital infrastructure. We are proud to help protect democratic institutions and are encouraged that cyberattacks were once again not a disruptive factor in 2026.
In this post, we examine traffic and attacks observed against those organizations on Election Day, analyze the most common types of attacks of the 2026 cycle, and provide recommendations based on those findings.
Election Day: significant voter traffic, minimal attacks
Ordinary user traffic to state and local government election websites was higher on Election Day (November 3) than any other day in 2026. Traffic to those sites increased to approximately 602 million requests, up from 130 million on November 1. By comparison, traffic across the rest of Cloudflare’s global network rose by only 12% over the same period.
State and local government election websites provide authoritative information to voters on how to register, where to vote, and who won. Because of their critical role, these platforms are often targeted by those seeking to suppress voter turnout, disrupt the reporting of results, or steal sensitive information.
On Election Day itself, Cloudflare did not record a single significant distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack across any of its 1,400 election-related websites. The only significant DDoS attack occurred on November 2, targeting a candidate for the U.S. House of Representatives in California and totaled 520,000 requests. By comparison, the Moldovan Election Commission experienced more than 898 million malicious requests in a single 12-hour period on their Election Day in 2025, with attacks peaking at 324,333 requests per second.
Prior to Election Day: the most common attacks in the 2026 cycle
Website vulnerability scans were by far the most common attack observed by Cloudflare in the 2026 U.S. election cycle. In the 12 months leading up to the election, Cloudflare mitigated 392 million such attacks on government election websites alone.
Website vulnerability attacks exploit outdated or vulnerable website code to gain access to internal systems and data. For example, cross-site scripting attacks inject malicious code into web pages in order to capture administrator credentials or deface site content. SQL injection manipulates database queries allowing attackers to potentially extract voter records or alter data.
Phishing and other malicious emails targeting political campaigns protected by the company occurred at rates consistent with Cloudflare's broader network, but showed signs of sophistication. In the 90 days leading up to the election, 3.9% of emails sent to organizations participating in Cloudflare for Campaigns were identified as malicious, closely tracking the 4.8 percent baseline across other Cloudflare customers. However, nearly 42% of those malicious emails managed to bypass basic email authentication checks, such as verifying sender identity or preventing in-transit tampering. These threats were nonetheless identified by Cloudflare’s advanced phishing detection tools.
Although website vulnerabilities were the most common attack overall, for journalism and election-related civil society organizations, DDoS was the most common. Over the same 12-month period, Cloudflare mitigated over 10.8 billion DDoS requests targeting these groups. The largest single attack occurred on September 10, 2026, hitting a U.S.-based news organization with 3.04 billion requests. This pattern is consistent with Cloudflare research released earlier this year, which found that among all Project Galileo entities in 120 countries, DDoS were by far the most common attack seen, accounting for 81% of all attacks.
PHP vulnerability
On October 21, security researchers disclosed serious vulnerabilities (known as php2shell) in PHP, an open source back-end programming language used by 70% of the world's websites. The flaws reportedly could allow attackers to execute malicious code on vulnerable servers, expose customer data, or disrupt services. Cloudflare deployed Web Application Firewall (WAF) protections for all customers, prior to public disclosure of the vulnerability.
On October 22, Cloudflare's PHP defense was triggered more than 9,000 times on a state government election website in the Western U.S. This attack was only detected on one election-related site and appears to have been an isolated incident rather than part of a broader trend.
Recommendations
Cloudflare research consistently shows that individuals and organizations participating in democratic elections face significant risk of cyberattack. Data gathered during the 2026 U.S. midterm election suggests those attacks continue to evolve, occur throughout an election cycle and not only on Election Day, and can vary depending on the type of organization targeted.
Based on the recent cyberattack trends in the 2026 U.S. midterms and other elections, we make the following recommendations:
- Prepare for surges in user traffic. Legitimate voter interest can create traffic spikes that overwhelm unprepared infrastructure and make essential election websites inaccessible. Organizations should prepare scalable, efficient infrastructure to handle Election Day traffic increases without straining budgets or staff.
- Maintain security protections year-round, not just on Election Day. Cyberattacks targeting democratic institutions occur across the entire election cycle, not just around voting windows. Defensive postures must remain active continuously rather than treated as a short-term, seasonal measure.
- Deploy automated defenses to counter rapid threats. AI has made it easier for attackers to find and exploit new vulnerabilities. Organizations should implement security services that update automatically, like managed rules, to ensure new protections deploy by default.
Ensuring voters have access to reliable information about elections not only helps encourage participation and deliver timely, accurate results, but also protects voter confidence in the democratic process itself. As more officials, more institutions, and the public increasingly rely on the Internet for those services, keeping that digital infrastructure stable, secure, and accessible becomes an essential civic priority.
State and local election offices, political campaigns, party organizations, journalists, and voting rights groups in need of cybersecurity services can access them from Cloudflare at no cost. Visit the Athenian Project (for state and local election websites), Cloudflare for Campaigns (for political campaigns), or Project Galileo (for civil society, democracy, and journalism organizations) to learn more about eligibility and sign up today.

articles.title: Gemini on Mac can now use your computer
articles.text:
Google’s Gemini app for macOS now has computer use, meaning it can help you “get multi-step tasks done across your local files, desktop apps, and the web,” the company says. Google suggests the feature might be useful for things like speeding up workflows, filling in forms, making presentations, and listing items for sale.
Gemini on Mac can now use your computer
With the new computer use feature, Google says Gemini can better help with things like filling in forms and creative workflows.
Users will be able to decide which of your apps Gemini can access, and be able to follow along as Gemini works because it has its own background window that shows a live preview in your chat, Google says. The feature is rolling out now in English for users in the US.
Gemini is introducing the new feature ahead of Apple launching new restrictions for apps wanting “full disk access” on Mac due to potential risks from AI agents with computer use. A preview of the settings rolled out with this week’s macOS 27.3 beta.

articles.title: Into the Omniverse: How Developers Turn Ideas Into Simulations With Frontier AI Agents
articles.text:
Turning a simulation idea into a working application means assembling assets, connecting physics and rendering, and checking that the scene behaves as intended. Developers are combining frontier AI models with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to help carry out that work — building applications for exploring scenarios, investigating failures and improving designs.
Developers direct AI agents through natural-language instructions, review results and guide changes. Omniverse libraries provide GPU-accelerated physics, rendering and sensor simulation capabilities.
Explore the projects below to see frontier AI models such as GPT-6 Astra at work, and check back for new examples from NVIDIA teams and developers across the ecosystem.
Physical AI Paves the Path to Autonomous Industrial Operations 🔗
AI agents powered by frontier models pave the way to autonomous operations. They use industrial tools and engineering data to help engineers build digital twins that test plans and processes and evaluate operational decisions.
Falkor, a KONGSBERG company, shows how this works in practice. The company’s Falkor Surface platform lets customers turn their computer-aided design and engineering data into facility-scale digital twins using the GPT-6 Astra model. The platform uses NVIDIA Omniverse libraries and NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Server Edition GPUs on Microsoft Azure to enable advanced physics simulation.
AI agents built on Falkor’s agentic engine understand dense technical documentation, spatial relationships and real-world physics. Engineers can create and test plans in simulation before traveling on site, reducing costly delays and mistakes. They can also inspect equipment and check clearances in a shared view.
Read Falkor’s article and watch the livestream for a closer look at how the company builds these tools and checks the agents’ work.
Build a Robot Pick-and-Place Simulation With SimReady Assets 🔗
Getting a robot model into a scene is only the start. Developers also need to assemble its components, add controls and check whether it can complete a task.
NVIDIA developers Dillon Bailey and Rishabh Chadha used 3D assets from the SimReady Central library to build a pick-and-place simulation of a robot moving a can using the NVIDIA Isaac Sim framework. They directed an agent equipped with GPT-6 Sol and Isaac Sim skills to assemble the scene and generate pick-and-place controls.
Testing the assembled scene shows how the assets work together, from joint movement and contact behavior to the gripper’s ability to hold, move and release the can. With that baseline in place, developers can adjust object positions and motion paths and repeat the tests to evaluate how each change affects the task.
Follow the walkthrough to assemble and test a pick-and-place simulation in Isaac Sim, with sample agent prompts and checks for robot movement and grasp behavior.
Build a Voice-Controlled VR Simulation With SimReady Assets 🔗
Bringing 3D assets into virtual reality (VR) requires more than rendering a scene. Objects need to respond to controllers and behave as expected when grabbed, moved or released.
NVIDIA Omniverse community developer Michael Wagner took on this challenge. He directed GPT-6 Astra to use Blender software to model a study environment from two reference images, balancing visual quality with efficient performance in VR.
He then used Claude Code to build an application that lets users find SimReady Central assets by voice and interact with them in an immersive VR scene. The Claude Code agent worked for about eight hours, and Wagner built the application over a weekend using an NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada workstation and a Meta Quest 3 VR headset.
The application ran on NVIDIA Omniverse libraries: ovstage shared the OpenUSD scene, ovrtx rendered it, ovxr enabled VR and ovphysx ran physics. Wagner later built a second version with ovnewton, which integrates with ovstage, to compare the physics libraries.
The biggest challenge for Wagner was checking what happened inside the headset. Automated tests missed problems he could feel, including objects shaking when grabbed. Wagner reported the symptoms, guided the agent through changes and verified the interaction himself. Updating the grab control once per frame resolved the shaking. His takeaway: Give agents renders and logs to inspect, then check the experience directly.
Explore his open source demo for build instructions, a starting prompt and reusable agent skills.
Send Microducks on Rounds in a Simulated Hospital 🔗
Before adapting a robot to a new environment, developers need to test whether its walking policy — the AI that controls how it moves — can keep it stable in that setting.
AI developer Maziyar Panahi directed Claude Code, using Claude Opus 5.5, to assemble an intensive care unit from 13 NVIDIA SimReady hospital assets and test Microduck robots inside it. The assets came with Newton physics settings, so Panahi didn’t have to model the furniture or create collision geometry from scratch. The Newton physics engine also helped replicate the ward so hundreds of copies could run together on one NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPU.
When the cloud containers lacked graphics support, Panahi and the Claude Code agent separated simulation from rendering, recording robot poses in the cloud and rendering them locally. They also treated the furniture as static collision objects, which enabled larger runs within the solver’s limits.
The robots walked using AI they had already been trained on and followed preset points along a route. Panahi checked how many robots remained upright: In a 256-ward run, 766 of 768 Microducks were still standing after 14 simulated seconds. He said the agent’s work took about two hours.
Explore the open source demo for a starter prompt, checks and instructions to begin with one ward on a CPU, then scale to hundreds on an NVIDIA GPU.
Create Editable 3D Assets With Houdini and AI Agents 🔗
Creating animated 3D content requires connecting modeling, simulation, materials and rendering. Nick Scarcella, a senior technical artist on NVIDIA’s BondLab team, directed AI agents — primarily using Claude — to work with CUDA libraries and Isaac Sim to create animations. The BondLab team uses SideFX Houdini and the NVIDIA ovrtx library to develop materials, lighting and the final rendered appearance.
In one experiment, Scarcella guided Astra to recreate an OP-1 portable synthesizer using product images, manuals and technical direction. He exported the model into the OpenUSD framework, tested it in Houdini and Blender, then used Astra and Opus to refine details before adjusting materials and textures for ovrtx rendering.
Scarcella also used a publicly shared robot-hand checkpoint in Isaac Sim, directing the motion and developing materials and lighting in Houdini with Claude’s assistance. Working with team member Steven Dvornik, the team created an “Echos” visualization: translucent versions of the hand overlap and merge into a single hand animation, offering a visual interpretation of robot training.
Figure: An artistic visualization of simulated robot-hand motion, developed with AI assistance and Houdini’s materials and lighting tools.
These workflows bring agent-assisted creation into existing artist tools, giving teams editable content they can inspect, refine and render across applications.
Explore Scarcella’s Houdini MCP tools and agent skill.
Test Robotic Disassembly With Computer-Aided Design and Simulation 🔗
Before a robot can disassemble a product, developers need to know whether its tools can reach and remove the parts. Jens Jebens, a senior product manager for OpenUSD at NVIDIA, directed Astra to model a car suspension in PTC Onshape and configure it in NVIDIA Isaac Sim.
Jebens used simulation feedback to revise the tooling, including a wrench designed to reach the suspension’s bolts, and reported successful removal of a suspension component in simulation.
PTC also connects computer-aided design (CAD) with simulation through Onshape’s SimReady Publisher, built with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries. Robotics startup Sensori uses it to transfer its Yuri robot into Isaac Sim, carrying geometry, joints and configuration data so the team can evaluate design changes without repeatedly rebuilding the simulation model.
Explore the Onshape importer guide.
Create an Editable Building Model From Site Scans 🔗
Planning warehouse automation requires a model of the building itself, but shelving and machinery can obscure its structure in site scans. Omniverse brings together real-to-sim tools and agent skills to help developers turn real-world captures into editable starting environments for physical AI simulation.
David Wehr, from NVIDIA’s simulation technology team, built on that work using Astra to develop a workflow for digitally reconstructing a building without its contents. The goal is an editable, simulation-ready building model where developers can add or reposition shelving and machinery to evaluate warehouse layouts and automation plans before making physical changes.
Wehr guided Astra to interpret panoramic photos, create building geometry and align it with point-cloud measurements. OpenUSD stores the models, while Omniverse’s ovrtx library renders results for inspection.
Explore NVIDIA Omniverse agent skills to help agents build with Omniverse libraries.
Test Gas-Turbine Operating Scenarios With a Digital Twin 🔗
Before changing how industrial equipment operates, engineers need a way to explore the consequences. Pradeep Kaushik, a member of the NVIDIA Omniverse developer relations team, directed Astra to build a what-if analysis application around a simulated gas turbine and generator.
The application lets users adjust conditions such as load, ambient temperature and fuel composition, then compare power, efficiency, fuel consumption and equipment response. Six test procedures explore scenarios including load changes, a stuck fuel valve and an exhaust-sensor error.
The prototype gives engineers an interactive way to investigate how operating changes and faults could affect equipment behavior, supporting decisions about which scenarios warrant further testing.
Astra used tools like Cantera for thermochemistry and SciPy for equipment dynamics. The application maps solver results to rotor animation and color-coded temperature, pressure and flow-velocity indicators in a 3D turbine. NVIDIA Omniverse libraries update the scene (ovstage), render it with RTX (ovrtx) and stream the view to the browser (ovstream). Engineers can rotate and zoom the cutaway, switch between indicators, and pause or scrub through a simulated response alongside charts and virtual instruments.
Build Simulation Scenes With Open Source SimReady Assets 🔗
With SimReady Central Library, announced at GTC Berlin, developers can access more than 2,000 simulation-ready USD assets from equipment manufacturers and asset providers for robotics simulations and AI factory digital twins workflows.
Paul Kind, a member of NVIDIA’s Omniverse documentation team, pointed an AI agent to the library and guided scene assembly through conversation. His kitchen scene included 180 placements drawn from 63 unique library assets, alongside 18 custom geometry pieces. Kind reviewed renders produced with Isaac Sim and guided further adjustments.
For robotics and factory workflows, developers can select SimReady assets with the simulation properties embedded to fit their required task then test in an assembled environment.
Find assets in SimReady Central Library, and learn how to contribute.
Stress-Test a Warehouse Simulation at Scale 🔗
A warehouse simulation needs to keep running smoothly as more robot arms, conveyors and boxes fill the scene.
When it slows down, developers need to identify what’s holding it back. Bhavik Sanganee, principal engineer at NVIDIA, used Astra with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to build a warehouse simulation, increase its complexity and investigate slowdowns.
Performance first fell below the target when the scene doubled in size. Running physics calculations, image rendering and video preparation concurrently restored performance and enabled further scaling.
With 80 conveyors, 40 arms and 800 boxes, the simulation sustained 30 frames per second at full HD resolution during a two-minute test. The arms completed 640 successful box placements.
Doubling the scene again reduced performance. Testing traced the slowdown to the physics and robot-control pipeline, giving Sanganee a specific area to improve.
Start building with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries.
Test Robot Control for Flexible Cable Routing 🔗
In electronics assembly, a robot may need to position a flexible cable around components before plugging it into a port. The cable bends as the robot moves it, and the connector must line up precisely to fit.
Oyindamola Omotuyi, robotics technical marketing manager at NVIDIA, directed Astra to build a robot simulation using NVIDIA Isaac Lab, Newton physics and Omniverse rendering with a Robotiq gripper handling the cable.
Astra also developed a reinforcement learning system that combined learned cable-routing movements with position-and-orientation feedback and corrective adjustments for USB-C insertion. The simulation gave Omotuyi a way to test cable handling and connector alignment before moving to physical-robot experiments.
The controller used information supplied directly by the simulation. Next steps include testing a friction-held grasp and using information a physical robot could obtain from cameras and sensors.
Get started with robot learning in NVIDIA Isaac Lab.
Turn Robot Computer-Aided Design Into a SimReady Asset 🔗
Before testing whether a robot can pick up and move a box, developers need a simulation model with joints that move correctly and with grippers that can hold the object. A computer-aided design (CAD) model provides the robot’s shape, but it still needs physics properties to perform the task.
Using an ABB Robotics YuMi robot, developers directed Astra with NVIDIA Omniverse content libraries to convert CAD files into OpenUSD, match the robot’s appearance to reference images, and configure joints and collision geometry. They checked the asset against SimReady Foundation requirements before testing it in NVIDIA Isaac Sim.
Both arms and grippers completed four cube pick-and-place cycles, using simulated finger contact and friction. These tests demonstrated behavior under the simulated conditions — estimated physical properties were not calibrated against the real robot.
Follow the five-step SimReady tutorial.
Build a Humanoid Simulator for a Warehouse Environment 🔗
Explore a gamified, physics-based control of a humanoid robot in first- and third-person view.
Before automating warehouse tasks, developers need an interactive simulation environment to explore task behavior and evaluate how the work gets done. Frank DeLise, Omniverse product manager at NVIDIA, used Astra to turn a SimReady warehouse and humanoid robot into an interactive simulator with first- and third-person views.
DeLise directed Astra to connect NVIDIA Omniverse libraries for physics (ovphysx), scene updates (ovstage), rendering (ovrtx) and the user interface (ovui). He also used Astra with SimReady (simready-foundation) to create the physical scene in simulation. Astra then generated animation and application code to bring those capabilities together.
Learn how to prepare and validate SimReady robot assets with frontier AI models and NVIDIA Omniverse libraries.
Connect an Autonomous-Driving Testing Workflow 🔗
Changing a scene, sensor or driving model can significantly affect autonomous-vehicle simulations. Doyub Kim, a manager on the simulation technology team at NVIDIA, asked Astra to build Zero to Alpamayo — a reusable simulation environment based on San Francisco’s Market Street.
Kim directed Astra to map out the workflow, then connect asset creation, traffic, Omniverse RTX sensor simulation and Alpamayo driving in stages, checking each integration. The resulting prototype was a testing ground for comparing models and tracing how scene or sensor changes affect downstream driving behavior. A separate Cosmos3-Nano experiment varied weather and lighting in recorded simulation videos, allowing Kim to compare the driving model’s responses to the same scenario under different conditions.
Use Sensor Differences to Create and Improve Digital Twins 🔗
Comparing recorded and simulated camera and lidar outputs gives developers key performance indicator-based feedback for refining a scene.
To test robots and autonomous vehicles, developers need to know how closely simulated sensors match real ones. Ashley Reid, who works on RTX sensor validation at NVIDIA, directed Astra and Claude Fable 5 agents to compare ovrtx camera and raw LiDAR outputs with recorded data. The agents created two digital twins from scratch and improved two existing ones.
Over about three days, Reid guided an iterative workflow in which agents measured differences, created or modified OpenUSD scenes, and checked the results. Changes addressed missing objects, geometry and materials, with acceptance depending on camera and LiDAR metrics. This gives developers a way to use measured discrepancies to guide scene creation and improvement.
Start by rendering an OpenUSD scene with the ovrtx minimal Python example, then define a sensor measure to compare with recorded data.
Robo Olympics: Test Robot Skills With Simulation 🔗
Teaching robots new movements means checking whether those actions work under physical constraints. Tae Kim, who leads NVIDIA Omniverse engineering and product, used sports videos and natural-language instructions to guide Astra in building Robo Olympics, an experimental project that tests simulated Unitree G1 humanoids performing sports movements.
Under Kim’s direction, Astra built controllers and refined them through physics trials. Newton Physics Engine simulated behavior, the open source NVIDIA Warp framework accelerated calculations and ovrtx rendered scenes and virtual-camera images. In one experiment, the robot cleared a single hurdle in 64 of 100 simulation trials. The trials gave Kim feedback for improving the robot’s timing and control.
Watch Kim explore building simulations with Astra and NVIDIA Omniverse libraries.
Bring the International Space Station Into the Browser 🔗
Turning 3D models into an application requires connecting assets, live data and an interface. Nic Johns, an engineering director at NVIDIA, prompted Astra to assemble NASA assets into an OpenUSD International Space Station model with telemetry. Johns built the application with a single prompt, then used a follow-up prompt to shift the scene to Earth’s daytime side so the planet was visible.
The workflow used Blender for asset preparation and Omniverse libraries for rendering (ovrtx), scene runtime (ovstage) and streaming (ovstream). The application brings 3D models and operational data into the browser, with Johns guiding its development through prompts and corrections.
Try the Omniverse Real-Time Viewer skill.
Turn Captured Rooms Into Testing Environments 🔗
A digitally reconstructed room needs editable objects and accurate physical behavior before developers can test interactions. Chirag Majithia, from the Isaac engineering applications team at NVIDIA, directed Astra to turn stereo camera captures into an editable OpenUSD studio.
The workflow combined PyCuSFM, FoundationStereo and nvblox for reconstruction, with user review guiding object selection and placement. Astra assembled generated and Blender-authored assets and used USD Content Agents to configure how objects move and interact in simulation. Isaac Sim tests guided collision and contact revisions for doors and drawers. The studio connects captured geometry to interaction testing, making gaps and object behavior easier to inspect.
Have a simulation idea? Explore NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to start building with an AI agent.

articles.title: Al menos el 10% de la población mundial sufre un uso problemático de internet: “Hay que priorizar la salud pública frente a la industria”
articles.text:
Al menos el 10% de la población mundial sufre un uso problemático de internet: “Hay que priorizar la salud pública frente a la industria”
La revista ‘The Lancet’ urge a gobiernos a actuar para combatir los trastornos por apuestas y videojuegos en línea, el consumo adictivo del porno o la hipocondría que genera la red
Existe un término. Se inventó durante la década de los noventa y se llama “adicción a internet”. Pero ya no es suficiente, se ha quedado obsoleto. Por ello, la Comisión de la prestigiosa revista The Lancet Psychiatry ha decidido emplear otro: “Uso problemático de internet” (PUI, en inglés). Y las razones no son muy halagüeñas. En un documento publicado este jueves, la Comisión estima que el PUI afecta al menos al 10% de la población mundial. Una situación que abarca desde los trastornos por apuestas y videojuegos en línea, pasando por el consumo adictivo del porno, hasta llegar a conductas “emergentes” como la cibercondría —los hipocondriacos de siempre, solo que ahora potenciados por las infinitas y aterradoras posibilidades de la red—. Los autores del artículo urgen a los gobiernos y a todas las instituciones involucradas a “priorizar la salud pública por encima de los intereses de la industria”.
En el estudio han participado más de 30 investigadores de universidades de cinco continentes que a su vez han sido coordinados por 26 comisarios —psiquiatras, psicólogos, economistas, neurólogos—. Es un esfuerzo por abordar problemas complejos y urgentes en salud mental y por emitir recomendaciones para políticas públicas. La dimensión del asunto se entiende a raíz de los datos que emplea la propia Comisión. Por los más de 6.000 millones de personas que usan internet en todo el mundo (cerca de tres de cada cuatro habitantes del planeta). Por los más de 5.790 millones de perfiles de usuarios en redes sociales (casi el 70% de la población mundial). O por los jóvenes de entre 16 y 24 años que invierten, de media, más de tres horas al día, al menos cuatro veces a la semana, en esas mismas redes sociales.
Un diseño problemático
Pese a que el trabajo reconoce que existen condicionantes genéticos, sociales o psicológicos que afectan la forma en la que un individuo se relaciona con, por ejemplo, las apuestas en línea, los investigadores advierten de que “el uso problemático de internet no puede explicarse únicamente por las vulnerabilidades individuales, sino que también está moldeado o amplificado por las características de diseño de los servicios digitales”. Es decir, las aplicaciones, algoritmos o sitios de internet se aprovechan de mecanismos como las notificaciones emergentes —ese aviso constante que aparece en la pantalla del teléfono—, los me gusta de las redes sociales, el mantenimiento de rachas o la obtención de insignias como parte de una estrategia “para desarrollar un uso habitual y automatizado (es decir, sin pensar)”.
Para la Comisión, hay evidencia suficiente de que las redes sociales, el comercio electrónico, las compras en línea y las plataformas de videojuegos usan “los avances en la comprensión científica de los mecanismos de recompensa cerebral”. Ofrecen lo que saben que el cerebro consume con voracidad. Pero no solo eso, sino que dichas funciones suelen implementarse “sin el conocimiento explícito de los usuarios, sin advertencias ni medidas para gestionar las consecuencias, a expensas del bienestar de los propios usuarios”, continúa el artículo de The Lancet. Todo ello sucede sin que existan límites regulatorios claros.
No afecta a todos por igual
El uso problemático de internet no es una fuerza universal. Puede afectar de distinta forma a una mujer veinteañera de clase media que vive en Pakistán que al flamante nuevo Agente 007, el cuarentón inglés Robert Pattinson. Según el estudio, el uso problemático de internet parece tener más incidencia “en los países de ingresos bajos y medios que en los países de ingresos altos” y, aunque puede perjudicar a personas a lo largo de toda la vida, los jóvenes parecen ser “especialmente vulnerables”. Pero el trabajo también ha identificado algunas tendencias por género. Los hombres suelen tener mayor prevalencia de problemas relacionados con juegos de apuestas, los videojuegos y el consumo de pornografía. Mientras que las mujeres tienden a tener más prevalencia en el uso problemático de las redes sociales, las compras compulsivas y la cibercondría.
Es una realidad que conoce de primera mano Susana Jiménez, jefa del Servicio de Psicología Clínica del Hospital de Bellvitge (Cataluña). Allí, el equipo que lidera atiende alrededor de 350 casos nuevos cada año, sobre todo relacionados con los juegos de apuestas, que representan cerca del 87% del total. A través de una llamada con este diario, Jiménez —que no participó en la investigación— matiza y señala que a la atención clínica llegan solo “los casos de mayor gravedad”. Por lo que celebra que la publicación de este documento de la Comisión ponga el foco en algunos fenómenos que usualmente reciben menos atención.
Las propuestas
El texto de The Lancet Psychiatry propone aprovechar algunas de las enseñanzas de la lucha contra el alcohol o el tabaco, como prohibir la publicidad en eventos deportivos o en escenarios masivos. No obstante, los autores invitan a tener una mirada que vaya mucho más allá de lo meramente restrictivo. Por ejemplo, frente a las limitaciones de acceso que han impuesto países como Australia —y que evalúan implementar algunos miembros de la Unión Europea, entre ellos España—, los expertos consideran que no pueden ser “la estrategia regulatoria principal”.
Es algo en lo que coincide el profesor de Psicología de la Universidad Santiago de Compostela Antonio Rial Boubeta. Para este profesor gallego, la eficacia de dichas medidas que restringen la edad para acceder a las redes sociales (como TikTok o Instagram) es “insuficiente”. Rial hace énfasis en que, si bien considera que el trabajo de la Comisión es “riguroso y necesario”, en el apartado de las propuestas de acción es justamente donde el texto “se queda un poco corto”. Este experto en ciberadicciones considera que la gravedad de la situación demanda acciones mucho más concretas: “Estamos siendo muy laxos con la industria”.
Jiménez —la especialista del Hospital de Bellvitge— converge en la necesidad de regular estas industrias. Es un elemento que también sobrevuela el texto publicado este jueves. Como si fuese patente que ya pasó el tiempo cuando se podía creer que las grandes empresas de este ramo, con las redes sociales a la cabeza, podían autorregularse. Los autores del trabajo son más diplomáticos cuando piden que “la adopción de modelos regulatorios no dependa principalmente de la autorregulación de la industria”. Jiménez, por su parte, recalca que “la responsabilidad de un uso saludable de las nuevas tecnologías no puede recaer ni en las familias, ni en los educadores, ni en los profesionales sanitarios, ni el individuo”. Rial Boubeta es el más combativo: “Debemos dejar de creer para siempre en la autorregulación de la industria”.

articles.title: Black Friday mit KI: Findet ChatGPT wirklich die besten Schnäppchen?
articles.text:
Schnäppchenjagd mit ChatGPT & Gemini: Warum du dich am Black Friday lieber nicht blind auf KI verlassen solltest
Wer in den letzten Jahren rund um den Black Friday auf Schnäppchenfang war, hat vor allem die gängigen Preisvergleichsportale wie Idealo, Günstiger und Geizhals bemüht, vielleicht noch mit einigen Preisrecherche-Tools wie Camelcamelcamel oder Keepa Preisalarme gesetzt und bestenfalls noch die Tipps in Communitys wie Mydealz verfolgt. In diesem Jahr dürfte sich das ändern. Denn immer mehr Nutzer:innen haben erkannt, dass künstliche Intelligenz nicht nur gut darin ist, das geeignete Produkt in der Beratung zu ermitteln, sondern auch nach den passenden Preisen und Angeboten fahnden kann.
Laut einer repräsentativen Umfrage des Preisvergleichsportals Idealo von Oktober 2026 sucht schon heute jede:r fünfte Verbraucher:in mithilfe von KI-Tools oder -Assistenten nach Sonderangeboten. Auch Yougov hat im Oktober die Vorlieben der deutschen Käufer:innen untersucht: Demnach wird in diesem Jahr jede:r Zweite KI für die diesjährige Angebotssuche im Vorweihnachtsgeschäft einsetzen und immerhin 42 Prozent der Nutzer:innen wollen die KI gezielt für die Recherche nach dem besten Preis verwenden.
Doch sind ChatGPT, Gemini und Co. dafür wirklich schon reif und ist das Vertrauen in die Treffsicherheit der LLMs gerechtfertigt? Unserer Erfahrung nach ist insbesondere ChatGPT schon recht gut darin, Kaufinteressent:innen im Vorfeld zu beraten, etwa „einen Saugroboter, der gut im Beseitigen von Tierhaaren ist, unter 400 Euro kostet und nicht allzu laut ist“ zu finden. Dazu wählt die KI anhand hinterlegter Eigenschaften und Daten etwas Passendes aus, berücksichtigt (mehr oder minder zuverlässige) Testergebnisse und Kundenrezensionen und zeigt die passenden Angebote einiger Händler. Hier hatten wir Anfang des Jahres in einem Selbstversuch noch einige Schwächen aufgedeckt, die inzwischen weitgehend verschwunden sind.
Dass das so ist, dafür ist vor allem das Bewusstsein der Händler und Hersteller verantwortlich. Denn – nicht nur wir predigen es regelmäßig – die Auffindbarkeit und Validität der hinterlegten Daten sorgt dafür, dass zunächst die passenden Produkte gefunden und im nächsten Schritt auch die Angebote eines bestimmten Händlers aufgelistet werden.
Nicht nur ChatGPT kann Preisrecherche vernünftig abbilden
Besonderes Augenmerk liegt hier offenbar für viele Anbieter und Service-Betreiber auf ChatGPT. Wer etwa in der Vergangenheit auf Idealo für die Preisrecherche gesetzt hat, kann seit einigen Monaten das passende Plugin mit dem OpenAI-LLM verbinden. Der eigentliche Einkauf erfolgt dann allerdings weiterhin wie gewohnt über die Händler. Die Frage, ob man sich bei der Suche also weiterhin auf eine Preissuchmaschine verlässt, ist also eigentlich falsch gestellt – die Zukunft wird auf die Preissuchmaschine innerhalb der KI hinauslaufen.
Für die Preisrecherche kann es sich aber auch lohnen, auf Google Gemini zu setzen, weil hier inzwischen mehr als 60 Millionen Preislistings angebunden sind – Google Shopping sei Dank. Durch den strukturellen Vorteil ist die Google-KI grundsätzlich gut aufgestellt im Hinblick auf Produkteigenschaften und Preisrecherche. Allerdings ist selbst für Nutzer:innen, die hierfür ein geschultes Auge haben, insbesondere in der Mobilansicht nicht immer ganz klar, welche der Angebote gesponsert sind und wie die Empfehlungen zustande kommen.
Auffällig ist auch ein anderes Problem, das auch eine Untersuchung von Shopsavvy bestätigt: Nur bei einem Teil der Preisrecherchen entspricht das gefundene Ergebnis dem von Google Shopping. Die Untersuchung kam immerhin in einem Drittel der Fälle auf Abweichungen (übrigens in beide Richtungen). Auch bei unseren Tests gibt es bei nahezu allen Konstellationen im Rahmen der KI-Preisrecherche noch Fehler zu beklagen – und das unabhängig vom eingesetzten LLM:
Nicht immer sind die Preise wirklich aktuell, was darauf hindeutet, dass hier nicht mit Echtzeitdaten gearbeitet wird. Demnach nutzt die KI unterschiedliche Datenquellen, Aktualisierungsstände und Angebote der Händler.
Defizite bei den Suchergebnissen
Defizite haben die Suchergebnisse der KI allerdings auch noch in der Aufbereitung, die offenbar in den meisten Datenquellen weniger aussagekräftig im Hinblick auf die längerfristige Preisentwicklung ist. Hinzu kommt, dass die Varianten (etwa verschiedene Farben und Größen eines Kleidungsstücks) nicht immer treffsicher ausgewiesen werden. Das war tatsächlich in der Vergangenheit auch schon bei herkömmlichen Preissuchmaschinen ein Problem.
Eine weitere Einschränkung für den Nutzen der KI in diesem Kontext ist die Gefahr, an Fakeshops zu geraten. So hat etwa das auf Markenschutz spezialisierte Unternehmen Podqi bereits in einem Test ermittelt, dass sowohl ChatGPT als auch Gemini und Perplexity teilweise Angebote auf Fakeshop-Seiten empfehlen. Dazu wurden fast 6.800 Antworten der drei KI-Systeme analysiert. In 15 Prozent der Antworten von Perplexity tauchten problematische Websites auf, bei ChatGPT waren es acht Prozent, bei Gemini vier Prozent. Als problematisch wurden dabei sowohl gefälschte Markenshops als auch Anbieter von Produktfälschungen verstanden.
Immerhin in 57 Prozent der Fälle wurden diese ausdrücklich als Einkaufsmöglichkeit empfohlen, in weiteren 34 Prozent wurden sie ohne Warnhinweis erwähnt. Auch wenn die Untersuchung sich explizit auf US-Quellen bezog, sollten Kund:innen bei von der KI empfohlenen Onlineshops vorsichtig sein. Es dürfte nämlich nur eine Frage der Zeit sein, bis auch in Deutschland ähnliche Fälle bekannt werden. Auch wenn die KI-Anbieter hier schnell tätig werden dürften, bleibt also ein Restrisiko.
Als problematisch im Zusammenhang mit den (Pre-)Black-Friday-Rabatten hat sich aber noch etwas anderes erwiesen: In vielen Fällen ließ sich eine KI wie Claude von vermeintlichen Rabatten auf den Listenpreis blenden, während der Straßenpreis schon über längere Zeit deutlich darunter lag. Erst durch gezieltes Nachfragen sah die KI den Fehler ein, fand dann bei einer Preisrecherche zwar den günstigsten Preis, benannte aber einen absolut unbekannten Händler, obwohl mehrere große Shops denselben Preis anboten.
Wie KI Beratung und Preisrecherche kombiniert
Die eigentliche Stärke der KI beim Einkaufen liegt also nicht unbedingt in der reinen Preisrecherche, sondern (noch) eher in der vorgelagerten Beratungsleistung. Hilfreich war die KI – vor allem in Form von ChatGPT – übrigens bei einigen unserer Recherchen, bei denen Vorjahresmodelle angeboten wurden, wenn diese im Laufe des Dialogs als ausreichend angesehen wurden. Das funktionierte etwa bei einem Internetproblem mit einem bestimmten Kabelmodem recht souverän.
Allerdings war noch nicht in allen Fällen die Transparenz der Angebote gegeben. Zum einen wurde nicht in jedem Fall klar, ob ein Suchergebnis gesponsert war oder es andere Anreize gab, zum anderen wurden in einigen Fällen auch andere Produktvarianten, die sich im Detail unterschieden, mit aufgeführt. Das ist etwa bei einem Fernseher, der bestimmte Features nicht hat, ärgerlich, weil man es erst auf der jeweiligen Website des Händlers erkennt – wenn überhaupt.
Widersprüchliches gab’s auch im Hinblick auf kompliziertere Preise, wie sie im Mobilfunkmarkt üblich sind: So wurden uns bei der Recherche auch die Kaufpreise von Vertragshandys angezeigt, da diese mit subventioniertem Vertrag niedriger liegen als der Kaufpreis für das Gerät.
Sinnvoll ist es daher, die KI bestimmte Informationen, die einem wenig plausibel vorkommen, noch einmal verifizieren zu lassen und dabei sowohl auf eine Websuche zu setzen als auch die jeweilige Uhrzeit und Quelle einzufordern. In einzelnen Fällen hat die KI auch Preisverläufe einfach geschätzt, sodass einzelne Ausreißer nicht mit abgebildet wurden – das sollte man ihr deshalb generell untersagen.
Blind vertrauen sollte man der KI aber vor allem auch nicht bei den Preisangaben und bei den gefundenen Händlern. Denn in einigen Fällen wurden Versandkosten unterschlagen oder das Produkt war erst deutlich verzögert lieferbar. Und einige der recherchierten Shops verwiesen auf wenig vertrauenswürdige Händler.

articles.title: Les Anneaux de pouvoir réinvente l'histoire du plus puissant dragon de Tolkien
articles.text:
Dans le lore de Tolkien, Smaug est certainement le dragon le plus connu : après tout, il est l’un des acteurs principaux du roman Le Hobbit, prologue au Seigneur des anneaux, et il a été représenté avec brio dans l’adaptation de Peter Jackson. Mais à travers les âges, d’autres reptiles volants ont su marquer l’histoire… et terroriser la Terre du Milieu.
La saison 3 des Anneaux de pouvoir, diffusée depuis le 11 novembre, vient justement d’en mettre un à l’honneur, de manière indirecte, au cours d’une discussion entre deux personnages majeurs de la série. Son nom émerge à l’occasion des épisodes 5 et 6, disponibles ce 18 novembre en streaming sur Prime Video.
Prudence, la suite contient évidemment des spoilers.
Ancalagon, monture de Sauron selon la série
Dans Les Anneaux de pouvoir, les showrunners puisent allégrement dans le Premier Âge et le Deuxième Âge. Si la série se déroule au Deuxième Âge, le Premier est une époque presque légendaire, des millénaires avant les péripéties actuelles. Une période où des légendes comme Tuor, Eärendil et Beren ont marqué leurs contemporains.
Cette fois, c’est un dragon qui sort de ce passé. Celeborn, le compagnon elfique de Galadriel, y parle d’un « dragon de feu » nommé Ancalagon, et Sauron affirme l’avoir monté. Si on n’a pas Le Silmarillion sur sa table de chevet, le nom ne doit pas dire grand-chose. Or, Ancalagon est le plus puissant des dragons de Morgoth, et du monde.
La scène arrive dans l’épisode 5. Cachés dans un arbre de Vertbois pour échapper aux orques, Galadriel et Celeborn rattrapent des siècles de séparation, car elle le croyait mort pendant la guerre contre Morgoth. Celeborn raconte alors qu’Ancalagon a réduit en cendres sa légion entière pendant la Guerre de la Colère, qui clôt le Premier Âge.
L’elfe n’a survécu que parce que son cheval l’a envoyé d’un coup de sabot dans un fossé rempli d’eau. Capturé en sortant, il a ensuite passé des millénaires dans les prisons de l’ennemi. Un peu plus tard, la série révèle que Sauron chevauchait le dragon ce jour-là, ce qui fait de lui le responsable direct du massacre.
Le plus puissant des dragons de Morgoth
Selon la fiche que lui consacre Tolkiendil, l’association francophone dédiée à l’œuvre de l’écrivain, Ancalagon le Noir était le plus puissant des dragons créés par Melkor (le premier Seigneur des ténèbres, plus connu sous le nom de Morgoth, dont Sauron n’était alors que le lieutenant).
Il était à la fois un dragon ailé et un dragon de feu, c’est-à-dire capable de cracher des flammes. Son nom se traduirait par « mordante tempête » en noldorin, une version antérieure du sindarin (l’une des langues elfiques) telle que Tolkien l’avait imaginée dans ses notes.
La première traduction française du Silmarillion, signée Pierre Alien, en faisait « le plus grand » des dragons, confondant ainsi taille et puissance. La traduction de Daniel Lauzon a rétabli « le plus puissant », fidèle à l’anglais « the mightiest ».
Ancalagon n’a pourtant combattu qu’une seule fois. Pendant la Guerre de la Colère, Morgoth voit ses armées faiblir et lâche une horde de dragons ailés. Eärendil, à bord de son navire Vingilot, affronte Ancalagon pendant un jour et une nuit, puis le tue juste avant l’aube, en l’an 587 du Premier Âge.
Le dragon s’écrase sur les tours du Thangorodrim et détruit dans sa chute la forteresse de Morgoth. Cet Eärendil n’est autre que le père d’Elrond, l’un des héros de la série.
Sauron sur un dragon, une idée de la série
Dans les textes de Tolkien, rien n’indique qu’Ancalagon ait porté un cavalier. La fiche de Tolkiendil ne lui en donne aucun, et on est très loin des dragons montés de Daenerys dans Game of Thrones (qui ne sont techniquement pas vraiment des dragons). La série prend donc une liberté, et ce n’est pas tout à fait la première fois que les showrunners remplissent les cases vides.
Cela étant, ce choix a au moins le mérite de donner un passé commun à Sauron et Celeborn, ce qui rend plus personnel leur face-à-face de l’épisode 6, quand Sauron torture l’elfe à Barad-dûr. Dans Le Seigneur des anneaux, Gandalf donne d’ailleurs une idée de la puissance de la bête : selon lui, même le souffle d’Ancalagon n’aurait pas pu détruire l’Anneau unique.
