articles.title: Ultraviolette X-47 Venom review: An electric crossover that makes more sense on the road?
articles.text:
Ultraviolette X-47 Venom review: An electric crossover that makes more sense on the road?
Ultraviolette’s X-47 Venom gets a 20kg weight reduction, improved battery cooling, more technology and better road manners, making it a compelling electric crossover. Here’s what we think.
Ultraviolette's X-47 was an interesting attempt at combining the performance of an electric motorcycle with the versatility of a crossover. With the new X-47 Venom, the company hasn't reinvented the motorcycle but has made a series of engineering and feature upgrades that could make it a more rounded proposition.
The biggest change is underneath the visuals. The Venom gets a new 100V VX-100 electrical architecture, an updated SRB-11 battery pack, a lighter motor and controller, and an improved battery thermal management system. Depending on the variant, it is around 13-17kg lighter than its predecessor, while offering larger battery options and a higher claimed range. Ultraviolette also claims faster heat dissipation, improved acceleration and a higher top speed.
There are some noticeable changes to the equipment list, too. The older 5-inch instrument display makes way for a 7-inch touchscreen TFT console, while cruise control, updated camera-assisted parking features and radar-based rider assistance systems add to the technology package.
But do these changes make the X-47 Venom a better motorcycle? We spent time riding it on a go-kart track, city roads and some gravel stretches to find out.
Design: Familiar territory, but lighter on its feet
The overall design remains unchanged, as do the motorcycle's dimensions. Swing a leg over and there is little to distinguish the new X-47 Venom from its predecessor in terms of ergonomics. However, once you kick off the stand, the reduction in weight becomes evident.
Ultraviolette hasn't made any significant changes to the styling or the core structural components, including the suspension and wheels. The chassis remains the same, apart from a few tweaks to improve its structural strength.
The Venom retains its crossover proportions, block-pattern tyres and upright riding stance. It may not look dramatically different, but the weight reduction is arguably more important than a cosmetic update, particularly for a motorcycle that has to balance battery capacity with everyday usability.
Features: A technology showcase
On the features front, the X-47 Venom continues to run on 17-inch alloy wheels at both ends, with USD forks at the front and a monoshock at the rear, both preload-adjustable. Braking duties are handled by disc brakes at both ends, supported by dual-channel ABS.
The technology package, however, is where the Venom gets more interesting. The first thing to catch one's eye is the new 7-inch TFT instrument console, replacing the older 5-inch display. It is touch-operated and allows riders to access a host of settings, including traction control levels, regenerative braking, tyre pressure information and ABS modes.
One feature I particularly appreciate is that the touchscreen functionality is disabled when the motorcycle is moving. Riders can only toggle between regenerative braking levels and riding modes while on the move. All other operations require the motorcycle to come to a complete halt. It is a sensible safety measure that prevents unnecessary distractions.
Other notable features include onboard front and rear cameras with parking assistance, along with radar-based systems such as rear collision warning, lane change assist, overtake alert and blindspot detection. Cruise control is another useful addition, particularly for longer highway rides, where maintaining a constant speed can help reduce rider fatigue. The company also claims better range when cruise control is used, however, this is something to test when we have the motorcycle for longer.
Underneath, the new SRB-11 battery pack gets an upgraded thermal management system. Ultraviolette claims up to 50% faster heat dissipation and twice the cooling performance compared with the earlier system. The company also says the battery can return to its optimal operating temperature in 15 minutes, against 30 minutes previously. These are interesting claims, especially for Indian riding conditions, although our short test ride wasn't long enough to evaluate the battery's thermal performance.
The new electrical architecture also brings improvements to performance. The UV LIGHTFURY motor delivers a claimed output of around 40hp and 550Nm of wheel torque, while top speed has increased to 155kmph. The 7.5kWh version offers an IDC-certified range of 227km, while the larger 11kWh variant claims 343km. Ultraviolette also says the Venom can accelerate from 0-100kmph in 5.9 seconds. While acceleration has definitely improved, real-world range is another aspect that we could not test.
Ride and handling: More at home on the road than on the racetrack
We had a go on the X-47 Venom at the Velocity go-kart track, before taking it out into the natural settings where this electric crossover is likely to spend most of its life: city roads, highways and some mild off-roading.
On the racetrack, the motorcycle reminds you that you are riding an EV. As I tipped it into corners, the transition felt like a small step rather than the seamless lean that conventional motorcycles offer. It did not feel quite as natural when changing direction quickly.
This could partly be down to the battery pack and how its weight influences the motorcycle's dynamics, or perhaps the block-pattern tyres, which are designed to offer versatility across different surfaces rather than outright track grip. The chassis, however, remains identical to the older X-47, with no fundamental changes apart from a few tweaks to improve its structural strength.
Move away from the racetrack, though, and the X-47 Venom begins to make much more sense.
On the road, the motorcycle felt completely natural. The rider triangle is excellent, with the rider sitting on top of the electric crossover rather than feeling enclosed within it. The handlebars are comfortably positioned and offer an easy reach, making the riding posture suitable for everyday use as well as longer journeys.
The acceleration is typical Ultraviolette. Riders can choose between a more linear power delivery and the sharper response of Ballistic mode. Regardless of the mode, the acceleration does not disappoint. The instant torque makes overtaking and quick bursts of acceleration effortless, while the different riding modes allow the rider to decide how aggressively the motorcycle responds.
Having shed weight compared with the older motorcycle, the Venom feels lighter and brisker. This is particularly noticeable when negotiating city traffic and changing direction on ordinary roads. The suspension also does a commendable job of soaking up Bengaluru's pothole-ridden roads. The experience remains reasonably composed even with a pillion, although the rear seat could do with better cushioning and comfort, particularly for longer rides.
The braking is predictable, and ABS intervention is not particularly intrusive during normal riding conditions. The motorcycle inspires confidence under braking without the system constantly making its presence felt.
Since our test rides were relatively short, we could not assess the battery's heating and cooling performance or the charging capabilities. However, one aspect worth noting is that the Venom comes with an onboard charger. This means riders only need to carry a charging cable, which does not take up too much space in a backpack. It is a practical addition, particularly for those planning longer journeys.
Off the road, the 200mm ground clearance provides enough confidence to tackle gravel tracks and uneven surfaces. The Venom is capable of handling mild off-roading, but it would be unfair to compare it with purpose-built adventure motorcycles.
It does not have the same off-road credentials as the KTM 390 Adventure R, its sibling, the 390 Enduro R, or the Royal Enfield Himalayan. These motorcycles are designed to handle considerably more demanding terrain. The Venom, instead, is better understood as a road-focused electric crossover that can take the occasional gravel trail or broken road in its stride.
Would I recommend it?
My answer is yes, provided you understand what the X-47 Venom is designed to do.
If your riding primarily involves city commutes, occasional highway runs and limited off-roading, the Venom makes sense. The lower weight, improved acceleration, larger battery options and added convenience features make it a more rounded proposition than its predecessor.
However, if you are looking for a serious adventure motorcycle that can tackle demanding trails, rough terrain and extended off-road journeys, KTM and Royal Enfield remain the more appropriate choices.
As a second motorcycle in the garage, though, the X-47 Venom is a fun proposition. It offers the performance and instant acceleration associated with Ultraviolette, while adding a degree of everyday practicality and versatility.
The Venom may not have changed dramatically on the outside, but the engineering updates make it a more appealing electric crossover. It is not trying to replace a conventional adventure motorcycle. Instead, it makes a case for being a versatile, technology-packed electric motorcycle that is enjoyable on everyday roads.

articles.title: Así se vería Lucía Caminos, Jason Duval y Mandy de GTA VI en el universo de Guerreras K-pop
articles.text:
La inteligencia artificial permite imaginar cómo serían los personajes de videojuegos y películas si pertenecieran a otros universos de ficción. Esta vez, Lucía Caminos, Jason Duval y Mandy, figuras del estreno de Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA VI), fueron reinterpretados con la estética de Las Guerreras K-pop, la producción animada de Netflix que combina música, cultura coreana y acción sobrenatural.
Las imágenes muestran a los personajes con una apariencia diferente a la que tienen en sus representaciones originales. En lugar de los escenarios urbanos y criminales asociados con el videojuego de Rockstar Games, aparecen en un ambiente de espectáculo musical, con luces violetas, pantallas gigantes y una identidad visual inspirada en el grupo HUNTR/X.
El resultado combina dos fenómenos del entretenimiento que cuentan con comunidades de seguidores en internet: la entrega de una de las franquicias más populares de los videojuegos y una película animada que convirtió el K-pop y la fantasía en parte de su propuesta.
Lucía Caminos adopta la estética de una guerrera K-pop
En la primera recreación, Lucía Caminos conserva sus principales rasgos físicos, pero cambia su vestuario por uno inspirado en la moda de las integrantes de HUNTR/X. La protagonista aparece con una chaqueta turquesa decorada con bordados dorados, accesorios metálicos y prendas urbanas que combinan elementos de la moda idol con una apariencia de guerrera.
Su cabello oscuro permanece recogido en una coleta alta y su expresión mantiene una actitud seria y decidida. La imagen la presenta junto a Jason Duval, en una composición que recuerda a un cartel promocional de una producción musical o una película de acción.
La reinterpretación también conserva la relación visual entre ambos personajes. Jason aparece con una chaqueta oscura, detalles dorados y una camiseta blanca, mientras mantiene sus tatuajes y su apariencia física. La iluminación de un escenario musical reemplaza los paisajes de Vice City y aporta una atmósfera completamente distinta.
Jason Duval también cambia de universo
El personaje masculino de GTA VI adopta una imagen más cercana a la de un integrante de un grupo musical. Su vestimenta combina prendas negras y turquesas, cadenas y detalles decorativos que encajan con la estética de Guerreras K-pop.
Sin embargo, la recreación mantiene elementos que permiten reconocerlo, como su cabello corto, su barba y el tatuaje que lleva en el brazo. La intención es trasladar su apariencia a otro estilo visual sin perder los rasgos que lo distinguen.
En esta versión, Jason deja de aparecer como un personaje relacionado con el mundo criminal de GTA VI para convertirse en una figura que podría formar parte de un espectáculo de K-pop. La propuesta no implica un cambio en la historia del videojuego, sino una reinterpretación artística de su imagen.
Mandy aparece como una integrante del universo HUNTR/X
La segunda imagen presenta a Mandy con una estética más cercana a la de una estrella del K-pop. Su cabello rubio ondulado y sus rasgos se mantienen, mientras que su vestuario cambia por un conjunto blanco con detalles dorados, una chaqueta corta y accesorios metálicos.
También aparece sosteniendo una tableta con el símbolo de HUNTR/X y haciendo un gesto con una de sus manos. El escenario está dominado por luces violetas y pantallas que refuerzan la ambientación de un concierto.
A diferencia de la primera recreación, en la que Lucía y Jason aparecen juntos, esta composición coloca a Mandy como protagonista. La imagen recuerda a las fotografías promocionales que suelen acompañar los lanzamientos de grupos musicales y producciones animadas.
La inteligencia artificial amplía las posibilidades del fan art
Estas recreaciones muestran cómo las herramientas de inteligencia artificial generativa pueden combinar personajes de diferentes franquicias y trasladarlos a estilos visuales distintos. A partir de imágenes de referencia, estos sistemas permiten conservar características físicas y modificar elementos como la ropa, los escenarios, la iluminación y la ambientación.
Este tipo de contenido también forma parte de una tendencia entre los seguidores de videojuegos y películas: imaginar encuentros entre universos que no comparten una historia oficial.
En este caso, la propuesta reúne a personajes asociados con GTA VI y la estética de Guerreras K-pop. Las imágenes son creaciones conceptuales y no forman parte de un anuncio de Rockstar Games ni de Netflix. Tampoco anticipan una colaboración entre ambas compañías.
La reinterpretación funciona como una muestra de cómo la inteligencia artificial puede transformar personajes conocidos y ofrecer nuevas versiones visuales para los fanáticos, sin modificar las historias originales de las producciones.

articles.title: November 2026 Top500 New Systems Are Few and Far Between
articles.text:
The November 2026 TOP500 list has only 28 new systems, the lowest count in our tracking series going back to June 2018. This dramatic slowdown from previous editions marks a significant shift in how often the list turns over with fresh hardware.
New System Counts Hit a Series Low
Just as a quick note, the official Top500 post says there were 27 new systems, but when we filtered the list on First Appearance 68 (with 68 being the November 2026 list), we got 28 new systems. We will use these new systems for our analysis. The 28 new systems on this November 2026 list mark the lowest count in our series since June 2018, dropping from 43 in June 2026. The previous low was 39 in June 2022, and while November 2024 rebounded to 54, this edition represents a clear step down.
The June 2018 list had 133 new systems, and November 2018 had 153. Those days of roughly a quarter or more of the list turning over with each publication are long gone. Today’s 28 newcomers represent 5.6% of the full Top500.
The 28 new systems together contribute about 1.0 EF/s of Rmax, or roughly 5.1% of the list’s total performance. That is the lowest share since at least November 2021, when new systems contributed over 12%. The prior low was 5.48% in June 2023, so this continues a pattern in which even the systems that do get submitted add little aggregate HPL capability. Part of that is because LineShine was added to the list in June 2026, so a recent new #1 tends to SKU the aggregate addition numbers.
Only five new systems made the Top 100. The highest-ranked newcomer is KISTI’s HANGANG at #12, an HPE Cray EX254n system using NVIDIA Grace CPUs and GH200 Superchips with HPE’s Slingshot 400 interconnect. No new systems made the Top 10. LineShine remains at #1, holding its position from the June 2026 list where it debuted with 2.198 EF/s of HPL performance using custom Arm-based LX2 processors.
With so few new systems and modest newcomer performance, total list Rmax grew from roughly 18.7 EF/s in June 2026 to approximately 19.7 EF/s now. That compares with nearly 25% growth on the previous list, which was driven largely by LineShine’s debut.
The #500 entry point rose from about 2.66 PF/s in June 2026 to roughly 2.87 PF/s now, an increase of around 8%. For context, the November 2021 threshold was just 1.65 PF/s, so the bar has been relatively low to enter the list. Just on a CPU basis, that was when a 64-core AMD EPYC 7003 “Milan” CPU was state of the art. Now, we have 256-core AMD EPYC 9006 “Venice” CPUs. CPU performance has gone up by more than a factor of four (since we get more performance per core), but we have only seen a roughly 74% increase in the “get-in” performance number.
The List Is Aging Rapidly
With only 28 new systems replacing 28 that fell off, the average system on the list has now been there for approximately 3.2 years. That is the highest in our tracking window, up from about 2.2 years in November 2021 and roughly 3.0 years as recently as June 2026.
The systems that dropped off this list had been on it for an average of about 5.4 years, measured as of the current list date. That is a long tenure in terms of list appearances, and it highlights how established these departing clusters were.
There is a stark contrast between what fell off this list and what came on. Of the 28 systems that dropped, 24 were CPU-only, with most using Intel Skylake or Cascade Lake processors from roughly 2017-2019. Seventeen of the departed systems were in the Industry segment, 17 were built by Lenovo, and 14 were located in China.
By contrast, 23 of the 28 new systems are GPU- or other accelerator-accelerated. The churn is slow as well as turning over from old CPU-only commercial clusters to newer GPU-accelerated research and academic systems.
China and Industry Submissions Have Collapsed
Chinese service-provider submissions and commercial Industry clusters have nearly disappeared as sources of new entries. Systems in China fell from 173 on the November 2021 list to just 18 now. China still holds #1 with LineShine, but it has otherwise largely stopped submitting at volume. The country added only one new system this edition: CTyun HPC – shanghai15, an eSurfing Cloud entry using a MetaX C588 accelerator and China Telecom C86 CPUs.
The Industry segment has fallen from 258 systems in November 2021 to 146 now, and only two of the 28 new systems are classified as Industry. The rest break down as 12 Research, 12 Academic, and 2 Government.
This is the same theme we raised in our June 2023 analysis. It feels like the Top500 submissions are not a census of all HPC or AI deployments, and the commercial systems that used to populate the list have largely stopped appearing.
Who Built the New Systems
HPE leads this edition with 8 new systems and by far the most new Rmax at roughly 615 PF/s. That total is dominated by HANGANG at #12 with 342.6 PF/s and ORNL’s Lux at #14 with 220.79 PF/s, an AMD EPYC 9575F system using Instinct MI355X accelerators.
Lenovo has 6 new systems, MEGWARE has 4, and Dell and Fujitsu each have 3. Notably, all three of Fujitsu’s entries are Supermicro-based platforms, including the RIKYU system at RIKEN using GB200 Superchips and Nagoya University’s Flow 2.0 subsystems.
By geography, Europe leads with 11 new systems, followed by Asia with 9 and North America with 8. Germany added 6 new systems, nearly matching the United States’ 7.
South Korea has 3 new systems thanks to HANGANG and its CPU companion system at KISTI, plus a Dell PowerEdge XE9680L with B200 accelerators at Elice Inc. Japan also added 3.
CPUs: Grace Ties Intel as AMD Leads x86
Among the 28 new systems, AMD leads with 13, while NVIDIA Grace and Intel each account for 7. The remaining system uses a China Telecom C86 processor.
All five of the new CPU-only systems are AMD-based, and four of them use Turin Dense (Zen 5c) parts: HANGANG-CPU at KISTI, Manta CPU at Navy DSRC, Nagoya’s Flow 2.0 Type I subsystem, and Lichtenberg NHR-1 CPU at TU Darmstadt. The fifth, ERDC’s Barfoot, uses Genoa.
All seven new Intel systems are GPU hosts. Six use Emerald Rapids and one uses Granite Rapids. There are no new Intel CPU-only systems on this list at all, which is a notable shift for a vendor that has historically dominated the Top500. Maybe more telling is that in the latest (pre-Venice/Vera) generation, Intel has only one Granite Rapids CPU system, while AMD’s Turin has 11 systems.
Across the full list, Intel’s share has fallen to 50.2%, down from 82% in November 2021. AMD sits at 39.8%, and NVIDIA Grace now powers 6.4% of systems with 32 entries.
NVIDIA Grace is the most common CPU among new systems with 7 appearances, all in GPU-host roles. Next comes the AMD EPYC 9655 with 3 systems, followed by several SKUs at 2 each, including the EPYC 9965, EPYC 9654, Xeon Platinum 8568Y+, and Xeon Platinum 8570.
The 28 new systems use 16 different CPU SKUs total. On the full list, however, the story is very different. The AMD EPYC 7763 from 2021 remains the most common SKU with 34 systems, and NVIDIA Grace is close behind at 32.
The EPYC 7742 has 26 systems, and the Xeon Platinum 8480+ has 20. These older models from roughly 2019-2023 still hold significant presence on this list, even as newer SKUs dominate among the latest additions.
Core Counts Split by Role
Most GPU-host CPUs have between 36 and 72 cores per socket. Grace has 72, Emerald Rapids hosts typically run 48-56 cores, and five GPU systems use 96-core EPYC parts.
Every new CPU-only system uses a part with between 96 and 192 cores. That includes the 96-core EPYC 9654 in Barfoot, the 128-core EPYC 9745 in HANGANG-CPU, the 160-core EPYC 9845 in Manta CPU, and two systems using the 192-core EPYC 9965.
The median new system has 72 cores per socket versus 52 for the full list. Five years ago, the full-list median was just 20 cores per socket.
Systems using CPUs with 24 or fewer cores have fallen from 75% of the list in November 2021 to just 19% now. None of the 28 new entries use such low-core-count processors, indicating a distinct shift in the CPU mix appearing on the TOP500.
The shift toward higher core counts reflects a clear division in new system design. GPU hosts typically use moderate-core CPUs, while CPU-only systems leverage high-density EPYC parts to maximize compute throughput per socket.
Accelerators: NVIDIA Blackwell Arrives, but Hopper Is Still the Installed Base
Fourteen of the 28 new systems use NVIDIA Blackwell accelerators, split between 12 with B200 and 2 with GB200 Superchips. Hopper accounts for another 6 systems across H200, GH200, and one remaining H100.
AMD has two new accelerated systems: ORNL’s Lux on MI355X at #14 with 220.8 PF/s, and C-DAC’s PARAM KAVERI in India using MI300X. MetaX has one entry with its C588 accelerator in the CTyun system.
Across the full list, accelerated systems now represent 58.6% of systems and 78.8% of Rmax. That compares with just 30% of systems being accelerated back in November 2021.
Blackwell systems nearly doubled from 18 to 32 since the June 2026 list, while Hopper reached 137 systems. In terms of system count, AMD Instinct across all generations is still roughly at Blackwell’s level.
The installed base story matters here. Even though Blackwell dominates new submissions, the full list still has more Hopper systems than anything else, and 61 Ampere-generation systems from the A100 era remain on the list.
Interconnect: InfiniBand Keeps Taking Share
Among new systems, 19 of 28 use InfiniBand. That breaks down as 14 with NDR, 2 with XDR, 2 with HDR, and one unspecified generation. Five new systems use HPE Slingshot, including the first Slingshot 400 systems on the list: HANGANG and its CPU companion at KISTI.
Four new systems use Ethernet. Two are RoCE-based, one uses NVIDIA Spectrum-X (the MEGARIDE system at CINECA), and ORNL’s Lux uses HPE Juniper with AMD Pensando 400G Ethernet.
Half of the new systems run 400Gb/s per port, and two run 800Gb/s XDR InfiniBand. These are nominal per-port line rates rather than achieved throughput, but they show where high-end cluster networking is heading.
Across the full list, Ethernet has fallen from 45% of systems in November 2021 to just 18% now. The old 10/25/100GbE commercial clusters that drove those numbers have largely aged off the list. InfiniBand now sits at 60% and Slingshot at 15%.
InfiniBand leads new submissions with 19 of 28 systems, while Ethernet accounts for only 4. Across the full list, InfiniBand has grown to 302 systems versus 88 for Ethernet and 73 for Slingshot, showing a clear shift in the reported interconnect mix.
Final Words
The November 2026 TOP500 shows a list with limited turnover, featuring only 28 new systems and roughly 5% performance growth. The average tenure of listed systems has approached 3.2 years, marking the slowest update rate in our tracking window. China’s presence dropped to 18 systems from 173 in November 2021, while the Industry segment fell to 146 from 258. Of the new entries, 23 are accelerators.
New hardware on the list highlights specific architectural trends: Blackwell accelerators appear in 14 systems, all CPU-only newcomers use AMD EPYC processors, and NVIDIA Grace matches Intel’s count among new entrants. The Top500 remains a useful gauge for tracking declared HPL system configurations and platform trends over time. However, it does not capture the full scope of current HPC and AI compute investments, which often prioritize different benchmarks or deployment models.

articles.title: A tiny supercurrent could unlock quantum information without destroying it
articles.text:
A tiny supercurrent could unlock quantum information without destroying it
Scientists have developed a promising new method that could read quantum information with 99.85% accuracy while barely disturbing the qubit itself.
- Date:
- November 4, 2026
- Source:
- Fundação de Amparo à Pesquisa do Estado de São Paulo
- Summary:
- Researchers have proposed a breakthrough technique for reading quantum information without destroying the delicate states that make quantum computers work. By detecting an electrical signal generated by the qubit itself, their method achieved up to 99.85% accuracy in simulations and could make future quantum computers simpler and more efficient.
- Share:
One of the biggest obstacles in quantum computing is surprisingly simple to describe: how do you read information without changing or destroying it? Unlike the bits used in ordinary computers, quantum bits, or qubits, are extraordinarily sensitive to measurement. Trying to determine their state can cause that state to collapse, potentially erasing the very information scientists want to retrieve.
Researchers have now proposed a way to overcome much of this difficulty by using an unusual electrical signal produced by the qubit itself. Their approach focuses on a special type known as an "Andreev qubit," which can generate an oscillating electric supercurrent through its own quantum behavior. By monitoring this current, scientists may be able to determine the qubit's state without directly measuring it or significantly disturbing the information it contains.
The research, supported by FAPESP, was published in Physical Review B Letters. It was led by José Carlos Egues, a full professor at the São Carlos Institute of Physics at the University of São Paulo (IFSC-USP) in Brazil, and Yugui Yao of the School of Physics at the Beijing Institute of Technology in China. If experimentally confirmed, their method could simplify quantum computing by removing the need for extra qubits used in certain measurement techniques.
Why Measuring Quantum Information Is So Difficult
Conventional computers store information in bits that have one of two values, 0 or 1. These values can be checked repeatedly without changing the information. Quantum computers work differently because their qubits can exist in superpositions, meaning they can combine the states 0 and 1 in ways that are not possible with conventional bits.
This unusual ability is central to the potential power of quantum computing. However, it also creates a major vulnerability. Quantum states can be disrupted by interactions with their surroundings, including the instruments scientists use to examine them.
"In the conventional formulation of quantum mechanics, a projective measurement causes the system to assume one of the states associated with the measured quantity. Thus, if a qubit has been prepared in a certain superposition of 0 and 1, its direct measurement tends to destroy that superposition and, consequently, the information it contained," says Egues.
To minimize this problem, physicists developed techniques known as "quantum nondemolition measurements," or QND. Many of these approaches use an additional quantum system called an ancilla. Rather than measuring the original qubit directly, researchers transfer information to the ancilla and measure that auxiliary system instead.
The term "ancilla" comes from a Latin word meaning "slave" or "servant." In modern scientific usage, it describes something that performs a supporting function. Here, the ancilla acts as an intermediary, allowing researchers to obtain information while preserving the original qubit as much as possible.
Although effective, these procedures come with practical disadvantages. Scientists must prepare the auxiliary qubits, connect them to the qubits being studied, transfer information between them, and perform repeated measurements. These additional steps require time and equipment, and the complexity becomes increasingly significant as the number of qubits grows.
"Our strategy is different. Instead of transferring the information to an auxiliary qubit, we seek to obtain it from a signal produced by the qubit under study itself," says the researcher.
A Special Quantum Bit That Produces Its Own Signal
The proposed technique relies on the unusual properties of an Andreev qubit. Its name honors Soviet physicist Alexander Andreev (1939-2023), who identified a distinctive quantum process in 1964 that occurs where normal materials meet superconductors.
Superconductors are materials that can conduct electricity without electrical resistance under appropriate conditions. At the boundaries involving these materials, special quantum states known as "Andreev states" can form. In the system studied by the researchers, these states are confined to an extremely small region between two superconducting materials.
These quantum states can represent the basic values 0 and 1, along with superpositions of those values, making them suitable for storing quantum information.
"In the system under consideration, this region is a quantum dot - that is, a nanoscale structure in which electrons are spatially confined - formed in an indium arsenide [InAs] nanowire connected to superconducting materials on both sides. It's in this environment that the states characterizing the Andreev qubit are formed," Egues explains.
The key to the new approach is an electrical phenomenon called a "supercurrent." Unlike the current flowing through ordinary electrical conductors, a supercurrent moves without resistance.
The researchers found that when the Andreev qubit exists in a superposition, the supercurrent develops a component that oscillates over time. These fluctuations arise from quantum interference between the different states making up the superposition.
Crucially, the oscillations are not random. Their behavior contains information about the qubit's underlying quantum state, potentially allowing scientists to determine what that state is without directly measuring the qubit.
"It's precisely that property that we use to read the qubit. It's that supercurrent that lies at the heart of our proposal," the researcher points out.
How a Tiny Electrical Current Reveals Quantum Information
To understand how the technique works, it helps to consider how physicists describe a qubit's state mathematically.
One common representation is the "Bloch sphere," a geometric model in which every possible pure state of a single qubit corresponds to a point on the surface of a sphere. Two angles determine the location of that point.
The first angle describes how much each of the two basic states contributes to the superposition. The second describes their relative phase, which specifies how the quantum components are aligned with one another. Together, these two measurements provide the information needed to identify the qubit's state.
According to the new research, both pieces of information can be extracted from the supercurrent. Its steady component and the size of its oscillations reveal the relative contributions of the two basic states. Meanwhile, the timing of the oscillations provides information about their phase relationship.
"Our study showed that this information is encoded in the supercurrent itself. The supercurrent has a constant component and a fluctuating component. The value of the constant component and the amplitude of the oscillation reveal the proportion of each state (0 and 1) in the superposition, and the moment when that oscillation begins reveals the phase relationship between them. Thus, by measuring how the current varies over time, it's possible to reconstruct the initial state of the qubit," Egues explains.
This means the electrical current effectively carries a signature of the quantum information stored in the system. By observing how that signature changes over time, researchers could reconstruct the qubit's original state.
A Supercurrent That Oscillates Without Voltage
Another surprising feature of the proposed system is that the electrical current can oscillate without an externally applied voltage.
Ordinarily, producing an oscillating supercurrent in this type of superconducting system requires a voltage. This familiar phenomenon is called the "AC Josephson effect."
The researchers predict something different in their Andreev qubit. Here, the current's oscillations arise naturally from the qubit's own quantum evolution. No outside voltage is required to generate them.
"Our system generates a supercurrent that varies over time like an alternating current but without voltage. It's the very evolution of the qubit's state that produces that oscillation," says Egues.
This behavior is important because it transforms quantum activity occurring on an extraordinarily small scale into a detectable electrical signal. The current provides a connection between the microscopic world of quantum states and the larger physical systems scientists can measure.
That connection is what makes the proposed reading technique possible.
Detecting Quantum States With an Extremely Sensitive Sensor
The researchers envision placing the Andreev qubit inside a closed superconducting circuit, allowing its supercurrent to circulate continuously.
Next to the circuit would sit a SQUID (superconducting quantum interference device), a highly sensitive instrument capable of detecting extremely weak magnetic fields.
Whenever an electric current flows, it produces a magnetic field. Because the supercurrent in this system oscillates, the magnetic field it generates also changes over time.
The nearby SQUID could detect these tiny magnetic variations and use them to determine the behavior of the circulating current. Since the current contains information about the qubit's quantum state, the researchers could then reconstruct that state without measuring the qubit directly.
Egues compares the arrangement to two compasses that interact through a magnetic field.
"We can think of the qubit as one compass and the SQUID as another compass. The current in the circuit produces a magnetic field, and the SQUID 'senses' that field. Since the coupling between the two is very weak, the effect of the measuring instrument on the qubit tends to be very small."
The weak interaction between the sensor and the qubit is especially important. It offers a way to gather information while minimizing the disturbance that normally accompanies quantum measurements.
Reading Quantum Information With Almost No Disturbance
In quantum physics, observing a system is not necessarily a harmless process. A measuring instrument interacts with whatever it is attempting to measure, and that interaction can change the system's behavior.
This fundamental difficulty puzzled the earliest researchers studying quantum mechanics. It remains an unavoidable feature of quantum measurements today.
The proposed technique does not eliminate this effect entirely. The SQUID still interacts with the circuit, creating a small amount of feedback that can influence the qubit. However, the team's simulations suggest that this disturbance can be reduced to a level so small that it becomes effectively negligible.
"Our method doesn't eliminate the fundamental problem of quantum measurement. But it can approach the limit of a non-destructive readout and, at the same time, avoid the use of auxiliary qubits - the ancillas - employed in other non-destructive quantum measurement protocols," Egues notes.
The approach could also remove another complication found in some existing techniques. Because researchers would not need to restore the qubit to its original state after every measurement, they could make repeated observations as the state changes.
This would allow scientists to follow the qubit's quantum evolution over time, rather than obtaining information only through separate measurement and reset cycles.
Simulations Achieve Up to 99.85% Accuracy
To investigate whether the method could work outside ideal theoretical conditions, the researchers performed computer simulations designed to account for imperfections that would arise in real experiments.
These calculations included measurement noise, as well as the small amount of feedback introduced by the detection coil. The goal was to determine whether the qubit's state could still be reconstructed accurately despite these disturbances.
The results were encouraging. Depending on the number of measurements used, the simulations produced accuracies of 99.52%, 99.81%, and 99.85%.
According to the researchers, these values fall within the standard thresholds used in quantum error correction schemes, which are designed to manage errors in quantum information processing.
The findings suggest that the method could provide highly accurate quantum state reconstruction without the additional complexity of auxiliary qubits.
However, the technique has not yet been demonstrated experimentally. The results come entirely from theoretical analysis and computer simulations, so researchers still need to establish whether a physical device can achieve comparable performance.
Could This Make Quantum Computers Simpler?
Despite the lack of experimental confirmation, the researchers emphasize that their proposal does not depend on technologies that have yet to be invented.
The calculations use realistic properties drawn from existing quantum systems, and SQUID sensors are already established tools for detecting exceptionally weak magnetic fields and electric currents.
What remains to be built is the specific arrangement of components required to implement the proposed measurement technique.
"All the numbers we used are realistic. In principle, this can be achieved. In fact, we used parameters from existing systems in our calculations. What doesn't yet exist is that geometry, that setup that we proposed," he argues.
This makes the approach different from theoretical concepts that cannot be realized until scientists develop entirely new materials or manufacturing techniques. In principle, the necessary components already exist, although assembling them into the proposed configuration and demonstrating the predicted behavior remain important challenges.
The research offers two potentially significant advances.
From the standpoint of fundamental physics, it predicts that a qubit can produce an oscillating supercurrent resembling the AC Josephson effect, but without requiring an external voltage. Instead, the oscillations emerge from the qubit's own coherent quantum evolution.
From a technological perspective, the study shows how those oscillations could serve as a measurable signature of the qubit's internal state. By analyzing the electrical current, researchers could recover quantum information while causing very little disturbance to the system.
If future experiments confirm these predictions, the method could make reading Andreev qubits substantially simpler. Eliminating auxiliary qubits and repeated resets could reduce the equipment and procedures needed to retrieve quantum information.
More fundamentally, the work points toward an intriguing possibility: information hidden in the microscopic quantum world may be accessible through an electrical current produced by the quantum system itself, offering a promising new way to observe delicate quantum states without destroying them.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Fundação de Amparo à Pesquisa do Estado de São Paulo. Original written by José Tadeu Arantes. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Xian-Peng Zhang, Chuanchang Zeng, Zhen-Biao Yang, Jose Carlos Egues, Yugui Yao. Andreev qubit readout from dynamic interference supercurrent. Physical Review B, 2026; 114 (8) DOI: 10.1103/6gkt-hghj

articles.title: Adieu Microsoft To Do : l'appli de tâches disparaît le 30 juin 2027, et Microsoft ne vous propose rien à la place
articles.text:
Microsoft To Do s'arrête en 2027 : comment exporter vos tâches et quelle alternative choisir
Voilà un nouveau coup dur de la part de Microsoft, cette fois porté aux nombreux utilisateurs de To Do. Le logiciel de gestion de tâches sera débranché en 2027, et rien n'est prévu pour le remplacer.
Les décisions prises par Microsoft autour de ses services et applications sont définitivement nébuleuses. Après avoir notamment bridé son logiciel Authenticator, cette fois c'est au tour de To Do de connaître un destin encore plus funeste. Sur une page de support, la firme a annoncé la fermeture pure et simple de son application de gestion de tâches dans quelques mois.
Microsoft tue To Do, sans véritable plan de remplacement
Bâtie sur les cendres de feu l'application Wunderlist rachetée par Microsoft en 2015, To Do va donc "prendre sa retraite" 12 ans plus tard. C'est en effet au 30 juin 2027 que To Do sera mis hors service, aussi bien sur le web, Windows, Mac, iOS et Android, pour les comptes professionnels ou scolaires et les comptes Microsoft personnels.
Microsoft précise que "le service To Do sous-jacent, les API et la prise en charge de la synchronisation associée seront mis hors service à des échéances distinctes et ultérieures." La firme ajoute : "Nous communiquerons ces dates et toute préparation requise séparément."
Pour les utilisateurs grand public, la douche froide est complète, puisqu'il faudra forcément se tourner vers une solution tierce. Reste à vérifier que des applications comme Super Productivity, Any.do, Todoist et autres Google Tasks proposent des fonctionnalités équivalentes et pourquoi pas l'import de données depuis To Do, qui ne simplifie pas réellement l'export.
Le Planificateur Microsoft, une béquille peu convaincante pour les pros
Pour les professionnels, le bilan n'est pas bien meilleur. Microsoft recommande de passer au Planificateur Microsoft, service qui n'est pas disponible pour les comptes personnels. Non seulement les tâches et listes To Do existantes ne seront pas migrées vers le Planificateur, mais en plus ce dernier s'avère beaucoup moins complet que To Do.
Si Microsoft promet que "l’expérience mise à jour de Mes tâches dans le Planificateur commencera à être déployée en décembre 2026", cette solution ne dispose pas d'applications natives, obligeant à passer par le web ou Teams. De plus, aucun support des pièces jointes, d'un accès hors ligne ou d'un système de rappel individuel n'est de la partie.
S'il reste quelques mois à la firme et à ses concurrents pour réagir et possiblement améliorer la situation, cette décision surprise de Microsoft ne devrait assurément pas aider la société à redorer sa réputation.

articles.title: Java4Shell Exploitation Attempts Begin as Vendors Rush Out Advisories
articles.text:
Threat actors have started targeting the recently disclosed Java4Shell vulnerability, as more vendors publish advisories detailing the flaw’s impact on their products.
Tracked as CVE-2026-114938, Java4Shell is a memory corruption bug in the way OpenJDK 17.0.6 and newer handle Base64 data. Exploitation requires an x86-64 processor supporting AVX-512 VBMI, a feature found in newer Intel and AMD CPUs. ARM-based systems are not affected.
Calif disclosed the bug on November 17, the same day Oracle and the OpenJDK project released patches.
Calif said it achieved unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE) against the default configurations of Jira, Confluence, Jenkins, Keycloak and other enterprise applications. However, it noted that no single exploit works against all of them, and that each needs a tailored attack chain.
Attackers are probing for vulnerable systems
As of early November 19, threat intelligence firm GreyNoise had recorded over 150 requests matching the shape of a Java4Shell attack, coming from five IP addresses. The company has not seen any successful intrusions on its sensors.
WatchTowr has also seen activity. “We are already seeing attackers spray the internet and hit our global honeypot network with requests decorated in ‘java4shell-recon’ User-Agents, alongside blind exploitation attempts using correctly shaped requests,” said Jake Knott, head of threat intelligence at WatchTowr.
“While what we’re seeing so far isn’t particularly functional or scary yet, it shows the clear signal that attackers want to leverage this vulnerability. Over the coming days, we expect attackers to iterate product-by-product to refine and build more reliable target-specific exploits, and that is where we start to see real exploitation happen,” Knott added.
Cloudflare’s Cloudforce One team has noticed that those scanning for the flaw are starting to conceal the tools they use. In one case, an IP address probed a target using a user agent that clearly referenced Java4Shell, then returned roughly 17 hours later with the exploit trigger while impersonating the Chrome browser.
On November 18, Cloudforce One also saw an IP address being used for both Artex and Java4Shell activity for the first time. Artex is an open source AI penetration testing framework that threat actors have been abusing to automate intrusions.
Threat intelligence firm Previdian says its sensors logged nine exploitation attempts from six IPs on November 18 and 19. However, it cautioned that its sensor data cannot confirm whether any targets were compromised.
Cisco’s product security team says it is aware of proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit code but has no knowledge of malicious use.
The PoC released by Calif only triggers the memory corruption. Meanwhile, VulnCheck has made a full RCE exploit available to its customers, and Immersive’s Kevin Breen has reported developing a working exploit.
Vendors confirm impact, but fixes are still rolling out
So far, Cisco has confirmed that more than a dozen of its products are affected, including Catalyst Center, Secure Network Analytics, Secure Workload, Smart Software Manager On-Prem, Splunk AppDynamics On-Premises Virtual Appliance, and Intersight Virtual Appliance.
The networking giant has yet to release fixes and says there are no workarounds. It is still investigating whether IOS XE and UCS Central are impacted.
Siemens says three of its Industrial Edge Management products are affected. The company is working on patches and, in the meantime, recommends taking these instances offline.
According to Elastic, every Elasticsearch release from 7.17.3 onward is affected. Attackers need valid credentials with read permissions or higher to achieve RCE, but they can trigger a denial-of-service (DoS) condition without authentication.
Logstash 8.6.2 and later are also affected, although exploitation requires a specific configuration and can only cause a crash. Elastic plans to address the issue in upcoming releases.
The company has already deployed a hotfix for Elastic Cloud Serverless and a configuration change for Elastic Cloud Hosted. It says only a small share of Elastic Cloud Hosted deployments run on vulnerable CPUs.
Red Hat has rated the issue Critical, saying that RHEL 8, 9 and 10 are affected, along with its own builds of OpenJDK 17, 21 and 25.
“No special configuration or non-default features are required. The accelerated code path is selected automatically whenever the JVM runs on a CPU reporting AVX-512 VBMI support, so affected systems are vulnerable out of the box,” Red Hat said, noting that patches are being fast-tracked.
The Keycloak team warned that its 26.8.2-1 and 26.8.2-2 container images bundled a vulnerable OpenJDK 21 build. On November 19, it announced updated images containing a patched Java runtime, including the 26.8.2-3 release.
Atlassian says it is working to address the issue in its cloud products, and that cloud customers do not need to take any action. For its Data Center products, until patches become available, Atlassian recommends disabling AVX-512 support as a workaround for the latest versions of Bamboo, Bitbucket, Confluence, Crowd, Jira and Jira Service Management Data Center in standard installations.
The Jenkins project says controllers are only at risk if they run a vulnerable Java 17, 21 or 25 release on a CPU that supports AVX-512 VBMI. It advises users to update to the November Java releases and restart Jenkins. Workarounds are also available.
Among Java distributors, Amazon, Microsoft, and Azul have released patched builds of their OpenJDK distributions.

articles.title: ANPD nega recurso do Discord e mantém lives suspensas no Brasil
articles.text:
Atenção: a matéria a seguir inclui uma discussão sobre suicídio. Se você ou alguém que você conhece precisar de ajuda, procure apoio especializado. O Centro de Valorização da Vida (CVV) funciona 24 horas por dia pelo telefone 188. Também é possível conversar por chat ou e-mail.
A ANPD (Autoridade Nacional de Proteção de Dados) rejeitou, por unanimidade, o recurso apresentado pelo Discord e manteve suspensas as transmissões ao vivo da plataforma no Brasil. A decisão foi tomada na quarta-feira (18) e confirma a medida cautelar em vigor desde 12 de agosto.
O órgão considera que a empresa ainda não demonstrou ter adotado mecanismos suficientes para proteger crianças e adolescentes durante as transmissões. A retomada depende da comprovação de medidas de segurança adequadas.
Por que a ANPD manteve a suspensão?
O Conselho Diretor confirmou a decisão da Superintendência de Fiscalização após avaliar que o Discord não implementou mecanismos capazes de tornar as transmissões mais seguras. A ANPD também considerou que a liberação poderia trazer de volta condutas já registradas na plataforma, inclusive criminosas, como tortura e morte de animais e automutilação.
O presidente interino da ANPD e relator do caso, Iagê Miola, afirmou que as evidências indicam a recorrência de situações graves de risco a crianças e adolescentes. Entre os episódios registrados estão violência, coerção, automutilação e indução ao suicídio durante transmissões ao vivo.
Miola ressaltou que a suspensão não constitui uma penalidade. A medida tem caráter preventivo, é provisória e reversível. Segundo ele, “o objetivo é evitar a continuidade de riscos graves enquanto a empresa demonstra a adoção de salvaguardas adequadas para proteger crianças e adolescentes”.
Para retomar as transmissões, o Discord precisa atender a três exigências estabelecidas pela ANPD:
- Implementar mecanismos eficazes de verificação de idade;
- Adotar controles preventivos de segurança;
- Demonstrar capacidade de identificar situações graves de risco e responder a elas.
A restrição não impede o uso das demais funções da plataforma no Brasil. A ANPD informou que mantém diálogo com a empresa para viabilizar a retomada das transmissões.
Morte de adolescente motivou investigação
A suspensão ocorreu após a repercussão da morte de uma menina de 13 anos, induzida ao suicídio durante uma transmissão no Discord. O caso é investigado pela Polícia Civil de Mato Grosso do Sul.
Duas operações contra suspeitos de envolvimento na morte resultaram na apreensão de 11 adolescentes, com idades entre 14 e 17 anos. Um adulto também foi preso.
O episódio também levou o governo federal a entrar na Justiça para obrigar o Discord a reforçar a segurança de crianças e adolescentes. Após uma tentativa de acordo sem sucesso, a Justiça Federal determinou a adoção de medidas de segurança no fim de setembro, sob pena de multa diária de R$ 100 mil por descumprimento injustificado.
Paralelamente, a ANPD abriu um processo para apurar possíveis falhas na moderação de conteúdo e na proteção de menores. A investigação abrange a verificação de idade, a retirada de conteúdos ilegais e a comunicação de casos graves às autoridades.
Valdir Antonelli é jornalista com especialização em marketing digital e consumo.

articles.title: Season’s Streamings and Savings: Black Friday Deals Come to GeForce NOW
articles.text:
GeForce NOW is kicking off Black Friday with more reasons to make time for gaming. Six-month memberships are back for a limited time. Save 30% on the first six-month term of a Performance or Ultimate membership. Big gaming plans, smaller price tag.
Keep the holiday savings going: Check out more NVIDIA holiday deals for gamers, creators and AI enthusiasts.

It brings console-style gaming to the TV, straight from the Amazon cart.
Bethesda fans have more in store, with five favorites adding GOG support as part of nine games joining GeForce NOW this week.

GeForce NOW handles downloads, patches and updates for Ready-to-Play games, freeing local storage and leaving more time for gaming. Choose a membership and start the season streaming.
More Screens, Major Savings
GeForce NOW officially expands to all three of Amazon’s Vega OS streaming media players including Fire TV Stick HD, Fire TV Stick 4K Select and Fire TV Stick 4K (2026 model) bringing thousands of supported games to more another screens in the home. Vega OS keeps Fire TV fast and responsive, so launching GeForce NOW and jumping into games feels quick and snappy, with no console required.

From cozy stories to epic adventures, turn-based tactics to co-op challenges, there’s plenty to build, explore and share with friends — all from the comfort of the couch.
There’s a fire deal to get the games going, too. Launching later today through Thursday, Dec. 31, get 90% off the first month of a Performance or Ultimate membership purchased directly through Amazon on supported Fire TV devices in participating regions. The cloud is ready. The next quest is calling.
GOG Big or Go Home
Five Bethesda titles expand their GeForce NOW support this week with their GOG versions: Indiana Jones and the Great Circle, Fallout 4, The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim, DOOM and DOOM Eternal.
Uncover an ancient mystery in Indiana Jones and the Great Circle, a first-person adventure set between Raiders of the Lost Ark and The Last Crusade. Explore the wasteland in Fallout 4 or trade the Pip-Boy for dragons and open-world fantasy in The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim.

articles.title: AI isn’t replacing your job. It’s turning it into low-paid gig work
articles.text:
The gig economy has arrived for cardiologists. Recruiting platform Outlier, run by Scale AI, advertises offers of up to $180 an hour for physicians in the U.S. to design complex cardiac scenarios, review artificial intelligence-generated reports, and rank model outputs. The site offers up to $7.50 an hour for Tagalog work in the Philippines for the same job, and up to $12.50 an hour for Swahili in Tanzania.
Companies like Scale AI first outsourced data work to wherever labor was cheapest. Now, they are recruiting physicians, lawyers, and Ph.D.s to generate and annotate data, rank model answers, and verify outputs. Higher credentials can raise the advertised rate, but the platform still controls payment and working conditions.
I’ve spent the last six years interviewing the people who do this work. Most were in Venezuela, where economic collapse has left a large, educated population online and out of options. One of them, Rogelio, taught computer science until the economic crisis and the pandemic left his family without work. His 13-year-old son discovered they could earn money labeling images of cars and roads on the platforms Hive and Scale AI’s Remotasks, using a laptop the Hugo Chávez government had issued to schoolchildren a decade earlier. The boy made 18 cents for a few hours of work. Rogelio joined him and made just over $2 on his first day.
For a while, the work paid. A task called Beast Mode where workers labeled objects in people’s homes paid more than any other work the family had done. In December 2020, with schools closed and the whole family working, it brought in $20 in a single day. It was the most they would ever make. By early 2021, Beast Mode had disappeared, and their earnings fell below Hive’s $5 weekly payout threshold.
This is how many platforms operate: They begin by paying well to build a workforce, then they cut the rates and move on. Remotasks ended its hourly program in Venezuela in 2021 and made a splash in Kenya the same year. In March 2024, it discontinued operations in Kenya, Nigeria and Pakistan. Scale AI attributed the closures to “enhanced security protocols,” and said notices had gone out three weeks ahead but later acknowledged that Kenyan workers never received them “due to operational errors.” Most workers who spoke to Rest of World at the time said the platform simply froze them out.
The pattern has a name, and it’s older than AI: extractivism. It is a system that takes resources and value from people and places for accumulation elsewhere, on terms set by the buyer rather than the worker. The term also stands for what is taken and what is left behind. The crisis that put Rogelio’s family online was the residue of an oil economy that built little else.
One woman I interviewed in Venezuela drew a pension from the state oil company. By 2021, it was worth about $1 a month, which she said couldn’t buy half a dozen eggs. She was labeling data on Hive to make up the difference, but that income was even less secure. An oil field stays put, while a platform can send the next batch of tasks to workers somewhere else.
AI is usually described as built on extracted data: authors’ books, artists’ works, all used to train models. But the extraction has another layer: the new examples, evaluations, and corrections commissioned to improve those models. That material has to be created by someone, for a fee, which is set by the platform — whether it is $2 for the teacher in Venezuela or up to $180 an hour for a cardiologist in the U.S.
Outlier’s terms let the company delay or suspend payment during an investigation of a worker’s tasks and withhold “some or all amounts accrued” where it finds a violation “in the company’s sole determination.” The company may also deactivate an account “immediately without prior notice for any reason.” The same language appeared word for word in the Remotasks terms that Rogelio’s family worked under in 2021.
Earlier this year, Josh Dzieza reported on the laid-off lawyers, scientists, and screenwriters now filling these platforms. Of the more than 30 workers he interviewed, nearly all described the same arc: Demands increased, target times shrank, and pay fell as a project went on. One designer was tagging videos for Meta at $21 an hour when the project ended for “scope changes.” Days later, the same job reappeared under a new name at $16 an hour — the same sequence that Rogelio’s family went through five years earlier.
Of course, workers can leave, and many do. But the ones who stay are often those who can’t leave. One woman I interviewed was confined to her home during the Covid-19 pandemic by a health condition and couldn’t risk losing the job. “This is my only source of income,” she told me.
None of this is unknown within the industry. In a 2024 meeting convened by the nonprofit Partnership on AI and the Fairwork project which rates platform companies, I sat with representatives of AI companies and the outsourcing firms that supply them. The AI companies said they didn’t employ the data workers; the outsourcing firms said their operations were determined by the prices the AI companies expected. Everyone agreed pay should be better, but when the question of representation came up, the room went quiet as no workers were present.
Workers have still acted. In March 2023, a judge in Kenya temporarily halted the dismissal of 260 Facebook content moderators, prevented Meta from moving their work to another contractor, and barred Meta and contractor Majorel from blacklisting workers. As workers fought in Kenya, Meta moved the work to West Africa.
American courts are also grappling with this issue. Claims by workers on Scale AI’s platforms led to a proposed settlement that has received preliminary approval in San Francisco. The company denies wrongdoing. A separate class action suit alleges Mercor misclassified more than 30,000 lawyers, doctors, and engineers while setting their pay and reviewing their work. Mercor’s clients have included OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta, but they are not named as defendants. The case is ongoing.
A cardiologist who is offered a three-digit hourly rate is not in the same position as Rogelio and his family. What connects them is the fact that the rate can change suddenly, the task can disappear without warning, and they have no say over any of it.
The work will keep moving, and the rules will continue to be set by the companies that commission it, wherever the next worker logs on, whether in Kenya, Venezuela, or the Philippines.

articles.title: Leaked images reveal Motorola’s wide foldable
articles.text:
New leaked images of Motorola’s next folding smartphone shared by SammyGuru add more credence to the theory that widescreen could be the default design for foldables moving forward. Following a single leaked shot shared to Reddit yesterday, this new crop of images reveal the Motorola Razr Flex from several angles in two finishes with its inner screen completely open and partially folded.
Leaked images reveal Motorola’s wide foldable
The Razr Flex will compete with the iPhone Duo, Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8, and other widescreen folding devices.
The photos show the Razr Flex in two finishes: coriander brown and dark botanical garden, according to SammyGuru. The brown option features a back panel with a bumpy leather-like finish, while the green has a fabric-like woven finish. The cover screen has a hole-punch selfie camera centered at the top, while the Razr Flex’s inner screen pushes the camera to the upper right corner. On the back is a pill-shaped bar with two cameras and a flash.
The Flex is expected to be a smaller and more affordable alternative to the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8, which has a 5.5-inch cover screen and a 7.6-inch main display when unfolded. But more specific details — including the size of the Razr Flex, its pricing, and when it’s expected to be debut — are still unknown.

articles.title: The best things in open source are built together
articles.text:
The best things in open source are built together
Introducing Replica and the Open Source Accessibility Framework, new open source projects for collaboration and inclusion.
In 2026, public contributions on GitHub soared to 2.5 billion, more than double last year’s total of 1.12 billion. It goes to show how open source remains a powerful mechanism for developers to build, share, and grow communities.
Open source is how I began my GitHub journey. I contributed to Processing Foundation by adding alt-text to images on the p5.js website. This was the first time I felt included in a software development space as someone with a background in traditional fine arts and design. It was the first time I made a fork, opened a pull request, and merged code on a repo that wasn’t mine.
Working at GitHub, you hear stories like mine everywhere. Open source is foundational to us not only as a business but also for who we are as the people who build it! We recently launched two new open source projects to share with the community: Replica, an open-source design harness, and the Open Source Accessibility Framework.
I attended John Maeda’s session with Qianqian Ye, Director of Creative Technology at Processing Foundation, at GitHub Universe titled, “Sketching with code in the age of AI.” This session talked about the power of the open source community and reminded me how important it is to our developer ecosystem. Open source accelerates innovation. It is the reason AI tooling understands different coding languages so well, how developers hacked agent harnesses to be more efficient, and why new AI companies have formed.
This moment resonated with me. Qianqian asked:
“What do you think the role open-source community plays nowadays in the age of AI?”
John replied:
“I worked in the WordPress open source community, where I learned that PHP stands for people helping people. And so if anything, I’m just sort of optimistic that the open source world is the way of how we should do things in general, in society. And I’m really excited how, at GitHub, we care so deeply about open source.”
Replica, a new open-source design harness
In 2025, 60% of the top growing open source projects were AI focused. At GitHub, it is no different. A few weeks ago, GitHub’s design team introduced Replica, which considers the role of designers in the era of AI and focuses on reinforcement learning. Replica started as an internal project, but it proved to be so useful that our design team shared the tool so developers and designers everywhere could also benefit.
GitHub Replica does a lot of reinforcement learning. It’s an open source design harness to enable you to do the kind of things you hope to do in prototyping playground
John Maeda, CVP GitHub & CoreAI Design
With Replica, anyone can create AI-generated prototypes within their design system and refine them side-by-side with GitHub Copilot. You can also publish prototypes to a Replica Hub to collaborate with teammates, receive comments, and iterate.
With reinforcement learning top of mind, the system learns what good looks like from each interaction and from the comments on the prototypes; it gets better over time. Because Replica is open source, you can hack it and adapt it to fit your teams’ products and workflows however you see fit.
A11y Framework, a new open-source accessibility framework
Developers pushed code changes to GitHub 17.9 billion times in the last year, more than 2024 and 2025 combined. Commits across all repo types (public and private) climbed even faster to 34.3 billion, more than three times where they stood two years ago. Merged pull requests more than tripled to 1.3 billion over the same period, an average of 3.5 million a day. AI has helped us all build faster. With this volume, and more to be expected, we must keep accessibility top of mind so that the code that is being shipped is accessible to all.
As the home for all developers, we want every developer to feel welcome and to be able to contribute to the future of global software development using everything GitHub has to offer.
Ed Summers, GitHub Head of Accessibility
The Open Source Accessibility Framework, created in collaboration with external contributors from the disability and accessibility communities, launched last month. It helps make accessibility an inherent part of how projects are created. It is an accountability model with four phases so developers can turn projects and accessibility goals into public, trackable progress. A core component of this is the new ACCESSIBILITY.md file, a file now visible on repository overview pages, giving a project one durable place to explain its accessibility goals, contributor expectations, supported environments, known limitations, and process for reporting barriers. Read more about the ACCESSIBILITY.md file.
The power of community
Going back to John and Qianqian’s Universe talk, John asked:
“How does an open source community keep something lasting that long? What’s the secret?”
Qianqian replied:
“I think the secret is one of the most obvious ones. Community.”
The GitHub repo firstcontributions/first-contributions ranked fourth among the fastest-growing community projects in 2026 by contributors, helping developers take their first steps into open source. We hope you can join our open-source community: hack away at our new projects or start your own.
Watch John Maeda and Qianqian Ye’s session 👇
